Freedom Planet is by far the best platformer I've touched in a long while
. And while it does have the style of a Genesis game, it's
a Sonic ripoff by any means.
Using one of the three playable characters, the gameplay involves high-paced rushes and close-quarter combat. Each character has its unique skills and playstyle, with one being able to dash in mid-air while another can wall climb as examples. Each level has its own unique mechanic to use, and as well as its own boss that requires certain strategies for each character. The game also has four difficulty settings, with Casual and Easy for those into the story, and Normal and Hard for hardcore gamers.
Speaking of which and without spoiling too much, the story is actually pretty dark to the case that I would not recommend for those under 13 years of age, despite having the comical appearance. The voices are pretty good and well-suited for their respective characters (with Lilac's voice actor, Dawn, being the best).
Lastly, the soundtrack. It's AWESOME. Woofle has not only just made soundtracks for the game, he revises some of them to fit the game perfectly with the help of Strife and Blue Warrior, and it's freakin' great. (For the record, Woofle also made cool arrangements for
and
soundtracks.)
If you're thinking about getting this game, but not convinced of buying it, you can grab the demo on the official website. If you want the soundtrack, get the one on Bandcamp for top-quality soundtracks if you can. (Some of the tracks in the Steam DLC have a lower bitrate for those who care. Otherwise, it doesn't matter too much.)

Lisa is a RPG made with RPG Maker, which was spawned from another RPG Maker game, Lisa The First.
You play as a alcoholic drug addict, known as Brad, in the wasteland of a world ruined by mysterious circumstances. You find an abandoned baby girl, possibly the last female in existance and decide to adopt her as your own, to protect her. When your child goes missing, you search the wastes to find her.
Lisa is an impressive game, not just with the writing, or the colorful characters or art, but with the direction it went, as a 2-D side scrolling RPG. From top to bottom, Lisa is a polished gem. The game has a dark sense of comedy that fits well within it's world.
Lisa also has an incredibly strong Earthbound vibe to it, which is a great thing.

After a 20 year break, I figured this summer it would be a good time to get back into the SimCIty franchise with 2003's SimCity 4.
This is one of those games where its greatest strength happens to also be its greatest weakness. The game is incredibly deep, which to a SimCity enthusiast must be the ultimate dream. For entry level players it is however a substantial barrier to entry. There is a tutorial, although I felt it could have been a little more in depth beyond the basics it does go over.
But once you are rolling, you are in command of all the tools you'll ever need to run your city. If you're like me, you'll become attached to your city as its very own life-form, and will want to nurture it along in its development.
And since this is an 8 year old title, it was a nice surprise to have a game today that isn't innundated with achievements and ceaseless updates.
SimCity 4 is a winner, I'm glad I made the trip back im gaming time to play it.

- You can drive around your city in one of many availiable vehicles, like cars, buses, trucks, sailing boats and helicopters!

I first played this game in 2010 after it first came out. I loved it back then and kinda forgot about it until I saw it on sale recently. After making the purchase, I decided to make trouble on the streets of Empire Bay once again. Five years later and this game is still an easy 9.5/10. The plot itself deserves a separate review and special recognition. It's so sophisticated and elaborate that the game does not need a movie adaptation. The cinematics provide a movie-like experience instead. Voice acting, radio songs and announcements, cars, clothing, etc. -- all of this is top-notch for a game about the life of Italo-American gangsters. The graphics are totally fine for a 2010 game too. The only downside perhaps is the rather boring free play mode that becomes unlocked when one finishes the game. But then again, this isn't GTA.
Overall, I would highly recommend this to those who are looking to play a game with a great plot and to those who, much like myself, are big fans of the movies like The Godfather and Once Upon A Time In America.

Sonic has had a bumpy road in 3D, but you already know that. That being said, I'm happy to admit that Sonic Generations may be the best 3D Sonic game. The gameplay is split between slower, momentum-based 2D Classic Sonic sections and fast-paced frantic 3D Modern Sonic sections. It's the best of both worlds, and both contrast each other beautifully. Seemingly small differences like Modern Sonic's boost mechanic make major alterations throught his levels and the slower more platforming centered Classic Sonic levels allow for more exploration, however both of these playstyles tend to merge and weave in and out of each other in some clever ways. You may find a section of a Modern Sonic level rithe with multiple paths and slower platforming segments or a Classic Sonic section in which you blaze by at ludicrous speeds. The game's presentation is solid, boasting bright, colorful visuals and a rocking soundtrack comprising of remixes from selected Sonic levels of the past. The whole game Sonic Generations for how much it holds on to the past, seems to be carving a new future for the blue blur that I hope SEGA will continue going down. Definatley worth you time and your money. A controller is HIGHLY reccomended and as there are little in the ways of graphical settings, make sure your rig at least meets the reccomended specs as playing this game below 60 frames per second feels very unresponsive and slow, something you don't want in a fast-paced game like this.

An out-of-character message from the developer in-game states that "This game is not a game. It is a portrait." The person it portrays is perhaps relevant to many who read this review - but it is in no way supporting of morbid things such as suicide (one doesn't have to relate to appreciate the Actual Sunlight experience, but someone interested in psychology and / or mental illnesses will probably be intrigued by Actual Sunlight.)
The out-of-character message was added to explain his concern for who comes across the game and possible negative reactions (or triggers, if you prefer) - and to switch and say out-of-character "That ain't you. So don't. Don't you ♥♥♥♥ing dare." (Here you have to remember what the game deals with - i.e. suicide.)
I agree with the reviews shown on the shop page that are taken from other sources than Steam reviews. It's a powerful portrait, perhaps because the developer refers to himself in the out-of-character message.
I recommend it to people who are not searching for the common perception of "video game", but a psychological experience. It would also have to be someone willing to pay its worth (base price 5 EUR / USD) for a short amount of game time. Few people will spend hours on it (including those who do several playthroughs, even though there's not really replayability), and most may just spend minutes on it before they complete the story and catch the point.
However, before considering buying, follow the trigger warnings. How do you react to powerful depression- and suicide-themed novels, music, real-life stories or whatever?
Actual Sunlight deals with serious topics, and I'm not sure how much courage it took the developer to create this. All-in-all I appreciate the developer sharing this portrait and do not regret my 4.49 Euro spent on it, but rather would do it again and will look for other interestingly-named titles from Will O'Neill.

The writing in this game is really good if you enjoy reading. I found myself screenshotting pages of text the way I would highlight them in my e-reader because I loved a turn of phrase. But in some ways the medium for this story took away from the narrative, and it might have been stronger as just text. For example, the artwork was disjointed and the delivery system for the text was more irritating than mood-setting. I felt like I would have carpel tunnel by the time I got through clicking enter at every comma and period in the game. In other ways, controlling the character through their depression added jarring reality that never would have been achievable in any other medium. Suicide is an option available to you at every single point in the game and it really drives the point home about how those urges keep cropping up. I think it's worth a few bucks if you would like to read some really stellar writing and see the potential a video game about depression has. It's a pretty interesting take on how to tell this story and overall I really enjoyed it.

Actual Sunlight is one of the best-written video games you're likely to play.
It's a deliberately simple experience, at least in terms of gameplay and interaction. The meat of the game is in text, observations and essays that are by turns hilarious, heartbreaking, acerbic, and sharply observed. Within the space of a few hours, as the story descends to the very darkest of places, you'll have experienced the full range of human emotion. That's not something you can say about many games.
This is an important game. It will broaden your perception of what a video game can be. It may well broaden your understanding of the world and the people around you - the quality of the writing is such that you really feel like you're walking in this character's shoes, and experiencing a life that may be very different to yours.
This all sounds very pretentious, I suppose. That's not something Actual Sunlight revels in. It's different to most games, sure, but it isn't flashily artistic or anything so ostentatious. It's a very honest game.
It looks great too, with some visually beautiful hand-drawn artwork and original music that dabbles in ambience and takes inspiration from the Toronto hip-hop scene (if you're into that kind of thing).
If you're even a little bit curious, I couldn't recommend this game more. It can be a tough experience, but your life will be better for having been through it.

I personally hope that that the developer was trying to scare people into taking that first real step towards a better life but the writing, design, and achievement suggest otherwise. The game is just an interactive, depressing, nudge in the wrong direction for those that suffer very common mental illnesses. There was no shock factor, beauty, message, or entertainment to be had and I find it sad that people will most likely call this art.
While I enjoyed the music and some of the art I strongly advise against purchasing this. I do not believe that most would enjoy it and those that might relate would just reinforce what they believe is wrong with them and the world.
If I missed some secret code or combo of interactions that allow any type of influence I apologize. These are of course just my opinions.

NOTE: This game isn't a game that you expect a happy ending out of. That said, it might not be for those who have conquered or are battling depression. Also, I played Actual Sunlight before its Steam release, but the game on the storefront is identical to the drm-free version, as far as I am aware of.
Actual Sunlight features extremely descriptive accounts of the mind of a man named Evan Winter. Through his eyes, you (The Player) will see how Evan sees the world, in all of his frustrating and cathartic perspective. For the short duration of the game, you will large amounts of text that provide some detail about how Evan sees the world. The game features humour that walks the line between Black Humour and the ranting of a broken, dispirited man; the title of the opening monologue ("Why Kill Yourself Today, When You Could Masturbate Tomorrow?") is a good idea of what you can expect.
The game's dreary tone is reminiscent of Cart Life; it is a game of a sad existence, told through the eyes of a man who is at the end of his tethers. Actual Sunlight leads up to a predictable and yet open-ended climax, and this will be the part of the game that will make you feel most strongly about the entire experience.
Actual Sunlight is a game that gives as much as you want to take; this is both its strongest point and its weakness. The game relies on your exploration of the environment to unravel the story of Evan. From his little musings in his apartment to his observations on the world outside, Evan has more or less given in to his depression. While this is effective in letting the player manage how much he or she wants to learn about Evan, you should be aware that you need to click the x button (there's partial controller support) on almost everything. Also, nearly everything in the game is text based, so be prepared to read. A lot.
On the techincal side. I couldn't get Actual Sunlight to run in fullscreen, so it will probably run in a window with a smaller resolution, just in case you are very particular about the resolution that you play your game at. If anyone has a fix for this please post it in the comments of the review.
TL;DR Actual Sunlight is a fascinating experience, and it will resonate with you if you have had any kind of experience with depression or with people suffering from depression. THAT BEING SAID, DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME IF YOU ARE DEPRESSED, AND THAT YOUR CONDITION MAY BE AFFECTED BY THE TRIGGER WARNINGS IN THIS GAME.

As a long term veteran of CoH 1 plus the addons, it still haunts me what has become of one of the best RTS titles ever made. This said, I am gonna try to give a 'short' review why I can't recommend the game compared to its predecessor.
First things first: Even though I can't recommend the game it has to be said, that I see it fitting for a growing group of casual gamers. Thus, if you wanna pretend to be a strategist but if you don't want to invest too much time into figuring out detailed game mechanics and tactics, this might be the game for you! Plus it might keep you motivated unlocking new skins, perks achievments etc. Hell, from a casual kind of view this game even makes fun and shines with its easy gameplay, which forgives you easiely the wrong macro and often also micro gameplay.
In addition the shop provides you with an almost endless combination of commanders. Thus, you can invest additional money to get the ability-combination you want. Eventhough, I don't get the concept of throwing extra money out of the window for a feature within a game I already bought.... I also have to say that I haven't seen yet any ability combination which would justify a 'pay to win' branding of the game, as I already bet people with 1000h+ gametime without having spent any additional money.
So let's sum up: if you are a casual gamer, who is searching for a 'strategy' game which is not too deep and if you just want to play it from time to time, go ahead and buy it! You might spend some fun hours and can stop reading the review at this point.
BUT if you are strategy game fan and/ or a lover of the first CoH, mark my following lines!
Coming back to my initial statement, it really creeps me out what they have done to one of the gratest RTS brands, men ever made. It seems like Relic/Sega took the content of the first part,  its DLCs and of some of its mods (looking at Blitzkrieg here), put it into a blender and mixed it hard until they got a soft strategy porridge without any profile or skills to need.
1. The menu structure
The first thing that struck me was how confusing the menues are: maybe I'm getting to old, but I got already overwhelmed and confused by the main-menu with all its blinking buttons, moving backround and popping up advertisments. WTF?! Why do I have to suffer from advertisment for DLCs, Commanders, Twitch etc. in a game I payed a full price for?
If you know the lobby from the first part (which had its weaknesses, too) you will miss MOST of the filter options to find a game: You can basically only specify if you are looking for games with or without mods! Filtering out eg. 2v2 games? -Impossible. Searching for anhilation games? -Well, literally search for it yourself, fool! Obviously the game designers found it more important to grand you access to your 'inventory' with all these perks, skins, badges and more nonsense at all time instead of implementing the clear menue structure from part one....
2. Gameplay
I think that many CoH veterans already commented on the very details of the gameplay, so I will only share my personal impressions! While CoH was celebrated for its strategic simplicity and depth at the same time, based on a simple rock-paper-scissor mechanic combined with offmap abilities and ressource managment, CoH 2 is only a shadow of the former strategic depth.
a) Ressources and sectors
While in CoH it was crucial to capture the right ressources at the right time to decide the game in your favor, CoH 2 took this aspect almost completly out by giving all the sectors almost the same priority. In CoH you had small, medium and big ressource sectors to supply you with differnet ammounts of fuel, ammunition and menpower. In CoH 2 there are only small sectors left which aren't differing much from each other. For what I have seen, it doesn't matter which one to capture since they all have the same worth. Sure, you can build an outpost on it to increase the output by eg.+ 5 fuel/min. Compared with CoH this is nothing, since it could be increased up to ~+15/min.... Thus, you will end up lacking every damn rescource but menpower in the longrun.
b) Units - Or how there used to be reliability
To sum it up, if you know anything about the units and their effect from CoH, forget about it. Rock-paper-scissor? -Nah, it's more like rubber mallet vs. rubber mallet. Almost everything can beat up almost everything! You spamed to many anti infantry infantry in the early game and get surprised by vehicles? -No problem, they sure have also cool antitank abilities. You spamed too many AT-guns and you are now getting attacked by Infantry? No problem since they now also feature HE ammo, no hard time to beat them! In any case, don't forget to build a mortar, since they don't miss much and make a lot of damage and often cause instand death!
The main weakness of the game is the uncertain unit effectifness itself. I have suffered a lot situations where I started a firefight which was pretty even and I gained the upperhand by starting to kill off the opponent until it was 5 men vs. 3, when luck started to turn, and I started to loose a figth I initially won.
How about tanks then? -They are even worse: They have the same HP bar like the infantry and thus it is almost impossible to determine how many hits they can still suffer. Plus, you have to save A LOT of ressources to get e.g. a Pather in the lategame. This is the biggest tank the Wehrmacht can build regularly! However, it somehow can be easiely defeated on the front by the allied's small tanks which cost less than half of the ressources. WTF? Why do I have to save ress the whole game for a premium tank if it is not really better than any other cheap one?! - Makes no sense to me. Also about reliability: one time your AT infatry makes no damage on vehicle, the next time they finish it off in three shots. One time an 'Easy Eight' Sherman almost destroys two panthers by itself, the next time it gtes owned by only one. This game has so much uncertanty or luck in it, that makes it hard to determine the outcome of almost any battlesituation. In addition, the game also excuses the loss of territory very generously: While it broke you your neck in CoH 1 to loose grip of all the ressources, in CoH 2 you can make an easy comeback just with your menpower featured jibber-jabber infatry. Thus, you can often still turn the whole (lost) game around within a few seconds.
Final Thougts
As a fan of the strategy genre, CoH 2 plays like they took the 'realism' and micromanagment of Men of War and tried to combine it with the 'casualness' of a command and conquer, creating a game which is neither of those and not even close to the quality of CoH 1.
I would even go further and say, there is NOTHING this game stands out for! It has neither the realism and micromanagment demans of Men of War, nor the easiness or arcarde-level of a command and Conquer.
Thus, if you aren't a casual gamer and you wan't to play a deeper arcarde game, buy CoH 1 + the DLCs because it costs not even half but gives double the fun of this clunky monstrosity.

This feels like a more thought-out version of the first BIT.TRIP RUNNER. Better said, a completer version! This time around there's an actual storyteller and the game's also a bit easier on the eyes. Personally I couldn't enjoy the first BIT.TRIP RUNNER because of it making my eyes hurt. But the developers made a lot of improvements. So, do I recommend BIT.TRIP Presents... Runner2: Future Legend of Rhythm Alien? Yes.
How high were they when they came up with the title of this game, though?

"BIT.TRIP Presents... Runner2: Future Legend of Rhythm Alien" is probably the most ridiculous name I have seen for game. Why did they feel like they needed to make this the name? I get that you want to get the company known, and I guess it has worked because I refer to the game as "Bit trip Runner" instead of "Runner2", but it is a pretty dumb title.
Anyway, this game is a lot of fun. The gameplay is pretty simple and slowly introduces you to new features and obstacles that make the game more interesting and challenging. The boss battles are done quite interestingly and don’t completely change the games mechanics just to incorporate bosses. They just test all the skills you have learnt from playing through the levels.
The music, luckily, does not get annoying seeing as you end up listening to it lots of times after dying repeatedly. It’s quite catchy and once you get into the rhythm, you can time jumps and dodges to fly through the level. The music changing depending on the area you are in is good as well. The Reggae inspired beats that are used in the second stage are pretty good and the timing is a bit off to try and throw you off and make the game a bit more of a challenge.
The costumes are quite fun to mess about with. There are some funny ones and some that are straight up gross. The Retro levels are fun and can be quite challenging, especially seeing as you only get a certain number of lives before you need to restart and unlock them again.
There is one thing that has♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off though. It’s not a big deal really but as someone who likes to get achievements and 100% games, it has put a bit of a sour taste in my mouth.
1. Why the hell have they added the Dancing task (You need to dance for 1 Hour when the action takes about a second, meaning you have to spam the trigger every time you play a level) I've played this game for 20 hours and have only just crossed 30 mins of dancing. Its absolutely ridiculous.
2. The achievement to triple perfect every level (Get every collectible and hit the bulls eye on all three difficulties on all 100-ish levels) was added to do nothing more than get playtime out of the game. It’s not a fun challenge. It just means that when someone looks at reviews and see's the playtime of a completionist, it looks like there is 30 hours of content, when there is actually only about 6 - 10 hours. It just seems pointless and misleading.
Apart from those last two problems, this is a very fun game. It only costs a couple of quid and you can have a lot of fun with it. Just be careful as it can make you feel a bit sick at points with the constant moving of the background.
7/10.

I have not finished the game yet but since the game has some major issues I'm making this review early.
Runner 2 is a rhythm platform game.
+ Good graphics
+ Good music
+ Fun to play
+ Many skills and collectables
+ Works on Arch Linux
- Noticeable motion blur (played in windowed mode to avoid this problem)
- Tearing when V-Sync is off
- Ackward fixed keyboard layout
- Gamepad is mapped only to the Xbox controller layout
Runner 2 is a rythm game where you control an alien that must avoid obstacles. You start by jumping over obstacles but as the game goes on you get more skills like kicking and sliding.
Unfortunately there are some technical issues with this game. The biggest issue is that there is a very noticeable motion blur. Having a 120hz monitor does not help since the game is fixed at 60fps. You can get more than 60fps by turning v-sync off but the price is a lot of tearing. The compromise I came up with was to play the game in windows mode instead of fullscreen. This can be very annoying and a major flaw for this kind of game since it requires precision at fast speeds.
Another issue is the controls. The game recommends a gamepad but there's not much of a difference between using the gamepad or the keyboard. The keyboard layout is a bit ackward and you cannot change to the keys you want but it's still easy to get used to. Another issue is that the gamepad controls are fixed to the Xbox controller layout so the PS4 controller buttons are incorrectly mapped in this game. You can however mimic the Xbox controller with another controller.
Apart from the technical issues the game is fun and well designed and for that reason I recommend this game. It's a fun game with excelent graphics and music if you like rythm-music platformers.

You can have a perfect level, which is collecting all gold bars in a level but then there's perfect+. Overall, if I was The Completionist, I'd give it a review of Finish It. Compared to many other games in my Steam Library, this one will be easy to 100% complete, achievement wise. My favourite SimCity game of them all (and they are all so good), simply because of its depth. Plan city sized commercial districts to feed residential and industrial sectors respectively, or build small villages across a region area that you (with a lot of donkey work, it must be said) can design yourself.
As in some other SimCities, you'll plan neighbourhoods, fund services, enact policies and balance a budget to build a working city.

SimCity…The definitive city building game…The time show on steam doesn’t show the amount of time I have spent since I bought the game in 2004. As a matter of fact, I have gone through about 5 copies of this game…SimCity4 has infinite replay value. No 2 cities will be the same…..don’t even attempt to make a duplicate city…it will not work.Simcity4 works a little differently from the previous version of SimCity in that, where the previous versions just gave you a plot of land to build on, SC4 lets you select a region, akin to a city or county in your state. You can import and export among the regions, sell electricity, water and import garbage. Build a police station with a helipad and be a helicopter pilot stopping crimes. Build a hospital with a helipad, and deliver a liver for a transplant. Build a small airfield and  spray crops for insects, or write messages in the sky. Built an airport, and watch the tourism tax dollars start rolling in…

A classic, and one of my all-time favourite games that even today, I occasionally revisit. Creating a working city is something I've alawys enjoyed, and in the most straightforward of ways, this old game delivers and has stood the test of time with it's fundamental attention to detail, whilst still maintaining it's clean, common-sense UI.   I've chosen to continue playing this over EA's newest incarnation, because this game works - on every level - it just works.
Have easily logged thousands of hours in this over the years and I consider it the definitive city-building title.
Sidenote: Found it to be slightly buggy in Win 7/64 bit, but so far it's played smoothly in Win 8.1/64.
Edit March 2015:  While this might be the original, it really isn't optimized for newer OS and topping it off, Cities:Skylines has made it what it should have been today. I recommend the latter if you're seeking out a successor to the original series.

Weapons duelers like Chivalry and Soul Calibur are based around using different types of weapons with different skillsets like hammers, nunchucks, and zweihanders. Blade Symphony takes this concept and narrows it down to just swords, and by doing this, they have a created a skill-based duel  game that is fun to watch and play.
Story wise, Blade Symphony isn't much to look at. Here's the gist of it: You're a blind swordsman trying to become the best in the world. Seriously, that's it. However that's not where Blade Symphony shines. It's graphics are very well done, especially at the particles when swords collide. All of the models, both sword and duelist, are very well done with textures fitting the weapons, like giving the katana "Serrated Serenade" a serrated edge. When wandering around the maps in free for all mode, it's a joy to be able to climb up onto a roof and take in the scenery. While playing I didn't notice any texture pop ins or jagged edges.
While Blade Symphony may be lacking a story, it more than makes up for it with its deep customization  and sword play. Upon entering, you're guided through a series of tutorials teaching you about basic things like sword types, all the way up to advanced side cancelling, with Puny Human planning on releasing more as time passes. You'll pick from one of four classes, with Judgement being your defensive tank, Ryoku being the nimble fiighter, Phalanx your long reach sniper, and Pure with her fancy spins and sword flurries. Along with your sword type, either katana, longsword, rapier, scimitar, or jian, and sets of fast, balanced, and heavy stances, you have an unlimited amount of strategies waiting to be learned. You'll see common ones like Judgement with a longsword to deal massive damage, or Phalanx with a rapier to deal bursts of damage, you can visualize more unique ones. A slow and bulky Judgement wielding the jian, which speeds up your move recovery, can help him compensate for his slow heavy attacks. Fighting tooth and nail with another player is electryfing, and the main reason why this game is so much fun to watch. When not slashing other players into bite-sized chunks, you'll be either waiting for the way too long load screens to disappear, or using your currency to purchase new swords and masks. While they certainly change how your character looks, they don't do anything to impede the balance of the game, since everything is cosmetic. This makes the game purely reliant on skill. The only way to get good at the game is to practice, practice, practice.
THE VERDICT:
Stuff I liked:
+Simple yet deep swordplay
+Vast customization
+Skill based gameplay
+Electryfing duels
Stuff I didn't like:
-Horrendous loading times
9.5/10 Outstanding
With how easy it is to get into Blade Symphony and how deep the strategies go, it's easy to lose several hours into one play session. If you want a multiplayer duel with a large amount of depth and customization that takes a minute to learn and a lifetime to master, stop reading this review and add Blade Symphony to your cart.

This is the Nethack of roguelikes - there's multiple different systems, all of which interact with one another, all of which will kill you if you're not careful.
Let's say there's a bunch of orks sitting around a table, and you need to get past them.
You could run in there swinging your weapon, and hope you're just better at combat than they are.
With the right spell, you can do anything from teleporting past them entirely to setting the whole room on fire
But you don't need a spell to let your inner pyromaniac out - a well-thrown torch will set the table (and all the orks) on fire.
You could lure a slime or bat into the room, distracting the orks while you run through
You could gain invisibility from a spell or potion, and sneak past.
You can find a boulder and roll it into the room; I'm not sure what good that would do but you can do it. Maybe you should set the boulder on fire first.

Firstly, have my personal "Why did it have to end, like, at all?" award.
Secondly, an actual review.
-
The characters that make up your team in this game are great. They, above all, are the main reason I did not want this game to end. The last time I felt so attached to a small amount of characters was in Mass Effect, and it took them 3 games to achieve.
-
Keeping with their own style, each character portrait seen in dialogue does a great job at communicating that characters personality. And they all manage to look distinct to boot.
-
Few games make me want the soundtrack, but when they do, they can take my money. I'll never get tired of 'Grendel' or how the music changes pace as the fight draws closer to it's conclusion.
-
The game has plenty of ways around the problems it presents you. Perhaps that mission would have gone a lot smoother if you had a drone? Or maybe a lost spirit would have been willing to help if you could have communicated with it?
-
Although the game kinda gives you and hint and a shove to play as a mage, since it is the one thing the team lacks, you are far from forced to do so. In fact, I loved running 2 Shamans with my totally safe strategy of placing cover around them both, in the middle of the enemy, with an arm that threw back the only counter to it. Projectiles. Delightful.
This part of the game could be better in my opinion. Taking much of it's inspiration from XCOM and it's cover system, they do a fair job at replicating it. But It is easy to question why some things are not considered cover when you'd otherwise expect them to be. And to this day I feel that the angle characters are considered as 'Flanked' is too... forgiving, I should say.
I loved the story, don't misunderstand this as anything but true. However, one thing I disliked was that your character has a much more 'defined' background. You are made to play more of a role, rather than make up your own background and have your character act more around that.
Give this game a try if you aren't so easily swayed by strange combat choices when it comes to cover. Pretty much everything else has improved over the previous games, including the combat for that matter.
The story is good, the characters are practically lovable when you get to know them and you can have an animal spirit.
Note for the next game HBS, I want my totem to be seen just as much as Gobbet's is. Don't be unfair on us player characters.
Good story, good choices, good combat good game.

A new Shadowrun campaign set in Hong Kong, this is the followup game to Shadowrun: Dragonfall but you don't need to have played it to enjoy this game. I actually recommend picking up both if you like turn-based RPGs. The chilling atmosphere of Berlin in Dragonfall is gone so if you wanted more of that, you may be disappointed. What you get gameplay-wise is very similar though: distribute points (known as karma) into your skills, assemble a team of shadowrunners and complete a bunch of missions through force/diplomacy/stealth/hacking.
+ Revamped Matrix is much improved although turn-based fans may not like the real-time, twitchy nature of the stealth sections and the time pressure of the "Simon Says" hacking minigame.
+ Graphically the maps are more detailed and intricate than Dragonfall.
+ More varied and memorable missions than Dragonfall.
+ Enjoyable soundtrack. There wasn't a single track I disliked, which is quite rare.
- One of the characters feels overpowered in combat.
- I played SR:HK on hard difficulty and thought the main campaign was disappointingly easy compared to Dragonfall. The developers then tried to remedy this by making the bonus campaign much, much tougher, throwing waves of enemies at you as you fight for survival. The abrupt change in difficulty is jarring - I really enjoyed the bonus campaign but you may not.
- Dragonfall kept the text fairly concise and I really appreciated that. SR:HK has a few NPCs that ramble on and on about irrelevant topics - this slows down the pace of the game and feels unnecessary.
- A really minor thing, but I thought the jogging animation of the main character looked oddly cartoonish in contrast to the serious nature of the plot.
tldr; Improves on the previous game in many ways but suffers from uneven difficulty and bloated text. I can't decide which I like more, Shadowrun: Dragonfall or Hong Kong - they're both pretty good.
Two years after the initial release and it's still a great game. I hope they don't abandon this franchise in favour of Battletech.

SRHK is the third installment of the Shadowrun reboot, and expands on the qualities of its predecessors with varying success.
While it's already a classic for CRPG fans, the casual audiences will be quickly put aside by the sheer volume of text, especially compared to the earlier entries (count one hour in-between missions of pure reading).
The combat gameplay, even though overhauled since Dragonfall by the addition of new mechanics and expansion of the old ones feel the same as in the previous iterations, taking no risks but avoiding downgrade/oversimplification in the process.
Where does it steps up from the previous games then ? Simple : its storyline is one of the bests for a game of this length and scope and is wonderfully complimented by the bonus campaign
that accomodates from radically varying endings and make them work within an epilogue that is enticing to play for both its storyline, shedding light on obscure plot points of the base game and adressing the fights that were too easy past the first half with a new batch of fiendish enemies to overpower.
The storyline in itself uses the same ingredients than in
, putting you in the shoes of a stranger stranded in a new place meeting a ragtag bunch of misfits and getting involved in a conspiracy too big for even the Great Dragons.
But don't let yourself be defeated by this simple premise : the execution is near flawless and to the player devoted to overcome the walls of text an incredibly rich world appears; one where even the smallest secondary character gets copious amounts of character development.
What's wonderful is that this writing does not exist within a vacuum, but always has a reason to exist and the game actively rewards the players that take the time to get to know their fellow runners and neighbours.
The graphics on their part are very crisp and render the electric atmosphere of dystopian Hong Kong with great detail, although one can regret no big improvement since the equally beautiful areas of Dragonfall.
The music of the third game is integrally composed by Jon Everist and features two dozen tracks that give Hong Kong a very different sound signature from Seattle and Berlin, that in the previous games reused the same themes.
Special mention to
, the combat theme that you'll hear a lot.
If you got there, congratulations on overcoming my own wall of text. Here's a brief summary for you.
"Should I get Shadowrun: Hong Kong ?"
- If you're looking for a sleek tactical game, other titles do that better. However if you're not afraid to dive in a complex universe with solid narration, SRHK is the title you want

Actual Sunlight follows Evan Winters, a man who is in the midst of one hardcore existential crisis.  I don't think I'd be wrong to say that much of society today are facing similar feelings and thoughts as Evan.  I have read articles on many kids and young adults that are dealing with depression and suicidal ideation and unfortunately, too many go through with it.  So I know this game will hit too close to home for many who give it a shot.  It's not so much a game, however, as a character study.  What you take from it I would assume is how much you can relate yourself to the protagonist.  If you are the literal equivalency of your facebook profile I can only imagine that you would find this game to be a nonsensical story with a whiny main character.  If that's what you take from it: congratulations.  Your life is perfect.  However, if recent stories on rising depression and suicide rates are any indication then you would be in a miniscule percentage of the human populace.  That is why I think this game is important.  Sure, we're making strides on "anti-bullying" campaigns but nobody is really touching these issues.
For kids in school with "no friends" and teenagers transitions into adulthood who are now getting socked in the head with their first existential crisis, and for all of those soon-to-be thirty somethings who feel like they've wasted their lives, I implore you, the next time something nice happens in your life take it in stride.  Much of life is unhappiness.  But those little things are what keep us going.  Sure, you may die alone and depressed, but what about all of those great games you've played?  What about that totally sweet thing you did the other day that totally mattered to you?
When you play this game remember that it is not you.  It's a character study and a damn good one.  I wouldn't exactly call it "art" but I would certainly say it's important.  It does what creative writing majors are taught never to do and that's to make your protagonist way too ♥♥♥♥ing depressed.  This game makes it work and makes it worth playing.

Just finished my second playthrough of Actual Sunlight.  If you have ever been even a little depressed, something will resonate with you in this game.  I expect that most people who have purchased this game either are depressed, have been depressed or care for someone who is depressed.  Personally, I teeter mostly between okay and almost not okay, but some parts of this game reminded me of when I was at my lowest.  There's comfort in knowing you're not alone, but sadness in the realization that some people will never teeter back to even remotely okay and that there truly is no comfort for some people besides to just end it.  "It gets better" doesn't apply to everyone, no matter how many times we insist it does, no matter how badly we want to fix someone or their situation.  I love this game and believe it can possibly help people who haven't completely lost all hope.  For those who have, maybe it will give their loved ones some understanding or solace.

Good game, short, but wow...sure hits awfully close to home with this one.  I've dealt with depression for half my life and playing this is like looking at myself on my darker days...
If you know someone who deals with depression, play this.  It's a glimpse of what they go through.

What is a game?
Actual Sunlight is an interactive work of fiction with minimal choices to make. Its job is to make its imprint on the player and not vice versa. Be malleable enough to let it impact you, but don't be so impressionable as to let it REALLY impact you. Not that you'll be able to help it.
You're not going to ever forget playing this game. You -will- see fragments of yourself in this protagonist succumbing to his own downward spiral. "There but for the grace of god," you may say to yourself. That's okay.
To face Actual Sunlight is to face yourself. Be brave and persevere. Buy, play, and finish this game. Wait 6 months and play it again. Reflect and find yourself.
A powerfully moving game, funny and tragic, taking on the issues of depression and suicidal thoughts in an honest way that affected me greatly.

This is easily one of the better Sonic the Hedgehog titles available today. To elaborate but keep it short, I'll boil it down to the basics. This game is the best possible outcome from a decision to re-tread the adventures of the blue blur over the last ~20 years. Several levels are reborn here from the various titles in Sonic's past. So here's a short synopsis:
Visuals:
This is a nicely polished Sonic game. The colors a vibrant, the graphics are worth of any HD release of its generation, and everything in Sonic's world is rendered with loving care to the source material. Every level looks loving remade in this game.
Sound:
Everything in this game is well executed in the main game. While There's a slight lack of voice acting with some characters, the game easily makes up for it with a mixture of excellent tracks, building new arrangements, so that each level in the game has a Classic and Modern Sonic variation of the original track of the game it came from. Along with the classic sonic sound-effects, this game is a joy to listen to for any long time Sonic Fan.
Game-play:
Starting it up, the menu and title screen is very simple. The main navigation through levels is done with whichever incarnation of Sonic (Classis side scrolling or Modern 3D plat forming) you have at the time. while there, you play through 2 acts (one for each sonic play style), either plat forming through a 2.5D environment like Sonics 1-3, or on a plat forming speed rollercoaster, Sonic Adventure style. After a few of these, you unlock a sub-boss (Metal Sonic, Shadow, Silver), then a main boss (Various Robotnic Mechs). This continues for 3 sets of levels and bosses, until you reach the final boss. All of these wonderfully put together in what just reeks of love and effort. Sonic controls a little floaty in his classic incarnation, but I quickly got acclaimed to it, while modern sonic is embed with a boost ability, easily facilitating the needed momentum to blast through the, again, speed rollercoaster segments.
Story:
This is the part where I say there's nothing to talk about here and then move on to the conclusion. I'll elaborate though. This game isn't much for story to go off. To not spoil anything other than the premise, Modern Sonic is sucked into a time warp by Doctor Rootnik (Eggman) who harnessed a creature called a Time Eater, to try and defeat Sonic, by correcting his past blunders. So now it up to our hero to free these time periods, maintain the time stream and reuse his friends, while defeating past enemies and Eggman in the process.
In conclusion, sets out to pay homage to Sonic games of the past. While not all of the material they're drawing from aren't exactly outings we'd like to revisit (Sonic the Hedgehog [2006]) but they manage to do what few sonic games have been able to put together, and that's a fun platformer, that is a loving re-treading of a franchise that has had better days. The stages are solid, the music is amazing, and sonic looks fantastic. While this game isn't for everyone, i would recommend it to any long time fans of Sonic, or anyone who wants to get into Sonic, but wants something more recent to reinforce their faith in this time-weathered hedgehog.

Seeing as Sonic's 23rd birthday is coming up I thought I might as well leave a review for this game. So what do I think? Well, apart from the return of a horrible level from a horrible game (I'm looking at you, Crisis City), SONIC GENERATIONS is one of the best Sonic games of all time. If you like boost-to-win gameplay with pretty much no challenge, modern sonic is your guy. On the other hand, if you grew up in the days of Blast Processing and being able to do what Nintendon't, then Classic Sonic is the pudgy little mascot for you. Effortlessly switching between Sonic and Sonic on the hub is great, whilst still keeping the loading times down to keep the immersion from breaking.
All of the 9 stages have been excellently recreated, my personal favourite being City Escape (both Classic and Modern). Whilst Omochao can be annoying, he can be turned off if you want to do so. Comparing this game to the HD Console versions is easy. This is the one to get, largely because of the modding community! From '06 physics to Adventure Style Sonics, from a Real Hedgehog to Rayman character mods, even from Shrek to Hatsune Miku character mods, this game's modding community has it all!
Final Verdict:
If you get the chance, spend the money! And check out the various mods available, as they will undoubtedly extend your playtime with this!
On a side note, for a better representation of that Blast Processing gameplay, check out the 3DS version of the game! The 3DS version isn't much, but will keep you Sonic Fans happy for a couple of hours, especially with some exclusive levels from past handheld Sonic Games...well, two (Water Palace, Tropical Resort DS Version).
The perfect gift for any Sonic fan, whether they want to learn the Boost-To-Win gameplay, or if they want to keep doing what Nintendon't, or even if they just want to celebrate the 20th anniversary of one of the best gaming mascots of all time!

Iron Snout features animal cruelty and gore, similar to what you would encounter in games like Manhunt and The Suffering. If you are planning on buying this game, think twice if you are sensitive to violence and blood. Jokes aside, in the game you control a pig that, after months of being constantly harrassed by the wolves, decides to break bad... and break bones. With a self explanatory and easy to understand playability, Iron Snout offers a challenging, yet, fun gameplay experience, that will entertain the player for hours on end. You will often find yourself trapped inside the game while trying to beat your own record (331 here).
One complaint I would have to make is that the replay feature of the game is fairly low. After I finished getting all of the achievements, I felt like I had already "played the game", and enjoyed whatever it had to offer to the utmost. The developers could have added more features to implement the game, like, for instance, a mode where the character could walk and interact with more objects, maybe find more guns and so on.
Nevertheless, if you want to challenge yourself (climb on the leaderboard), skip some time or just procrastinate, you would surely want to play this one, as it's an "outside the box" game, and maybe have a couple laughs with it.

I recently got into this game again since I refused to play the new Battlefront II from EA. I can honestly say that this game is still a total blast even if it is an old game. I previously played the game as a child on my X-box and loved it and I still love it. It offers so much content that the new game doesn't.
For starters, Battlefront from 2005 offers a great singleplayer campaign were you get to play as the 501:st legion of clone troopers, that later became Darth Vaders personal elite troopers. This campagn starts of in the Clone wars and goes through the entire story of the third and into the fourth movie from the perspective of the clone troopers.
The game also offers a unique mode called Galactic Conquest were which combines on foot battles with tactical gameplay on a campaign map of the star wars universe. This mode is also available in multiplayer were you can face your friends in an epic war across the galaxy.
There is also a instant action mode were you can hop directly into battles alone or with friends. Here you can create a mixed list of battles of different modes. Conquest, were you battle for control of different command posts and try to make the opponents run out of reinforcements. Then there is a classic capture the flag mode which is not different from other games. Assult is a typical team deathmatch mode were your team are supposed to kill as many enemies as the the host has decided. Then there is the Hunt mode where you get to play as different races.
There are also several space battle maps were you can play either assult or capture the flag.
Given that the graphics are not the best compared to current games and there is no cockpit view in space battles. However this does not take away from the fact that this game offers hours of fun, especially if you have three to five friends you can play with.
Played this on the PS2 for longer than I could possibly imagine in my youth, and to this day I still consider it one of the greatest games ever made.  Thanks for nothing EA.

LISA is a beautiful game. Like a flower with many petals, it is layered with so much colour, each one begging to be picked. Do not let its Earthbound-esque visuals or its RPG Maker origins discourage you. This is a game that will sit in your memory banks for a long, long time.
LISA follows Brad Armstrong, a reclusive martial-arts master encumbered by a bad childhood and a world without women. Amidst one of his usual drug-fuelled escapades, he finds the last female alive: a little girl called Buddy. From there, he is catapulted into a land of a few strong men, dip♥♥♥♥♥, and perverts, and must fight the past and the present to keep his adopted daughter alive.
LISA's RPG system is a chest of wonders. With so many playable fighters and a variety of different attacks, each with their own animations, there's no shortage of damage to do to your many enemies. Whether you're launching combos, shooting fireballs, lullabying enemies to sleep, or licking them, there is something new to see in every battle. It's easy to play, yet unique at every turn, and gives plenty of other RPG systems a run for their money in the content department.
But the pleasure lies not in the fighting. It's in the world. Olathe is a place of desolation and decadence, where the absence of women and the abundance of narcotics have turned its people into licentious violence junkies. Each character, minor or major, spits their personality into the dialogue. Cutesy art and witty writing give every encounter a reason to make you smile, laugh, cringe, or even tear up. Above the blood and sun-baked deserts stands the most ragtag ensemble of psychopaths you'll ever see in a videogame. Yet, the balance is good. Things never get repetitive or annoying. Nothing outstays its welcome, and I can guarantee that you will never find a dull moment when you start a conversation or dive yourself into a game of Russian Roulette, a wrestling championship, or a shopping-cart race. There is so much to do, so much to remember. Rarely do you see an open world that takes advantage of every space it owns.
And that's what makes LISA. Its themes. It broaches depression, abuse, genocide, promiscuity, addictions, and the lengths that a parent would go to in order to protect their child. The character development and the clever use of its art makes LISA's plot multifaceted. So much can be interpreted in different ways, so much can elicit different emotional responses. When the final boss is slaughtered and the credits roll, the game's events will flash through your mind, be they lewd or comical or solemn. LISA's writing and cinematics achieve so much, and have done so on a molehill budget. You'll laugh, you'll cry, and you may even learn something from the capriciousness of LISA's characters.
Problems do exist. Decisions can have an impact on what certain characters do or how specific communities change, but the ending ultimately comes out the same. To top it off, LISA's concluding DLC chapter, The Joyful, is a letdown. Dissatisfying ending, horrible characters, and a narrative filled with too much angst. It's a huge drop from the height that LISA stands on. If you decide to finish LISA's ten-hour campaign and leave it at that, I wouldn't blame you. If you do progress to Joyful, please drop your standards, and don't expect a jaw-dropping conclusion.
But overall, LISA astounded me. It's big and ambitious and, given how small a team it had, it should have crumbled in on itself. But it didn't. It's funny, it's sad, it's educational. Scarcely will it bore or chide you. Frequently will it reach into your mind and test your fortitude. It plays, sounds, and reads so well, and will follow you to your grave. If you want a good RPG with a character of a world and a wealth of wit, you owe it to yourself to play LISA.

Company Heroes 1 (the predecessor to the is game) was, and maybe still is, one of the best RTS games of all time.
Company of Heroes 2 has the potential to be even better.  Both games share the following: a game not centered around base building, or swarming/zerging units, but tactical positioning of individual units.  A smaller, well played, or in good position force, can easily defeat a larger force. Good use and skillful employ of mico is rewarded, and it's more than just pressing a units special ability the right time, but also smart use of cover, engaging and disengaging at the right time, correct use line of sight and ranged units, manipulations of counter units, careful resource management, etc.  The are few games that use the retreat mechanic like Company of Heroes 1/2, and well made use of it will have battles ebbing and flowing the whole match.  Any minor skirmish loss can become a game win in the long run, if you play well.  Resource management is also extremely well done, and is played out on the map level, with key resources in constant contention the whole game.  At high levels of play, it's not at all uncommon to have a cheek clenching, nail biting game that can go either way, straight down the last few seconds of play.  Finally, for added measure the different factions are not just the same factions reskinned, but genuinely different, and play differently, offering  large degree of variation in abilities and strategies, and general replayability.  All of what I described above was in Company Hereos 1, Company of Heroes 2 takes all that, and adds to it some small additional features such as visual upgrades, an improved (or different line of sight system), snow/weather effects, and even an additional faction.
…so why is this review negative? The reason is, Sega/Relic added a horribly grinding, rng perk system in Company of Heroes 2 that rewards you with some objectively “more powerful” abilities and/units.  Of course, the grind, which isn’t meant to be done by any normal person through normal play, can be avoided through micro-transactions.  Now, if you buy this game for solo play, or just to skirmish the AI, or co-op and comp stomp with your friends, your money cannot be better spent.  However, if you value PvP, or the on-line competitive scene of an RTS, in my opinion, the micro-transactions make this game a hard pass.  You can’t disable them, so you will never be able to stop some random dude from having some kind of minor advantage over you in what would otherwise be a tight, intense, balanced match. It’s a horrible design, and it just destroys competitive rankings and tournaments.  I used to play very competitively in Company of Heroes 1 on-line and had an exceptionally high rank, and I never once played an on-line game in Company of Heroes 2 for the reason I stated.  Company of Heroes 2 is a great game for solo and co-op play, and as such I’d recommend it to all my friends and I don’t regret my purchase at all, however, because on-line PvP is such a staple of RTS games, I simply can’t recommend it positively given it’s current game design.

This game may hurt you. This game will taunt you. This game will probably give you stockholm syndrome. This game will probably blow your mind. Lisa is a survival RPG, but a little more hardcore and a lot darker than the norm. Think of this as a depressing dark humor version of the Mother series of games. Recently added easier difficulty modes should give you a hint of what is in store.

Death can be found commonly though this helps fit the narritive of this post-apocolyptic narritive of suffering, struggle, and redemption. It has a crazy amount of vteriety of characters many with unique battle styles, all of which can perminately die throught your journey. The story will pull you in all sorts of directions, from moments of crippling depression to pure obnoxious humor. Along with this, the game forces you to make choices. Hard choices. Each choice has an impact to the story, each of these choices will have you struggle on decisions.
The combat system is strange at first, this is only due to the need of creating combos with certain characters but other than this it's a pretty standared turn style battle system. Besides basic status effects, the game adds it's odd ball humor with other effects such as crying, depression, drunk, etc. and adds a new layer of strategy even for RPG diehards. Enemies in the game are just as obscure and wacky as the game and characters itself. This ranges from unnerving creatures, to hardened wastelanders, to beautiful majestic deer.
The struggle is real in this game, especially on pain mode. This is'nt reccomended on a first play unless you want the game to really grind against you. It's pretty challenging, but possible even though this was what i started with for the full struggling pain experience. This includes: single save points, new enemies, different areas, more hard choices, and a secret ending. This game however gives you a decent motivation through it's tough love. The risk versus reward system all depends on you, except for some obvious points in the game. Even basic mechanics such as resting are affected by this. Your members can be kidnapped or even just abandon you, other times you party is poisened because spiders slept with you, or a creepy mask appears on you face, but likely a full party heal as per RPG normes.
I don't think i've had this kind of experience in a long time. It's like defeating an old boss that takes too many tries to defeat, but worth the reward in the end. Playing this is a test of will, fully knowing that the end would be painful no matter the choices. Beating this game will toughen you up and show how much motivation you really have. So if you're ready for a depressing dark humor hardcore RPG that relies on the choices, here's your chance.

Before the review, I'd like to say this is my first time reviewing any game, and I have been hyped for this game since 2013, so this review may be slightly biased.
Where to start... most things about this game are excellent! The controls are excellent IF you use a controller (I'll get into that later), the enemies are really fun to fight, the combat feels pretty nice, and mechanics are what makes this game stand out.
About the controls, I say it's excellent with a controller because the keyboard is a little weird, however that's just my opinion. It's not unmanagable though, and if you prefer keyboard, go for it!
The enemies are really interesting, since the grumbles, which are the main enemies, tend to have a lot of health, however are easily predictable. The slimes, goos, and byats are all easy meals, which is great. When you descend deeper, more types of enemies start to appear, making the game a little more difficult each floor.
The combat is something that made this game really great. With blocking, rolling, parrying, and dismemberment, you have tons of options. There are a variety of melee weapons, aswell as tomes for those who prefer the mage class. Speaking of tomes, the spells in this game are each unique, and are all good in their own way.
The mechanics, however, are what makes this game what it is. For example, you can heat up a boulder using a fire spell, then push it into water, pick up a poison mushroom and cook it, ridding the poison and making it safe to eat. You can beat enemies to death, create distractions, or activate traps or switches with JUST a rock! You can melt balls of slime or goo, and consume them for health, or use them as weapons against grumbles by blinding them. You can knock over torches and create a fire, burning enemies in the vicinity. Plus how each kid is randomized with different traits just adds more variety to this game!
That's the end of this review. Keep in mind, this is my first one, and it may not be clear. If you're interested in difficult, but fun rogue-likes, you'll definitely want to pick this game up. 9/10.

Being a long-time Jedi Knight player (JK2 and JK3), and also an app/mod dev for JK, I had quite the expectations regarding this game. Devs promised me exciting fights, exhausting duels, a lot of skill-based gameplay and... I got it.
For those who didn't really fall for lightsaber dueling or don't think Star Wars Universe has anything to do with Blade Symphony I'm gonna try and convince you to this game without any further comparisions to my favorite franchise.
The whole idea of this game is to create a competitive environment for players to duel with various melee weapons (but really mostly swords and such). The goal was to make it pleasurable, fast, dynamic while keeping it more advanced/difficult than just your average arcade game in TPP where you hack and slash your way to victory.
It's a game of strategy, analysis and customizing your gameplay to fit your style. I wanna talk about the latter first: It's really well done, you get to choose from 4 characters, and each one of them has got a completely different moveset and playstyle.
I've noticed 1-2 similiar moves but then again they follow up into something else, have different range, different purpose, are from a different "string" (I'll talk about it later).
Each one of them has got different properties and different "defensive" ability. You also get to choose what the sword looks like but that's a detail.
Let's talk about the gameplay: It's brilliant. How do you mix dynamic fights with tactics? You put 4 categories of attacks, each one of them countering 1 of them, at the same time being weak against another. Attacks also have exact "trails" - some leave you open, some attack from the left, some attack from the right, some make you spin and attack everything around you, but there are still openings your opponent can use. So can you. Combat is still fast-paced and you feel the adrenaline rush. Add "strings" to that. Attacks come in patterns but you can break the pattern, reset it and completely confuse your opponent. It's truly a game of skill, predictions and observation.
There are a few gamemodes but really you should know you can take part in FFA, duels (1v1, 2v1, 2v2) and Hero mode. Hero mode chooses one of the players to be the "hero" - he gets empowered attacks but all the enemies are trying to kill him at the same time.
As for the audio: it's neither bad nor good. I didn't really puy much attention to it and for the most part I just had my own music running in the background. Have to say I've played a bit with the in-game music and it wasn't irritating at any part. Only thing I could wish for is some better hit-sounds.
Graphics are just ok, living up to standards but still pretty simple. That's ok, you wanna stay focused on the fights and there's no irritating visual stymulus coming from the game itself. Some of the fighting areas seem a little bit empty and poorly designed but it's not much of a deal at all. Lastly I'll just say that camera work is intuitive and you can actually adjust it in any way imaginable (e.g. angle, yaw, shaking, moving, rotation, height, distance).
I can really recommend this game. If you like dynamic sword fights with a bit of tactics you will enjoy this game. It's simple, but holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ in its simplicity it's beautiful.

Super Time Force Ultra is an entertaining game with a rather hilarious plot. Whether it is interacting with your CO who has TWO eye patches or heading back in time to stop the asteroid which killed the dinosaurs (irrespective of the number of dinosaurs you kill on your way to the impact site), there is a charming and hilarious disregard for that pesky time space continuum in the epic quest to make time more AWESOME.

But with each death, the level becomes a little easier as your previous lives continue fighting (and shooting) when you replay it. The pictures and videos make it seem like this is an arcade-style retro action platformer.
In a way, you could say it is. But then, not really. I'd actually classify it as a *puzzle* game, and a very very good one at that.
The premise is that you control a character in a level which is much too long for the time limit you have and with death being ~everywhere. Only, when you die or at any given time you can stop time, rewind, then from that point spawn a new character (of the same or another class, there are a lot of classes which you unlock throughout the levels, each with their own unique skillset). You'll move again, but the previous character still does the stuff you controlled it to do.
This leads to a very puzzle-like way of approaching levels. You will constantly branch and rewind, using new characters to protect older ones (which allows you to pick them up again) which died originally. Bosses result in a giant carnage of 15-30 characters blasting various weak spots at various points in time.
At the end of each level, the game plays back everything in "normal time", which is very interesting to watch.
It's a really good game. Graphics are solid, controls are very tight, the mechanic is quite unique and works well, enough stuff to do, the only thing I would criticize is that unless you're going for a minimum-rewinds approach, difficulty is often on the low end.

After finishing Shadowrun Dragonfall, I was kinda sad there were any more campaigns to play to continue my story. Sure I could download a mod, but a huge part of the charm of Shadowrun is the writing, and I'd be missing out on that. When I saw Hong Kong, I immediately put it on my wishlist to get once it went on sale. It was definitely worth it. Dragonfall had a sort of Dystopian anarchist feel in addition to the overarching theme of fantasy mixed with cyberpunk. But Hong Kong managed to avoid re-treading the same ground that Dragonfall covered, and found its own unique charm in a crime-ridden oriental world with plenty of its own appeal.
I enjoyed the main character's personality more in Hong Kong than Dragonfall, as you had a greater ability to come off as sassy or joking. The companion quests were a mixed bag, but ultimately I think Gobbet, Racter, and Gaiju had compelling conversation options. Duncan was intersting to talk to, but didn't have much depth to his story. Isobel was basically a brat the whole time to me, which may have had something to do with me choosing a decker as my profession, and so I barely used her on missions.
Combat, skills, and progression were the same from the previous two, which I appreciated because it meant I could learn my my mistakes in the past on how to spec out and gear my character most effectively. As tempting as it can be to lure enemies into an easy killbox on some of the harder scenarios, I appreciate the timer mechanism which forced aggressive gameplay. I greatly appreciated the enhanced hacking mechanics in both Dragonfall and Hong Hong, especially since you spend so much time in the matix in both.
Overall, I think the biggest boon to this franchise is its immersion. There's no way I'd play, let alone pay, for a game where you literally just read text all day with scattered turn-based combat unless it was really compelling. Fortunately, it is.

First of all, this is a mature game. I don't mean mature as too much violence mature. Actual Sunlight tackles a very tough subject. Depression. If you are depressed, don't play this, because it will get you even more depressed. Even if you're not depressed, this game will very likely make you sad if you pay attention to its story.
My hours played do not seem like much here, but I bought this game before it's steam release and played it through, and it was amazing.
Actual Sunlight is probably the most accurate depiction of depression in a game to date. It can hardly be defined as a game, really. It is more of an interactive story. Don't let that stop you though, if you're not depressed, you'd be doing yourself a favour by buying it. I can't go into a too in depth review without giving to much away, but it is about a young man named Evan Winters who is suffering from depression. I believe that a lot of people can relate to what he's going through, even if not depressed.
The game was made with RPG maker, so expect the graphics you see in the screenshots. If you don't like reading too much, you may not want to buy it, but that would be a mistake.
At this price, this is a story worth reading and seeing.

It accurately portrays what it's like to be severly deprssed. That's literally all I can think of to say about it. Do not play if you're currently sufferring from depression. Otherwise, play it and be prepared for hard hitting storytelling.

(played the original and indiegogo funded versions) I'd consider this game up there with the likes of Gone Home, The Novelist, and Depression Quest, if not even being better at them and more powerful at some things. A powerful reflection on depression and the workplace, Actual Sunlight is a pretty harrowing but worthwhile experience, and definitely a steal at this price. It doesn't give you much choice or agency over what you do in the game but that's somewhat the point, and it's an interesting few hours to say the least. To quote a few reviewers -- ‘it is quite possibly a dangerous game […] a game that could drive someone to depression or worse’ (TP Review), ‘this game probably shouldn’t be played if the you have suicidal thoughts, a tendency towards self harm, or are just plain not having a good day’ (Penny Arcade), the game is ‘written in such a way as to make the player consider their own lives, and there are clear attempts to draw parallels between the gamer and the character’ (The Indie Game Magazine). One reviewer appeals ‘to anyone who finds their own feelings echoed in Actual Sunlight to recognize the catharsis of being understood, certainly, but to hear another voice, one saying that hope always exists’ (RPS), going so far as to give numbers for suicide prevention hotlines.

Actual Sunlight is more an interactive novel than a game. It's the story of someone who is permanently mired in depression, self-hatred, and crushing hopelessness. The narrative is primarily the protagonist's own twisted introspections and personal observations of the world around him. The gameplay brings you through his life, as he lives it. It feels like taking a tour through an exhibit of someone's mental illness.
The game is short, but the story is fairly compelling. It has a fullscreen mode, but no configurable video settings beyond that. It has controller support, but the analog movement lacks precision and the d-pad doesn't seem to work (I use an Xbox 360 controller), so you might be better off with keyboard controls (arrow keys and Z).
Overall, I'd give this game a solid recommendation if you like stories that deliver a strong message, but aren't necessarily meant to be happy.

Do two Sonics really make one great adventure?
Heck Yeah!
Seeing as Sonic's 23rd birthday is coming up I thought I might as well leave a review for this game. So what do I think? Well, apart from the return of a horrible level from a horrible game (I'm looking at you, Crisis City), SONIC GENERATIONS is one of the best Sonic games of all time. If you like boost-to-win gameplay with pretty much no challenge, modern sonic is your guy. On the other hand, if you grew up in the days of Blast Processing and being able to do what Nintendon't, then Classic Sonic is the pudgy little mascot for you. Effortlessly switching between Sonic and Sonic on the hub is great, whilst still keeping the loading times down to keep the immersion from breaking.
All of the 9 stages have been excellently recreated, my personal favourite being City Escape (both Classic and Modern). Whilst Omochao can be annoying, he can be turned off if you want to do so. Comparing this game to the HD Console versions is easy. This is the one to get, largely because of the modding community! From '06 physics to Adventure Style Sonics, from a Real Hedgehog to Rayman character mods, even from Shrek to Hatsune Miku character mods, this game's modding community has it all!
Final Verdict:
If you get the chance, spend the money! And check out the various mods available, as they will undoubtedly extend your playtime with this!
On a side note, for a better representation of that Blast Processing gameplay, check out the 3DS version of the game! The 3DS version isn't much, but will keep you Sonic Fans happy for a couple of hours, especially with some exclusive levels from past handheld Sonic Games...well, two (Water Palace, Tropical Resort DS Version).
The perfect gift for any Sonic fan, whether they want to learn the Boost-To-Win gameplay, or if they want to keep doing what Nintendon't, or even if they just want to celebrate the 20th anniversary of one of the best gaming mascots of all time!

If you ever wondered what being the captain of a spaceship in hostile space was like, this is the game for you.  Like "Star Trek", your experienced crew and technological advances will save the day again and again.  Unlike "Star Trek", you have to foot the bill.  Hull repairs cost.  Weapon upgrades cost.  Ship systems cost limited power.  Better trained crew costs.  Fuel costs.  Even the Missiles your ship can fire aren't free.
Tough choices abound.  Do I upgrade the weapons or the shields?  Do I purchase that awesome weapon or use several smaller ones?  Do I get involved in the conflicts I come across and try to be a hero or remain content to simply survive?
Which crew member do I send to repair the broken Oxygen system and which stays at their post during the heated battle?
This game is full of random events in a randomly generated galaxy.  There are countless strategies to employ, new ships to unlock, and suprises along the way.  As many different ways there are to win, there are even more ways to die in the infinite coldness of space.  And believe me, you'll find them, and be even more motivated to start up a new game.  "If only I'd purchased that shield upgrade instead of installing that shiny Mind Control device..."
Space is unforgiving, but the Space Bar is your best friend!

Calling this game a clone of Sonic the Hedgehog is a serious disservice. This game is not a clone; it's a love letter, and like most love letters, it expounds on the subject's greatest virtues while downplaying its flaws. Like most love letters, it contains a portion of the heart and soul of its author and is the product of an obsessive infatuation: every "i" has been dotted, every "t" crossed, and—I suspect—each and every paragraph rewritten again and again until it everything was perfect. Most of all, like only the greatest love letters, Freedom Planet proclaims its love publicly. It may be adressed to the Sega Genesis era of games, but it was intended to be read by everyone.
Unlike most love letters, however, one of the main characters is a dragon. Honestly, there's a distinct lack of dragons in most love letters that I've read, but this game fixes that. It also has motorcycles and giant airships. Oh, and aliens! Lots and lots of aliens. So basically Freedom Planet is like the most badass love letter ever written.
Highly Recommended.
