Freedom Planet much like Shovel Knight, harkens to an earlier era of gaming. Whereas Shovel Knight was to the 8-bit NES era, Freedom Planet leans towards the late end of the 16-bit era, taking cues from games like Gunstar Heroes and Sonic the Hedgehog (in Particular Sonic 3 & Knuckles)
I heard about this game a long while ago, and was intstantly interested. However, the extent of my interaction with the game has been no more than the few hours I played today.
As a disclaimer, I play a lot of games, and absolutely love the original sonics, so my gaming level may be considered advanced (everyone has their strengths and weaknesses though) So take this as my opinion, there is no unbiased review folks.
Let us begin, this game is not just a mere ripoff, this game borrows some good things from 16 bit era games that you never realized mattered so much.
Tight controls - This game is extremely responsive, and the controls are solid. One thing from Sonic that was always important was he was never too floaty, the speed never exceeded an amount that made it difficult to play, and each button press connected properly. Freedom Planet copies this important detail.
Simple controls - The game does not overload you with controls, it keeps things pretty simple, but with unique controls for each character. You are limited in your moves, so it doesn't take a lot for you to figure out what you need to do, where.
Innovative Gameplay - Now, I say "innovative" as a relative term - the game relies on 16-bit era game design as a model, and relatively, it innovates. The unique combination of beat'em'up aesthetics with the speed of sonic creates a unique experience. One could also argue it takes the coin-hoarding from the latest entries into the "New Super Mario Bros" series.
Your pace - The game never forces you to go that fast, the timer does not tick to an invisible deadline. This game does not use the improper and often misinformed recollection that "sonic games are about going fast" Instead, it captures the accuracy of Sonic games - It has good platforming, and mild exploration, and chances - qoute,
, to go fast. Sonic was often seen as being fast because it made the platforming and exploration so tight and simple, and I feel Freedom Planet copies this well. You can run fast, you can jump around, or you can hunt down every damn gem in a level.
Challenging bosses - Some people made an issue of the bosses being difficult, for me, they were just right. The game is fair about checkpoints, so jumping right into a boss is simple. Additionally, this is not a matter of rings = life. A lifebar is present, and you are given fair warning about certain attacks.
Female protagonists - I'm just generally pleased with the choice of having female protagonists. It is not a gameplay point, but a personal point.
The game has flaws, and I won't just ignore them, I'll go over them
Cluttered level design - by no means a deal breaker, but players of Sonic 3 & Knuckles will recognize the issue of having levels where you backtrack, and levels that are very large, sometimes, you get a bit confused. This game copies many good aspects of Sonic, but ended up copying this flaw as well.
Zoomed viewpoint - The game could stand to have the area zoomed-out a bit. once again, not a deal-breaker, but simply a flaw you may find yourself frustrated with once.
Unclear checkpoints - I wish the checkpoints were made clear, a spinny ball, a flag, something. The checkpoints themselves are fair, but just an indicator would be nice.
Things I cannot comment on are things like:
The story - it is a bit of a stock story, but by no means it is the "worst of fanfiction" (trust me, I've seen that) It gives us a clear goal, we have a protagonist, and we have an antagonist, it does that right, and it quickly gives our characters a motivation to keep fighting. That said, it is not The Last of Us, or even Saints Row IV, but it's a decent enough story. Plus, you can ignore it completely by going through a "classic" mode.
Voice Acting - I am just pleased to have some voice acting, it's not good or bad to me. I'm not a professional voice actor, and I also don't expect the best from a non-AAA game, they put their heart into it, that's good enough for me. Nor do I expect to be emotionally moved by the game.
Always remember folks, reviews are of personal opinion, I try to go over the good and the bad, but those two categories will always be influenced by a reviewer's experiences, likes, and dislikes. In the end though, I hope if tihs review convinces you to buy the game, that you enjoy it, and if notm I offer my sinceriest apologies.

I haven't played this game for as much as I'd like to thus far, but it's pretty clear already how impressive it is.
Going through all of the tutorials gave me a grasp on the fighting system works. I understand the basics, but still can not reliably win in a duel for the life of me. This is and of itself isn't a bad thing. In fact, part of me is excited for how much more I have to learn. Unfortunately, another part of me is upset by the fact that there's no easy or convenient way to do so.
This game does not hold your hand. It very much tosses you into the deep end and lets you sink or swim of your own accord. If you've ever played 'Toribash', you'll probably understand what I'm talking about; you've got an incredibly complex fighting system that you can start with a friend to be on-par with (though only because neither of you are any good yet), or you can play against bots or foes online that understands the ins and outs of the system and as such, at least for a reasonable while, tend to beat you without contest.
The game makes a point of saying that it will include further tutorials at a later point, which would certainly be welcome because as it stands one has to figure out most of the mechanics by themselves after seeing somebody else do it. YouTube for now remains the best place for in-depth tutorials to be best of my knowledge.
In any case, this is definitely a game that will take a long time to master. If you're genuinely willing to spend many, many hours playing and perfecting this game, then good for you, I recommend it. I fear for many, though, it could end up sitting in their library as ‘that one game I really should really get better at some time’.
Character customisation is decent – you can chose one of four characters and one of a lot of swords, both affecting gameplay stats, and you can also make a few aesthetic changes. Unfortunately the character and sword you fancy most for the looks mightn't necessarily be the best for actual competition, but I find changing up your style to match a new, cool sword you unlock is refreshing.
The modding community is certainly not lacking - there are plenty of custom items and maps to download, if that's your bag.
I tentatively recommend this. I think you can already tell whether or not you'd be wasting your money.

Roguelite Platformer with tons of RPG mechanics. There are only two classes to choose from right now with another four to be released at a later date.
I think my only real complaint is that it's local co-op and not online co-op.

Despite my (currently) low play time, rest assured I've put at least 30 hours into earlier kickstarter-exclusive builds. This a simply fantastic roguelike platformer. To me, it feels like a combination of Spelunky and Super Smash Bros in a fantasy environment.There are four big selling points I'll discuss below. TL;DR: Very fun, fluid movement, challenging skill based combat, incredible variety of organic environmental interactions, and all play styles are equally supported
The thing that initially drew me to this game is the way the player moves throughout the environment. It's the smoothest system I've ever played with, and traversing the environment is not just a means to an end, it's a pleasure. The only gripe I have with it is there are occasionally environmental hazards you can't protect against, but they're few and far between.
This game is extremely difficult, make no mistake. In my opinion, not all of the stats are as balanced as they should be; it's very difficult to survive hits from Grumbuls (humanoid enemy, think orc) early on, and getting good will definitely take practice. That said, the combat is very fun. Killing the enemies is always satisfying, and your deaths feel horribly brutal, but never unfair. The magic system is very intuitive and is useful both in and out of combat.
The third and perhaps biggest selling point for me is the interactions that happen organically in the world. For instance, within the game there are poisonous mushrooms, boulders, pools of water, and fire magic. Let's look at the interactions possible between these four objects. If there are fish in the water, a mushroom can be thrown in to leak poison into the water and weaken the fish. Using fire magic, you can burn up the mushroom and it's poison cloud to safely pass. Using the same magic, you can super heat the boulder, and hit it into an enemy to deal extra damage and potentially set them alight. If you need food in a pinch, you can heat the rock, push it into a pool to boil the water, and then throw in the mushroom, which will cook and become edible.
The final aspect is that this game supports playing essentially however you want. In many roguelikes, leveling up is based on getting experience from fighting enemies, completing objectives, and so on. In Catacomb Kids, each floor has a leveling orb, which, once picked up, allows the player to level up once. Nothing else matters, as long as you get the orb, you can level up. That means if you want to play by dodging dangerous situations with teleportation magic, no problem. Want to slaughter everyone you come across? Cool. Tackle the levels however you want, because you won't be punished for skipping rooms and opponents like you would be with an EXP system.
Overall, it's a very fun and unique experience that I think is absolutely worth $16 in the current state. The developer is very communicative as well, and does weekly Dev streams on Twitch.
Edit: I forgot a HUGE aspect (equal playstyle representation), so I've updated the TL;DR and added the section.

I'm a long-time Falcom fan and have been playing and loving their games since the SNES days.  As such, it pains me to say that I honestly don't like Tokyo Xanadu very much.  I've tried to give it a fair chance and have pushed myself to play it, but I'm just not enjoying it.
People have sometimes called it a "combination of Ys and Trails of Cold Steel," and that's true, except it combined the worst parts of both.  The plot moves at a glacier's pace; every chapter follows the same formula of one of your friends getting into trouble, getting sucked into a portal into another dimension, you have to go rescue them, and then their personal problems are fixed.  Each chapter is bookended by a few mysterious characters doing mysterious things that you're supposed to be intrigued by, but the answers to the mysteries are not nearly as interesting as they lead you to believe.  The out-of-combat gameplay is very Trails-like, in that there are countless NPCs you're expected to talk to between every scene, except rather than being set in an interesting fantasy world, TX is set in modern Japan; if you've ever watched an anime series featuring high school students, you'll automatically recognize all of the tropes.  There's nothing new here.  Occasionally something interesting will happen at the end of a chapter, but then it's right back to the mundane.
The gameplay is decent, but not up to the level of any Ys game.  Movement and action are relatively slow; there are many characters you can play as, but each character has a very limited move set, and most of the characters' move sets are very similar to each other.  There's a wide variety of accessories you can equip to increase characters' stats and upgrade their abilities, but none of them offer any fundamental changes to the gameplay.  Palette-swapped enemies fill every dungeon, and after a while you'll even start running into palette-swapped bosses, which would have been inexcusable for an Ys game.  The Ys games are great because they're short and sweet and constantly throwing new things at you, but TX felt the need to pad out its gameplay enough to match the padded-out story, and it didn't go well.  In chapter 6, near the end of the game, I went through two entire dungeons in order so that I could fix an alarm clock and a broken TV.  They were both filled with enemies I had killed a dozen hours before.  Yawn.  I could have done a speed run of Ys: The Oath in Felghana in that time.
If you've played every other Falcom game on Steam and are jonesing for more, TX might give you what you want, if you can handle pushing through the boring parts.  There are almost certainly better options out there.

This is another great game from the Shadowrun series. Thus, if you liked the previous ones, you will probably going to like this one too. Since I am a fan of Shadowrun, I loved it!
The only issue I found in this game is that it needed “a little less conversation, a little more action”, as Elvis would put it. Between combats, there are tons of texts to be read and people to talk to if you want to explore the whole game and get all information from the side characters. Hence, although the story is amazing, it may get a little boring to catch up every time, especially in the cases you were able to finish the mission very quickly.
It is worth mentioning again that the story is amazing. The plot development is really cool and got me hooked up since the beginning.
On the game itself, there are many improvements in cyberware and melee weapons that are worth checking. Also, the game is much more generous in granting karma for the missions. However, it is much less generous in money. Thus, this game has a lot more possibilities to develop your characters, but you have to choose wisely... Moreover, the matrix system changed to an annoying mini-game thing that you have to beat in order to advance, instead of the previous version of blasting your way through it. If you fail too much, you will be overwhelmed by enemies and will probably fail the mission if using the matrix was necessary. Personally, I preferred the previous version, but it is fine to explore other possibilities.
In sum, this is a great game and certainly worth playing it. I hope the developers keep’em coming, but, sadly, it seems that it will take a while to release another one…

8/10. Great game, almost awesome, even... almost.
+ Overall feeling that game is polished, solid, and completed - something that two it's predecessors lacked.
+ Wonderful storytelling (our character finally has a real name and surname along with the street name - that alone is ground-breaking), all characters and dialogs are well-written and feels alive. Same way goes the world - you really want to read all that colossal amount of text that game has to offer.
+ Various nice quality-of-life improvements, from better game optimization to the ability to enter combat mode without stumbling your face into the enemy's hairy chest and managing items between party members during the run (still kinda unbelieveable, gosh, finally) that makes gameplay way more fluid.
+ Amazing soundtrack, worthy of your music player's playlist.
+ More, like, much more ways to outtalk yourself from unnecessary bloodshed, and less unskippable battles that previous games had.
+ Reworked Matrix gameplay really feels nice and refreshing.
+ Tons, no, TONS of references to the events of the previous parts, and events that happened in-between. Heart-warming.
- Shooting mechanic surely was severely altered, and it's goddamn b a d. It's nearly impossible to land more than one or two bullets/pellets from something with auto-fire or shotgun. Even with high Quickness and Ranged Combat skills. Even in point-blank range. Still, that one or two bullets that will mercifully hit their target will often do strangely high damage - something about 2/3 from overall shotgun blast damage from one pellet, for example. Still can't quite get how exactly is wrong, but it IS wrong - most of the projectiles will miss all the time, yet *technically* you'll get some of your promised damage from that few bullets that will land on the target. Tried with different chars, so it's not a bad luck. Not a real problem either, sure, but it's groan-inducing to see how all people involved in a gunfight miss most of their shots even standing next to each other, even with >90% hit chance. Interestingly, guns from bonus campaign tend to be the opposite - they have almost no spread, both visually and mechanically. Guess that's B a L a N c E. Speaking of which...
- Everything that relates to equipment is dull and undeveloped - a problem that originates from the first title, problem that was widely discussed, and problem that HBS just left as is in the end - yet with the visible traces of attempts to solve it, which makes it even worse. Armor now doesn't gives any stat bonuses, which was logical - like, it's more comfortable for a rigger to work in the industrial-grade west that has many pockets with many tools within, shaman appreciates magic garb riddled with magic trinkets and so on. But nah, armor now just plainly gives armor points - each tier of it gives 2 more, and that's absolutely all of it. Was that an attempt to ease the burden of fashionistas? Quite crude one, i'd say. Weapons follow the "tiers" rule as before, and as before, you just know that tier 2-gun will be better than tier 1-gun only because it has a smaaaall increase in damage. And maybe it'll have a burst fire option. Wow. In the end, it kind of kills the purpose, kills the joy from obtaining a new hardware - it's all the same, essentially, absolutely same minus the damage it does. Guess all this tier-system with almost non-existent differences between guns wasn't changed at all because of "simplicity" and "clarity of purpose" (quotes from forum, srsly) it provides, but no, it damn doesn't. It's uninteresting and rigid. It's understandable, though, that Shadowrun: Hong Kong mainly revolves around storytelling and dialogues, but that's no damn real excuse for leaving the whole equipment game part so crude, especially knowing what needs to be changed, and how it needs to be changed. Magic, though, suffers from tier-system less, which leads us to...
- Spell bounce that ley-lines, oh, pardon me, Dragon Lines now provide. Interesting concept, maybe, but such lame outcome. It oversimplifies things way much. Place your mage on the dragon line, cast blind/mind wipe/confusion, wipe out enemy without much retaliation. Or heal all your party every 3rd turn, because healing bounces too! Seriously, when you're stating to *restrict yourself* from the feature that developers encourage you to use, because it makes almost any encounter trivial - that feels uneasy. And combat magic still blows, even with ability to be the pinball wizard.
- Shamanic spirits. They are now tied to 4 primal elements (although Eastern philosophy has 5 of them... was it too hard to make thing a bit more logical? Seems so), and just a mere reskins of one model. While spirits in Dragonfall greatly differed in shape and gave some narrative about the location just by summoned spirit's type. Lame.
- Almost each and every gunfight in the game is just too easy, even on Hard difficulty. Again, compared to the Dragonfall and Returns. Even without abusing disable bouncing and Duncan's Subdue, it's null sweat, including the final fight too.
- Storytelling is awesome, but the plot of main campaign itself isn't so brilliant. Better than one from Returns, but not even close to Dragonfall. Plot of bonus campaign is outright cringeworthy, sometimes. Isn't a real downside, though, more like personal opinion.
- Plot-involved teammates (and a good portion of hired runners, to be honest) are a walking cliche. Especially Is0bel.
Saying straight, most of the downsides listed above consist from the legacy problems that Shadowrun series kept from the beginning, and from the things that people who's first Shadowrun will be Hong Kong will barely notice at all.
So, buy it, play it, enjoy it. This game is really worth it's price.

Tokyo Xanadu is a game that not many will probably come to purchase simply because it doesn't seem like the sort of game that's worth the price for what it presents in trailers and screenshots. But after completing the game (and all the extra content) in its entirety I can honestly say it's definitely worth the price tag for the amount of content you get.
Playing through the story is sort of like watching an anime set in the modern era with fantasy elements--- one that you would normally rate a 7/10 in your book. Solid, but hardly innovative in the genre. However the same story presented and executed well in video game format warrants this particular one a 9/10 in my book. Again, whilst it does nothing innovative in the genre in terms of storytelling, it does execute it in such a way that makes the story worth more than it is on paper.
Many reviews have compared this to the Persona series and the Ys, and while I can't attest to it being similar to the latter (due to not having played any of the Ys games), it does have the makings of a Persona game in terms of how characters interact with one another, as well as the tropes used in said interactions.
Combat is simple yet fulfilling when you play the game 'right'. With the player skill cap mostly coming from how you deal with the bosses and less about each character's (similar yet slightly different) mechanics. Grinding can get tiring as most of the dungeon monsters can be regarded as 'fillers' but I find the story was enough to keep me going-- and me being me, I didn't want to be 'weak' when it came down to fighting the bosses.
As someone who is interested in the world-building aspects of video games in general, I do hope that the developers continue this "Xanadu" world which they've built-- as the game leaves a lot of room for more stories to be told. Hopefully more people pay attention to this game and with luck, we'll get to see Nihon Falcom deliver more of it for us in the future-- perhaps with different characters in other parts of the Xanadu world.
All in all a well rounded package if you like an ARPG with a Persona style characters and tropes. 9/10.

:::THINGS TO KNOW:::
1) Cards work passively, and can be consumed for health.  You pretty much need 10 points in any card stat to get any benefit.
2) Hold Space to switch between weapons and head gear.
3) The crypt can store cards and equipment for you.
4) You can find powerups in chests (cards, etc) but the regular chests cost health to open.
5) You can carry a combo through rooms for massive points.
6) Use windows to leave the tower and store any gains you've acquired in the crypt or to pump points into the wall.
7) The big wall with guns and head gear is like a "shop."  You can pump your points into different gear.  When it's red, you can claim it, or keep pumping points into it to upgrade it to Blue (level 2) and then Green (level 3).
8) Guys you free from the cages become worshippers and provide you with a steady trickle of points.  If you hit Escape, go to the "exit" option and show up in your room, you can walk on the treadmill to increase the speed at which you gain worshipper points (a great way to boost up some gear while you're at work or school).
9) You can equip stuff you find on the "dead body" in the crypt storage room to create a follower who you can send into the ruins on their own to get stuff for ya.
10) I have no ♥♥♥♥ing clue what the damn telescope does or how to get the code for the goddamn briefcase to open it in the room...

There is something unique about a game where you play a dangerous and secret mercenary group employed from the Shadow World to break into a museum and smash cheap artificats.
In another mission I spent time breaking into a corporation tower block and had to move things half a milimeter to break the overall flow of Qi
I enjoyed the previous game in the series which was called Dragonfall. This time we are based in Hong Kong and it is really, really, REALLY nice to see an oriental themed game.
Persecuted for a crime you did not commit, you and your brother are given safe haven by a crime lord in Hong Kong and you take on missions to pay of your debt, build resources and find out what happened to your father.
The missions are quite varied and combat when it occurs is turn based and involves guns, grenades, magic, summons and drones. Many of the missions include cyber levels which initially can seem complex.
There is a lot of text to read, some of it is vital for progressing through the game and other text adds flavour to the world. There is a tendancy to zoom through this stuff and I would urge any potential player not to do this. Without the reading it becomes a completely different game, much poorer.
The writing is pretty good and above the standard level we find in most pc games. Seeing concepts, places and ideas from the other side of the world is no bad thing.
As I progressed through the story I found the end game a complete surprise, nothing like I expected.
Probably the strength of the game. It can be tough until you level up your character and your team and until you find shops to stock up on healing items and grenades etc
Some of the combat missions involve getting stuff done in a certain amount of rounds and other missions can’t be completed unless you delve deeper into how mechanics like cover work.
They made some changes to this area from Dragonfall. Initially it’s almost impossible to understand how things work. I had to find out on a video tutorial. Then I found my groove and enjoyed these sections.
Another strength. As you complete missions you receive Karma points that can be spent on character development. The best thing here is that you have complete freedom to build your character as you want. I played a pistol in your face character first (guns and HP) but found more joy with a shaman (summons and charisma).
You can also save these points until you really need them, for example if you come across a mission where high strength or intelligence is needed.
Generally your mission party is based on four people so as you build your own character, you can hire or go with the NPC party members the game makes available to you. One of these is your brother who is a rifle man former police officer. Another is a shaman and another a Decker.
There are two games here. The first one I played on my laptop without reading much of the storyline and conversations. That game was poor.
The second game I played on my main PC and gave the writing a chance and it was really interesting, educational and enjoyable game.

After just now completing my first playthrough (there will absolutely be more) of this game or any Shadowun game, it just awes me.
First off, the incredibly well written narration gave me a much more immersive experience than any game that solely relies on awesome graphics. I saw much more through this text than I'd ever expect. The writers are talented for sure.
The whole Shadowrun universe is also intriguing and very fascinating. As I love both sci-fi and fantasy this is a perfect match for me. Combining demons, ghouls, shamans, and magic with hacking, sci-fi prostetics, and droning in the midst of a near-future dystopian environment ruled by big corps and mafia leaders running a war with information, military and mercenaries. It's just amazing.
The characters are also so lovable. hatable and diverse. The conversations feel like actual conversations. Creating your own character with such detail makes it truly a personal experience and immersion. The character progression makes the player taking on many parts of the game in just one playthrough. The progression of the game is also very personalized due to your actions impact on the future.
I can't recommend this enough. I also saw some comments downvoting the game due to heavy text. Expect to play a book. Everything except the combat is text. The loading screen is text, explaining how your team feels after and before a mission. Coming in a room explains what they see and smell. The text explains how anyone looks. As the game, do have amazing graphics, the text narrative is the core focus.
The only thing I have to complain about, is the damn decking. I absolutely disliked the whole running around in the cyber-space or whatever you wanna call it. It took away a big chunk of the immersion. It felt like a filler due to not coming up with a proper engaging way to simulate the hacking.

Positives first - great stylised art and overall atmospehere. The shooting feels rather good. Alt+F4 closes the game pretty quickly.

Now for the negative - basically the game does all it can to rob you of any sense of achievement - when you die you lose everything. And any new equipment you get eventually runs out of ammo and is lost. The only thing that is persistent are the little followers you free from cages that dangle from the ceiling. These are the "clicker" element of the game in that they generate the in-game currency at a steady rate and the more of them you have the faster it regenerates. You can use the quit game menu to enter the "real world" and run on the threadmill to advance time faster and quickly regenerate more points. Leave it for a couple of minutes and you would probably have a decent amount of points.

You also get these same points for in-game actions with a neat combo system. But if you might as well idle for them what's the point of earning them?

Anyhow, beyond that the game punishes your efforts, as previously mentioned the weapons will run out of ammo and with better weapons the enemies upgrade as well - so what's the point?

You do improve as a player and start reaching the boss room more often, but then the boss has a VERY long health bar and basically is just an annoying bullet sponge. Couple that with not perfect controls and it just gets annoying.
Summary: A game that looks promising, but turns out being way more annoying than it is fun. If only they actually let us achieve something more - keep the weapons you unlock/find, vary the locations, actually have some progression. It might be less of the popular "roguelike" and probably shorter to complete, but it would be a better game.
PS. I see on the forums that the devs are decent people and the fact that this is built with Construct 2 is quite impressive. But still - got this game with Humble Monthly and still sort-of regret not trading it for something else. Perhaps they could add another "easy" mode where your progress matters (even in Dark Souls you keep what equipment you find and that game is the "git gud" poster boy). I'd play that.

To say this game is absurdly ♥♥♥♥ed up is an understatement. But it's all the more amazing for it.
Out of all the games I've played, indie or otherwise, few have really dug at me like LISA has. This game does NOT sugarcoat the suffering its characters go through or the horrors of its universe, and yet it's such an entertaining and well crafted game regardless. The universe and tone of the game is bleak and littered with dark humor and violence and yet once you start playing its impossible to put down. It might seem like another one of those over-hyped meme games, but it's not by any means whatsoever. In fact, I'm genuinely shocked it didn't get more attention than it did.
There's some annoying flaws with the gameplay like the cliffs and some of the perma-kills, but its otherwise very fun and the combo/timed button skills add quite a bit of depth to the combat. The story is pretty much flawless as far as I'm concerned; it's clear Austin Jorgensen knew what he was doing. It's very tightly written, with complex themes, sympathetic yet tremendously flawed characters, a mercilessly bleak yet engaging atmosphere, brilliant usage of storytelling devices and some of the most twisted symbolism I've seen in any game in recent memory. Which altogether makes quite possibly one of my favorite games, and without a doubt the best game I've played so far this year.
Quite simply, don't let the fact that it was made with RPG Maker fool you. LISA is a goddamn masterpiece and overlooking it as a fad and cheaply written game would be doing it a massive disservice. HIGHLY recommended.

Company Heroes 1 (the predecessor to the is game) was, and maybe still is, one of the best RTS games of all time.
Company of Heroes 2 has the potential to be even better.  Both games share the following: a game not centered around base building, or swarming/zerging units, but tactical positioning of individual units.  A smaller, well played, or in good position force, can easily defeat a larger force. Good use and skillful employ of mico is rewarded, and it's more than just pressing a units special ability the right time, but also smart use of cover, engaging and disengaging at the right time, correct use line of sight and ranged units, manipulations of counter units, careful resource management, etc.  The are few games that use the retreat mechanic like Company of Heroes 1/2, and well made use of it will have battles ebbing and flowing the whole match.  Any minor skirmish loss can become a game win in the long run, if you play well.  Resource management is also extremely well done, and is played out on the map level, with key resources in constant contention the whole game.  At high levels of play, it's not at all uncommon to have a cheek clenching, nail biting game that can go either way, straight down the last few seconds of play.  Finally, for added measure the different factions are not just the same factions reskinned, but genuinely different, and play differently, offering  large degree of variation in abilities and strategies, and general replayability.  All of what I described above was in Company Hereos 1, Company of Heroes 2 takes all that, and adds to it some small additional features such as visual upgrades, an improved (or different line of sight system), snow/weather effects, and even an additional faction.
…so why is this review negative? The reason is, Sega/Relic added a horribly grinding, rng perk system in Company of Heroes 2 that rewards you with some objectively “more powerful” abilities and/units.  Of course, the grind, which isn’t meant to be done by any normal person through normal play, can be avoided through micro-transactions.  Now, if you buy this game for solo play, or just to skirmish the AI, or co-op and comp stomp with your friends, your money cannot be better spent.  However, if you value PvP, or the on-line competitive scene of an RTS, in my opinion, the micro-transactions make this game a hard pass.  You can’t disable them, so you will never be able to stop some random dude from having some kind of minor advantage over you in what would otherwise be a tight, intense, balanced match. It’s a horrible design, and it just destroys competitive rankings and tournaments.  I used to play very competitively in Company of Heroes 1 on-line and had an exceptionally high rank, and I never once played an on-line game in Company of Heroes 2 for the reason I stated.  Company of Heroes 2 is a great game for solo and co-op play, and as such I’d recommend it to all my friends and I don’t regret my purchase at all, however, because on-line PvP is such a staple of RTS games, I simply can’t recommend it positively given it’s current game design.

Holy moly, Freedom Planet. What a game.
This game holds true in what its reviewers state: it is not in any way a Sonic copy.
Freedom Planet, at its heart a platformer, is probably one of the best if not the best platformers I have ever played. Having played through the game entirely, I can safely say it is my favorite platformer ever, and it goes right in my top 5 favorite games of all time.
The creators of this game really knew what they were doing. The story is so compelling that I found myself impatient through the levels because I wanted to know what happened next. Captivating voicing and absolutely pixel perfect graphics make it that much more amazing to me. To go along with that, the game features probably one of the most amazing soundtracks I've ever heard in a game.
Graphically, it's a throwback to an older generation of games. Having never played a game from the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise (unless anyone at this point counts Sonic the Hedgehog 2006 as a game at all), Freedom Planet did what it could to make me feel that nostalgic connection anyway. Boy did it do that. Galaxy Trail picked a theme that's easy to get wrong: China. WOW is this so GOOD!!! China is prevalent throughout the entirely game, and it is truly beautiful as it stands in this game, visually and culturally. Every color in the game is vibrant and wonderful. Every object pops out in full screen and doesn't bring up the common problem that pixelated games have (when objects that can be interacted with blend into the background). The backgrounds are truly stunning and well put together. This entire game to me is eye candy of the best kind.
Graphics bring me to the art style. The art style. Just the art style alone was what pulled me into the game in the first place. I looked at the title card on the Steam Store and instantly fell in love with it. The characters are so well designed and they move smoothly and amazingly. The art style is the kind of style that makes me beg to see more. It looks GREAT.
Next up, characters. The characters. Galaxy Trail couldn't have gotten this aspect more right. Every character in the game is developed well and are given personalities as they are introduced. This is one of the few games I know of that does this, as opposed to introducing a static character and giving them a personality afterward. The establishment of character so quickly leads to an easier time getting into the story, which I will go over later in the review. The characters all have unique and interesting designs, and the voice actors put a lot of work into their jobs. It really shows that they have, as the characters' dialogue are captivating, with full voice-overs for every bit. I felt truly amazed at how easily I could connect to every character (of course with the exception of the antagonist side of characters).
Music. I don't have to say anymore.
The music is AWESOOOOOOME. It's so well composed, and it fits the overlying theme of the game perfectly. Even through the music, China is prevalent throughout the entire thing. Truly beautiful, and it fits the gameplay and the environment perfectly as well.
Gameplay. It's tight. It's solid. It's responsive. Every death and every victory you have will make you feel fully responsible because of how good they are. This game's control is comparable to Super Meat Boy.
Throughout the game, you have the same set of moves. But while you're playing, it STILL feels like you evolve as the player. I was a fish out of water at the start, and by the end, I knew the characters like the back of my hand. I don't know what else to say, other than that the challenge this games offers is daunting, yet possible, and I mean that in the best way I can (GAME MEANT FOR GAMEPAD).
The story is truly wonderful. Right off the bat, tension is established, and you meet your antagonist, Brevon. This game does well with its immediate establishment of an antagonist. With the accompaniment of a few tertiary characters being introduced, you're immediately presented with the game's protagonists. A dragon(oid)(?) named Sash Lilac and a cat named Carol Tea, later an alien named Torque and later a dog(?) named Milla Basset. All of these unique characters fuel the story so well and progress it in the most sensible way. Freedom Planet presented me with probably the most captivating story of any game I've ever seen. I'm not even going to explain any of it. Anyone reading this who hasn't played the game MUST PLAY IT FOR THE STORY.
Of course, every game has its flaws.
There are a few graphical errors in this game (objects on the wrong side of other objects). As I said, though, there are few, and the truly beautiful environment of the game distracts from any of these errors.
The dialogue is perfect, except for just one little grammatical mistake (the word "I" in the place of the word "It"). Of course, any and all games that HAVE dialogue and subtitles coinciding with each other have at least one grammatical error.
An issue I have is that nothing in terms of gameplay changes at all. The Sonic-style speed is the only thing that can be considered to change, and by that, I mean that often times it is unclear what direction Lilac or Carol are meant to go in. In conjuction with that, there is plenty that impedes the forward motion. Despite that, it isn't too much for me that I'm going to bash the game too much. It isn't too much that bashing is warranted, anyway.
This issue I have is a little bit nit-picky, but I feel it's got to be said. The character you play as normally will stick to the ground, meaning that whatever angle the ground they are standing on is at is the same angle at which the sprite is standing. This particular fact isn't what I dislike, but rather it is the self-righting mechanism in the sprites. After running up a wall or something of the sort, the entire sprite rotates from a central point back to being right-side up. To me, this is unsettling and it breaks the contingency of the character as being believable. A simple way for this issue to be fixed is to implement some sort of movement sequence in the sprite that would take the place of the awkward pivotal rotation.
Another problem I had with this game was that it felt lonely. Most levels are lengthy, meaning a lot of time may be spent in each level (unless you're a speedrunner of sorts or get stuck in spots easily, which happens on occasion). The dialogues constantly reference the fact that the protagonists have conquered a certain aspect of a level together. This is strange, considering the only time any of the characters move and fight WITH the character you control is during a boss battle in the middle of the game. This disappointed me, as I find the Donkey Kong Country-esque character switch to be nice.
My only other problem with Freedom Planet is exposition. Whether or not it was intentional is beyond me. But being a minor issue, I still found myself having troble understanding the beginning of the story until I started a second file and experienced the beginning again.
But overall, this game (in my opinion) is near perfect, and a true work of art. It shows how much work, time, effort, and love went into this game's creation. And having played the whole game from start to end in a single sitting, here's what I feel like:
THIS GAME IS PROBABLY THE BEST GAME I'VE EVER PLAYED IN THE PLATFORMER GENRE!
Never has any game left me wanting more as much as this one. This game is perfect in my eyes, and it leaves me wanting more from it. I hope that the people at Galaxy Trail are working on a sequel to this, because the ending of this game has set itself up perfectly for that. If it already has a sequel, I NEED TO KNOW AS SOON AS POSSIBLE. The game is short, but it's fantastic, nonetheless.
Plus, this is the first game that has ever made me cry because it ended.
This game is a work of art. Worth every cent.
Buy it. Play it. Love it.

Usually I'm the one ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on games for micro transactions, but in this case, I'm here to defend this one. For example Paradox has extremely cancerous micro transactions and expansions for games like CK2 that I've wasted over 100 dollars on with almost no perceivable change in my gaming experience. Unlike almost every game out there, the little expansions for this do radically alter gameplay and give you tens of hours of new content worth playing. They also have completely different visual and audio qualities to them that can change the flavor of the symphony of battle that is this game.
Outside of that, the game is a very solid one. Its story(s) is above average, not particularly memorable, but not cancerous at all, it does its job and gives weight and importance to the campaign battles. The ability to move around the camera is a huge plus, and you will be able to set up some truly awesome visual spectacles for yourself the likes of which you wont find in many other games. Combat is fun and challenging. Online gets into the typical exploitation of mechanics which the nolifer autists will always do in any strategy game, but the AI is competent and fun to play with, very rare. Its attacks are never overly predictable, and you really can achieve victory in more ways than any other game I've so far come across. The factions are truly unique but all reasonably balanced. The visuals and attention to detail are nice, if not the most graphically advanced, but the art of them is hard to top for strategy games (color/design/general look). Best of all the community is extremely active and makes tons of super detailed maps that are usually as good or better than the ones included with the game. Destructability is great too. Overall its a buy people, its 20 bucks.

After playing the previous games, I was expecting this one to be great: and you know what? For the most part, it did. However there's a surprising amount of problems with the game, things that seem way off and should have been fixed by now. As usual I'm gonna start the review with the negative parts, then moving up for the stuff the game does best, so you know what you're getting yourself into.
First and foremost, the glitches. After Returns, Dragonfall and♥♥♥♥♥♥you'd expect this one not to be broken... But I've found a surprisingly amount of bugs. The worst ones no doubt have to be the missions that bug themselves out; things like suddenly facing unlimited enemies but being tasked to kill them all, being told to kill them all but having one enemy stay in an unreachable area, the mission reaching an unbeatable state because you somehow didn't get a mission related item, stuff like that. Because of it I heavily suggest saving often, I somehow ended up getting these in a few missions and that was a pain in my butt.
Something that also seems way off is that in the extra chapter of the game there seems to be many typos and errors in the texts, and in a game where 90% of the story is being told by text then that seems way off. Thankfully it was still easy to see what they meant, though.
Another weird issue are weapon related games. I have NO idea how I did it, but I somehow got weapons that I wasn't supposed to get. For example, the Basic Blaster 2.0, a weapon that's used inside the Matrix. No idea how but I got it on the normal game and it's completely and utterly broken, killing pretty much any enemy in one hit. I also somehow duplicated items that only other characters have, such as Is0bel's deck or Duncan's armor.
I also gotta comment on how... Lame and dissapointing easy is the final boss. Not the one from the extra chapter, the one from the normal game. It was stupidly easy, anti-climactic as hell.
Lastly, I feel like some characters aren't as balanced as others. Is0bel being the main offender here, her grenade launcher is just stupidly broken. It also doesn't help that just like with the previous games, cover feels off. Like, you get flanked from pretty much anything that isn't dead center in really weird ways.
That being said, the game does feel like it fixed some of the other issues on the previous games and I honestly feel like it's the best one so far in the series.
The story is quite good. Think of Star Wars; Knights of the Old Republic but in a slightly modern setting instead, with similar dialogue and♥♥♥♥♥♥ And honestly, it felt more interesting than the previous game. It's well paced and it rarely got boring. My only complain would be that there weren't enough side missions like in previous games.
The characters on this game also feel more interesting, even having their own secret missions and♥♥♥♥♥♥ Only complain I have is that some don't feel as great in combat... But they all can work out. Kinda sad that
The setting? Great! Really liked it, Dragonfall felt like it didn't use much of it but Hong Kong does feel like it's on a damn chinese triad-filled city that's gone to hell.
Surprisingly there's also a few cutscenes in the game, even voice-acted. It would have been better if the game had one or two more, but hey.
Lastly, the extra chapter was surprising, specially since the ending on your normal story does matter into this one and they get more developed. I would totally recommend playing the game a second time just to see more endings.
Would I recommend the game? Yeah! I was honestly expecting it to be worse than Dragonball and it was pleasantly surprised. However I do feel like I should recommend the previous two games as well, you should play them too. On a sale it's a really good purchase, specially if you pick all of them together.
TL;DR Edition: As usual with Shadowrun games, it's a bit buggy... But really good! If you can overlook the glitchy missions and weird errors, you'll find a good game with quite good lenght that's also worth replaying to see more of the stuff on it.

As much as a fan I am of the original two Dark Forces games, something went amiss for me afterwards that began in Outcast that made the game underwhelming that I could not enjoy finishing it whereas I have completed previous games several times. This isn’t a problem of its shoddy beginning or its lacking level design but more so about how the new developers changed the priorities of previous games from the endearing bounty-hunter who became a Jedi into focusing on another game flaunting the abilities of the Jedi and lightsabers.
The improvements made to the overall combat mechanics as well as the cryptically linear level design are only the beginning of changes that led to my dissatisfaction with Outcast as the greatest sin of all is how much the storyline that has deviated away from the canon falls back into the trap of making a Star Wars game that can’t escape the grandeur of its name.
Dark Forces 1, to an extent, was often criticized for being a DOOM-clone; Dark Forces 2 (Jedi Knight) was in a sense a Half Life 1 inspired game that utilized the large-scale environments with old-school FPS design and mechanics. In both of these games, the emphasis on traditional FPS gameplay, resource management and the interchange of bounty-hunter and Jedi abilities were the qualities that made these games unique amongst other Star Wars games as relying on the lightsaber quickly showed how much Katarn was untrained and reliant on his skills as a bounty hunter. Jedi Knight 2: Jedi Outcast (Dark Forces 3), however, abandons the Dark Forces lineage all together by foregoing the importance of the FPS mechanics in order to emphasize the third-person light-saber gameplay and force abilities.
This is why as much as the game wants to be a tech-demo improvement for the series it’s ultimately a step back from the previous games’ greatness. As previous mentioned, the greatest detriment to the series is Outcast’s change to a more cryptically linear design that relies more on an FAQ to progress rather than natural exploration of the labyrinthine DOOM environments of the original or the level-design itself naturally taught the player where to go through visual cues and focused level-design in Dark Forces 2. This change can be easily felt when players are asked in Outcast to shoot a barrel through a window to progress rather than find a switch to unlock or look around the environment for the next place to proceed, or they must pass through a trash compactor rather than find another way around to proceed.
Even when the game allows more open-ended environments than previous games, enemy placements like sharpshooters promote a slower paced game of hiding and sniping or rushing in with the lightsaber to avoid attacks as much as possible. Health, ammo and other items are more stringent than before that promotes more active use of the Force powers than allow players to take some hits. These changes, as well as the general shift in focus into being more of a Jedi than previous, are all contributing factors of how the game aggressively and defensively promotes the player to abandon the blaster in favor of a total Jedi—and even when fighting enemy Jedis they are somehow immune to rockets or explosives whereas they were exploits in the past game.
Perhaps what is somewhat of a more subjective concern is how Jedi Knight: Outcast cannot help but to fall back on its canon for characters like Luke Skywalker and Lando as well as for places familiar to the Star Wars films such as Bespin, Yavin IV, etc. to make up for its lack of identity and originality.
In the two previous games, the canon was used to establish the place and time within the films, and then the stories they told explored mostly new regions, character and conflicts. Dark Forces 1 established this through stealing the death star plans; Dark Forces 2 mentioned Skywalker’s journey, but focused more so on the mystery of the Valley of the Jedi. Contrasting these two examples is Outcast having you wander around Yavin IV with Skywalker at his academy to relearn the Force as well as teaming up with him at the end to fight against the Sith, and the situation with Lando is similarly reliant on fan-serve rather than focusing on the story of Katarn.
As a result of this shift in focus, Katarn’s story is put towards the side when the previous games focused entirely on his personality and his conflicts, and in Jedi Knight: Outcast they retread the previous story of Katarn walking the line between a Jedi and Sith that he already had faced once before when he became corrupted to the Dark Side and gave the Force up. Had the story delved more into this one interesting angle for Katarn perhaps the story could have been redeemable, yet instead it falls prey to the alluring trap of the Star Wars brand name itself.
None of these complains are to suggest that the game itself isn’t without its merits or its fanbase for good reasons, but I think there are valid reasons as a fan of the prior games to look upon this game as a squandered opportunity that gives up too much of what makes the series unique in order to please the more wider audience of Star Wars fans who dream only of the Jedi. This is perhaps the result of the change in developers from LucasArts to Raven Software who fell victim to the desire to emulate what they loved about their favorite series rather to create something new.
In perhaps the only time an instance of Star Trek and Star Wars can coexist in the same sentence, the greatness of the original episodes of Star Trek were the episodes written not by the diehard writers but the writers with little to no infatuation for the series in order to create new experiences that were beloved because they explored the unknown beyond the audience’s expectations.

This game is simply not enjoyable. A lot of stuff that is just plain awful gamedesign-wise.
+ the music is fantastic, even though its basically the same melody throughout
+ artwork looks good, Im not a fan really, but it still has its charm to it
- absolutely nothing is explained in the game and there is no text ingame, normally this wouldnt be that bad, but the game has some more complex mechanics that actually needed explaining
- altough the levels are randomly generated, they feel the same, there isnt much variation to it and you will start to see the same rooms in just a couple of minutes
- the game has clicker elements, meaning that when standing idle you get points, you can increase these points by shooting(clicking), these points are currency for the shops to buy power-ups, so basically you have an infinite amount of money, but have to click like mad......not very fun and the grind is tedious as can be
- you can find chests on your way, but everytime you open up a chest it takes away health from you....it just drags out the game by a lot as the only way to regenerate health is to kill enemies (which only gets you back a very very small amount of health) or to jump out of a dungeon window, bringing you to the starting point (at full health), where you can go back in and generate a new dungeon.....this is abnormally tedious and not fun at all, as you have to do this several times in one run
- power ups come in form of cards and only boost stats, like crit or damage up. You can at any point burn up those cards to regain health, its just so unneccessary that you loose health to begin with when collecting these cards from chests.....meaning once you collected a couple of cards you need to restart the dungeon
- your character starts headless, you can collect a head which acts like a power up, that grants you a special ability.....the huge problem is all I got so far, were absolutely useless. Like blinking one step(!) ahead, it doesnt benefit you in any way. Same with the double jump, it never comes to good use and in the challenge rooms, where you could actually use your ability, you are prohibited from using it or else you dont get the chest at the end of the challenge room.....
- you can find weapons but they run out of ammo and you cant find any ammo in the dungeon, meaning you will only use these cool weapons on the boss
- the controls arent as good as they should be, you cant shoot upwards (only when doing a slide, which is awkward to pull off) but a lot of times enemies come from above and you are pretty much screwed, even more so when the space is tight and you cant slide
- when going through a door you start at the next room/screen behind the door still and have to press "right/D" no matter which direction you actualy wanna go you always have to press right to come out of the door, as minor as this sounds, its really annoying
- the controller button mapping is not good, you have to constantly press RB to shoot, which is the weakest, most easily to break button on the controller and since this has clicker elements (clicking fast and like mad), you are going to wear out your controller super fast
- there are no options whatsoever, no windowed screen, no keymapping, no resolution
- this game tries way too hard to be deep and edgy, sort of how Binding of Isaac has more to the gameplay mechanics as you would think at first (secret rooms, item combinations, transformations), but BoI was fun and not hard to figure stuff out, where here you have no clue whatsoever and no motivation to try further, as the grind and gameplay is so unbearable
- there are a couple of situations where I absolutely couldnt avoid being hit, like a jump across a hole, that has spikes on the edges, but I had to jump over there to advance in the dungeon.....not even the stupid blink got me over without a hit
- when leaving the game, you get into this weird stage where you are a dude, that just stands up from his computer (like he was the one that just played the game) and is in his room. You can control that guy and then click on certain stuff to make him have a look at it, like the treadmill that generates the clicker points for you. Its kinda neat and completely unneccessary at the same time, even leaving the game gets annoying as its way too long to actually do so

If you grew up on Star Wars, be it in the original or prequel era, it was probably your dream to somehow adventure across the galaxy as a Jedi. Before game tech allowed it, this dream was mostly reserved for pen-and-paper RPGs, books, and multimedia. When LucasArts decided to create a game about being a Jedi Knight, it was one of my personal favorite decisions they've made. The original Dark Forces took Doom's successful shooter formula and made a Star Wars adventure with the same kind of thrill. The sequel, the first in the Jedi Knight series, was the first in which a lightsaber was introduced. After one expansion for that game, they returned with Jedi Knight II - Jedi Outcast.
My childhood was practically built on this series, but this was the game that truly made me a fan for life of the entire series, as well as the whole Star Wars franchise. If you wanted to give this game a name based upon the films, this could have been called "Return of Kyle Katarn", as Kyle has left the Jedi Order to resume mercenary work for the New Republic. Half-way through the game, a certain event transpires that drives Kyle to desiring revenge: something Jedi are forbidden to aspire toward. He rejoins the Order initially to gain that revenge but eventually realizes that revenge only killed him more than what had happened.
Graphically, this game still can hold up to some of the more modern games to a certain extent. Some of the engine tech was pretty advanced for the time, and it is a very immersive atmosphere. They did a wonderful job at capturing the Star Wars spirit as well as giving us interesting areas to explore and play through. The only complaint I have with this game comes from the environment design: they designed it to be less linear in an attempt to force (pun semi-intended) the player to explore their way through the game. While this was a good idea, the lack of direction often makes the player scratch their heads in defeat as they wander the same paths over and over again.
The sound design is great as well, with a fully-voiced cast of characters, original John Williams pieces, and perfect sound effects. Interesting fact for those who watch the new show, Star Wars: Rebels - the voice actress who portrays Hera Syndulla portrayed Kyle's copilot and love interest, Jan Ors. The voice actor who voices Kyle gives both a gruff and sarcastic mercenary bad-to-the-bone feel without making you feel like the character is a jerk, and the voice actors who portray classic movie characters (such as Luke) all do a good job at mimicking the sound of the original actors.
As for the gameplay itself, they refined almost every element of what made the first JK game amazing, but the most obvious refinement is the lightsaber combat and powers like force jump. In the original JK game, there was one lightsaber style that you could use, and force jump was an entirely different feature from the standard jump. In this game, there are three -- light, medium, heavy -- and force jump is intertwined into standard jump. Lightsaber combat flows very well and allows you to piece together different styles to create borderline cinematic duels against other lightsaber-wielding opponents.
In general, while this is my least favorite in the JK series, that does not mean that it is a bad game. Not in the least. It is STILL one of the best games ever designed, and is worth every penny.

Simcity 4 was, and still is, the best city-planning simulator.
It have very deep game mechanics, which ensure the city simulation is dynamic. It is nearly impossible to just "pan out"more zones without many different issues. Most of these issues will have  affect on the population, and this would cause other issues, etc. All the city planning simulators came after it failed to reach its level in terms of complexity. And it is friendly toward beginners. ( Hint: After go wild building for a while, you may want to go back to check the tutorials.)
Its graphic is outdated.The game engine is not very effective. (One of the devs explained that is because the game was built before DirectX 9) The camera is fixed. Look at the screenshots and determine yourself.
The game is "moddable". The UI and the engine can not be edited. But all the data and the models are. This results in a great collection of building (and other thing on ground) mods. Most of them requires manual install, and sometimes need additional dependency. They can be found on Simtropolis or
.
The most important mod for Simcity 4 is Network Addon Mod, or NAM. It is a great improvement, if not overhaul, of traffic system. I recommend anyone who plan spending more than 10 hours on this game to install it. Due to engine restrictions, build a tram-in-avenue/tram-on-road interchange or underground tunnel is more complex than it should. But at least you can do it, with patience and time.

"On Exactitude in Sim City," ... "In that game, the art of mapping attained such perfection that the map of a single city occupied the entirety of a zone, and the map of the region, the entirety of a city. In time, those unconscionable maps no longer satisfied, and the modding community struck a map of a region whose size was that of the region, and which coincided point for point with it. The following gaming generation, who were not so fond of the study of mapping as their forebears had been, saw that that vast map was useless, and not without some pitilessness was it, that they delivered it up to the inclemencies of incompatible versions. In the abandoned websites, still today, there are corrupted files of that map, inhabited by broken links and bugs; in all the Internet there is no other relic of the disciplines of geography." - Suárez Miranda, Viajes de jugadores prudentes, Libro IV,Cap. Tokyo Xanadu eX+ is a proper Action RPG from Nihon Falcom and is a welcome addition to the PC roster of JRPGs. So far, this is perhaps the only JRPG with a modern urban fantasy setting in the PC market and that makes it unique to some extent
.
First off, yes, the game borrows heavily from Persona in terms of some settings but the similarities end about halfway into the first chapter. The biggest change being that the protagonist here has a well-defined personality and is not a blank slate unlike in the Persona games. Other obvious differences include the action combat, the way the bonding events take place and of course, the packaging of the game. The game also goes the extra mile of fleshing out the NPCs, on whom you can collect trivia which will flesh out their characters throughout the entire length of the game.
The packaging is the best part of this game, as every chapter is its own self-contained story arc which has one of the playbable characters as the focus but also advances the overarching plot. Every chapter has its prologue and an epilogue which is followed up immediately by an interlude like Side Story. These Side Stories are short episodes featuring the characters other than the main playable character which give a definitive end to their individual story arcs. These also set up the
as well as flesh out the characters as individuals. However, the main plot develops these same characters as a collective. Every chapter also has an opening theme, making the chapters feel like episodes of an anime (which was a major appeal to me, I admit) and is a signature of other Falcom games as well.
The plot and setting are quite intriguing, placing the players in a world fraught with mystery and intrigue filled with esoteric organizations springing around an unexplained phenomenon called "The Eclipse". The main characters decide to unravel the mystery after they are inadvertently drawn into a series of incidents which may have connections to an event
that happened 10 years ago in the game's timeline. The lore is rich and the enemy designs are pretty good.
The game is fairly long and like me, if you take time playing the various mini-games (there are a LOT and some even have great prizes like master cores and helpful elements) and farming materials for upgrades and equipment, it will take quite a bit of time. The eX+ in the title isn't just for show either as the game has a very pronounced post-game content along with a new game+ mode that has extra dungeons not found in the first playthrough. The music and the three songs featured in the game are good.
Finally, the localization might be spotty at places but it is still enjoyable and some of the translations have quite the comedic value (both intentional and unintentional, Aksys employees love the Cthulhu mythos and World of Darkness). Other miscellaneous additions include the boss rush mode where you can replay the boss battles in the game. The Gallery and Character Viewer are also fun additions.
Overall, for the asking price Tokyo Xanadu eX+ is engaging and enjoyable. This is the true definitive edition of Tokyo Xanadu and comes with all associated bells and whistles so the DLCs (which are atrociously priced) can be igonred without issue. That's about it, I guess. Hopefully, we get a sequel for this sometime soon.

Tokyo Xanadu eX+ is a Action RPG by Nihon Falcom, best known for the Legend of Heroes series and the Ys Series, that is certainly not their best work and has its fair share of flaws however in the it it still manages to be a good game that is fun to play.
The gameplay can be described as Ys with (I have not played Ys 8 yet so this based on the old series that are on Steam) extra resources to spend in battle along with the inventory system of Legend of Heroes.
This does cause that the game can feel quite easy at times, I was playing on hard, since the only limit on items is the 99 cap and a cooldown on certain difficulties.
It also has an orbment system alike to the Legend of Heroes series, mostly to the Cold Steel entries although with the names altered. Also has cooking and several mini-games inside the game. The Dungeons are very basic most of them are just simple "go down this corridor, kill some mobs and then get to the boss" with sometimes "oh yeah press these buttons on the way" so there isn't much to write about this. What is fun is how the game plays and the feeling of going fast and killing a lot of enemies.
Story wise, The story is not bad but it does suffer from an abundance of generic anime cliches that make the story quite predictable in places, the characters are the strong point of the narrative though that is a pattern with some of Falcom's games. But at least in my opinion it does things worse than those games. Also might get a bit formulaic at times.
However, and while this is a Falcom standard, what I really do appreciate is the huge amount of NPC flavor text and whilst the quests that the game has are quite few compared to other RPG's with open world elements, the quests that are there are interesting since they often times offer a mini-story that affects things in the world and even has effects for longer then just right after doing the quest.
Graphically it is pretty standard, nothing to write home about I personally enjoy this style and I wouldn't mind if the graphical levels didn't change. The options for this game are rather lackluster compared to other Falcom games but this is a port by a company that doesn't really do PC ports that often and whilst barebones it does run solid at 1080p60fps on my machine.
The soundtrack is pretty good but that is to be expected from Falcom since they just have a way with soundtracks.
Aksys Games translated this game and whilst I did notice some irregularities(and I generally don't pay attention to those) on the surface level it seems like they translated it just fine(though serious from "this is our final stage lets do this or something" to "this is it" is a bit.... lackluster I suppose?).
- Should you buy this game?
The amount of content that this game has to offer is good for current price point but that only applies if you like it.
Right now I'd say it is a hard sell if you aren't a fan of Nihon Falcom or if you haven't played most of the flagship titles by Falcom that are on Steam(Trails in the Sky, Cold Steel and Ys series).
However if you are a fan of the games they have made, then I'd say the game currently is worth it at the price. Even more if you buy via humble bundle if you have a monthly subscription.
Otherwise, I'd say buy the flagship titles of Nihon before this one because they excel at certain points where this game is good to great at those points.

Up front I will say that I have never been a fan of Sonic. I never disliked the games, but none of them ever grabbed me. After having played through the entirety of Sonic Generations, I will say that hands down THIS is the best Sonic game. Taking levels from all of Sonic's history and offering two seperate versions of the levels (classic mode, which plays like the genesis games, and modern mode which plays like the daytime stages of Sonic Unleashed or Sonic Colors), as well as providing many challenges for each of the levels. The gameplay for both modern and classic modes feel great, and aside from a few very minor issues, this is an incredibly enjoyable game, if a little bit easy to get S rank on the times.
Definitely would recommend, but perhaps not at full price. The game took me about 8-9 hours to complete including all challenges, so it's not incredibly long. If you have been growing tiresome of the continuous flops that Sonic Team has been shooting out over the past decade, Sonic Generations will serve as a blunt reminder that the Blue-Blur still has some life left in him.
Sonic Generations is a monumental tribute to fans; boasting large and beautiful recreations of iconic stages from past games. (FYI, said games are Sonic the Hedgehog, Sonic the Hedgehog 2, Sonic & Knuckles, Sonic Adventure, Sonic Adventure 2, Sonic Heroes, Sonic 2006, Sonic Unleashed, and Sonic Colors). The nostalgia will be strong with this one; but make no mistake, the actual game here is genuinely good. You alternate between both modern and classic versions of Sonic throughout the course of the game; each level featuring both a classic and modern section.
Classic Sonic plays as you might expect.  Entirely 2-D platforming and the lack of a boost successfully replicate the formula that made classic Sonic the Hedgehog installments so great.
Modern Sonic plunges you into EXTREMELY fast-paced mayhem that made it's debut in the form of daytime stages in Sonic: Unleashed.  Quick reaction time is needed to take full advantage of numerous shortcuts that riddle the maps.
Also, the mod community has actually managed to find ways of adding new content to Sonic Generations on PC. As a matter of fact, there is a mod out now that allows you to play nearly all of the levels from Sonic Unleashed, despite the fact that it is a console exclusive.
Overall, I recommend this game with complete confidence that most will enjoy it.  If you have been discouraged at all by recent attempts to reignite the gaming icon that is Sonic, you NEED to restore your faith right now by playing this game.  In all honesty, the story IS slapped on and completely laughable, but it's refined gameplay and undoubtedly nostalgic nature makes Sonic Generations a crowning achievement for Sonic Team.

I will get to the point - your character's backstory in Shadowrun: Hong Kong is somewhat more restricting than the other usual Roleplaying Games.  You were a street kid from Seattle, and now you have followed the man that has adopted you to Hong Kong, where the folks are friendly and the shadows are welcoming.
However, if you don't mind the limiting factors to your character's backstory, Shadowrun: Hong Kong will give you one hack of a story. That is not to say that the story is linear. As common of good well-written RPGs, your choices and what you say and do matters in the game, and it is highly recommended that you take your time exploring around the game thoroughly.
The combat itself is very reminiscent of X-COM: Enemy Unknown, with a myriad of magical spells and techno buffs here and there.  Nevertheless, Shadowrun: Hong Kong, at least in the vanilla play through, will not give you a large amount of combat if you invest in non-combat traits like Charisma.
While I wish to tell you how well I enjoyed the story, I do not wish to spoil. Just note that you are going into the universe of Shadowrun: Hong Kong - and that you should probably spend no time in getting familiar with the culture and the people of this dystonia, corporate-run, always-raining city of Hong Kong.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong fixes a lot of the mechanical mistakes of its predecessor, Shadowrun: Dragonfall, and includes a lot of brand new content and polish to further differentiate itself. The matrix levels are well designed and function a whole lot better, the combat has seen some improvements, and the party/item interface was completely redone, and the missions are generally better structured. All for the greater good, I think. There's also Qi, a new adept system that I think is fantastic (from a mechanical perspective), and it also ties in well with the events of the game.
The only downside is that the main story doesn't feel quite as thrilling as the original; it's got a lot of twists and turns, and the final conflict feels appropriately epic, but it doesn't have that sense of urgency as Dragonfall. The Walled City is only a small part of the Shadowrun world versus the events that happen at the end of Dragonfall—should you choose to join with the antagonist, even more so. On the flip side, the companions in Hong Kong feel stronger, more thematically tied into the fate of the events taking place. The two optional companions are especially noteworthy, and the game is overall better for including them.
Also worth noting is that there is an epilogue story that takes place after the main campaign. It isn't terribly long, but it does tie up the loose ends left hanging. The missions in it are also pretty neat, some having several solutions, and are generally fun to play through. If you liked Dragonfall, definitely play Hong Kong.
