Small review from Yellow Lotus member :)
Music
Big improvement since Dragonfall. Great samples and tunes make the atmoshpere thick but at the same time fresh. Added oriental vibes to battlemusic from Dragonfall hits the spot. I am blasting the OST on loop!
Graphics
Not much improvement since Dragonfall. One thing I didn't like is how they changed the appearance of some races.
Orks look like elves with tusks, Trolls look like Orks from Dragonfall. I liked more the old look where Orks looked like steroids was their everyday breakfast. Trolls looked like hulking anabolic beasts. Now they are all 'smoothier'. If this was made on purpouse like making them more slim and more 'asian' then the change is welcome.
Mechanics
As previous games, battles are smooth, readable, and not boring. I like how they added cyberweapons. My character was a Troll using only Spurs Cyberweapon. Playing like that on Hard was easy as day - unfortunately. At least there were encounters where more than 8 guys attacked at the same time so then I was able to show all my skills. At the begining I had to watch out for receiving damage, but later when I put some armor, Killing machine was my second name. Spurs + Barrage = Bloodbath. Never used the Whip, because I was only going for Strenght, Body and Close Combat. Later some points in Charisma came in handy. There is one new weapon since Dragonfall - something like rocket launcher. I used it only once - Qiu used it. It was devastating. When enemies have that even my Onslaught Tank of character had to watch out. One critical hit I received was for 65 dmg :D
NPC
Racter was awesome. His story was interesting though. Same with Gaichu. Rest of the guys I tried to ignore, but as I was playing through, I had to read all of the lines. The most interesting to me was Racter as stated above. He seemed like JC Denton from Deus Ex hellbent on destruction. My kind of guy! Gaichu was a Japanese spice to this game. His loyalty mission was the most interesting.
Plot
The dialogues are long in this game, longer than Dragonfall. The main story was good but not as interesting as Dragonfall, but the side quests.. DAMN those were awesome! I was sitting on the edge of the seat at few times. Main story events tend to slow down if you focus more on the side quests.
When I play RPG games I look at the "whole" of it. If side quests are better than plot but you still feel that all of this is connected in some way then I have no problem with that.
Setting
To me Hong Kong is a lot more interesting than Dragonfall. First of all - I hate german words - this made me gaze only at the words in Dragonfall instead of reading them. Second of all - Berlin was boring (the hub location for example). In Hong Kong Heoi looks a lot more interesting to me. The colors, the rain, the water, boats and neons. All of this gave me more Blade Runner/Deus Ex feeling than Berlin did. Third of all - I always liked the idea of crime boss who is a chinese lady - this one here is exactly what I wanted.
Shadowrun Hong Kong is a basically a dish made in a Wok. Inside you get Shadowrun Dragonfall mixed with spicy oriental sauce sprinkled with spices which contain awesomeness.
If you like Dragonfall and Asian vibes - this game is for you.
If you want to play a really interesting RPG with cool story and awesome side quests - this one is for you as well.
If you don't want to read then don't buy this game.
TL;DR: this game is awesome, better than Dragonfall. Buy it!

This game brings out 2 emotions for me: Happiness and sadness.
Freedom Planet originally started development as a Sonic The Hedgehog fan title but over time it evolved into its own standalone title.
Visuals:
Vibrant and smooth. In todays gaming world of brown and gray it is nice to see a title that is awash with primary colours. Stages each have their own distinct theme and the colour choices fit them perfectly. The only thing I can liken it too is Dynamite Headdy or Ristar The Shooting Star on the Sega Megadrive (Genesis). If those games appealed to you and you like speed then this is the game for you.
Sound:
I only have, at the time of this review, 1.5 hours  on record so its not really enough time to judge accurately. However,  from what Ive heard so far it is great. Voice acting is a bit hit-and-miss at times but for a fan game its good. Each stage music fits the stage perfectly and has a very Saturn-esque vibe going on with both a mix of synth and CD-quality audio.
Story:
Again, as above, Im not far into the game but it is quite a light-hearted story with some occasional dark moments.
Gameplay:
The most important aspect and it delivers in spades. You take the role of 3 characters Lilac (dragon), Carol (cat, I think) and another I forgot the name of. Each have their own powerups and abilities to help navigate the expansive levels. Despite being heavily influenced by Sonic you dont have the standard "collectible items that stop you dying in 1 hit" mechanic here. There are blue gems to collect with 200 netting you an extra life. You do however have a life bar which is replenished by collecting red leaf looking items. Above your health is what amounts to a mana bar that powers your secondary attacks. This refills over time and moves cannot be performed until it is refilled.
Perhaps the hardest thing to get to grips with is enemy behaviour. In most 2D sidescrollers simply touching an enemy results in a hit. Not here, the enemy has to be in an attack animation. Although a good idea in theory, it can make enemy hitboxes seem a bit....off :/
Final Thoughts:
An underrated gem that fans of classic Sonic and classic platformers will enjoy. Story, from what Ive read, is a good 5-6 hours long. Characters are well fleshed out and the music is brilliant

Many people are not into turn-based combat and I happen to be one of those, so I'll address that really quick: LISA does it best not to feel slow in combat by giving you combo abilities and very few to no random encounters at all. There is no need to farm, the game pace is suited to be possible without it. No complicated skill trees, just some equipment you can find and buy for the ingame currency "mags" (yes, magazines; yes, that kind of magazines). Also, you rarely fight the same enemy twice, so it doesn't get boring.
I hope that helped you decide; I sure as hell recommend it! If you like it and want to know more about the story, check out the DLC, it's pretty good as well :)
Oh, one last thing. Don't you dare walk into this game without hair, or it might be your last mistake.

When Sonic The Hedgehog came out, it was followed by a series of micking games that tried to capitalize on it's popularity. Games like Bubs the Bobcat and Aero the Acrobat were, for all intents and purposes, replicas of Sonic right down to the title of the game. Some were good and some were fairly derivative. Freedom Planet, much like those games, recaptures what we loved about the Sonic 2D platformers of the Genesis age, but it lies in the first category. With multiple characters to choose from, individual gameplay styles, fantastic production values, and an interesting story, Freedom Planet is a fun platformer that feels like a true homage to the Sonic series. If you were a Sonic fan, Freedom Planet is most definitely a must buy.

Were you a Sega Genesis fan back in the day? Then this isthe a must buy. Were you not a Genesis fan? Then this game is still really good.
Freedom Planet is a platform similar to Sonic the Hedgehog. Similar is the key word here. Do not goin expecting this to be exactly like Sonic. There are plenty of differences. While the speed based gameplay is there, it borrows elements from many other Genesis titles as well including Rocket Knight Adventures, Gunstar Heroes, and Vectorman.
There are three playable characters and they all play differently from one another to balance them out. Some levels and bosses are harder with some characters and some are easier. Try all three to figure out which you like best.
The game has three modes; Adventure, Classic, and a trial mode. Adventure is the story mode andpersonally this is the game's greatest weakness. The story is not bad, but not good either. It is very uninteresting. There are plenty of cringe-worthy moments as well as a few engaging moments but for themost part it is very hard to get invested into it. It is worth playing through once with each of the two characters available in the mode just to see, but unless you really want those achievements, it is best to leave this mode once you have done that.
Classic mode is much more similar to a classic platformer. In this mode you play through the levels without the story in between. The gameplay is very good and responsive, thus his is the way to play the game once you have seen the story. You have access to all three characters here, which offers even more playability.
Time trials are as the title would say. Beat the levels presented as fast as possible. The most notable thing about this mode is that you do not just play through all of the levels from Adventure and Classic mode. There are other trials unique to this mode which is a nice addition and gives this mode a purpose aside from being Classic mode with a time challenge.
The visuals in this game are just amazing. The artstyle is very reminiscent of games like Sonic CD and Ristar. This is the right way to do retro graphics. They aren't Atari 2600 graphics put through filter; they're real 16 bit graphics. Some may be put off by the character designs, but this is only noticeable in Adventure mode. It becomes a non-issue in the other modes since there isn't any attachment to the characters. You just play the game. The music and sound effects are very well done as well. I can definitely hear Sonic CD style music in there, but I get hints of Streets of Rage and Gunstar Heroes all the time. It's good enough to be memorable. I still have themain theme stuck in my head.
On a side-note, I have heard this game was originally a Sonic fan project and just looking at the characters in the story a lot of them could easily be replaced by Sonic characters from the SATAM series. This is not a knock on the game nor is it praising it. It is just an observation and makes me wonder what could have been.
Seriously, this is a game for Sega Genesis fans and platformer fans alike. The gameplay blends Sonic the Hedgehog and Rocket Knight Adventures, the boss fights are reminiscent of Gunstar Heroes and Vectorman, the level themes have similariies to Sonic, Ristar, and Shinobi, and a great soundtrack that reminds of Sonic CD, Streets of Rage, and Gunstar Heroes. The story is this game's biggest downfall but is just a small portion. If you write this game off as furry trash, you are not only closed minded but missing out on a really great game. This game is easily a 9/10 with an uninteresting story dragging the score down just slightly.

I got a ton of Star Wars related games at the Winter Steam Sale, and oh boy I was glad this one was one of them. Now, I'll do my best so my love for this game doesn't hide it's problems, and I will start right off with them, as usual:
The biggest problem this game has, is that it was NOT build for computers of this generation. The resolution is not the only problem you'll have to face, but there are also glitches, such as strange shadows and even (at least on my case), strange brightness errors, as I everthing was strangely bright and I had to lower it, making me see it right, but all screenshots show the game to be really dark. If you want to play the game, have patience and look for guides arround the Internet on how to get over these problems.
The second problem it has, and really the only other I have, are the difficulty spikes. There are areas of the game that don't f#ck arround. Take Nar Shadda (did I type that right?) as an example, a huge map FILLED WITH SNIPERS, which can easily 1-Hit kill you with barely any time to react... And yet you're supposed to do all kinds of platforming arround it, on which missing a platform will kill you. There are other examples, such as your first encounter with the shadow sith jedi guys, which are WAY MORE POWERFUL AND TOUGH than any other Reborn you've faced so far (even more than the boss before that), and you're supposed to take on two at the same time. Even with all of your powers later on, just one of these guys might get tricky, just get the idea. The game ain't a walk in the park, and you should expect it to be a tough journey.
However, is the game good if we look away from those two problems? You bet your motherf#cking♥♥♥♥♥ The game is a sequel on the Jedi Knight series of games, and follows up Kyle Katarn's adventures, but it ain't really needed that you play the previous games to understand it. However, you might need a bit of knowledge about Star Wars to understand most of it. It starts as a classic FPS with tons of enemies, no regenerative health, armor (or shields, in this case), and a ton of enemies who are pathetic and weak in comparison with you. However, the game changes itself mid-way, as soon enough you have a light-saber and can use the power of the force, AND THAT'S WHEN THE GAME TRULY GOES FROM GOOD TO F#CKING GREAT. Light-saber combat on this game is insanely fun to pull-off, specially against other Light-saber users.
The force also feels natural on the game, neither being useless or broken: just like in the movies, it's a tool. You can push stuff, pull stuff, slow-down the game, mind-trick people like old Ben Kenobi did on the movies, a ton of cool stuff. There are a lot of powers in the game, and you unlock them as you go through it. Some enemies also use them, and eventually you'll find a use to most of them on your play-style.
The story and the characters also feel great. I won't spoil much more (I did spoil that you get a light-saber, BUT COME ON, KYLE HAS IT ON NEARLY ALL THE ADDS OF THE GAME ANYWAY!), but the only thing I didn't like about them is that Lando doesn't appear nearly enough, and characters such as Han Solo would have also been great. Oh, and the game goes after Episode VI and before the new one.
The multiplayer was fun, also. And I say "was" and not "is", as I doubt there are many servers, anymore. If you want the game for the multiplayer, look for Jedi Academy instead, it's sequel. But if you want a really GOOD and solid singleplayer experience, look no further. This game on a sale is quite the steal, and if you like Star Wars, you're garanteed to like it. And if you don't... Well, refund the game, seek medical attention.

At this point, SimCity 4 Deluxe is a creaky classic, and no longer an indispensable one. If you're considering a citysim game you should weigh this alongside its predecessor SimCity 3000 and its figurative successor Cities: Skylines. If you already love the game, it's probably worth a Steam purchase if you haven't already. If you're still undecided, read on.
SimCity 4 was and still is commonly regarded as the pinnacle of its series by citysim enthusiasts. With the release of Cities: Skylines however, many of those same enthusiasts have seen that game as the new king of the genre. After a decade and change, it seems SC4's life as the premier citybuilder is coming to an end, and Skylines' is just beginning.
Mind you, SC4 still delivers a great citybuilding experience. Whether you should actually
it depends on your affinity for the SimCity series, your attitude towards its complexity and your appetite for tinkering with the game to get it working.
SC4 is unquestionably the deepest, richest SimCity game, but for some people it can probably get too complicated. It was released in 2003, and it doesn't play nice with newer computers. Custom mods truly bring the game to life, but each one has to be manually downloaded and configured.
This can become annoying if not downright anal when you take into account the multiple separate dependency files that contain textures, items and other things that most mods use; a holdover from the waning days of dial-up...that morphed into creator pride which refused to allow the distribution of files with the mods that
. Also, if you don't organize your plugins folder, hunting down trouble with your plugins can be a nightmare.
If none of that sounds appealing? SimCity 3000 is older, but it's
and delivers the series' best balance of accessibility and challenge. Meanwhile, Cities: Skylines is easier to run, has Workshop support for mods and takes inspiration from SC4 while improving on it in certain aspects. With the release of additional expansion packs, patches and Workshop mods, its depth may come to rival and even surpass SC4's, all while still maintaining a little more accessibility. Skylines is new too, so if you're deciding between SC4 and Skylines, the latter will probably give you more value.
I suppose SimCity 4's primary draws at this point are its pedigree and its region play. If you already know you don't like SC4's region play on the other hand then I guess it won't matter to you. For genre and series enthusiasts, it can at least be interesting seeing how SC4 remained a dominant game for so long.
Cities: Skylines gives you the option of purchasing more land to make into new districts, and the amount of land can be increased with mods. SC4 though gives you entire geographical regions of varying sizes to build multiple interconnected cities on, not to mention the capacity to download others' or make your own.
Region play is fascinating and very in-depth, which enhances the depth of the actual citybuilding. Unfortunately, there's no option to build a singular city by itself like in Skylines or previous SimCity titles, and you pretty much need to start other cities to have them grow past a certain point.
SC4 also has over a decade's worth of custom content from its dedicated community, some of which is truly excellent & high-quality and extends the game considerably. Having a lot of mods however makes the game slower and sometimes more prone to errors, and you still need to manually download and place them in your plugins folder, so strategic downloading is advised.
If you're into it enough, it's worth it to go to the
and download everything there so you don't have to hunt for them when you download a mod. Even that list was last updated in 2008 though, so you still need to cross-reference dependencies for what you download. Since Skylines is easier to mod for and download mods for, that game will catch up eventually anyway, so this isn't as big of an advantage.
If you're gonna play this game, here's a couple things you should keep in mind.
As mentioned above, the game's over a decade old and can be finicky on newer machines. The game still chugs when running large cities. To optimize the game, I recommend the tips in
.
You ABSOLUTELY NEED a couple of mods to make SimCity 4 playable. The Network Addon Mod in particular unscrews the traffic algorithms so your transit network doesn't degenerate into a kafkaesque nightmare. There's a couple other quality-of-life fixes floating around that aren't as important, but still go a long way towards making the game more playable.
Patience is a virtue, and saving is important despite whatever the tryhard idiots on /v/ will tell you. SimCity 4 will remind you of both whenever it crashes, which is always more often than you'd like.

The classic and original Sim game - as good as it gets minus performance issues. SimCity 4 offers great replayability and complexity, with an insane amount of player-created content available on the internet. The learning curve is less than linear, with basic city building as easy as it has ever been, but end-game being at least as complicated as it has ever been (GameFAQs has some good write-ups to help newbies). The only notable drawback (other than tame gameplay, but hey, it's a SIM!) is how poorly SimCity performs on budget and entry-level PCs. Just lower the default settings to the lowest and slowly crank them up and you won't have a problem.

Tokyo Xanadu is fantastic. I waited almost 2 years for it to get localized and it did not disappoint me in the slightest. The PC port is really well optimized. The game is similar to persona in regard that you spend 70% of the game talking, watching cutscenes, doing side-quests in the city or playing a mini-game and 30% in combat or dungeon exploration. The story is somewhat predictable. Not saying it's bad It's just that it lacks any plot twist until the final chapter. It has great character development. Final Score: 9/10 If you wanna scratch that Falcom itch or just wanna play a good dialogue heavy action RPG. Get this game It's awesome.

The below review is taken from my original post at
There are some ‘sort of’ spoilers up ahead. Some people may wish to go into this game completely blind and work out the mystery of the game mechanics for themselves but in order to review the game, I’ll have to explain how the game works.
If you are in this category and just want to know if it’s any good without knowing anything further, then yes, it is. It’s completely awesome. Now stop reading and go and buy it.
When I received the game to review, I installed Nongunz to try out for a few minutes, check if it ran on my PC, get a feel for the genre etc. before then setting an evening aside later in the week to delve into it properly….four hours later I was still playing it.
It’s good, it’s REALLY good.
First, the bones of the game. Nongunz is a side-scrolling action/platform game with a muted visual palette and heavy gothic overtones. As mentioned above, I do suggest diving into the game without any prior knowledge to get the full effect. The game’s basic mechanics are briefly explained via stained-glass windows (obviously) and then you are off on your own.
You play as a silent protagonist who starts with a pistol, each time you fire your gun, a counter at the bottom goes up by one point. Initially, I thought (due to the games’ title) that I was meant to go through Nongunz firing as few bullets as possible. I was VERY wrong. It turns out that this counter needs to go up, up, up. Leaving the underground section and emerging into the game ‘hub’ (a massive graveyard, but what else would you expect from a game which counts Ingmar Bergman’s ‘The Seventh Seal’ as an influence?) you walk around and discover a few initial points of interest. A crypt which contains four coffins (more on these later) and a sarcophagus (more on this later), a huge altar filled with animal skulls and weapons (more on this later) and some underground walled-off areas (you guessed it…) finally, off to the far-right, there’s Theresa May an enormous, towering cathedral, not ominous at all.
Upon entering the cathedral, the top-right of the screen shows the layout as well as the location of the boss, item-store and occasionally a room with a new gun or skull in it. You traverse the rooms but locating doors which move you to corresponding areas. The rooms are randomly generated and filled with grotesque monsters, dismembered fingers leaving an acidic blood trail, mounds of flesh and eyes that drag themselves across the floor and strange pig-beasts are but a small selection of them. The cleverness in the game comes from, among other things, the balance of risk and reward. You can find chests in the game, but it costs a portion of health to open them. You can try and get to the boss, but if you fail on the way or during the battle itself, you die losing all of your items and weapons. To escape, you can leave through the windows scattered around which take you back to the graveyard, replenishing your health and allowing you to spend your points wisely. In this section of the review, I’ll break down the game mechanics in more detail.
Points – You get these by firing your gun, raising combos from chain-killing enemies and rescuing worshippers from the cathedral. When you save a worshipper, they return to the graveyard and pray to the altar of weapons, slowly raising your points in the background, even if in the game you remain idle.
Crypt – in here, the cards you collect from the cathedral are stored. You can either keep them on your character for their passive buffs (more health, stronger weapons, less recoil etc.) or you can choose to destroy them in order to regain a portion of your health whilst in the cathedral. Also in the crypt, you can place the bones you have collected, along with a weapon into the sarcophagus and raise a warrior to fight with you.
Altar of Weapons – here is where a lot of my points were spent. You can put your raised points into a vast array of skulls (which grant various powers) or weapons (they shoot things) in order to unlock them to help out on your journey through the cathedral to the boss.
I cannot express how perfectly balanced this game is or how well it works out for various playstyles. Like a ‘clicker’ style of game? Fine, just keep pressing the fire button as you wander around raising your points to unlock the best weapons and items.
Want a challenge? Ok, head straight through to try and kill the boss using just a pistol and your wits.
Like grinding? No problem, do a few rooms, pick up some cool stuff, get out of there, store them up and repeat.
Struggling? Just leave the game on overnight and in the morning you will have thousands of points to use unlocking some saucy firepower to give you a fighting chance.
Honestly, this game caters for everyone.
I couldn’t believe how addictive it was, whenever I died and was sent back to the graveyard, it always felt fair and I knew I’d pushed myself too much when I should have left with the items I had, maybe unlocked a new weapon and re-started, maybe I shouldn’t have lost a load of health greedily opening chests willy-nilly, it never felt cheap or a chore. The music in the game really adds to the oppressive, nihilistic atmosphere and, the whole game is engaging and dark with rich, fleshy sound effects and smooth animations (I especially like the rolling animation whilst wearing a skull, very cute).
The random generation of the cathedral’s layout each time you enter ensures that each run through feels unique. Every time you enter a room with a swinging cage holding another of your followers or you find a new gun which you desperately try to keep aside for a boss, it all adds to the tension and enjoyment, I can’t remember another game where I’ve thought, “ok, one more time, THIS is the one!” so often.
Summary:
I know I’ll be playing Nongunz for weeks to come and at a fiver, it’s insane value for money. I really hope this gets a PS Vita release because it’s the perfect game for the system and it would sit perfectly in my library next to Downwell and like Downwell, it would never leave it.
There’s such a layer of mystery to the game, why does the screen only fuzz at the graveyard?
What’s the strange room that shows up when you quit out of the game?
What’s in that secret case?
What does the ukulele do?
I heartily recommend Nongunz to everyone; it is an absolute gem of a game which has such intense depth and rewarding gameplay. Brainwash Gang do NOT mess about.
I’ll see you in the cathedral.
P.S – The developer has released a brief overview of the game mechanics and items etc. which explains everything far more clearly than I have here, definitely worth a read if you find yourself getting lost or need clearing up on a few things.

Nongunz is a game that I could easily see appealing to people, but just does not for me.
The game bills itself as a purposefully obtuse, nihilistic roguelike. What might not be immediately obvious in the teasers and trailers is that the game is also an idle clicker game. (Yes, I know it says it in the description and am probably stupid for not realizing it. I know.) Much of the game revolves around managing your economy properly, and grinding for followers for a better idle economy, to get different boosts to start runs with, entailing leaving the game running for hours in the background. It's a neat idea in theory.
The problem with this is that as soon as you activate any of the boosts, the game immediately ups the ante and spawns stronger monsters. Your upgraded guns have limited ammo, which means using them just spawns stronger monsters in exchange for a gun that will run out of ammo. All true roguelikes with no saved progress are inherently nihilistic in a way, because you always start again from scratch with a new run, but this one takes it a bit beyond: you spend hours idlnig for weapon or item boosts only to be repaid in stronger enemies right off the bat - so you don't even really benefit from the upgrades. There also appears to be crafting you can do with bone items to construct skeletons - but I never finished a skeleton, and everything goes away if you die, so I could never claim any rewards.
There is little to zero text in the game, so you need to suss out what upgrades do on your own. The iconography is pretty intuiitive for the most part, which is a plus. My problem is that once collected, none of the item cards seemed to actually do anything. I didn't jump higher, run faster, or shoot faster (a worthless upgrade as all the weapons I ever found shot as fast as I could click, and much slower otherwise. I admittedly never found a machine gun. Probably relevant there.) Consuming your item cards gives you health back, but then you lose the boost (? - maybe an obtuse mechanic I missed here? Again, could not tell any differences.) You can also idle-grind to start with, and find skeletal heads that give unqiue active abilities, like dashes, teleports, slow-time, and gravity manipulation. Unfortunately - opening chests costs you HP. So you could spend life to get an item card that doesn't benefit you at all, but because it's a bad card, you won't even get much HP back by consuming it. Even the 'rewards' in the game feel like they're working against you. Nihilism may be the theme, but it wears thin quickly.
The gameplay itself is pretty standard jump and shoot, and really isn't terrible. You can't free-aim, so shooting little enemies is either done by constantly jumping, or using the slide to shoot upwards. Most enemies are bullet sponges right off the bat, so the most dangerous enemies tend to just be a cloud of flies tat you have to awkwardly jump 'n gun at, and dodge roll from. Platforms can only be passed through upwards and not dropped back down through, and enemy projectiles play by different rules than yours, making some rooms feel inherently 'unfair'. I didn't find the game particularly difficult in and of itself once I grasped the ropes, just not very fun, and not very engaging.
The presentation is super slick, the aesthetic and sound effects and music and graphic design are very cool and very thematic for what the game is doing. It's just that, what the game is doing isn't all that fun for me. Your mileage may vary pretty wildly. I'm going to give the game a positive recommendation out of an appreciation for what the game is doing and for the excellent presentation, but understand that the game outside of the 'nihilism' and 'figure this♥♥♥♥♥♥out yourself' theme, and the clicker game wrapping, it's a pretty standard roguelike jump and run and gun. I'd rather play Risk of Rain or 20XX. You need to decide for yourself if that's worth playing.

A common trait in these kind of games is that part of the difficulty lies in being confusing at first, and for starters nongünz is really confusing. However, you progressively learn how the game works in a natural way and you'll be learning and trying new stuff probably till the end of the game. In this game you really feel like you are the one getting better with time, and not your character, since permadeath is a thing here and the thing that remains when you die is knowledge. The art for the game is gorgeous and the ending muic always gives me the chills. If you like weird and cryptic games and you enjoy difficult roguelikes this is definitely a game you'll enjoy. Oh, and it's pretty cheap as well.

Basically this game is what would happen if you took Mother 3, Mad Max, Children of Men, NiER and We Happy Few, and mixed them all up in a blender. A gruesome and dark game that is sometimes hilarious and other times downright creepy. It is quite polished for an RPG Maker game and feels like something that could have been made by a AAA team, albeit with the movement a bit unavoidably clunky making the game's platforming harder than it should be.
It chronicles the adventures of a man traveling through a post apocalyptic wasteland of sex starved men trying to find your daughter, the "last girl on earth", after an apocalyptic event killed all the women. Unusually for an RPG, it works a lot like the Fire Emblem games in that you will recruit a huge amount of party members and you must decide who to kill for the greater good (or risk losing your own abilities instead, if you're a masochist). The battles are livened up from the typical RPG Maker style with the addition of button based combos and all kinds of weird attacks that are unique depending on the party member.
The music is downright superb. The game also uses sight gags (or sometimes, horrors) in a masterful way that calls to mind Undertale. The game does have some rough around the edges and very frustrating parts... mainly when it moves away from the RPG gameplay towards more platformy stuff, or russian roulette... but overall what I played so far is really unique and accentuates what makes indie games so important for gaming.

Do not enable
on your first playthrough. You don't need it in your life. The primary difference between Pain and Normal mode is that save points in Pain mode can only be used once before exploding and being gone forever. No explanation is given in game as to what it does and the default selection is Pain mode. I played for 4.2 hours before restarting the game to get out of Pain mode; at that point my save file only had 1 hour 52 minutes recorded because of a couple very costly deaths. This nearly ruined the game for me. Don't make my same mistake.
You know when you see a macabre painting and you're like "Damn, that's some great artistry, but I just can't get into the subject matter."? For me, this game is often like that. I can intellectually appreciate the mature themes that LISA tackles in a kooky, comedic way. However, the dark comedy can't fully wash away the emotional muck that this game submerges you into as it shows you some of the worst sides of humanity. Your views on whether these heavy topics have a place in your entertainment and if you can laugh at them are the biggest determinants on whether you'll like this game. If you can stomach the rest, LISA's writing, characters, visual style, soundtrack and combat won't let you down.
Welcome to a world without women. It is brutal, perverse and often hopeless. Adult magazines have become this land's currency and addiction to a new drug called Joy is rampant. You play as Brad Armstrong as he seeks to rescue his adopted daughter, Buddy, from this world that sees her both as a savior worth safeguarding and a sexual object to be used and passed to the next guy. He found her as an infant and hid her away from the world as he raised her. He sees protecting her as a means of redemption for past failures... And this is just the game's setup.
A colorful cast of characters bring their own quirks and vices to this story. Some are addicted to Joy and will suffer withdrawal during combat if you don't feed their addiction. Others are simply lonely and are easy to convince to join your band of misfits. There are 30 characters to recruit and seeing a slice of each of their stories is a delight. A number of disparate antagonists make regular appearances, some to make your life miserable while another is surprisingly cordial. It is refreshing to see such a diverse, nonstereotypical supporting cast of both playable characters and NPCs.
Some of the themes in this game couldn't have been addressed as successfully without stellar writing. It deftly blends humor in with displays of abuse, addiction, hopelessness, insanity, questions on child rearing and other parodies of real world issues. I welcome less black and white, good vs evil narratives in the game industry, but at the same time I feel like this game took it a little too far into the dark side. Its depressing elements frequently outweighed its funny ones. The general flow of text, the text box style and the comedy itself are all reminiscent of the Mother series (Earthbound), and I mean that as a great compliment.
LISA's art style fits the world beautifully. It, too, compares to the Mother series, but with a more grungy, bloody take on it. It is not always the most detailed or varied, but characters stand out as distinct from one another. Perhaps even better is the soundtrack. It consistently sets the oddball tone of this world and what happens in it. There are a few repeated melodies, often in very different styles, that really help to tie the soundtrack together as a singular whole. I, for one, am very glad to have bought the game packaged with its soundtrack.
Combat is an enjoyable turn based system where each party member can play very differently. Some, like the main character Brad, use a combo system where you string together small attacks to trigger special moves. Others use something more akin to a traditional mana system. Others still need to build up points by using basic functions before they can unleash more devastating attacks. Rest assured that you'll be able to find a group that fits your playstyle among the many options. Be warned that there are situations both in and out of combat that can permanently kill party members. With such harsh consequences I reached a point where I felt like I needed to play with the excellent LISA wiki open for reference in the background.
Adjusting for my restart time, a single, thorough playthrough took me roughly 18 hours. I consider that a good length for this type of game and an excellent value compared to its cost. Looking at Steam global achievement rates, there is a concerning drop off between those that get the first achievement (85%) and those that finish the game (16%). However, most of that occurs near the beginning where only 28.2% defeat the first real boss. Still, it's worth noting that clearly this game isn't everyone's cup of tea.
With all said and done, I don't regret having played LISA. I do not, however, plan to play either its prequel or sequel. It is a more memorable game than many others but I will remember it with conflicted emotions.

If you liked the other Shadowrun games, you'll probably like SR:HK. Its gameplay is pretty much identical to that of its two prequels, though it has a slightly adjusted Matrix hacking minigame that is annoying at first but a welcome challenge later on.
The Shadowrun games overall do a great job with their storylines, and Hong Kong carries on that tradition. It's got some really unique and fun missions (such as one where you have to subtly disrupt the feng shui in a corporate office), and the characters are all memorable and interesting. It also allows for diverse approaches to each problem, so the way you spec out your character will affect the overall way the campaign plays out.
Bottom line: though nothing new or grounbreaking, it's a lot of fun. If you, like me, feel the urge to get lost in a vivid world of corporate intrigue and arcane secrets every now and then, Shadowun: Hong Kong will scratch that itch nicely.

Cause i'm lazy i'm gonna wrap all 3 'Shadowrun Returns' games here.
Overall and across all 3 games i rather enjoyed each of them very much and gameplay is solid and varied with multiple routes and ways to accomplish almost every mission, which makes having different builds and styles more interesting and replayable. There are some styles that you'll need particularly in Dragonfall and Hong Kong, namely decking, as in Returns decking helps with some major quests but isn't necessary and offers some loot. Dragonfall and Hong Kong you NEED reliable decking and fortunately the ones they give you for those do the job and still allow you to handle freely. The music and graphics are pretty solid across the games and the interfaces and menus are increasingly more friendly the farther down the conga-line you go. My biggest complaint is they are unoptimized and run like someone trying to strangle a walrus with toothbrush, Returns being the biggest offender, and Dragonfall having worked the smoothest for me.
Returns: This is one's story isn't great but holds okay and holds a solid intro to the style and setting and escalates in insanity and scale the further you go. As you'd expect of the first game of a trio, it's the clunkiest and offers the least variety. If you're interesting in playing them all i advise to start here as it offers the least features to get used to, as well as difficulty.
Dragonfall: The story starts big, and ends just as big, unlike the pace of the linear Returns which offered 1 side mission, Dragonfall is all about the side missions, whether for your fancy new personal team to learn their stories and personalities, or just doing the sides to progress the main plot, or just doing them cause they're side quests. Aside from the team building it only lightly expands on interface changes and building content, like a few new guns and some modified perks.
Hong Kong: So they kinda ran a bit of hit and miss with the story as it tries to sell you as someone who is already established and that you either LOVE your new life, or HATE it and only continue as a means to an end. On the flip side the arcing plot is more solid than Returns and holds well as you have to nitpick through your new world to find the answers you seek as it grows darker and darker and people become worse and worse. The characters held exceptionally well and loved all of them. Now to the game. It's more established and varied than the last two games, with a host of new weapons, perk changes, and even whole new perk lines to try all wrapped up in a brand new easier to manage interface, this interface also extends to your combat menus and inventory management. The progression for the story is as mentioned above, but the progression is largely the same as Dragonfall. Also gonna note that HK was a laggy buggy mess to play, ranging from the 2nd to last mission not loading cause you aren't playing in HD, to crashing, screens not loading textures, to characters just outright having turns skipped cause Xom said so.
Despite the flaws and grotesque amount of bugs in the game(s) i thoroughly enjoyed all 3 games. If you like more classic RPG with some more strategy element to it kinda XCOM style, i guess would fit, i'd definately reccomend any of them and suggest playing them in release order.
Also all 3 have workshops setup for playermade campaigns so if the base stories run dry for ya, there are always those. I didn't include them in my reveiw cause i really stuck to playing through the primary campaigns.

Better off buying Dragonfall instead. Dragon had better characters, more memorable combat and missions, much faster load times, and a better plot. The Flux state and the nature of Dragons and AI was a lot more interesting then work for triad, learn about demon in last mission, fight demon.
Has a few more flaws than Dragonfall - the incredibly irritating Matrix sections being my biggest complaint - but still a solid CRPG in an era where, let's be honest, that genre is dead.

This game--as well as the other two games in the series--is more novel than game, I would say. I'd probably put it about 75% and 25%, respectively. That being said, it is absolutely bad♥♥♥♥♥ From start to finish, it is an incredible work of art. It speaks to the inner bookworm and subbed-anime-watcher in me.
Let me start at the basics, I guess. The backgrounds and sceneries are beautifully "painted," and are worth zooming in on. There's fun little snippets of graffiti and interesting shizz lying around to look at. The characters themselves are not so bad; they kind of don't fit in with everything else, however. Easy to ignore. The top-down tactical gameplay is addicting and makes you want to read faster (or skip through dialogue) just to get to more action. To that, I go back to my original disclaimer. If you don't want to read, don't buy this game. All of it is important and very well put. Nearly every part of a conversation has choices for you to pick from, and the characters will respond accordingly. I also dig the race and class system they've been using. It gives many options for different kinds of characters. For first time players, I'd recommend being a Decker for your first play-through as it will really help. Trust me. Learn those ropes and you'll learn to hang with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Decker later. It's worth mentioning that your race, class, and skillset also affect the conversations you have with characters, opening you up to more dialogue options that will help you out... in most cases (I'm referencing the part in SR:DF where I gave a women a heart attack for choosing to intimidate her).
I am a completionist, for the most part, when I find a game I really, really enjoy. I come back to this series every once in a while for more play-throughs, just to try out different races/classes and to snag those other achievements. There's only two things that come to mind that bug me about these games. First of all, in my personal opinion, the game takes too long to load. To quote Joe Dirt, "That's just me talking." Shadowrun: Hong Kong is the latest entry in the Shadowrun Returns franchise of games, based in the Shadowrun tabletop setting, big shock. It's the last of the three current games I played, and by far my favourite of the bunch. But it still has some serious problems.
The story: Your foster father sends you a message begging you to return to Hong Kong to help him in some undisclosed way. The intro makes it clear that he's in serious danger of some sort, and no matter how you choose your character to be disposed towards the man, you do return to Hong Kong. Your adoptive brother and his girlfriend await you, and at the designated meeting point, you are met with a group of Shadowrunners. Then a sniper shoots half of you and you have to escape to the sewers. From then, it's a long story of getting in the good books of a local triad boss named Kindly Cheng (who is about as pleasant as a devil rat down the trousers), doing a lot of runs, recruiting new, very curious party members and finding out where your father is and what the big looming plot behind it all is.
While the actual intro is a bit weaker than those of the other games, the story from then on is the most well executed in my opinion. The biggest two factors? Cast of characters, and mission variety. Hong Kong continues the trend from Dragonfall to have a small group of dedicated characters under your management, with the other runners you can hire in being entirely optional. Though the casts in the other two games were already very good, this one is the most intriguing to me. I won't give away their stories here, but suffice it to say that it's colourful.
As for mission variety - I am happy to say that not every single mission involves a shootout with the police now! My dislike of the combat structure in the other games has gone well documented in my other reviews, and there was a point late in the game where the combat became grueling to me once more, but it was much later and to a much smaller extent than in Dragonfall. The runs you can go on now stretch from crime scene investaigations with entirely avoidable combat to fighting ghouls and goblins in a museum cellar, like in that one movie, just with more violence. It's refreshing, and it never gets as stale and repetitive as it did in Dragonfall. The second-to-last mission was especially great, but saying any more would be spoilery, so I shan't.
Sadly, though, there is one big negative I have to mention - I encountered a couple of bugs that forced me to replay certain sections. In one particular instance, meeting a group of NPCs under the wrong circumstances made it impossible to complete the mission because they wouldn't hand you a necessary item. It was frustrating to say the least. A little bit more playtesting wouldn't have gone amiss.
All in all though, despite the bug problem, Shadowrun: Hong Kong is easily the best of the Shadowrun Returns franchise. With this level of quality, I sincerely hope that it won't be the last.

This game is a visually charming, musically brilliant, sort-of-a-rhythm-game that I scoffed at before playing, because I assumed it would be devoid of anything I would like. I was very wrong, because the look and music of this game are phenomenal, and if you've got the dexterity for it, this game can be a blast!
That said, if you're like me and have poor dexterity, you may end up cussing every 10-30 seconds because you weren't fast enough and are having to replay the same sections of a level for 10x longer than it actually takes to complete the entire level successfully. It would be like playing Guitar Hero, except hitting one wrong note backs the song up 10-30 seconds back to a predetermined point to do it all over again. If I recommended this game, I would be doing a disservice by giving people the illusion that this game is for everyone, but that simply is not the case. People with crap dexterity, and/or who hate artistic charm and wonderful music should avoid this game.
In short, I would love this game if I had the skill, talent, and sufficient short-term memory to keep up with the quick actions needed to succeed in this game.
An excellent Rhythm game.

I'm very aware that one of my most hated reviews is Star Wars: Republic Commando (as it's the only one with three comments that attempt to insult me), but I never flinch when it comes to a game that didn't do well with its gameplay and narrative. I'm sure you know where this is going (especially, since I've got a big thumbs down on my review as it).
Yeah, I didn't really enjoy Jedi Outcast. I mean, I like the lightsaber combat. No, I love it. It's astounding. It's fantastic. It really makes you feel like a Jedi without all the strings attached (like when the blade is made out of plastic). But I don't like everything else around the lightsaber combat and occaisionally polished level design.
For starters, the biggest complaint that I see from many other critics is the incredibly dull first five hours of the game. Yeah, I'm right there with them on that. I actually set the game aside for a couple months (while I actually beat Jedi Academy in that hiatus), just because the level design was so vague and the FPS mechanics so bland and story so thin I couldn't find any enjoyment whatsoever. Even when you get your lightsaber, Nar Shaddaa is an absolute nightmare of level design. However, for some strange reason, once you get to Bespin the level design and fun rocket off high into the sky for the next 7 hours. The story's still garbage, but the level design and fun lightsaber and Jedi-related objectives are really fun and engaging.
I guess I should address my problems with the story. Well, for one, Desann is one of the most boring villains ever. The only thing you could say that's slightly interesting about him, it's that he's reptilian. And sure, the last villian you fight in Jedi Academy wasn't that great, but she functioned more as a conduit for a Bowser-esque final boss that provided an ultimate challenge. Desann had a lot of opportunities to shine, but he's just like every other bland, forgettable villain you've seen before.
The animation is also very wonky in this game. Characters move stiff and interact with each other in very robotic manners (matching their stiff mouth movements perfectly). Near the end, two characters kiss, and it looked like someone pressed them together, forcing them to make lip contact, but they actually had no attraction for each other. Besides that, the story as a whole is pretty samey. Big bad Empire tries to take over the galaxy, Rebels (or New Republic) fights back, become a Jedi, yada, yada, yada...
I prefer Jedi Academy much more than Jedi Outcast, because Academy was tailored around making each level as unique as possible (probably since they knew the story was pretty much the exact same as Jedi Outcast, but with a predictable plot twist near the end), and centered each level around a mechanic or attraction that didn't take up too much time- like fighting with Chewbacca, avoiding a Rancor, or freefalling down caverns to land on small ledges. Jedi Outcast has fewer planets and fewere situations for you to adapt to to get invested more. But the biggest reason I think I'm more apt to play Jedi Academy a second time, would be because for the 10 hours I played Academy I had tons of fun. I had fun for about a fraction of the whole time I played Outcast. It's not a terrible game, that's not what I'm implying. It's just got some massive flaws, that Academy eventually smoothed out.

I don't like recommending games, b/c capitalist propaganda etc.
But I recommend this one, it deserves more players. It offers some great and refreshing ideas in the action-platformer genre and in the rogue-lite genre as well (looping runs by abandoning levels and starting over, grinding and stashing equipment, card deck building, farming an 'economy' by idle gameplay). The mechanics are bewildering at first but it's really fun finding out what is happening in the game, it's not just a superficial cover. The gameplay itself is old-shool, slow and kind of punishing platforming and combat, slow but deadly enemies and even harder bosses. You are responsible for balancing your own difficulty as using higher tier guns makes short work of the bosses but levels up all the common enemies. There's no rush toward the final boss either, you have strong incentives to explore every room and loop back to the hub town to stash your findings before you lose them. It creates some nice incremental progression. Managing decisions of cost and reward is big part of the game. You can clear rooms, but that will reduce your ammo, you take damage, but heal from kills, cards offer stat boosts, but consuming them heals you more, take too much time and your cards get used up, take even more time and you can gain enough points over time to buy new skulls and weapons and die to a boss and lose everything.
But what I most love about it is the visual design. So many game tries to show gore and macabre themes and ends up being timid and boring. This game really grabbed me with its desolate death-ridden cathedral and its tormented squirming inhabitants. Resurrecting bones to do your bidding, freeing caged imps to worship you, paying their sacrifice to an altar of weapons, dying to a small bit of bouncing flesh gagged up by shapeless hunk of meat and bone and then resurrected climbing out of your own grave without a head back to the demons. Makes me feel warm and fuzzy.

Jedi Outcast has all the fundamentals of being a good game, and it definitely shows promise in parts, but too much of the game is spent slogging through utterly terrible levels of the worst design imaginable.
First, the pros:
- The lightsaber combat is fantastic, and while it isn't as advanced as in Academy, the game's sequel, I actually had more fun with it here than at any point in Academy. Something about its simplicity feels better. It isn't as flashy, but it has more weight to it.
- The cheat codes are brilliant. By far, the most fun I've had with the game has been spawning 30+ Reborn and engaging in enormous battles, or pitting Luke against 100 Stormtroopers, etc. It's simple, but kind of amazing.
- The game definitely will make you feel like a Jedi doing cool stuff.
Now the cons:
- Godawful level design. Far too often, you'll end up wandering around wondering where the hell to go next. I loathe games that hold my hand and point me in the right direction with giant guide arrows, like I'm a little child, but this game takes it so far to the extreme that it gets infuriating. At the time of writing this, I'm on the last level of the game, where, after getting stuck for about an hour, I realized that the way forward was under dark, solid-toned water (I.E. not clear) and behind a rock wall, which, from above the water, looks exactly like the rest of the environment. Many of the solutions to the player's pathfinding woes are similarly esoteric; you'll get stuck until you notice the tiny two-foot grate on the ceiling, which looks exactly like every other grate, except this one is breakable because... video games. So much of the level design feels less like an intended path and more like you're hunting for secrets. Some people tell me that this is just how games were back in the day, but I know that isn't true. Doom wasn't like this. Neither were Quake, or Thief, or System Shock, or Deus Ex, etc. Jedi Outcast's level design is frequently just obtuse and frustrating, and not fun.
- The random difficulty spikes out of nowhere. I like a good challenge, but a fair few parts in this game are just ridiculous and poorly designed. The second area, Artus Mine, is often even more difficult than much later parts of the game. The Nar Shaddaa Streets sniper-dodging will have you tearing hair out of your head, as they seem to have perfect reflexes, perfect aim, and about three buddies to shred your health at any given time while you hopelessly try to take aim at just one of them. In the second-to-last area of the game, you have a completely unnecessary, unfair and horribly-designed stealth gimmick forced upon you; even though, by this point in the game, you've pretty much incinerated half the Imperial army single-handedly, suddenly Kyle decides that there's one too many enemies on the map, and if any of them see you, it doesn't matter how well you're hidden or how good you are at fighting them, because the game immediately cuts to an arbitrary "you lose" cutscene with Kyle getting captured. The Jedi fights throughout the game, as well as a few bosses, can often be frustrating, purely because they have abilities you can't do anything about. At any time, they might decide to eat half your health with the Force Grab - a move which you can also do, except that every time you try using it on them, they're completely resistant to it. In Academy, at least you could make yourself resistant to their cheap Force powers as well, but not in this game.
- Everything before unlocking the lightsaber. No, you don't start the game with the lightsaber. Instead, you have to go through a number of mind-numbingly horrendous FPS maps before you get your trusty laser sword. What's so wrong with these early levels? A few things. For one, nobody played Jedi Outcast for a tedious FPS, they played it for Jedi action, and holding it back from the player for so long is just mean. Another issue is the shooting: it's absolute garbage. Your lasers move at a snail's pace, making any moving targets a chore to hit. Remember when I said the second area was one of the hardest parts in the game? This is exactly why. You enter enormous rooms with 15+ enemies all shooting at you, all at once, and your only defense is a painfully inaccurate, weak laser rifle, and grenades, which, if you ever try using in a big fight, will probably just result in little more than you getting shot a whole lot. In one of the later parts of the level, you take an Imperial officer at gunpoint (or grenade point, or shocky stick point), and lead him on a sleep-inducing walk at about 0.5 MpH to get him to open a door, at which point he unsurprisingly attacks you and you are (once again) ambushed by about eight enemies. By that point I was half asleep! What a rude awakening.
There are other things to comment on; some positive points (Lando's appearance is great, and every level he's featured in is also a lot of fun), but mostly negative ones (the terrible platforming that gets shoved down our throats at every turn, the AT-ST bit in the last area, the fact that the online multiplayer seems to no longer work). In general I'd say this: buy this game if it's on sale. You might like it, and odds are, you'll definitely enjoy cheating and creating some cool battles and stuff. If it isn't on sale, I couldn't recommend it at $11 CDN. Instead, if you're in need of a quick Jedi fix, go play Academy instead. Or, if you're looking for an actual good Star Wars FPS, try the first two games in the series (Dark Forces 1 and 2), or maybe the old Battlefront games, even though the multiplayer is down.
Whatever you do, make sure you have fun.

If you love isometric RPGs and cyberpunk settings, this game is a must-try.
This game takes place in the slums of near-futuristic Hong Kong, the underbelly of a society with advanced technologies and a great amount of fantasy. Think cyborgs, the virtual space like the Matrix, Ghost in the Shell hacking, orcs, elves, dwarves, and a healthy dose of Chinese folklore. That's Shadowrun: Hong Run in a nutshell.
The visuals and soundtrack are beautiful. For an ugly and depressing world, the game captures the grimeyness of a dying world both in the environment maps and the writing. The game's story throws you right into the mess, and leaves you a breadcrumb trail of unanswered questions as you progress along the main quest and some of the larger side quests. You take each quest from your terminal or other characters (important NPCs, party members) in the general hub and set out for each one through the subway metro station. The general hub is a living town, where you can stock up on supplies through the shops, learn more about the world through NPC interactions, and bond with your party members after each mission. The game is about 20 hours worth of content, good enough to satisfy an appetite for a cyberpunk indie RPG.
The regular companions are great and stand out from each other with their niches (zombie street samurai, drone operator, support shaman, decker/hacker, standard rifle grunt) . You can also hire mercenaries to fill some other niche not mentioned for your party. It's still highly recommend to roll with the the regular companions since they have backstories, and are fairly powerful powerful. It's better to save the money for buying consumables, new gear, magic, etc. Your main character is flexible enough to fill in missing desired roles such as offense mage, sniper, etc. Just be aware that the limited amount of skillpoints and money restricts you from being a jack of all trades. It's fairly expensive to go above 5 in a stat since the level of the new stat is the same amount of skill points that it costs.
The difficulty curve on normal mode feels relatively the same throughout the game. Your party grows at a fast enough rate that even the endgame isn't that difficult. After you learn about all of the mechanics, everything becomes pretty easy to breeze through. The same applies to decking/hacking, the stealth/combat portions don't really scale that hard even up to the endgame.
This game's merits are more in the fun of leading a fantasy cyberpunk crew than being a strategic genius, The games' world, writing, and overall gameplay are good enough to let the lack of min-maxing and simple combat slide.
There are fair share of game breaking bugs but they're rare to the point where it shouldn't take too much away from the experience. Just keep a good amount of saves just in-case.
Pro-tip: there are multiple endings, the good ending requires a good amount of paying attention during key moments in the main quest and also bonding with the regular companions. It's fairly simple to figure out in the final moments of the game. Have fun shadowrunners.

There's a lot of options for how you make your character and what equipment you use, what you say in dialogue and how you fight battles. But for most of the missions there's a pretty set path for you to go through, don't get me wrong I think the linear style really works for this game and I feel too much openness would have ruined it. And it's not devoid of replay value either as the game feautures multiple endings (btw I haven't finished this game which is important to know).
If there's something I can really praise here it's the missions and the character writing. Seriously, most of the fun in this game comes from the reading and the walking around sections where you're clicking on♥♥♥♥♥♥ There aren't a lot of companions, if you replay the game you're still going to have the same party as before with like the odd one out (unless you hire mercenaries, meaning companions that go with you but don't join your team). But the few companions that are there are well written and have hours worth of dialogue.
The missions don't assume you're an idiot, there's usually some mystery to them with dots to connect. Figuring that stuff out doesn't really have a visible impact on the mission but it's enjotable and when it's important so far it has. It kinda reminds me of the side quests in the WITCHER 3, in that they have their own story and things to contribute to the overall theme.
They're not unispired fetch quests like what we're used to, nor do they scream exposition at you. What I mean is they allow you to figure out what's going on for yourself, they don't pause the action to explain everything to you like some kind of condesending parent, which is rewarding narrative wise but not gameplay wise as they never combine the two. Narrative rarely compliments the gameplay, instead gameplay is used as pacing in between the "story" sections. Which is a shame I guess but it really isn't a problem here, the combat is fun and I enjoy it and the writing can stand on it's own regardless considering how strong it is.
Missions usually alwasy end about the same way, every missions always has a choice to make. Sometimes this just changes the rewards you'll get afterwards but that's not what it feels like,  in the moment your choices feel really important.
As an example from my early game there's this quest wherein the game hides a story inside what's disguised as a standard MMO fetch quest. It was actually really memorable and I think it might be a favourite gaming moment of mine.
The part I liked so much wasn't even technically part of the quest but it was the chat that followed with the NPC afterwards, it changes nothing and it's completely optional. It's literally like a well designed side quest you cleverly get pulled into where you learn about an NPC and his life completely on your own free time with no discernable profit to be made.
That and seing how OP your character has become. Combat is cool, there's a diffuculty selection and it could be worth cranking it up. Then again the point of combat is basically just to deal with pacing issues in the story so it's fine playing it on easy if that's what you prefer. Personally I find normal a bit too easy although the first few missions had some challenging combat if I remember right.
The circle of combat is basically: do missions -----) get money and experience -----) unlock combat and roleplay options -----)  start over. The more options you have the more combat depth you get.
The depth of the combat comes out of deciding what options you have to utilize, sure there are hit percentages and♥♥♥♥♥♥but they kinda take a backseat to skill management because you could always just cast a spell to increase accuracy. Same with cover, you can always just give take some Bliss (expendable item) or cast an armor spell. Hell, my samurai is so tanky I just leave out in the open.
Overall it's a very unique game with a suprising amount of depth and humour and I reccomend it.
For a game that's based on having a smaller scope it's got an impressive amount of internal ambition (shoutouts to the sound design and soundtrack). Also kudos to implementing good enviromental design that fits into this "connect the dots" mentality.

In this game you play as both classic Sonic in levels reminiscent of the Mega Drive era Sonic as well as modern Sonic (or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Sonic as i prefer. I hate the way Sonic is now) in 3D levels.

The Bad:

This has some fun gameplay and is artistically gorgeous. The gameplay starts to be problematic though. Even if you like first person jumping challenges, brace yourself for some rage.
The story is ok, sort of  the Twilight Zone meets Fraggle Rock. The story aspects of the game could have been better, but that wasn't my real problem. I didn't mind needing to account for momentum, the physics seemed fine. But then you add the level difficulty spiking and the registering of the grapple feeling inconsistent and you have a recipe for frustration. The devs seem like they knew what they were doing so it seemed almost sadistic that one second I felt like electric-whip-Spiderman and the next I felt electric-whip-JoeBeerbelly-guy. There should be a range of difficulties, but there is not.  The soothing music and the stunning visuals help, but I decided to avoid a heart attack and watch the end on YouTube.  I think if you like SEUM speedrunners you'll probably like this even though it has a more kiddish flavor to it. Despite it's flaws I still recommend this game because it is fun for a while and the level design is on my short list of prettiest ever. Just get it on sale or in a bundle.

Another Falcom game comes to PC, this time courtesy of Aksys & Ghostlight.

Your first thought when seeing the game is very likely "This looks like Persona 5".  A common one, but shallow, as the commonalities start disappearing well into the first act.  Progression is closer to the way Cold Steel does it, and combat is completely different, more akin to Ys. Also has decent, rebindable controls for both controller & kb/m , although I can't comment much on kb/m.
Music-wise, this game obviously delivers, with Falcom's JDK team continuing to make rock-solid music pieces that generally fit the tone and enhance an already great game.
Localization-wise,  the game is sub-only. The translation is still a bit spotty, but should be far ahead of the VITA version, at the very least.
Port-wise, it mostly delivers on the basics. 1080p60 with reports of the game doing 4k with not too much trouble. If you're expecting a "Cold Steel" quality port with Durante magic in it, you will come out disappointed, as aside from resolution, it's a match-4-match with the PS4 version.
Although the game is a tad bit pricey, I still think the asking price is worth it, if you have the money,at least. This only applies to the main game, the DLC is preposterously pricey and I confess I'm rather surprised Aksys went with that value, specially for the basic cheat ones.

Also keep in mind this game does not have english voices, its only in japanese voices. This is the first time in years that I bought a game full price (ok not full price it had a -10% but still), and I don't regret it at all, indeed it's a bit expensive for a game so you might want to wait for a bigger sale.
The story is simple and effective, there's no useless dialogues (unless you want to talk to every npc), pretty fast, it's really easy to follow and very enjoyable. You'll get into it in no time. Plus it's like watching an anime, that's really the sensation that I got while playing this game.
Free time is a lot like the free time you got in the Persona series, you have a "bonding time" with other characters, you get to know your friends better that's really interesting. But this isn't Persona, you won't get an insane amount of free time. Actually you're just playing few days.
You can also walk freely in various places, there's some littles things to do, there's a lot of npc moving around it gives you the impression that you're living there, it's very lively. And even randoms npcs has some backgrounds.
The combat is fast paced, each characters has their own style (slow attacks but hits like a truck or fast light damages for exemple). You don't need to grind in this game, that's something I like. Overall the combat system is pretty fun. Bosses can be tricky/challenging if you're on a high difficulty but you have your best weapon : The roll. It makes you INVINCIBLE for a short time rolling into an attack nullifies it (even lasers) and you can spam it there's no stamina, time it well and you'll destroy everything (there's also an element that can enhance the duration of the invincibility if you're bad at this), it's pretty fun to read bosses attacks/pattern. But in the end it's fairly easy.
The OST has some nice epic tracks, but what did you expect ? It's a game from Nihon Falcom.
I would really love to have more games like this one.

I'm shockingly impressed with this game. I'm enjoying the story and characters, I adore the music, and the action-RPG gameplay is great.
It absolutely is Persona-inspired in terms of setup. In fact, some of the camera angles in the school building are so close to Yasogami High School from Persona 4 that I'm surprised more people haven't noticed.
However, it doesn't feel like a rip-off as a game. Nihon Falcom took Persona's world building and fused it into their own style of story telling and gameplay, and I really like the result.
I'm a huge fan of the Persona series but its turn-based combat is definitely not my favorite part about it.
While I'm not going to try to claim that Tokyo Xanadu's story so is better than Persona 3, 4, & 5 (Atlus are probably the best at what they do) but it's good enough that I'm actively enjoying it rather than simply tolerating it. The fact that I enjoy the combat as well means at no point am I just waiting to get through one aspect of the game to hurry on to the next.
I discovered this game by chance. I've seen almost no marketing for it so I'm worried it won't reach all of its potential audience in the West. It seems to have sold "ok" in Japan, so I really hope Nihon Falcom and Aksys Games both exceed or at least meet their sales expectations.
I really want Tokyo Xanadu to continue. It doesn't need to be the same characters or continuity (in fact I hear the ending of this one is pretty definitive), but Nihon Falcom is off to a great start with this new IP and I want to see the results of them taking time to refine what they've created here.
(Also, I'm fine with them continuing to make it for handheld. If that means the series will continue to be graphically minimalist, I'm good. A great art style/aesthetic and sharpness is more imporant than realistic graphics anyway.
In fact, Nihon Falcom - it seems like this would be a great game to port over to the Switch as well.)

One should note however there are lots of "St" weak monsters early in the game before you can use "St" attribute, possibly poor planning on the developer part but I'm not one to tell the devs how to create their game.
5/10 could do with some tidying up around the graphics and some nicer / more distinct characters.

The above quotation sums up the whole idea of this new Sonic installment pretty well. What You get in Sonic Generations is more of the same, proven experience known from some of the
Across the course of the game we revisit some iconic locations from the Sonic universe both in 2D and 3D incarnations, and once again roll through them with a blazing speed.
Unfortunately the game does not introduce anything new, except more of the old ideas. Even challenges (called acts) assisting each main level feel somehow repetitive and in most cases waste their own potential. There are a few promising moments, but in most cases they’re ruined by
As I said earlier, the whole idea about the game, and it’s main plot twist is an emergence of a mysterious time-eating fellow who “erases time”. This allows our heroes, namely Sonic and Tails, to team up with their previous incarnations on a quest to save all well-known Sonics friends. During our task we’ll be forced to beat each area twice, both with our “new” fully 3-dimensional Sonic, and his old-2D-only-self, once again collect all chaos emeralds, and finally beat time-eating creature.
The plot is almost nonexistent, dialogues between Sonic and Tails feel stiff and does not encourage to explore the world. The case is similar with our friends, who once rescued reappear only to help us during certain, usually 2-3 minutes long acts, by performing certain special actions. Sadly those certain acts are usually affected by the highest number of glitches.
There are only
I could say about this game, while recommending it to any non-hardcore Sonic fan would be the music and the modds. Music in this game is simply a collection of best pieces from the previous Sonic Games, which more than once proved itself to be one of the strongest points of the series, perfectly accompanying our high-speed runs through the world.
As for the modding system it’s unofficial, but in my opinion the game improves dramatically after a few modds are installed. Luckily most of them come equipped with a guides allowing us to change the game drastically. Not only we are able to change our playable character, add new levels or even add new game modes, but also change already existing levels, or even affect controls of both Sonics.
Summing up, the game is not bad, and I’d risk saying that it’s still, despite all its flaws, a solid Sonic experience. Unfortunately numerous bugs, glitches, poor plot, and terribly broken on-line mode make it feel like an unfinished product. So if You’re not some kind of hardcore-hedgehog fan, better avoid this game and get Yourself one of the older, proven editions.
•	Refreshed classic levels
•	Old music brought back to life
•	2D and 3D gameplay mode in one game
•	Extremely sloppy controls both with keyboard and X-box controller
•	Booring plot, and repetitive side challenges (acts)
•	High number of bugs and glitches
•	Broken on-line mode
•	Visibly unfinished product with a lot of wasted potential

Another good Shadowrun game, although it took me quite long this time to really get into it (compared to the two predecessors). The first few missions didn't take me long to complete. Inbetween missions I found myself spending an equal amount or longer just walking and talking to NPCs. In other words, I spent a good deal of this game reading text instead of playing a game. This made the story unfold quite slowly which somewhat annoyed me. And there is so much information that just isn't relevant to the story. The game mechanics didn't change too much from Dragonfall or the original Shadowrun. The notable exception here is Decking. In the previous two games decking was just fighting in cyberspace.
