Freedom Planet began its development life as a Sonic the Hedgehog fangame, but the final product is so much more than that. At its heart, the game feels like an amalgamation of so many gaming memories from the nineties. Sonic is one, but there are also doses of Rocket Knight Adventures, Gunstar Heroes, Blaster Master... the whole thing is one big high-octane sixteen-bit thrillride which (apart from more modern touches like completely voiced dialogue and a rather lengthy story element in Adventure Mode) feels like it would have been considered a classic without question if it had come out back in the day.
That's not to say the game is perfect by any stretch. The story, while entertaining in terms of individual cutscenes, has a weird pace (occasionally taking ten minutes or so to get through a dialogue sequence), and shifts tone between dark and lighthearted a bit too jarringly, not to mention the plot itself is fairly simple (you can select Classic Mode to play the game through minus the story sequences, though). If I had to register a balance complaint, it would be that the game's bosses, while elaborate and certainly well-designed for what they are, feel like they belong in a much harder game--if you want anything resembling the sort of comfortable platformer difficulty that games like Sonic and Rocket Knight generally provide, you'll need to play on Easy difficulty--the bosses will kick your butt and grind it into a paste while you're working to get a handle on their patterns of attack, otherwise.
But the gameplay is solid and flowful, apart from some very rare collision-issue moments that I only suffered on replays; there are three characters, one unlockable, each offering a very unique gameplay style (the main character Lilac is my personal favorite and the one I recommend starting with). The level designs are all unique, if nothing wildly revolutionary for the genre, and the sense of pace, while somewhat slower than Sonic the Hedgehog (due in part to the greater emphasis on action elements) remains consistent throughout.
Put frankly, in spite of what flaws there are, I love this game and want nothing more than to get the word out there that it's a near-must-play for fans of the style of platformer that was popular back in the SNES and Genesis/Mega Drive era. It's only about five or so hours long at a stretch, but it provides more than enough fun factor and content for its $15 price point, as well. At the very least, do yourself a solid one and try out the demo. That in itself is fairly substantial, featuring a full stage and one "act" of a second level.
As a side note, the music is also fantastic and el gasp, an indie game using pixel art that looks like it isn't just trying to look like pixel art because RETRO NOSTALGIA! I am almost in awe. Almost. Did I mention the game's very pretty-looking? Because it is.

Preface: I have played a small of amount of CoH, but am a big fan of strategy games. I bought this on a whim in the summer sale, and got the "master" collection, which has all factions.
Singleplayer: The singleplayer overall is decent- like many strategy games, the story is largely an excuse to string together a bunch of missions that you've played in games like this before. Defend the bridge(s)! Use the sniper team! Destroy the enemy base that is 8 times bigger than yours but can only send two squads to attack! We've seen it before, but there's nothing wrong with it per se. The game has two campaigns, one soviet the other american. The soviet campaign is linear but has more going for it in the story department, while the American is nonlinear and you can lose a game of you fail too many times and your company's strength falls, but is even more game-y. I have yet to beat either, as while decent they do get repetitive and the skirmish is much more fun.
Singleplayer (Skirmish): The skirmish, is in my opinion, the best part of the game. If you enjoy getting some friends to battle AI in co-op matches, you will be more than satisfied. All five factions are very different, both in their tactics and abilities, (For example, rather than build structures, the US army deploys officers that unlock better units while being combat units themselves) and the faction variety is easily the best part of the game to me. Additionally, you have 3 commanders (replacing the doctrine system) that have further specialized abilities and unique units, such as Fallschirmjäger or the IS-2 tank (more on why this is good and bad later). The game is extremely replayable with user generated maps and constant updates by the devs. If you enjoy comp-stomping, this a great strategy game for you.
Multiplayer: I’ve only recently dipped my toes into PVP, but I think I understand why this game receives the flak it does, and it is perhaps a bit too harsh. Essentially, the Three commander system I mentioned earlier has additional commanders that you can unlock via loot crate, but they can also be bought for three dollars. This means a player you are going up against may be able to deploy a unit you can’t, and vise versa. Defenders of the game say it doesn't matter, while gamings white knights say it ruins the game, when the truth is somewhere in between. I’ve yet to play a game where I feel like I lost because he had better units than I did, or at least commander supplied units. The commanders aren’t a terrible idea to spice up the rapidly stagnating RTS Genre, but the randomness of loot crates coupled with a huge variety means you’ll rarely get the commander you want, let alone one you’ll use.
Verdict: With an entry fee of 20 bucks for eastern armies or western armies, i don't think any RTS fan should pass this up. Is it perfect? No. But what game is? Pick up the game next time you've got the cash. Or don’t. I'm not your mom.

STFU is a fun action platformer with a different take on the time rewinding mechanic. If you die and rewind time, your past self is still there shooting along next to you. Instead of using it to rewind and fix a mistake (ala Prince of Persia), rewind and shoot twice as many bullets! Half the fun of STFU is having 20 copies of yourself running along with you firing wildly. There's still interesting time tactics you can use, like spending one life to clear out baddies so your future self can run through faster. And there's a whole section of Portal-esque puzzles in the "Helladeck". Top that off with some excellent pixel graphics, humorous writing, and a variety of different characters to play.

This game packs a retro-look with unique and innovative gameplay mechanics that put you up against challenges quite unlike any other game. Its frantic "single-player cooperative" nature allows you to pause and rewind at any time, choosing the same or a new character (each with their own unique style) and having them fight on simultaneous to your previous "recorded" actions. Lose one of your characters in battle? Come back with her time-travelling clone and destroy the bad guy before the final blow was struck - thus saving them, and earning you an extra hit point. Beating the game once unlocks a "SUPER HARDCORE" mode, which presents a new, greater challenge where each character has a single life, so saving them this time becomes extra important.
There is also plenty of collectables, some harder (or nearly impossible!) to get that present themselves as useful in-game objects. This means, no going out of your way to collect something useless just for the achievement. The exception are (no spoilers!) objects unlocked later on that serve as a time attack, tasking you to collect them in a certain amount of time before they disappear. This adds on an extra layer to each level as you try to find ways to speedrun them!
I was actually disappointed there wasn't an achievement for doing this on every level. Otherwise, I did get 100% achievements on this game - something I almost never do. All of the achievements felt accessible yet challenging, unlike some games that present you with nigh impossible goals just for a few internet points.
The story is fun, but predictable, but it's not supposed to be anything deep or dramatic. It drives the humor home and keeps you wanting to see what crazy adventure the Super Time Force will go on next. Maybe, mostly, it's just about what you get to blow up next and potentially ruin the entire space-time continuum...
Note that this version is superior to the less than "Ultra" versions available on consoles. It includes bonus "challenge levels" and a few Valve characters, such as the TF2 Pyro.
It's not perfect, but it's damn near close. I highly recommend this game. Now STFU!

A very good game with a great concept and really, really annoying writing, Super Time Force Ultra is a side-scrolling shoot-em-up with a cast of interesting and diverse characters. A mix of Contra's shooting, Braid's time manipulation, and a bad Saturday morning cartoon's writing and plot, STFU has fun to spare, though a few elements can get repetitive.
The gameplay itself is the standout here, with a mix of rapid shooting action and precise time control, letting you repeat sections while your previous character carries out the actions you just did, allowing you to do a lot of things within the same timeframe. It's a neat gimmick, and one that rarely ends up feeling forced. The one downside is that every single boss fight in the game boils down to repeating the same 60-second chunk of time a ton to bring their health down, often 10-20 times. It's a slight complaint, because a few bosses have their own quirks such as an object you have to defend, or minions that attack you, etc.
Each character has their own interesting normal and charged shots; characters have varying amounts of usefulness, but every one is fun to use. The combat feels good, and enemy health is set to a manageable level that keeps them from being bullet sponges (Cough cough, Mercenary Kings). I found that mostly you'd use 4 or 5 characters a lot, with others mostly being relegated to a few extremely situational uses. You gain more characters as you play, often in hidden, missable areas, which provide a fun reason to explore the levels.
Other reasons to explore include pink sparkly items that, when touched or shot, slow down time; this allows you to get in a lot of shots in a short amount of time, letting you use crucial seconds to easily defeat tough enemies or bosses.
There are also gold items to collect which add another life to your counter, and little.. sparkly things that I have no idea what they do. (Upon researching, apparently they activate time trials. I don't know what the reward is, because I was never good enough to finish them, since I didn't know that was their point.)
A neat gameplay mechanic is that if you die, then go back in time and prevent that character from dying, you can absorb them to gain an extra hit point as well as their charged shot mechanic, letting you become a more powerful character (until your inevitable death). This means that you have a lot to keep track of when you're rewinding time, as you can figure out how to save a character's life, absorb them, and attack anew.
The game's low-res pixel art aesthetic might initially look trite and overplayed, but the use of muted colors and few outlines on things overall adds up to a pleasing look, though not wholly unique. The levels all look different from each other, however, which helps sell the interesting time travel theme; future levels are gleaming futuristic chrome, whereas the levels set far back in the past are full of dinosaurs and interesting flora and fauna.
The soundtrack is passable, though I didn't note any particularly great or horrible tracks. The sound design itself is fun, though, with punchy gun noises and loud, goofy character screams as they die in slow motion.
The only real complaint I had aside from the slight repetition was the writing. It's just so overly WE'RE A VIDEO GAME that it takes me out every time the mission commander says "LOL" or uses other awful internet slang. It's distracting and immature, and almost all attempts at humor fall flat, closer to a child shouting for attention than a witty pun or joke.
Overall, I enjoyed my time with STFU, but I wish the characters had done just that. The gameplay is fun, the level design is interesting, and the game doesn't outstay its welcome. There's a lot of stuff I didn't get; I came nowhere close to 100% completing the game, so completionists will have a lot of fun collecting collectibles and beating time trials, unlocking characters, etc.
I give Super Time Force Ultra an 8/10, and I'd like to see Capybara revisit this concept because the core gameplay is a blast. Recommended.

This game is a work of art. It is both filled with dark humor that kept me entertained beginning to end, as well as sad moments that will shatter even the most solidified of hearts. It is an rpg maker game, so controlls are pretty basic. However this isn't just a standard "build your party, kill the guys" rpg. No no. This game features a ton of party members, each unique and memorable on their own, as well as situations where your playthrough can become very challanging depending on your choices, some of which can permanently cripple Brad, the protaganist of this story, or kill your party members off. Yes, kill. In this game your party members face the chance of permadeath, whether it be from strong enemies, russian roulette, being kidnapped by a gang, or your own hand. Not only that, but there is another major thing that can hault your progress. Joy. Joy is a drug in this game that Brad, as well as a few of the better party members, suffer from. Joy, when used restores your health completly, and makes you do crits every turn until the effect runs out. However, the bad side of this is withdrawl. Withdrawl makes you do almost no damage, and will pop up more often every time you take joy. So you have to balance everything well, or you may get stuck. And if you think that this game is too easy, you can choose to play pain mode. You can only save once per point, and all the enemies are much harder here. This game is pretty difficult, and will be a good time for fans of titles similar to earthbound. I would rate it 8/10, with the only real fault, in my opinion, being a few unforgiving spots, and a lack of ending variety.

Not a standard hidden object game; a resource-management game with "objects" that need to be collected; it costs money and energy to search for them in HO scenes. (Money to open the locations; energy to search.)
Each scene has only a handful of objects at first, all easy to find. Each location will have the same scene with different object selections several times. They alternate between text descriptions and silhouettes - but the silhouettes don't actually match the items. (You can tell it's a "knife" shape, but it's not the same shape as the knife you need to click.) As you visit a scene more often, there are more objects to find, and sometimes complications are added (like a fog over the scene).
Obvious port of a mobile game; plenty of distracting details and resources to manage; impossible to follow the storyline. Pretty sure there is no "win;" this is "keep visiting locations; collect objects every time you do a hidden object puzzle; make collections of multiple objects to earn money." And it has "connect with friends!" options, but I think those aren't fully functional for Steam players; names with photos are from the mobile version; steam players get random-number IDs.
Some of the scenes have bugs: you can find all the objects shown/listed, but it still shows one missing, and there's nothing you can do to make that one appear. You have to close out or wait for time to run out (the HO scenes have timers), and lose the energy you spent to open the scene.

Preface: I have played a small of amount of CoH, but am a big fan of strategy games. I bought this on a whim in the summer sale, and got the "master" collection, which has all factions.
Singleplayer: The singleplayer overall is decent- like many strategy games, the story is largely an excuse to string together a bunch of missions that you've played in games like this before. Defend the bridge(s)! Use the sniper team! Destroy the enemy base that is 8 times bigger than yours but can only send two squads to attack! We've seen it before, but there's nothing wrong with it per se. The game has two campaigns, one soviet the other american. The soviet campaign is linear but has more going for it in the story department, while the American is nonlinear and you can lose a game of you fail too many times and your company's strength falls, but is even more game-y. I have yet to beat either, as while decent they do get repetitive and the skirmish is much more fun.
Singleplayer (Skirmish): The skirmish, is in my opinion, the best part of the game. If you enjoy getting some friends to battle AI in co-op matches, you will be more than satisfied. All five factions are very different, both in their tactics and abilities, (For example, rather than build structures, the US army deploys officers that unlock better units while being combat units themselves) and the faction variety is easily the best part of the game to me. Additionally, you have 3 commanders (replacing the doctrine system) that have further specialized abilities and unique units, such as Fallschirmjäger or the IS-2 tank (more on why this is good and bad later). The game is extremely replayable with user generated maps and constant updates by the devs. If you enjoy comp-stomping, this a great strategy game for you.
Multiplayer: I’ve only recently dipped my toes into PVP, but I think I understand why this game receives the flak it does, and it is perhaps a bit too harsh. Essentially, the Three commander system I mentioned earlier has additional commanders that you can unlock via loot crate, but they can also be bought for three dollars. This means a player you are going up against may be able to deploy a unit you can’t, and vise versa. The Loyalist fraction adds another layer of strategic depth, the new Garbage Dump building allows you to manage pollution more effectively, wind turbines allow you to generate clean and cheap electricity, and even the Garages are now reasonably-sized. Fortunately, you can still play through the original campaign with the new buildings and Loyalist faction, and having played Tropico 3 without this expansion pack, I have never regretted the upgrade.

The best way to describe "Operation Kursk K-141" is to call it a missed opportunity.
I really hate it when adventure games are bad, because just making the effort to make an adventure game confines its creator to a very select niche.
The most part of the budget was clearly devoted to the graphics and animation part, which might not be exceptional, but is above the average 2D, pixelated indie efforts.   However, after finishing the game and realizing they must have run out of money at the end, I wish they had gone the 2D route and invested more in story development.
Puzzles are the bread and butter of any adventure gamer. If they are good, they keep you invested in the story. If they are bad, they ruin everything.
While there are some good, smart puzzles in the game, they are mere exceptions to the "WTF" reactions to the step-by-step walkthrough one has to use in order to finish the game. Random objects apearing and disappearing without reason in different rooms - check; uninteresting, unidimensional and useless characters - check; combining objects in illogical ways - check; have to click objects several times in order to be able to use them - check; open, unsatisfying ending - check and so on.
So don't get this game unless it's on sale and you are desperate for adventure.

Whether you're a fan of oldschool point & click adventures or into mystery and crime solving, you should definitely give this one a try. It may be lacking a bit in regards to polishing, but if you dare to look beyond that, you won't be disappointed!

Undercover Missions: Operation Kursk K-141:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

You are part of a very small and special unit of the Russian Secret Service called the URPO which is fighting against organized crime but especially against the Russian Mafia. As are all agents from this elite group, you have been given a new identity upon your appointment! Your new name is Milena Belyaeva and you have been given the task to look into a new criminal organization, “VORY,” which recruits former members of the Russian Secret Service, and is suspected of stealing their own military equipment. You will be thrown in the deep end – you will have to investigate the activities of the personnel aboard the submarine Kursk K-141 in order to find out who the traitor is.
Undercover Missions: Operation Kursk K-141 is a point and click adventure game divided into 9 sensational and captivating chapters. You are going to embark on a thrilling adventure that will keep you constantly thinking about what do to next, and where to go to in order to move forward into the story.
I consider myself well known to this genre of games, but I can tell you that I did not feel too smart about my methods of deduction or logic in more than one occasion!
On the bottom right of your screen you will have a magnifying glass, a car and a setting button. The magnifying glass button will help you to find all clues in each of the locations that you will visit. You will use the car button a fair bit when you are on-board the Submarine (I would prefer a map icon rather than car) where you will constantly move from one room to another to find more clues. I really enjoy the combination between the objects which, when put together, become a new brand item.  Sometimes the objects are not so obvious and you might find yourself in a pickle, really not knowing what to do next. Perseverance will prevail and your effort will be rewarded by entering a new chapter. YES!!
The graphics are good and the game runs really well, I did not encounter any issues throughout the entire game which took me a good 16 hours to finish. The voice-over is not the greatest, to be honest, but this should not put you off purchasing this game. The mini games are fun and can be a bit tricky.
This is a really solid and well-constructed point and click adventure game but it is not an easy one, which is what you want.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good and well-structured story
-	Good graphics
-	Makes you think all the time
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Voice-over could be better
-	No  games achievements
-	No trading cards
A good and well-structured point and click adventure game - you can’t afford not to have this game in your game library!

If you want a quick yea or nay, know this: Freedom Planet is one of the best-designed and most compelling titles I've played in my twenty five year history with video games as a whole, and it continually managed to impress me throughout. It's not perfect, and there are a couple of seams showing, but if you have any fondness for the action platformer genre and are willing to take the game on its own merits, you owe it to yourself to try this one; it sits with Shovel Knight as one of the best of its genre. Be warned that it can be legitimately challenging in the late-going, and if that worries you, dial the difficulty down to Easy for your first run, or even Casual.
The Good:
- Great stage design that's well-paced and leads the player admirably
- Fun presentation and colorful cast
- Legitimate challenge
- Fantastic soundtrack
- Surprisingly long and replayable
The Bad:
- Moderate learning curve on each character
- Lilac's special meter regenerates a little slowly, causing unwelcome waiting at times
- Plot occasionally loses focus and drags
- Some bosses can be a little unfair
The Weird:
- For a plot so animated, why are Milla's bizarre block-summoning, laser-shielding ways never explained?
Now for the detailed version.
Let's start by getting this out of the way: the average independent game, like the average game in general, is terrible. My hope for a new generation of developers was new, fresh takes on the ideas that they grew up with, homage to the sensibilities of old while adding new elements, and subtracting outdated ones.
Instead, most independent developers use a retro aesthetic because they either don't have the money or talent to do anything else, frequently poorly in their own right, and rather than use the design elements of a bygone age to create new experiences, or at least compelling rehashes of old ones, they frequently miss the point altogether, or simply use the format as delivery for some ham-fisted art project, with little-to-no focus on the gameplay. The results are an overall waste.
It took about ten years, but this new generation does occasionally create an exception to this rule, and we were fortunate to see a major one in the way of the aforementioned Shovel Knight, a wonderful romp through one of the earliest periods of video gaming, re-interpreted with a new perspective and vigor that entertains throughout. Freedom Planet somehow pulls off the same feat with a different era, it also making showing its own flavor, and in many ways improving on its source material.
Its first and arguably greatest crime, though, isn't even in the game itself. The cover art sells it extremely poorly, and fails to tell the player anything about what it is; I took one look at it and passed it over immediately, not the least bit interested in whatever game it could be. I came across the game again in a random related Youtube video for a totally different game, compelled by the thumbnail, and was immediately intrigued by the gameplay. I expected that, at worst, it couldn't fail to impress more than the generally woeful Sonic the Hedgehog 4: Episode 2.
What followed was the surpassing of that and nearly every other expectation I had of it, starting with the surprisingly involved and animated plot. The characters are lively and expressive, and feature a surprising variety of sprites to accompany their dialogue, and the voice acting, which is present for every line in the game, is capable, if a bit too hammy here and there. The whole thing can get cheesy, but it fits, and absolutely feels like it came straight from the 32-bit age. While it's a bit long in the tooth, and takes itself a bit too seriously sometimes, it sets the tone well for the adventure, and can be skipped should one feel so inclined, besides.
Whether you get to the gameplay at the story's pace or your own, though, it's immediately comfortable and tight -- Lilac, the character representing Sonic the Hedgehog's style of play, handles well, her gliding double jump gives welcome control in situations where Sonic may otherwise end up in places you didn't want him to be, and her multi-directional air-dash, while requiring some getting used to, is also handy. Carol, a bizarre hybrid of playstyles reminiscent of Mega Man X's Zero, complete with wall jumping abilities, is a riskier and more challenging contrast, and her trademark motorcycle is hilarious fun. They're eventually joined by a third character, whose playstyle is a slower, more deliberate brand that brings to mind, of all things, Tails' Sky Patrol, an old Game Gear game featuring Sonic's fox friend, though bombs are replaced by throwable blocks here.
The player guides one of these three through some surprisingly high-quality and well-paced stage design, full of interesting elements and trials to overcome, but mercifully almost entirely devoid of its source material's fondness for sudden drops into pits or facefulls of enemies and spikes. The game very rarely punishes you for not knowing what's coming up, and little is totally missable the first time around. Small design tweaks like these improve the experience without hurting its feel, and you don't realize how much you hate what it deliberately omits until you notice it's not there. Even water, the bane of many a Sonic player, manages to be nothing more than a part of the obstacle course, adding to the experience rather than impeding it. The results are frequently a treat to play, rarely frustrating or discouraging, and surprisingly technically sound, with few glitches and mishaps, something the game's closest inspiration still can't get right with any sort of consistency. Every now and again the stage design doesn't properly direct you or breaks flows in unnatural ways, but overall the game just feels remarkably tight and well-designed.
Each stage is capped by a boss, often interesting itself in design. This is where the game bears its true difficulty, and many of your foes, while frequently thrilling, often featuring exciting chases and brisk brawls, are just as frequently challenging; I'm above average in terms of playing ability, and even I died a total of thirty seven times on the default difficulty setting -- although I never ran out of lives -- as in addition to their overall difficult, if welcome, design, the bosses' attacks are sometimes poorly telegraphed or approaching genuinely unreasonable. Extra chances are plentiful, checkpoints are forgiving, and Game Overs are essentially meaningless, but be prepared for the game to get the better of you until you learn to deal with some of the challenges the bosses present, or swallow your pride and dial the difficulty down in advance if you're not up to the potential frustration. Hard mode in particular is aptly named, and even seasoned veterans may find themselves face down more often than expected on the way to the credits roll.
Wrapping this package up are charming graphics, if not spectacular ones, and one of the best soundtracks scored. I find music to be the second most important aspect of a game, behind the play itself, as it sets the tone, helps draw the player in, and can excite them for what is to come, or what is currently happening. Freedom Planet delivered beyond my expectations, and every track during the gameplay fails to disappoint, with certain stages and the boss themes enhancing the experience and adding to the enjoyment in ways that wouldn't be possible without it.
On the whole, Freedom Planet grabbed me with its sharp production values, and didn't let me go through the entire ride, surprising and delighting me time and again. It has some rough edges, but is regardless a legitimate classic, a game I can genuinely see myself playing and enjoying years from now, just as I have many of the games of the time it borrows from and subtly evolves the ideas of. When you think about how many games you can say that about -- and mean it -- you may realize that that is among the highest praise I could give it.

Freedom Planet is a pretty tight platformer that's kind of like a mishmash of Sonic and Ristar with one character, or like Sonic and Gunstar Heroes mixed with some other thing with another character. The way these characters play so differently while being able to play the same stages is a pretty good indicator that the devs had at least some idea what they were doing. Maybe some of it was a happy accident, who knows? Point is it's good and it's fun.
Look, I grew up on the Genesis. Maybe that's why the game grabbed me at first. Honestly though, it doesn't really make me feel like I'm playing one because of the fully voiced cutscenes and dialogue, which would be a problem if it actually mattered. I'm not crazy on the cutscenes, the story or whatnot, but they're nice enough to consider 'hey maybe people just want to play the game,' so there's a mode that's just playing the levels, and if you accidentally started story mode you get to just skip over all the cutscenes. Good feature.
Now I know a lot of you are saying that the bosses are unfair, that you have to try multiple times to figure them out before you even have a chance. While that's not entirely true, I will say you're probably going to lose a life or two before you pick up on some of the later boss patterns, even if you're perceptive. I know a lot of people would rather die before they tone down the difficulty, but there's actually a great feature where you can lower the difficulty before you load your file. (I mean not that I needed it, but as I said I grew up on the Genesis so I might be more used to the challenge.)
I guess what I'm saying is the game's good and the biggest complaints I'm seeing have workarounds.
...One complaint though, maybe patch in an audio slider. It's not a big deal in the era of audio mixers but it's a good feature to have so you don't have to mess around outside the game to adjust it to your liking.

I'll put this bluntly: If you were a fan of the Sonic franchise before it lost all sense of speed, overall production quality, and respect for its players' skills, then you will absolutely love Freedom Planet.
Not only does it emulate what made classic Sonic games good, it surpasses them;  Combat is more fun and complex than just jumping on things (or using cheap homing attacks like the modern games), Bosses are BRUTALLY challenging (and you beat them through SKILL, not cheapness) and the levels are masterfully crafted, with tons of secrets and achievements to hunt for.
All of this is available in either a Story mode, where you'll be treated to fully voice-acted in-engine cutscenes between every level, or a Classic mode if you don't care for the voicework or just want to keep the action flowing. Additionally, there are THREE characters with very separate and unique sets of gameplay mechanics (two available in Story mode, the third only in classic).  I've played through the entire game with all three, and I can say that even when visiting the exact same level or fighting the exact same boss (some levels/bosses are unique to certain characters, but most are shared) it became a different experience just from these characters' unique abilities. For example, Sash Lilac can periodically rocket herself in any primary or diagonal direction (and be temporarily invulnerable while doing so) while Carol Tea has wall-jumping, rolling and claw-strike attacks, and a truly awesome motorcycle. The third character, Milla, has very little health but can reflect most projectiles, and pick up powerups or generate blocks out of thin air to throw, while traversing verticle space with a klonoa-style limited flight.
If I had to nitpick anything about the game, it's a lack of multiplayer, and the voicework (while I personally enjoyed it) was for certain characters done with recording hardware of noticeably lower quality.  Neither of these small details made the game overall any less spectacular.

Brad Armstrong is a violent man and a reprehensible character, yet you can't help but sympathize with him starting at the very beginning of the game. LISA takes place in a post-apocalyptic world where there are no more women. One day, Brad stumbles upon an abandoned baby, and in shock (and slight horror) discovers that the baby he found is a girl.
This game has very complex themes including addiction, the cycle of abuse, attempted redemption, depression, and the meaning and implications of gender, so if that is something you don't want to be confronted by at this moment you best leave this game alone. However, complex and mature themes aside, this game is also really funny! It's really tongue-in-cheek with some dabbles of dark humor thrown in at some very unexpected (but highly appreciated) moments. LISA is also quite unforgiving sometimes, but mostly in the choices you are forced make in the game and the consequences that follow, but hey, you’re living in a post-apocalyptic world, life is rough! The art style and the character design is also fantastic. I'm really tempted on buying the art book because the style is equally as cute as it is weird, which is also a good description of the soundtrack too, which I also like for those exact reasons.
If you want to play an absurd, disturbing, complex, but also super funny RPG that will make you laugh and cry (I know I did), then I highly suggest LISA.
Awesome, Funny and relaxing, just buy this gem!

Bit Trip Runner 2 besides bringing a needlessly complex title, is an excellent rhythm-runner platformer that's an improvement in almost every way from its predecessor. It's a real treat playing and looking at this game.
This time Runner 2 brings a beautiful and joyful 3D graphics and style at the forefront, with large amount of details to every scene and characters that you are going to run past through at great speed. Everything is crisp and fluid, without ever dropping a single framerate, no matter how cluttered a level is with details, nor how fast the player is moving.
Again, story revolves around Commander Video, a music and rhythm-loving alien in another outrageous, silly and nonsensical adventure across the time and SPACE!!! There are more than 100 levels across 5 different thematic worlds, where the player's goal is very simple: Reach the end of every level without hitting a single obstacle while getting as much gold bars as possible. The trick is that Commander Video doesn't stops to smell the roses, ever, and the player has to navigate him across the carefully balanced levels of ever-increasing difficulty. Every couple of levels you are going to see a few new obstacles or alternate paths that you can take, making this game fairly long and almost never dull.
The second biggest improvement in Runner 2 is the control responsiveness. The first game had that delayed response when you were pushing a key, thus breaking the rhythm older levels had. This time control responsiveness is superb, with Commander Video reacting in a micro-instant as soon as you push a key, which adds to enjoying levels more and gradually becoming a master of the game.
Make no mistake, Runner 2 is only a slightly easier game than the original: it is still very difficult and sometimes frustrating game that is, however, more forgiving to player's mistakes. And this is the third most noticeable improvement: thanks to introducing an optional checkpoint system at the middle of every level, Runner 2 is a lot more forgiving and a lot less frustrating experience than the first game. You can still make this game as much difficult as you want, by increasing level of difficulty, taking more dangerous alternative routes, picking up optional unlockables and skipping checkpoints on purpose in order to get a large boost in overall success score.
There are only two major downsides to this game: problematic visual aesthetics of the later worlds and playing poorly on a keyboard. First two worlds, besides feeling vibrant, are also well defined and simple for player to get his bearing where Commander Video is and where he needs to go. The other three worlds, due to excessive color palette and outrageously unnecessary background details, can make navigating very difficult and can cause severe eye tiredness. If you are not switching game characters, like me, you are going to find very difficult controlling Commander Video as he easily blends with the level background and simply vanishes out of sight to your eye. Also, and this is the first time I admit it, having a controller to fully enjoy this game is a must have. While keyboard works well and feels extremely responsive, it's very inaccurate and unreliable to pull off more difficult moves and stunts. Runner 2 is made with an analogue controller in mind, and it shows on more difficult levels.
Overall, Bit Trip Runner 2 is a great indie gem and a game I wholeheartedly recommend to everyone who are looking for well-balanced and satisfyingly challenging, mechanics-focused game that also looks and plays wonderfully :)

Shadowrun Hong Kong may be the most mechanically superior game in the series, with improvements to the God-Aweful matrix aspect of the previous games, improvements to magic and skills etc. The combat, unlike Shadowrun: Dragonfall is very much improved and does not rely on enemies with a bunch of hit points for it's fights. The soundtrack has become much less techno, which could be considered good or bad. I, personally think the soundtrack is very good, more emotional and atmospheric. The greatest improvement in my opinion is to your team. In Shadowrun Returns you had no team, just a few story characters and a bunch of mercenaries. In Shadowrun: Dragonfall you had a team but they where terrible mechanically, had bad stats and used trash weapons. In this game, every unit on your team is good, you can justify the use of all of them regardless of your Player Character's role. Duncan Wu, aside from being the best story character ever, is an amazing Street Samurai character with good damage potential and utility, Is0bel is a solid Decker who can dish out great damage with her Grenade launcher, Gobbet fills a good support roll, has a great area of effect spell called Poison Cloud which is just amazing. I cannot speak for the optional characters, I killed Gaichu and never recruited Racter.
Anyway, besides the mechanical superiority to previous games, the story is much different. And may be offputing to fans of the series. But I say give it a chance, it's worth it

A huge disappointment after playing the excellent previous game in the series.  I wouldn't recommend SR: Hong Kong unless you are keen on Shadowrun games and it's on sale.
I enjoyed the main plot, art and music.  The devs clearly spent a lot of effort making assets for the new setting.
However, most aspects of the game are lacking.  There is no meaningful difficulty or balance, although some characters may be strapped for cash.  The Very Hard setting from previous titles is missing and on the Hard setting everything is laughably easy aside from maybe 2 fights in the entire game.  The shadowruns are short and simplistic, which is a shame because some of them could have been awesome had they been more than a mere concept sketch.  I felt like I spent twice as long outside of missions, running around being dripfed plot and subplots, as I did on actual shadowruns.  NPCs and party members are boring and uninspired, sometimes from blandness, sometimes from being a collection of too many adjectives.
Sadly, the devs seemed to think they were clever by frequently working in references to Dragonfall, which only served as a reminder of how much better that game was.

I don't usually make reviews but I just felt I had to make an exception for this game.
Disclaimer:
I recieved this game for free as a prize in a giveaway, while this does not change my opinion of the game itself in any way I want people to know this just so people can take this review at face value.
This RPG made by Harebrained Schemes as another title in their Shadorun series, this game is my first experience with the development team and the series itself outside of the actual Shadowrun RPG system.
They absolutely nailed the themes, tones and all around atmosphere of this game. It is one of the most immersive gaming experiences I've had and it really made me feel invested and 'part of' this rough futuristic society where the majority of the world is run by Megacorps and if you want to live 'freely' you usually need to turn to the shadows.
The music score in this game is part of what makes you feel so strongly about everything in the game, the vibes it gives off are almost always exactly what's needed to spice up a shootout or make you feel the high stakes of a delicate operation.
I would also like to mention the game's writing, the way world building is done in this game is executed very well imo, most of the NPCs you encounter in the game may not have a stake in your overall story but almost everyone has their own interesting story to tell you or some intriguing morsels of information about people you may of already met or just hear distant whispers about shadowy figures that you should watch out for. (Basically, the game really does a good job of putting you in the Shadowrun universe and not making it feel like a 'shallow' experience where only you and your party have actual personalities, everyone feels 'alive' in this game.)
The writing of your fellow party members is also one of my favourite parts of the game, because of how you get to chat with your party members between every mission and slowly learn more about them it really feels like you are bonding with them and it is an amazing experience to feel character development between your PC and an NPC just by remembering to chat to them when you have the time after missions.
Decking is a cool and unique (At least to me) system in the game that has Deckers navigate cyberspace in a blend of stealth, turn based combat and hacking games. (They involve following keypad button presses and figuring out patterns of code symbols.) I think that this system does bing more flavour into the game by giving Deckers a fleshed out area to show their skills but I dot hink there are a lot of program combinations which you can equip to easily force your way through every cyberspace encounter.
Finally, I would like to mention the combat system, while I overall enjoyed the combat a lot in this game I can see possible issues with it for other people, I played on normal and while a few encounters in the game were tough I never actually came close to dying once in the game. While I still enjoyed the experience since the turn based combat system is well refined (except for the annoying issue when you have several characters clustered together so it becomes extremely awkward to click on a tile nearby to move them into cover.) but the difficulty being too low on normal may turn some people away if they want a hard experience, while I haven't tried the hard mode I would advise looking up reviews which did play on hard mode so that you can come to a conclusion if you would enjoy the game yourself. ^^
Overall, I think this is an amazing RPG with a Cyberpunk setting that anyone with in interest in good writing, the Shadowrun universe or story heavy games should definitely check it out. (Sorry for making such a longwinded review but I wanted to cover everything I felt needed saying.)
Thanks to the devs for creating an incredible experience.

Another standalone entry in the Shadowrun series by HBS. Although the third entry in the series, it fails to really improve upon or even meet the quality of the masterful SR: DRAGONFALL. Imperfect, it still exploits a very rich campaign setting, pulling in some fun and fascinating characters to help you run the shadows (Gobbet being an absolute highlight), and weaving an interesting story of intrigue through its missions and LOADS of dialogue.
If you liked the previous entries in the series, SR: HONG KONG is still a must-buy. If you have yet to play a Shadowrun game, DRAGONFALL is still the best of the bunch by far. HONG KONG does little to improve technically or visually upon its prececessors, instead aspiring to play things safe and provide a new story using the same tools. Regardless, it's still a delight, and further proof that the Shadowrun series is in good hands.

This game is so much fun to play for any who miss and love the old style RPG. Good storyline to play through, interesting characters. The game is limited in that it follows a linear story arc, and of course it's not an open world; but it's no less fun. When I finished the extended play, all I could think was, I wish there was more.

As the third game in a trilogy SR:HK clearly learned from the minor mistakes and missteps of it's predecessors. The gameplay here is tighter and more responsive, the menus and interface are more streamlined and less clunky (although the inventory management is still cumbersome) and HK is a marked improvement on the previous two games in every technical sense. Bravo, HBS. It's rare to find a team of developers that listen so actively to the (mostly) constructive criticism of their fans.
The story is great: more personal than Dragonfall, longer and more complex than Returns and the general feel of being a Shadowrunner is more present in HK. From having a fixer set you up with runs from your base of operations to seeking out your own side gigs, you feel much more like an actual working Shadowrunner than the previous two games.
I only have two major criticisms of Shadowrun: Hong Kong:
-The long winded dialogue and expositional text-
When you play SR:HK be prepared to wade through thousands of lines of dialogue: both expository and conversational. There is a STAGGERING amount of text to read in this game and the criticism here is nothing to do with the content of the text, but the inefficient and long winded manner in which it is delivered.
Both Returns and Dragonfall had the same text driven mechanics yet those games were far tighter and more focused, they rarely if ever felt like a chore to read. HK loses it's edge here; It takes too long to get the point in many dialogue exchanges and simply put, many exchanges are rambling, long winded slogs that detract from the story experience and could easily be shortened.
Additionally, if you find yourself tiring of these novel-esque dialogue exchanges and choose simply not to explore a few of them, you can hamstring your chance at completing the game and getting the 'good' ending. Interactions with plot advancing NPC's are filled with text walls that could easily have been condensed to streamline the gameplay without any sacrifice to the story.
Diehard RPG fans are very quick to defend this criticism and label anyone who takes this stance as missing the point of RPGs, almost as though there is no middle ground between a total lack of world building dialogue an drowning in wave after wave or coldly delivered text boxes. The issue is not with the content, just the sheer volume and the manner in which it was delivered.
Look at the Elder Scrolls games; much of what you learn is delivered via books that you find in the world, conversations that you overhear walking through open world towns and cities. by nature of that game being voiced, the information is delivered more quickly and with greater clarity. When a game relies solely on text to convey story beats it needs to be more creative in the delivery of this text or it becomes repetitive.
Shadowrun Hong Kong has a great story to tell but the writers seem to have forgotten the single most important rule of storytelling.
Show, don't tell.
SR:HK doesn't show you anything, everything happens via expository text and after a while you just become numb to it.

-The companion characters-
Of the available companions in this game, I found only two the be worth the effort talking to. Gaichu and Racter. Both are awesome, well written characters: nuanced, complex and brimming with humanity. Ironic when you consider they are arguably the two least human members of your team in terms of their stories.
Duncan. one dimensional and cliched, his presence detracts from your connection to Raymond and the main story: his exclusion from the story would've made no difference whatsoever to your journey, if anything removing Duncan would've created a stronger bond between the player and their surrogate father. A forced subplot involving you, Duncan and Raymond comes up every now and then and you get to make a series of text based choices that are ultimately meaningless.
Gobbet and Isobel are utterly forgettable, especially Gobbet. Isobel's story at least ties into the main plot but her character is so forcefully unlikeable that it's a challenge to see it through. The problem with these two characters is that we don't SEE them do anything, their entire characters are already developed by the time we meet them and they've already known each other for years. Unlike Dragonfall where you slowly build the trust of Eiger, Glory and Dietrich, Or Coyote whom you forge a connection via saving her life, Isobel and Gobbet are like a pair of friends that just hang out with your character and occasionally drop in, they never really feel like part of your team. HBS again drops the ball here, telling us instead of showing us.
In closing, Shadowrun: Hong Kong is an amazing game and a truly stellar experience that I recommend to all Shadowrun fans, RPG fans and Cyberpunk enthusiasts. It has amazing artwork, engaging combat and great music. Unfortunately, while it has all the required elements for a top notch story, the game fails in the presentation. It relies too heavily on explaining every little thing instead of just letting the player experience the game and fill in the blanks themselves. You often feel like a spectator in your own story, something I never felt in the previous two games.
In spite of this jarring disconnect, the game is still magnificent and well worth your time and money.

It's been a while since I finished the game, so I won't dive in much details on how the game is. I might even consider a rerun of the game in the future, as there seemed to be a bit of replayability I can take out of the game, especially with choosing a different character progression.
Overall my experience was rather postiive.
The story was entertaining, with enough compeling plot lines to keep the action going. It never felt like I was going on pointless sidequest, as each mission explored more about the world of Shadowrun set in Hong Kong. Being someone who actually lives in Hong Kong, the references of locations are quite neat and are not too absurd. The character progression/customization you get to make when you progress through the game is enjoyable. I ended up being a dwarf(think it was a dwarf) with hacker capabilities and mostly use long ranged weapons.
Combat wise, I didn't find myself picking only certain companions for the mission, and used pretty much everyone, so I felt it was quite balanced.
My favourite part about the game was the lore, and the setting. The little quirks such as a note from a technican, was highly relatable for someone who does programming for a living and gave me a good laugh. I would mention some of the side characters you get that were quite unique, except that may just spoil the experience.
In conclusion I feel like this game would be a hit or miss, depending if you get into the lore. It was easier for me to get into it, given the setting (Hong Kong) it is based in. It was always fascinating for me to see how the developers gave their take on a cyberpunk Hong Kong.
My apology for a not so detailed review, but I did enjoy the game, so I figured I'll at least leave a positive review based on my own experience.

I have played Shadowrun Dragonfall and Hong Kong extended edition, both are excellent in their own setting and story. These games are for people who really like stories, reading to get inmersed in a reality that gives meaning to your actions. If you want constant purposeless action and you hate long dialogues and reading, this game is really not for you.
What I enjoyed about SR: Hong Kong is that the city and the culture hooked you to make you feel like you were really there and not just in any place, and definitely NOT in Berlin. Also the story is great, slowly growing and gripping you from the inside just like it grips everyone else around you. I'll never forget this story.
To add even more quality to the game, the extended edition is completely worth it. The ending I got from the bonus made it so worth it to the point that I'd like to play the game again some day, and I'm the type of guy that never plays games a 2nd time. Shadowrun's story and the way decisions impacts your game just makes me love it so much. Shadowrun games have officially become some of my favorite games.
*PERSONAL PROS*
+Great dystopian story.
+Decisions really impact your game in ways you sometimes can't imagine.
+Level of skills impact some of your dialogues and ways to solve problems.
+All the dialogues and long explanations push you to imagine you're actually there and some of them might be
rewarding. (some people would find this painful)
+Battle system is quite interesting with a great range of weapons, skills, cyberware and classes.
+Your characters have developped personalities and personal stories, that make some of the conversations really interesting and are strongly questionning morality. I loved getting to know my team.
+Definite replayability material.
*PERSONAL CONS*
-Difficulty could be tuned a bit better. Hard mode wasn't hard enough, I kept most of my med kits, grenades and drugs.
-You can't change the equipment of your teamates, though they get upgraded on their own as some of their abilities but you can still buy abilities to some of them. It would have been nice to at least be able to add or change a weapon to each one of them.
For me this game gets a 10/10 and I do not give a grade like this lightly. However everything depends on personal taste.

Imagine if you will instead of just tapping R to reload a gun you had to tap P to open your pocket cover, then hit G to grab the bullet in it, then hit P to pull the bullet out, then hit C to chamber the bullet, then hit T to♥♥♥♥♥♥the gun. There's a reason most action games don't overcomplicate the controls in combat.
That's the problem with this game. It pours buckets of needless complexity into it so the more used to it you are the better you'll do - which sounds better than it really turns out to actually be in this case. You can't just pick this game up and play like most offline fighter games. Every stance beats a different specific stance: Heavy beats balanced, balanced beats fast, fast beats air, air beats heavy. These stances (aside for air) are all changed by selecting the stances
. In addition to this every time you click the attack it'll be a different physical move. In many cases veering in a way entirely unlike the previous attacks. So you also have to deal with having to memorize the number of each attack in each stance to make sure they'll land somewhere that the opponent is standing.
What makes it so glaring is you have to tell it to tap 1, 2, 3, and spacebar to switch stances constantly if you want to have any honest chance of doing anything against an experienced player. You can't just rush in with a favorite stance and do anything. They'll switch to the perverbial paper that beats your perverbial rock (because for some reason it displays what stance you are in to the opponent). So you're forced to mess with the stances constantly lest they simply get all the hits.
Sadly the problems with this game don't end there.
Some moves are simply useless compared to other moves. Charge Attacks give the user an
. That's nifty except for the fact the user can release the charge anytime they like (including early) and they can start another one immediately after - there's nothing about it that leaves them open and in fact even makes them even more dangerous to approach due to the extra speed.
The game engine is clearly not designed with platforming in mind yet a lot of the stages require you to platform to compete. Whether you're fighting on catwalks, rooftops, balconies, rafters, or trying to run on walls (yes you can possibly do it, but seriously try fighting on those and tell me that felt like a good forumula of controls and environment).

The fact there is finally a game like this is a miracle. A sonic fangame gone rogue, its become some kind of astonishing hybrid of all the best Genesis titles, blended together in a fine puree. Some critics will argue that the game suffers from being slower-paced than the Sonic games we are all reminded of by this title--this is missing the point. This is what Sonic should have been all along. Let's get real, the Sonic franchise is not self-sustainable. I've played the old Sonic games and then thought to myself, what if I could have more? I thought about what that would mean, to have Treasure-inspired bossfights in a Sonic game. How would that look? How could you do that with the ring system? I've dreamt of working on a game like this, hoping that it would exist at all, but I kinda gave up on that concept many many years ago.
But here it is. Here it goddamn is, in a glorious mix of Rocket Knight, Ristar, Gunstar Heroes, Pulse Man, and yes of course Sonic. Hell there is even some Megaman in the stage design if you pay attention.
Is it a perfect game? No. Is it the perfect game for me? Oh my god yes. There is not much of a clear difficulty curve until the very end. The first two levels are easy enough but its hard to pick out a boss fight that's anything less than an adrenaline rush. If you don't like the pacing of oh say, Gunstar Heroes... No nevermind that thought. Gunstar Heroes is awesome, screw you.
Voice acting, not perfect. There's a super adorable character who the writing and acting side of me can't stand and yet I still find her cute? Without a doubt the main antagonist's voice acting steals the show. Look forward to that!
You will also notice some curious sprite imperfections. I won't call them errors just oversights.
Game can slowdown at times and will cause button inputs to get lost in translation, sometimes at critical moments. That could use some work if possible, but its something you can compensate for by acting quickly.
Some of the boss attacks are slightly cheap. You won't know they're coming the first time around.
Pretend its a Sonic game made by Treasure, then give it an actually attention holding plotline. Real basic stuff but they told it right and most of the characters are actually 3Dimensional. Those that aren't are 2Dimensional and that's more than I can say for the Sonic franchise (or Treasure for that matter).
But don't let any of that fool you. References to Treasure and Sonic team aside, this is GalaxyTrail now. Look what they did. They deserve a career. Give them a career. I will hunt you down if you don't give them a career. Cuz if they get and maintain some momentum people will be comparing future games to GalaxyTrail and Sonic Team and Treasure might become relics.

When I first heard of this game, I expected something I'd really love.
I wasn't disappointed.
Freedom Planet is a 2D platformer that takes elements from many other games and combines them into a new and interesting game. Yes, there are elements from Sonic. And Rocket Knight Adventures. And Gunstar Heroes. I haven't even played two of those three but I probably will if this game is any indication of their quality. It's not a rip-off of any one game/series in particular though.
Now that that's out of the way, what is there to like about this game? Well, a lot.
First off, the art is gorgeous, every level looks unique and there's a lot of detail put into every level. The music is also fantastic as well, not a bad track found here and the level themes all fit very well for the stages/bosses.
Also, the gameplay is, simply put, fantastic. There are 14 levels in all (though only 12 per storyline) and each is a rather large and rather diverse. They're all designed so that you can speed through them if you want, but also explore them to your heart's desire (as there are very few points of no return aside from screen transitions). The stages may take a while to get through the first time, especially if you explore around them, but soon you'll find that the speedrun achievement times are pretty darn generous.
Each of the three characters (with two more planned) controls differently and interestingly. Lilac has a double jump/attack and the aforementioned Rocket Knight dash, as well as an uppercut and downward kick that are both useful in combat and in platforming. Carol has an air dash that can lead into a powerful slash, an infinite wall jumping ability, and a close range flurry of kicks that also double as invincibility frames. Plus, finding a gasoline can gives her a motorcyle with contact damage at higher speeds, a double jump/attack similar to Lilac's, and the fastest base speed of any character in the game. Milla's a bit of an odd one out, with primarily ranged attacks and a shield that can be used to reflect projectiles back at opponents. She also has a flight ability similar to Tails (though far, far shorter). Though I personally prefer Lilac over the others, I have seen plenty of evidence to suggest that all three are quite good in their own distinct ways.
A few other comments about character controls: The lack of invincibility frames after being hit provides a further incentive to avoid damage, while also making some boss attacks especially deadly. All three characters can swim, and quite swiftly, making water stages much less something to be dreaded and actually quite enjoyable, though there aren't a large number of them. There are 5 different shields that all have their uses, every single one providing an auxillary function aside from protecting from a certain attack. And there's no knockback when you lose your shield, one of the worst mechanics that the classic sonic games had.
The bosses in the game start off pretty tame but ramp up in difficulty fast. You are expected to fail against many of them before you figure out how to dodge their attacks while dealing damage, but they almost never feel unfair and it's very rewarding to finally knock down a boss that's been giving you ire. The difficulty curve throughout the game is also very smooth, no sudden spikes or wildly varying difficulty curves. The game starts off fairly easy yet you hardly notice it when it's suddenly really bloody hard, because there's nothing that comes out of nowhere and puts a huge roadblock in your way. It's tough, but fair.
Unless you play on easy/casual mode, you wimp.
So yeah. The negatives, then. While I personally don't have a problem with it, the voice acting and story may put some off. There are, at the very least, a few scenes that go on too long or could've been cut entirely to keep the pacing of the game better. The story isn't amazing but it's passable, and the voice actors all do a pretty good job, though I'm not blown away by any of their performances. A few off the bosses aren't quite that great either, most notably the stage 6 preboss/boss segment as Carol, and the Lilac stage 7 and everyone stage 8 final bosses are also a bit on the tedious side. The lives system also seems a bit unnecessary, as there is, as far as I can tell, no real penalty for game-overs.
There's not much about this game that I can knock it down for, though, it's a very well designed game as a whole and tons of fun. I've clocked nearly 30 hours in under a week, which probably says something about how much I'm enjoying it. I bought an awesome game expecting an awesome game and I got what I came for.

I'll start out with the positives.  The character animation is great and the graphics overall are very nice.   There's also three different characters you can play as and they play differently.  The devs clearly put in a lot of time and effort on this game.
Now to the bad stuff.  The bosses are too hard, and bad part is they're hard for cheap reasons.  This is tied into the the character field of view being too close the character.  If the camera was pulled back a bit, a lot of the frustration of the bosses would be removed since there are many instances of attacks coming from off-screen blindsiding your character.  I'm not ♥♥♥♥♥♥ at games but from the halfway point on, some of these bosses aren't even coming down to memorization, just a matter if I'm getting lucky with not getting hit by some off-screen projectile at various points of the fight.  The close-in camera also makes navigating the large levels not as fun as it should be.  This leads into my next point.
Levels are also too large.  I know a lot of people will disagree with this but the stages just go on and on and by the time I get to the third or fourth screen of them, I'm more than ready for them to be over.  Pathfinding is also a bit of an issue since there are times when you have to go what appears to be backward to go forward.  I do give the devs credit for making the levels multi-tiered but they took it to far.
The story is bad and the voicework/audio recording is very inconsistent.  I normally wouldn't care about this in this sort of game since the gameplay is the thing that matters but there is a ton of story bits going on in Freedom Planet.  Your character also has audio cues every time they jump/attack/whatever and it can be annoying since you can't turn it off.  Unless you read or wrote Sonic fan-fiction at some point, you'll probably want to play the game on classic mode, which from my understanding, skips the story bits.
In short, a game with great animation but unless you're really down with hard, cheap bosses, you'll probably play the game and enjoy it enough until you hit a frustrating road block and just put the game aside.  It's not that the game is hard, I've played and beaten a lot of hard games, it's just that the hardness feels like it stems more from poor design in the later portions than a true sense of difficulty. That said, if you're into hard 2-D games, you're likely to have a good time with Freedom Planet.

I love this game. Imagine if Megaman and Dark Souls had a love child. Nongunz would be that glorious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
The design is great. It doesn't hold you by the hands and actively encourages you to experiment and learn the game mechanics on your own. There is some trial and error involved. There is a strong theme of death, gore and violence within the monochromatic 8-bit world.
The game is a metroidvania-esque rogue-lite shooter, with 8-bit enemies clawing, stomping, chewing, and even shooting caustic mucus at you. There is a risk-reward element in place to encourage you to play defensively and not rush in like leeroy jenkins on crack. You can burn your stat cards to get a bit of health back and continue exploring the mausoleum, or you could keep the stats and try to recover a tiny bit of health by viciously murdering enemies in quick succession without getting hit. You can invest your points in your loadouts, like purchasing ability skulls, stat cards, or weapons.
The weapons themselves feel satisfying. The shotguns are beastly at close range, while the rocket launcher vaporizes most enemies. You inner murder beast will feel sated.
The minimalist approach to story is very reminiscent of the Souls series. You know there is a strong thematic connection between the elements in the game's world, but it is up to you to dig deep and find out what that is for yourself.
The cemetary hub and funeral parlor world of the early stages let you know youre in for a dark treat.
The game is well worth the price of admission, so check it out!

This is, without a doubt the most fun I've ever had playing a platformer. It's the best platformer I've played with Rayman Origins and Ducktales Remastered right behind. Everything about it is so...perfect. The music, the animation, the visuals, even the gameplay for once, just fantastic. It's really the perfect Sonic the Hedgehog game. Basically what happens is that a mysterious monster has erased Sonic and his friends, as well as the young Sonic (Sega Genesis era) and Tails. Now, Sonic(s) must race through their past to restore it and their friends. Young Sonic's gameplay is more 2D, and is like the Genesis games with a modern touch (although light), and its great, as good as the old sonic games. In the modern Sonic sections, that's where the game gets great. They really finally did it. They made 3D sonic great. It combines the fast paced nature of Sonic Adventure 1, with the platforming of Sonic Adventure 2, and it works fantastic. Overall, I can't say enough good things about this game. Believe it or not, I was actually like, close to tears when I played this. The good kind of tears, it was just completely overwhelming to a long time sonic fan, its just so great.
There are a couple bad things. One is very minor, and is that the main stages are a bit too easy. You have to try very very hard not to get below a B rank, and I only remeber running out of lives once, on a boss fight. Not to say that there aren't challenges though, there's lots of sub-missions that are plenty challenging, and there are a lot of them. And there are time records, all sorts of stuff to add lots of replayability. The collectibles are great, and its fun to team up with other sonic characters to accomplish them.
Another thing that is a minor complaint is although the diversity in the levels is astounding, there are some times when I said "wait, wasn't there a segment just like this in the previous level?" This is also minor, and is present in most games, so its no big.
Pretty much the last thing I can possibly say about this thing is that its kinda cheesy, it's adorably cheesy though, I'll be rolling my eyes, but honestly, this is pretty great for a Sonic game, which has had lots of uh...groan worthy writing in the past.
Lastly, there's pretty much no story, its there, but it is pretty generic, but its fine, and obviously is there to provide context for this remix of games.
Oh, and the boss fights are mixed, they're not great, but there's been worse, and the only real problem with them is the gameplay of it, in that they're simple, but I don't mind, really, they're not really awful like some.
All in all, all of these complaints, I'm just trying to force myself to say something bad. You have to understand, it is a sensational game. If you haven't got it already, get it. Do it. Honestly the only reason that you wouldn't at least enjoy it a little bit is if you really, really, really hate platformers, or uh, action games, or fun.
Buy it
do it

You finally did something right, Sega.

Wow. Just... wow. If you like sonic, or even just platforming in general, get this game. Period.
It runs at an amazing 60 fps on my PC at high settings on a 32" hdtv, and looks absolutely gorgeous. Like, really. This is the best a sonic game has ever looked. It has full controller support that's as easy as plugging in a wired xbox 360 controller, going into this game's settings, choosing to use the xbox controller, and starting the game. And unlike other games designed for a keyboard/mouse that are just compatible with a controller, this game is truly designed for a controller and is 70 times better with one. So, if you have a wired xbox 360 or ps3 controller hanging around, use that.
This is a perfect combination of classic and modern sonic. It literally has a remade version of levels from nearly every one of the main console sonic games for both classic sonic (who makes an amazing return in HD), and modern sonic (who is even better then before!).
If you're a sonic fan, get this. There's so many references to sonic games from all eras that even if you've only played one sonic game you'll probably understand a lot of them.
But that makes you think "Oh. Well, I have to be a sonic fan to enjoy this." No. Not at all! Even if you're not a sonic fan and/or have never even played a sonic game, I still say get this. You may not understand all the references, so it won't be AS enjoyable, but it's still the best sonic's ever been in 3D (in my opinion) and it really isn't complicated. It's a platformer, after all. It's still built off of the basic platforming base. Just run and jump. There's just more stuff added on top of that.
My only complaint is that this game is too short. They put a lot of effort into it, which is great, but they took so much time on making sure it was enjoyable that in the end they had to make a huge amount of rehashed missions for each stage just so they could actually sell this as a game with enough content to keep you going for more then a day.
However, there is an online mode. That's right, this game has a mode in which you can race to the end of a stage as fast as possible and put your best time on the leaderboards. It's great fun replaying a stage 100 times just to try and beat that one record. It also has a "30 second trial", in which you have 30 seconds to try and see how far you can get in one stage. Once your time runs out, the length you traveled in the level is posted to the leaderboards.
The best part, though, is that the PC version solves the "too short" problem entirely because of mods. There are so many mods for this game you'll never run out of stages to play. One mod ports all the levels from sonic unleashed on xbox 360/ps3, one ports stages from Sonic 06, one ports stages from sonic adventure, there are even mods that have entirely new stages in them, such as "Meponterations". And with new mods being made every day, you'll never get bored.
In brief, this is an amazing piece of art and probably the best sonic's ever been in 3D. Well, maybe not the best, but at least the best in the last decade. Overall I recommend this. 9/10.

Hi, after a little more than 20 hours of playing (didn't use any help) I want to share with you my impressions of this game!
First of all, I love watching documentaries on history, espionage and conspiracy theories, so to me the game's setting based on the Russian nuclear submarine Kursk K-141, which sank under unclear circumstances in August 2000, is quite compelling. Playing a Russian secret agent, your investigations in the murder of an undercover partner imply that a criminal organisation stealing Russian weapon systems might be interested in the nuclear submarine Kursk K-141.
The story then takes you onboard the submarine to conduct further investigations and covers 9 chapters. My first playthrough took me ~20 hours which I find sufficient for a game priced at 18€. I've seen games three times as expensive offering a considerably shorter playtime. Furthermore, unlike many other games which I stopped playing after a few hours because they just didn't thrill me, Operation Kursk's storyline was overall exciting and I always felt motivated to keep playing.
However, the last two chapters felt a little like recycling to me, I personally would haved merged them into one chapter.
Focussing on the technical aspects, the game honestly can't compete with blockbusters like GTAV in terms of graphics and animations. However, that didn't really bother me because I think it still creates an authentic athmosphere. Yet, I have to agree with Gwynlar that the voice acting isn't good (both in English and German versions) and generally lacks some passion. This actually disturbed me a little but after some time I got used to it and I felt it got better after the first chapter.
On the other hand, I have good news for all of you who are annoyed by the fact that hardly any recent game was released or even patched bug-free: I did not encounter any bugs throughout my entire playthrough!
Most of the item combinations and interactions were pretty logical, some required a little creativity, and a few weren't really conclusive to me and I didn't know how to proceed in order to advance the story - especially when I needed to use one item multiple times in a row to trigger a reaction. But probably this is the nature of a Point and Click Adventure and makes up its charm - sometimes you just have to find out by trying things which don't seem obvious at first.
In summary, the aspects I liked and did not like about Operation Kursk K-141 were:
+    overall thrilling story and setting, authentic athmosphere
+    no bugs
+    sufficient playtime
+/- item combinations/interactions and puzzles
-     technologically a little outdated
-     rather passionless voice acting
I would give the game an overall rating of 7.5/10 and recommend it to fans of Point and Click Adventures in particular and generally to anyone who likes to uncover the truth about a conspiracy theory, set against a thrilling background. If you are someone who doesn't put state-of-the-art graphics first (people who don't mind playing GTA San Andreas or  Minecraft know what I mean) and if you want to enjoy a stable game without bugs, you will be fine provided you accept the rather passionless voice acting.
