When gamers think of a spiritual successor to the Mother series, they tend to think of Undertale. However, having played both games I can say without a doubt that the LISA series deserves that title more.
I don't want to give away much of the story, as that is one of the game's greatest strengh; what I can say is that it is gritty, and thought provoking to say the least. Much of the setting is inspired by Fist of the North Star; for those who don't know what that is, basically the game has a post apocolyptic setting in a barren, dry wasteland.
Unlike the Mother series, the main character is not a blank slate.
LISA The Painful is the only game that I have ever played where I actually cared about the story.

•	Developer: Dingaling
•	Publisher: Dingaling Productions, LLC
•	Genre: Adventure/RPG
•	Release date: Dec 15, 2014
•	Played on: PC
•	Price: $9.99
•	Play time: 11 hours
**Spoiler Alert*** This game is demented!
The man sees some kids playing with fire and asks me if I can grab a bucket of water and put out that fire. I oblige by grabbing the nearest bucket and tossing the liquid on the kids, setting them aflame. The startled man quickly informs me that I just used his bucket of gasoline, the water one is further up the hill. Panicked, I climb the hill and grab the bucket of water only to return moments later to piles of ashes where the children once were.
They say the road to Hell is paved with good intentions and that would be a fitting tagline for this game. Lisa is a 2D side scrolling RPG set in a post-apocalyptic world full of weird characters and some of the most disgusting degenerates all wrapped up in a charismatically drawn world. Players take control of Brad, a Joy addicted empty husk of a man seeking redemption by raising and safeguarding one of the world’s few remaining females.
Lisa begins with a series of flashbacks to show Brad’s life and how he became the man he is at the start of the game. Bullied as a kid, an abusive father, drug addiction…but all that seemed to have changed when he came across an abandoned infant one day. He brings the child home to his flat to show his friends and they’re all surprised to find out that the child is a female. Brad then enlists his friends to help take care in raising this girl. They build a basement for her, cover her face in a mask to disguise the fact that she’s a female and Brad even comes to grips in taming his Joy habit for the benefit of his new daughter. However, things don’t always go well in this world and Buddy is kidnapped, most of brad’s friends are murdered which sends Brad on a hunt to rescue his daughter. Occasional hilariousness and often a metric ton of depravity ensues.
I found the game full of dark humor and even some touching moments but there are also some deranged portions so some people might be put off by some of the situations that occur. Lisa is pretty much the opposite of last year’s Undertale in overall tone even though this game does have a few life lessons to be learned.
Traveling around the world takes place in 2D; people are met, ladders are climbed and caves are explored all using adequate graphics. The artstyle isn’t impressive but it is creative with a style of its own. There are roughly 30 companions ranging from clumsy wrestlers, to a two-legged fish that is a lawyer. There’s not Obsidian level depth in these characters but each one has a personality of their own which is seen through the level up screens and the initial dialogue. The biggest example of all the differences between the characters come from their abilities in combat. There’s a slew of different weapons, attacks, buffs and debuffs to choose from and it’s almost a challenge to find out which characters deserve a space in the party.
It’s sort of good that the characters aren’t too memorable or that there are so many of them that their abilities are pretty interchangeable because they can be taken and even perma-killed occasionally. There are a couple bosses that have instant death attacks, resting can get one of your party members ransomed for a fee and other unfortunate endings can await the player character’s companions if the player so chooses. Of course, this sort of misfortune often befalls the PC also and the player will be called upon to decide if a companion is worth one of Brad’s limbs. Choosing to disfigure Brad will usually rescue a companion but will limit Brad’s effectiveness in combat by reducing the number of combos he can do.
Combat is turn-based and the various RPG stats determine the order of turns, amount of damage done and accuracy while equipment boosts attack, defense and resistances. It’s all standard fare. The characters’ attacks however, is where the variety comes in with Brad and a few other characters using a button combinations for attacks while others use words to debuff the enemies and others use special abilities with their weapons to be useful. As I mentioned before, it takes a while to swap out characters and test out their abilities but it’s fun to give each character a test run and see what they are capable of.
The game is pretty good when it comes to choice and consequences besides the limb vs companion choices I previously mentioned. I had some somewhat friendly guys approach me and offer to buy some Molotov cocktails from me only to find that they used them in a most heinous way. This prevented me from meeting certain characters and removing what could have been a bunch of side quests from the game.
Another thing I found satisfying is the world’s economy in the game. Porno mags have turned into a form of currency and it’s something that, while found in abundance, isn’t always easy to keep with the party members being ransomed, new characters sometimes taking a large amount to hire them and new equipment being so expensive. There are certain areas in the game that random encounters occur and I could grind my way towards more cash but I gave up my grinding days years ago.
In the end, this game just stuck in my head a lot longer than most RPGs due to the story and the way the world’s situations were handled. Lisa left me wondering if all my decisions were worth it in the end. I still have yet to play through the DLC just because the end of this game has really stuck with me. Lisa does a good job of separating itself from other RPGs but the dark nature might not be right for everyone.

Probably one of the best strategy games available anywhere right now. If PC is good for one thing, it is the strategy genre, and Civ V exhibits everything that this genre is capable of.
The gameplay is simple enough to be engaging, while complex enough to plan and strategize in a meaningful way. The leveling in this game is great, and different units don't counteract one another after they level up, at least not in a way that they probably would in other games; there is always a balance in your units, at least if you know what you're doing. I have only played domination games (which is how this game should be played), and i can say that the warfare in this game is solid. Whether it's shaka surrounding you with hoppi warriors, or persia nuking your air bases, when in warfare, the game ALWAYS forces you to think of a contingency to something.
If there are some gripes I have with this game, it stems from the AI. While not as bad as the AI in 6, it is very inconsistent, and does not always make smart moves when it comes to warfare. The AI is usually good with technological strides, however. The difficulty does not imrove or lower the AI, only gives them benifits beforehand.
tl;dr, if you like strategy games, Civ V has to be in your library. I would definitely reccomend it, even over Civ 6.

WARNING: THE FOLLOWING REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS...somewhat
This is a true love letter to fans of old-school, 16-bit 2D platformers. Freedom Planet takes the best elements of other retro platformers such as Megaman X and Sonic the Hedgehog and combines them into an extremely fast-paced, and incredibly fun 2D platforming adventure.
The stages are massive and are quite lengthy, but they are so incredibly detailed and crammed with alternate paths and hidden goodies that will have you revisiting them either for finding collectables or for speedrunning purposes.
The characters all control really smoothly and are very responsive to button imputs. They are all balanced along with having unique abilities that let them travel to different parts of stages. And some characters will visit their own exclusive stages in the story mode.
The boss battles are excellently designed as they prove to be challenging and rewarding but not unforgiving.
The music is amazing. Every song fits each stage perfectly and the music during the cutscenes in the story is also really good. The music is catchy, upbeat, and are good tunes on their own.
The difficulty is gradual as it naturally scales upward, increasing in difficulty the further you are in the story mode.
Speaking of which, the story mode itself is done well and does make you feel like you are on an adventure and the game gives you the feeling that you're fighting for freedom. In terms of the tone, with the exception of one VERY dark scene in the middle, the story is light-hearted and the writing is innocent, cute and cheesy. It basically plays out like any ordinary Saturday morning cartoon. Though I will say it is unusal for a 2D platformer to have a story with cutscenes and voice-acting.
Unfortunately the voice-acting is not very good. In fact it borderlines on being cringe-worthy at times. Sometimes the voice actors try to sound overly dramatic but it just comes out flat and laughable (I'm looking at you Torque). Maybe that's more of a personal preference but I didn't particularly enjoy the voice acting that much in this game. The only exception to this however is the voice of Brevon, whose voice and acting for that matter is AWESOME!! Everyone else is below-average to meh. Not the worst I've heard and I give the voice actors credit for doing their best, but it's not that good either.
However the animation for the characters during gameplay and in the cutscenes is extremely well done. The characters are very expressive and all have unique, emotional and even some humorous animations.
So in conclusion, well taking a step back for a second, it's easy to see where Freedom Planet gets its inspiriation from. The selection of multiple characters, each controlling differently and having different paths in the story mode is definitely akin to Sonic 3 & Knuckles' structure. I mean heck almost all stages have a mid-boss and an end boss and both the mid and end stage bosses have their own theme songs. Also the fact that the music changes between the acts of a stage is definitely reminiscent of Sonic 3 & Knuckles. There are also a lot of other Sonic tropes, shall we say, that are quite noticable in the stages such as springs, loop-de-loops and the fact that Lilac's running animation is similar to that of Sonic's running animation. Carol even has a rolling attack that follows the same physics as the rolling ball and spin dash in the classic Sonic games. Though I'm not sure why she has the Megaman X wall jump, huh. The game moves at a very fast pace and it's easy to say that this is just a Sonic clone. To which you wouldn't be completely wrong.
However, if the whole "This game looks like a Sonic clone" is the one thing that is preventing you from buying this game, then don't you worry. This game may look like a Sonic clone but trust me, put aside any doubts you might have in your mind because Freedom Planet is one hell of a good time. Sure it might not be completely original, but it combines and, in my opinion, improves upon elements of other games and is superior to the old 16-bit style 2D platformers of the Super-Nintendo and Sega Genesis era and mostly importantly the game is just incredibly fun to play. It's $15.00 that you'll love. I give this game the strongest recommendation that I could give to any game as it has become one of my favorite games of all time.

Castle Invasion: Throne Out isn't really much to look at overall. It's a simple lane defense style game on par with Plants vs. Zombies, but with a little more action involved. You control an archer who just bought a castle and must defend it from the evil king and his hordes by running along the outter rim and shooting arrows, spears, etc., at the approaching foes. You can also upgrade them for maximum damage, as well as your speed to race from top to bottom.
That said, I absolutely [em]loathe[/em] the controls. Up and down arrows control the direction of your hero, q and e survey the land and return to the castle, and time trial levels use a and d to speed up or slow down approaching enemies, while space bar fires. It doesn't seem like much but it's actually quite the complicated, uncomfortable controller scheme, especially when you have to use the number keys to switch out weaponry.
The muscles in my arms are actually tight and in a bit of pain from the tension I put on them playing this. Although that could just be from stretching for the proper keys or how fast (and near uncontrollable) you become with fully upgraded footwear. Plus, there are certain levels (like stage seven) where you can just replay constantly and quickly upgrade your weapons as far as you can take them.
Overall, for a little casual game made in Unity (no, not the broken Unity that most horror games on Steam are made from), I'm honestly having a lot of fun. The price point seems a bit steep at nearly $5, but what you get is something simple, well crafted, and quite addicting. I intended to only play a few rounds and wound up sinking in over an hour just advancing to level eight and then grinding for coins to upgrade my gear. If you enjoy a good lane defense but want a little more mobility than what most will offer, Castle Invasion: Throne Out is worth checking out.

With an evil curse cast upon the Carrot Kingdom and the local hamsters turning into flesh eating groundhogs.. It's all up to you Sir Knight! Time to defend the Kings carrot crop, save the day and possibly win a few hearts.
Knight of the Hamsters is more about highscores and
fun, then in-depth story or game mechanics. Each level tasked with a simple goal, survival through waves while defending the royal carrots. Killing hamsters rewards gold drops which could be spent on upgrading several pieces of equipment. Shoes (runspeed), Sword (melee-dmg), dagger (range-dmg), cross (magic-dmg) and armour. While treasure chests randomly spawned which contained both health and mana for spells. Day/Night cycles become critical, during the day hamsters require less damage to kill and during night were much more aggressive, so you needed to plan your spending accordingly. Progress further through the game you will come across several boss-like species of hamsters while also gaining the ability the unlock several heroes each with their own unique abilities.
As someone who plays a lot of platformers I did find the game challenging. Some people this may be a little bit of a turnoff while others will thrive on it. Game did include a family friendly mode which I thought was a nice touch, basically removed all gore and you won every round (while still having fun!) To the developer I would suggest adding a 'normal' mode with simple tweak. 1) Initial waves should have lowered gold costs on upgrades. Would
to see online co-op implemented if viable and the ability to pickup chests or upgrades while moving would be a big plus for all modes.
Simple, clean artstyle which is more then suitable with 200 odd hamsters nipping at your heals. Great soundtrack that really ramped up during the nighttime sequences and very responsive controls, though I would suggest a gamepad else you might get frustrated quickly. Price might be a little high but it's enjoyable so gets my recommendation, Quick pick-up, play while releasing the fury kind of game. Worth keeping shortlisted at the very least. Cheers. :)

edit: Thanks to the developers recent update improving the difficulty spike of the game I have decided to change the review to positive and have updated my review with changes to reflect my new opinions.
This game is mad fun! I never expected so much from this game.
At first glance I thought the gameplay was really standard and was unintuitive. However as I got further through the levels surviving longer it became extremely fun and tense to play. The controls consist of a ranged attack, melee attack and a special ability. The goal of the game is to protect carrots from being taken by the hamsters. The levels are designed really nicely in a way that you need to run about consantly jumping from carrot to carrot to be able to protect them successfully. And then at night time the hamsters turn into zombies and start attacking you. This makes for a nice contrast between the day and the night and instead leaves you running for your life.
The hamsters themselves have a nice variety of different species/classes that make them fun to fight. You have types such as armoured hamsters, mages or flying hamsters and a tonne more. This variety keeps you having to switch up your gameplay tactics to survive successfully.
The upgrade system also adds to the gameplay. You are able to upgrade your weapons, speed and armour. These are bought during levels via the coins you earn while playing. It is pretty much impossible to play without using these as you will die very quickly.
Unfortunately this game is very difficult to play at currently with a keyboard. When loading the game you can't even access the options menu with the keyboard from the initial menu as far as I can tell. The game is also flooded with xbox button prompts no matter whether you have an xbox controller plugged in or not.  I wouldn't recommend buying this game unless you have an xbox controller.
The graphics are not the strong point of the game. Although they do have some very nicely designed character models for the hamsters that I would like to praise. The problem is the textures on things like grass aren't particularly well done. The background on the level select screen in screensot 2 on the steam page does look really nice though. Because of how fun the gameplay was I decided the graphics didn't really matter and could be overlooked.
The story is another weak point of the game. It is a fairly boring and cliched story. However this is another point that I decided I could overlook due to the absolutely amazing and fun gameplay!
The absolute highpoint of the game has to be the soundtrack though. This adds amazingly to the experience. The soundtrack is full of a great mixture of tracks such as oldschool video game music and dance tracks. It is truly incredible and a great pleasure to listen to.
So overall these are my thoughts in summary-
Overall I would definitely recommend this game to anyone. The gameplay is insanely fun and is really addictive. I myself will definitely be playing a lot more of this game.
Disclaimer: I was given a free press key by the developer of the game.

As a huge fan of Dragonfall, I was very excited to play Hong Kong. Despite having a good story and incredible atmosphere, it is unfortunately plagued by technical problems, the worst of which is the loading screens. More than half my playtime was spent staring at loading screens, and this just isn't fun no matter how good your game is. Selecting enemies is a pain, as it seems you have to put the cursor directly over their ankle or else it won't register them, and many times I tried to click on an enemy only to have the character run directly beside them and do nothing, because my pointer was a centimeter off.
Sometimes, you can run out of an area fast enough to cause NPCs to become trapped. This happened in the bonus campaign with the NPC who takes you to your missions, which is pretty game breaking. HD textures will also cause your game to crash at a specific end-game level, for some obscure reason.
Also, the "matrix" secitons were truly ruined, one of the highlights from the previous games. It feels like they just throw tons of enemies at you and turn hacking into a series of obnoxious minigames, and it gets to a point where it's just too much. I stopped bothering to try Matrix runs because I would set off the alarm every time, even when I got a near-perfect run.
There are dozens of minor issues that make playing this game more of an annoyance than entertaining. It's a shame because once I actually finished the game, I could appreciate what they were going for, but I would never replay it and sit through hours of loading again.

This is by far the most fun I have had in front of my PC in a long time, and some of that time I was actually sitting by the window of my room enjoying the atmosphere it created in my mind. That is something this game does like very few others: It draws you into the story and the setting so well, you almost feel as if you ARE leading a team of shadowrunners. This is mostly due to the incredible detail of the scenery as well as the expertly crafted character conversations.
However, if you are looking for a fast-paced adventure with RPG elements set in the Shadowrun universe, I would recommend "Boston Lockdown", which puts a lot more emphasis on the action than the story. In this game, you can complete entire missions by talking and hacking your way around having to fight people, which often results in really cool dialogues. This is made possible because, like in the pen and paper RPG "Shadowrun", you get experience at the end of a mission, so the amount of "kills" you get are irrelevant (unless otherwise specified of course).
DO get this game if you:
- enjoy well-told stories
- enjoy leading a team of operatives in more ways than clicking on orders
- enjoy finding alternative routes to solve missions other than gunning people down
- love cyberpunk in general or Shadowrun specifically
DO NOT get this game if:
- long meandering conversations about a character's past or what they had for lunch bore you
- you love fast-paced action sequences (it is turn-based)
- you think magic has no place in cyberpunk
- you hate east-asian settings in general or China in particular
If you've played the others, don't miss out on this one.  If you haven't, what are you waiting for?

TL;DR:  If you already like Sonic games, this is an easy recommendation.  If you're new to the series or not well-informed, this is a great way to see what you've been missing.
I've had this one for a little while.  Since I accidentally deleted my save when I screwed up my graphics settings, I decided to give this game another go-through.  Once again I'll mention
Sonic Generations is both a new game and an anthology of sorts.  It's Sonic's birthday (and this was Sonic's 20th anniversary as of the year it was released), and this mysterious Time Eater thing kidnaps everyone and takes them to this white void where time stands still...and where familiar locales are also present.  And it is in this white space where Sonic meets his past self.  What is the Time Eater, and why has it stolen all of these Zones away?
Gameplay in Sonic Generations is split between two characters, Classic Sonic and Modern Sonic.  Classic Sonic plays much like he does in the Genesis games.  He doesn't have the Homing Attack, but he
Spindash, and most of his gameplay is focused on sidescrolling platforming.  His stages are "2½D" in that even though the course can turn and bend, he still really only follows two planes.  This is most evident in some parts of Sky Sanctuary.  Modern Sonic plays like a cross between the day stages of Sonic Unleashed and Sonic Colors.  He lacks the Spindash but he has a Boost Meter powered by rings and defeated enemies for a nigh-invulnerable surge of speed, his Homing Attack returns, he grinds on rails, he can quickly move to the side or drift for a hard turn, he does tricks off of ramps for more Boost, and he has some 2D sections too, though there are a few 3D platforming sections.  Both characters need to get to the end of their respective Acts to clear the Zones.
The game is split into three sections representing three eras of Sonic:  Classic, Dreamcast, and Modern, and each section has three Zones and are guarded by a boss that comes from that era.  Every Zone has two Acts, one for each Sonic.  Just clearing the Acts isn't enough to progress to the boss however--clearing all six Acts for the era unlocks Challenge Gates for every Zone in that era.  To get the three keys to unlock the boss door, every Zone in that era needs to have just one Challenge Gate cleared (and you need to physically go get the key from the hub world too).  It doesn't matter which Sonic completes which Gate, so long as each Zone has one clear to its name.  And this isn't even enough to open the final area.  The Chaos Emeralds are once again given to you through gameplay, though they're mostly given for boss battles.  And in each era, there are Rival Battles where Sonic faces off with an era-relevant hedgehog.
Even though this is a "greatest hits" of sorts for Sonic, the returning Zones aren't copy-and-pasted rehashes of old locales, and they're more like remixes with plenty of callbacks to old features, even if they aren't represented as Zones in this game.  Green Hill Act 1 has the corkscrews from Emerald Hill, the spinning top platforms from Marble Garden get a makeover for Sky Sanctuary Act 1, the street boarding section from City Escape is greatly expanded, and the Mad Convoy section in that Zone returns...with a vengeance.  The returning bosses also get amped up, so old tactics won't work as well this time around.  But this is the perfect opportunity to mention the Skill Shop, a shop set in the hub world where you can use the points for clearing Acts to buy skills to customize each Hedgehog.  While there aren't very many to start, you can unlock more by clearing challenges or beating the game.  The issue is then keeping the cost of all of the skills below 100, which can be pretty tricky since naturally the more powerful ones cost more.  And yes, Super Sonic in stages returns, but you'll have to clear the game first and it'll take up all 100 of your skill points to use.
There's a lot of content here, though if you want to blow through it all, you can probably go from start to finish in a few hours no problem.  If you're a completionist though, look out.  Clearing every Act and boss fight is just to get to the end of the game--can you finish every Challenge Gate?  Get all of the Red Rings scattered through both Acts of every Zone?  S-rank every Act?
Getting Red Rings will unlock artwork in the Collection Room to the far left of the hub world, and every cleared Challenge Gate will have a bell to ring, which releases a music note you have a short amount of time to chase down and collect which will reward you with either more artwork or music to listen to in the Collection Room.  Said Collection Room also has a section to review character profiles and rewatch the movies from the game if you want.
I can safely say when I do a review of a Sonic game, I'm going to mention the music.  This game is no exception, and I really liked how both Sonics had a variation of the same theme for each Zone, much like how the music for most Sonic games starting with Sonic 3 did.  Better yet, all of the music you collect through the Challenge Gates and Red Rings can be used for the music for whatever Act or boss fight before you begin.  If you want to fight the final boss to Green Hill Zone, you're free to!  You'll just need to unlock them first.  The hub world also has its own spin on the Zone or boss music when you're near the entrance, so that's a nice touch.
There is a level of polish here I could appreciate.  Consider you free one of Sonic's friends for completing a Zone's two Acts.  The comments they each say differ depending on which Sonic was the second one, though most comment about Classic Sonic looking different than the one they're used to.  One of the movies is also different depending on which Sonic you're using, though unfortunately there's no way to view the "other side" version of it or hear the other friend responses without starting a new game and erasing your old save (or you can back it up first, naturally).
Getting hit in this game is an exercise in frustration.  Both Sonics tend to do the "dazed for a second" thing that started in Sonic Heroes, though there's a skill to negate that.  The big issue I had was that the rings are especially difficult to grab once they've flown out.  Classic Sonic is stuck to the 2D plane but it seems like the rings aren't, and a few times it seems like Modern Sonic's rings were just fake trying to pick them back up.  There aren't any shields in this game (except as skills for Classic Sonic), and while you only drop a portion of your rings when hit if you have enough, just trying to retain those last few can make survival a bit of a challenge.
I honestly didn't like how there was so little mention of the handheld titles apart from a small handful of songs from the Gameboy Advance and Playstation Portable games.  This is more of a personal issue, but I grew up with a Game Gear and never owned a Sega home console, and it's a little disappointing how all of those games just got glossed over.  For as popular as Sunset Park Act 3's unique theme is, even it didn't get a remix here.  Sad.
My rig chugged at a few times, but that's not something I can really hold against the game.  It doesn't scream "bad port" like some games, but if you're looking to buy this, make absolutely sure you have a good enough machine.
This will be a nostalgia trip for many.  For those like me where it isn't, there's still a lot of fun and enjoyment to be had here.  Can't complain about the controls, and while a game clear won't take very long, 100%ing this game will keep you busy for a while.

If you've ever been a fan of the Sega Genesis and its games, then I can guarantee you'll love this game. It's got great gameplay, excellent spritework (barring a few inconsistencies) and splendid music! Freedom Planet is easily my favourite indie game I've played this year!
There's even a demo that you can try out, if you're still on the fence on buying it:

A game that, honestly, I was apprehensive about buying. I was so wrong. Freedom planet make look like "Deviantart the Game" on the outside, but once you get into it, it's alot of fun.
The controls can be a bit loose sometimes, but overall there aren't many major problems there. The gameplay is incredibly reminiscent of many Sega classics such as Ristar, Rocket Knight and , of course, Sonic the Hedgehog. Rather than jumping on your foes to kill and damage them, characters have a variety of punches, kicks and dashes to deal damage up close.
Fans of Treasure games (Gunstar heroes, most notably) might feel right at home with many of the visuals in Freedom Planet. In fact, there's even a boss that i'm certain is a reference to Gunstar Heroes itself. The art is incredibly well done and has alot of personality to it, with great care being taken in making the levels and backgrounds look very pleasing. Some of the characters seem a bit off at times, but nothing glaring.
Audio-wise, the soundtrack is amazing. It's incredibly similar to many sega classics and, to quote an actual reviewer, feels incredibly "video game-y". For a videogame, that's good of course. The voice acting is a mixed bag. Yes, there are voice acted cutscenes. If that's not your bag, they've even added a "Classic" mode that's just the gameplay! The voices range from "I hope this guy got more work after this" to "Hilarious".
All in all, if you enjoyed classic Sega platformers and can get past the whole "these look like sonic fancharacters" shell, you'll find a fun game with a goofy saturday morning cartoon-like story loosely tying it together.
After all, it could've been worse. It was gonna be a sonic fangame.

Company of Heroes 2 is a small-scale WWII real-time strategy game where players build, equip, upgrade, and control diverse Allied and Axis forces in a semi-realistic tactical battle. It features combat mechanics such as dynamic cover, indirect fire, suppression, garrisoning, pinning, retreating, smoke and concealment, weapon facing, healing and reinforcement, squad merging, and more. The gameplay favors smart tactical decision-making and use of diversified troop types over massive blobs of one or two dominant units that you see in some other RTS games.
Unit micromanagement is an important part of the game, but the micro is more about positioning, movement, and map control - using your assets tactically - than about managing tons of activated abilities for individual units. The units that do have activated abilities are typically things like grenades, sprinting, or temporary boosts to firepower; most units only have one or two active abilities if they have any at all. CoH2 is not as focused on Actions Per Minute as a game like Starcraft II.
I've had this game for years and still play regularly; there's really nothing else out there that fills the role that CoH and CoH2 do. If you enjoy RTS games in general and Relic's RTS games (well, aside from DoW3) in particular, chances are you'll really enjoy CoH2.
WHAT TO BUY?
- The base CoH2 game will give you the main Soviet SP campaign and the two MP factions, Ostheer (Germany) and Soviets.
- The Western Front Armies add-on will give you the Oberkommando West (another German faction) and United States Forces factions for MP and skirmish games.
- The British Forces add-on will give you the United Kingdom Forces faction.
- Ardennes Assault is a single-player USF campaign with a territory map that consists of scripted scenarios and skirmish-like battles against the AI. Lots of fun.
- The Mission Packs are single-player and co-op scenarios for Ostheer and Soviet factions; IMO these are totally optional and not necessary unless you are already a big CoH2 fan and want more SP content.
Looking over some other reviews, I'm disappointed to see people calling out "pay2win!" and "microtransactions!" without really understanding or explaining the actual situation. A few points to clarify misunderstandings here:
1. You do NOT NEED TO BUY ANYTHING to be competitive in MP. The stock Commanders are fairly effective for each faction.
2. VERY FEW DLC assets impact gameplay. Yes, there are lots of small assets you can purchase via the in-game store, and almost all of them are cosmetic: vehicle skins, faceplates, post-game victory strikes, and vehicle decals.
3. The two items that can impact gameplay are Commanders and Intel Bulletins. Of these, Commanders are the only meaningful change to gameplay; Intel Bulletins generally have negligble impact and aren't worth purchasing, IMO.
4. You can win ALL of these DLC assets via an immediate reward for playing any CoH2 game, including skirmishes against the AI. (At the end of a round, everyone gets a random loot drop, which can include "supply," skins, faceplates, victory strikes, Intel Bulletins, and even Commanders.)
5. You can earn in-game currency called "Supply" by playing ANY match - even SP matches against the AI or matches with mods - and you can use Supply to buy ANY of these DLC assets from the in-game store without paying ANY real-world money.
Now, purchasing a Commander enables you to use a slightly customized version of a given faction. (The Heavy Cavalry commander for USF gives you the ability to call in Ranger infantry squads and Pershing tanks in the late game, for example.)   None of the Commanders are so OP that someone who has purchased that content will automatically win against anyone who hasn't. They're a way to tweak an existing faction, not a method to buy easy victories.
TDLR: If you're interested in CoH2, you don't need to purchase DLC or do any microtransactions to have a viable shot in multiplayer. The game goes on sale all the time and you can get bundles for very cheap, sometimes just $5-10 dollars for everything. Try out the base game and see how you like it, and if it works for you, pick up the Western Front and British Forces add-ons on sale. Ignore claims of Pay2Win, they're largely unfounded.

We currently don't have dragons and elfs casting magic while running the streets, however while playing this game I couldn't stop to wonder how far our life is getting close to this game (and cyberpunk in general). The pollution is not as critical but although the ecology technology and regulations are improving the pollution is large, and the smog is really bad in many large cities. The news about brain with chip synchronization technology advancing, the cooperations that introducing so far "voluntary" chip under the skin to their employs, working holograms, virtual reality sets, small drones, hacker attacks... all this makes you wonder. And cooperations in general are already having huge power, changing governments decisions with the threat of high unemployment rate, providing many times under our noses what should we buy, and how should we live.
The story of the game is very intensive, player really wants to meet those people out there and listen to their stories, wants to be part of their lives, and feels their emotions. And the choices many times have consequences. This is the strongest part of the game. The game also is having really great, deep  music, check some stream service to get the idea.
The missions could be usually completed in few ways and many times not necessary through brute force. The fighting system is easy to begin with, but with luck factor, covers, explosives, dragon lines, cyber implants, summons and generally quite nice bunch of spells and equipment becomes quite hard to truly predict and fully master. The karma system is nice, I really like that specialization skills depends of the level of the main skills, also I like the balance between magic and cyber implants. However I find the system to be a bit wasted. Don't get me wrong, the idea that you can be a specialist only in one or two fields is nice, also that you cannot buy everything, but I really like my character to discover and test new things. Also I have impression that game could be longer, especially side-missions. The bonus content is less stable then the main story and you may trigger some bugs and clitches, still story is worth that discomfort.

[Original Review] Disclaimer: I have only played through about 12 hours of the game as of this review, but since I don’t know when or if I will finish it, I feel alright about posting this.  Also, GET US A NEUTRAL REVIEW BUTTON STEAM!!!  This is a 6.5/10 score, not a 0/10.
I like – no, love – reading in video games.  I love the writing and stories of PoE, BG, Planescape, Tyranny, and my one of my all-time favorite games, SR: Dragonfall.  Hell, I used to just sit around and read the codex in Mass Effect.  Reading is a great medium in games, especially RPGs.
But something is off about the writing in SR:HK.  I can’t quite place my finger on it.  It seems like it is heavy for the sake of being heavy.  There are a TON of words in each conversation, yet nothing is ever really said.  It’s just… flat.  This is something I am having difficulty objectifying, but subjectively, where I was hooked on Dragonfall within minutes, I find myself questioning whether to return to HK.
The lackluster writing is exacerbated by the fact that, for the time I have played anyway, it is primarily talking.  Sure, you have a fight up front, and a few in the middle, but in the 11.7 hours I have put in probably 2 hours of that has been in a fight.  10 hours of reading subpar cyberpunk fantasy and walking around?  That’s extremely low, even for a guy who loves his non-combat RPGs.  80% of HK’s skills are combat based, after all.  More to the point, if there’s not a lot of gameplay, your writing better be phenomenal.
Sadly, that’s not the end of it.  I like role playing my conversations, even if the outcome is linear.  That’s cool; I dig cosmetic roleplaying like that.  Dragonfall’s conversations were actually fairly linear.  What I don’t dig is when there are clearly outcomes hidden behind stat checks THAT SHOW UP EVEN WHEN YOU DON’T PASS THE STAT CHECK.  That is incredibly immersion breaking.  Case in point:  I am conducting a murder investigation with my cyberweapons decker build.  I can’t examine the body or its spirit because I’m neither a doc nor a shaman.  The game isn’t allowing my other party members to do it either.  No biggie, move on.  Get to the end, and I have conversation options showing that I examined the body and spirit.  You can’t do this.  There is roleplaying a conversation, and then there is poor implementation of choices.
So not only does the writing fail to grip me and is too voluminous for its quality, but I can safely skip things and reach the same outcome.
Not good.
Up to this point, I have talked mostly about the writing.  That’s because the rest of the game is still a solid piece of work.  The character building makes sense and is fun, the combat is enjoyable when it is there, the universe it amazing.  The foundation is all there.  Sadly, the execution of this story based RPG just doesn’t hold up.  If you loved Dragonfall or are looking for some slightly above par cyberpunk fiction, I would say this is safe to grab on sale.  But if you don’t particularly care for reading in RPGs or have other games that will scratch the cyberpunk itch, stay far away from this one.

You could call it a "Sonic clone"... if the clone was a smarter, stronger, and more likeable version of the original, who then chose to murder the original and take its place as a more productive member of society under the clone's newly chosen name.
The levels are designed surprisingly intuitively, allowing you to maintain a fast-pace throughout. All of the characters allow for a varying level of speed, but each has her own unique style of play, pretty analogous to the play style differences between Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles.
Though there are plenty of enemies and you're given a few combat abilities to fight them, you can often choose to ignore most of the combat entirely and rush to the boss fights. All of the bosses follow a pretty strict pattern, but solid execution is still critical to winning the boss fights, especially the late game bosses, which spike in difficulty relative to the first 3/4ths of the game.
The game itself is beautiful. It has a consistent and colorful style that isn't too chaotic to understand at first glance. Occasionally, you see platforms and walls that aren't actually walls and platforms, but they aren't frequent enough to where you'll regularly be jumping into mirages.
Finally, what really brings everything together is the fantastic soundtrack. It hits all of the right notes you'd expect from a classic Sega game. Sonic CD and Virtual-On come to mind. Though it adopts that similar style, it's not just some riff on old content. The soundtrack is clearly this game's own and each track does a great job at complementing each stage or boss fight.
Galaxy Trail really stepped forward and brought back a style of platformer that really hasn't had many hit games since Sonic CD. Even then, Sonic CD had a number of problems that just aren't present here. Freedom Planet really brings out the best of the platforming genre that otherwise would be a sea of slow-paced puzzle platformers, "deep" 8-bit experiences, or super-hard death fests.
If I had to describe Freedom Planet in a single line, I'd honestly say, "Sonic 3 and Knuckles... but much better."

Freedom Planet is the best Sega Mega Drive (or Sega Genesis depending on where you live) game released this year.
OK so it isn't really a Mega Drive game, but it takes a lot of inspiration from notable games of that system (Sonic 1, 2 & 3, Gunstar Heroes, Rocket Knight Adventures to mention a few of the Mega Drive inspirations), the fact that the game also lists it button inputs in the menus as 'A' 'B' & 'C' helps with that impression too.
What we have here is a 2D platform game rendered with high quality pixel art reminiscent of the 16-bit era of video games with a crazy amount of detailed sprite animation.  The level design is where the Mega Drive/Genesis Sonic inspiration is most felt.  The layouts aren't as sprawling & labyrinthine as the Sonic games but the later levels especially offer lots of different routes take to reach the end of each stage, stages which culminate in exciting & very challenging boss battles.
If you do not enjoy very difficult games or games which feature anthropomorphic, cutesy animal characters as the protagonists then maybe Freedom Planet is not for you, but the exciting boss battles, incredible soundtrack & surprisingly in-depth game mechanics with 3 very different characters to master (with more on the way) has me gushing praise for this game every chance I get. Runner2 is an incredibly addictive music-based autorunner. Every successful action in the game is accompanied by an assortment of musical sounds, so you feel that (when you do well) you're a part of the soundtrack. This is such a great way to provide the player with positive feedback that really hooks into your brain. It's lovely. The player input is simple, based solely on the 4-way dpad, but as the levels become more complicated and start scrolling faster, requiring ever increasing tandem combinations of these inputs, the game becomes quite hectic. That said, the difficulty curve is consistently gentle and the most difficult sections are often entirely optional - mainly being alternate paths leading to bonus exits in each level. Simply put, this game is just a ton of fun. It's so colourful and once it clicks in your brain, you're left with a zen-like connection between music and puzzles that is impossible to stop playing.

I remember when years ago I played it many times. Got it from some gaming magazine and it was fun. I loved to play it around Easter - it was my yearly tradition to play it when there was Easter coming up. I probably wasn't the only one who did that. It was really hard game - I mean, how can you avoid all those eggs? How do you beat the first or second level, it's impossible! After some time I forgot about this game and didn't even wanted to look around for CDs, only to install a game that I would play for short time. In 2014 I got Chicken Shoot Gold from some bundle but also I didn't feel like playing it. Now, in 2016, I wanted to relive some of memories. Nostalgia trips from time to time aren't a bad thing. I played for some time and I was surprised how easy it is. While playing it for the first time after so many years I got rather good score and beat more levels then earlier in every try. It was fun to discover something new when it wasn't really possible as kid. Chicken Shoot Gold reminded me once again what gaming should be like - it's fun to play a game which have a good story, and same goes for graphics and new ideas but sometimes you don't need all of this and something simple, like getting rid off chickens in this case, can be really enjoyable too.
There is only one thing I'm not sure about - price. While for me, I would probably buy it at full price if there wasn't a bundle with it but for new players, for somebody who never heard and never played it, it's way too big price for content it offer. If there will be some promo, and you enjoy simple AND I MEAN IT, really simple games when everything you could brag about is your highscore - grab it.

A good way to fix these would be to have some kind of sheild that you can deploy at anytime by pressing a button. I can tell you, after the first installment of Chicken Shoot I was blown away. My expectations were low. I truly doubted that the dev's could improve a perfect game, yet somehow they did. How could such a small company on such a small budget create this classic, gem of a game? But they pulled through and delivered on promises I could not even dream of.
It has the pace of GTA, the storytelling only a Telltale game could perfect, the responsive combat of Counter-Strike. The weapons, though few in number are brilliantly balanced and feel fantastic. When you fire the sawn off, you almost feel your arm coming out of it's socket and the excrutiating pain that comes with it, because you're firing it one-handed. I feel the name "Chicken Shoot" undermines the games full potential. All in all it does not just boil down to shooting chickens; Those who played the game would know that. The deep connections with the player, twists and turns in the story tell you so much more.
For those of you who are intelectually inferior and cannot fathom the potentcy this game, perhaps it is transcendant of your tiny chimp brain - Not meant for you, as it were.

Company of Heroes 2 is a small-scale WWII real-time strategy game where players build, equip, upgrade, and control diverse Allied and Axis forces in a semi-realistic tactical battle. It features combat mechanics such as dynamic cover, indirect fire, suppression, garrisoning, pinning, retreating, smoke and concealment, weapon facing, healing and reinforcement, squad merging, and more. The gameplay favors smart tactical decision-making and use of diversified troop types over massive blobs of one or two dominant units that you see in some other RTS games.
Unit micromanagement is an important part of the game, but the micro is more about positioning, movement, and map control - using your assets tactically - than about managing tons of activated abilities for individual units. The units that do have activated abilities are typically things like grenades, sprinting, or temporary boosts to firepower; most units only have one or two active abilities if they have any at all. CoH2 is not as focused on Actions Per Minute as a game like Starcraft II.
I've had this game for years and still play regularly; there's really nothing else out there that fills the role that CoH and CoH2 do. If you enjoy RTS games in general and Relic's RTS games (well, aside from DoW3) in particular, chances are you'll really enjoy CoH2.
WHAT TO BUY?
- The base CoH2 game will give you the main Soviet SP campaign and the two MP factions, Ostheer (Germany) and Soviets.
- The Western Front Armies add-on will give you the Oberkommando West (another German faction) and United States Forces factions for MP and skirmish games.
- The British Forces add-on will give you the United Kingdom Forces faction.
- Ardennes Assault is a single-player USF campaign with a territory map that consists of scripted scenarios and skirmish-like battles against the AI. Lots of fun.
- The Mission Packs are single-player and co-op scenarios for Ostheer and Soviet factions; IMO these are totally optional and not necessary unless you are already a big CoH2 fan and want more SP content.
Looking over some other reviews, I'm disappointed to see people calling out "pay2win!" and "microtransactions!" without really understanding or explaining the actual situation. A few points to clarify misunderstandings here:
1. You do NOT NEED TO BUY ANYTHING to be competitive in MP. The stock Commanders are fairly effective for each faction.
2. VERY FEW DLC assets impact gameplay. Yes, there are lots of small assets you can purchase via the in-game store, and almost all of them are cosmetic: vehicle skins, faceplates, post-game victory strikes, and vehicle decals.
3. The two items that can impact gameplay are Commanders and Intel Bulletins. Of these, Commanders are the only meaningful change to gameplay; Intel Bulletins generally have negligble impact and aren't worth purchasing, IMO.
4. You can win ALL of these DLC assets via an immediate reward for playing any CoH2 game, including skirmishes against the AI. (At the end of a round, everyone gets a random loot drop, which can include "supply," skins, faceplates, victory strikes, Intel Bulletins, and even Commanders.)
5. You can earn in-game currency called "Supply" by playing ANY match - even SP matches against the AI or matches with mods - and you can use Supply to buy ANY of these DLC assets from the in-game store without paying ANY real-world money.
Now, purchasing a Commander enables you to use a slightly customized version of a given faction. (The Heavy Cavalry commander for USF gives you the ability to call in Ranger infantry squads and Pershing tanks in the late game, for example.)   None of the Commanders are so OP that someone who has purchased that content will automatically win against anyone who hasn't. They're a way to tweak an existing faction, not a method to buy easy victories.
TDLR: If you're interested in CoH2, you don't need to purchase DLC or do any microtransactions to have a viable shot in multiplayer. The game goes on sale all the time and you can get bundles for very cheap, sometimes just $5-10 dollars for everything. Try out the base game and see how you like it, and if it works for you, pick up the Western Front and British Forces add-ons on sale. Ignore claims of Pay2Win, they're largely unfounded.

Lisa is bound to give most a new, fun, humorous, and most likely uncomfortable experience that you will remember for a long time like I have. I personally think that the less you know about the game, the better and more impactful the experience will be, so I'll keep it short.
The game's strongest asset is it's story, which contains some dark tones, dark humor, and very unique plot with interesting characters. It's story is also particularly engaging due to the fact that it forces the player to make some decisions that will permanently affect their playthrough.
Gameplay is the usual turn based rpg combat system with a slight twist with some unique mechanics, like dial combos for certain characters. Throughout your journey you will be introduced to a lot of choice in play style, with many party members to choose from as you progress through the game. This party system allows for a lot of variety and strategy.
The pixel art style has a nice charm to it, and does a good job in portraying the world of Lisa.
Soundtrack is odd, but very catchy. It does a great job in creating the desired mood of the current scenario of the story.
I know this is a short and very brief review, but this game is definitely worth checking out if you are looking for something new, unique, and a bit of an eye opening/disturbing experience.
From what I have seen, Lisa is one of the best examples so far on how video games can be a great platform for engaging storytelling.

This is the best isometric RPG I've played since Fallout 2, or at least it's tied with its sister game, Dragonfall. I don't know how I could put my recommendation much more clearly than that, if we're honest.
The visuals, sounds, and environments are as good as they need to be. The gameplay is solid. It's both easy to pick up and yet varied enough to keep the overall concept interesting for multiple runs, especially given that fan-made campaigns can be created for it to keep the overall style fresh.
But the story here is very well done, it's engaging and interesting. It's also a good length: it doesn't feel too short, and it doesn't start to get overbearing or drag on endlessly. It's this kind of writing that takes an RPG and transforms it into a Great Game.
HBS, in general, did a great job with its Shadowrun games, and I have to admit I Kickstarted their Battletech game too. If it matches the quality of these, then it will have been completely worth it.

The storytelling is very good, but the developer seems to have pushed their aging game engine beyond its capabilities.  The performance is horrible for a game with such low system requirements. Most disappointing of all is how little workshop content there is.
Check out Dragonfall instead.

A fun game where you can control your favorite historic world leaders, and mod in others to have even more fun. Civ 5 is a turn based strategy game full of war and strategy. I recommend it purely for the times you have while playing with friends, like Ghandi the warlord.

Would reccomend to: true strategy fans, Fire Emblem fans, and Total Empire Fans.
The base game is excellent.  Turn based, strategy game that revolves around building your civilization by researching different technologies, using resources wisely, managing your people, fighting invading intruders, and trading with friendly and opposing civilizations to further yourself.  The game is very simple in cocept you start out in the anciet era and play till you reach the modern age, assuming you can survive until the.  The game board is made up of hexagonal tiles with various different resources, environmental elemnts, and climates appearing.  This means that an area can be vary desirable to settle and make for quick work of building a city or a long, difficult process for building one.  Meanwhile other civilizations are progressing, and how do they compare to yours?  Are they beating you to building different wonders or researching technolgies before you so their units are more advanced?  What does that mean for your society?
Are your people satisfied with your reign and producing the most they can?  All these questions come across your thoughts as you play this game, trying to find a way to victory.  Don't worry there are 4 ways to victory and many different leaders to pick from (all of which come with their own unqiue bonuses), so you won't be getting bored any time soon.  That doesn't include all the achievemnts, scenarios, and mods that you can play and get hours out of doing.  The graphics are very nice and make for a satisfying and fun gaming experience. Plus there are lots of different customizable options that allow you to pick what kind of gaming experience you want, for those of us less high matience pick your difficulty setting, set the rest to random, and click play. In addtion, this game has lots of fun and worthwile DLC that add to the game, in paticular I reccomend the Gods and Kings expansion as well as the Brave New World one.

Chicken Shoot Gold consist of two games, Chicken Shoot and Chicken Shoot 2. They are similar to each other, could say that CS2 is more of mission pack. Anyway, they came out around in 2003, developed by some Toontraxx and published by TopWare. They come from the era of shareware games, mind it, and seem to ride on Moorhuhn/CrazyChicken success, both being shooting gallery where you just shoot at many chickens.
Actually, as I found out from a friend, original name of this polish series was "Kurka Wodna". And what you see as Chicken Shoot Gold is combination of the second and the third game. The first game isn't all that known, but you can YouTube gameplay out. It's quite primitive.
It also for whatever reason was ported to GBA, DS and Wii (in 2007!). Which is way past the intented audience of bored office workers. Reviewers weren't afraid to dumb the game on those platforms. PC version seems to be the best anyway.
Technically it's as-is. For 2003 game. Which means low-resolution in forced full-screen which will go "we smoke everyday" if you alt-tab. No Steam Overlay. Nope, no widescreen. You can only increase resolution up to 800x600, but it will just increase in-game space. Meaning that you will see more. Which affects gameplay, making it harder, as eggs thrown at you will hit you only if they will be on screen.
Also, it doesn't usually remember CD-Key and scores, so check Steam guides to find out how to fix that.
Also, nope, Internet multiplayer doesn't work. It can't "connect to host". Local seem to function up to server browser, but you know, I don't have friend nearby with computer with local net to connect by to check this out. Not 2000 anymore.
And so it begins, you got two games, with 5 usual levels in the first CS and 6 exotic levels in the second. Then you choose one of the two modes to play. Classic is score based, you worry less about being hit by egg and more about not accidently hitting other non-chicken living beings. With weird exclusions to both rules. Like owl-looking ones, who are too gross, I guess. Just try to get enough score in time to go to the next level. And arcade mode, where you got usual lifebar and have to avoid eggs by either shooting them down or scrolling away.
After which you are shown intro where a farmer of sorts will wake up and starts shooting chickens who were eating spilled seeds of sorts, instead of trying to lock them back. After which chickens will suddenly learn how to fly away. And then you will murder all the chickens by getting even more disturbed, whether young or old. Which gets a bit wicked when you find out that some don't just fall over, but turn into angels.
And well, really, it is what it is. Shareware-age moorhuhn-clone "me too". Albeit it has more content that Moohruhn in levels. And you can get more weapons to use and such. Final boss. This stuff isn't easy. Both games also have secret levels that I couldn't find how to get to.
But really, it ain't Virtua Cop. Or House of the Dead on Steam. It doesn't have much going on outside of shooting gallery. Just some chickens, some throw eggs, and interactive level objects you can shoot mostly for score. In all honesty, I wasn't sure whether to recommend it or not. It didn't♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, so I guess it's good if you know what you are getting.

At first glance, it might be tempting to dismiss Freedom Planet as a rip-off of the old Genesis Sonic games.  But while it's clear that those games did provide a lot of inspiration for this one, such a dismissal is a disservice to an excellent piece of entertainment.  While its level layouts, character designs, and gameplay definitely take cues from Sonic, Freedom Planet is its own game.  It's less about speed and more about exploration, control, and combat, a game that rewards observation and thinking in addition to quick reflexes.
The game's bosses deserve special mention.  While the first few are fairly simple fights that one can clear without much effort, the latter half of the game features some genuinely challenging fights that require speedy reactions and good pattern memorization.  They're very challenging without being unfair, and are, on the whole, superb.
There's a story too, and it isn't bad, but it's secondary to the game's beautiful aesthetics and great gameplay.  If you're a fan of challenging, old-school platformers, it's hard to go wrong with Freedom Planet.

This is a game that surprised me quite a bit, and it was worth every penny!
While yes, starting out I couldn't help but compare it to sonic like pretty much everyone, I rather quickly realized I was dealing with a different beast altogether. It's less a jump on things to pop them kinda thing, and more a "pummel enemies to a pulp" kinda game that primarily uses attack moves as hit detection rather than collision like most games of the platformer genre. The game also has three characters that each play with their own unique fighting style, and seeing as the enemies don't pull any punches learning how a character flows and the proper combos is pretty much essential.
The storyline was simple enough, although it managed to throw a surprising amount of emotions into the later levels (particularly the last zone.)  While I won't say the story was spectacular, the storymode kept me engaged enough. Sadly storymode doesn't differ much depending on which of the two primary characters you pick to play as, although it does give a slight bit of variety to a few levels, particularly the fact the two primary characters have their very own unique level attatched to them.
Music was great. 10/10, bought the album.
As for replayability, while a second playthrough with the other character might not offer much in the way of story to keep you interested, the fact Carol and Lilac don't exactly move in the same way or have the same moveset means you're going to have to take quite a few situations you encountered in the first playthrough in a completely different way.  Despite knowing how the various bosses work, I've found that bosses I got down perfectly with Lilac were suddenly giving me a lot of trouble again after I switched over to the other character.  Also, if you're the type who enjoys challenges hard mode is quite unforgiving.
Now then, problems I've seen. I could say some of the obstacles seem a bit badly designed, but that would be innacurate. As I said, certain terrain types flow a lot more fluidly with certain characters. If the game was made specifically for just one of the characters the flow of the other character would be completely shot and probably seem a bit frustrating.  The main problem I can point out (other than the glitches) isn't so much a problem as something that's a bit irksome. The game defaults onto hard mode, and players who don't exactly want a challenge in their game might find that a bit of a problem. Granted, I personally LOVED the challenge of it so I wouldn't really count that as a black mark.
In summary, if you enjoyed the games this was made to pay homage to this game is a must get.  There's no real penalty for failing so just learn the controls at your own pace, enjoy the soundtrack, and have a good time.

This game does a lot of things right:
Gameplay is really good. You are highly mobile due to boost-boots and grapple-hook. It is easy to understand what you can do, but it's not easy to get all the jumps right at first try. You always know what you can change so that you get it right some tries later, which is perfectly balanced difficulty. Sometimes you need a few seconds to look around and see where you have to proceed.
That's it. That may seem little, but it's okay, because of several points:
- It works really well. (Some other platformers just have unpolished gameplay destroying the fun.)
- It is enough for a platformer as gameplay elements. There are a lot games with less to offer.
- The game is not long enough to need much more. (It's exactly as long enough as it needs to satisfy you, though.)
- Environments are so beautiful and diversified, that helps the game not getting boring.
Atmosphere is what really shines. The world you visit in this lighthearted yet emotional story is simply gorgeous. Graphics are nice and the places sometimes remind me of bioshock infinite, but are more peaceful.
When the story is finished you might come back to get the achievements, to get collectibles or to do some speedruns. That are after-story-tasks which make sense for this kind of game.

Experience epic, free-to-play naval combat when you helm one of over 200 historic vessels in an exciting balance of strategy and real-time combat in World of Warships. Outfit your fleet with flags, camouflage, modifications, talented commanders, and more!
World of Warships is one of the World of X titles in Wargaming portfolio, next to World of Tanks and World of Warplanes. It's a clash of 16-24 ships in PvE bot battles, scenario missions or PvP combat. You take control of a ship - quick and agile destroyer, slow and tanky battleship, somewhere-in-between cruiser or a plane carrier - and destroy other ships while trying to control strategic points on the map.
WoWs looks very pretty and if you're interested in navy battles just play it. It's free after all. If you don't know if you're interested... It's a rather slow and strategic, mostly PvP, naval fight game. It's extremely fun even if you don't like PvP games and it can really suck you in. It's a squad based game, so your enjoyment greatly depends of the quality of your team. If your team is bad you will lose. Most often than not it's not possible to carry and, as there are no respawns, the margin for error is slim, even if you're amazing but have a bad team you will fail. And failing is not fun. I have to say I have a love hate relationship with this game as I love the idea, looks, music and pretty much everything, but bad teams make me hate it very much. For that hate moments there are bot battles though, these are easier and more fun even if less rewarding.
As to the f2p aspect. The game can be enjoyed free for a long time. Having said that mind that in higher tiers - there are 10 - you can lose in-game money, needed for resupply, when playing normally. You can gain money playing lower tiers though, so it's not like you have to pay to play. If you want to pay the game can be extremely expensive with ships costing up to 50 euro per one (that's normal for these kind of games unfortunately, WarThunder is the same). Real world money gives you some more in-game money (needed for resupply and parts), xp (for captain skills) or cosmetics, but doesn't give you any additional power (like special ammo). Also while you can buy premium ships for money without any grinding you will not be proficient enough to succesfully play them. And most of them are great for collectors but so so for competitive play.
One more thing, you have to invest time into the game. To not suck much in PvP you'll need ca. (20hrs * tier) of playtime, more or less, so for tier V you'll need about 100hrs of playtime to be proficient enough not to be a burden. Your milegae may vary.

Get this if:

* you like PvP games that don't require twitch reflexes

Don't get this if:

* you cannot stand the grind (~100hrs are needed to get not bad, way more to get good; ~300hrs to get to tier 10 ships without buying premiums)

This is a mild recommendation. I was a big Sonic fan as a kid, so this game has a huge nostalgia value for me. The 2D Sonic levels feel great, the 3D levels are usually pretty good, and hearing a lot of the classic music from the games being remixed is fantastic.
But I was a little disappointed in this game, too. I wasn't expecting to finish the game in 6 hours. That feels REALLY short to me, particularly since the game's currently selling for $30 at full price. (I, luckily, got it on sale.) There are a lot of optional challenges which I mostly haven't done, but I didn't feel like the gameplay was compelling enough to make me want to.
And in the 3D levels I stumbled across some of the flaws that have plagued the series since the switch to 3D--glitches (one time I fell through the floor and died), a wonky camera (which is REALLY frustrating when you go fast) and occasionally frustrating controls (a lot of times I didn't home in on an enemy with my homing attack when I thought for sure that it should've worked--I'm not sure if it was a glitch or if I was just unclear on how it should work but either way, it was frustrating).
I ended up feeling pretty luckwarm on this game, which was really disappointing considering all the praise I've been hearing about it. It DID tickle my nostalgia so I'm giving it a rec for that--the game sets out what it wants to do, pay homage to the Sonic series. If you're a fan and that's what you're wanting, pick it up. Otherwise I find this hard to recommend--there's a lot of better platformers out there on Steam nowadays. At the very least, I'd wait for this game to go on sale rather than paying full-price.

So about Blade Symphony. Let me start off by saying if it hadn't been for this free weekend I'd never have picked it up.. or rather never would have tried it, as I didn't pick it up.
I absolutely loathe the asian theme, the futuristic art-style, the over-the-top animations, the character design...basically the entire presentation of this game doesn't so much speak to me as it does shout "Stay away. Far away".
However that is a personal preference and even though I'm essentially right in this I am also aware of the fact that there are people who have the audacity to be wrong and like this sort of stuff. Not much you can do about that.
But the game isn't just looks, so let's ignore those for now.
The fighting, the heart of this game.. well it isn't bad. It is actually rather enjoyable to begin with.
It is however rather repetitive after a while. This is not - as some other people commenting here seem to think - due to a lack of content but rather due to a lack of input.
I actually like the fact that weapons are uniform across characters and I could do without the different character-traits as well. Purely cosmetic characters - making the outcome of a fight only about input-skill&speed rather than character attributes feels cleaner to me.
Input however is the problem.
You have far too little actual control to actually do something creative in your attacks, which means it all comes down to timing. Once you have ascertained that your timing is better than the opponents the fight is more or less over and will play out accordingly.
I'm not going to go into balancing because I haven't played enough of it to actually notice - or care - and I've also limited myself to the Longsword, as it is the only of the weapons in this game I actually give a toss about. So while there might be balancing issues - there almost certainly are, would be the first multiplayergame not to have those - I can't comment on those.
I can however comment on performance.
Some of the maps are rather mess as far as performance is concerned and - as with all melee games - if your ping rises or isn't stable it will have significant impact on your experience.
The performance-drops I noticed aren't significant enough to be blamed for getting defeated in combat (outside of really close matches on a very high skill-level which didn't really affect me all that much) but they are really irritating and a drag on the amount of joy the flow of combat delivers.
This flow sadly isn't all that great either. If your opponent is fast enough you can get locked-in by combo-attacks which basically drain most of your life before you are able to defend yourself (as you can't block mid-combo, you can block it entirely or not at all in my experience). Similarly you can get yourself locked into the combo-animation and killed because you didn't hit the opponent but also were unable to respond to his attacks. Cancelling animations to perform new actions would obviously break the animation-style the game aims for, so unfortunately there is little to be done about this.
This highlights the input problem, combo-animations may look nice (to other people) but fighting with individual attacks&strikes gives you much more control over your character and combat in general.
Right now the game is very heavily discounted and I can't bring myself to buying it, even though - despite the named issues - I had a couple of really enjoyable fights in this game.  Not even worth the 4€ they are asking for it right now, at least not to me.

Life in a Cold War banana republic probably wasn't as much fun in the real world as it is in Tropico 3. Fortunately, this little bit of historical revisionism is one of the few complaints you can make about this city builder.  Not every aspect of this game works smoothly, however. The interface is a little wonky when it comes to placing buildings. It's hard to understand why you can't build in certain areas, which makes it easy to put down a building that cannot be connected to a road. Economics are also a touch obtuse in spots. It takes a few years for farms to start producing, and they seem to go through fertile and fallow periods in later years of operation. Garages operate as public transit, sending out cars that get workers to and from jobs. These new wrinkles are just fine, though, because they add extra strategic depth that needs to be taken into account when planning cities.

With the amount of content added to the game in this DLC, its hard to justify the price (2/3 the cost of Tropico 3 itself).  A must have for the hardcore Tropico 3 fan, but the average fan can easily pass on it until it lowers in price.

Oh the nostalgia, I remember in the holidays/weekends, I'd used to get up early in the morning and turn on my Xbox (Original) and put in the disk and wait. ---------------Multiplayer-----------------------------
Now, I don't remember going into multiplayer alot. But when I did, no-one would be on. It's like a desert out there. Even with bots it still felt pretty lonely. I'd always get my next door friend over but we wouldn't have fun.

I'll keep this brief, with the Cons then Pros.
Cons:
-Cutscenes, while most offer story,  are long and some are a bit too frivolous.
-Multiple Characters, but only one feels 'Good' while the others are gimmicky.
-May leave you with a sense of wanting more.
Pretty short right?  Well, that's why I put them first, and why you don't see a 'No'.  Let's move on to the Pros, shall we?
Pros:
-Yes, this is a Sonic the Hedgehog
game.  Not a carbon-copy.  They've taken the bits and pieces of mechanics, gameplay, level design and all that and then put that all into one package.  The end result is a game that will tickle your nostalgia if you're a fan for sure.  Even then, you don't need to have played sonic, or even know of its existence.
-The Gameplay itself is fluid and fast-paced, to a point.  Sure you can speed through it, or you can take your time.  Maybe collect all the goodies to get that completionist feeling.  Plus, multiple game modes!  Time attack mode, 'Adventure' Mode for those that love story(Even with the long cutscenes), or just straight up 'Classic' mode.  As in, You beat a boss, onto the next stage.  No stopping.  Just gameplay.
-The game, even with pixel graphics looks absolutely gorgeous.  From level design, enemy design, effects.  Whatever you look at is sure to catch your eye.
-The soundtrack is equally as amazing as the art.  The kind that fits each stage through and through, and helps you appreciate both all at once.  Especially the boss music.  Oh man, if you ever loved some fitting boss tracks this game has some that'll please you.
-Different Playable characters, while the other two besides the 'Main' character aren't that spectacular, offer multiple ways to explore the levels and dispose of your enemies.  On top of that, they have some pretty neat designs to boot!
-The bosses are fantastic.  From the first to the last, I found myself loving every moment of the intense battles they offer.  Even if I died a ton on my first playthrough, almost every moment was as thrilling as the last.  Then there's that sweet sense of satisfaction when you finally beat it.  I don't remember how many times I threw my fist up in triumph.  It was probably a lot.
-It's 15$.  Super cheap for what you're getting.
All in all, I have to say after playing through it once this has got to be one of the best platforming experiance I've had in a long time.  Forget whatever negative thoughts you may be having about it and just pick it up, especially if you read this far.  After all,  it took me just a few minutes of looking at all the positive reviews to decide to purchase the game.  They were right about it after all.  It's worth playing, and you should buy it.  You won't regret it.

If you buy this game, you buy it for the platforming, and you get a helluva experience. I find the characters to be rather well designed and voiced.  All in all its a really good game that platformer fans and sonic fans will enjoy.
