You know what to expect if you've played Shadowrun: Returns, and Shadowrun: Dragonfall. Formulaic as it may be, it's a pretty cool CRPG-styled game that won't go stale so long as you're not burnt out on the other games, like I am. Being the 3rd game in the series that I played (underrated FPS aside), I didn't have patience for glitches that forced me to restart chapters or character who whined a little bit too much. Maybe Dragonfall was just a tough act to follow, but I understand there are plenty of people who prefer Hong Kong. The setting is more exotic, the weapons are more varied, and the UI is nicer than previous installments. So there's that.
If you're new to the series and enjoy games like Fallout and Baldur's Gate or even the tabletop game, you'll feel at home.

If it could be a gray " - " instead of an up and down, I would rate this that way.
If it's your ONLY Shadowrun game in your library, you're probably going to like it. It won't be EPIC, but it will be a good enough story and game.
However, when you actually compare this to Dragonfall, you literally see the "Quantity over Quality" kind of thing: Hong Kong offers a LOT of content, and a LOT of gameplay time, atleast 10 or 20 hours more than Dragonfall.
However... the quantity were a bit too much to test thoroughly, so you end up comparing Hong Kong, your average game with a good story, with that tight-knit special piece of Dragonfall. Hong Kong has a lot of ups and downs, and has got SOME improvements over Dragonfall.
Options to resolve situations are, again, very different and cool. You can go gun-blazing as usual, but the dialogues for NOT going gun-blazing literally killed me a couple of times. I went from giggling sometimes in Dragonfall - which, in turn, I felt was much more VIVID and fresh than Hong Kong - to literally laughing in Hong Kong. (DECKER LOOKING FOR CREW)
Speaking of the Extended Edition BONUS campaign, I'm sorry. It feels too rushed, too... crumped up. It feels like they were going to do another 20-30 hours campaign with it, but butchered dialogues and stories up. A couple of other in the original Hong Kong feel butchered aswell, but those are scarce. The Bonus Campaign, instead, while I enjoyed the final resolve, it felt off, incomplete. Also, it LOCKED dialogues from NPC away if you started combat, or did some things that, supposedly, do NOT mean you can't speak afterwards with some NPC. Felt really cheap.
Writing, as I said, has its ups and downs, aswell the combat: some characters are better written than others (Gobbet wins, hands down, sorry Gaichu, you did good) but, unlikely Dragonfall, it is harder to grow attached to them. Even so, I felt like they had a lot of depth in character building anyway. Is0bel is a bold move of a character: she's hideous, hostile, bottomed up, and even if you may not like her, you can only think "well, that's her, that's her way". All in all, if it weren't for Gobbet... screw Cheng, I'm gonna get out of this damn China thing.
What really killed a lot of fun were the bugs: even at 3.1.2 - well fixed up in comparison to the original version - it still had a couple of gamebreaking bugs, which forced to reload a save. Hell with it: I had this Merc or Fuchi Mage which, in the HUGE warfare I couldn't avoid in that mission, kept getting stuck between two motorcycles, running infinitely. It happened with three reloads, until I forced here to take another route and stay away from the motorcycles.
All in all, Hong Kong is a bit bugged here and there and may occasionally feel like the sheer amount of dialogues and options and content COULDN'T be tested throughly.
All in all, Hong Kong is more your run-on-the-mill RPG than Dragonfall. For a better writing and - IMO - a better combat system (albeit missing a lot of funny things like the JoltArm) I suggest Dragonfall. Otherwise, Hong Kong feels ok and as all other Shadowrun games, it comes with the campaign editor. I've already picked up a couple of titles for community-made mods which look promising.
TL:DR : good enough, but wait for a sale if you already own Dragonfall.

I really don't understand why everyone takes a dump on this game. It's a slightly different style of than writing Shadowrun: Dragonfall was, but that's because Shadowrun: Dragonfall was up there with Planescape: Torment, and the other gaming literary greats.
Shadowrun: Hong Kong makes close to the cut, and is a riot to play - I consider its characterization, writing, and mechanical systems even better than Shadowrun Returns. It's just not Dragonfall - which is really fine, to be honest!
The new matrix system is harder - in my opinion, too hard as I'm personally not as much of a fan of it, but the old system *was* too easy. It's doable, just aggrivating, but I won't argue that it needed improvement.
The music is great. Just, absolutely awesome. I love it more than Dragonfall and Returns, and the music for both is amazing, so that says a lot.
A lot of people whine about the flat, stereotypical, or 2 dimensional characters. I have no flipping idea what they're talking about. The characters come across as real people; maybe not the fully flawed/figured entities of Dragonfall, but real people nonetheless. The interparty commentary is as good as Dragonfall, better in some places. I don't think I've ever cracked up as much during a game, especially one as dark as this one. A certain ork Rat shamaness is just a nonstop barrel of laughs, to say nothing for the others.
"What's the moral of the story?"
"That fire solves everything?"
10/10 would take morality lessons from Gobbet again.
EDIT: After finishing the end game and going through the Shadows of Hong Kong bonus, I have to add that it equals or EXCEEDS Dragonfall. The main story plot is actually pretty awesome - and the post game campaign actually adds a lot of content and characterization. RATPARTY!
Also forgot to add that they added additional equipment to rebalance the classes. At least as a Adept, it really shows, but it seems like it does for the others too.

I wanted to love this game, I really did. It's both beautiful and deadly.
The main issue I have is that I am just flat out bad. Now this is where it's easy to think therefore that because I'm not recommending it, that I'm raging. Being utter crap in this game spells doom for a very good (or is that bad?) reason.
If you don't have great reaction time and/or you are not a natural at this game there is no effective way for you to practice. Unlike other games where practice does indeed make perfect, here you don't get the chance. You'll be very lucky to come across enough bad players in a row for your own skills to develop. You'll most likely be matched up against advanced players who have been around for a while, and any hope you had of liking the game would be sliced to ribbons, like your face will be. Being able to practice and develop your skills shouldn't be down to match making luck.
The AI training opponent doesn't solve the problem either. It's actually not much help, so you're still stuck in the same situation (if you're rubbish). It doesn't behave human. That's true of many games but you need an AI here who will mix things up a bit. It doesn't have enough options to make it helpful or fun. There's not even a proper offline mode to keep you interested and to help you develop your skills. That's the whole crux of the problem, no way to improve your skills. How about more advanced matchmaking, putting players of similar ability together? Handicaps to help players? Speed settings?
I would only suggest buying this if you and your friends want to have a bit of a laugh. It's not worth the risk to your wallet if you could be bad at it with no mates. Yes it may be cheap. However I just purchased Killing Floor (which is excellent) at under £4. With sales like that on Steam you can get a deal that makes saving a tenner worth it.

OWH (and the accompanying content in +) is a bit of a sexed up turn based RPG that features randomized gameplay in a variety of fashions.
Games can be quick, moderately long, or take quite a bit of time - regardless of whether or not you die in the process.  If you do though, starting back up in the same world or a new one is pretty easy and rewarding.  I'm reluctant to call it a rogue-like since it really isn't like rogue, and beyond that, these days who's actually played rogue?
Music is pretty solid, and the art style is fine/cute.  Never had a problem with any of the translation in game.
Anyway, the usual stuff.  A smattering of different classes, equipment, enemies, terrain/environments.  The big thing that sets OWH apart is that the game features a crawling 'darkness' that is sweeping across the land - from the left side of the screen to the right.  Since the game is turn based it only moves when you move, and depending on some settings, the speed can be mixed up.  Think of it as playing 'The Neverending Story' with The Nothing creeping up on your heels... if you know the movie anyway.  Darkness catches you - you die.  Makes for some interesting gameplay because you have to prioritize your actions, fight monsters to level up, go digging for loot, all while trying to keep pace and stay ahead of the darkness.  One major positive for me is that the game tends to 'play fair' with a lot of items and status effects.  It doesn't fall into the "but that character is a boss/powerful!  X is useless!" kind of stuff.
Really easy game to sink quite a bit of time into, and it's rewarding as well.  While each individual character will either succeed at their quest or die trying, there are elements in the game that allow you to carry items forward to new characters, or to progress in different ways; unlocking other classes, starting options, etc.
Best of all?  It's a really cheap title, so it oozes value for money.  If it doesn't wind up being your jam, I suppose you could always refund it, but you won't need to get that much playtime out of it to justify the purchase anyway.
For the negatives:
- It is a highly repetitious game, so if you're not into that, this game is definitely not for you.
- Even after playing the game a lot to figure/find out all the story elements, it's nothing to write home about.
- The random nature begets replayability, but the way this is fashion can result in you getting totally and completely unfairly screwed.  Doesn't happen that often, but something to be wary of.
- No full screen/widescreen if that bothers you.
All in all, this one is a keeper for me.  I still come back and play games of it from time to time because it's really easy to just crack one off, and it still manages to be fun.
Worth every penny. The richness, depth, replayability, all make this a worthy game for a ridiculously low price. Play with a controller to make it easier.

A story about my uncle is a smooth and pleasing platform puzzle game, with stunning scenery and a classical storyline.
Graphics 9/10
The graphics are ecstatically pleasing, reminding me of good quality 3D movies that i watched as a child. The game had stunning views and since it basically revolves around floating islands the game is full of them. Its basically a couple of hours of eye candy.
Sound 9/10
The sound fits the scenery really well and it creates a relaxed and laid back atmosphere. The ‘safer’ areas with pleasing sceneries have relaxing music the more ’sinister’ areas have more sinister music, the game pulls this off very well. Not much to say, it fits like a glove
Story 6/10
The story is a classical tale beginning middle and an end told by a narrator. The reason why i didn’t give it a lower rating on the story is because it feels as if there aren’t many games that have that nowadays.
Gameplay 7/10
The gameplay revolves around jumping, rocket jumping and grappling. Personally i love all three of those things and they exist in abundance in the game but in principle they are the only things you do. If you do like such mechanics then the game is definitely for you.
Characters 6/10

A little masterpiece. After playing the demo last year, I was anticipating this game with very high expectations, and it surpassed all of them.
The short story is that this is Sonic, on the top of his career, as programmed by Treasure (on their Gunstar Heroes/Alien Soldier days), with a colorful cast of characters, a decent sense of humor, very nicely-voiced cutscenes with in-game visuals, and vibrant boss battles. All accompanied with excellent digital music and colorful, crisp sprites, all very 16-bit, but without limitations of the era.
The game's story brings an old-China-styled world, pitted against a technologically advanced warlord. On the side of the good guys, we have Lilac and Carol, two adventurers of sorts, who get involved into the events of the game after coming to the rescue of Torque, a commander who was fighting against the antagonist Lord Brevon, a rare relatively intelligent villain, who crash-landed in the planet and attempts to take over a powerful energy source for his own ship, while causing infighting amount warring nations as a distraction.
The game is divided in stages with two sections each. The setting and music of the stage changes with each section, so the game keeps changing environments pretty fast, with each stage having a number of unique gimmicks to them. The structure of the levels is a good reason this can be compared to a Sonic game, because it uses very large levels, with massive individual tiles, designed for speed and throwing in loops and curved terrain and so on. However, this is only at a visual level, as it plays in a fairly different fashion.
Each character plays radically different to each other. Lilac herself plays very similar to what you'd expect from a Sonic game, with emphasis on speed, but also good melee combat abilities and combat moves. While running she plays like Sonic, while fighting she plays like Zero from Megaman X4, with upper and downward attacks, a double jump (that also serves as a low-power high-rate attack) and a damaging dash attack.
Carol however has weak but fast melee attacks, and can't double jump, but can instead leap forward during jump, giving her pretty good movement capabilities, and she can also walljump, so she navigates the maps in a radically different fashion than Lilac. Her best thing is an unique powerup, a motorcycle she can ride until she receives enough damage. Her speed becomes as good as Lilac, can double-jump, speed boost, and she's even able to ride over vertical surfaces or stairs, while retaining her kicking abilities. If you are skilled enough to keep her bike, she's easily the best.
After playing a bit of story mode, you'll unlock Milla, a younger character who also plays even more radically different than the other two, being able to summon energy cubes that she can toss as a projectile, extend barriers that reflect enemy attacks and dispel in a directional short-range burst, and combining both things to create a mid-range beam attack. She can also dig items from the ground and has a limited form of flight. Because of this, she plays nothing like the other two, and traversing maps with her is even more different with the same architecture. She is also far, far stronger than her cutesy looks suggest, being able to demolish bosses with little effort if played right (and she also has the most effective range)
Boss battles are plain memorable and intense. Except the first, which is not a taste of things to come. From stage 2 onwards, bosses scalate in intensity, becoming bigger, more aggressive and way more over-the-top, some even having your companions join in battle, culminating with an really memorable fight against Brevon, who is no definitely no pushover, and pulls off a magnificent display of villainry, using everything he has to fight your heroine of choice. And the best is that you even are motivated to go kick his green♥♥♥♥♥due to certain events in the late game, making the fight even more satisfying.
Some can be tough for some players, but some reflexes and memory will be enough to succeed. It's that kind of game where dying is your fault, as it has no artificial difficulty added to it. Tough but fair.
The story starts off pretty weak, a bit rushed perhaps (Milla becomes best friends forever with the other two main characters in 3 seconds flat), but after stablishing itself, it grows on you and becomes interesting enough to care. All the three main girls are really badass in their own right, and some of the NPCs and enemies are also very memorable as well. Some are even actually kinda funny. And the villain is a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but actually does things instead of sitting on his throne waiting for the story to reach him. You get the impression of the guy being an actual threat, and succeeds at doing many things, which kinda motivates the player to keep going to see how things unfold. But well, as good as he is at being a bad guy, nothing can fight SOMEONE WHO CAN JUMP-KICK HELICOPTERS IN THE FACE WHILE RIDING A BIKE.
Also, the amount of enemies makes the fact that you are fighting an army quite believable. Which is a nice touch.
Presentation is spectacular. It uses the same design principles of old-school console games, but with no technical limitations, so it looks old, but shiny enough to look good. Sprite art is animated pretty nicely, uses plenty of vibrant, saturated colors, using many color motifs for each background and playfield. Lots of nice effects give emphasis to every relevant action, with tons of little sound effects mixed in. The result looks very polished and you can tell the ones behind it have a genuine love of the craft.  It looks like a high-profile 2D game in the PSX era, perhaps even a bit better.
Sound design is also notoriously well done, with lots of catchy tunes of great quality, every sub-level has its own unique theme and most bosses have their own unique theme as well, so the soundtrack is quite rich and varied. Stage themes range from cheery to relaxed, to calm to fast-paced, and tend to match the environment pretty well. Boss themes are very fast-paced, intense pieces that add to the showy feeling of the game. Sound effects are placed quite well, and voice acting is surprisingly good for an indie game, specially in the cutscenes. No one comes off as sounding bad, and some characters like the Magistrate or Lilac herself have really good voice actors, and no voice sounds like it doesn't belong to a given character.
Replay value is not the best, but if you like old-school games, it's that kind of skill-based game that you can run in half an evening and have fun while at it once in a while. You can collect a number of hidden items in stages, as well as trying score and speed runs for achievements or personal bests. You can also play a simpler mode without story, just gameplay sections, and a time attack mode. There's also a challenge mode of sorts, and a couple difficulty levels. Playing the game with each one of the heroines is really different though, and each one has an unique stage suited to her abilities.
Overall, Freedom Planet is a really competent sidescrolling action game, with a lot of careful polish and dare I say, love into it. It looks great for the chosen aesthetic, sounds great for the chosen style, and while it might look like a Sonic wannabe, it's definitely everything the Sonic Team has failed to deliver after the golden age of Sonic, and much, much more. It is an old formula given years of refinement and care, and the coolness feels more genuine than some 90's 'tude.

I don't even know where to start with this game. Where should I begin...
- The fluid movement and tight, responsive controls evocative of the best Genesis and Saturn-era sidescrollers?
- The three unique gameplay experiences including the Sonic-speed brawler, the technical wall-climbing combatant, or the tactical and exploratory summoner?
- The large and varied environments featuring excellent level design that match the pacing and abilites of each of the three protagonists' skills?
- The gameplay gimmicks that completely transform each experience without being tacky or overbearing and bring about multiple ways to progress through any level?
- The gorgeous and flowing sprite animations that cram detail and character into every pixel of screen space?
- The varied enemies that change from level to level and have their own attack patterns and weaknesses, making no two zones even remotely similar?
- The independent story paths that bring about unique levels and all interweave in a compelling story line?
- The absolutely fantastic soundtrack that never fails to set the right tone and mood for any encounter, and never become repetitive?
- The fully-voiced dialogue by, for the most part, well-matched and competent voice actors that give a proper charisma and personality to each character in the story?
- The boatloads of easter eggs and subtle attentions to detail that keep the game lively from start to finish?
- The compelling achievements and collectibles that make replaying the game desireable?
I mean, honestly. I am at a loss. If Shovel Knight is the "Super NES" indie game of the year, then Freedom Planet is the "Super Genesis" (so, Sega 32X or Saturn!) indie game of the year.
My two biggest let-downs with this game have nothing to do with the game itself. It has to do with the fact that this game received nowhere near as much publicity as some other indie platformers this year, and the fear that prospective gamers will write it off as a "Sonic clone" without so much as a second thought and miss out on one of the greatest retro revivals this side of a Gunstar Heroes re-release.
With a free demo available on the developer's website, there's no reason anyone should skip over this without at least a sample.

I've got a lot of great things to say about FTL, but keep getting distracted from writing a review, at least in part because I'm playing FTL.
The game starts you off with a spaceship with a small crew, viewed in a top down, 2D layout. You jump from encounter to encounter, trying to outrun a pursuing enemy fleet which vastly outguns you, whilst acquiring equipment, new crew, and weapons of your own.
If you run out of fuel (of which you have a limited supply, sometimes replenished in encounters), it's probably game over.
If your crew are murdered by a boarding party of battle drones, it's game over
If your ship is torn apart by beam weapons in a nebula, it's game over
If you open your ship to hard vacuum to murder a boarding party, forget to close the bulkheads afterwards, and asphyxiate your own crew, it's game over.
There are a myriad of ways to fail, and only one way to succeed - to get to the final sector and save the Federation.
Succeeding is much, much harder than failing, but both are massivley entertaining - and the allure of doing just one more jump, to see if you can pick up that extra fuel/crew/that one other thing you need...will keep you playing for days.

Company of Heroes 2 is a fun World War 2 RTS, featuring the newest playable faction, The Soviet Union. I haven't explored much into the multiplayer yet, but the game does offer many co-op missions from historic World War 2 battles with either co-op versus another player, or co-op versus an ai; there are singleplayer challenges as well!
I bought the master collection for the game when it was on sale for $6, so I cannot fully attest to the DLC scamming that the devs have done. If any DLC is most notable for the game, it would be the Ardennes Assault campaign. This is a non-linear American campaign featuring dynamic map interactions where conflicts are not following a linear story per-se, but instead occur as a result of intercepting German counter-offensives, and making strategic moves to capture territory.
I would recommend the game, but make sure that you get in on sale. The DLC is good, but follows the stupidity of abundance for things that could have been included in the game from the start.

Decent game, and I definitely had fun with my one-hour spent with it. The community -- that is, people who have stuck with the game and are experienced -- were very polite and helpful.
Unfortunately, I'd have to advise getting against this game because of the lack of a player-base. I had the luxury of playing during the Free Weekend which saw a big boost in player-population, but according to SteamCharts[0], the game's population always bounces back to pretty frighteningly-low levels after every sale/Freekend. And this isn't the type of game a noobie would want to get into, where only hardcore, experienced and dedicated people are playing it, ready to wipe the floor with someone who doesn't even know what they're doing yet. The accounts of other people also corroborate this problem (see the other reviews).
The forum community is also pretty toxic. So don't go there hoping to get a decent discussion about the game going.
Anyhow, as far as mechanics go, the swordplay felt good and balanced, and I really enjoyed out-witting some of my foes, as well as the prospect of further polishing-up my technique/understanding and participating in mind-games - but that's likely because I was mostly playing people who weren't part of the dedicated player-base. I do question how the character/weapon balance will pan-out in mid-to-high level play. That always becomes an issue in these types of games.
So yeah, I wouldn't spend money on this unless it was a $1 or something. Play it if it ever goes on for a Free Weekend again.

Blade Symphony is a good idea....executed poorly. Sometimes it only takes a couple of matches to figure that out. If you've ever played Warframe then this game has the same idea; only with just PvP. The first thing I noticed was just how the whole layout of the game was going to be. Upon completing the tutorial I instantly knew that I would be facing players just simply spamming attacks. The blocking system isn't a smart one. You just simply go into a block stance and hope you block. So basically there's no skill involved. Even I just went in and mostly spammed my attacks because there's no real smart system.
The second thing I noticed was the projectile system. In order to block them you need to face them. Otherwise it'll home in on you and take about a quarter of your health. I don't much mind the damage so much as the fact that it acts as a heat seeker and you don't always block when you should (I mean come on they throw them at half a mile an hour). Running up walls is a chore to do as well since you have to run a little and jump and repeat (not asking for super running but a little more distance with it would be nice). The constant team changing also threw me off. One minute I'm fighting a person and the next minute I'm fighting with him. I like to stick to the team I'm given in a match.
The graphics, sound and music are all nicely done and the moves flow fluidly. The only thing I was irritated about was the fact that heavy attacks seemed too quick to be heavy and the hitboxes already seemed a little off. I realize I'm throwing a lot of negativity about this game. I know it's an indie game and that it isn't going to be perfect...but there's a lot of annoying elements that I unfortunately can't get past. I personally don't recommend it.

For those of you who have played Sonic the Hedgehog and enjoyed it, you will love this game. For those of you who probably avoided teh Sonic games, I suggest getting the demo. This game is great, and runs remarkably smooth. The game has a mere 18 levels over 9 different worlds. Not particularly amazing, but those levels provide tons of replay value as you attempt to get all the S ranks.
Classic Sonic is fun, but doesn't particularly evolve past what you start with. Probably why it's considered the easy mode of the game. Modern Sonic is where all the best stuff is though. Levels are varied and the speed is ever more intense. You'll find a lot of the games better moments in the Modern Sonic portions. (Though Classic is still tons of fun as well.)

Sonic Generations represents a return to form for Sonic. While recent 3D sonic games have been... lackluster, Sonic Generations has Sonic finally hitting his stride. Sonic and Classic Sonic are the only playable characters, each handling the levels in different ways.
Sonic finally controls well, and though there are frustrating moments, the game is still overall enjoyable.
I found it enjoyable to replay levels that I had previously beaten to try to get a better time or find all the secrets, something that will take quite a while.
Anybody who considers, or has considered themselves a Sonic fan owes it to themselves to play this game. It's a bit short, but sweet.

Mafia II is burdened by the fact that it is a game - and maybe not even a very good one. But Mafia II is also one of the greatest games I have ever played. A here's why.
Mafia II is your basic Italian steroetype mobsters versus some other gangs flick. The gameplay is fairly simple, shoot and cover and make your way from point A to point B, nothing special. However, Mafia II is beautifully directed, acted and designed. The attention to period detail is fantastic, and the character interactions and story are absolutley fantastic. Mafia II would suit much better as being a movie or TV show, because all in all it is a cinematic experience and I would even go as far to say a cinematic masterpiece.
Mafia II has such a heart-pumping and wrenching narrative that really makes up for the sub-par gameplay mechanics and the lack of a traditional "free play" mode. At face value, this game may not seem much to you. But I assure you the sale price it is at right now is WELL worth the price and is an absoloute steal. Since it's release, Mafia II has never really left me and the announcement of Mafia III is just as much a reason to pick up this game than any.
- Lackluster gameplay
- No free roam
+ Cinematic experience that is golden
+ Beautifully executed
+ Fantastic story and acting that would expected to feature in a AAA Holywood Blockbuster

Merge the servers, give the option to play any Zone in PvP, with increased rewards, and the population will start growing again. It will not grow if it stays like it is now, it will bleed out.

So I've been playing this game for the last two years on EU (now started a second account via Steam on NA), and I have to say this is my goto game whenever I just want to play a few games and dont want to immerse myself in a big open world RPG or similar 50+ hours game. It isn't as fast paced as normal shooters (or even games like World of Tanks) offers a much more relaxing style of gameplay, relying more on positioning, good aim and teamwork than reflexes - while still having its fair share of high adrenaline moments.
While it is a F2P game with the usual grind and monetization, it is the first one I encountered where you can have fun without being robbed left and right. Gameplay is fun on all tiers, and silver ships (i.e. the ones you can grind) dont suck compared to premium ships (yes, there are some stronger premiums, but they dont affect your enjoyment). So while the grind to top tier without premium time or ships is a long one, its a fun time nevertheless - and if it isn't at some point you still earn some free xp to skip the odd bad ship or you can simply switch to another line of ships that fits your playstyle more. Also there's many ingame events that allow you to win flags, cammos, premium time or ships for just playing the game.
As for loot boxes: yes, they exist. You earn up to three boxes a day for simply playing with a small chance of the container being a 'super container', i.e. one that can contain premium ships, gold, special modules or big amounts of flags or free XP. Normally you can't buy extra loot boxes for real money, except on special occasions (like xmas) or for specific events. You usually get at least your money's worth compared to buying the loot items directly (which is possible for most items except some special event camos).
For me the monetization scheme is fair (for tthe time being), but then I don't expect F2P games to be completely free - servers and further development have to be funded, so I buy the occasional premium ship or loot crate and usually run premium time. What I get in return is a fun arcade game of boats with a lot of variety in ships and gameplay styles - and (in general) a great community.
Note that the game itself is easy to join and play on the low tiers - but the tutorials and initial handholding is absolutely lacking. Nothing that watching a few 'for beginners' introduction videos on youtube (by one of the many community contributors like The Mighty Jingles, iChase, etc.) won't fix, but you have to look for these outside the game itself. In general: know the range of your guns and torps, avoid friendly fire, learn about angling (i.e. dont show broadside) and using the sights to aim correctly (recommended: switch to the dynamic sights). Dont go YOLO - this is a team game and throwing away ships or exposing youself to concentrated fire is a sure way to loose the match for your team. It will take you a good 1000 games in a mix of classes and nations to be proficient at aiming and getting the best out of your ships, but as I have repeatedly stated here: its fun playing throughout.
tl;dr: if you like slower paced gameplay with big guns and explosions, beautiful ships and sneaky torps this might be your cup of tea. Monetization is fair, gameplay fun and the community is great.

Freedom Planet is a side-scrolling action platformer that is heavily inspired by Sonic the Hedgehog and the Genesis/Megadrive era of Sega video games. After playing this game for a bit, I have come to a realization that I, in fact, have a love/hate relationship with this. Before you go off and say "WHAT?! You hate this game?! I don't find this review helpful at all!", let me explain why.
The appearance, and gameplay, delivers exactly what I heard about it, and it's incredibly fantastic. The controls are smooth and easy to use, the gameplay is crisp and fresh, using mechanics from older Sonic the Hedgehog games, and mixing it up with others, Ristar, for example. The graphics, being 16-bit graphics seeming to be have been built from a similar engine to the Genesis' "Blast processor" unit, and it's incredibly well done to look at. The worlds are all unique and colorful, with no lag whatsoever. you play as three different characters, all with different, but similar in a way playstyles to keep the gemplay fresh and addictive. All in all, as a game, it's very well done, and it's a game I can sink my teeth into, just like the older Genesis/Megadrive games.
However, this game is not without its flaws. In this case, the lowpoint of the game is the actual Story/Adventure mode. The levels are fine, as I described above, but the way the story is presented could have been done loads better. Don't get me wrong, I'm not saying the story and lore itself is bad, it's just... "Unnecessarily Complicated." The basic story is that the evil Lord Brevon and his forces have invaded the world, so it's up to Sash Lilac, a cutesy anthropormorphic dragon girl to stop him. This would be the perfect basic story for this game, but suddenly, we get thrown with the fact that three different nations/kingdoms are all at war with each other, blaming the crisis on everybody else, a bunch of side characters get thrown in, it all becomes a complicated mess. I would expect a story like this to be featured in a game such as Final Fantasy, but a game that's heavily influenced by the older Sonic games? It seems unfitting. While the Lord Brevon himself is a cool villain, he seems to be way too evil and cold hearted to be in this cutesy world. Take Dr. Eggman from Sonic, for example: He is a bumbling, tempered, quirky fat man who would do anything to be rid of Sonic, most of his plans failing and him throwing a tantrum. That would be the kind of villain that would fit perfectly with this world, but instead, we have a more serious villain being thrown into a non-serious world. You could argue that it would be fine, but take one look at this game, the artwork, pretty much everything about it, and it's unmistakingly a Kids game. It has the cutesy-ness, the bright colours, the simplistic gameplay and controls to make it a kids game, but the complicated storyline, and some incredibly, and I do mean INCREDIBLY dark scenes in it, including a long drawn out "Torture scene", makes it seem like in a way, the game itself is confused on what it should be. People could also argue "Oh, if you didn't like the story, just play it in Classic Mode!" That's the thing. Without the cutscenes, the story does not make any sense at all. There is no transitions from the levels to make it a believable world without the cutscenes, so it's basically necessary to understand just what the heck is going on. Take, for example, games like Sonic the Hedgehog 2. A game that has no cutscenes at all, yet you can clearly feel between levels, that there is some sort of transition between the worlds, that it feels like it's all one big world. Now, I'm not saying cutscenes are bad, and a story is bad for this, but let's take another example, this time, from Sonic 3 & Knuckles. Unlike Sonic 2, this game does have cutscenes, but they only last a few seconds, with no dialogue, and acted out with simple actions. This is, without a doubt, the best story telling in Sonic history ever, because it's more complicated, yet it doesn't take the general feel out of the game, it still gives you the fast paced transition that the older Sonic games were great for. In Freedom Planet here, between each level is a long, drawn out cutscene where you sit there, pushing the button, listening to the characters speak. For a game that's fast paced, this can be a bad thing, since it breaks off all illusion from this world. The Voicing, I honestly am unsure about the voice acting, all together. The voices do sound like they would have been better if it was said once or twice, and just small basic stuff, but the game is fully voiced acted. To me, the voices seem unfitting at times. They don't feel genuine enough for me, so I can't quite relate to or like the characters that much. It's like the gameplay was inspired by older Sonic, but the story and cutscenes were more inspired by the more "mid-2000s" Sonic, which is not a good thing at all.
All in all, the gameplay and presentation of this game is fantastic, but the main problem with it lies with the over-complicated story and way too many characters to keep track of. The game does deliver what it promises, a Genesis-styled platformer, and it has made me want to actually nab an old Sega Genesis and start playing on it again. Just keep in mind that the story could have been worked on more, and granted, I do appreciate the time and effort that went into the game itself, and also the artwork and stylized characters it made.
In fact, why can't we have more games with the Genesis feel? Has everyone suddenly forgotten that Sega made one of the most kickass video game consoles ever? The same console that gave us Sonic the Hedgehog, Mortal Kombat, NBA Jam, Vectorman, Comix Zone, Gunstar Heroes, and Ristar!

The game Sonic should've evolved to...
(More in-depth thoughts after the lists below)
The Verdict
++ I LOVE this game. At $15, this is a steal for the quality of entertainment value it brings, one that I would've gladly paid more for. I cannot recommend it highly enough, this is pretty much everything I wanted in a game of this genre. The developer did such a great job making everything come together.
If nothing else, try the demo and see what you're in for.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
The lengthier thoughts
This game wasn't on my radar, at all in fact... mostly because I didn't know it was in development or existed for that matter. What got my initial attention was a chance encounter with a couple player reviews as I was browsing the (non-specific) section of the Steam Community hub. Seeing the game compared to other titles I was familiar with (Rocket Knight/Sparkster, Megaman, Pulseman, and Sonic), as well as mentions of the difficulty included within piqued my interest enough that I decided to check the store page to see what was up. When I saw the gameplay trailer, I was more or less hooked to the point where I decided that I wanted the game, and didn't want to wait for a sale.
Indeed if you have any fond memories of the aforementioned games (preferably their 90's versions), you likely will recognize many familiar elements scattered throughout, but with a fresh take on their iterations in this game. Regardless of whether those memories are present or not, you should be able to create quite a few new ones from Freedom Planet.
The gameplay itself is the shining star here as it should be. There are currently 3 characters available for play and one additional on the beta branch.
- Lilac has your Rocket Knight elements built into her skillset, being able to boost in almost any direction when her special meter is full. She is in general a very fast fighter and makes great use of open spaces with the rest of her moves, particularly her cyclone attack which can be used on the ground or in the air to unleash a devastating flurry of attacks, and even increase her maneuverability.
- Carol is your wall jumping, fierce melee fighter who can make best use of tighter spaces. What she lacks in her open-space mobility (when she doesn't have her motorcycle power-up), she makes up for by being able to pull herself out of danger by scaling any nearby surfaces. With her motorcycle, she gains the ability to double jump, boost her speed when on the ground, and ride up walls rather than having to jump up them Megaman/Super Meat Boy style.
- Milla is a more defensive-based ranged character, who summons 'phantom blocks', projectiles which can be thrown, or used to enhance her shield blast which also doubles as a means to reflect/absorb most enemy projectiles. She also has the ability to fly temporarily while in the air, and dig into the mostly sparse, softer surfaces to find items to help her along her way. Mastery of these attacks will allow for more aggressive gameplay.
Enemies themselves for the most part do not wound you on impact. This typically tends to be the standard for games of this genre, which also tended to lead to some aggravating, not to mention avoidable damage/deaths and slowdowns. Make no mistake, many will hurt you, very badly in some cases, but you'll at least have time to react so that any mistakes will be player side and not because of bad design.
The bosses are some of the best moments of the game due to the fact that they evolve in many different ways over the course of the fight. Some of the encounters have a bit of randomness added to make the fight unpredictable, others add new attacks/patterns as you bring them to different damage thresholds/phases, a couple speed up as they become closer to death, some even behave differently if playing on 'hard' difficulty. All in all there's a nice variety of elements to each boss fight to make them fun (but not necessarily any easier) with each subsequent playthrough. That said, it is worth noting that you will likely meet with a few cheap deaths on your first playthrough as there are a couple "surprise!" moments that will badly hurt you toward the later levels, whether from an unexpected attack, or just the number of instances you take damage from failing to dodge something particularly painful. I like to think that it will increase the fun factor though after the initial shock wears off.
The music is phenomenal as well, we're talking the kind of quality that stays with you after you stop playing, that, assuming you don't also buy the soundtrack, you will listen to over and over outside the game.
I could go on and on, but the main thing that any perspective buyer needs to know here, is that this game does essentially everything right that matters and where it matters.

Jedi Outcast is the third (though officially second) part of the Jedi Knight series. I began playing this after completing and enjoying Jedi:Academy and bit of dark forces.
Story is strong. Following, the protagonist from the previous games, Kyle (former jedi) and Jann (pilot) continuing working for the new republic as mercenaries. As plans back fire, Kyle will be forced to re-unite with the 'force' again in order to seek answers and vengeance. I found the plot better than Jedi: Academy, as it was less vague with a better antagonist and motive behind the player's actions.
Gameplay is good. The beginning sequences of the campaign plays homage to 'Dark forces' with you having no lightsaber and forced to use guns instead. As you progress through the campaign, you will finally get access to the glowing blade as well as force powers. The force powers available include force lightning, heal, push, pull, speed and mind control. You only start off with a few powers which are at level 1. As you play, you will automatically unlock new powers and upgrades. You light saber skills will also upgrade, unlocking more powerfull offensive and defensive moves. Unfortunately, you can't customize you light saber or fighting style (ie two sabers or Darth Maul's one) like in J:A. Some people may find that starting without a lightsaber and forced to use guns for the first few levels, annoying. Another issue may arise from the level design, which by the way well done, but will leave you confused and lost some times (forcing you to use a guide like I did).
There is also a multiplayer mode available. Just like in J:A, there are variety of game modes including capture the flag, deathmatch and duel. You can customise your character and light saber (color and hilt). There a variety of maps to choose from which are mainly inspired by levels in the campaign such as the Yavin temple, while others like the death star are unique. You can play the game with bots or players with a maximum of 16 in total. As of this review there were a few players online.
Graphics are alright. Although they are not as good as J:A, there isn't much difference between them. However, outcast definitely has better detailed models and textures compared to the previous Dark Forces games. I tweaked the game and played in widescreen, which made everything look clearer.
Audio is great. Soundtrack is awesome as usual. Weapons like blasters and light saber slashes, sound as they should. Voice acting of characters are good as well.
If you want to play a star wars game with good combat, story and characters, Jedi: Outcast will not dissapoint.

It's a beautiful, simple game. Greatly recommend it. Here's a bit of a breakdown:
*Graphics: It's your standard basic NES/SNES overworld view with some portraits that arent great but are good enough. Portraits seem to be the extent of the artwork. It's not meant to be beautiful, but it doesnt really take much away from the game itself.
*Music: It's fantastic and it's worth the time looking for it and downloading it (don't worry, it's free, hence it couldnt be packaged into a DLC, which I would've gladly spent money on). No, really. The music is beautiful and outstanding, reminescing of SNES era. Especially the game recap/clear data tune and the loading screen.
*Battle system: Simple hack and keep moving. Simple item usage. Simple magic using if you can get to it. A bit bothersome to get to the menus to cast magic or skills, but hack slash is a click away.
*Gameplay: Controls are very easy, mechanics are simple, objective is clear from the get-go. Menus are a bit cumbersome as mentioned previously. Other than that, it has some neat mechanics like the dimension vault where you can store some valuables to use at your next rebirth. Perks are nice to have, and all classes have a plus and minus, they feel fairly balanced. I can axe walls with my mage, or cast fire with my pirate. It's a joy to play.
Difficulty: Up to you. It has several modes you can play, and though I've only been playing on the Easy mode, I haven't found it too bad. I still die if I'm not careful, but not like I am struggling to survive... except when all of my weapons break at the 375km mark and the evil lord is about to show up. Without the dimensional vault, it can be slightly challenging, but MUCH easier if you do use it to store valuable weapons and equipment.
*Story(?): Well, it's very simple really. Run from the darkness before it gets you. I've read the more you play the more you get to know what's going on (what's the darkness? Why are you the hero? Who's the evil lord? Why at 402km?). I'm not there yet, but it doesnt bother me not having 200 tomes of history shoved down my throat as I am just trying to get by. And get by you must, or darkness will get you.
*Replayability: I havent beat every single aspect, but I aint even mad when I do die because I wanted that treasure and my weapon breaks in the middle of a dungeon and darkness gets me. Each class is a pleasure to play with (last being hunters... not sure why, I just cant get along with them). Each try is different, maps, treasures, weapons.
All in all, best cheapest game I've ever bought. Would purchase at full price for sure.
PS: I haven't played the Plus version, so this is based on the basic version.

The difference between Chicken shoot Gold and Chicken shoot is quite astonishing. This game is a must buy, it brings together the full package which the original just cant. The orignal barely lives up to the sequels glory.
Story: The game throws you into an apocolyptic scene from the get go, which makes for a very engaging start (+1). The universe is set in 1934 Nazi germany... BUT WITH A TWIST!!! Instead of Nazi german humans the villans are actually portrayed as chickens, which, i believe, gives the game a deeper poetic meaning (+1). Perhaps the Nazi's have been portrayed is this manner to hint to the fact that not only were the nazi's villans they were cowards too, but its all open to interpritation (+1).
The protagnist of the game is a nameless man, you may be wondering ''Why isnt the protaganist a chicken too?? And Why am i reading this review??!'' Two very good questions. To answer the first one i would say that the devolpers of the game have tried to use the nameless man to represent the allied forces as a whole (+1). Now i know this game may seem slightly xenophobic, but you must keep in mind that this game was released in 1936 as a propaganda method for the allied forces to brainwash the minds of the succeptable younger generations (-1).
After a few levels into the game we meet one of the co-protaganists of the game 'Jesus Christ'. The introduction of the son of god unlocks some new interesting features to the game (+1), but we will get to that later. The game then goes onto an amazing twist, i wont spoil much, but the story turns into a battle against time as you and 'Jesus Christ' go on a perilous quest back in time to stop Hitler from coming into power (+1). Ill leave the rest of the story for you guys to find out.
STORY POINTS = 5   Next up is the Graphics.
Graphics: Not much to say here. Sure the visuals may not be as amazing to games such as call of duty and Kick♥♥♥♥♥2, but you must keep in mind that this game was released in 1936 which makes it quite revolutionary in my opinion. (+5).
GRAPHIC POINTS = 5   Lastly up next is gameplay.
Gameplay: The way the game plays is simple yet genius, alot like minecraft its a 3rd person side scrolling adventure. The game then sugar coats this with the addition of magic, you may remember me mentioning 'Jesus Christ' earlier in the review. Well after a few quests you earn his trust, and in return you revieve the holy bible. This alows you to cast spells which really spices up the game and kept it fresh for me. And personally this game comes under both of my faviourte game genres (FPS and RPG) and i would recomend anyone else who enjoy games under the same catergory to pick this up immediantly. (ONE BIG +1)

Though a fairly short game I found I rather liked this game.
First Person Platforming tends to be something cringeworthy, but this game's mechanics of a grappling hook and in-air control makes platforming in first person a really good experience, which is good since it's what you're going to spend all your time doing.
No guns, no cover mechanics, no "Press U to wallrun and tag the wall for big points". You get movement, a jump. Then a charge jump forward and upward. A grappling hook to swing from and finally something to save you from falling to your doom. But with those mechanics A Story About My Uncle presents you some not too tough challenges running, jumping, swinging across bottomless pits.
Graphics wise, this looks really well. Up close you might find some jaggy edges or not too pretty textures, but the visual style as a whole and the environments made me stop to take in the view several times throughout the game.
Storywise...there is one, told sparsely as you explore the (linear) world. Some might derive a deeper meaning and message from it. Personally it was a nice background to why you were doing death-defying jumps.
Overall, I can recommend the game to anyone who likes the idea of first-person-platforming. It isn't a very taxing or long game and you might want to wait for a sale, but I certainly didn't feel it a waste of my time.

One of the Star Wars games to get close to emulating the authentic feel of the movies, Jedi Outcast was also one of the titles that helped change public perception of SW games from cheap cash-ins to heartfelt, fan-made adventures. This is the game in which you get to hang out with Lando Calrissian on the Millennium Falcon. It's also the game where you drive an AT-ST in a jungle and then get taunted by a dark Jedi with a deep voice in a temple while the throne room theme from Return of the Jedi plays.
It's a very 'Star Wars' experience - its attempts to summon nostalgia for the movies succeed much more than in its predecessors Dark Forces and Jedi Knight, or its sequel Jedi Academy. All of those are quality games in their own right, but Jedi Outcast has Lando in it. It feels effortless.
Outcast is far from perfect - its visuals and choppy lightsaber combat have aged poorly even if its blaster-blasting is still fun. Its plot, for all its Star Wars-y-ness and syruppy nostalgia, is pretty silly (a dinosaur is involved). The nineties/noughties obligatory stealth section and needless keycard hunts are a bit of a pain. But I will be god damned if Lando Calrission isn't right there sat next to you with Billy Dee Williams doing the voice and everything.
A fun adventure that gets its tone just right, while the gameplay varies. Recommended easily for fans of the films (Lando cameos btw), but for people who are after a quality shooter/platformer by modern standards, it's just a blue milk run.

Back in the heady NES era, auto-scrolling levels always seemed to cause people the most stress. In a game like Mario or Castlevania where you normally get to explore or measure your movements, scrolling forces you to think on your feet and act under duress. As tends to happen in this eclectic genre, someone took that concept and applied it to the traditional roguelike formula. But rather than simply turn a stressful game design into a pressure-cooker, One Way Heroics expands on every aspect to produce something unique, engaging, and addictive.
The Land of Generic Fantasy is in peril, and the evil Demon Lord is to blame. For any other game this would get an eyeroll from me but here the drama plays out over dimensions, not continents. Each world is threatened by an inexorable wall of darkness that moves ever rightward, consuming all in its path. Only by defeating the Demon Lord  can the darkness be stopped, at least in that particular dimension. With little time to prepare, you must scour the land for equipment and allies before running afoul of your nemesis in a climactic final encounter.
Don’t let the ceaseless march of oblivion put you off, because this is a traditional roguelike at heart and that means everything is turn-based. You can sit there as long as you want, staring at the unmoving void or frozen enemies, all waiting for you to take your damn turn so they can get back to terrorizing the land. That time will be invaluable for planning your moves, especially if you get cornered in a dungeon being consumed by the darkness or end up stuck behind a mountain range. It’ll also give you time to use your special abilities or consumables you’re inevitably going to hoard your first few runs.
Once you get a feel for the game, staying several steps ahead of the murderwall will be of little concern to you. Instead, you’re going to have to come to grips with the off-beat progression system this game has. If you’re coming off other traditional roguelikes you may be expecting a fair spread of weapons, armors, and consumables spread across the land for you. On good days that’ll be the case but One Way Heroics has no qualms with denying you any of those, even simple foodstuffs necessary to keep your heroic avatar chugging along. New gear is extremely sparse, food items need to be bought if you hope to keep a reserve of them, and enemies rarely drop anything besides some modest coin. Even treasure chests hidden away in dungeons or lakes must be bashed or lockpicked open, and so are worthless without a special skill or plenty of time to get through their unexpected defenses.
The game’s uneven power curve will keep this from appearing much of a problem for awhile, but soon enough you’ll run across a minotaur or a golem or just a really beefy bandit who explodes you in a hit or two. I’m sure your first few deaths will be quite sudden, and the game is nice enough to advise you post-mortem about how to improve your chances. You’ve got some powerful innate abilities to overcome tough monsters and tight spots with the darkness, and you’ll need to use them freely to get through the sudden difficulty spikes. The bright side of the difficulty curve is that it’s still easy to learn and overcome, and once you start sticking it to the Demon Lord the real fun can begin.
One Way Heroics does more than stick a pursuer onto the roguelike formula. The dimensions your adventures play out in aren’t just called that for kicks, they can have wildly different topography, unique landmarks and treasures, or powerful house rules like no leveling up or no item drops. Every time you start a game you can pick a new random dimension, a specified dimension, a dimension you failed to conquer before, or one of three daily challenge dimensions featuring those wild house rules. And this is on top of the numerous character classes and unlockable perks which can start you off with handy stat boosts, extra skills, or even a pet. Plus there’s the dimensional vault which lets you carry over helpful items from one world to the next.
It’s the simple fun of running riot over a fantasy world in short sessions, mixed with an expansive backend full of unlocks and game modes, that makes One Way Heroics special. That key one-more-round appeal is here in full force, taunting you to try again every time you get crushed by a skeleton or devoured by the darkness. There’s something to be said for the unique presentation as well, a veritable circus design of windows, text panels, indicators, and progress bars. It can be daunting and downright ugly at first, but after awhile even that starts to feel comfortable and familiar.
The graphics are certainly not a strong point of the game, featuring basic RPG tiles, tiny sprites, and a disappointingly bland palette. Nor is the sound design of much note, though it succeeds in capturing that JRPG upbeat heroism as you travel from fields to deserts to tundra. But it fortunately lives in a genre dominated by ASCII art and silent combat, and besides none of this stops the game from just being flat-out fun. One Way Heroics starts out with a bold gimmick and builds it into a vast and entertaining experience, one that gets deep hooks into you once you learn how it all works.

So I'm guessing there was a meeting at galaxy trails ( the company who made this game) that was something along the lines of this: " you know what's cool Sonic the Hedgehog and rocket Knight and other awesome Sega Genesis platformers we should make a game the combines all those elements". and they did and it was freaking awesome.
Fans of platformers will love this game. It's a fantastic mix of high-speed action, thrilling combat, interesting story, fantastic music, and excellent and expressive art.

If you're a fan of classic platformers like Mega Man, Sonic the Hedgehog and Rocket Knight, you have NO REASON to not own this game. The levels are superbly designed, the bosses are intense and challenging, and it gives awesome incentive to be replayed multiple times as you have three different characters (four in the later future) that not only play entirely different from one another, but also have their own levels and branching paths!
The only thing that might turn you off is its plot-hole ridden and inconsistent story. It's fanfic material, escalating between lighthearted GIRL POWER kid-friendly stuff, to dark and serious territory involving politics, war and TORTURE. And keep in mind that the characters are a bunch of adorable, simple minded furries that want to save the world from an unstoppable evil. Its transition from kid friendly mindsets of saving the world, to the characters having realistic notions of stuff just doesn't work. I won't spoil anything, but the tale that Galaxy Trail made is filled with eye rolling "cringe" moments and that's kinda disappointing. The story tries so hard to be mature for its own good.
But that doesn't stop Freedom Planet from being an excellent game. I'm not even a huge fan of old school platformers and I still adored every minute of it. Let that be a tip to any who are shy of the genre, because Freedom Planet does an excellent job balancing its mechanics by being both a 2D action game and an obstacle course platformer. You have the best of both worlds, and it never becomes a Jack-of-All trades kinda thing where it fails to achieve quality gameplay by doing too much; both aspects are next to flawless. Movement can be a little slippery and sensitive, and the physics are sort of wonky as of this moment, but the developer intends to improve the game as it treads towards its inevitable release date.
Buy it, support the developers, and hope that they will make a sequel.

Advance: I backed this on Kickstarter.
I didn't play Dragonfall until well after it came out where I played Shadowrun Returns almost entirely within the first week it came out; something about the advertising and the art just didn't catch me.  And then, on a whim, I dove in - and once I finished, I immediately turned to Hong Kong to get more of a fix.
It's good, but after the mastery of Dragonfall, Hong Kong left me feeling a little wanting.
To give context within the series of games, Shadowrun Returns felt like a nostalgia trip while Dragonfall was a crafted, almost cinematic, experience worthy of a movie.  Hong Kong is a lot of fun, but where Dragonfall had moments of ambiguity and the constant looming feeling of being the pawn of much larger forces, Hong Kong feels very binary - there is never any ambiguity to your choices.  You're being a♥♥♥♥♥♥or you aren't.
In many ways, Hong Kong feels like the Shadowrun your friends would craft around a table - the story is servicable, the characters are fun if a bit one dimensional, the setting allows for some fun and wacky runs (the feng shui one was hysterical), but there are also a lot of plot holes and details that just kind of fall flat; when Dragonfall ended, it all came together cohesively and even if the whole story didn't *end*, you felt satisfied with the ending of this particular chapter.  With Kong Kong, it just kind of stops and then you get a bit of an exposition that's mostly "and then everyone lived happily ever after!" and there's a moment of "Is that it?"
Don't get me wrong - it's a lot of fun and if you played the other two, Hong Kong is definitely worth picking up and playing if you need to get your fix of being a decker or street samurai.  But of the three (all of which were good!), it feels like the middle child.  It isn't a nostalgia trip like SRR, it isn't a first class experience like Dragonfall - it's very good, but not *great*.

This game is enraging... and I love it. The music is great, the art is cute, and the controls are tight and responsive. The game is all about rhythm. If you play without the sound on you will be screwed. This game is about a hero known as Commander Video trying to rescue his friends. Now, the only reason I bought this game is because there is a Slenderman easter egg in world three. But, now I like it for what it is. I highly recommend this game.

This game isn't some average day Banquet TV Dinner, let me tell you. Bit Trip Runner 2 is, actually, a very simplistic side-scrolling platformer with some slick rhythm elements and a very unique, whimsical style.
You play as Commander Video and your task is to reach the end of some levels, DOMINATE your robotic nemesis, and save your friends.  The first level starts off pretty chill, just jumpin' over some lil' bumps in the road, look out for some robots. Not a big deal. Everything is going great until you see- OH MY GOODNESS-  an airborne robot threat! You can't jump over him, so you're forced to hit down and SLIDE underneath it. You might be thinking "Dang, now I gotta jump over things AND slide under things too, this is getting a little outta control".
Fortunately, things only get crazier as new mechanics and abilites are introduced. Over time you'll be hoppin' on springs, grinding on rails like a skater dude, karate kicking through your enemies, deflecting power cubes with your force field barrier, and dancing 24/7. Trust me, its too sick. The game offers 3 different difficulties, but the overall challenge is pretty tame. Fans of the 1st Bit Trip Runner may be disappointed at the drop in difficulty.
One of my favorite aspects of the game is it's musical magnificence. Not only is the soundtrack itself killer, but the ways in which sound is integrated into the platforming is a real juicy treat.  As you progress in a level the soundtrack will increase in complexity, and every single action that you perform in the level, like completing a jump or hitting a spring, will make sounds that add to the beat.  It's little things like this that make Runner 2 stand out and make me say "I LIKE THIS GAME."
There's plenty of costumes and characters to unlock, and 100+ levels to complete. If you go for 100% completion, this game can occupy you for quite some time. I must say that, for me, it was truly a slamtastic experience. So, If you are thinking of purchasing this, I'd recommend looking at some videos of the game in action so you know what to expect, but rest assured that you will be buying excellence.
To sum it up, if Bit Trip Runner 2 was a wild animal, it would definitely be a funky lookin' rainforest ape.
Thank you for reading this review.

A Story About My Uncle has amazing gameplay and almost nothing else.  That being said, this is the best first person platformer I've ever played, not that it has a whole lot of competition.  The game is centered around a grappling mechanic, which accounts well for the age old first person platformer problem of not knowing where your feet are.  Platforming is fast and exhilirating.  Zipping onto and off of floating rocks feels great, and the game balances its challenge very well.  It also knows exactly when to end, not stretching out the mechanic needlessly; however this does mean the game clocks in at around 2-4 hours.
With that said, now I'll talk about my problems with every single other aspect in the game.  The graphics on everything look muddled even on the highest resolution but otherwise fine, except the character models.  With the exception of one model at the very end, they all fall deep into the uncanny valley.  The characters aren't human, so Coffee Stain may have been going for that, but they did their job too well in making the creatures look awkward and unsettling.  The sound design is uninspired, and unremarkable.  I struggle to remember a single piece of music from my entire experience, but what I do remember was generic kids' movie fodder.
Speaking of kids' movies, that transitions badly into the plot that's hyped up by a lot of commenters.  It's completely generic, getting from point A to point B with no twists along the way, and knowing exactly what will happen if you've seen a kids' movie in your life.  The plot isn't the main focus here, but it is worth noting that it's mediocre.
Despite those issues, it's still worth buying because soaring from stone to stone, across miles in a single jump is one of the most enjoyable platforming experiences I've ever had.  Just don't go in looking for more than that.

Chicken Shoot Gold/2 won’t revolutionise the light gun shoot ‘em up genre and they probably won’t entertain you for more than 20 minutes, but they are perfect to just whip up a simple little game to pass the time when you feel a bit tired or lazy.
Trust me, it has been proven numerous types, your little brother/sister or your young child can sit in front of it for hours on end while you will be free to do anything. Especially if you show them there are more levels so they can play with a goal to progress.
Chicken Shoot Gold and Chicken Shoot 2 are actually cash-in games that rode the success of Moorhuhn (Crazy Chicken), a franchise that lasted 10 years and 30 games. Apparently Germans really like to shoot chickens around the turn of the millennium; during that time you could find dozens of these themed (usually cartoonish) shoot ‘em ups on the internet and on gaming magazine CDs.
Chicken Shoot’s primary selling point is the hand-drawn graphics, and I have to admit, they look good even in 2014 on a full HD monitor. While the game itself is simple as a stick (you get a gun, you shoot chicken, you reload, then shoot more chicken), the small details can really add a few layers to it here and there.
For example all levels (there are five of them in the first one, six in the second, plus an end boss screen in both) feature hidden bonuses you can shoot for additional points: shooting a mine cart into an abandoned mine, blowing off the top hat of a snowman and so on; this also emulates Moorhuhn’s crazy level secrets. And these are just a few of the Easter eggs you can find in the game– apart from those the chicken throw in your face of course.
Yes: the games have several levels. Most people who try the games out will never notice that, because you either need to kill all chicken (Arcade) or get to 2500/3500 points/level (Classic) to advance to the next stage.
And yes, there is actually an end boss in both games, and in the second one beating the Chicken King can be a really difficult task. So… good luck if you try it.

This game has the same magic that catapaulted the classic Sonic games to fame. The characters feel like extensions of you - not an avatar that you are manipulating. Slopes let you catapault to soaring heights, and you can blast through a stage once you learn it. If you're like me and have been waiting since 1994 for an honest successor to those games, your wait is over. It easily rivals Sonic 3 and Knuckles as one of the greatest platform games ever made. You don't need to wait for this one to go on sale - it is worth far more than its launch price.
This isn't to say that it is a Sonic clone - in some ways it is, but in other ways it is completely unique. The parts of the game that could qualify as 'sonic cloning' are cloned so well that the brilliance of the originals shine through. All of the parts that are unique are thoughtfully designed and fit in with the whole.
As a fellow game developer, my only critique is that I would tweak the checkpoint system a little bit. There were many times where a checkpoint would occur just a little bit too early before a boss fight or other notable encounter, which would slow me down when I wanted to just get back into the action. I'd make it abit more like Nitronic Rush or Super Meat Boy with the 'immediately back in the action' principle. Still, this is a trivial issue and doesn't detract from the experience at all.

It's not possible to review this game without drawing comparisons to Sonic the Hedgehog. It's not. But if I had to choose between Sonic the Hedgehog 3 and going another round with this game, I'd have to say Freedom Planet would own my afternoon.
At first, I was leary of this game. The graphics didn't look all too impressive from a glance at the screenshots, and $15 seemed a little steep for me to take a risk. But for whatever reason, I did. And after playing through the first few levels, I deeply regret ever doubting the quality of this game. The levels, characters, and just EVERYTHING were all lovingly crafted by the developers, and it shows. And while the game hosts a number of obvious similarities to the blue hedgehog's glory days games, I daresay that Freedom Planet does it all far better, right down to the core mechanics of the game. Even if you didn't really enjoy any Sonic games, I'd still recommend this game, because it is something else altogether.
Admittedly, I don't care terribly for the difficulty curve. Because while the difficulty raises over time throughout the course of the game, it fluxuates wildly within the level, ranging from a gentle summer breeze to DEAR CHRIST IN HEAVEN SPARE ME THIS TRIBULATION. You also accumulate lives way too easily. If it were my decision, I would abolish lives altogether, and rather start the player off at the beginning of the current board whenever you die. But I suppose it's a little late to be going back and making such colossal redesigns as that. Also, the game has VOICE ACTING! And it's not atrocious! It's nothing amazing, but it's still good. And that's pretty damn impressive.
Difficulty aside, it's a great game that I would easily recommend for any fan of the action-platformer genre.

Sonic has had a much bumpier career than Mario with his missing appearance on the Saturn, his first adventure into 3D having not aged too well, his first anniversary game being one of the worst games of all time (Sonic '06) and the attempts to fix the franchise afterword resorting to ripping off other non-related games (like God of War). That said, things have been looking good for Sonic ever since Colors came out and Generations does to some extent build on that momentum and even fix many of the problems with the previous 3D Sonic games. Of course much like Sonic's career, Generations has numerous flaws that keep it from reaching the peak of platforming bliss that old Jumpman set.
Let's start off with the good: Generations looks and sounds great with crisp graphics, beautiful environments and some of the series best tunes in one package. Both the 2D and 3D levels are mostly fun (with a few disappointing exceptions) and in some cases even fix what weren't really fun levels before (such as '06's Crisis City). The controls are spot on and it seems they have almost perfected 3D Sonic's move set (almost, one of the missions proves that the Homing Attack is still a bit tricky) while 2D Sonic feels just like he did in the old games, which is funny given how odd Sonic 4 felt. The Story is nothing special, but it's not contrived and stupid like in Adventure 2 and '06, plus there are some funny lines here and there. Also the new not-4KIDS cast is great (even though Robotnik is still played by the same actor) and they fit the roles well without any weird ear bleeding voices making you reach for the mute button.
As I said though, the game does have flaws that keep it from being a proper classic. For one thing, the game just feels padded. There are 9 levels (3 from each era: the Genesis Era, the Adventure Era and the Modern Era) with 2 acts each, 4 boss fights and 3 rival bosses. Given the general brevity of a standard Sonic level, this makes the game sound a bit short, even compared to other Sonic games. This is where the missions come in. In order to gain access to a boss of a given era, you have to get a key from each of the 3 levels. You get a key by completing missions (there are 5 for each level for both old and new Sonic), which you really only have to beat 1 of in each level. This is thing though; if you are only expected to do 1 per level, then why not just add a 3rd act? Reusing the existing level's assets for random missions just feels like they were tacked on at last minute or added to save money and really they just feel like filler. Franky, adding a 3rd act and just having the missions be completely optional would have been the better option.
The other issue is that the missions them selves are mostly not fun. In fact a few are what I'd call "anti-fun" (the Vector music note one is one of the worst things I've ever played in my life). I can think of several that were no fun at all, but can't think of one that was fun off the top of my head. I'm sure there were a few, but they just don't leave an impression on you. The other issue is that while they fixed many levels that weren't fun in old games, they actually ruined one that was fun, that being Planet Wisp. I personally love Sonic Color, so I was excited to see what this level was like, but I was saddened to see that they didn't use any actual level from the game. I can understand for the 2D act (which was even less fun), but not the 3D one. How could they keep the '06 level mostly intact and then just ignore all the levels in Colors? What a waste.
Those problems aside, Generations is still a fun game overall and well worth any Sonic fan's time. I'm not sure if I'd recommend it for new fans, maybe check out Colors or even Unleashed first or hell, just buy the Steam bundle that comes with 12 games for free and play the old games in order. There is really no reason not to.
I give Sonic Generations an 8.0 out of 10.
