Shadowrun Hong Kong is that rare gem (for me): great story AND great gameplay. I might even like it a bit more than Dragonfall, as I appreciated the concept of what was ultimately going on. The characters are interesting, I felt genuinely attached to some of them by the end. Like Dragonfall, it's dripping with atmosphere, most of it expressed through speech or descriptive texts, so it's a good thing I like reading.
Quests can be completed in a number of ways, such as infiltration/hacking, charm, or just bashing your way through. There's some moral calls to make, some of which have consequences you can see later on in the game. It's a pretty nifty package all in all, no buyer's regret here.

You find yourself in a bright passage, with only one door at the end. Approaching, you observe that the door is made of a study section of oak. On it, at eye level, is a small brass nameplate. It reads "Shadowrun: Hong Kong Review". Seeing no doorknob, you push the door open.
It takes your eyes a few seconds to adjust to the light after stepping into the room, moodily lit with a fire blazing on the hearth. The room is tastefully fashioned in what you recognize to be a rather old style, mahogany bookcases, a classical globe on an axis, a ship in a bottle; very relaxing decoration. Your attention is drawn however to the furniture placed near the fireplace. There are two large wingback chairs, one of which contains a silhouetted figure.
"Ah, so you're here at last", you hear the figure say, his voice lined with friendliness. "Come on in, take a seat. Don't be shy."
You casaully make your way to the vacant seat by the crackling logs, soaking in the heat of the fire as you sit down. The chair is surprisingly comfortable while still being supportive of your back. It seems to make you sit attentively, as if to listen to a story.
You can see the man more clearly now. His appearance would suggest him to be middle-aged but his features are worn. He has signs of slight wrinkling on his cheecks and around his eyes, eyes which you can tell from a glance, have seen many things. He's pouring two tumblers of whiskey from a decanter on the side table, finishing the act with a few cubes of ice each from an ornate ice-bucket that sits beside the decanter. He offers one to you, which you gladly accept.
"So", he begins, "you want to know about Shadowrun: Hong Kong, do you chummer?"
He pauses, but you remain silent, sensing his question to be rhetorical.
"That is why you have found yourself here. Well you've come to the right place. Make yourself cosy, because I'm about to tell you a story. A story that features good and evil, where the lives of many hang in the balance while the world itself weakens. A legendary and epic tale about the dark and dangerous shadows of Hong Kong, the city Heoi and how an old friend of mine forever changed the lives of the people that lived there. If only I could recall a name..."
As he speaks, you feel as if the words are reaching out to you, and this man feels somewhat familiar. Do you know him from somewhere? He reaches the end of his sentence and you suddenly know that you've heard this story before. You are the friend he speaks of after all. But how did that story go again? You shiver with excitement, and close your eyes as your vision fades and you suddenly recall a story you never knew, starting back at how it all began when you first arrived in Hong Kong...

I am giving this game a reluctant non-recommendation.
For those who rate the validity of a review based on hours played, I want to stipulate that a 15% of my hours logged playing this game are atributed to load times.
Shadowrun Hongkong was my first exposure to the Shadowrun cannon. When I started, it I liked it. The graphics are crisp the music is apt, and I have always had a softsopt for games set in Hongkong.  Shadowrun has acted as a wonderful surrogate for table top RPG's that I no longer have time to play. (Think cyberpunk 2020)
Alas! I was betrayed be a party of menacing glitches !!!  Roll for initiative:
1)The inventory system in this game is cumbersome and unreliable.  Access to your over all stash is only accessible in when shopping or at your hideout in Heoi proper--the hub town. The game is designed so that you are only responsible for your own equipment so when shopping you can only compare weapon/ armor stats to what your playable character has. if you want to figure if handing down your equipment is worth your time you have to wait until you start a mission.
When starting a mission you can loan equipment to your party, and at the end of the mission you are supposed to get your equipment and unused items retuned to you. This is not always the case. Sometime your equipment dissapears somtimes you get mystery equipment. There are also times once usable items in your inventory become unequipable or you cannot sell them.
2)Load times between mission areas are painfully long.
3)The fatal blow:  my copy of shadowrun will not load past the "Prosperity" mission.
I worked around the inventory problems and load times because I wanted to keep playing. The game is entertaining, but ultimately it is non-functioning. I would stay away from this one.

I kind of forgot that I owned this game, and I guess that probably should tell you all something.
Not even going to go into what kind of game this is - if you're on the store page at all, you know what you're here to buy, and in all honesty, Runner 2 is not what you're here to buy. Like me, you were probably expecting BIT.TRIP RUNNER, but with fancy graphics... and at its core, it is indeed BIT.TRIP RUNNER with fancy graphics. Only at its core.
A lot of complaints in the negative reviews are complaints that seem to suggest the player just doesn't like this kind of game. If you truly are new to the scene of BIT.TRIP, it's a rhythm game that integrates what you're doing with the background music, and you're technically supposed to be able to use the audio cues to help you improve your gameplay,  but that seems to have gotten lost here. The first RUNNER title was a huge leap away from the previous trilogy of BIT.TRIP games, and remained simple to pick up but challenging to master. Your movement options were essentially limited to run (which the game does for you), jump, and crouch/slide. That was it, not hard to manage.
With Runner 2, the game just dumps features on you. You can jump, you can couch, you can kick♥♥♥♥♥♥apart, you can bring up your shield and bounce squares around in homage to the first BIT.TRIP trilogy... it becomes overwhelming and a little unintuitive. Maybe the dev team changed, but it almost feels like they forgot what they were doing, most importantly, forgot the difference between the depth of gameplay and the complexity of gameplay. With limited, almost one handed controls, RUNNER was able to match the feel of classic games upon which it was clearly based. Runner 2 on the other hand tries to make itself challenging and give itself more depth through the use of new mechanics, and stacking those mechanics on top of each other, and it starts to become like trying to pilot a jet - there's a ton of buttons and it's almost impossible to remember on the fly which one is doing what and which one needs to be used to stop yourself from crashing into whatever is in front of you.
Story wise, it's nothing special. This is one of those games with a story that just doesn't really need a story. No one cares what's going on here.

It's kind of hard to describe exactly what this game is, but I freaking love it! Essentially a rouge-like, but very unique, It's an action RPG with very lite turn-based elements. The whole goal is to keep moving right as the entire world is engulfed by this black wall of death. Fighting monsters along the way, leveling up, finding new gear, and eventually battling the demon lord.
You start each run by picking a character class and up to 3 starting skills. You then get to choose from a list of worlds to join. Some are harder or offer different challanges, you can join up with other players or even use the random seed generator. Playing the game at first might seem weird, but it is fun. The game and enemies don't move until you move, attack, or use an item. Although, I still consider this an action RPG because of how fluent you can move, it almost does have a real-time feel to it. It seems like the whole turn-based element is only there because it has an in-depth system with skills and inventory management. It actually makes the game more interesting because you can play it at your own pace.
Like mentioned, every time you move so does the black fog destroying everything in it's path, forcing you to always move right. This adds a lot of strategy. Knowing when to fight monsters or maneuvering around obstacles and terrain to pick up items, all while managing a hunger meter and conserving energy. Along the way you'll encounter several NPC's. Being able to buy, recruit, identify items, or save your game among other things, but even they are not safe from the death mist. Leveling up is simple and automatic to specific character class, but you are given opportunites to trade stats at certain points. You can also upgrade weapons and armor, and use various scrolls, abilties, and a wide array of items. After a certain distance traveled you will face the demon lord. Prioratizing a well built character is key to survival, and when playing on harder difficulties there is no telling when the boss will show up.
When you win or die you will be rated based on your performance with a quick recap of your entire playthrough. You get points to spend on more skills and characters. You also get a vault to store some of your best items to help better your next run. The vault is universal for every playthrough, but taking an item out is only for that specific run. This is a good way to level up weapons and armor by playing multiple times, as long as you don't allow the durability to break. Another cool thing after winning, is you can see other players stats and progress that also beat the same world, even when using a random level seed.
What I originally considered a hidden gem has turned into one of my favorite rouge-like ARPG's. The game even has a deluxe dlc which adds tons more content, similar to how much Binding of Issac Rebirth added. Even though it has a very Japanese feel to it with the story, the gameplay is superb. I highly recommend this game if you're looking for something new and unique.

Eventually when the player has mastered the movement and the rhythm of the game, then the real interesting parts start.  Classes unlock, you learn how to survive with different classes and play styles.
You will die.  You will die often.  You will die stupidly, wondering why you did something that dumb.  You will learn, and then you will start to win.  Each victory brings you closer to uncovering what's really going on, and each death can contribute to your survival later on.  Many hours later you'll probably look at the clock and wonder where your day just went.
Do yourself a great favor and get the plus version of this game.  Give it some time and love, and before long, you'll have something that you can turn to for a quick round, or for a day of amusement and rewarding activity...  And don't forget to talk to Iris before the first day, or she'll totally sulk.

I liked this game at first.  It definitely has some good points.  But the bad just dragged me down at the end and I honestly can't recommend it.
The good - I enjoyed the storyline of the main campaign and liked the characters that they introduced.  Your team for the most part was interesting and didn't feel like throwaway characters.  I also like the implementation of Shadowrun RPG stuff (levelling up, cyberware, gear in general etc..) that they've used since Shadowrun Returns.  And in general the missions in the base game were good - lots of options, from all out combat to full charisma/stealth.
So far so good right?  In fact until about 2/3rds of the main game was done I would have thought that this would have been a thumbs up review.  But then the bad started to outweigh the good.
The bad - Repeatedly having to chat with the same 15 dudes in the main town hub after every mission gets kind of old after a couple of times.  But if you want to make sure you don't miss a mission or option of some kind you sort of feel like you have to do it.  Related to that, I would have liked a bit of voice acting for some of the main missions at least, so I don't have to read through quite as many walls of text.  You don't have to hire expensive voice actors, just use your own staff.  I don't care if the person is an amazing actor, I'd just like to actually listen to a mission description or conversation once or twice rather than having to read pages of information on it every time.
There's also a pretty significant bug regarding save games (and the game came out a year and a half ago at this point).  I noticed as I played into the game that loading times were getting longer and longer (occasionally to the point where the process would hang and I'd have to kill it and start the game up again).  Looking into it, apparently for some reason the number of save games you have causes loading a game (and some in game interactions as well) to slow down significantly.  In a game with this much choice, you want to be able to save often.  I shouldn't have to delete half of my save games just to be able to load a game faster than Skyrim...
If you really loved Shadowrun Returns and Dragonfall I'd say maybe buy this but just skip the Extended Edition content.  The base game was fine minus the things I mentioned but the EE stuff just wasn't good.  The storyline didn't really make any sense from the start.  And maybe they had a different person working on it or something but the missions weren't designed with nearly as much care.  The first couple of missions were combat after combat after combat (which might appeal more to a certain playstyle, but one of the appeals of Shadowrun is that you can design your character many ways, combat is just one of them).    Maybe I could have skipped one or two of those but in the main game, until you got to the final stuff, combats were spaced out, maybe one or two per mission, unless you really wanted to just kill everything. Shadowrun Hong Kong takes the better elements of the earlier games and fine-tunes them, including a noteworthy transition of the Matrix scenes to stealth encounters that, if failed or rejected by the player, become the earlier meatspace-mirror of isometric battles. The environments and music are sublime: the world is the playground of corporations, whether you're delving through ancient tombs or penthouse parties, you're certain to know it with the deft scene-setting.
If there is any problem I have with this game, it's asymmetric information. As with Dragonfall, where a very specific allotment of Karma points awards a negotiated allegiance with an important adversary, there are scenes in Hong Kong where your stylistic gameplay decisions will reject your idea of enjoyment. A well-planned suite of your decker, shaman and muscle can usually overcome this, but I still found myself (for example) without the ability to hack a spider tank in the DLC's conclusionary fight(s), and selecting a single dialogue option that seemed neutral but proved to turn two sides against me, both of which were just super-uncomfortable, salt-inducing bummers. As for technical operation, I experienced one game-breaking progress bug, a noted issue on Gobbet's optional backstory missions which I am disappointed is not fixed this long after release.
I have more than a few characters and storylines that've worked their way into my favoured gameplay experiences from this title: I'm unlikely to forget the charm of Rats! Rats! Rats!, my labours for a snarky dominatrix of a Fixer, or the way the game seamlessly manipulates the player's expectations of the antagonist throughout.

Mafia II is a 2010 action adventure third-person shooter that takes place between 1945 and 1951 at Empire Bay. You play as Vito Scaletta, who reluctantly joined an Italian mafia in order to payed off his father's debt from a loan shark, "pressured" by his best friend, Joe Barabaro, and making quick bucks. The story evolves from a facade fantasy of having so much wealth and power to the dire consequences of losing friends, betrayal, and a power struggle to know who you can really trust.
For a video game, it is very refreshing that the setting takes place in the late 1940s and early 50s. Heck, there's authentic soundtrack from the 40s and 50s that are featured in the game. Police interaction to the player is surreal and a bit immersive. For an example, a police can give you a ticket for speeding, or you can bribe them...or you just go on a rampage. Want to rob multiple stores? Go right ahead. The best feature in Mafia II is the story and voice acting. The plot will immediately capture you attention from start to finish.
A summary of positive features...
+ New York City-like setting (which is the fictional Empire Bay) that takes place from 1945 and 1951 that delivers the authenticity and surreal effect that you are in post-WWII era
+ Multiple vehicles to choose, drive, and customize
+ Strong story, excellent voice acting and casting, including well-established character developments
+ Police realism that ranged from ticketing you for overspeeding to authorized orders to kill you if you commit serious crimes (i.e robbery and mass shooting on NPCs)
+ A great selection of good music from the late 1940s and 1950s which are worth listening to
The game does have its faults. Few problems have to be noted, including varieties of technical issues that were unable to find a specific solution to fix them. Basically, a trial-and-error method to see if the problem is fixed or not. Example: Slow-motion bug or random CTDs. The gameplay mechanics are a bit basic, which is the simple shoot and cover and hand-to-hand combat. Major gameplay issues that I had that sort of ruined the immersion for me was the lack of side missions, semi-lifeless NPCs and little interaction, and the Mafia II world was... semi-open worldish, but is very linear and broken into a series of chapters. Mafia II was overhyped back in late 2009 and early 2010 with numerous trailers and promotions, including heavy expectations that it was supposed to be a game of the year contender.
A summary of negative features...
- Various technical issues that have trial-and-error solutions to fix these problems such as put the monitor at 60 Hz or delete certain folders within the Mafia II folder...you get the picture
- No side missions, at all (What the f*ck, seriously?)
- Deceptively open-world, but it really isn't and very linear (A few wouldn't mind about it, but it has to be taken account)
- Some collectable-related achievements are very ridiculous like the Card Sharp and Explorer achievement
- The game was really overhyped before the game was released in 2010
Mafia II is a good game, and probably a great game to some. In its own merits, Mafia II has really great positive attributes that can convinced a potential buyer that the game is good. It is. For me, Mafia II is one of those games that really have the true potential if the negative attributes above were taken seriously. The lack of a true open-world, post-WWII era game is what Mafia II turned me off for a bit, but the story is what kept me playing from the beginning to end. Do I recommend it? Yeah, sure. However, for $30 or regional equivalent? I don't think so. I strongly suggest that the game has to be -75% off (or -80%) to get your money's worth.

You enter the room, and see five stormtroopers - two of which have heavy repeaters - accompanied by three officers and turrets on the walls to the sides. Could get tricky considering the numbers, but not too much of a challenge. You adjust the grip on your lightsaber for one better suited to deflection and get to work, a flash of blue bringing out the cries of falling Imperials. The battle's over in a matter of seconds, and you move through the door at the back.
It's a narrow walkway with what looks to be an open room behind it, but standing in the doorway you see a Dark Jedi, and a fairly powerful one judging by the green hue to his tunic. You stand and wait for him to make the first move, but he remains motionless. Fine, you think, let's do this. You run, jump, use the Force to push him while activating your lightsaber in mid-air to bring it down over his head, but he's fast, he rolls backward and brings his own blade up against you. You barely manage to parry the strike, and there's a heated exchange of blows, a flurry of blue against crimson, a true test of your skill. You dart one way and he darts the other, he somersaults above you, you pull him to the ground and he collapses on the floor. You're about to strike him down for good when he pushes himself back to get on his knees, but this is the endgame for this particular battle. You let loose an unrelenting barrage of attacks until at last his guard breaks, you slice cleanly through his arm and he falls.
You continue through the large doorway ahead, to see two more Dark Jedi in front, but the yellow trim of their robes shows them to be novices. You run straight between the two, igniting your lightsaber just as they move to engage you. Your blade locks with that of the rightmost opponent, you put your strength into overpowering him, but before you can finish the job the other Dark Jedi rushes you from the side. He brings his lightsaber up, and at that moment you break off, swing your own blade to the side and through the torso of your attacker, who drops to the ground. The remaining enemy steps back, regains his composure, and strafes around you, clearly not wanting to repeat the mistakes of his compatriot. He tries to push you down from afar, but his power is no match for yours and the effort is barely perceptible; seeing this, he decides to use it as a distraction as he then leaps over you in an attempt to cut you down from behind, but he's too slow and predictable - you turn, and just as he lands you throw your lightsaber at him, embedding the blade in his chest.
You press on, but just as you turn the corner you hear the telltale clank of an AT-ST and hear yourself say "I've got a bad feeling about this..."

Freedom Planet is a platformer that takes on an identity to resemble the old Sonic the Hedgehog games on the Sega Genesis(Mega Drive). It has the sense of speed of those games with the simple platforming and gravity defying movement. Despite that, it is strictly not a Sonic clone. The characters in this game play quite differently and there's more of a choose your own flavor in this game. You can explore the levels at your own pace, or try to set speed records by zipping through them as fast as possible.
The boss battles are some of the most fun things about this game, with a great sense of difficulty and this game even has difficulty settings if you find it too rough for you. Anyone can get into this game and play it quickly without the story or just enjoy the simple storyline.
Freedom Planet is a game that one should try if they love fast paced 2d action platforming. I wholly recommend it for carving out its own identity and making us forget about that blue hedgehog that hasn't seen better days for over a decade.

This is not a complete Sonic clone. I just have to get that out of the way.
The game actually takes a number of elements from various titles made during the 16-bit era. Gunstar Heroes, Mega Man X, even a little bit of Vectorman and Ristar. But yes, at its core it does possess a lot of elements that you can identify with Sonic. Though, as the developers pointed out, they are not the first to try and replicate the basis of the Genesis titles and do their own thing with it.
The level design and bosses speak widely to the combination of Sega Genesis games I mentioned, where the levels do carry a lot of Sonic elements in them, the bosses usually do not and feel a lot more like bosses from Mega Man X or Gunstar Heroes. One or two of the bosses feel a little cheap, but ultimately that may be down to my own lack of skill and perception. The only manner in which I can have problems with the gameplay is that Carol is rather unbalanced and has difficulties with those boss battles. Though you can use some cheap tactics to make boss battles way easier, and in many ways I prefer Carol simply because her attacks are more precise and fun to use, but Carol's motorcycle is detrimental to some boss battles and should really not be used in a lot of places they provide it. Lilac has no problems just punching through bosses with her dash, though. I actually kinda dislike Lilac's gameplay because of that.
The story is not amazing, but it's not really that bad, nor does it really bring the game down since you can just skip it anyway. It is predictable at points, it has its plot holes and unanswered questions for sure, but it's not fanfiction bad if that's what you're expecting. I was actually pretty invested in the characters by the end of the game, and Brevon makes a cool and intimidating (but still very cheesy) Villain.
The soundtrack is amazing on the same level as Shovel Knight and I'll certainly be recalling tracks from the game for some time, it similarly evokes the feel of Sonic and Mega Man X in it's music as it does with it's gameplay, all full of energy and not disappointing at any part of the game, at least to my ears.
The voice acting is not
bad. I realize this may be a hot button issue to focus on when dealing with a game that's completely lacking professionals, but if 4kids actors can be considered professionals, I think these guys are doing okay. A few of them even stand out as being above average, in my opinion.
Freedom Planet is a shoestring budget game with almost the same amount of polish as much more expensive projects like Shovel Knight, while also having an extra degree of substance. It has flaws here and there and the voice acting isn't triple-A, but I think it deserves whatever praise it gets. I personally think it's worth your time if you're looking for a nostalgia trip, or even just a game that's easy to just sit down and have fun with.

Saw some summer sale dorks posting lousy, unfair reviews on this and had to write a counter.
It's a roguelike with a very solid premise in that you have to run away from a constantly moving darkness on the left side of the screen. If you are consumed by the darkness your run immediately ends, resulting in a forced sidescroller type game. It's actually quite intuitive, and the game teaches you to adapt very quickly. Expect to fail a lot in the beginning.
The system is subtlely brilliant in that it requires you to play in a number of different ways. Even if you make mistakes or a bad situation RNGs itself upon you, you can use your resources to play your way out. And if you do make a mistake that is actually fatal, it will definitely feel deserved. "Bad luck" is more often the result of ill preparation and poor management.
To make the game more interesting, there are various objectives and classes to choose from that vary the play experience. Additionally, you can choose from different 'perks' in order to build your character how you choose, or to even make the game more difficult for yourself.
Each of the ally NPCs in the game are charming to look at and have their own unique personalities and dialogue. I won't spoil any of it, but the bonding process and backstory of the game that slowly comes to light through them is a delightful experience that adds a lot of color to the game. The art is handdrawn from the looks of it, and is pretty refreshing to be honest. Sprites are mostly what you'd see in RPG maker games, seeing as how the original engine is based off of Wolf.
I won't say it's impossible to get random'd (darn teleport pills), but the decision making in the long run is what makes the experience. If you want a challenge, try tougher win conditions on harder difficulties! There are many ways to customize your run, so you can adjust the edge as much as you like.
The least satisfying thing about the game is probably the content. This is remedied quite a bit with the Plus Edition DLC, which I STRONGLY recommend for the sake of balance and expansion. If you are playing vanilla and you don't think it's enough, I definitely think Plus is the way the game is meant to be played. Of course, this means shilling out more $$$ for a more complete game. However, purchasing Plus not only supports the localization, but the original developer of the game as well.
This is a really quick RPG roguelike experience with an easy to understand system, but it comes with a surprising amount of depth that's fun to explore. Daily worlds make completionist goals much easier, and adds a bit of fun to the game by comparing your runs with other participants in Online mode.
At the very least, I would recommend giving this indie classic a fair try. If you can get your hands on Plus, the game is priceless.

A classic.
The flexibility in how you approach this game in order to have fun is its genius.  Do you jump right into its single player and conquer the world in various ways?  Do you let the AI duke it out in a massive battle royale alternate retelling of world history?  Do you jump online and square off against players in free-for-all or teamers?  Do you want a massive, epic game lasting eons, or a quick, speedy couple-hour match?  It really is up to you -- you're only limited by how much free time you have, and the limits of the massive amount of mods and extra civs in the Steam Workshop.
The only real caveat with buying Civ 5 is that you pretty much NEED all the expansions packs.  Not only does this give you all the bonus civs, but it balances the game out much better compared to when it first launched.  However, since the game is cheap, especially with Civ 6 around, it's well worth the purchase at its price.  It also helps that Civ 5 is far, far better than Civ 6 in its current state.
While Civ 5 is far more balanced than Civ 6, it's not without its limits.  Some Social Trees are far better than others, to the point of having a cookie-cutter meta (4 city Tradition into Rationalism into *yawn*), but your decisions are certainly far more meaningful than in Civ 6.  Civ 5 also has a couple technical issues, from the occasional crash to the objectively worse netcode.  Beyond that, though, this game has far, far, far more content than Civ 6 -- and that's not taking into account the mod scene.
It seems like Civ 5 is just far less of a hassle to mod and support the Steam Workshop, compared to its successor, and it shows.  Tons more user-made civs await, as well as mods that rebalance the game via social policies, techs, wonders, ideologies, religions, and so on -- making for a far more enjoyable experience with many more working strategies.  Two mods I know of, for example, are the NQ Mod and Lekmod, which are both still supported and played online.
Online play, should you care to try it, is still played by a number of dedicated people (many of whom are still waiting for Civ 6 to become an actual good game).  The netcode can be sketchy, as there are desyncs and rejoining lobbies at times, but most people are good for attempting to play through it.  These games are usually done on quick speed, with most games lasting from 2 to 8 hours.
But, really, the meat and potatoes of Civ 5 is its single player, and there's just so much content and so much replayability.  As mentioned above, you can pretty much choose how you want to play this game, and there are lots of scenarios to play through as well as free-for-all and teamer modes.  To top off, the maps are almost always randomly generated, so no experience is the same as any others.  The replayability in this game is off the charts.
I'm one of many examples of people who got caught into Civ 5's addictive replayability -- 2000+ hours is as concrete of such proof as one can get.  There are tons of people with similar amounts of time or more in this game, so one should not really worry about Civ 5 getting old shortly after purchasing it.  It's addicting, it's got tons of content, and it's tons of fun.  You can't beat that.

I've been playing WoWS since the closed beta test and was really excited to see it appear in the Steam Store, though due to blatantly illegal action by Wargaming, I have uninstalled and will never play again.
The Good:
Graphics and Audio are the best among WWII naval combat simulators.
Attention to detail with the ships is excellent.  Layout, armaments, and wartime retro-fits are historically accurate despite not always being better.  (Some retro-fits actually cause you to sacrifice offense or defense in favor of the other.)
Map layout has evolved to create more balanced battle scenarios (mostly).  During CBT, some maps were heavily in favor of DDs or BBs.
The Bad:
Gameplay is dumbed down compared to other naval combat sims.  The game used to rely on careful shot placement and timing, now it's all governed by random chance.
Due to this, Flags and Signals that nullify the above RNG nightmare become a must very quickly.
The Ugly:
are a pack of thieves.  I was in port post match and brought up the Steam overlay to respond to a message.  After a quick conversation and reading an article, I go back into WoWS to discover that I had somehow made a $15 purchase while I wasn't even in the game.  I immediately closed WoWS and reported the unauthorized transaction to Wargaming along with a bug report.  They have acknowledged the bug but steadfastly refuse to reverse the transaction or even refund the amount in gold doubloons (their in-game currency) despite the fact that I have not played a single match since it happened.
The Bottom Line:
WoWS is a mediocre game made by a dev not deserving of your time or money.

LISA: The Painful RPG is an RPGMaker game with striking sprites; a bleak and gruesome, yet often flamboyant, post-apocalyptic setting with morbid comic relief; and cheap, janky music that still grows on you and perfectly fits the whole f-d up aesthetic of the game. It was definitely in my top 3 favorite releases of 2015 (technically late 2014 but still) in particular due to its grim, depressing storyline and character development, unique soundtrack, and the overall lasting impression it made on me.
I also wholeheartedly suggest you play LISA The First prior to playing The Painful. It's an entirely different kind of game, a surreal Yume Nikki-style exploration game, as opposed to a proper RPG, available for free but not on Steam. It's short, only a few hours long, but it helps set up the hellish backstory that led to the events in The Painful.
And finally, LISA: The Joyful is an expansion to The Painful, a new storyline taking place directly after the ending of the first one. Has a new combat system, incredible writing, and though it too is pretty short, it nicely wraps up the LISA series. Would recommend buying it too if you enjoyed The Painful.

"Lisa: The Painful"  might be the most interesting, funny and depressive game I've ever played. It was made by a single person named Dingaling and is the successor to the free game "Lisa - The First". It was designed with a version of the "RPG Maker" and comes with original art and an original concepts.
The post-apocalyptic rpg is set in the land of Olathe, a brown and joyless wasteland. Only males survived the big catastrophe, leaving them in a somewhat desperate situation. The main character Brad, a former drug addict, Kung-Fu master and son of an abusive father finds a female baby and raises her isolated from the rest of the world, together with the few friends he has left. As she gets abducted, he is hell bent to find and to rescue her, having to travel through the wasteland, roamed by madmen, homosexuals and mutants.
The story gets more and more twisted and insane as you progress through the game. You will meet some unique characters and have some absurd and crazy encounters. Some of them made me laugh out loud, some of them were so sick, that I almost couldn't make the required moral decision.
Gameplay itself consists of much grinding and a lot of walking from point A to point B. It's a turn based fighting system with many different optional characters to choose for your team of four. What makes this game really special is the story and the characters itself, as well as the atmosphere. The situation and the world you'll find yourself in is absolutely hopeless/ridiculous and it's presented with a brilliant sense for twisted, black humour.
If you love an impressive, funny, sickening and interesting story and don't have a huge problem with a repetitive fighting system, then this game might be something for you.

Having reviewed the previous two games in the Shadowrun Returns Franchise, there isn't much left to be said so I'll keep this short.
Shadowrun Hong Kong is a solid turn based tactical RPG set in a well developed and detailed world. If you are a fan of cyberpunk or tactical RPGs it is well worth playing. Just be prepared to read A LOT.
For fans of the previous games -
The mechanics are fairly close to Dragonfall. The matrix (virtual reality internet) has been upgraded and has generally been praised by the community over the old version. The amount of descriptive text has also been dramatically increased. At points it felt more like I was playing a visual novel rather than a tactical RPG.
For new players -
If you haven't played the other games in the franchise, then I suggest starting with Dragonfall instead of this game. Unless you are an avid reader, the amount of descriptive text can be daunting and Hong Kong setting comes across as more complex than the others. The game has decent, if simple graphics, so it relies largely on descriptive text to set the scene and mode.
TL;DR - Definitely worth playing, but you may want to start with Dragonfall instead.

Freedom Planet is a 90s style platformer that hits nearly all the right notes to deliver an experience that I've not felt in ages.
This game and Shovel Knight have been godsends for an avid platform gamer like myself.
The initial looks of this game give off a very sonic vibe, but even a few minutes into the game that feeling fades, Freedom planet is a game that borrowed ideas from sonic at first (it had fangame roots after all) but quickly improved and evolved into its own thing.
I came into FP late so I didn't know of it at all during its fangame state, and you wouldn't know it originally was looking at it or playing it. It all feels very solid and professional; stages have multiple ways to progress and many paths utilize the character's unique abilities to progress, the stages are very colorful and varied taking you across much of the game's world, and the stages are backed by fun but challenging bosses and a kickass soundtrack that make playing the whole game a wonderful experience from beginning to end. The only small complaint I had was the first two stages are "humble beginnings" and take place in backwater parts of the game's world so it may not pull a player in fast enough, but even then these stages are colorful and fun to play and the game picks up completely at stage 3.
The game has 3 playable characters currently each with their own unique move sets and they do offer some variation in the stage patterns. Carol and Milla being the ones that get to play Trap Hideout while Lilac is the only character that gets to play Pangu Lagoon. Millia currently lacks any story mode but its been discussed that she will have one in the future and other character playability is planned in the future as dlc.
A  word of warning for people getting this because they think its like sonic. In many ways its not at all so don't go in expecting that too much. Plot is important in this game unlike sonic and the game takes a far more serious tone with it's story than sonic ever has. This is NOT a bad thing however its just something you need to adjust yourself for to enjoy.

In this good old fashion 2D platformed, its up to Soni....er...Lilac the Dragon to recover the Chaos....um....Kingdom Stone from the evil Doctor Egg....I mean....Lord Brevon.
OK, in all seriousness, this game did start out as more or less a Sonic fan game, but it was also always really intended to be it's own thing. The game is well paced and simply a lot of fun to play, with a good story.  The Sonic influence shows, but the game also feels like it has it's own identity.
Critics of the game like to criticize the physics and speed.  Yes, it's not often you actually do go super top speed in this game, but it's also not often you need to.  Even though you don't move at the speed of sound, you never feel like your moving too slow. (and I think you still move faster than some of the classic Sonic games.) There are times you kind of walk up walls, (you really only need momentum and a slope to get up walls, no matter how little speed you actually have), but I find that to be more helpful than bad.  And as for Carol the Wildcat's bike....well, breaking the laws of Physics is just one of it's features.
Each playable character is fun to use, and different enough that it actually warrants playing each stage with each character.  Each character also has there own story, which shows you extra story tidbits.   (well, at the time of writing this, Milla doesn't have a story mode, but she will soon, and new playable character are planned too.) And each character has a level exclusively to them. (well, Carol doesn't get one all to herself, but there is one clearly designed with her in mind.)
The story itself is great.  Yes, it's a bit cheesy, but it's in the style of a classic early 90's Saturday cartoon.  Cheesy but also serious at points.  It works well.  There were defiantly moments that had me laughing, and other moments that had me on the edge of my seat.  Of course if you just hate story in retro platformers you can always play classic, and just skip the story.
The voice acting is good.  Maybe not the best ever (I wouldn't even begin to claim to be an expert in that department), but defiantly not the worst voices I've ever heard.  Defiantly quality work.
Overall this game has a classic feel and charm, but at the same time feels fresh and new.  I didn't really feel that nostalgic when playing this.  Maybe that's because I entered the video game world in the N64/PS1 era (save some original NES), or maybe it's because I was too caught up in the game itself as a title today.  Freedom Planet gets a 10/10, and is a great game for anyone who loves Sonic platformers, Retro platformers, or just 2D platformers in general.

At first glance you'll probably think this is a Sonic rip off, but you'll be wrong (very very wrong).
Freedom Planet shares the same gameplay style as Sonic, but still has many aspects that make it different.
Let's start with the levels. There are 9 stages in total (the last stage being split into 4 acts), and instead of splitting the stage into two acts the stages transitions to different areas. For example you'll be in a hill area and then you'll move onto a forest area. You'll also come across two bosses in each stage. It might be the same boss or two different bosses. The stages are also very large and expansive, with many unlockables and power ups hidden in each part of the stage.
Now let's talk about the gameplay. It plays a bit like Sonic, but has a mix of combat and exploration mixed into it. You can choose between two modes Adventure or Classic. Adventure shows you the story and Classic goes straight to the game without the story. You can also easily speed run the game since you can't get damaged from simply running into enemies. The only exception is if the enemy is attacking and your in it's line of fire. There are three characters to choose from: Lilac, Carol, and Milla (only on classic). And each character plays differently, each with their own skills, attacks, specials, strengths, and weaknesses.
Sash Lilac: Lilac is the Sonic the Hedgehog of the game. She is able to move very fast and speed across the levels. She can perform a spin to give her some extra height while jumping as well as damage enemies in the air. And her special is a speed dash that allows her to move extremely fast as well as damage enemies who get in the way, and reach up to hard to reach areas.
Carol Tea: Carol is much more offensive than Lilac. Her special makes her perform a kick attack where she attacks an enemy multiple times. When jumping she can perfrom a pounce, which does nothing, but makes up for it with her wall jump that allows her to reach up to hard to reach areas. Also to make up for her lack of speed she also has a (gravity defying) motorcycle that can make her move even faster than Lilac, and can... climb up walls?
Milla Basset: Milla is much more defensive than Lilac or Carol. Milla is capable of hovering into the air like Lilac but can't damage enemies. She is the weakest of the characters with only 4 health points, but makes up for that with her energy based attacks. Instead of a basic attack or special, she has the ability to conjure up energy blocks and pick up items she can throw at enemies. Along with the blocks she can summon an energy shield to deflect and attack enemies. She also has a unique special where she can combo the energy block with the energy shield to unleash a powerful energy beam.
Lastly there are many bosses you'll come across. As mentioned before you might come across two, maybe three bosses in one stage. The first boss is easy, but then things get seriously difficult. As you progress the bosses only get harder... and harder... and HARDER!!! The bosses go with a certain pattern but can be difficult to fight. When I first started playing I thought I was going to breeze through the game and get the "no death clear" achievement. But when I came across the 4th stage boss I was in serious trouble. I died like 6 times trying to fight him. Once you figure out the pattern you should be able to beat the boss. But the most trouble I had was in the final stage. The final stage literally tests your skill and the bosses won't hold back. When I reached the first boss in the final stage, my final time was 20 minutes, and it only took me 6 minutes to reach the boss. The second boss was just as hard as the first boss. The third boss is not as hard, but still pretty difficult. The final boss, I'm not going to reveal a lot, but I will say: you better get used to seeing that continue screen, cause your going to see it a lot.
Well I think I rambled on enough about the gameplay, so lets get to the story (no spoilers of course). The story goes on like this: An evil general known as Lord Brevon has crash landed onto a planet and now seeks an ancient relic called the Kingdom Stone to power his ship and leave the planet, as well as help grow his army. The Kingdom Stone is a power source for three kingdoms: Shang-Mu, Shang-Tu, and Shuigang. Lord Brevon and his army raided Shuigang, killed their king, and brainwashed the king's son: Prince Dail into following Lord Brevon's orders and now seeks to find his father's killer (even though he is taking orders from him). Then comes Lilac the Dragon and Carol the Wildcat, who caught sight of a crash landing ship and met Torque a "Shell-Duck", and later on met Milla the Hound. Now it is up to the group to stop Lord Brevon and bring peace to the three kingdoms before it goes into war.
The characters are very entertaining in the story. Literally the best part of the game are the cutscenes where the characters are talking and interacting with each other, as well as being every expressive. Lilac being a no nonsense leader, Carol being a wisecracking rebel, and Milla (who is plain out adorable) being very enthusiastic, acting more like an asset instead of a liability. In fact all of the characters are very fun and unique. Even though the voice actors are amateurs they seriously do a great job. The dialogues are cheesy, but they have a certain charm that makes it enjoyable, and makes the characters very memorable. Pretty much the entire story feels like a Saturday morning cartoon.
Overall Freedom Planet is a fun and enjoyable adventure with memorable characters, large levels, a fantastic soundtrack, and challenging bosses. This game isn't afraid to be hard, and you'll be determined to finish it.

It's a pretty good platformer. However, while a decent game and probably worth the cost to platformer fans, it has a host of minor things that hold it back from greatness:
1) It holds your hand in regards to unlocks/secrets. Signposts tell you when a fork in the road includes a harder route (usually has a costume unlock) or an '?' route (can have either a costume unlock or an alternate exit to unlock a side-level). Even easier platformers (Super Mario World, etc.) had less hand-holding with secrets. The only semi-tricky secrets are the retro-level unlocks, which often appear in areas of the level that are moving quickly and/or demand a quick but unmarked detour.
2) Unlocking new characters is merely cosmetic. After playing something like Super Meat Boy, it's surprisingly disappointing to unlock characters that don't vary whatsoever in speed, jump height, gliding, etc. It wouldn't be a big deal in other games, but in a game where you constantly move forward and have far less choice in how you approach a level, it would have been wonderful to have slight differences in characters (like maybe one can glide longer, or one can double-jump, or so forth). It would have been hard to do, but I feel like characters could have been given slightly different abilities.
3) There's nothing in-game to delete your save-state, and there's nothing in-game to allow multiple play-throughs to be going on simultaneously. This is inexplicable, as even NES games had multiple save-files at times, and, barring that, most at least had a password system. For a game made in the 2010's era, it's hard to explain why there wasn't a basic 'Start New Game File' option for a PC platformer.
4) Levels are a bit repetitious... there's enough variety, but there could have been more. The last two worlds really blend together the different moves of the game and force a player to extremely quickly determine what moves to use. But even here, there are only so many moves: because you never stop moving forward, and because nearly every move you can do thus is always at the same speed and height, this means that levels cannot be as varied as in other games. In most platformers, you control how fast you are moving as you approach a jump, and you also control how high you jump. Not so in Runner2. And this means that, while there are a number of interesting moves you have to use, you still end up feeling like levels are not as different from each other as you might have first imagined.
For all of that, it does get enough right:
+ moves/abilities are described quickly enough to allow the last worlds to really be interesting
+ getting a 100% on a level is a challenge even on normal difficulty
+ there are a number of optional moves to master to increase your score
+ graphics are rather good
+ soundtrack is quite good (though not exactly diverse)
My overall opinion:
Runner2 is a good change of pace for platformer fans, and definitely has some replayability if you're trying to 100% levels and compete for a high score. But it's not really a rhythm game, at least not in the way that fans of AudioSurf and so forth would expect.
If anything, Runner2 is like if the music feature from Mario Paint had a baby with Sonic the Hedgehog games, thus giving birth to a fast-paced, linear platformer with a variety of moves to pull off (including optional ones) to keep the beat going as you play through the level.
Ultimately, a decent game, and worth getting for platformer fans, but not as open as Super Meat Boy felt in level design and what moves to pull to get by.

A Story About My Uncle starts with you as a father, tucking your kid in at night. The kid requests you tell them a bedtime story about adventure, and the game starts as you play through the adventure you are telling your child. Your uncle has gone missing, and you follow him through a weird wormhole-type-thing to a land of floating rocks and caves. Using your special adventure suit, you follow your uncle's trail by running, jumping, and grappling through the world. As you progress through the story and discover more about the world you've been transported to, you gather more components to the suit which grant you additional options, such as using the grapple multiple times in one jump.
It's an addicting platformer based around parkouring around the skies and caves of some fantasy world. Grappling becomes a simple dexterity mechanic and once you get comfortable with it you will find yourself running through the world quicker and more instinctively. It's rewarding when you chain your jumps together, but there's still a challenge in timing everything correctly so you don't plummet towards the ground.
The narration is interesting. There's a certain charm in listening to the narrative unfold in the form of a father telling his kid a bedtime story. But there's always something off- whether it's the voice acting or the script I'm not sure, but when you reach the sections of the game with narration it takes you out of it. It's nice when the game gives you a chance to slow down and appreciate the setting compared to the faster-paced grappling, because the caves and worlds are beautiful, but I still got taken aback by the narrator.
As for the gameplay itself, the whole thing is rather linear. You follow your uncle's path, and there's usually only one way through. Sometimes you get to choose how you approach the path, but even then the choice is often just a challenge of "do this part only running and jumping, no grapple" or "do this part only grappling, no touching the ground". There's no impact on the game whether or not you do the challenges, just a voice line saying "yay you did it", "haha you didn't do it", and then a Steam achievement to go with it. It's definitely more like a puzzle game than a sandbox, but that's fine.
My biggest complaint is that some of the jumps you have to make are so specific it's maddening. The difference between you beating the section or restarting at the checkpoint is so miniscule that there's really nothing you can do to improve with each attempt. I was breezing through most of the game until I came to one part I spent a half hour on, and when I finally succeeded I didn't feel like I actually got better and beat it, it felt like I randomly got lucky with timing. Thankfully, occasions like this are rare, and even when you get to these parts the checkpoints are literally right before them so you don't have to replay long sections of the game just to retry a specific section that's giving you trouble.
All in all, I enjoyed the game. I don't know if I'd pay full price for it, but when you get it on sale for $2 there's not much that can go wrong. It's a great way to spend an evening.

A Story About My Uncle is an amazingly smooth and beautiful puzzle platformer. You follow a breadcrumb trail to find your Uncle, Fred, through magical floating islands. I had a few issues with this game though. About half way through the game, you get a pair of rocket boots that gives you a boost mid air. Most of the jumps don't require a boost, and I ended up using it as a crutch 90% of the time. I think that this should’ve been given to you in the beginning of the game, and then taken away halfway through. This would help players just learning the system, and add a layer of challenge to the latter half. Also, I found myself getting caught on the geometry of the last level.

Overall, A Story About My Uncle is a heckin’ good game. It has flaws, and I don't know if I would buy it for $13. I’d wait for a sale.

Age of Conan is one of the older MMO:s,
Like many others people were bored with World of Warcraft and wanted something new to try out. Back then the first 20 levels of Age of Conan and tortage were amazing and fresh feel for the mmo genre.
However after that you could notice how unfinished the game world was, you were supposed to grind monsters to 80, as you quickly ran out of quests. In starting area there was more than plenty of voice acted quests.
Thats how things were at launch and why me and my whole guild quit the game back then. Funcom has improved the game since and added more content, quests and bug fixes. While they no longer have big updates for the game, i recommend everyone to try the game, if nothing else the first 20levels are great.
Pros:
* Unique Graphics style
* Sound & Atmosphere
* First 20levels are fun to play
* Fun combat with combos and fatalities
Cons:
* bugs
* combat can feel a bit clunky
* no voice acted quests after first 20lvl
* no major updates planned for the future
Total:
Graphics - 8 (back at release 9)

Gameplay - 8
Story - 7 (Starting area story 9)
---
;TLDR awesome early game, that everyone should try out.
Overall a nice free MMO for those who like the genre.

Sometimes older games seem superior in certain ways. This game is one such example. Yes, the graphics are somewhat primitive by today's standards, but it beats the days of rendering using sprites like Dark Forces, etc. Unlike the rich graphics that are mostly non-interactive (like The Forced Unleashed), this game has worlds with vast layouts of buildings and rooms that you can get yourself lost in (can be overwhelming at times, but it's an exercise for your brain). Be prepared to think outside the box and to solve puzzles (not overly complicated, but can require some legwork). Also, this game has a LONG story line by most standards. I finished TFU in about 17 hours; this one took me 33 hours. You will die again and again; you almost have to die just trying different ways of advancing in the game. The checkpoints are few and far in between relative to how often you will die, so be prepared to save the game after winning a difficult battle (or when you anticipate one).
To summarize, this game is a rich experience, and well worth the sale price when those come around. Enjoy.

When first looking at Freedom Planet I honestly didn't expect much other than a Sonic clone. It had the old-school feel, some familiar patterns in what was seen of the levels in the trailers and on screenshots. Still, back then I wasn't calling it a clone as a bad thing - it was a welcome taste of the familiar nostalgia in a slightly different package.
When I finally got the game and played it though I was in for a treat. More than once I'd go "Oh hey, that's just like good old <insert classic SEGA or SNES game>". The callbacks were almost affectionate and made me grin. At the same time it proved far more challenging than I'd expected (I played on normal) had a memorable soundtrack and characters you could actually get attached to. Furthermore since each character plays completely differently, having finished the story as Carol I can look forward to a different experience of playing it as Lilac.
Altogether it's a very enjoyable if occasionally challenging platformer. If you're in it for the cutscenes, colors and plot you may want to set your difficulty level lower to avoid the frustration of multiple deaths. If challenge doesn't scare you - go right ahead and be ready for a real rush.

Just as Shovel Knight is a throwback to the NES, Freedom Planet is a heartfelt love letter to the Sega Genesis. The difference comes not only in the influences and (simulated) limitations of the hardware, but more importantly in the nature of the creators: where the Shovel Knight devs were seasoned veterans who knew the right games to reference and the right self-aware design conveyance to make sure those reviews came in positive, Freedom Planet feels like more of an amateur effort with some janky physics, strange hitboxes, and inconsistent sprite work marring the first impression. Make no mistake, the game's rough around the edges. Despite that, it manages to be more spirited, challenging, and experimental than its major-league counterpart.
A glorious return not only to the flashy design of the Mega Drive era, but also to a more playful side of the indie scene that I thought had been long buried.

I can't stand the new matrix mechanics with its real time stealth and flashy distracting code breaking system. It's actually not difficult if you don't mind grabbing a pen and paper to quickly scribble down the symbols, but you know what? I don't want to do that while playing. So that was a huge turn off even though the new matrix LOOKS amazing.
Story wise I loved the setting and atmosphere, and morality was even more vague than the previous games. And every mission up until the final one felt very flexible and solvable in various ways.
However the final mission was frustrating and a kick in the balls. Instructions were convoluted and you'd have to reload a lot of saves if you want to even get to the final objective in one piece. I'm sure with multiple playthroughs, a guide, and time you could get through it without trouble, but playing through for the first time is not fun. It was a huge let down and was the final straw for putting up with the series. For me difficulty is a delicate matter. A game should still be rewarding and enjoyable despite it, but this wasn't. It just was too bogged down with negatives.
That said I would still recommend it on sale. The interface is a lot more polished than the previous games and the writing is top notch. But it started going south when I felt like I was playing just to finish it rather than enjoying the experience.

Modern Sonic's gameplay in this game is basically what it was in Unleashed, except with 90% of the issues fixed. And, with no night time stages to hold you back, the only disappointing thing about Modern Sonic is the lack of levels, since you only get nine levels with four boss fights, and some(lame) modified layouts of those levels. As someone who enjoys Sonic, you really would owe it to yourself to buy this game, especially during a sale.

1.) It's not full of rainbows, tigers with wings, colorful fairies or Asian characters. The atmosphere is somewhat more serious and interesting.
2.) No toxic community. So far, the community answered my questions, even the silliest ones, with a friendly approach.

4.) Fatalities. Fatalities are animations when you kill a NPC or player. They are very cool to watch.
5.) World bosses. There are different world bosses and it requires a VERY BIG group to kill it. It is very fun to attack it with a lot of different people.
6.) Nudity. You can see ♥♥♥♥♥♥s of naked woman and even buy a "pleasure company". Because of this, the game attracts more mature audience than kids.
7.) The game includes blood. Sometimes its good to see your enemy bleed.
The things that I don't like:
1.) The servers seem somewhat empty. I wish there were more people playing it.
2.) Occasional lags. They are rare and does not affect the gameplay too much.
Overall, this game is very good if you are looking for a new game.

The Tortage opening chapter is the only chapter that has full voice acting for pretty much every line of dialogue and every NPC; after you finish that, only the main plot quests have voice acting. I don't think this detracts from the overal experience, but I'm sure some people would complain about it.
The game offers a good variety of paid content, but you can play a ton without paying a penny, if that's your thing.
My favorite bits: Music, graphics, combat, customer support team (one of the most helpful I've ever interacted with in any game, ever)
My least favorite bits: Only 2 character slots available to free players, in-game items with in-game currency being very expensive (particularly horses), party function glitching relatively often

Действие игры разворачивается спустя три года после событий Mysteries of the Sith. Боясь вновь соблазниться темной стороной Силы, Кайл Катарн отказывается от неё и своего светового меча. Он вновь работает простым наёмником на Новую Республику, вместе с Джен Орс, участвуя в разгроме последних сил имперского Остатка. Во время очередной миссии Кайл и Джен встречают тёмного джедая Десанна, который, узнав известного джедая — победителя грозного Джерека — похищает Джен. Кайл пытается помешать ему, но Десанн легко справляется с ним при помощи Силы и заставляет Кайла убедиться в гибели своей соратницы.
Кайл в ярости решает вновь стать джедаем и отправляется в Долину Джедаев, где снова получает Силу. Он не знает, что Десанн все время следил за ним и теперь знает расположение Долины. Кайл же летит на Явин IV, в академию джедаев, чтобы забрать у Люка Скайуокера свой световой меч. Люк заставляет Кайла пройти несколько испытаний, и только затем вручает Катарну его меч. Люк наводит для него справки и помогает выйти на крупного бизнесмена в сфере мусоропереработки, Рило Барука, который помогает Кайлу выйти на след Десанна. На базе Рило Катарн встречает одного из лидеров повстанцев — Лэндо Калриссиана, который находится в плену. Освободив его, герой попадает в Облачный город, где по воле случая встречает Тавион Аксмис — ученицу Десанна. В схватке Кайл побеждает её. Однако перед тем, как Кайл собирался убить её, она успевает раскрыть все планы учителя и то, что Джен живая содержится на флагмане Остатка, «Хозяин судеб». Кайл пощадил её, так как понял, что если в гневе убить Тавион, он может пасть на тёмную сторону.
В планы Десанна входило с помощью особых технологий создать армию «Возрождённых» (обычные бойцы, искусственным путём наделённые Силой). Собрав немалые силы, имперцы намеревались уничтожить всех джедаев, а также разрушить Долину джедаев. Кайл проникает на флагман и освобождает Джен. Попутно он встречает Люка, который шёл по следам Десанна (не сумел однажды в бою его одолеть). С «Хозяина судеб» Катарн подаёт сигнал флоту Новой республики и истребители уничтожают флагман, а Кайл убивает его командира — Галака Файера.
На Явине IV Кайл пробирается через джунгли из капсулы, на которой сбежал с погибающего крейсера Остатка. В жестоких боях с «Возрождёнными» погибает немало джедаев. Под Академией Кайл находит Десанна, который воспользовался агрегатом Силы и стал ещё мощнее. Кайл говорит ему о безнадёжности ведения войны, и что все его воины уничтожены. Десанн ему не верит, но связывается с адмиралом. Тот не отвечает, и Десанн приходит в ярость. Он пытается склонить Кайла на тёмную сторону, но в ответ он предлагает Десанну самому вернуться на светлую сторону. Тёмный джедай, придя в ещё большую ярость, включает свой меч и бросается в атаку. В тяжёлой дуэли Кайл одолевает его.
После этих событий он с Джен отправляется на отдых, после чего возвращается к преподаванию в академии.

If Earthbound decided you should be an awful person, this would be the game Nintendo would have made. LISA the Painful creates a world that is both full of life and colorful characters, and simultaneously barren and dead. The music is wonderful, adding to the feeling of an 'anything goes' Western atmosphere, not entirely unlike the Fallout Series.
The combat is difficult, and sometimes downright unfair, in how it plays out. Even just bad luck in a fight could permanently kill one of your party members and ruin your composition, as could just sleeping at a fireplace to heal. As annoying as this sounds, the difficulty fits the setting perfectly and never felt like a hindrance nor unenjoyable.
In conclusion, if you like Earthbound or Undertale's sense of adventure and humor, LISA is the perfect cynical counterpoint to either game. A single playthrough takes about eight hours, though to get all the endngs you'll need to go through at least three times.

BTR2 does an excellent job of improving over its predecessor by distilling down the fun parts of the original and rebuilding itself around those concepts. Functionally it serves as a kind of pure-reflex rhythm game, with musical themes which bear repeating and creative use of an xbox-style controller. The visual upgrade to faux three-dimensionality does not accompany floaty or imprecise controls as is so often the case – in fact, the sequel has even tighter controls than the first, and every obstacle is clearly delineated without interrupting the overall graphical style.
Playing BTR2 can be a soothing, cathartic experience, but with variable difficulty levels and lots of hidden secrets there are plenty of challenges floating beneath the surface. This game is perfect for gamers of any age and ability, so long as they can enjoy Katamari-style quirkiness and the sense of achievement that comes with well-honed reflexes.

Combining old school rpg visuals and feel with a rouge like creates One Way Heroics, a very fun and distinct game in the Rogue like genre.
You pick a character, level up, and traverse the map one turn at a time (most of the time very very fast turns) as you try to reach the end and beat the dark lord.  With several classess, weapons, and ways to play, the game manages to have a lot of variety.  In addition, the out of game level up system lets you become stronger with every game you play and is a great addition.
The only warning here is Rogue like.  This game is first and foremost a rogue like.  If you like rogue likes you are golden.  If you like old timey RPGs but hate rogue likes it wont matter; you won't like this game.
With all that said, its a very fun game that can be played in long goes or short bursts.  There really isnt anything here not to like if you are a fan of the genre.

The game costs $3.50 cents and there is enough replayability for several hundred hours. You do the math.
Think about it like this, a movie ticket costs roughly 8-10 dollars, we'll say 8. Movies range anywhere from 1.5 hrs to 3.5 hrs. So 8 dollars gets you (for the sake of argument I'll use the higher number) 3.5hrs of entertainment. This game is less than a large coffee at Starbucks, only with this you will get at least 20 hrs of fun out of it.
What makes this game so good is the way it is set up. You are constantly walking to the right to avoid a black cloud of smoke that kills on contact. The story is randomly generated each time, as are the zones. Also, this is a roguelike, so once you die, you die forever, however there are things you can save such as new classes, etc.
The music is excellent, and the entertainment value is incredibly high. If you've ever played Tome of Maj'Eyal, and enjoyed it, this is basically the same game, only better in absolutely every way.
Highly reccommend. Worst case scenario, if you don't like it, you can always return it as long as there are less than 2 hrs played and it's been less than 2 weeks. With that said, even if you only played for 2 hours, you'd still be getting a lot more than your moneys worth.

To start, I'd recommend you try to separate this game from others because the changes might result in frustrating habits.
In short, this game has excellent sounds, visuals, and a very adaptable gameplay style with challenging enemies (both mooks and bosses) and great level design. It's strongest aspects for me is the pacing of the game that is helped immensely by it's soundtrack and audio, gameplay rules that allow yourself and enemies to be on equal footing, and a story that is not distilled for the sake of being harmless.
The story does not try to force morals and lessons on you but instead gives you a interesting, fun, and animated experience that I feel I can say attempts elements that aren't typically featured in such a cartoony setting.
Gameplay-wise, most of the opponents are dangerous, down to the most dormant and the level design is varied. Often you will come across situations where enemies will challenge your speed in ways that will require you to fight, use an ability, change direction, slow down, or keep to your speed until you can escape. I feel it noteworthy to mention that enemies do not damage you on contact unless they clearly can. There are moments of slow platforming and times where you can progress at a relaxing pace with each character having their own methods of progress and are equally well equipped to do so. I also appreciate that bosses act a lot like they look as a "human" boss does not rely on soaking up hits or ramming into you as much as a robot or a manned machine.
This game, while it does get very difficult, is a great blend of many game practices and I would easily recommend it. Thanks for reading.

I felt bad about my last review, and upon further investigation, it turns out that improperly applied Thermal Paste was the cause of (some) of my prior issues. So I feel obligated to give the game a proper review, even though I don't normally give games reviews on Steam.
The game bleeds 90's design but without the hardware limitations of the time. This means extensive cutscenes and full voice acting for the entire game is the norm, perhaps slightly too extensive at times, but it does drive home the liveliness and personality of the game's starring characters.The story is worth viewing once, but a bit too long-winded to suffer through repeat playthroughs.
The game does feel sloppy at times though. For me at least, the "Screen Resizing" option simply doesn't work even post computer-fix, freezing up the game's video until I restart the game (this was the issue that made me assume the game was bugged before... because it IS, just not to the extent I believed). Also there are many stage gimmicks that seem designed one way but simply don't work properly. Similarly to "Sonic the Hedgehog" there are many springs placed around stages that seem positioned to rocket you in the appropriate direction, but don't give you the momentum they should, instead giving you a gentle nudge in the right direction and leaving you to slowly trudge along in that direction.
There's a lot of little things in the game that don't work quite right, some rough patches here and there that keep it from being the seamless experience you get in a real 90's AAA title, but it's still a great game with a lot of heart and soul, and wonderfully realized characters.

It does become increasingly very difficult however, which for me makes it all the more fun... but playing it on Normal difficulty, I found it getting roughly as difficult as an Ys game towards the end. But only barely, mind you.
You can choose from Lilac or Carol for adventure mode, or Lilac, Carol, and Milla for classic (just the stages, no story) and Time attack modes.
A must buy for any fan of classic sidescrolling action platformers.

It's taken me a long time to finish this game. 3 big attempts over the years before getting distracted.
I was a huge fan of Mafia 1. It was pretty amazing the way the game simuated a city. One of the biggest disappointments in Mafia 2 then is how the city is dumbed down a bit. There no ability to call up a taxi to get around easily, theres no functioning train system like Mafia 1. Instead you'll drive, a lot. This was hugely immersive in Mafia 1 talking to characters while walking around the city.
Combat is a bit average with a weird regenerating health system that sees you insta killed behind cover often. The weapons also seem underpowered and inaccurate.
In terms of technical glitches I had to install DX9 again as it wouldn't load and there are FPS drops at some points for some reason. Nothing too game breaking but I hate the weird DX9 motion blurring and glow that used to be popular. Turn that off.
The story writing is also no where near Mafia 1, with a lot of being lead by the nose you lurch around the fairly jarring story. The great thing in Mafia 1 was working closely with characters who were experienced mafioso's making collections until the story escalated in a really feature film storyline. You really worked each mission from the family to cement your position with the boss. In this sequel you hang around with a fat wannabe, Joe. He has his thing but it's not very mafia. This in turn leaves you with very little feeling of being in the mafia and more like a GTA thug.
That said, it's an open world game in the 40's and 50's that's worth seeing. Get it cheap for a reasonably fun time. I was pretty impressed with the graphics, voice acting and animations considering it's 5 years old.
Here's hoping they get back to the great parts of Mafia 1 which is graphically dated now.

Deserves far more attention than it gets. The Conan setting is compelling and Funcom did a great job bringing it to life. The art direction and soundtrack alone are unmatched by other MMOs and the gameplay's on par with other titles out there today. The community does a disservice to this game with the incessant complaining, painting AoC as a "dying" game, when there's plenty of activity to be found in-game. I've had no problem finding groups for every dungeon on my way to the level cap. Had I listened to the vocal people out there claiming "AoC sucks", I'd have never even tried this game. I encourage new players to not be put off or take these comments seriously, they come from old veterans of the game who've grown bitter... they want to see the game receive new updates, but that won't happen while they're here to scare away newcomers and keep the game's revenue stagnant.
The MMO market is saturated with generic weeb Asian trash, WoW and other dull titles, full of glitter, kawaii and rainbow-farts. If you want something darker and more mature, Age of Conan delivers an immersive and gripping world, it got right what every other game in the genre got wrong. After having played WoW, FF14, SWTOR, GW2 and other MMOs for years, Age of Conan managed to suprise me and is now my absolute favourite game in the genre.

I love this game, and I think everybody should give it a try at some point. The game really makes you feel like a powerful ruler, and there are many different ways to play the game. You can go to war and try to dominate the world, try to become supreme ruler by getting small city states to back you in a plea for power, or even win by blasting off into space with a rocket.
That said, I have a few recommendations. Play this game with friends. Play with hybrid turns on so the game goes faster. This will cause turns to automatically take sequential order for players at war with each other. Just bear in mind that when two or more players are at war, the game slows down dramatically. This is why I recommend playing with a dynamic turn timer. This will automatically give more and more time for turns as the game progresses and everything gets more complex.
Oh, and beware of Gandhi. He will reduce your population to mutant fish people with nuclear technology.
