A very short version of should you buy this game is do you enjoy casual sandbox games? Did you like Saints Row: The Third? Then you'll probably like this game as well. It has the same ridiculousness, characters, engine, and writing that you enjoyed from the previous game, however it takes itself even less seriously. This might put off some people but I personally enjoyed it for what it was. Now to go into detail on what exactly does this game have to offer.
WHAT THEY DID RIGHT:
Gameplay - A previous complaint I had about Saints Row: The Third is that a lot of the missions felt the same. Kills these guys for x amount of time until the mission is complete. Not too many mission deviated from that formula. However Saints Row IV mixes it up a lot more with different options as you progress though the story missions and some side missions. I didn't feel myself get bored with what they had to offer me, however it can feel grindy by the end if you want to perfect everything. Not to mention checkpoints can be infrequent in some areas of the game.
New game mechanics - They added superpowers into the game. You can jump super high, run super fast, and set people on fire just by being around them. Not only do they fit perfectly within the game, I don't find myself missing when I didn't have them. I don't think it takes away from the gameplay in any capacity as the game changed along with you gaining these new abilities so you don't feel like the game is lessened for using them.
Writing - I think the majority of the humour of the game comes from the banter between the characters. I love hearing the interactions between the boss and everyone on their team. It doesn't feel forced at any point in the game. Now if you are looking for any unique deviations from the story, I'm sorry to say that it is as generic as it gets. There are no surprises when it comes to what you expect next, but it's a fun time getting there.
Music - The music this time around is SLAMMIN'. There are not many tracks I dislike while listening to one station, while in Saints Row: The Third I found myself turning off the radio a lot of the time. And best of all you can listen to it from anywhere in the world which means you can always have background music as you go around claiming the city for your own.
WHAT THEY DID OKAY:
Story - As I said before there is nothing too interesting that they did with this. It's your generic invasion story that ends in a way that you can easily predict. It might be fun getting there but there is no fun in watching what is going to happen next. If you are looking for something unique in this department you won't find it here.
Game Length - The main game is relatively short. A lot of the length of the game comes from conquering the city that you have already taken over just in different ways. I don't necessarily think this is a bad thing because I'd much rather play a short fun game rather than a drawn out one with a lot of bad game mechanics just to pad out how long everything takes, however I can understand people wanting to get their monies worth out out it.
Difficulty - To me there is nothing too difficult about this game. I don't think it's meant to be challenging as much as it's meant to be engaging. There can be some difficult parts here and there but this can ultimately be negated by upgrading your character and weapons and destroying whatever comes your way. And while your character can't get damage immunity like they did in Saints Row: The Third, this game does give you arguably the best gun via DLC called 'Merica. Which when fully upgraded and coupled with infinite ammo will kill everything before you in a matter of seconds making any fighting gameplay nonexistent.
WHAT THEY DID WRONG:
Weapons - I don't feel like the weapon balance is as good as it was in Saints Row: The Third. In the previous game I always felt like switching weapons for the occasion. Use rockets when in a tough spot, AR for long range enemies, SMG for a lot of short range enemies, and the pistols for everything else. In this game as soon as you get the Dubstep gun that is all you'll ever use because not only does it do great damage, it's rechargeable. Meaning even before you get infinite ammo you will have two ways of dealing with enemies. When you are using the Dubstep gun and when you are waiting for it to recharge. Sure you have more fun weapons to play with but ultimately you will be using one to two guns your entire playthrough.
References - In my opinion there is nothing funny about pointing to something and saying "Hey remember this? We did that once." There is no joke in that, you have to do something with it in order for it to be considered humourous. Unfortunately Saints Row IV is full of self-referential observations about the previous games that after a while gets annoying. It plays on your nostalgia rather than actually doing anything with it. I'm all for new, I want everything to move forward. However it's hard to say Saints Row IV was new, because of how much of it was a walk down memory lane.
Old game mechanics - When you introduce new game mechanics some of the old mechanics that you had might become obsolete, this means that there is no reason for them to be there anymore. This is exactly what happened when they introduced super jump, gliding, and super sprint within the game. The old mechanic of driving airplanes and cars is not needed, and is slower than you just going there yourself. It's odd that you can still get a car and upgrade it with top speed when you can sprint faster than any car in the game no matter how tuned up it is. Unless you are doing this for old times sake there is absolutely no reason to do any of that.
Collectibles - So I believe that there is nothing inherently fun or interesting about running all over town finding clusters you need in order to upgrade your powers. It's a chore. I don't want to do chores while I'm playing a game. Sometimes they are just there to get while climbing towers that you are going to do anyway for an objective, and sometimes they are just on rooftops you go on one at a time. Sometimes you have to throw a ball to get them. It's annoying, and this is partly because there is so many of them as well.
Multiplayer - Now this might just be a couple of people, but myself and some others in the forums have complained about constantly getting disconnected when trying to play with a friend. This could be in the middle of a long mission or when you are just chilling in the simulation but it is seemingly random and incredibly frustrating. It is funny to see two main characters when a certain part of the game wasn't designed with that in mind, as well as both of you showing off your outfits and powers. However I just wish it would actually work consistently.
DLC - I've already mentioned how the DLC gun Mercia' completely breaks any fighting gameplay, which means all the other DLC guns are obsolete as a result as well. The added outfits are okay, but not worth any of your money. And the two added DLC mission are definitely not worth any of your money in my opinion. Enter the Dominatrix to me was boring, didn't add anything to the characters or gameplay, and I actually don't remember most of it if that tells you anything. I did get a chuckle or two out of it but if I didn't play it I wouldn't lose anything of value. How the Saints Save Christmas was comparatively better, and I liked that we got to see more of the bosses personality. However it's still not worth buying separately. They are add-ons, but they do not add to the game as a whole.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
I don't think that this game was worth $60 with the content we got. Especially when it uses the same engine as the previous game. Overall I had fun with Saints Row IV, but this is not a must play for all gamers. I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes this style of game and can get it on sale.

Comparable to GTA, Saints Row IV is an open world sandbox(ish) game where you play as the former President of the United States in an alien simulation world.
The game features fantastic writing and humor, addicting superpowers and abilities, and is jam packed with ♥♥♥♥ing huge explosions all out the wazoo.
The humor is spot on with funny characters, brilliant pop culture references, and a fair share of sex jokes just for good measure. Serious props to the writers on the humor. God damn is it good.
Recognizability and memorability (is that even a word?) of the characters is also where this game does pretty well, especially for the returning players from previous Saints Row games. Each character has their own personality that is original (At least most of them), funny, and memorable.
Gameplaywise, the game is also quite fun. Blasting through aliens with your telekinesis mind-powers and good old Johnny Gat at your side certainly has it's memories. The absurd amounts of customizability options also make each individual's game even the slightest bit different.
BUT, with all good things there are bound to be some flaws.
Whether this is a bad thing or good thing is up for debate, but the game is really collecting-oriented. To progress at an optimal pace in the game requires some time deticated to going around the simulation and collecting clusters and other such collectibles, which can feel tedious and useless. Again, this may not be a bad thing in a few's eyes, but I don't like spending what feels like hours collecting stupid pieces of data.
The game also seems a little too short for what it could have been, as the main storyline and sidequests can be burned through in a couple days of gameplay, with the rest of the game being simply minigames, collectibles, and customization possibilities. The dlc remedy this problem slightly, but they still don't feel satisfying. It makes the game feel rushed and a sense of lost potential can be detected.
Basically, Saints Row IV is one of those games that makes you feel like a badass, most of the time by giving the player so much power over the game. It may not be a great game for hardcore gamers as it may feel like a hand-holder, but it is by no means a bad game.
Even then, the writing and whacky style of the game make it worth every cent already.

"What the ♥♥♥♥ did I just play?" That's the question this game is designed for the player to ask themselves when they're done with it. It's not something bad, as in this case it can be a fun question. In a sense, I'd compare it with a night where you had too much too drink, you can't remember what you said and have flashes of what you did and when you see someone familiar the next day, you don't know whether you're feeling cool or embarrassed. Like a parody, Saints Row IV captures many quirks from the other games of its times while blending it all in through comedic formulas.
There's no denying the game's abundance of quests, challenges and activities of the sort that are on the side for completitionists that always want more than what the main narrative offers. Sure, they're design is the same as others that are seen to be repetitive and nothing more than a grind for rewards that don't add much to the table, but in SR IV's case, those quests&challanges are not meant to be taken seriously, leaving the possibility that going through the side content can actually be fun. Having something to collect in a visible spot in pretty much every place may seem boring at first, but the fluidity of the movement, character remarks and screen effects can add enough spice to turn water into wine, an impression that only someone who never drank wine could really believe to be so.
Making things different this time around and lifting the ridicule a couple of notches, the plot this time revolves of the Saint's Boss becoming president of the USA and facing an alien invasion soon after. Without giving too much away, I'll tell you the rest of the story revolves around the Saints running around in a simulation, the boss having superpowers akin to the ones seen in Prototype and the obvious ones, like sprinting faster than sports cars, jumping high in the air, gliding, crashing into an aimed spot, throwing fireballs, telekinesis, plenty of powers to give you reasons to dress in hero latex other than looking like a submissive ♥♥♥♥♥. Being a Sci-Fi story, it parodies elements from Mass Effect, making the Boss pursue romances with their crew, by the press of a button, perform loyalty mission which gets them new outfits and a superpowered status. There are separate quests they'll give you, which when done, there will be new weapons given for you. Unnecessary, but they are fun to use.
When taking a closer look at the chemistry between the characters, their tropes and the Boss's lines, I can't help but feel like they've drawn inspiration from Archer, an animated show that in two words I'd describe as "satisfying comedy". Frankly, I'm glad it feels that way, despite the fact that even so, nothing is better at doing "Archer" than "Archer", a fact I'm open to be proven wrong yet still feel like it's right. Still, it adds to the SRIV's dynamic.
Character creator is great. While it doesn't let you change the mesh of a character or anything of the technologically advance sort, the huge numbers of features that add to the personalization can really make a character your own. In fact, if one is up to the ridicule that Saints Row offer, they'll feel more at home in this character creator than in any other game. Aside from the large variety of hairstyles, a body slider and a slider to adjust the pitch of your voice which comes with a selected accent and personality, you have all the little things like cat eyes and face paint. Not to mention the tattoos and clothes you can buy in virtual Steelport. There's something for everybody.
Sprinting in a virtual Steelport that will have a retro dark theme throught the main narrative, bystanders being set on fire just for getting to close for you, probing aliens in the♥♥♥♥♥ collecting clusters from all over the place while occasionally chasing after golden orbs pretty much covers the gameplay. During some loyalty mission you'll have to fight without your powers, but that won't set problems in the game's difficulty, even in the main game where aliens will shot orbs that temporarily disable your powers. Enemies stand still to get head-shot, some changing their position mostly to their side and others running some place else at a speed that you'll still have an easy time to aim and hit.
Co-op is there and it works. In a game such as Saints Row IV, it can be fun to bring a friend into it.
The problem of this game is that it's nothing original, it doesn't try to be, despite the plot-line leading you to believe it has an actual story to tell, a conclusion for the series. While there is a lot of bang for the buck you'll give, especially on sale, it's not a bang you'll remember much of. Great cast of characters in a weak story, fun gameplay elements that aren't new, retro and glitchy visual effects in an open sandbox, small glitches that can be considered hillarious and freezes that can be frustrating by coming out of nowhere at random spots, all make for a game that I'm not recommending but can't blame anyone for buying and playing it. Like internet porn, there's nothing about it worth an award but everybody finds themselves enjoying it.

If Earthbound decided you should be an awful person, this would be the game Nintendo would have made. LISA the Painful creates a world that is both full of life and colorful characters, and simultaneously barren and dead. The music is wonderful, adding to the feeling of an 'anything goes' Western atmosphere, not entirely unlike the Fallout Series.
The combat is difficult, and sometimes downright unfair, in how it plays out. Even just bad luck in a fight could permanently kill one of your party members and ruin your composition, as could just sleeping at a fireplace to heal. As annoying as this sounds, the difficulty fits the setting perfectly and never felt like a hindrance nor unenjoyable.
In conclusion, if you like Earthbound or Undertale's sense of adventure and humor, LISA is the perfect cynical counterpoint to either game. A single playthrough takes about eight hours, though to get all the endngs you'll need to go through at least three times.

This is by far one of the greatest star wars games to date. Best know for its advanced lightsaber gameplay mechanics; Jedi Outcast's campaign, which for a new player is about 12-14 hours (8-10 on reply) is a real challenge compared to modern day releases. Some levels require precise gameplay but give you mines, outposts, and city districts to explore, with many hidden treasures.

Levels are challenging, espically on harder difficulties and show a real sense on progression through the unlocking of new force powers and leveling them up.
While this game has less customisation then it's sequal, Jedi Acadamy, I still argue this is by far the better game. More interesting story, better villian (Deissan is a bad a**) and has more stand out moments, such as the invasion of the Jedi Temple. The soundtrack comes straight from the films and there is only really one section I have had quarels about, Simply because I don't like the AT-ST which you have to pilot.
The multiplayer is also fun and even though many don't play it anymore, you can still take advantage of the game's bot system which was not really matched until Call of Duty: Black Ops combat training mode. There are lots of maps and customisation is great with, saber's powers and character skins and dyes.
Overall a great game and is incredible good value. A classic gamer without having this on their play list is really missing out. 9.8/10

Many other people have already reviewed this game, much better than I could ever hope to. I just want to add a very simple "thumbs up" and recommendation here as well. This has to be one of the finest games in the cyperpunk genre, and the best SHADOWRUN thus far. Brilliant writing and artwork, as usual from HAREBRAINED SCHEMES. Just about every area of the series has now been vastly improved and fine-tuned to perfection, a huge update from RETURNS and even DRAGONFALL. My rating for SHADOWRUN: HONG KONG (EE): 9 out of 10.

Not as good as Shadowrun: Dragonfall.  The main problem is the plot: where Dragonfall and Returns had a steady escalation from street-level crimes to world-shaking calamities, Hong Kong just faffs around for a dozen missions of random shadowruns before finally advancing the main story all in one go.  There's no sense of threat, no sense that you're closing in on the villain or that things are rushing to a conclusion.  They introduce the main plot at the start and then don't do anything with it until the finale.
Also, the changes to Matrix combat just plain suck.  The previous gameplay was perfectly fine, but now they're trying to put real-time stealth gameplay into it, along with a hacking minigame where you play Simon Says for a while.  It's just not fun and it really breaks up the flow of the game.
The characters are still fun - Gobbet and Racter were my favorites - and the final set of missions is excellent.  And the new cyberweapon options are cool.  But the bottom line is, this is a story-driven game, and I just didn't like the story very much.

Freedom Planet. This game has managed to sneak it's game up my favorite games list as my all time favorite video game ever concieved.
The development story of this is that Stephen "Strife" DiDuro originally created the game as a Sonic fangame, with one of the protagonist: Lilac the DragonGirl, originally being concieved as a hedgehog and the main antagonist: Lord Brevon, being a replacement for Dr. Eggman.
The Story is that you play as Lilac, Carol, Milla, with playable Torque and Spade coming later, to stop Lord Brevon from taking Avalice's prized treasure: the Kingdom Stone.
The cutscenes may be long, but I originally didn't skip them, but now I do as I know the story of the game. Voice acting is superb and one of the actresses: Dawn Michelle Bennet, was late hired by FUNimation studioes. The presentation gives off a mid 90's vibe of playing 2D platformers on a Sony PlayStation 1/SEGA Saturn, with crisp artwork and one of the best soundtracks ever made.
Each character plays differently, and are a blast to play, such as Lilac being Sonic  with Sparkster's jetpack, a Shoryuken, and a dive kick; Carol being Zero from MegaMan X with a motorcycle, Chun Li's Hyakuretsukyaku AKA the spam kick button attack, and Sonic's spin attack; Milla is like a Super Mario Bros 2 USA/Doki Doki Panic character, with Cream the Rabbit's ear flap flying; Torque looks like a sort of MegaMan X from current gameplay footage I've seen of him, and Spade looks like Gabit without the staff from his boss fight (I didn't like to play as Milla personally, but that's just a tiny nitpick).
Overall, this is probably the best game I played in 2014, and everyone should play the game. This game is worth $15 and your time. If you're still unsure or need to make sure the game works on your computer, play the free demo.

Question: Did you enjoy old 2d Sonic the Hedgehog?
If yes, then prepare to have your mind blown.
This game is similar, with most, if not all of the little problems that plagued sonic fixed, resulting in a damn near perfect game. The story itself is the weakest part of the game, but it still gives each charactar their own personality and makes them relatable, which is all you can ask for. There are also a couple of heart wrenching moments in it, which is totally surprising.
The platforming and combat themselves and honestly, fantastic with every boss being the right mix of challenging and yet, fair. A little thought and understand of the game mechanics will enable you to formulate a plan of action for just about every attack pattern, meaning the only thing to blame for your failure is you.
So if you don't mind a bit of a cheesey story and anthropomorphic animals (which means, you didn't watch a tonne of good stuff on tv as a kid), then you're in for a near perfect gaming experience.
The one complaint one might level is the price point, but frankly, those people don't realise that all 3 playable charactars have completely different play styles, meaning the same boss has to be beat 3 different ways, essentially trippling the lifespan of the game.

Runner2 is a lot less frustrating than the original Bit.Trip Runner, but it still requires too much memorization of the levels and too much repetition-until-perfection of levels to be consistently fun. The addition of mid-level checkpoints means you now only have to repeat half the level over and over again until you do it perfectly, but that still becomes rather tedious. Runner2 may very well of perfected the 2D forced running, avoid bad guys, collect gold mini-genre, but the mini-genre itself is fundamentally flawed.
On a more constructive note for the potential Runner3, the inability to remap controls is a real pain. In the original Runner, kick was mapped to the shoulder buttons in addition to the face buttons on a 360 controller. This made it much easier to jump and then kick mid-air barriers. Now jump and kick are both face buttons and neither can be remapped, so you're left awkwardly covering two buttons are once with your thumb. This is completely inexplicable since most of the shoulder buttons do nothing.
I would only recommend this game to gamers who enjoy memorizing patterns and repeating the same sections of levels over and over until you do it perfect.

As an avid fan of the Conan Franchise, from the Arnold Schwartzenegger Movies, to the original Novels and even some of the Comic Adaptations over the years, I was actually surprised to learn a Conan based MMO even existed, how did a 7 year old game fall under my radar?! It was a great idea with a large scale universe that is easy to immerse oneself in and explore for themselves. And it was Free to Play on Steam!? Of course I would try this out, I heard some less than favorable things about it but I figured I'd try it for myself.
But was I satisfied with this game? No. Why? Well first off the combat system, now I know the game is old and that it wanted to try something new in regards to the typical MMORPG style of Combat; but seriously, it is tough to pull off, from what I can tell; many of the special attacks outside of one's main three left-right-upward thrust attacks, are executions one has to pull off by pressing the key to activate it again AFTER pressing it the first time (WHY!?) and then pressing the basic combat thrusts to fully execute the executions. I like the idea but the fact that the tutorial on how to do it is easily forgettable and very easy to mess up makes your attempt to pull off these executions pretty much a failure and no extra damage out of them will happen.
That would not be so much of a problem if this games idea of difficulty scaling wasn't basically making every enemy you face off against when doing a side-quest literally 3 levels higher than you by the time you do it. The last time I played this game (and trust me, it will be the LAST time); it was when I was doing the lowest level possible side-quest for my character which was level 8 by the time I was doing it, and the quest involved me just having to kill 3 pirates; easy right? Not really; because they were level 11, and you CAN'T fight them one at a time, eventually they'll all join in and tackle me and kill me. I cannot even complete the lowest level side-quest in the game at Level 8; it's like the moment you reach level 6-8; the difficulty spikes up to levels that could reach Jupiter!
Maybe if I can buy some good items from the shopkeeps; maybe that'll help me? Nope; not even high enough level for me to even buy them. And enemy grinding doesn't work because the cap for XP gains dies out at 2 levels or lower! The only time I have EVER seen ANYONE in game (which is rarity because the games' servers are empty), they have paid for the exclusive weapons via-microtransactions. That means the only way possible to beat the game after level 6 at minimum is to pay for good items with REAL MONEY. Now look; I know Free to Play and Microtransactions go hand in hand and you're probably saying; "What did you expect!? How else are they going to make money!?" And to be fair, I am not against Microtransactions; I think they are a necessary evil for games like these, however; I do NOT believe they should be forced upon the players to the point where it is only possible to continue with such (might as well put a paywall), nor do I think the exclusive items should be so overpowered that they create an imbalance between players who pay and players who don't.
That said, why is it that a game that is so beautiful and enriched by the Conan Universe so lackluster!? I can only guess that my feelings are the same as others. I don't recommend this game for anyone, the game itself is not strong enough to stand on it's own and only got my attraction because of the Conan name. Conan deserves better.

This game held me for quite some time and replaying it never gets boring.
The story that is somewhere in the background is not that significant - as the captain of a space ship you are tasked with breaking through several sectors in a mostly hostile galaxy and carry vital intelligence to its destination.
Along the journey you build up your vessel, expand its weaponry and systems, harden your crew and recruit new members - everything to be prepared for the more and more difficult challenges.
The most entertaining thing for me is the micro-managment in this game. During encounters with several types of hostile ships you have to decide real-time where to assign your crew members, to which systems allocate the energy to and which parts of the enemy's ship should be targeted and with what. This very often turns into hard live-or-die choices, like for example: should I send the crew to repell the boarding party that just teleported in or maybe have them fixing the hull damage that is sucking air out of the ship, or put out a fire that is ravaging the engine room? Usually you end up doing everything at the same time, constantly switching your resources from offense to defense. Even if at some point you'll strike a steady balance and think that you are prepared for anything, you will always find that one enemy ship that employs tactics you are not prepared to counter and will have to "make do".
The simple design of Faster Than Light packs a ton of features, so if you value content over looks you will be most pleased. Trekkies, Star Wars and other space-franchise fans will also feel at home. Since each playthrough has a different randomly generated galaxy, with different directions, enemies and encounters the replay value is extremely high. Be prepared to get addicted!

To sum up: a masterpiece.
This game has the essence of the roguelike genre, combined with a good story (you don't even have to know the story to fully enjoy FTL), a sublime soundtrack, a perfect graphic design, very interesting combat mechanics and a neverending of posibilities.
10/10

This is probably my favorite Sonic game of the last 15 years. It's not something I plan to go back to and doesn't get visited near annually like 3&Knuckles, but I still enjoyed it a lot. It improved on the few things I liked about Unleashed and Colors and the added PC benefits of a rock solid framerate and higher resolution makes it more of a spectacle to play.
I don't have the metrics or straight comparisons to validate this, but Generations felt a bit slower to me compared to Unleashed in the 3D sections. Either that or the zones were designed with Sonic's movement in mind more. While Unleashed felt like a game that rewards rote memorization and simply has too much "speed" for the sake of speed, Generations felt like a game that rewarded good reaction time and doesn't punish as harshly. It seems like windows for finding the alternate paths, ducking the obstacle, etc, are more lax. This sounds like the game was simplified a bit, and that's maybe true; however it just felt more balanced, and more fun to fail and more rewarding to succeed (and more likely without commiting the map to memory.)
2D gameplay is great. And while I feel it is also slowed down a bit, it manages to hold my interest compared to other platformers which haven't. Wisp powers change things up without being too abundant.
The story and dialogue and everything outside of gameplay is garbage. Or, extremely silly and simple. Which I suppose is a direction I don't mind compared to melodrama or whatever you want to call what was vomited out of the mid-2000s games. If you've played Colors it's mostly more of the same here.
The various challenges are hit or miss. Many require playing the game in an extremely unituitive manner with questionable gameplay, Espio challenges are especially bad. However, the time-trial esqe challenges were extremely fun to undertake. The act 2 Planet Wisp challenge offered a great deal of enjoyable frustration as it required me to really learn the stage in order to succeed.
Basically, I feel Generations is a platformer worth playing, even if it still has the stink of modern-day Sonic on and in it. Hearing both original and remixed tracks of various sonic themes is quite the trip down memory lane, even if the songs get a little less familiar once you get past the Genesis era games.

Game: Sonic Generations
Genre: Adventure
Developer: Sonic Team/SEGA
System: Steam/PC
Total Score: 96/100
Value Score: 9.6/10
• Story: 9/10
o Sonic the Hedgehog was having a birthday party with all the friends he has made in over the past couple of years. However something off in the distance a dark ominous being appeared and sucked everyone up and leaving both Sonic and Tails confused at what happened in a unknown mysterious space void. There they find themselves in a familiar location and as they traveled around they managed to find younger form of themselves. Now both Sonics and Tails will be going on a new journey to save their friends and their own respected times and worlds.
• Characters: 10/10
o Almost every single Sonic series hero and villain appear in this game. There are some ones who do not make an appearance but all of the major characters from the past few generations do appear. You have characters like Sonic and Tails from both the past and present, Dr. Eggman of the past and present, Amy, Shadow the hedgehog, Rouge, Knuckles and the rest from Colors, Unleashed and etc. The enemies are also the same depending on the level of which game it reflects off from. Some of the notable bosses as well from the past games also make an appearance. Sonic Generations is pretty much like a reunion for the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise.
• GamePlay: 9/10
o Sonic Generations plays differently from the older Sonic games. For one thing levels and stages are divided into different areas from past Sonic games and you can access them through as Classic Sonic or Modern sonic in a world map like sidescroller style. Playing as either sonic will alter the gameplay and changes the whole design of a level/stage. Classic Sonic's gameplay style is more old school 2D view while Modern Sonic's is mostly 3D view like recent Sonic games. There are three levels with each area having a mini boss and a boss at the end of the three levels. Defeating each mini boss and boss earns you a chaos emerald which is used to fight the last boss at the end of the game. Each level consists stages from different eras of Sonic - in the PC version which is the same as the home console versions, the levels and stages are included as : Classic Era - Green Hill from Sonic the Hedgehog, Chemical Plant from Sonic the Hedgehog 2 and Sky Sanctuary from Sonic the Hedgehog 3 & Knuckles. The Dreamcast era includes Speed highway from Sonic Adventure 1, City Escape from Sonic Adventure 2 and Seaside hill from Sonic Heroes. The Modern era which is the last era has Crisis City from Sonic the Hedgehog 2006, Rooftop Run from Sonic Unleashed and Planet Wisp from Sonic Colors. The usual gameplay rules apply to both modern and classic sonic - collecting rings and racing your way towards the exit marker at the end of the stage after avoiding all sorts of enemies and obstacles. For Modern sonic you can super speed dash upon a limitation bar which can be increased by collecting rings while classic sonic mainly plays like the old Sonic games with little to no difference. The level designs for each type is completely different even though it may be in the same stage. You have the usual power ups such as invincibility, shields which range from the regular green shield, the electric shield which absorbs rings, the fire ring which can make Sonic shoot like a fireball and the water shield which Sonic can use to breathe underwater or to have a extra bounce. Upon completing stages you will get access to additional missions which base around the level of where these missions are located (which is above each level entrance). These missions also vary depending on which Sonic you play as and will have a different requirement or goal as well which can range from completing a level, fighting/competing with a rival, collecting certain number of rings or simply surviving amongst other things. Completing these missions will earn you a point towards the achievement of completing all the missions and allows you to unlock a artwork or a music track which can be used optionally on other stages. Red stars also make an appearance in which goes towards your achievement scoring and is counted towards the completion of the game. A new feature introduced to the Generations game is the ability to buy power ups or abilities which can be equipped upon purchase with a limitation on how many you can equip by the number of points it requires compared to how many you have in total. Abilities and power ups range from simple power ups depending on certain situations happening automatically, the inclusion of new speed abilities or the ability to protect yourself with some bonuses such as keeping a few rings even after taking a hit instead of losing all your rings. There's also a special room where you can go and check on character profiles, listen to the game's OST or to even look at some promotional artwork designed for the game. The online feature of the game introduces you to a competitive circuit where you are forced to do a level and are ranked by the time and score upon completion which then gets displayed in a leader boards for bragging rights.
• Graphics: 10/10
o Sonic Generations use a new style of visual design and fluidity for its cutscenes however the in gameplay seems to be similar to what you would expect see in a HD version of Sonic Colors and of Sonic the Hedgehog 4. The new cutscenes seem reminiscent of a typical western influenced platformer which isnt a bad thing. The visual designs for the characters look great especially on the older versions of characters. The environments re-done from past Sonic games look incredible with the new style and brings a whole new depth to whatever the player had imagined beforehand in the past games. There are some slow down and FPS drops but that is only because you would need a stronger CPU than what is recommended but by not that much and not very noticeable.
• Sound: 10/10
o Sonic Generations have managed to keep majority of the voice overs for their characters from all eras including the eras without voice overs are nicely done and you can tell the difference in the quality/type of voice. However even though Sonic doesnt talk might be a bad thing - what was worse is the fact that Shadow and Rouge's voice actors were changed but it isnt bad to the extent where they sound completely off. The sound effects which were made famous in the older sonic games and all of the other games make a complete return.
• Music: 10/10
o Sonic Generations consists of a mixture of old classic tracks, original tracks from modern games and remixes of all of the songs with a bit of new tracks exclusive to the game. The remixes are actually quite well made and some of them are even BETTER than the originals. Another nice thing that they added is the ability to change the music when you play in a stage. Simply upon clicking to start on a stage change the music to whatever you have unlocked via playing missions.
• Length: 9/10
o Sonic Generations although might seem a bit short but it takes a lot of time and dedication to get all the red stars, perfect score points upon completion and to get every single music/artwork unlocked. At the most you will complete at least 12-15 hours on a straight way playthrough with minimal missions completed. For a platformer that is a pretty decent amount since most platformers are usually done within 7-10 hours.
• Replay Value: 10/10
o Sonic Generations most powerful aspect is possibly its replay value aspect. With the ability to play in over 50 different stages over the choice of 7+ maps that seems to be a pretty hefty amount considering if you add the mini bosses and the bosses you fight along the way along with some of the things you need to collect such as Red stars which will eventually make you play through the levels multiple times.

This is a very clever little VN with a strong “meta” aspect. While the core story is nothing that special, the game is very decently written and rather endearing when it goes to the main intrigue/romance (can’t say much more without spoiling it). The most fun aspect though is exploring the various story routes, while interacting with your guide Lycoris and trying to uncover the meaning behind the story-within-a-story setting. There’s a ton of achievements connected to that very idea and while I didn’t have the patience to hunt for them all, looking for hidden content and story elements was quite amusing. The whole experience took me around 5 hours and I was very satisfied with it.
The art and music are rather simple, but apart from one sprite I quite enjoyed them. Backgrounds are very few, but rather nice to look at. I think I’ve noticed a few typos in the whole game but that’s hardly a serious issue. Production qualities simply felt adequate, never getting in the way of the story.
What is important to point out is that this was made for a game jam and from that point of view is very much an impressive achievement. While it’s not the best thing ever in the storytelling department, it’s really original and ambitious with its structure and meta-narrative. As a free product it’s definitely worth looking at and has more heart and fresh ideas than many VNs I’ve paid money for here on Steam.

TL;DR: "Realistic" long primary ranges hurt class balance and result in slow and passive gameplay, and no one seems to care.
The bulk of my time in-game was spent on the standalone verison, not the steam version. Only downloaded the steam verison for convenience.
The game is very visually impressive, i don't think i've seen anything more beautiful in a vido game than firing a full broadside in a battleship, or having your machine guns light up enemy aircraft.
The issue i have is the gameplay. PvP is extremely passive, slow and unfun, for me at least. Wargaming seems to have an inconsistant method of applying "realism" to the game. They make the ranges for primary guns realistic (but not the sceondaries, for example) to the detriment of gameplay.
WoWs is devided into 4 classes. A generalist class, being the Cruiser, a Support Class, being the Aircraft Carriers, and 2 Specialist Classes, being the Destroyers and Battleships, holding the roles of Harassers/Pickers and Tanks respectivly.
Battleships, the "tank" class, has the highest Armor and Health, and the most powerful Primary Guns, as well as a large compliment of secondary guns for use at close range. A big issue here is that Batlleships primaries are also the longest ranged weapons in the game, which is realistic, but feeds into a few major issues. A High-Health class with that has a long-ranged attack is, by nature of the long range weapons, encouraged to hang back at maxium range to pick people off with the high burst-damage attacks, rather than push in and brawl with opponents at close range, as the secondary armament, as well as the supposed teamplay and counterbalance between Battlehsips and other classes such as the more versitile curiser would entail.

From this you might conclude that battleships are Overpowered, but, removing thier range advantage, they're really not. With thier pluses comes their minuses. Battleships have the tankiest armor and health, but also have poor speed and trash manuverabaility. Thier Primaries are powerful sources of damage, but require a long time to reload inbetween shots, generally around 30 seconds per shot, and turn extremely slowly. Secondaries provide useful support damage at close range, but can *only* fire at close range, and are very innacurate, especially against small a nimble destroyers.
All these weaknesses would be very exploitable in close-range battles, but because the Battleship's long range can allow it to sit well outside close range battles, rendeirng all these weaknesses irrelavant. Slow reload time and turret turn speed would hurt a brawling Battleship's ability to respond to new targets attacking at different directions, but because the Battleship is at long range, there's only ever one direction it needs to face. New targets are always a quick couple of degrees of turn away. Anything past that, and you're out of position, and will get focused or ambushed to death. Poor secondary range and accuracy is only a factor to consider if secondaries are given the oppuritunity to fire, which a Battleship at long range never provide. That minor extra damage isn't considered worth pushing forward to get focused by enemy long-range fire
Cruisers are the generalist class, supposedly good at everything, but not *great* at anything. It's medium damage, but fast-reloading primaries ideally would make great support fire for allied ships in brawls, being particularly decent at attacking destroyers, and chiping away at Battleships with fire damage form explosive shells, as well as providing specialized anti-air support against enemy fighters. The long range of battles hurts Cruisers, however.
Cruisers have less range than thier Battleships counterparts, and so generally play second fiddle to them if they are present, relying on numbers advantages to attack enemy Battleships, since they cannot take advantage of map terrain due to the longer range, and so sit at a "meh" grade of power in the game.
Destroyers, the Picker and Harasser class, are represented as the rock-paper-scissors counter to Battleships, which they are... at close range. Thier torpedos deal heavy, heavy damage depsite being slow-moving, which battleships (and some larger cruisers) at close range are generally unable to avoid very easily. But because, like we've well established by now, Battleships, and now Cruisers have no reason to come into close range, Destroyers are relegated to a vulture role of patiently wiating behind map terrain waiting for someone to overextend so they can be ambushed, since closing the distance regularly is a harder task. Destroyers have the highest manuverability and speed of any ship class in the game, as well as the smallest and thus hardest-to-hit profile, which gives them an advantage at avoiding slow-moving enemy shells at a distance, as well as the ability to deploy a smokescreen to provide artificial cover for themselves and teammates, but all of trivial effect if they are not within fighting range to begin with. All it takes is one lucky Battleship volley to take down a lightly-armored destroyer, and if an enemy destroyer at range is always inside an enemy Battleship's line-of-sight, a hit will happen at some point.
Aircraft carriers, the indirect fire support class, are affected by the range issue in both ways. By nature of controlling planes in an rts-like fahsion, Carriers have the freedom to sit at extreme ranges, letting thier planes quickly fly to thier targets over the heads of allied ships, exceeding the range of even battleships by technicality. Carriers however, have no primary guns with which to defend themselves, armed with only secondary guns, if any at all, making them very vunerable to focus fire when in-range of an enemy, and so, like battleships, are encouraged to sit at maximum range, generally behind an island, or at the edge of the map. This is an issue in a couple ways. Firstly, it causes aircaft support to have long periods of downtime, as planes must travel long distances to and from thier target, reducing thier ability to play the game, and relegating aircraft to an ocasional danger to outliers in the group, rather than a near-constant threat that affects player positioning and movement, even if Aircraft are a powerful weapon. The second issue is that, again, carriers have poor abilities to defend themselves, and so, unless guarded by an escort willing to take themselves out of the battle, are essentially screwed if any enemy ship - generally destroyers - finds them at thier end of the map; Carriers are unable to recieve the passive support of thier teammates due to the danger of ranged focus fire, and so in turn are less able to support thier teammates.
For these reasons, I personally find PvP to be very stale, passive and unfun. Matches very often pass the 20 minute limit due to how slow games are. I personally find Co-Op and PvE gamemodes to be more enjoyable, for the simple reason that Bots aren't afriad to be agressive. How to begin with this?, I was told this game was great and also read about it, watched reviews and decided to buy on a steam sale (fortunately!), I was excited and had high hopes over the hype for this game, unfortunately, Mafia 2 falls short to my expectations and excitement.
Vito Scaletta, our main protagonist, born in Italy arrives to the US looking for a better future along with his family. He didn't wait too long to get into trouble along with his friend Joe, he ends up being caught by the police while robbing a store at a young age, he is given two options either going to jail or joining the army. After getting wounded in war, he comes back to the US to meet his family once again, and of course old time’s friends.
Being poor and having no money is no life for Vito, so he joins Joe into getting more money and doing "jobs" before joining one of the three families in Empire City, mid 40's and the whole world in changing after the war. After a couple of these jobs, Vito ends up in jail serving a long sentence, but he meets somebody, an important member of one of these families who helps him survive in jail and teaches him the value of what he is doing, after six years of imprisonment, he is free once again, eager to get rich, be respected, and make a name of his own. Along with Joe, Vito's best friend, they make their way into one of the families that conform all of the mafia underworld getting into all of kind of deals, missions and contracts for the bosses.
To sum the story up, it is not groundbreaking nor has original elements, but it does have really strong characters which make it a likeable one, Joe is funny and always adds some humor to the density and tension of conversation or the different situations, Vito is charming, determined and is always ready for action and to shoot first and ask questions later if necessary, along with other support characters that are part of the story, Vito and Joe are the ones that truly shine here.
Mafia 2 offers the typical open world combat mechanics, cover-shoot-cover, and move to the next room, repeat. It doesn't offer many variations to be honest, almost all missions have the same mode, the ones that have something different that may add some contrast come every time you drive a car and have to escape from the police, besides that, Mafia 2 is really monotonous to say the least, it's always the same: mission is given, drive from point A to point B, shoot, cover, repeat, mission done, drive back home, sleep, receive phone call, mission is given once again, drive from point A to point B, that's it. Nothing extraordinary to my taste.
To add some variation to this world, we have some fillers, like selling cars to get some easy money, collectibles like Playboy magazines, which entertain the eye a bit, and some posters that are all over the city with information on criminals, besides that, there is not much to do in Empire City, which is really a bad point in my opinion, games like this that offer an open world experience should have more things to do, for example, there are weapon stores where you can buy ammo, but I felt they were totally useless, I visited some shops like twice and that was it, all of the ammo and weapons I had, I got them from missions, perhaps the only extra that it's really worth it being the mechanic, a place where you can customize your cars and really pimp them out to look cooler! But overall, Empire City is a very boring and dull place to do anything exciting.
Despite Empire City feeling alive at times, I had the idea the devs could have used this chance to add some mini missions or real time fights, maybe rival bands getting into our territory, shootings, police chasing other criminals, all this just to have the chance to do something out of the ordinary for a change, none of that happens at all, there is nothing else to interact with in the whole place and Its citizens, this is only limited to rob stores, buy some awful clothing and nothing more, a pity.
What can I say about the music? it feels like a mid 40's and 50's city, or at least, I felt it that way, songs play on the radio every time you drive a car, making your driving experience musically rewarding, classics of that time play all over the stations we have access to and I must say, they nailed it, they pass this with flying colors! We can also hear the news regarding our missions and all the bodies we leave behind, as well as the news about the final stages of the war in Europe.
The voice acting is great as well, all main and support characters feel really alive and with intention, the Italian accent is awesome and makes the conversations amusing at any time, nothing bad to say here, top notch acting.
I think Mafia 2 could have been more, I believe the devs should have added some more details in relation to the city and the way it develops during the game, it had potential and room to add what I said before, some more action into the dullness of Empire City. With strong characters and a story that could have been a little riskier, Mafia 2 offers an uninteresting city, a monotonous mission system, repetitive combat mechanics, boring boss fights, to put it that way, (though, I would not call them boss fights) and a terrible and unexciting ending with no ambition nor any sort of cliffhanger, Mafia 2 gets my thumbs down. I could have been harsher, but the soundtrack and awesome voice acting are the game’s shining stars here.

One Way Heroics is a rougelike RPG with a twist.  All the normal conventions of an RPG are present--stats, classes, gold, weapons, random monsters, chests full of loot, towns, a sprawling overworld--as well as the start-from-scratch different-every-time staples of a rougelike.  The catch is no backtracking, and no dilly-dallying: the left edge of the screen is a mass of darkness consuming the world, and is constantly moving right, so the player must move even faster while still spending enough time to level up and find better supplies for whatever dangers lie ahead.  The game is pretty entertaining in its own right WITHOUT the one-way gimmick, as it boils down an entire RPG fantasy adventure into a bite-sized 30 minutes, with victory unlocking more options to use for the next run.  It does nothing particularly new, but takes a ton of old ideas and simplifies them for a fun little game that's easy to play and replay.

Overall, a fun take on the randomized dungeon RPG.

As CRPGs go Shadowrun: Hong Kong - Extended is a short but fairly sweet example of the species. While the graphics have gotten an upgrade from earlier entries in the series, it is the writing and text that takes center stage here. If you fully explore the game you will spend far more time reading than anything else.
Not only do your fellow shadow runners who make up your party have back stories to explore, a good many of the local color, who will have nothing to do with any mission, have robust dialog trees in which you can learn about their lives and the larger Shadowrun setting. There are even narratives playing out in cyberspace you can follow on the in game BBS used by shadowrunners like yourself.
Fortunately, the writing is generally very good. The characters are vivid and unique, while the world is complex and fully fleshed. The game and its characters show a lot more creativity than we have become accustomed to in run of the mill RPGs. While the narrative is relatively fixed, the way it plays out and the choices you make do color the story nicely and the player dialog options do a good job allowing you to express your character's attitudes and ambitions even if they don't have a dramatic effect on the world around you. It has some of the best writing I've seen in an RPG though there were times I got tired of dialoguing and yearned for a bit more action.
The combat is solid but not especially well balanced. I played on the hard difficulty and found most of the game fairly easy. My few losses came from not understanding clearly what the objectives were in a given fight and thus failing to achieve them. That said, the combat is interesting and varied with very distinct classes and approaches to building a strong character. There is not a great deal of combat, perhaps 30-50 encounters in the game, many of which you can avoid through dialogs or careful exploration. While a few fights are short, many are nicely staged with reinforcements and other interesting complications.
The mission design is a high point for the whole series. Each run typically involves a mix of exploration, dialog, and combat. Clever and observant players can gain significant advantages. A real high point involved a moment where you are giving verbal instructions to an NPC through a com link, telling her what to say. Just as she is being questioned by a suspicious official your character is confronted. You must try to choose dialog options that will work for both situations simultaneously. Super clever and super fun.
The extended edition adds a post story scenario about half the length of the core game. It offers a satisfying conclusion to the story of the main character and his comrades and I think the narrative really benefits from its inclusion. Thus, I absolutely recommend the extended version.
The weak point in the series remains the cyber combat. Deckers aka hackers are integral to the Shadowrun world so it makes sense they would do their best to include it in the game. In prior editions it was simply a much duller version of the regular combat system. Here, while it does occasionally become a simplified turn based combat game, it has become a collection of mini games. There is a stealth/action section as you dodge scanning droids. Then a simon-says game and a kind of simplified memory matching game, both with a countdown timer. While a bit less tedious, it still feels a little disappointing compared to the rest of the game play.

This is extremely similar to "Shadowrun Returns" and "Shadowrun: Dragonfall". If you've played those then you'll like it. They all run on the same engine and are adventures of approximately the same length. This is the most recent of the three and has the most up-to-date graphics.
For the uninitiated, it's an isometric turn-based RPG. The rules and setting are based on the pen-and-paper RPG of the same name - it's a quirky cyberpunk setting with fantasy elements.
The pen-and-paper background means that the rules are strong. The game is well balanced, challenging without being too difficult. The rules are explained well through the user interface with tooltips and the like.
I enjoyed the story and cared about the characters. The writing is really good. The game took approximately 15 hours, including the "bonus content". If anything, this was a little fast - I would have enjoyed a few extra side missions.
If you enjoyed the other Shadowrun games then you'll enjoy this one. If you're wondering which of the three to buy, this wouldn't be a bad choice - perhaps "Dragonfall" edges it on story, though that's a matter of taste. It has better graphics and more finely turned than "Shadowrun Returns" though, and I'd recommend it over that.

There are plenty of quest givers scattered around the starting zone with plentiful rewards of armor and weaponry. The thing I like most is the idea of a `night-time` zone that is used to persue your individual `destiny quests` as opposed to `day-time` which you share with other players.
My favourite aspect is the ability to have armor items on a fashion tab which have no effect on your actual gear ratings. If you want to run round nekkid whilke defeating your foes then have at it :)

How to begin with this?, I was told this game was great and also read about it, watched reviews and decided to buy on a steam sale (fortunately!), I was excited and had high hopes over the hype for this game, unfortunately, Mafia 2 falls short to my expectations and excitement.
Vito Scaletta, our main protagonist, born in Italy arrives to the US looking for a better future along with his family. He didn't wait too long to get into trouble along with his friend Joe, he ends up being caught by the police while robbing a store at a young age, he is given two options either going to jail or joining the army. After getting wounded in war, he comes back to the US to meet his family once again, and of course old time’s friends.
Being poor and having no money is no life for Vito, so he joins Joe into getting more money and doing "jobs" before joining one of the three families in Empire City, mid 40's and the whole world in changing after the war. After a couple of these jobs, Vito ends up in jail serving a long sentence, but he meets somebody, an important member of one of these families who helps him survive in jail and teaches him the value of what he is doing, after six years of imprisonment, he is free once again, eager to get rich, be respected, and make a name of his own. Along with Joe, Vito's best friend, they make their way into one of the families that conform all of the mafia underworld getting into all of kind of deals, missions and contracts for the bosses.
To sum the story up, it is not groundbreaking nor has original elements, but it does have really strong characters which make it a likeable one, Joe is funny and always adds some humor to the density and tension of conversation or the different situations, Vito is charming, determined and is always ready for action and to shoot first and ask questions later if necessary, along with other support characters that are part of the story, Vito and Joe are the ones that truly shine here.
Mafia 2 offers the typical open world combat mechanics, cover-shoot-cover, and move to the next room, repeat. It doesn't offer many variations to be honest, almost all missions have the same mode, the ones that have something different that may add some contrast come every time you drive a car and have to escape from the police, besides that, Mafia 2 is really monotonous to say the least, it's always the same: mission is given, drive from point A to point B, shoot, cover, repeat, mission done, drive back home, sleep, receive phone call, mission is given once again, drive from point A to point B, that's it. Nothing extraordinary to my taste.
To add some variation to this world, we have some fillers, like selling cars to get some easy money, collectibles like Playboy magazines, which entertain the eye a bit, and some posters that are all over the city with information on criminals, besides that, there is not much to do in Empire City, which is really a bad point in my opinion, games like this that offer an open world experience should have more things to do, for example, there are weapon stores where you can buy ammo, but I felt they were totally useless, I visited some shops like twice and that was it, all of the ammo and weapons I had, I got them from missions, perhaps the only extra that it's really worth it being the mechanic, a place where you can customize your cars and really pimp them out to look cooler! But overall, Empire City is a very boring and dull place to do anything exciting.
Despite Empire City feeling alive at times, I had the idea the devs could have used this chance to add some mini missions or real time fights, maybe rival bands getting into our territory, shootings, police chasing other criminals, all this just to have the chance to do something out of the ordinary for a change, none of that happens at all, there is nothing else to interact with in the whole place and Its citizens, this is only limited to rob stores, buy some awful clothing and nothing more, a pity.
What can I say about the music? it feels like a mid 40's and 50's city, or at least, I felt it that way, songs play on the radio every time you drive a car, making your driving experience musically rewarding, classics of that time play all over the stations we have access to and I must say, they nailed it, they pass this with flying colors! We can also hear the news regarding our missions and all the bodies we leave behind, as well as the news about the final stages of the war in Europe.
The voice acting is great as well, all main and support characters feel really alive and with intention, the Italian accent is awesome and makes the conversations amusing at any time, nothing bad to say here, top notch acting.
I think Mafia 2 could have been more, I believe the devs should have added some more details in relation to the city and the way it develops during the game, it had potential and room to add what I said before, some more action into the dullness of Empire City. With strong characters and a story that could have been a little riskier, Mafia 2 offers an uninteresting city, a monotonous mission system, repetitive combat mechanics, boring boss fights, to put it that way, (though, I would not call them boss fights) and a terrible and unexciting ending with no ambition nor any sort of cliffhanger, Mafia 2 gets my thumbs down. I could have been harsher, but the soundtrack and awesome voice acting are the game’s shining stars here.

Have you have been searching for a tough 2-D platformer designed with care, classic 16-bit to 32-bit era sensibilities, and a superb soundtrack? Is so, look no further than Freedom Planet. Despite the similar character art direction to those familiar with the Sonic the Hedgehog series, Freedom Planet is its own beast sporting elements from a number of classic games perfectly blended into its own unique entity. Featuring the sense of speed from classic Sonic the Hedgehog games with gameplay elements from Megaman X and a boss design approach reminiscent of Gunstar Heroes, this game will provide a unique sense of challenge rarely found in games anymore as of this writing.
The game offers a number of character each with their own strengths, weaknesses, and special traits which will make you think differently as to how you would approach the same situation. For one small example, Lilac has a direction amiable airdash, Carol can either wall jump or drive up the wall on her motorcycle, and Milla has a flutter jump that is most useful for tricky platforming segments. This isn't to imply all the characters go through all the same, carefully crafted stages and encounter the same challenging boss fights however as some stages are limited to few characters or even exclusive to a single character. These stages can be enjoyed accompanied by a fleshed out story in Adventure Mode or if you are looking for just gameplay you can just select Classic Mode.
Other features this game has to offer include a time attack mode that not only includes your standard ability to replay stages and tally the top results, but it also houses a series of obstacle courses that are designed around breaking all the targets in the fastest time possible alongside a snuck-in mahjong minigame in the time attack menu's on the stage select screen. The game also features collectable in-game cards scattered across most of the stages, incentivizing the player to approach and explore each stage utilizing the branching paths of each stage or explore them in creative ways with each character. The options menu also sports a variety of different difficulties, which is great news for allowing the game to be accessible or challenging depending upon your skill level.
The story itself in this game gave me the impression that it is one of those "Either you will love it or you will hate it" sort of situations. At its core, the story is about trio of friends and their ally from space stopping an evil space tyrant from stealing a precious valuable from the planet on his way off the planet. The story contains cheesy dialogue and a decent amount of humor as you'd expect from the story given its cartoon styling but the story also manages to have some shockingly dark moments, almost jarring by contrast. The narrative managed to make me personally care about the cast and their struggles, but as I previously stated your mileage may vary on the story depending on your personal tastes.
To summarize, Freedom Planet is an absolutely fantastic game and it deserves to be in your library if you are a fan of 2-D platform games or a fan of classic style games in general. This game has plenty of content to keep you busy for hours on end and provides a unique sense of challenge that will make you want to replay levels to test to see how much you skills at the game have improved. You will not be disappointed.

Ill get it out of the way, this game is very “Sonic” In character design and level design. That’s where the similarities end though, Freedom Planet is a very different beast and really deserves to be judged on its own merits. Freedom Planet is more a action game then a speedy platformer. Sure there are parts where you will be booking it through loop-de-loops but it blends combat in with it seamlessly and the levels lend themselves well to it. See most enemies don’t hurt you on contact, so you have two options. Blaze through the level and hit the occasional enemy on the way or stick around and fight it out. Both options are fine and both have there rewards and the game gives you everything you need to do it.
From the offset the game has three characters to play and all of them play drastically different. There’s Lilac who is more well rounded and great for first time players, Carol who can really kick♥♥♥♥♥with skillful play and Milla who is meant to be played slowly and more carefully and is really built for exploring the levels and finding shiny things. All of these characters are viable in all the different levels and they even each have there own levels unique to them. Each character is like playing a different game and most of the levels are balanced so every character has there own way of getting around them. There are even areas that only certain characters can access. It can be very difficult to build levels with multiple characters in mind and they have done a great job of it.
I will say some of the bosses can take a while to really get a bead on however the game pretty much lets you try again as much as you want until you finally get it right and that moment when you do can really be satisfying. The game does use a lives system but with how the continues work its really just kind of window dressing which is a bit of a oversight but it didn’t bother me too much. Though that makes going for the games main collectible Crystals kind of moot since all it really does is give you lives unless you care about high scores or bragging rights. I do really wish they could have reworked it cause the idea of doing away with lives period wouldn’t hurt me in the slightest. The reason I stuck with it til the end was because I DIDN’T have to start a level over, I actually had a chance to learn instead of drop the game out of frustration. Lives are a product of the times, when the games were all about eating quarters. I feel like lives are a outdated relic of the past and its just not good game design anymore, hardcore gamers be damned, but really its just a small nitpick on a otherwise great game.
I do want to end on a positive note though. I’m proud this game opted to have not one, not two but THREE female protagonists who are fun and interesting. I will say that while the story itself is pretty good its not super spectacular, But I do like how you get different pieces of the story depending on who you play and it does add good replay value. The characters are what really saved it for me. The writing is fun and the voice acting is also well done for having a lot of unknown actors. Having three female protagonists is really a breath of fresh air in a game industry ruled by scruffy white guys.
I highly recommend Freedom Planet especially if you’ve been craving a Sonic styled platformer like the good old days that feels like a long lost Saturn game. They plan on adding more content for free later including 2 new characters with there own parts of the story to play which frankly im very excited for. Give this game a look.

If this was a recent release, I'd say "Wait and see, they'll hopefully fix it." Since it isn't, I'll say "Abandon all hope, ye who enter here." Then again, who knows? Maybe you'll be able to dodge all the bugs, glitches and general issues. Do ya feel lucky?

I can't really say I enjoyed this. The first Runner's charm (or even the original Bit.Trip series charm as a whole) was the combination of simplicity and insanity. The art style was simple, the music was simple and enjoyable, the commands were simple and difficulty grew on chaotically (though in a seemingly natural way). Runner 2's mistake is all of this. The art style is fancier, but forgettable; the music is tiringly repetitive (excluding the third world's - Supernature's - themes); the commands try to be unnecessarily a little bit more complicated; and difficulty by level design doesn't make you feel like you're being challenged. Actually, the few more challenging parts are so misplaced that you feel like "finally I beat it, I was getting bored" instead of "hell yeah! I DID it!" Moreover Charles Martinet's narration, albeit short, isn't as brilliant as you'd expect. Also the game fails when it tries to be funny - yep, I'm talking about the costumes and the dance moves.
Overall the game isn't bad. It just feels like just another game you'll forget soon, or worse, like a ripoff of the original Runner instead of its sequel. I definitely can't say I recommend it.
Give it a shot, though, if it has at least a 70% discount. Otherwise, stick to the originals and you'll save some good bucks.
Score: 5/10
Eu não posso dizer que eu gostei de verdade desse jogo. O charme do primeiro Runner (ou mesmo o charme de toda a série Bit.Trip original) era a combinação de simplicidade e insanidade. A arte era simples, a música era simples e agradável, os comandos eram simples e a dificuldade crescia caoticamente (mas de uma maneira que parecia natural). Runner 2 peca em todos estes aspectos. A arte é mais trabalhada, mas é esquecível; a música é cansativamente repetitiva (exceto pelos temas do terceiro mundo, Supernature); os comandos tentam desnecessariamente ser um pouquinho mais complicados; e a dificuldade através do level design não faz com que você se sinta desafiado. Na verdade as poucas partes mais complicadas são tão mal distribuídas que você se sente "até que enfim consegui vencer, já tava de saco cheio" ao invés de "AE ♥♥♥♥♥, CONSEGUI". Além de tudo, a narração do Charles Martinet, mesmo que curta, não é tão brilhante quanto você esperaria. E o jogo fracassa quando tenta ser engraçado - sim, tô falando das fantasias que cada personagem pode usar e das danças.
No geral o jogo não é ruim. Você só sente como se ele fosse mais um jogo qualquer que será esquecido rápido ou, pior, como se ele fosse uma cópia do Runner original ao invés de sua sequência. Eu definitivamente não posso dizer que o recomendo.
Mas experimenta, se for o caso, se ele estiver com tipo uns 70% de desconto. Caso contrário, fique com os originais e você vai ter poupado uma grana boa.
Nota: 5/10

Once on a windswept night looks like a nice little VN, and it is! But it's also a lot more than that. The story has many layers and it is a really interesting experiment with the limits of the VN genre and interactivity within it that's very well integrated within the story of the game.
The writing is really lovely, funny and sharp at some points and highly emotional at others, and gives the characters depth with few words. If you've already played (and liked) games written by this dev, you'll definitely enjoy this ; if not, as a free game, it's a great way to see if you do. It's also a game with several well-written and complex f/f relationships, which is also rare on Steam. The art and music are mostly nice (the music especially), and serve the story well.
If you're intrigued by the summary and presentation of the game, or want to play games that mess with interactivity and metanarration, I definitely recommend trying out Once on a windswept night. It almost definitely will surprise you.

Fun at the first few tiers, but the terrible ship balance and grind wore on me quickly.
The game has newbie deathtraps, like the Kawachi, that are terrible terrible ships compared to everything else. It doesn't help that the game forces you to grind though awful ships to reach the next tier (unless you pay, of course). You can also simply buy better ships. It leaves the impression that some of these ships are intentionally bad to encourage the player to pay money to advance.
I originally wanted to play the aircraft carriers, but I had to slowly grind through multiple battleships first. Why? Not worth it. And would it really hurt the game if it only required 10 or so matches to progress to the next ship, instead of hundreds?
If you do play it, avoid the Kawachi at all costs. It is a low damage battleship, even compared to cruisers of the same tier. Low damage and battleship should be a contradiction! I think I sunk more ships with fires, flooding and ramming than direct hits with its cannons.
I do congratulate the game for its historically accurate ship models and good sound design, but these positives are lost in the sea of questionable business models, balance issues, and slow progression.

Skill aside, some ships are simply better than others.  When it comes down to it, there's not a lot of tactical variety to this game.  Big ships beat small ships.  Carriers beat big ships.  Small ships suck.

Freedom Planet is a fantastic platformer with tight as hell controls and a good difficulty curve to it.  The story, while pretty simple is enjoyable enough.  Just don't expect to much out of it however.  The voice acting is pretty good as well.  There are some points and characters where it could have gone better but other than that it's fairly well done.  I think my biggest complaint with the game however are the boss fights.  The first couple of bosses are fine, but as time goes on it seems that bosses get way to hard out of nowhere.  The normal sections of the game like I said have great difficulty curve but the bosses are a different story.  The biggest problem with this being is that a lot of the later bosses attack rediculously quickly and telegraph their attacks in little to no way.  It begins to boil down to having to memorize their exact attack patterns if any after countless deaths and exploiting your characters I-Frames just to pull through the abrupt damage that comes your way.  If you don't mind difficult boss fights than I guess you could ignore all that and find a wonderful platformer in Freedom Planet
