One-Way Heroics combines turn-based combat, side scrolling arcade style gameplay, limited saves, and a hearty dose of classic RPG nostalgia. It also ranks in difficulty with the likes of Mega-Man, Ninja Gaiden, and Castlevania.
The foundation of Heroics would make it seem like two things that should never go together.
On the left side of the screen, the world fades into a Darkness that consumes men, women, children, small animals, dungeon bosses, buildings, eveything. It is your job to find out what is causing the darkness by travelling to the ends of the earth and defeating the source (oh, and the final boss has finally attained some common sense, and will randomly spawn in an effort to kill you before you get enough power and equipment to wreck his world.) It would start to sound as if it's an infinite runner (akin to Temple Run and Flappy Bird).
And then there are the RPG elements.
Randomly generated worlds, item upgrades, exploration, looting, unlockable perks and classes, the element of permadeath between save points (random enemy drops and treasures will not be the same after continuing from a save file), and the random enemy attributes lead one to question their sanity.
Each playthrough is different. You have the option to create a new random world every time that you start a new game, but you can also play through the same world as different classes.
There are 8 different classes in total, (Only the Knight and Swordmaster are available at the start, but with additional playthroughs, the roster expands with Hunter, Pirate, Bard, Adventurer, Force User, and Hero) with very different play styles. Swordmasters are tough, but it comes at a cost to stamina and carrying capacity. Hunters, however, are better suited to stealth, ranged weapons, and have a special ability that allows them to see off-screen enemies before they encounter them.
All in all, it's got great addictive gameplay, the sprite animations are charming, the music is fantastic.

I wouldn't reccomend paying full price for this game, but if it ever goes on sale, it makes for a fun afternoon.

The re-telling of Ancient Asian mythology and its portrayal of Asian society in the Sixth World in a totally non-stereotypical way makes it all the more interesting. The dark and brooding atmosphere makes for a unique and memorable setting, unlike the Hong Kong one is familiar with in - say - the Wan Chai of Deus Ex or the Kowloon District in Project: Snowblind. The core of the story itself is also a memorable one, and the characters have quirks that make them relatable. Indeed, the best part about the game is the wittiness of the writing. The Matrix runs can be tedious at times but the game's concept and approach to it is nonetheless entertaining. 9/10!

First let me say I play a lot of MMORPGs and am subscribed to three of the largest and play others.  Age of Conan was a game I was excited for when it was released in 2008, as were many of my friends I played other MMOs with.  It was a hopeful challenger to the older and "Gold Standard" of MMOs, World of Warcraft or WoW.  It appeared to be a hit for the first couple of months by the sales and the community, patient as they were for the promised game, hung in for a few more months. Hawever, by the 5th month the game qucikly died off, like several other MMOs that didn't meet expectations of the consumers, leaving only the hopeful fans.
The game in general is lack luster by todays standards.  For a game still trying to get money out of your wallet via micro transactions and subscriptions, Funcom has done little to the graphics engine, combat system, and UI to make it  feel current, fluid, and fun. Play this if you are a fan of the Conan lore and old school RPGs and can adapt to the awkward combat system.
The chief complaints were that the game was buggy and the zones following the starting area felt unfinished and lacked end game content.  Although Funcom has fixed many of these issues over time, the game struggled to produce revenue with a small community.  As a result it was repackaged as a FTP in 2011 (Unchained edition) with a business model that limited your ability to play this game as an MMO if you do not purchase the expansions/subscription packages. This also had problems, much like Rift faces today, with step prices for content and pay-to-win/ pay-to-progress debates.
Funcom has recently removed some, not all, of the pay restrictions for non-subscribers to access content such as zones and instances.  You can purchase game packages including expansions, T1 & T2 gear sets, mounts, loot boxes, consumables, and bonuses via micro transactions. A set of Tier armor will cost you $60 USD while mounts range between $10-20 and expansions will cost just under $20 each.  Subscribers still pay $15 a month and recieve increased XP, loot, and currencies.
Age of Conan offers a unique love/hate combat system.  The combat system is designed so that you can attack and block in multiple dirrections with combos.  However, the system feels unnecessarily complex, slow, and clunky with animations that lack a wow factor.  The combat performs more of what you would expect from a small indie team rather than a triple-A studio supporting a giant MMORPG. And compared to a MMORPG like Black Desert Online (BDO), the combat system is aweful.
You can chose to play in two game settings, PvP and PvE, on three server types, PvE, PvP, and RP.  Player vs Player is enabled when you want to play in the sunlight with other players. On a PvE server, enemy NPCs are in the world to attack rather than actual players. Player vs Enviroment is the night phase and you will not encounter other players as well as have completely different quest lines. This is a open world game however some areas are instanced and the world lacks the size of WoW, ESO, Rift, and BDO.
Age of Conan was a beautiful game when it was released and pushed the boundries of MMOs of the time period. However, by today's standards it is lack luster at best. The game lacks brilliant attack/spell animations leaving you with a feeling of blah when fighting with your character. Some people may not mind this but when combined with the slow awkward feel of the attacks, it is not very satisfying.  While other MMOs have updated the engine, combat, and textures to ncrease the graphical fidelity of the game world to current standards, Funcom has done very little to Conan. Compared to other triple-A MMOs you can play for free like WoW, SWTOR, ESO, Rift, and BDO, Age of Conan is a jewel in the rough and only shines in the story.
The story is set in a great lore based world and this would be the only reason to recommend this game to anyone. The writing is great and interacting with the quests NPCs can be very enjoyable. I found myself laughing several times at the dialog. The voice acting isn't bad, but I wouldn't call it great either. You will encounter a wide range of accents which can aid with immersion and also break it when the large white viking looking barbarian suddenly speaks to you with an East Indian accent.  However, this is by far some of the best dialog I have experienced with NPCs in an MMO.
If you are a fan of the Conan lore and enjoy RPGs, then this may be a game for you provided you can adapt to the awkward combat system.  If not, then there are several other FTP MMORPGs that offer a more enjoyable experience.

8/10 despite 100% positive reviews? Let's help with that.
Once on a Windswept Night (you can see how I'm annoyed by the lack of capitalisation) is a Visual Novel about girls' love, for other girls that is. It's free and small, first and foremost, so it's always going to be a good deal no matter which way you look at it. As with a traditional Visual Novel, there are a few categories to consider:
*Writing: Not the best, though that's a tall bar to pass. Leans a lot on cute and characterisation. The plot itself has quite a few twists and turns in it, however, and greatly emphasises reading between the lines. Subtlety is always appreciated in a piece that appears deceptively straightforward as this. It's decent enough, as good writing is hard to come by. Everything is explained in the end though, so take that as it may. Despite the game's short length, the story is rather dense and not accompanied by much change of scenery, so it can feel tiresome at times to read.
*Characters: A bit one-dimensional at first, but unlocking more endings really portrays the sort of effort which went in here. Everyone has something to hide, and that's good, even those bearing their hearts on their sleeves. There are
characters in this game, and though they regrettably are not all adequately developed, they are at least fairly distinct and relatable in certain ways. That's good, because you wouldn't want to read what they have to say otherwise.
*Art: Quite here and there, has the "no difference but hairstyle" effect. Overall serviceable, but I would've liked to see a lot more full screen art to accompany the non-true endings, especially some much needed love between
. Bonus points for those being subtle too, if that's at all possible.
*Music & Sound: Positive. Nothing too stand out, but fits well with what's happening on screen instead of being just filler.
*Novelty: Quite a bit, especially if you're going through the achievement list (check with the guide if you're interested). There're some serious fourth wall rustling here that made me laugh out loud a few times (your genuine reactions are not guaranteed to be the same), especially as my computer puts itself in a deep sleep in protest.
It was overall not a bad hour of free entertainment, and is clearly made by someone with a real standard of quality in mind. Here's to helping it get that Overwhelmingly Positive rating.

I've changed my mind again. This is the second time I've flip-flopped on my opinion on Jedi Outcast and I don't know if it'll be the last, but I'm going to have to give it a negative recommendation if for no reason other than the fact that it IS so polarizing for me.
The Dark Forces Saga is as a whole a very contrasting series. It's simultaneously some of the best Star Wars games out there and some of the most mismatched, poorly-handled games I've ever played. This might have something to do with the fact that they've changed developers and formats something like three times, but even within the games themselves the quality level wavers wildly between timeless action-adventure classics and incredibly dated, poorly designed claptrap. Dark Forces 2, for example, would be my favorite game in the series if it didn't both handle poorly on modern machines and essentialy set its entire second half in one Imperial base in a desert canyon.
Jedi Outcast, on the other hand, has its own set of problems. While it has some of the best characterization in the series and smoother controls, to say nothing of the graphical improvements, its level design is easily the weakest and somehow every single time I play it the enemies become even more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t than before.
I've played Jedi Outcast all the way through at least twice and done partial playthroughs on at least three additional occasions, and no matter how many times I play I can't seem to get used to how blatantly unfair some of the enemies are. From Gran who can spam an endless stream of grenades in your direction with impeccable aim and seemingly limitless range, to Rodian snipers who can kill you in one or two shots and will tag-team you from three different directions at half a kilometer away, to saber duels that basically boil down to luck, no matter how much you adjust your mindset to the game's tactics, somehow it always turns out to be even worse than that.
As much as I love the series for its galaxy-spanning adventures and lovable - if inconsistently written - protagonist (for whom this game really is the defining basis of his character), and will likely keep coming back to it, continued exposure tells me I can't really in good conscience rate this entry over the others when its flaws permute through most of its runtime, while Dark Forces 2 is easily the superior game if you simply stop playing it at a certain point.

What is it about Jedi Outcast that makes it worth revisiting 13 years on (and counting)?
Its predecessor, Dark Forces II, was the last great Star Wars title to be developed in house by LucasArts, at a time when the studio was just at the peak of its creative powers and not yet in decline.  We might even remember DFII as the best shooter of the 1990s, were it not for a little game by Valve that came out just over a year later in 1998.
Of course, 4.5 years is an eternity in gaming.  By the time Jedi Outcast hit market in 2002, LucasArts' catchet had taken some major hits, thanks to post-Episode I Star Wars titles that were lazy cash grabs at worst (Jedi Power Battles) or disappointing failures at best (*cough*Force Commander*cough*).  Jedi Outcast was developed by a third party, Raven Software, using the Quake III engine; gone are the quirks and charms of the proprietary engines that powered the earlier games in the Dark Forces series.  Moreover, there's a definite emphasis on straight-up action, rather than the vertiginous, puzzle-filled vibe of the first two titles.
So why is this game so much damn fun?
Although JO takes a while to hit the ground running with its blaster-only prologue missions, there's an immensely satisfying payoff once the player begins Jedi training.  If wielding the lightsaber for the first time in JK:DFII was a cool feeling, then in JO it was absolutely mind blowing: there is a level of fluidity, control, and power that is unique to Raven's treatment of the lightsaber here, and it's apparent from the moment you first use it.  One can honestly say, even after all these years, that there has never been an objectively better representation of lightsaber combat in a Star Wars game,
And the Force powers?  While some players will miss JK:DFII's RPG-lite system, which allowed one to invest in some powers instead of others, it has to be said that Raven took an interesting approach here: not only are most of the iconic powers retained (push, pull, jump, speed, choke, lightning, etc.), but the leveling is handled so discreetly that it's hard not to be impressed by how POWERFUL you really are late in the game -- and, wow, is it a treat to take down entire rooms of enemies with nothing but your saber, the Force, and the extremely tight controls you'd expect of a Quake III-powered game.
The story is hardly award winning stuff, but it's conveyed effectively within the gameplay itself.  As a result, JO has a solid momentum that builds in intensity as the game progresses, until the player is continuing on just to see what crazy cool thing they'll get to do next.  (DO, not WATCH; take note, present-day devs.)
Throw in a multiplayer mode that's just about everything you'd want a sabers-and-Force-powers multiplayer experience to be, and there's not much else to say about this game.  Raven might not have made a 1:1 follow-up to the Dark Forces games -- how could they? -- but they more than made up for it by delivering the most exciting Jedi action yet seen in the series, or really any Star Wars title.  I still fire this game up once every several years just to see how it's aged, and each time I'm impressed by how much of a blast it still is.  It's not mere nostalgia at work; it's quality design and honest fun delivered by a talented group of people who set out to capture a very specific kind of action-gaming experience, all while remaining true to the spirit of a classic game series.
If you're a Star Wars fan, or even just a shooter fan looking for something slightly different, this is really one of the most entertaining titles out there.  This game lives up to its pedigree in a big way.

If you're a fan of old style side scrolling games with oldstyle highly detailed pixelated artwork, fast paced action, and intense bosses from games such as Sonic the Hedgehog and Mega Man, then you'll probably love Freedom Planet.
Let me make one thing clear, I have not beaten this game yet at the time of this reviewthing, with any character. However, this game gave me a very refreshing experience because I am a very dead on fan of the old 80s and 90s side scrollers, and this feels just like one. What Freedom Planet has what the old games don't, is very good modern music, very amusing and sometimes very emotional voice acting, and a very engaging story plot that see's quite a bit of branching based on which character you play. Controls are simple, graphics transition smoothly, and this game can easily be ran on even my old potato computer box. So all you with laptops that have trouble running larger games? We got a good package right here.
The only thing that I do NOT like about the game is that some of the bosses are insanely difficult and have made me want to punch something really, really hard. Be prepared to stop playing for a bit, walk away, and drink a glass of water to regain your sanity, because you WILL find yourself thinking very nasty thoughts while fighting some of the bosses.
To those who dislike this game before even playing it because it's "furry based" I have one thing to say. Sonic the Hedgehog is no different (oh god Im going to get a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥for saying this), the only reason why you don't dislike like sonic is because it's been around for a very damn long time, and we've grown used to it. If this game came first and evolved the same way sonic has, and, I'm willing to bet you my australium flamethrower that people would loathe sonic if it was released here in 2014 because it would be a "ripoff of Freedom Planet".

I never really heard of the Kickstarter for this at all, and only heard about it a few days from release. I'd heard talk of a "Sonic fan game" that became it's own thing, but never really looked into it, despite being a huge fan of the older Sonics (some of the new ones are okay, too).  A friend of mine pointed me to this, and I downloaded the demo, and I was hooked. The day the game launched, I was right there at 10 AM when Steam updated to download it.  I expected a fun little game, but what I ended up getting is perhaps one of my favorite games of the year, thus far.
Visually, the game looks like an early sprite-based PS1 or Saturn game, and that's pretty neat. The sprites are detailed, the style is great, but the only gripe is the use of real time rotation. It always looks kind of cheap... why not just do how Sonic did? Then again, Sonic didn't have 3 characters (to begin with), each with attack animations and whatnot, so, whatever. It's a small gripe.
The music in Freedom Planet is spot-on, a fantastic OST. Pretty much every time I heard Brevon's theme, it stuck with me. The main theme itself is fantastic, too.
The story and the acting have caused a bit of conversation, I've been seeing. Personally, while some of the lines are rather.... bad, most of them are fine, and most of the actors themselves do a fine job, stand out characters being Mayor Zao and Carol.  The story itself gets surprisingly dark at times, as well. No real plot twists here, just a straightforward adventure, but it does end mostly satisfyingly.
The three characters play VERY differently, with Lilac being faster, Carol being a tad slower but having more focus on combat, and Milla being a puzzle game of sorts, with her ability to create blocks and such. Milla, unfortunately, doesn't have a story mode yet, and bits of her exclusive content in her Classic Mode stages look unfinished (that Minecart, guys, it looks like something you made in MSPaint).
However, all in all, I stand by what I said. This is right up there with Shovel Knight and Super Meat Boy as perhaps my favorite indie games, if not some of my favorite games, period. To Sonic fans, Freedom Planet is better than Sonic 1 and 2. Perhaps not better than 3&Knuckles, though. That said, though, this does enough to separate itself from Sonic, and I hope we see more in this story.
PS: Lange, if you're reading this, thanks for answering people's questions on that forum. I'm sorry for some people being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, but your honesty was refreshing, amid the PR jungle that most games traverse.

Now...What I was expecting when I saw this and downloaded it was a fun little romp of sonic styled gaming with voice acting with some unique looking twists...What I got...Well ya, was that but ooooh so much more.
The Good!: This game brings everything about 90's gaming together, Elements, of Sonic, Rocket Knight, Megaman X, Mario, Gunstar heros and castlevania and goes even further beyond that to not only blend these elements beautifully, but do it while maintaining it's own identity. The level design is brilliant for the different styles of gameplay with the various characters you can play, having each character able to tackle the level in different ways. It's a fresh feeling being able to blaze a level as Lilac and then play it again as Carol to take a slower but more action and explorative approach...Till you get the motorcycle and just rocket off having a blast. The Music is catchy and beautiful and I don't thing there was a single track I wouldn't just sit down and listen too. When I get a 1up and it plays a jingle, I'm♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at the jingle for cutting off the music cause it's so good...The same doesn't apply for the invinciblity tune, I wish that one would play forever...The last gem to me is the story, something I wasn't expecting to be as good as it was. I enjoyed the character immensely as each felt unique with well fleshed out and likeable personalities...IN A PLATFORMER...Seriously back in the genesis and SNES days, what was Mario's character or personallity? Sonic had more personality, but what was his motivation. The old games were just BAM Here's the level off you go. As this game goes their motivations are done up very well as to why the villan needs to be stopped and the impact it has on the characters and the voice acting, though not the best, is rather engaging and gives it a great charm that further helps establish it's own identity.
The Bad...: The biggest draw back for most and most glaring is gonna be the lenghty cutscenes. If your not expecting it and aren't into long cutscenes it's gonna be a downer for you. They're skippable and if you want to avoid them completely you can play a classic mode to play the game just like the old Sonic and Mario games of yesteryear. Another problem is there's a bit of a difficulty curve when it comes to the later bosses. I breezed throught the first 3 levels or so without a single death but from then on bosses started unleashing heavy damaging attacks and not seeing them for the first time resulted in me unable to react fast enough and taking a ton of damage. It gets pretty bad at the end where the final boss killed me about 30 times before I finally figured out a strategy, but for oldschool gaming, higher difficulty could be a welcom challenge. Lives don't seem to be a big issue as even if you game over, you can continue pretty much where you left off...See dying to final boss 30 times. I continued 3 times and picked up right where I left off, didn't even need to fight the previous forms...So what was the point of lives? The most shocking aspect of the game was how DARK the story got at times, I mean the villan is cold blooded to the point I wonder how the hell this game is rated E...
Over all I adored this game, I expected a quick little game to past by weekend off on and got a Gem I hadn't expected. I highly recommend it for any classic 90's gaming fans, sonic fans, or even just platformer fans.

So after spending a long time playing this game before finally beating it, I really do think this is one of the best indie games out there. If you've ever played an old Sonic game or maybe and old Mega Man X game and liked them, you'll be happy to hear that this game is in a sort of in between place for those games. Its got the exhilerating high speed of Sonic with the action and fights of a Mega Man X game. Gameplay involves running through well designed levels made to complement either Lilac or Carol's (the two characters you can currently play as in Adventure mode) individual unique abilities, all while traveling at high speeds (or taking it slow if you like), fighting awful baddies sent out by Lord Brevon, and enjoying the fun of going through loop-de-loops and running up/down walls. Levels are varied, with them going anywhere from taking place in a sunny mountain to a scientific lab. The game starts off easy (perhaps even a tad bit too easy) but picks up steam as you progresses, all the way to the point to where the game can get extremely difficult (average death amount for the last few levels made its way to over 100 deaths). But even so, there are multiple difficulty settings to change how hard the game will be, so if you don't think you're very good at these sorts of games don't worry.
The game has a nice length and load of content for an indie game (or any game really). While the main adventure mode itself, cutscenes left in, will probably only last around 8 hours if you're playing on a normal difficulty, higher difficulties can drag the game out, and character specific cutscenes depending on what character you play as add replayability. And besides that, there's also a special time attack mode with more levels to play along with the option to play as Milla (another character) rather than Lilac or Carol. Added to that, there's a bonus Mahjong mini game, lots of secrets to find and collect and plenty of achievements to unlock. As of this moment, while its not out yet, it was also stated by the game devs that the game would later allow one to play as the characters Torque and Spade (they're introduced in the adventure mode of the game along with Milla), perhaps with Milla even having her own Adventure mode too, all as free DLC. In the end, the game offers a lot of replayability and should last a really long time. As of right now I've put about 18 hours into the game and I've only scratched the surface (and that DLC isn't even out yet).
The adventure mode of the game has all the levels of the game in it with cutscenes and a storyline attached. If you aren't in it for the story or don't like the cutscenes, you can skip them or play the classic mode of the game (which already features Milla as a playable character, though you may have to unlock her through play. I'm not sure). In doing so however, you might find yourself to be missing out, as the game offers a decent though compelling enough story to keep the player interested. The basic idea is that this evil dude named Brevon has come to take the Kingdom Stone (an item full of energy or electricity or whatever you want to call it) and who else but you will have to stop him. In idea it sounds extremely simple but that's really the tip of the iceberg. The game genuinely has a decent amount of focus on story, with a decent amount of surprises and a couple really shocking moments in this game, most of which are well built in showing just how dangerous Brevon really is. He's no Eggman. He's a man with a plan ready to kill. It even shows in the opening cutscene of the game, as Brevon is extremely brutal. Its done so well in fact that it sets this game apart from other games that have really lame antagonists, or gams that have antagonists that are hatable for all the wrong reasons. Brevon is a genuinely cool, simple yet well built well characterized villain. The story also benifits not only from how well the villain was done, but by the characterization of Lilac, Carol, and even Milla. You grow to care about these characters as the game continues(it helps that some cutscenes exist entirely for characterization), and that makes any story events all the more impactful. Now, while I say this game has a decent emphasis on story, by no means does that bog the gameplay down. At a few moments the cutscenes seem to last a little longer than they should, but overall they rarely overstay their welcome and you have plenty of opportunity to enjoy the gameplay, especially in the later stages when the game cuts down on the cutscenes and the difficulty increases.
Disregarding the gameplay and story, this game has a fine soundtrack, on par with Mega Man X's music. Its also similar in sound, as, just like Mega Man X games, the music doesn't seem to be orchestral (note that this does not hurt the game in the slightest, and actually improves the game). The main theme is catchy and easy to remember (and it appears even when you get temporary invincibility), some boss music (boss track 3 in particular) sound fast paced and action packed, and some of the main stages have some great music to suit the stage at hand. Some of it is dramatic as if something big just happened (one even has a couple lyrics in it, with a person starting the song with "If this is my destiny...There is no turning back"), and others are a tad mellow and are meant to be a bit more relaxing and calm, or perhaps sound more ancient. Other times it sounds like you're going to your doom, especially on the later Final Dreadnaught levels and the Brevon theme. The game comes with the soundtrack in its Steam folder too (in ogg vorbis format), and you'll be able to enjoy it (though the dev has stated that he'll release a higher quality OST with unused tracks later on). Now while we're talking about sound, it might be worth mentioning that while the music is great, the voice acting is all over the place. Some characters have great voice actors and great voices, while others sound like they're overacting or don't know how to act period. This doesn't harm the game too much; most events sound how they need to and the story and meaning behind things aren't hurt by it, but nonetheless it is a problem, which can especially seen with Prince Dail's father's voice in the opening cutscene. The quality of the microphone being spoken into also appears to vary between voice actors, with some sounding incredible and others sounding slightly amateurish, though overall the sound quality itself is all right.
If you'll notice, the game has the graphical style of older games, but despite this it doesn't hurt from it. Sprite art is a dying thing these days and even sprites can be cool to look at, show emotion, and even be endearing, and this game delivers. The game is also full of color, and it winds up being very pretty to look at, much moreso than old Sonic games, so if you're worried they'll look like that you have nothing to fear. The art is great.
So in the end, I REALLY recomend buying this game, especially if you want to support more games like it.

I just finished this game and boy, I'm glad I decided to buy it. It was an interesting experience from start to finish. First of all, let me say that before playing Mafia II, I was expecting a generic GTA clone. I never played the first Mafia game, and I didn't even watch any gameplay before purchase. What I got was not a GTA clone, but rather a story-driven game that tried, at times, to pretend that it was an open-world game. I think that Mafia II definitely could have worked as an open world game, giving the player the opportunity to work for the different families as they progressed through the story. But Mafia II doesn't need to be an open-world experience. It's made something new, and it really works.
Yeah, yeah, I know that during the game the player can drive or walk around the city of Empire Bay at their leisure. The world is open. But the missions are, for the most part, linear. There are no big letters on the map telling the player that they can go talk to their various Italian coworkers. The player completes the objective, then moves straight to the next one.
PROS:
-The characters feel real and alive. The main characters show real emotion. I was most surprised by a moment fairly far into the game, when a certain character who I had marked as one dimensional shocked me by showing a new emotion. This is helped by Mafia II's great voice acting and writing.
-Shooting♥♥♥♥♥♥is fun in this game. It feels great.
-A wide variety of cars from the time period. There are even military vehicles driving around in the earlier parts of the game, seeing as it takes place while America is fighting in World War II. Furthermore, players are rewarded for progressing with shiny new sports cars to drive around. My personal favorite was the Ascot Bailey.
-The music. There isn't a lot of it, but most of it is great. It just adds flavor. If Mafia II was a bigger game, I would complain about the music. But there's just enough to make the radio feel fresh. As the game goes on, newer songs are added, making time progression feel real.
-The story was compelling, and I wanted to keep playing just to find out what happened to the characters. Every mission brought something new to the table while continually convincing me of how fun it was to fill people with bullet holes. As I mentioned before, the cast of characters was varied, interesting, and deep. This served only to help the story grip me as I played through it.
CONS:
-Man the civilians just cannot drive. I wasn't alive during the 40s and the 50s, but was everyone at the time inept at driving? They have one mode. Forward. It just makes for some frustrating situations.
-For how small the world is, there are a lot of cops. They seem to materialize police cruisers out of thin air. While some of the features reguarding police were cool, such as bribing them to leave you alone, their rules were a little wonky. I can drive through as many red lights as I want, but as soon as I hit 41 miles per hour, you're going to write me a ticket? Hm.
-I already covered this a little bit, but other than the story missions, the world was dead. Civilians bustle through the streets and sidewalks, but there isn't anything to interact with. There was one moment where I helped a woman fix her car, and another where I beat the spit out of someone. There are stores, but for the most part they all carry the same merchandise.
Mafia II's gunplay is good, its driving is good (for the most part), and its story is excellent. I highly enjoyed it. If you are a sucker for mafia stories like I am, this game has a little something to do with that. Who knew. Just don't be disappointed when you find out it's not a real open-world game.

A beautiful example of a game made that has everything it needs and more without manipulating its customers into spending ridiculous money. Every map is well crafted with plenty of options for players to use in order to defeat their enemies. The classes are diverse and fun to play. The heroes only mode, Assault on Mos Eisley, is pure fun, allowing you to play as whatever iconic character you wish while clashing with every enemy that character could face. Galactic Conquest mode is brilliant fun, adding the ability to command your armies and attack planets in a turn based system. Lastly, the campaign is simplistic, running you through a series of maps where you complete unique missions such as defending a fuel well on kashykk from the droid army. All while you follow the 501st, the legion of clones who would eventually come to serve as Darth Vader's personal force. I love this game and I hope that more people see this and realize that the only thing stopping a good Star Wars game from being made is greed.

Mafia II is nearly a solid mafia themed open world game, but it's held back by some technical issues and an unsatisfying story.
The Good:
-If you don't want to be chased by the cops you actually have to drive the speed limit and behave somewhat discretely.
-Solid shooting that feels pretty satisfying.
-The tone of the game is pitch-perfect.
-The graphics are pretty good for a game that is five years old.
-The driving feels more realistic than in most games of this type, if a bit unwieldy at times.
The Bad:
-I encountered a game-breaking bug that required me to backtrack an entire chapter. This bug repeated multiple times and I've read about it happening to others.
-The story feels completely unresolved.
-For a game about becoming a mafioso there is really no progression. You start out poor and you end the game poor, despite becoming a made man. There is really no point to accumulating wealth in the world since everything you can buy is either cheap or you can steal it easily.
-The camera can be extremely annoying while driving.
-The game, despite being open world, is entirely story-based and there isn't much to do outside of story progression. There are very few unique NPC faces so the world is laughably one-dimensional.
I got some enjoyment out of the game but I can't recommend it unless it's on sale for under ten dollars.

Walk in a straight line, attack what-ever you want, die. Wash, rinse repeat. That is how the general gist of this game progresses. There isn't a whole lot of depth to the game, there aren't many weapons, aren't many variations of enemies, no characters you really connect with, the map areas are general generic type fanatasy locales, and no real story line (other than to stop The Darkness) which is stated in the opening 3 seconds of the game. However this game has something going for it... charm.
If that sounds silly just run with it for a moment. There is very little to do, or really unlock that can't be done easily. Unlike the game that drew me to this (Faster Than Light) you can unlock everything in nearly 5 hours, the remainder of the time will be playing with these unlocks. However the goofy commentary from the few NPC's you do find are enough to distract momentarily from the humdrum of walking to your right. That is where this game gets its charm from. The constant breaks in the basic mechanics of the game for a fun, light hearted gab between pixelated characters.
Finding all the secret endings and characters endings will be what make you come back to this. The small morsels of charm that you get are what will make you enjoy coming back to it. However, don't expect to be able to play this for long periods of time. I found that the game is best when played a few run throughs at a time. Any longer than that and the charm kinda wears off and the simplistic nature of the game robs from its potential.
Additional peripheries were pretty decent as well. The music is fun to listen to but after prolonged time periods begins to grate at your ears. The graphics are simple enough and give it a classic RPG feel that allows me to relive the days of early Final Fantasy's. Mechanics are simple and will be picked up with one minute of playing.

One Way Heroics is an auto-scrolling rogue-like. As you move about and act in the game, the screen will slowly moves to the right - and should it reach your character it will devour you in darkness.....
The goal of the game is essentially all about keeping ahead of the encroaching darkness as you travel across various lands. You get stronger, collecting items and leveling up, stop in settlements (before they can consumed by darkness) and eventually you will battle across the lands against the Demon Lord behind it all!

I would consider this game the peak of the Sonic franchise. As with every Sonic game since Adventure, there is some relatively boring content you'll have to slog through. But the other half of the game is absolutely fantastic and well worth the full price of the game. Classic Sonic doesn't quite capture the essence of the Genesis games and has physics that don't make for great platforming, but it's inoffensive and just boring at worst. The modern Sonic stages, however, have some of the best design in the entire franchise. The stages are multi-layered and reward quick decision making and have great replay value if you want to cut down on completion times or get the collectibles and complete the missions. After almost 20 years of trying to get fast platforming working in a 3D space, this is the only game that does it and remains fun from beginning to end.
The modding scene for this game is pretty good as well. I would recommend the improved FxPipeline renderer (it adds nice rendering effects from Unleashed but disables anti-aliasing, although you can fix that with DSR/downscaling) and Unleashed Project, which ports over the fantastic daytime stages from Unleashed.

How do you define a good Sonic game?
The series was struggling with the right answer for this question. The Sonic Generations attempt was one of the last possible calls for SEGA to do things right and... they succeeded! This game single-handedly revived the franchise for me and gave me the kick to check out the old classics for the first time (I'm the Dreamcast Kid). This game is really this good!
Imagine that the famous band tries to set up "The Best of..." album. They take one song from each previous album. Some of those releases were horrible and you think: "Remaking this track is a bad idea! This was a dark age for this band!". You are relieved when you notice that the "that one" dreaded song sounds so new and fresh! Even more... you notice that every song has one version for the original vocalist and second for the new one that came into band recently. This is Sonic Generations in nutshell. They took a level from every single game in the main series and remade them to fit for both: the old and cute Classic Sonic with 2D gameplay and the Modern Sonic with the boost mechanic. Fear Sonic '06 no more! Crisis City in this game better than ever! And you can cure your PTSD from the Silver boss fight here! Don't like him? IT'S NO USE! He will suffer and you will be satisfied!
I think that the good Sonic game is the one with the good controls and clever level design. While the controls of the Modern Sonic aren't still at the level of Sonic Adventure's one they are acceptable. Classic Sonic rolls and hops nearly just like in the Genesis era, only with few inconsistencies.
The level design in this game is near GORGEOUS. They look extremely well and they are designed around the idea of the multiple paths in the single level. There is still one start point and one goal post, but there are many routes for the run through the stage. The exploration is highly rewarded by the Red Star Rings that are layed on the different pathways in the level. You may find yourself replaying the level multiple times to finally reach the highest, fastest and the most skillful route. Even when Modern Sonic still has the Boost Button, the levels have much more platforming this time around and it is not bad implemented. This level design single handedly makes up for the all replayability of the game - just look at my playtime.
The graphics are... oh my... they are outstanding. The Surreal Realism fits the series like a glove. There are pretty water effects, plants and locations and yet still the game have a incredible, cartoony artstyle. Unfortunely, this game really needs a good computer to run smoothly, but if you have a nice power PC, 60 FPS in this game and the art style will make you laugh on the nice visually but weak artistically games like Crysis.

Soundtrack of this game is a pack of music all well known to the fans of the series handled with the nice remixes. "Escape from the City"? "Live and Learn"? Crisis City Stage music? Chemical Plant? Awesome disco remix for the "Classic" Speed Highway? Do want!
Controller is a must here... Sorry keyboard-exclusive guys. Story is kinda weak too. Don't buy this game for the SA2-like story. You won't find it here. The nods to the previous games are fun, but the writing and plot is nearly non-existent. The online mode is very buggy and may crash your game when you are attempting to unlock the achievement. Final boss fight is not well designed and Side-missions are hit or miss, but still, I was happily to finish this game on 100%. 4 times.
This is a extremely solid 3D platformer. This is one of the few Sonic games that I would easly recommend to the people who are not fond with the series yet. This is really a high note in the franchise and you are really missing out if you put a fold on it. It is definitely not perfect with various bugs, weak story and the short playthrough, but the replayability, level design and the presentation is top notch.
Side note: kids REALLY like this game! Tested on several individuals during the babysitting. It may be too hard for the less skilled, but with supervising parent this will be a really good time!

Company of Heroes 2. Oh, how I looked forward to purchasing this! I had played, on disk, the Opposing Fronts standalone expansion from CoH1 and I adore it.
If that was such a great addition to a great game, who had the bright idea at Relic to take one step forward and then one step back? Now... Bare with me here. This is a review, not a bash, so let me explain, and don't worry. There is a TL:DR at the end, but I assure you the body of this review is more in-depth.
I only ever had the chance to play Opposing Fronts, but that alone was outstanding. There was diversity in the play-styles between Germany and Britain, and even more so with the different 'focus trees' you could go down, which there were three of and who had 7 unlockable abilities and perks within each (if memory serves me correctly. It could have been 5), really allowing you to explore a lot of different options in approaching a task.
To add to it, the cutscenes were a joy to watch. Even if you ignored the story, the cutscenes would pull away into actual gameplay, seemlessly. This was genius for immersion and made me feel a lot closer to the beginning of the action. Durring gameplay, even, everything was satusfying. The tanks felt like butter when you hit them and felt like rock when you bounced-- The ragdolls were all over the place, and were almost fascinating to watch, halftracks displayed the men inside the actual truck based on how many men you put in, and so on.
Why, then, would you take this all away?? In CoH2, you have cutscenes and ragdolls and tanks-- but none of the fun or feeling to them. Ragdolls are sometimes replaced with death animations, the bodies are still stiff after being blown to peices (which can't happen, really), and the tanks feel hard and not very satusfying to destroy in comparison to the CoH1 tanks. The cutscenes, too, look just like the ones from CoH1, but they ruin the immersion, I feel, with removing what made the CoH1 cutscenes special, being in-game rather than played over the game.
Of course, I understand these points are nitpicking at best, but what really dissapointed me was the lack of any and all focus trees. You have command points, but what is the point of racking up 32 in any given battle without anything to spend them on? You've already unlocked the three to five abilites you can use, and command points sit to collect dust. With that, teams are really only ever given one way to play, and for the Russians, that's conscript spam. I mean, who values human life, amirite? but seriously, it takes away the ability to taylor your own play-style.
Perhaps I've squabbled a bit too much for now. There is a lot of good to the game. Especially upon purchasing the Ardennes Assault expansion, which is just worth the price of admission for what it brings. The expansion does wonders with playstyle customisation through unit skill trees in between missions, the ability to choose a roster of your choosing being three divisions you want to fight with, and an active battle map, where you usher your units through to an objective, moving battle-lines and so on. This sort of action is what the vanilla serise needs, really. There's also this really interesting, intuitive and fresh concept with freezing to death. While I don't feel it was utilized to its full potential, being relegated to two missions each campaign if that, it certainly has an exciting future in the workshop, and if I can find out how, I'd like to build a map centered around an assault in a blizard.
However, I was very dissapointed in Fox Company. Fox Company is a DLC, locked off for a whole five dollars, and all of the annoying purchases that nickle-and-dime you really feel like a sham, and kind of buffeted my enjoyment of the game, feeling like a peice of the game had been taken from me for the money I paid for it, and left a sour taste in my mouth.
The stories are a what you'd expect, and the gameplay isn't too different-- perhaps just a tad more stale that the original game, but it isn't by any means "bad".
-TL;DR-
In short, the game isn't bad, but the profuse amounts of DLC left a bad taste in my mouth, and they sort of traded off with innovation with the Ardennes assault capaign (which has to be bought alongside the base game if you want to play it), but a few noteable advances and neat ideas are found in the base game, as well.
In comparison to the first Company of Heroes, number 2 is a bit number 2, but if you're content with more CoH, a few locked squads and a whole other capaign taunting you from the other side of the fence, I would buy this game on sale. I still got pleanty of enjoyment out of it, and the workshop really does make me happy.
So if it's on sale and you want the game, go ahead! Otherwise, I'd say stick with CoH1: Opposing Fronts.

Do you have to pay for commanders? Yes, you do. Sometimes. AND they forgot to mention the currency you pay in.
Every 4 to 6 games (Depending on whether you win or lose those), you get a free loot crate that can contain anything from skins over commanders to upgrades or currency.
Looking at that, plenty of luck or time will get you what you want - for free. And you seem to always get loot for the faction you played as for the last few points before the crate.
You read that right up there: You can obtain currency through those crates. I wonder what that currency could be used for... but surely not for making purchases with real money optional, right? *Kappaface*
It is possible to buy commanders with currency or actual money, while upgrades and victory strikes are only available through said currency.
In other words: You can get any item you desire just by playing the game.
But why is THEIR greed in their way?
That is because the impatient kind of player strives to unlock anything instantly. This kind of player will tell you you have to pay real money because you have to, most likely, actually do that in order to obtain items THEIR way. The way that won´t shy from costs in order to be the fastest possible.
It is, however, NOT NECESSARY TO PAY REAL MONEY FOR EXTRA CONTENT FOR YOUR FACTION. You will, sooner or later, get either the stuff you want or plenty of currency to buy it.
Saying there was no way to progress without expenses might be true in war, but in terms of items, simply playing your faction of choice will get you what you want.

Shadowrun is a world where it is as literally magical as it is unfair. Dragons and Megacorporations control everything, including the government. The tititularly named Shadowrunners do crime jobs for anyone with money, fighting with guns and fists and magic for the highest bidder. Unless they choose not to, because successful ones have that luxury.
Hong Kong is the third game in this format, and improves cybernetics and hacking from the previous game, Dragonfall. Pretty much all trees feel reasonably effective at this point, and all allow for you to become a ridiculous powerhouse.
One of the best RPGs in recent years, only arguably beaten by its predecessor Dragonfall. Get both, ignore the mainstream chaff like Pillars of Eternity.

Good game.  Refinement of what was in Returns and Dragonfall, with an extended post-ending extra bonus campaign to finish up the Hong Kong storyline.  When you pick up items, you can give them to anyone in your party (a pet peeve of mine  in Drangfall, where you could only give items to the main character only), matrix sections are now a mix of stealth and rhythm / puzzle based hacking in addition to just plain combat, and you can start combat manually instead of having to run into enemies to start combat.
Mechanically, everything's much better, and the storyline is still good.  I liked it better than Dragonfall personally, and liked how it didn't get bogged down in endless combat like Dragonfall, especially near the endgame.  There is a lot of fighting yes, but it doesn't feel as much of a grind.

This is the second visual novel by Ebi-hime that I've read and enjoyed. The whole experience is crafted in an unusual but compelling way, by telling a story within a story. You and your mysterious companion delve into a book to unravel all of its mysteries, which shifts your perspective to one of the characters inside the book. Multiple routes exist, and these are integrated in an immersive way with commentary from your companion after each route's completion, followed by the suggestion to start from the beginning or turn back the pages. Even quitting the game is charming - it's described as
, and your companion welcomes you back once the game reloads.
Besides the intriguing experimentation with the VN medium and extra immersion that adds, it's a fine story, with characters that have distinct personalities, a dramatic reveal, and a true ending that was uplifting after all of the sorrow and difficulties along the way. It's a testament to the power of love, but also the power of self-doubt and the inability to trust and take risks for your own happiness. Furthermore, Ebi-hime's writing is suited to dialogue, and she excels particularly at making character interactions sound natural and bringing those characters to life without resorting to needless exposition. Exploring the darker, more vulnerable parts of the human heart and mind is done quite well.
I have two criticisms, but these are minor and do not detract much from the experience. Firstly, there are two characters that serve as substantial parts of the plot, but a conclusion for them isn't reached. They have their own dilemmas which could have been explored more thoroughly during the story, and so there is untapped potential. Secondly, advancing the plot past a certain point hinges on a very specific set of choices, which eluded me for longer than I expected and required too much backtracking. For anyone who's coming into this fresh, use the CTRL key to skip text you've previously seen!
Altogether, this is a real treat that is being given for free. It's more than worth the few hours to complete.

Having experienced other titles from this developer, one could argue that its not unusual to be presented with something that is completely unexpected. While this is true in the case of this visual novel, it goes far beyond that. I'm not sure I've ever experienced anything quite like it. I do not write many reviews, but given the absence of any other reviews at this point, I felt the need to make sure people did not pass up this story for lack of feedback to gauge their interest. If you were unsure about whether or not to give this story a chance, heed my advice and purchase it immediately. The price is right, although it feels criminal to have this game without being asked to pay a dime.
There are many paths to take, and each adds to the overall story. Or rather, each path is a story within a story. What’s stunning about this novel is that it is an interwoven story of stories, and each attempt to find new paths reveals more and more of that story. This probably sounds confusing, but it will make sense as you begin to progress through the novel.
As I mentioned before, there are elements of this visual novel which I have never experienced before. There is no title screen, it is instant immersion. Certain choices made make it simply close. When you relaunch, it welcomes you back. There was even a choice made which caused the novel to refuse to let you back in unless you agreed to wipe the slate clean and start from nothing [no more skipping/sub paths seem to be locked again/save file is gone.].
This has been a very deep and thought provoking visual novel. Do not let the label of "Yuri" convince you this is nothing but an erotic frolic between some shallow/ditzy female anime characters. Each character encountered has been complex, and more importantly, damaged. It’s this damage which has served as an element to bring substance to the plotline. You empathize with them and wish to know more. The "best" ending is completely heart warming and you'll probably find yourself shedding a few tears.
There are some bugs which make it possible to get stuck if you do not pay attention [See Discussion tab for my thread], but this is a release day review, so I hope to see updates made in the future, as no release is ever bugfree on day one.  Some of the achievements are a bit strange as well. Some depend on knowledge of the developers other stories, while others are left to pure chance. Despite that, I still give this a 10/10 rating. I'll definitely come back to this VN for a replay in the future.

Up to level 4 (IV) ships, the game is fun, and you feel like you accomplish alot.
Once you get that IV level ship, you have to decide if you want to start really grinding.
The problem, is the difference between a level IV ship player and a level V (5) player is that a players will get put into games with High Level V all the way to low level IV or even III.
If you are a III or a IV and come up against a level V player, you are toast.
They can snipe you from distances that you can't even detect them from, and if they hit your ship, 80% or more of your HP are gone in an instant.
If you want to grind past IV, be prepared to run away from level V ships a lot or get extremely frustrated.
If you are okay with grinding like a mother after level 4, then go for it.
However, don't be surprised to find all the enjoyment and sense of accomplishment you were getting before to vanish once you hit level 4 ships.
One thing to consider, is this game is always being adjusted and tweaked.
For example, before the last patch, a Destroyer (DD), basically a fast but weak ship with torpedoes, could reliably fire off a salvo of torpedoes at the AI with about a 70 to 50% chance of at least 1 or 2 of the torpedoes hitting the ship if you played correctly, however, the AI now seems to have a 6th sense and immediatly knows when you launch torpedoes at them and can counter them.
I have recorded two instances where I was less than 100 feet (30 yards) from a ship, broadside, launched torpedoes and they magically where able to twist their ship to miss evey single torpedo lanuched (I had launched six in two sets of spreads)
So, you need to understand what worked good for you this week, might not work at all next time you log on.
Not so much an issue on lower tiers, but when they expect grinding and even money from you at higher levels, that shouldn't be a thing.
Now, this isn't really an issue in PVP, as the players lucky don't have AI subroutines that cheat, but the AI is clearly cheating to a point after the latest patches (Mid-Dec 2017)

Mix together Sonic+Megaman X+Sparkster/Rocket Knight+Pulseman heck, a bit of Chip and Dale with Millia (one of the three characters in this game) and some of Treasure's magic together and you have a heck of a crazy game here. This game feels like the devs heisted people from the Saturn era to bring a game that not only looks but feels like an old school platformer.
That's not to say it's like other games claiming 'retro', no this one actually has the feel, the characters have the ol' Genesis/Playstation/Saturn era weight/ feel of 2D platformers. No havok physics engine just whatever the heck made them feel like they did.
Fun levels, awesome music, cheesy cutscenes and gimmicks that don't require obscure hardware to make fun. Took around 3 hours to beat the first time through (took my time, was enjoying the game) and there's 2 other characters to beat it with. Lots of different routes to go with this game and replayablilty to bring you back.
Speaking of the characters, all 3 of them play differently.
Lilac runs, jumps, kicks, has a double jump that acts as a spin attack lasting till she hits the ground, she can uppercut or kick down (which can speed you up if you do it down hill).  Then her her dragon dash which spins her up and fires her off in a direction Rocket Knight style where she'll bounce off walls and smash enemies which relies on her power gauge.
The gauge very quickly (5 seconds maybe?) making her very mobile.
The other Carol, is able to wall hop Megaman X style, claw around a bunch and ride a bloody motorcycle that does spin jumps like Sonic, can drive it up walls and up ladders and ...it's so cheesy and damn fun becase of it. The motorcycle is a powerup and can be lost and regained by gas tanks laying about.
So I got to play as the third character, Milla. She's very different in terms of gameplay  she floats like Yoshi, throws blocks Chip-N-Dale style and can form shields to bounce enemy attacks or even turn her block into a big short ranged beam. She's the only character so far who does not use a special bar and it's fun. Her boss fights are also drastically different since you're not as agile or offensively able.
The game clearly has a LOT of effort behind it, there's a lot of detail put into the game like holding a button to access bloopers while the story is playing out. Dancing around disco balls while fun music plays. My favorite: while in some boss fights your friends will come in to help you fight, Carol leaping in on her motorcycle to kick the boss and Milla straight up dropping health from a plane. It's really charming to see all this in action.
If you're going to blow off this game because it looks like a Sonic ripoff you're missing out because that's not what the game is.

This is a game that I've been hearing about for the past 2 years, and now that it is finally released, I've decided to play it to see if it is worth the hype. Short answer: Yes, Yes, A Million times YES!. Long Answer: A platformer with excellent music that is not only ambient but catchy as well, fantastic visuals, a great story that is VERY well voice acted, intricate boss fights, and solid gameplay. It seem to be a hybrid of the obvious (*cough* Sonic the Hedgehog *cough*) and the playstation Mega Man games (namely Mega Man 8 and X4) and a touch of Rocket Knight. The game feels like an old Playstation/Sega Saturn game (whether or not that was intentional, I have no idea), and that is something that "retro inspired" games don't really try to emulate. Often they try to be 8-Bit like the NES or 16-Bit like the Genesis/Mega Drive, and it is nice to see a retro inspired game try something different. However, this game also does it's own things and isn't just your average "Nostalgia" fueled game. It has plenty of originallity and charm to be it's own game. Overall, this is an absolutely fantastic game that is worth every penny! I highly recommend it!

Do you have a fondness for traditional Genesis platformers, such as Sonic and Gunstar Heroes? Do you miss games that were actually difficult, and required you to anticipate boss patterns to succeed?
If so, look no further than Freedom Planet, a game that through it's use of traditional gameplay, manages to remain engauging in a modern market because it's simply unlike anything released in the last decade.
The gameplay mechanics of the levels are remanicent of traditional Sonic games (loops, fast speeds, etc) with combat mixed in (you have to physically attack enemies to stop them, not just jump towards them). Bosses on the other hand, are inspired by other Sega greats, such as the previously named Gunstar Heores. What may appear cheap or unfair at first, unfurls into a intricate set of moves to anticipate and counteract as the game continues. No boss in unbeatable, and forthought as well as planning can go a long ways in boss fights.
The story, while melodramatic at times, rings true with the time period the game mechanics reflect. I can easily see the cutscenes being the "Freedom Planet Saturday Morning Cartoon" while the gameplay being the game tied to the same franchise.
Taking Freedom Planet as what it is, a love letter to the games and cartoons of the 90s, it is FANTASTIC.
If you have any fondness or those times, or want a more modern take on traditional formulas, Freedom Planet is WELL worth your time.
All the nostalgia and still fun after all these years!

One Way Heroics is a surprisingly good roguelike.
The gameplay is pretty straightforward: whenever you move, every monster on the map moves as well. You attack monster by running into them, and your stats determine how much damage you do, and how much damage they do to you.
This is pretty standard for a roguelike, but One Way adds in a twist: every time you move, the screen moves a little to the right. If you get caught on the left edge of the screen, you die, so you always need to keep moving forward. Not only this add to the difficulty, it also ensures that every run moves at a good pace: there's no time to loot or backtrack when everything in the world is disappearing on the left side of the screen.
One Way Heroics uses permadeath, so if you die, it’s game over. Fortunately, a successful run in the default mode only takes about 20 minutes to complete, so even if you die right at the end, you (usually) don't feel like you've lost a lot of time. You also have the option to keep a few pieces of equipment from previous runs, so if you die right after finding a great piece of equipment, you can carry it over to the next game. The difficulty is also balanced very well. I was able to beat the game after only two or three attempts at the easiest difficulty, but there are several difficulty levels above that, with each one being significantly harder than the last.
Overall, One Way Heroics is a solid game. The different difficulty levels offer challenges to players of all skill levels, and the randomly generated worlds keep every run feeling fresh. I’d recommend this game to fans of roguelikes and roguelites at any price, but especially if you can grab it on sale.

There's also quite a bit more story than you'd expect from the game's description; each recruitable party member has their own backstory they'll slowly share as you progress through a run with them, and each has their own unique ending (and a few have more than one). As you do more things and undertake harder runs, you'll also learn more about the world, such as the true nature of the Darkness enveloping everything, and even how it affects the land after it has done so. Resultingly, there's even more endings based on how you go about stopping the Darkness, and generally, the more difficult of a run you complete, the better the endings you get tend to be, ranging from "We stopped the Darkness... but at what cost, and what's really going on?" up to
.
It can be fairly hard to "win" a run early on, though it won't be long before you've polished your skills and learned enough tricks that the Demon Lord isn't terribly hard to defeat. If you're having trouble, I've found that the easiest difficulty isn't always the easiest place to get your first victory, as unlike other difficulties, you can't just run from the Demon Lord if things aren't going well. Unlocking more perks and classes also helps a lot, and one of the easiest builds is available early on. (If you feel you need the help, it's:
)
The One Way Heroics Plus DLC is along the lines of an expansion pack; adding more classes, perks, party memebers, items, more challenging runs, and essentially just more of everything, like any good expansion pack should. As stated earlier, it's also the only time the game's creator earns money from the game, as the Japanese version of the base game is actually free, and the price for it on Steam only exists to pay the translators (who have done a very fine job, by the way. I've yet to find any issues in the game's translation). Eventually, when the game became really popular, the creator added the paid One Way Heroics expanion, both to update the game and to have a way to earn money off his creation. So I strongly recommend buying the OWH+ DLC, even if you haven't played before. Even with the added cost, the game's still an incredible value; almost criminally so when it's on sale.
All in all, the game is a hidden gem that's far better than the price point would suggest. As cheap as it is, there's no go reason not to grab it, and makes a great choice for using that last bit of cash in your Steam Wallet, or funds you've gotten from selling trading cards from other games.

A Sonic fan gets Sonic Generations. What happens?
MIND BLOW.
Sonic Generations is a fantastic addition to the Sonic franchise. From the nostalgic setting of Green Hill Zone, to the bright and fresh Rooftop Run, I was hooked.
Classic Sonic feels much like he did in the old days of the Genesis. He runs, he spins, you get the drill.
Modern Sonic is the same as in Sonic Unleashed, but with a few tweaks to improve his control. His boost is no longer necessary for certain parts, meaning players who didn't like the boost gameplay can go back to Sonic Adventure style gameplay.
The stages are a ton of fun to rush through, but they're also fun to explore. Often, if you speed through the level, you'll miss some secrets and easter eggs. City Escape is one such case. If you don't slow down, you'll miss tons of throwbacks to older titles.
The graphics are INCREDIBLE. Often times, the graphics are the best I've seeen on a PC.
So the game is a masterpiece, and you should get. The end, right?
No.
Sadly, Sonic Generations has its fair share of issues.
Towards the end of your adventure, three obstacles will arise.
Planet Wisp, Egg Dragoon, and (SPOILERS) the Time Eater.
Planet Wisp is a mess. Not only is it 95% bland factory, but it's INCREDIBLY LONG. New players will most likely spend 7-10 minutes in this place.
Egg Dragoon suffers from the length as well. The boss drags on for while, eventually succumbing to the constant homing attacks you've been spamming for the past 8 minutes. God help you if you play it on hard mode.
*SPOILERS*
The Time Eater is a boss that ALSO suffers in length. Maybe that was Eggman's plan: to bore you to death. Sadly, not only is this fight long, it's completely one-sided. Often times, you'll be RIGHT infront of him, about to land a hit, when he desides to jump fifty feet back!! Oh, and those, "helpful" friend of yours? Get used to the saying, "It looks like a homing missle!! Be carful, Sonic!!"
Thankfully, those are all the problems I had with this game.
Sonic Generations is a wonderful platformer for gamers old and new. It offers a bunch of new things to keep the expierience fresh, while also borrowing just enough ideas from Sonic's past to make the ultimate Sonic tribute. If you haven't already, do yourself a favor, and BUY IT!!

Do you like fighting games?
This isn't one.
Sure, two players enter an arena and attempt to beat the crap out of each other, best 2 out of 3 wins.
If that's the only way you define fighting game, then go ahead and call it one.
BUT
Blade Symphony is lacking in the depth present in a game like Skullgirls or Street Fighter. It's less about knowing what your opponent will try and more about exploiting the game itself to gain an advantage.
The third person over-the-should view obfusicates much of your ability to gauge the actual range of your own attacks, as well as those of your opponent. Hit detection is often quite spotty. Which results in awkward advances followed by swinging wildly while backing up. Hit and run tactics are the way this game is played for the most part.
Blade Symphony lacks the consistency of fighting games too. Frame rates aren't consistent, so good luck trying to gracefully and skillfully link sword attacks into one another.
What you'll really end up doing is clicking and wildly swinging your camera around to manipulate your attack's path and speed.
It doesn't have the careful balance of fighting games, either.
The project's leader, Flux, set out to initially balance the attacks each character possesses using a very simple method.
He played against the "knight" character, who for the purpose of this process used only his slowest, strongest attack. Clicking over and over, using only this attack, Flux then played each character and gave them tools to counter or get around this attack.
Then he was done balancing. The characters were done being iterated on, for the most part.
The dev team tweaks the numbers, at this point - sword swing speeds, damage values etc, but the ongoing balance meetings really only involve Flux asking the "top players" (read: most popular/vocal at the top of the leaderboard) what should be done. And of course, you can imagine the clamoring for the weakening of characters that they have trouble with, and the buffing of their mains. To be fair, it's not really the player's fault - it's natural and unavoidable to be biased in your own favor, no matter how impartial you think you are. The blame lies with the devs for outsourcing it's finer balance decisions to the most highly competetive players.
Several characters have attacks that are so fast, they actually exceed the game's ability to display and often detect. Which can have wildly inconsistent results.
This game plays more like a third person action game, or an extremely bare-bones character action game.
That's multiplayer only. Very little realism to be had, with characters defying physics with certain attacks, outlandish Errol Flynn techniques, and in some cases outright flying.
If you can look past some very bizzare balancing philosophies (ie none at all) and don't expect to play more than one character (ie the one everyone at the top of the leaderboard plays) then you might enjoy this as a unique competetive experience. But all I can see is a whole lot of potential wasted by poor decisionmaking and direction.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong is one step forward, two steps back for the Shadowrun Returns games, but it's still a long way from being a bad game, it's simply a step down from its older brother Dragonfall.
On paper, Hong Kong is excellent, sporting improved graphics and redesigned aesthetics, as well as new music and more gameplay features. In execution, it suffers from performance issues ranging from slower response from the environment (and your party members pathfinding) to much, much longer load times, as well as a decline from the top-notch writing quality present in Dragonfall and Dead Man's Switch. There is also a change to the way the Matrix works, which I have no opinion on. It's not bad, but it's nothing to write home about either.
The story itself has very few issues, being filled with plenty of magical corporate and criminal conspiracy, barring the backstory forced onto your character which put me off early on. Though I did get used to it, the nagging feeling of disconnection I had from the character I'd envisioned at creation and what was forced into my lap after the first mission never quite went away. The issue comes from the bloated amount of text that fills each conversation, which are just as numerous as in previous games. The problem doesn't come from the amount of text, but how it's broken up. In Dragonfall, conversations felt like conversations, with plenty of back and forth between your character and those you conversed with, leading to incredibly digestible 'page-turners' that kept you invested. In Hong Kong, you're forced to deal with incredibly long dumps of narration or exposition all at once from characters in a stilted, unnatural manner. There is also less action relative to the dialogue, making this bloat of text even more noticeable.
The runs themselves are also not nearly as memorable or intricate as those found in Dragonfall, with nothing like the Mark VI or Humanis runs to stick out in your mind long after completion. Coupling this with the shorter length, and the ending feels incredibly abrupt.
The characters are also not quite as memorable or interesting as the squad in Dragonfall, though certainly leaps and bounds ahead of the likes of Coyote or Sam Watts. Is0bel, Duncan and Gobbet are no Dietrich, Eiger or Glory, though Rachter and Gaichu are very, very deep and complex individuals, playing with existing tropes and conventions that you'd expect from the philosophical mad-scientist or the honor-bound warrior types. This is, of course, subjective, and I certainly didn't hate them nor did I not care about them.
The villains, however, do not stand nearly as strong as Dragonfall's nearly perfect antagonists. Though extremely interesting conceptually, they remain uninvolved with the plot for the entire game while you simply waste time on runs, and by the time endgame hits, it's difficult to care. It feels like wasted potential, as they are certainly interesting in theory, but in execution fall short.
Hong Kong is incredibly disappointing when it really shouldn't have been. Perhaps it was a change in writing staff, or perhaps the team was simply overambitious after their previous success. I certainly hope they compare what did and did not work in both Hong Kong and Dragonfall for their next endeavor, because there are certainly enough good ideas to create a game that surpasses both.
