i'm sorry, devs, but...
Management summary: nicely done but tedious to work through because there's too much talking and not enough skirmishing.
Yes, i played it all the way through. Yes, i mostly enjoyed it. But... despite the changes and improvements from the first two in the series, two major problems make Hong Kong the black sheep of the three:
1) the load times between levels are so long that i often walk away or switch windows while waiting, and then forget that it was running at all. At least an hour, possibly two, of the time Steam recorded was a loading screen (either me waiting on it or having forgotten about it). The load times range anywhere from 30 seconds (which is bearable) to 2 minutes or more.
2) My gawd, the text! i felt like a good 80%+ of the time in the game was reading the tremendously long, way-too-frequent dialogs. i felt like i was reading a choose-your-own-adventure novel, rather than playing an adventure game. There were lots of interesting, sometimes difficult, choices to make burried in those dialogs, but a large percentage of the dialogs just add color, rather than carry the story along, and i got rather sick of reading them. "Oh, no, not _another_ talky sequence!"
Both of those are, for me, tremendously distracting. The first one rudely pulls me out of the game and the second one makes the game feel like a book. (Not that i'm against reading - i've read at least 10 novels in the past 3 months - but that's not what i play Shadowrun to do!) Yes, one could argue that more text provides more background and more color, and one would be correct. But more text is most certainly not what i want in a tactical adventure game. If the conversations had been a good 50% shorter, and possibly less frequent, i'd have been happy. i.e. it needs more combat scenes and less talking.
In short: i dislike SHK because i play the Shadowrun series for the tactical combat. This episode in that series seems somewhat lacking, compared to its predecessors, in that regard. The combat itself is just as good, if not better, there's just less of it. (Tip: the auto-reloader cybernetic upgrade may seem overpriced, but it's worth its weight in gold when paired with a grenade launcher!)
Other than that, it's remarkably good. While i would play the first two in the series a second time, i could not stomach doing so with this one.
Depending really on how much one likes to read, this game may or may not be worth playing. Other than text-centric software (e.g. Fighting Fantasy Combat books), Shadowrun Hong Kong easily has the most text of any game i've played, and a correspondingly large amount of game time is required to navigate through dialogs.
If you decide to try it out, be prepared to put your reading glasses on.

It is a great game, very engaging and fun to play. I really cant find a major negative fact about it. It is one of the few strategy games that is balanced, relatively realistic and most importantly fun to play.
The only minor negatives I find is some payable commanders (the comanders have some special abillities and sometimes a vehicle), skins and stuff but all these can be purchased with in game money you earn when you play so its not that important. Some people say its unbalanced but i dont belive that because every faction (there are 5 factions Wehrmacht, Red Army, US forces.The British and OKW, another german faction, I think they are sold in a DLC) is good at something and every tactic/weapon can be faced.
On the other hand, the game has many positive features. It has a good campaign, coop campaign where you can play with friends on BOTH GERMAN AND RUSSIAN side, which is relatively rare, multiplayer battles up to 4v4 with many maps to choose from (including community maps), a normal player base (5k-10k usually), historical accuracy, realistic values (penetration of tanks, weapons etc.) and many available tactics and to lead you to victory !
I would definately recommend this to anyone, especially to those who want realism, historical accuracy and for those who like many strategies. This game has something for every (WW2) strategy player.

If it's not their choice of preferred control scheme, I understand, but still would expect some option to change it like in every PC game since the 2000.
This made the game unplayable to me, so if you have the same problems with hard-locked keys and limited camera level(restricted to what feels like 20 meters above the ground) I cannot recommend this game. Can't say if the gameplay was fun, cause this issue is so frustrating. On the note, I played almost every other Relic game just fine, but this one is an infuriating slog, fighting with controls to actually 'see things on the battlefield' just as much as the enemy forces.

From a single player standpoint.  This game is awesome. Here at the end of 2017, I still consider it the best in the series and would recommend it to anyone who loves this type of game.  The only negative I can think of, is that mods disable achievements.
From a multiplayer standpoint.  The game is still good, but suffers in features I will list below:
1 - Mods are not supported in multiplayer.  It doesn't matter if you and a friend have the same version of whatever you will be using, it's simply isn't allowed.
2 - If you start a game with a friend as "private" and save the game, when you load it back up it is no longer private and anyone can randomly join it.  There is no option to keep it private other than to kick people once they join. I hate doing that, but it's the only way I've seen to keep games for just me and who I want to play it with.  On the upside, once the game is in session, it disappears from the sight of others.  Or at least that seems to be the case.  But you'll need to kick people who try to join it before the session starts.
3 - This goes with number 2.  You setup your game how you want things to be, like victory types, whether to have a turn limit or not, etc. and it will be that way on day one.  But after you load up a saved game, that save defaults to all victory types and you cannot change it.  You simply cannot uncheck those in the game options when loading from a saved game, even if that game may have had only one victory condition when you originally started it.  Also, it throws the max turns of 500 back in, and while you can remove it in the game options by backspacing it out, its annoying having to do that every time.

Runner2 Future Legend of Rhythm Alien
Your task: run forward, collect gold and powerups, but dodge the various obstacles of living and nonliving genesis.
Unlike its predecessor BIT.TRIP RUNNER, Runner2 Future Legend of Rhythm Alien made with good graphics, without a touch of retro bit styling. This means that the probability of vertigo and epilepsy reduced to minimum.
Compared with BIT.TRIP RUNNER, gameplay became softer - to the levels added checkpoints. Checkpoints are located approximately at half of the distance.
Highly recommend to use a gamepad for playing, as well as stock up soothing. :)
For support gamepad you need to purchase additional software, example Pinnacle Game Profiler or Xpadder.
Runner2 Future Legend of Rhythm Alien
Ваша задача: бежать вперед, собирать золото и поверапы, да уворачиваться от различных препятствий живого и неживого генеза.
В отличие от своего предшественника BIT.TRIP RUNNER, Runner2 Future Legend of Rhythm Alien выполнен с хорошей графикой, без налета ретро квадратизма. А значит, вероятность головокружения и приступов эпилепсии сведена к минимому.
По сравнению с BIT.TRIP RUNNER, геймплей стал более мягким - на уровни добавлены чекпоинты, с которых игра возобновлятеся после натыкания на препятствие. Чекпоинты расположены примерно на половине дистанции.
Очень рекомендую использовать геймпад для прохождения, а также запастить успокоительным. :)
Для поддержки геймпада потребуется приобрести дополнительный софт, например Pinnacle Game Profiler или Xpadder.

This game is THE RPG for those that want a faster paced RPG, while being turn-based, but don't want to invest too many hours going through lengthy cutscenes and dialogue, and be able to enjoy its various challenges. The roguelike nature of this game provides many hours of adventures with the many randomly generated worlds that you can play through (and go back to if you want) and the 4 difficulty settings that allows new players and veterans at the game to enjoy at various levels.
Each run is quick, simple, and fun, being able to quickly go from a fresh, level 1 character to an unstoppable hero with hundreds of levels, provided you can survive long enough. The world is being consumed in darkness, and you must run from left to right and outrun the darkness while going on your journey. There are several win-state goals in the game, each of which with varying difficulty. In other words, just because you've defeated the Dark Lord doesn't mean you've finished the game. There is more to the game than simply defeating the Dark Lord.
With the different classes with different play styles, the potential allies that you can recruit, the different worlds and encounters, there are many unique adventures to be had in your quest to save the world. The amount of content and hours of gameplay you will get out of this is well worth the very cheap price of this game. I also highly recommend getting the One Way Heroics + DLC as well as it adds more classes, content, and functionality.

This guy is a very mixed bag when it comes to the setting. Imagine trail mix, with the chocolate at the top, then the rest at the bottom. It begins with a really enjoyable tour through the golden age of Sonic games, but then peters out as you begin to play the levels from more recent entries.On top of that, I felt that the story kind of sucked, and the voice actors are passable at best, whether you like the older Sonic games or not. I would recommend it on it's gameplay alone, however, which gets a solid nine out of ten in my book. For me, it was an absolute joy to play through, I just ignored the story outright.

Sonic Generations is a breath of fresh air in a series that has been shifting from "hit or miss" to "mostly miss" since the move to the third dimension. However, perhaps by going back to the old games and trying to cash in on the nostalgia factor of the series in its 20th aniversary, the designers managed to recreate what made the Genesis games great, which was good level design. Both the 2D and the 3D versions of levels taken from past games just capture the correct amount of flow that makes a platformer game swim rather than sink. The powerups vary throughout the game, but they add enough variety to the gameplay to avoid making it feel dull while never feeling like a gimick. The game encourages the replaying of levels in a fun manner as well, with unlockable music that can be played in any stage, concept artwork, and red stars that mark alternate routes that you can use to optimize your runs. Furthermore, there are a number of special challenge stages for each zone that choose to focus on combat or exploration of levels or just create fun scenarios where all the enemies are large or you need to navigate a course purely on a skateboard.
In the end, Sonic Generations is one of the best games in the series, and an all around solid platformer.

So my first proper review, and what way to start it off with one of the best Sonic games ever, even if it is simply a load of past stages recreated.
The cutscenes are greatly improved from the Xbox 360 version, no longer looking pixilated, well for me anyway. It also runs at a very nice and plesent 60 FPS, making Sonic and his vibrant surroundings look georgous no matter what. The game as a whole looks fantasic as it is, from the cheerful rolling hills of Green Hill Zone, to the gritty and action-packed Crysis City.
The stages are so much fun. Each course is littered with secrets and alternate routes that I am still discovering every time I go back to shave precious milliseconds off your high scores. They really are a blast to play and feel unique from one another but not too gimmicky, which Sonic games have felt like in the past. As well as stages we each fight a classic boss at the end of the Era, either being the final boss of a previous game or a rival character (wait, how is Silver here?). The rivals are cool and interesting ideas, and well executed, along with the other bosses. I would have to say my favourite rival is Shadow, it feels just so... right, and it's an amazing update to fight in Sonic Adventure 2. I also love the Death Egg Robo as one of the bosses, all it's phases are just awesome and mix up the battle.
But obviously, the highlight of this game is the music, as expected. I love every single one of the remixes (errr... minus Planet Wisp and another Open Your Heart remix, they got butchered) and is my favourite soundtrack next to Sonic 3 & Knuckles and Sonic Adventure 2. From the incredible violins in Rooftop Run to the tears of manliness I cry when I hear City Escape for the 7 billionth time.  Just take some time to listen to it, you'll love it.
However, having said that, there are some minor complaints. The game as a whole is a bit short, it'll take you roughly 2-3 hours to complete and even less if your a veteran of the series. The Red Rings add a little more time to 7-9 hours and are a nice reward and incentive for you to discover and explore the stages and it's many routes. Also, the game is very easy. For me anyway, I got most S-Ranks first time. I also find myself going back to Modern Sonic more than Classic Sonic, despite so many people yarning for his return.
Overall, this game is amazing, for what there is of it. It may be short, and easy, but if your just looking for some high-speed-nostalgia-trippin'-rocking-beats-blue-burred blast, this is the game for you. A great way to celebrate Sonic's 20th anniversary and a perfect example that the hedgehog is still on top.

In Age of Conan you play a barbarian or a wizard of your picking, you start off as a slave(totally not a Morrowind ripoff) on a ship that crashes and then ghosts whisper sweet nothings to you as you are washed on the shore where a friendly local old man tells you to head for Tortilla in order to gain freedom.
As you move through jungle, slaying pirates, natives and gorillas alike, you finally reach gates of Tortilla. There the guard tells you that your shackle fashion is not okay in the city and you are forced to conform to the local acceptable dressing code instead.
After that you're free to do nothing as there is a severe lack of low level quests, which changes at around level 9-10 where you get far too many quests, even though they're all the same under the hood. You spend most of the game at the local inn getting wasted and talking to the local cat.
Leveling is slow and there is no one around to help you since the game seems to be on its last legs as there is barely anyone else to be found. Your days are spent creeping around static NPCs whose only purpose in life is to do barely anything.
Sometimes you use a boat to teleport to another location full of natives and crocodiles but nothing much changes. You slay them or they slay you sometimes, repeat repeat. 
Combat was fun until I realized that essentially you get 3 of the same basic attack and to use a special attack you have to press two buttons in a sequence instead of one like in most games. All this does is reduce your keyboard lifespan. It does not add to the gameplay much besides having to remember which direction an ability needs.
Playing alone is really tough since world NPCs respawn really fast and when you're done with one group, it will start respawning, locking you into an infinite wave survival.  This game could work a lot better if you dealt a bit more damage and enemies did not respawn as fast. 
I wanted to invite my son to play with me but the game mechanics were a bit too complex for a 9 year old. Though it is for the best since I would not want to damage his mind with how poor the game plays.
I played until level 15 and could not do any more as it felt more tedious than a manual labor job. All you do is run from one bland place to another doing bland quests killing mostly bland enemies. There is no strategy, just monotone grind. Maybe it gets better in higher levels but if after 6 hours it is all the same, that is more than enough to say no. I originally intended to play until when you leave Tortilla but I changed my mind after all the mind numbing experience.
After runnig the game from Steam, the launcher has to download more content. This puts up false expectations of being able to play as it is done downloading. Sorta like when gifting your nephew a Wii U but then having it to update for 3 hours straight.
The game does not use steamworks and forces you to register a separate account with their system. That's more nonsense to go through before you can jump into the world of Conan the Barbosa.
Every time you open the game, launcher needs to rescan everything which takes longer than it should. Every. SINGLE.
.
I don't know which server I was assigned to, but the game would constantly average at 140ms which is ridiculous considering there's total of three other people playing. Though this is most likely due to them being unable to afford more servers since no one is playing.
You cannot have more than 30 active quests at a time. If you want new quests, you need to delete old ones. I get that this is an old game, but come on, update it once in a while to allow more than that.
You can only have 3 quests being tracked at one time and you cannot have 0 tracked quests as at least one needs to be tracked at all time. The UI to track/untrack quests is also painfully clunky.  
Seriously!? Can't even try out other classes unless you either delete your existing character or create 10 new accounts. I suppose you need more registered accounts to show some activity to your bosses.
It feels like a ghost town. During all of my playthrough I saw 5 other players, one of whom invited me to a Russian clan where admin proceeded to purge all inactive accounts, dropping clan member count from 80-something to 7 including me.
Typical mmo quests of going here killing X of that. Very monotone and it gets annoying to walk back and forth.
Armor, weapons and clothes are rather enjoyable to look at with the realistic barbarian style. It is always fun to just take an ax that does not have any glowing elvish inscriptions and smack some pirates with it.
Not many MMOs have fancy executions. This is not one of them, but the executions Conan does have are fairly decent. Sometimes they go all wonky and animations don't exactly match but hacking someone's head off or taunting your target while your ax is embedded in their chest is rather fun as far as this sort of stuff goes.
Enemies with much lower level than you will stop being hostile and will allow you safe passage. Saves some time when you have to go to same place a hundred times for all the different quests that unlock one after another rather all at once.
It is a dying game standing on its last legs. Wish it went open source so that others could turn it into an actually epic adventure rather than having this mess of a tryhard mmo.
Final rating
Not worth the weight

i'm sorry, devs, but...
Management summary: nicely done but tedious to work through because there's too much talking and not enough skirmishing.
Yes, i played it all the way through. Yes, i mostly enjoyed it. But... despite the changes and improvements from the first two in the series, two major problems make Hong Kong the black sheep of the three:
1) the load times between levels are so long that i often walk away or switch windows while waiting, and then forget that it was running at all. At least an hour, possibly two, of the time Steam recorded was a loading screen (either me waiting on it or having forgotten about it). The load times range anywhere from 30 seconds (which is bearable) to 2 minutes or more.
2) My gawd, the text! i felt like a good 80%+ of the time in the game was reading the tremendously long, way-too-frequent dialogs. i felt like i was reading a choose-your-own-adventure novel, rather than playing an adventure game. There were lots of interesting, sometimes difficult, choices to make burried in those dialogs, but a large percentage of the dialogs just add color, rather than carry the story along, and i got rather sick of reading them. "Oh, no, not _another_ talky sequence!"
Both of those are, for me, tremendously distracting. The first one rudely pulls me out of the game and the second one makes the game feel like a book. (Not that i'm against reading - i've read at least 10 novels in the past 3 months - but that's not what i play Shadowrun to do!) Yes, one could argue that more text provides more background and more color, and one would be correct. But more text is most certainly not what i want in a tactical adventure game. If the conversations had been a good 50% shorter, and possibly less frequent, i'd have been happy. i.e. it needs more combat scenes and less talking.
In short: i dislike SHK because i play the Shadowrun series for the tactical combat. This episode in that series seems somewhat lacking, compared to its predecessors, in that regard. The combat itself is just as good, if not better, there's just less of it. (Tip: the auto-reloader cybernetic upgrade may seem overpriced, but it's worth its weight in gold when paired with a grenade launcher!)
Other than that, it's remarkably good. While i would play the first two in the series a second time, i could not stomach doing so with this one.
Depending really on how much one likes to read, this game may or may not be worth playing. Other than text-centric software (e.g. Fighting Fantasy Combat books), Shadowrun Hong Kong easily has the most text of any game i've played, and a correspondingly large amount of game time is required to navigate through dialogs.
If you decide to try it out, be prepared to put your reading glasses on.

For what it is worth, I never got around to playing this game back in the day.. Played Dark Forces, Jedi Knight I, and Jedi Knight III. I've heard great things about it, but... it's really broken on modern machines. Like, entirely broken, unable to function properly if you have certain configurations, and impossible to fix. The game is clunky, likes to crash, doesn't deal with widescreen well, and after a few hours of trying to get it to cooperate cleanly, I gave up. I know there is a quality FPS experience to be had here, but I don't happen to have a copy of XP with an older computer laying around.
I've seen people get the game running, and I know there are guides to get it running cleanly, but I never quite got around to trying to make it work, despite following PCGamingWiki, steam forums, and other sources of information. Did a few .ini things, played with some config files, tried unofficial patches, and then I eventually gave up after it crashed when I opened a door.
I came to find out that It doesn't work, period, if you have a newer AMD card with newer drivers (Catalsyt 13.2 or higher), no matter what you do. It doesn't like to cooperate with multi-cored systems. If you try to play it in widescreen, the FOV will get messed up, and if you try to adjust the FOV, you'll crash randomly. If you try to rebind keys, you might end up with a white screen. If you try to run it in a compatibility mode, it'll either work fine (If you have an NVIDIA card) or it'll hard-lock your computer.
If you happen to have an older laptop laying around, or an old desktop for whatever reason, you should be fine. If you have an NVIDIA GPU rather than an AMD GPU, you should also be okay, I think. I can't personally test it. I do sincerely wish I could play it, but I can't recommend it in the state it is in. It's an old game that doesn't want to work properly, unfortunately. Every other Jedi Knight game plays relatively well, but this one just doesn't like to work... Although Dark Forces 2 likes to run in hyperspeed sometimes. But, that's for another review.

I liken the Saints Row series to the Evil Dead series of films. Not because of similar subject matter, but becasue of the way they've evolved. The first SR was a pretty bad GTA knock off, but it had a certain charm. Just like Evil Dead was a pretty bad horror movie with some great ideas. Saints Row 2 was essentially a remake of the first game, but with more presence and a sense of humour, and is regarded by many as being the best in the series (even though it isn't). This parallels Evil Dead 2 - it was essentially a remake of the first film, but we had the first glimmer of what was to come.
Saints Row The Third went pretty damn crazy for a GTA style open world game, and embraced the elements of SR2 which made it unique - over the top silliness and self-referential humour, together with a bunch of pro wrestling movies. SR:TT doesn't really have a direct parallel with the Evil Dead films, but when taken as a prelude to Saints Row IV, it matches up nicely with Army of Darkness. It's ridiculously over the top, laugh out loud hilarious and has cut itself so free from its roots that it might as well be a different tree. Consequently it's adored by many (I hold SRIV as the greatest open world sim of all time, bar none), but looked on with some amount of disdain by those "purists" who think that GTA clones should be permanently trapped in the early 2000s (in the same way that Army of Darkness is often held up as a poor successor to Evil Dead 2, despite being superior in every way).

This is a great game, for several reasons. I will break this into categories to make this easier on us both.
Vehicles: There are some truly sweet cars in this game, which you can easily save for later access. You can also customize your vehicles heavily, with both cosmetic and functional upgrades available. Add kneecappers and nitrous for the heck of it.
Agility ability: I just mentioned how great the vehicle customization is, but why would you wanna drive when you can upgrade your abilities enough to be able to run ridiculously fast, run up the sides of skyscrapers, and glide through the sky like a d@mn sugar glider? Answer- you wouldn't.
Muscle power: You can also customize your weapons, again both appearance and functionality. There are also some crazy cool weapons, some of which are DLC but in my humble opinion, well worth it.
Goof factor: What other game allows you to slap aliens to death with large, suggestive tenticles? I'll wait.

I was eagerly anticipating the release of Hong Kong after playing Dragonfall and this installment of the series definitely delivered.
Pros:
- In terms of plot the concept of Qi plays a huge role in this this game and overall atmosphere. That is not exactly to my taste, but Harebrained Schemes presents solid storytelling and managed to reel me in despite my bias.
- Just about all the characters are interesting and well written. The cast easily endeared itself to me through the generous amount of dialogue between missions. Some people found that quite annoying, but I always appreciate well written character interactions. Not only your party members, but several npcs found in the main hub have interesting stories to tell. To me it made the world feel more fleshed out and most games don't have that much attention to detail outside of the main cast.
- I absolutely loved the soundtrack to this game. There are several fantastic songs that enhance the atmosphere and are just plain cool. My only nitpick is that it would have been nice if there were more tracks for various parts of the game, but what we did get was quite good.
- The battle system is just as fun as Dragonfall and perhaps more so. Hong Kong improved greatly in how you can build and progress your character. In particular you can install more cyberware and even invest in nifty cyberware weapons. They also made mediocre builds much more viable and way more enjoyable this time around.
Cons:
- No increased difficulty mode. Not sure why the option to play on a harder setting was taken out when Dragonfall had it, but Hong Kong was a bit too easy. Both games definitely could have been a bit more difficult without just making your hit chance garbage.
- After the last update Harebrained Schemes hasn't gone back and fixed any bugs which is rather frustrating. Nothing absolutely game breaking (that I have experienced), but definitely vexing.
- A bit controversial and completely subjective: The revamped matrix system. I do very much appreciate the developers listening to feedback about how boring the matrix was in the first two games and trying to make it less dull for the sake of the community. Unfortunately, the sneaking and timing aspects of the matrix ended up severely getting on my nerves.
If they had introduced ways to subvert those aspects via programs or skills I might have been more receptive, but as it stands the matrix in Hong Kong typically frustrated me to no end. My buddy and plenty of other people absolutely loved the revamp, but it just wasn't for me.
Overall, I'd be weary of purchasing this game if you want extremely hard gameplay or dislike lots of dialogue. If you are a fan of well crafted characters and story with a ridiculously fun isometric battle system you should definitely consider buying this gem.

A great addition to the Shadowrun series. It improves on the existing systems, adds new weapons and cyberware and has an interresting story.

The matrix system has been changed. You are no longer in combat the moment enemy IC shows up. Instead it works as a real time stealth game until you get spotted and have to kill all IC in the area. Getting spotted enough will raise the alarm, which happens a lot faster and is a lot harsher than in the previous system. It can feel kind of wonky since the isometric view and movement was not originally meant for this kind of gameplay.
Be warned that it involves
of reading. The story is mainly told through conversations and descriptive text. Rather than an animated cutscene, you will often read stuff like "he looks at you menacingly and steps closer". There is no voice acting.
The upside to this is it allows for a lot more "fluff" answers, where you decide how your character responds to stuff and sometimes what happened in the past. There are also a lot of conversation skill checks, meaning a straight up combat character build is not necessarily the best option. You level by completing objectives rather than killing enemies, so there really is no downside to avoiding a fight by passing these skill checks.
Combat is turn based and works well. You need to manage your cover, buffs, healing and so on. If you bring a diverse team it's not too difficult.
This is an extremely fun old school RPG.

Another fun romp in the Shadowrun world. I liked the new cyber-weapons (monowhip FTW!) and how you could stealth/talk past your way through a lot of the missions, but really disliked the new implementation of the Matrix. Enjoyable, but I must say Dragonfall had a more engaging story and more interesting characters.

Mafia II provides a great atmosphere to experience a city during the late 40s and 50s. The strongest aspect of this game is its ability to create a world that feels full, and has substance. Many open-world 3rd person shooters often feel like a sandbox for mayhem, but the Mafia II cityscape feels like a living, breathing city, where you actions have consequence. Story builds a strong mafioso web of interactions based around deceit and betrayal.
Gun gameplay is strong, comparable to a looser GTA-style of shooting. Driving is realistic in difficulty, have to actually try to not crash.
Checkpoints are the most frustrating part of the game.
8/10
"This wasn't how I imagined it when we were startin' out. I dreamed o' money, cars, women, respect, freedom... I guess I ended up getting all of that more or less, but along with it came prison, living in constant fear, and the blood of my friends. I ducked it as long as I could, but it was finally catching up with me. It was all just a matter of time..." - Vito Scaletta

Immersive, exciting and atmospheric, this game is really, really good. The gunfights have great sound effects and a lot of the big set piece battles have wonderfully destructible and damageable environments. The cars look really authentic, and the handling of them someone feels 'real' and proper. The radio stations with their 1940's jazzy tunes really help to keep the setting and atmosphere immersive and involving. The story is somewhat standard in plot and outline, as one would expect, but the dialogue within the story is witty and often quite funny. A lot of aspects of this game are superior to GTA 4 and 5, which it will be inevitably compared to. The citizens walking around the streets are a bit more lifelike, repairing cars, loading baggage into trunks, posting mail, chatting and strolling the streets of Empire City.
You can't go wrong with this game, it's well made, runs beautifully and the gunfights are awesome.
9.1 out of 10.

The chronic oversaturation of the mafia in our international media has taught us much. Mafia II is an attempt to chronicle these teachings in game form. Fact number one: mafia men do lots of killing. Fact number two: they like suits. Fact number three: mafiosa don't call each other mafiosa; they use the term 'wiseguys'.
I've cross-referenced facts one and two with Mafia II, and they're definitely right – a lot of killing and a lot of suits. Fact number three isn't. 'Wiseguys', with its implied streetsmarts and cunning, doesn't fit Mafia II's mobsters. It certainly doesn't fit the mid-level gangster the game asked me to tail early in its middle act, who didn't have the presence of mind to check his rearview mirror as he drove away from a literal hatchet job. Had that guy done so, he'd have seen Sicilian-born WWII veteran and new-boy mobster Vito Scaletta about 20 feet behind, dressed in a red and white cod- Hawaiian shirt, driving a hot pink corvette with 'BUMS12' proudly displayed on the numberplate. That guy was not very wise.
The other guy was me, and I was trying to be too wise. As Mafia II's protagonist, my first attempt to trail the escaping mobster ended in failure after my original car choice – an inconspicuous '50s saloon – was outpaced with ease on the motorways. I only chose that car, snatched unattended with a bit of pavement minigame lockpicking, to satisfy the mission briefing, which said my mark would notice anything too obvious. Dutifully I wrested against the vehicle's slightly clunky era-specific handling to try and keep pace. But after my AI target had pranged his own vehicle six times against anything and everything in his path, I realised that such forwardthinking wiseguyishness wasn't entirely necessary on my part.
That Mafia II so effectively harpoons its illusion of real life, showing its characters to be machines acting out prescribed paths, is to its detriment. But the fact that I bought into it in the first place is the game's greatest strength.
It's not that Vito is a sympathetic character. Returning from a war he held no moral stake in – after a botched robbery, it was that or prison – he joins the local mafia, even though his mum told him not to. Naughty. From there on, he relies upon menace through the typical mafioso triple-threat: punching, shooting, and scary staring. Best buddy Joe occasionally dips a toe into 'comic relief' territory, but then ducks back into 'just a bit nasty' land, gets his pistol and shoots everyone in comic relief territory. Those poor clowns.
The player's supporting cast eschews any chance to get really creative, instead furnishing the game with another layer of dark-suited, dark-haired professionals, hitmen and higher-ups that blur into one mass. Driven by his need for money and respect, Vito is encased in a series of ever-widening shells, each step up the mafia ladder (a ladder made of guns) giving a new set of faces to watch in cutscenes: but they're all congealed clichés, culled from a hundred Bronx Tales and Godfathers. The dialogue is wellwritten and excellently acted, but it feels mechanical, the spoutings of a supercomputer sat in a shady office with its dials set to 'lightly-accented macho threat.'
It was the city that drew me in. An amalgamation of New York's streets and Hollywood's hills, Empire Bay is as interactively sterile as all other 'open-world' game-cities, but it's been coated in a veneer of dreamy credibility. Each street and hallway has a feature – a man shouting at an open window; a woman pressing her ear to a door; the sound of an argument. It's easy to see these details written down in a design document, but it gives Empire Bay a genuine rhythm, a pulse that Liberty City lacks. Plus, it helps that it is – on hefty machines – stunning. Turn up in the city in winter, and the streets are caked in snow, with layered bands of crystalline white on the untrodden paths contrasting with slush on the roads. And the lights! Even as the game transitions out of the 1940s and into the '50s, Mafia II's waxy lighting remains consistently arresting, casting pools of gold and yellow on windscreens.
But there's no point to any of it. The city breathes and grows, changing as the missions span the years, but it never moves or cries out. The game is presented in chapters, and each chapter has you wake up in your home. Vito, I can inform you, is a man who sleeps in the same vest and pants for nine years. Before the poor, smelly bugger can even get dressed, he's hit with news and a job. The game forces you to drive to a location: once there, Vito either shoots some men, punches some men or drives to another location.
As their cheery local mafia man, I'd pop in to see my contacts. Need any guys whacking today? Anything nicked? Want me to punch a lady? I was good at all these things. But, always, no. To deviate from the missions just wastes time: you can rob shops, but won't procure much loot; you can pester civilians, but will only get police pressure. For a city dripping with incidental detail, the game slapped on top of it has none. Not that this is a mechanical problem – 2K Czech have never made any bones about Mafia II being a linear experience – but when the city itself looks so inviting, it's a shame you can't do more.
Unless you make your own fun, that is. I enjoyed people-watching in a city where every pedestrian and car driver has the situational awareness of a frightened rabbit. Drive near one of the AI humans on foot and their preset reactions kick in, launching them in a seemingly random direction. Sometimes, this would be toward safety; more regularly, they'd hurl themselves into speeding traffic.
Having a woman – a few moments earlier happily strolling down a sunny street – chuck herself in front of a nearby van is certainly a surprise. Having that van then swerve to try to avoid her and plough through another three pedestrians is brilliant. Having that van then be spotted by a police car, having those police open fire before getting squished by the panicky, blood-leaking van driver, is better than another cover-shooting 'kill 50 goons' story mission.
And those are too regular. Combat is supported by a pleasing system of gunplay that leads to weighty, inaccurate firefights heavily reliant on ducking behind cover. The enemy AI – so stupid at the wheel - doesn't redeem itself through Mafia II's battles. Bad guys just pop up and down from the same spots of cover like sharply dressed moles: whacking them is simply a matter of waiting. Early in the storyline, Mafia II displays a convincing unwillingness to murder indiscriminately, surmising that the repeated and wholesale murder of swathes of humanity isn't the mafia's major focus. This was the time I built my connections, prepared my lip for wobbling when my contacts became friends and my friends went to sleep with the fishes, as all mafia friends do. But then, three quarters of the way through, it forgets all that, and puts you up against waves of baddies, dehumanised after all that work to build Empire Bay's factions into tangible things.
Mafia II is a mafia movie run once through a game grinder, and that's simultaneously the worst thing about the game and the compliment it was developed for. In telling a story as convincing as most Hollywood depictions of the Cosa Nostra, 2K Czech have accomplished exactly what they intended to: only at the end does the artifice topple slightly, piling one too many game-cliché mass-battles onto the pile. But detach the story from its very familiar housings, and we're not left with much: a bit of walking, a lot of driving and too much shooting. Each is good, but rarely superb.
Even supported by a neat script and great voicework, Mafia II is treading ground already chewed up by cinema's very best. On that level, it can't compete.  80/100

A wonderful celebration of one of the gaming industry's most beloved icons, Sonic Generations brings together both Sonics, classic and modern, to face a new crisis between multiple timelines. By focusing on the most important part of the series, going really fast, Sonic Generations manages to transcend the numerous problems that plagued the other Sonics in the transition to 3D. With a wonderful soundtrack, inspired updates of levels from Sonics old and new, Sonic Generations should be played by any fans of platformers.

If you're a fan of Sonic Colors, and/or a fan of Sonic Unleashed's daytime stages, then I suggest you pick this game up. This game offers a set of nine individual levels from three eras of the Sonic franchise, ranging from the Sega Genesis to Nintendo Wii.
The gameplay is a combination of Sonic Colors and Sonic The Hedgehog (Genesis Titles). Throughout Classic Sonic's stages, you'll be doing a lot of platforming in a 2D realm, whereas Modern Sonic you'll be doing a lot of boosting. The game offers two acts with every level- one for each Sonic.
The graphics are simply superb. Playing this on the consoles doesn't do it justice. The console version runs at 30 FPS where the PC port runs at 60 FPS. The attention to detail in the levels are stunning as well. Green Hill Zone looks fantastic, and City Escape is absolutely beautiful. You can really see where San Francisco was the inspiration for that level.
However, before purchasing this title, do realize that this game can get be very heavy on your PC at times. While I never experienced problems, my friends reported having some slowdown during some areas such as Chemical Plant and Planet Whisp. Also, it's recommended that you use an Xbox 360 and/or PC controller for this game.
The game is worth the price, and it's a must have for any Sonic The Hedgehog fan. I suggest giving it a purchase and playing it now! If you're not sure, how about you click that "Download Demo" button up there at the top and give it a try. I gurantee you that it'll change your mind. ;)

First off, yes, this game started out as a Sonic fan game a long time ago.  However, after a lot of work and a successful Kickstarter, it has become so much more than that.  Now it would be more accurate to say this game is a little bit of several sidescrolling classics I had played growing up.  The running and general movement feels like a cross between Sonic and Rocket Knight Adventures, while the combat evokes memories of playing as Zero in the Megaman X series.  The sheer amount of action on screen can remind one of how hectic games like Gunstar Heroes were, as well.
On to the graphics.  The spritework is mostly good, but there are some not so great background elements you probably won't notice right away (e.g. some of the trees in the snow area look like someone took a turd and slapped on a few shades of brown).  However, the characters, and animation on them, are fantastic.  Overall, the graphics are nice, but when lots of action is happening on screen, sometimes the game's framerate will drop.  The reduced FPS isn't unplayable, and frankly, reminds me of the slowdown in old 16-bit games, but this is still a downside, nontheless.
The soundtrack is amazing, and something I will be humming in my head for quite some time.  Many of the tracks are very catchy, and can sometimes remind you of other games (for example, the first stage, Dragon Valley, reminds me of Chrono Trigger's music just because of the style).  All is not perfect in the sound department though.  The cutscenes are fully voiced, and while some actors are decent, others clearly haven't done much voice acting at all.  There is no way to turn off all the voices sadly, but playing in Classic mode does at least let you skip the cutscenes, relegating the voices to simple grunts and stage clear exclamations.  The actual sound effects themselves are nothing special, but they fit the game well, and don't sound out of place or misused at all.
The gameplay itself is an absolute blast.  While the physics engine used is more reminiscent of Sonic 4 than the classic Sonics, it does a much better job than that game did of allowing you to build up speed and actually *feel* like you're going fast (which was Sonic 4's biggest flaw, imo).  When you fire off a perfectly aimed air dash with Lilac and hit a slope at the right angle, it feels so good.  You'd think speed like that would make fighting annoying and something you'd rather avoid, right?  Actually it's the opposite, the combat is pretty fast paced as well, but since you only take damage from attacks and not from contact with enemies themselves, you can also just pass some of them by, so combat is mainly for building up your supply of orbs for the bonus level.  Enemies do also collect gems as they go along too though, so if you're hunting every gem in a stage then you might have to kill a few bots to get them back.  All of the characters you can play as so far (more are coming as free DLC) all play very differently and are all fun in their own way, with Lilac being a bit more like Sonic, Carol being a bit more like Zero, and Millia being a bit like Mario/Yoshi.
So, to sum it up:
PROs
+ Fun gameplay
+ Great soundtrack
+ Character sprites are well done, even if it doesn't look 100% like some of the promo art
+ Works well when using either a keyboard or a gamepad, and only uses directions and 3 buttons plus pause, just like a Genesis game
+ Is better at Sonic style gameplay than most of SEGA's recent games
+ Characters all play uniquely, and more are coming as free DLC
+ Can choose to play with cutscenes or without, and unlocks do not force you to play a certain way
+ Controls perfectly
CONs
- Occasional slowdown when playing in fullscreen and there is a ton of sprites on the screen
- I guarantee you will have to rebind controls the first time, as the gamepad detection is not perfect by any means (this can be considered minor, but still worth noting)
- Voice acting that ranges from decent to mediocre
- No way of turning off the voices altogether
- Combat can seem somewhat pointless if you're only playing for speed
- Most of the sprites are great, but some backgrounds are obviously in need of touching up
- The bosses can get pretty frustrating sometimes, especially later on in the game
When it all comes down to it though, the main reason I recommend this game is because it fills a niche that most other "retro styled" games don't.  Genesis/Megadrive Sonic games were classics, but few people try to emulate what made them so fun, and even fewer succeed at it.  Do yourself a favor, and check out the free demo, you just might become hooked like I did.
UPDATE 11/25/16: This game runs much better than it did on launch. While we still don't have all the characters, what is there is still a complete package, and I'm anxiously awaiting the sequel.

1. I kinda figured this would be a walking sim w/ some platforming thrown on top but it is the opposite. It is a platforming game first w/ cute, sentimental fantasy plot thrown on top.
2. I start playing a 3D platformer and I immediately reach for the controller out of habit. This was the wrong move.  Or, I guess it is the right move if you like your games good and frustrating. The accuracy of a mouse is very helpful and I don't find that to often be the case.
3. While I was using the controller, I stacked a bunch of pillows on the side of my couch so I could have a place to safely chuck it, which wasn't as satisfying as crushing the thing to smithereens in a fit of nerd rage but a whole lot cheaper.
4. It's not really the same kind of game but this reminds me of
as much as anything. There is a story overlayed via narration but you are not really involved in it. It just comes at you bit by bit as you progress. It's also a first person game where you have to aim and shoot things but can't kill anything.
5. The way the game works is, basically, you are Spiderman w/ rocket shoes. This is pretty sweet. Grappling is the name of the game here. There is a bit of challenge puzzling your way into finding the best root through a given set of obstacles but it's mostly about getting the timing right and aiming quickly. This works well and for the most part the game flows smoothly.
6. You play as a young boy who goes off looking for his uncle. In his house, you find a magic space suit and somehow manage to transport yourself out to a bizarre world of floating rocks and frog people. Adventure and grappling ensues.
7. I don't know where the hell the voice actors for this game from but they all speak like people who learned English as a second language and spent years perfecting it but still ended up like 1% short of speaking exactly the same way as a native speaker. They are in the accent uncanny valley. It is strikes me as kind of creepy at times but sort of works for the fantasy setting. If you tell me frog people from outer-space speak like northern Europeans who majored in English, who am I to say any different?
8. I found this much more difficult than most people. That is partly because I stubbornly stuck w/ a controller for longer than I should have and also because I was drunk half the time. Not gonna lie.
9. The graphics here are not a technical marvel or anything but are quite pretty and alluring so I feel the artists accomplished what they wanted to so good for them.
10. Number 10 being said, I did have two issues w/ the graphics here. Firstly, there are spots where it is too dark to see your various grappling points in the distance. Towards the end, I had to crank the gamma way up to see what I was doing and I liked the look of the game much less once I did that--but at least I could see. Also, often, I felt that at times it was not clear based solely on their appearance what points you could grapple. This made some sections a little more trial-and-error based than I thought they should be.
11. I played this solely on Linux. Thanks for the support! It worked almost perfectly but I did have some trouble w/ menus becoming unresponsive. Still, not nearly bad enough to avoid the Linux version.
12. Most of the replayability here is going to come from just wanting to play it again. There are opportunities to find collectables to encourage some off-course exploration and a time trial mode if you are into such things.
13. It'd be a stretch to call
a perfect game if I'm being honest. The plot wasn't great, the platforming certainly had annoyances but it's cute, almost always fun and is the kind of thing you can knock out over the course of a weekend w/o having to block off a huge section of time so it doesn't overstay it's welcome. People looking for a little something different in a platformer won't go wrong by checking this out.

Hands down the best Star Wars FPS/Action game I have ever played. (Admittedly I never played the prequels)
You play as Kyle Katarn, a Mercenary that works for the New Republic. You start the game by infiltrating a remnant imperial forces base armed with a basic blaster pistol, and as the game progresses you will get your hands on more weapons (like the iconic E11 Rifle, and a variety of other weapons). You and your wife (Jan Ors) are the only two people in the galaxy who know where a certain "Valley of the Jedi" is located, it contains a Force Nexus so powerful, that anyone who enters it will have their force sensitivity massively boosted. (In other words it can artificially create Jedi, or make Jedi who enter it much stronger) and this has been the focal point of the series up till this entry.
The difficulty curve for the first couple of missions isn't exactly forgiving, but after a certain point you start using force powers and a lightsaber which would make everything significantly easier... If you wouldn't have to be facing grenadiers and snipers (which the lightsaber can't block) as soon as you get your hands on the saber. I'd say the real relaxing fun of making minced meat out of stormtroopers doesn't start until after the point where you first start fighting other Jedi in the game, which is about a quarter into the game.
But the difficulty of the game is really just what you select when you start it. Hard is hard, medium is medium and easy is easy.
Sadly, the game's age does show on modern high resolution displays, it was made for the era of 1024x768. You will see some artifacts (like green tinted shadows) and some heavily upscaled textures. But it's still worth it. It's also worth noting that the multiplayer gameplay in these games is quite fun. How many games allow you to switch between third person lightsaber and first person shooting on the fly when you're fighting other players? Not many.
The Force is strong with this one...

OWH is a Rogue-like/lite with RPG element made in the WolfRPG editor, which is also made by the developer of the game. For a true rogue-like experience you'll not want to use the vault at the least - for more casual players though the vault helps make the game far more accessible as well.
Gameplay is turn-based (though turns merge together smoothly enough to look like it's real-time to viewers at times) with a wall of darkness advancing from the left side of the screen, forcing you to constantly move to the right. The goal in each run is to either defeat a boss or reach the end of the level in 1 piece - with numerous different rewards depending on how you won and who helped you to encourage you to try every method as well as points based on your score even if you failed to help you unlock more stuff. It uses seed-based procedural generation for maps and there is a variety of classes to play and companions to find.
If you have at least a bit of patience and are willing to think before taking action (i.e. take a more tactical approach) when necessary you'll no doubt spend tens of hours on this before you know it and I strongly recommend you try it out - honestly, you've not got much to lose either with how cheap the base game is and any reasonably modern system will play it without any difficulty.
Even if you're impatient, you may well still enjoy this game playing as certain classes that can get away with just charging through a lot of the time - the optional online feature and campaign worlds let's you see other players progress (and deaths/victories) on the same world, with ghosts that leave behind a random item from the dead hero when other players (or your own previous runs) die - potentially something very powerful, or it could be something fairly useless. There's enough seeds that there's no doubt some that no one else has ever played even now if you're lucky for glory of being the 1st to conquer a dimension too.
There's a ton to unlock to keep you coming back to it as well, with the DLC adding a ton more once you finally get everything and find yourself craving for more - the DLC also comes with some rebalancing and an improved UI. You can still play the original with the DLC installed too as the original save data is unaffected by importing it in OWH+ and the loader lets you play both.
Basically: Try it, it's easy to get into and dirt cheap for what it offers, even if it wasn't on sale frequently. You may well find yourself pleasantly surprised....and possibly somewhat addicted to moving to the right.

I liken the Saints Row series to the Evil Dead series of films. Not because of similar subject matter, but becasue of the way they've evolved. The first SR was a pretty bad GTA knock off, but it had a certain charm. Just like Evil Dead was a pretty bad horror movie with some great ideas. Saints Row 2 was essentially a remake of the first game, but with more presence and a sense of humour, and is regarded by many as being the best in the series (even though it isn't). This parallels Evil Dead 2 - it was essentially a remake of the first film, but we had the first glimmer of what was to come.
Saints Row The Third went pretty damn crazy for a GTA style open world game, and embraced the elements of SR2 which made it unique - over the top silliness and self-referential humour, together with a bunch of pro wrestling movies. SR:TT doesn't really have a direct parallel with the Evil Dead films, but when taken as a prelude to Saints Row IV, it matches up nicely with Army of Darkness. It's ridiculously over the top, laugh out loud hilarious and has cut itself so free from its roots that it might as well be a different tree. Consequently it's adored by many (I hold SRIV as the greatest open world sim of all time, bar none), but looked on with some amount of disdain by those "purists" who think that GTA clones should be permanently trapped in the early 2000s (in the same way that Army of Darkness is often held up as a poor successor to Evil Dead 2, despite being superior in every way).

This is a great game, for several reasons. I will break this into categories to make this easier on us both.
Vehicles: There are some truly sweet cars in this game, which you can easily save for later access. You can also customize your vehicles heavily, with both cosmetic and functional upgrades available. Add kneecappers and nitrous for the heck of it.
Agility ability: I just mentioned how great the vehicle customization is, but why would you wanna drive when you can upgrade your abilities enough to be able to run ridiculously fast, run up the sides of skyscrapers, and glide through the sky like a d@mn sugar glider? Answer- you wouldn't.
Muscle power: You can also customize your weapons, again both appearance and functionality. There are also some crazy cool weapons, some of which are DLC but in my humble opinion, well worth it.
Goof factor: What other game allows you to slap aliens to death with large, suggestive tenticles? I'll wait.
TLDR: The characters and story in this game are hilarious, and a pleasure to play through. The game looks good, has plenty of customization options, is well-polished, and has pretty much infinite replayability (I've played 100+ hours on my old Xbox).

Mafia II provides a great atmosphere to experience a city during the late 40s and 50s. The strongest aspect of this game is its ability to create a world that feels full, and has substance. Many open-world 3rd person shooters often feel like a sandbox for mayhem, but the Mafia II cityscape feels like a living, breathing city, where you actions have consequence. Story builds a strong mafioso web of interactions based around deceit and betrayal.
Gun gameplay is strong, comparable to a looser GTA-style of shooting. Driving is realistic in difficulty, have to actually try to not crash.
Checkpoints are the most frustrating part of the game.
8/10
"This wasn't how I imagined it when we were startin' out. I dreamed o' money, cars, women, respect, freedom... I guess I ended up getting all of that more or less, but along with it came prison, living in constant fear, and the blood of my friends. I ducked it as long as I could, but it was finally catching up with me. It was all just a matter of time..." - Vito Scaletta

Immersive, exciting and atmospheric, this game is really, really good. The gunfights have great sound effects and a lot of the big set piece battles have wonderfully destructible and damageable environments. The cars look really authentic, and the handling of them someone feels 'real' and proper. The radio stations with their 1940's jazzy tunes really help to keep the setting and atmosphere immersive and involving. The story is somewhat standard in plot and outline, as one would expect, but the dialogue within the story is witty and often quite funny. A lot of aspects of this game are superior to GTA 4 and 5, which it will be inevitably compared to. The citizens walking around the streets are a bit more lifelike, repairing cars, loading baggage into trunks, posting mail, chatting and strolling the streets of Empire City.
You can't go wrong with this game, it's well made, runs beautifully and the gunfights are awesome.
9.1 out of 10.

The chronic oversaturation of the mafia in our international media has taught us much. Mafia II is an attempt to chronicle these teachings in game form. Fact number one: mafia men do lots of killing. Fact number two: they like suits. Fact number three: mafiosa don't call each other mafiosa; they use the term 'wiseguys'.
I've cross-referenced facts one and two with Mafia II, and they're definitely right – a lot of killing and a lot of suits. Fact number three isn't. 'Wiseguys', with its implied streetsmarts and cunning, doesn't fit Mafia II's mobsters. It certainly doesn't fit the mid-level gangster the game asked me to tail early in its middle act, who didn't have the presence of mind to check his rearview mirror as he drove away from a literal hatchet job. Had that guy done so, he'd have seen Sicilian-born WWII veteran and new-boy mobster Vito Scaletta about 20 feet behind, dressed in a red and white cod- Hawaiian shirt, driving a hot pink corvette with 'BUMS12' proudly displayed on the numberplate. That guy was not very wise.
The other guy was me, and I was trying to be too wise. As Mafia II's protagonist, my first attempt to trail the escaping mobster ended in failure after my original car choice – an inconspicuous '50s saloon – was outpaced with ease on the motorways. I only chose that car, snatched unattended with a bit of pavement minigame lockpicking, to satisfy the mission briefing, which said my mark would notice anything too obvious. Dutifully I wrested against the vehicle's slightly clunky era-specific handling to try and keep pace. But after my AI target had pranged his own vehicle six times against anything and everything in his path, I realised that such forwardthinking wiseguyishness wasn't entirely necessary on my part.
That Mafia II so effectively harpoons its illusion of real life, showing its characters to be machines acting out prescribed paths, is to its detriment. But the fact that I bought into it in the first place is the game's greatest strength.
It's not that Vito is a sympathetic character. Returning from a war he held no moral stake in – after a botched robbery, it was that or prison – he joins the local mafia, even though his mum told him not to. Naughty. From there on, he relies upon menace through the typical mafioso triple-threat: punching, shooting, and scary staring. Best buddy Joe occasionally dips a toe into 'comic relief' territory, but then ducks back into 'just a bit nasty' land, gets his pistol and shoots everyone in comic relief territory. Those poor clowns.
The player's supporting cast eschews any chance to get really creative, instead furnishing the game with another layer of dark-suited, dark-haired professionals, hitmen and higher-ups that blur into one mass. Driven by his need for money and respect, Vito is encased in a series of ever-widening shells, each step up the mafia ladder (a ladder made of guns) giving a new set of faces to watch in cutscenes: but they're all congealed clichés, culled from a hundred Bronx Tales and Godfathers. The dialogue is wellwritten and excellently acted, but it feels mechanical, the spoutings of a supercomputer sat in a shady office with its dials set to 'lightly-accented macho threat.'
It was the city that drew me in. An amalgamation of New York's streets and Hollywood's hills, Empire Bay is as interactively sterile as all other 'open-world' game-cities, but it's been coated in a veneer of dreamy credibility. Each street and hallway has a feature – a man shouting at an open window; a woman pressing her ear to a door; the sound of an argument. It's easy to see these details written down in a design document, but it gives Empire Bay a genuine rhythm, a pulse that Liberty City lacks. Plus, it helps that it is – on hefty machines – stunning. Turn up in the city in winter, and the streets are caked in snow, with layered bands of crystalline white on the untrodden paths contrasting with slush on the roads. And the lights! Even as the game transitions out of the 1940s and into the '50s, Mafia II's waxy lighting remains consistently arresting, casting pools of gold and yellow on windscreens.
But there's no point to any of it. The city breathes and grows, changing as the missions span the years, but it never moves or cries out. The game is presented in chapters, and each chapter has you wake up in your home. Vito, I can inform you, is a man who sleeps in the same vest and pants for nine years. Before the poor, smelly bugger can even get dressed, he's hit with news and a job. The game forces you to drive to a location: once there, Vito either shoots some men, punches some men or drives to another location.
As their cheery local mafia man, I'd pop in to see my contacts. Need any guys whacking today? Anything nicked? Want me to punch a lady? I was good at all these things. But, always, no. To deviate from the missions just wastes time: you can rob shops, but won't procure much loot; you can pester civilians, but will only get police pressure. For a city dripping with incidental detail, the game slapped on top of it has none. Not that this is a mechanical problem – 2K Czech have never made any bones about Mafia II being a linear experience – but when the city itself looks so inviting, it's a shame you can't do more.
Unless you make your own fun, that is. I enjoyed people-watching in a city where every pedestrian and car driver has the situational awareness of a frightened rabbit. Drive near one of the AI humans on foot and their preset reactions kick in, launching them in a seemingly random direction. Sometimes, this would be toward safety; more regularly, they'd hurl themselves into speeding traffic.
Having a woman – a few moments earlier happily strolling down a sunny street – chuck herself in front of a nearby van is certainly a surprise. Having that van then swerve to try to avoid her and plough through another three pedestrians is brilliant. Having that van then be spotted by a police car, having those police open fire before getting squished by the panicky, blood-leaking van driver, is better than another cover-shooting 'kill 50 goons' story mission.
And those are too regular. Combat is supported by a pleasing system of gunplay that leads to weighty, inaccurate firefights heavily reliant on ducking behind cover. The enemy AI – so stupid at the wheel - doesn't redeem itself through Mafia II's battles. Bad guys just pop up and down from the same spots of cover like sharply dressed moles: whacking them is simply a matter of waiting. Early in the storyline, Mafia II displays a convincing unwillingness to murder indiscriminately, surmising that the repeated and wholesale murder of swathes of humanity isn't the mafia's major focus. This was the time I built my connections, prepared my lip for wobbling when my contacts became friends and my friends went to sleep with the fishes, as all mafia friends do. But then, three quarters of the way through, it forgets all that, and puts you up against waves of baddies, dehumanised after all that work to build Empire Bay's factions into tangible things.
Mafia II is a mafia movie run once through a game grinder, and that's simultaneously the worst thing about the game and the compliment it was developed for. In telling a story as convincing as most Hollywood depictions of the Cosa Nostra, 2K Czech have accomplished exactly what they intended to: only at the end does the artifice topple slightly, piling one too many game-cliché mass-battles onto the pile. But detach the story from its very familiar housings, and we're not left with much: a bit of walking, a lot of driving and too much shooting. Each is good, but rarely superb.
Even supported by a neat script and great voicework, Mafia II is treading ground already chewed up by cinema's very best. On that level, it can't compete.  80/100

Vito and Joe are psychopaths.
They go through life extorting, stealing, robbing, mugging, shooting, murdering and pushing drugs for no other reason than that it makes them a buck.
You think those guys are the enemy in this game?
Nope: you play Vito, and Joe is your best buddy.
Is there a excuse for being a bunch of murderious psychopaths?
There is a flimsy story that forces Vito to cough up two thousand dollars quickly to pay off  the loan his dearly departed dad has with a loanshark. But once that debt is settled there is no excuse for them for doing the psychopath things they do..
The mafia II story is the story of Vito, an unlikeable character at best. He kills because people point a finger and give the order, just like he did in the war. So Vito tells us. He does so without any change of expression or feeling of guilt. Violence is second nature to him. And so he has no problem with beating up a dockworker because that makes him pay the extortion money and gives a message to all the other dockworkers. Or beat up the husband of his sister Francesca because he is beating her in turn and cheating on her as well.
Joe is more charming perhaps, but in the end just as crazy as Vito. Incidently, Joe looks and acts remarkably like Telly Savalas.. aka Kojak.  Is that bad? Well it ain't right to me.
You might think that this is all to establish their psychopath personalities, but it feels more that it was just an unintended sideeffect from a game that meant to have some guys be like the mafia.
The story itself is divided into fifteen chapters and is simply not good. For one, the makers of the game haven't done their homework as they would have known that the mafia of the fifties wasn't the mafia of the thirties.  The most important change was that shootouts became increasingly a thing of the past.  Such shootouts, like the Valentine's Day massacre, brought inevitably retaliation from the authorities who couldn't let the mob rule in the street, at least not outwardly: it made for angry voters.  In addition the law enforcing agencies started to become better at pursuing the mafia. Overall the fifties were a turning point that marked the height of the mob's influence and also hailed its demise.
In addition the story simply fails to do the basic work of establishing a background for Vito and Joe,  fails to provide for a memorable antagonist and fails to follow a consistent storyline.
Instead it seems as if each and every chapter has been created almost in isolation from the others thus a lot of characters are introduced, then killed before you have any idea who does what. Some characters might disappear in one chapter just to suddenly reappear some chapters later.. No less than three times in the game Vito's life will make a drastic change that seriously impacts his life.
There is a chapter in which a sidekick of Joe is killed, which makes Joe go on a drinking trip, getting so drunk that he accidently kills a bartender. Why Joe is heartstricken by the death of his sidekick requires some explanation as he is otherwise an emotionless killing machine. But we have to just accept that Joe has a tender side.
The gameplay isn't much to write home about either. Mafia II is not an open world, although it has the looks of one. There is just one linear storyline that you can follow. Most of the time you will be driving from one end of the map to the other, often just to witness a cutscene before you have to drive to another part of the map.  One such drive has transporting a rotting corpse and two drunken buddies to a remote part of town where you can ditch the body. It is probably meant to be funny in a pulp fiction kind of way. Unfortenately it isn't really funny.
There is one redeeming factor about this game, which is the gorgeous look. You will ride around Empire Bay during the wintern and during the summer and it looks amazing. The same can be said about the cars, which are fun to watch and ride for a bit.
With a linear short storyline that offers you no choices, with overlong rides that bore and with a shallow story that mostly consits of cutscenes, the game has nothing much to offer but gorgeous eyecandy. If you still want to give it a try, than buy it when it is on sale  for less than eight bucks or euro's. It isn't worth more.

Having put over 75 hours into this game, it's about time i reviewed it.  Don't expect much from me though, as i've never reviewed anything before.
Firstly, it's big, and it's beautiful.  Yes, the graphics are dated, and can't compete at all in regards to most games nowadays, but, if like me, you regard graphics secondary to gameplay, then you wont be the least bit disappointed, because they still look great.  At the risk of sounding sacreligious; i'm not that big of a Star Wars fan, so if you aren't either, don't worry...the way this game is executed, even if it had no Star Wars Related themes, it would still tower over many other Action / FPS games.
To sum it up:
Great dialogue throughout; keeping the story moving, interesting, and consistent.
So much to do, so so much!  It's not the most challenging game out there, but there's barely any 'grinding'...the pace remains throughout, and some of the challenges will force you to engage your mind more than you would expect.
But most importantly!  It's fun, and interesting.

Sonic Generations marks the 20th anniversary of the Blue blur, and with celebrations of our beloved gaming icon, a game also joins the club. And what kind of game is it?
The game allows you to play with 2 Sonics. One from the good old genesis days and one from the modern Sonic days. Sounds confusing? Well, time travel is always confusing so don't point at me. The two Sonics are on their way to save their friends, speeding through stages of the past and fix the timeline.
The gameplay is fun for everyone, either an old skool Sonic fan or a new one, or even someone who has never been part of this franchise. Like playing old platformers with speed added, classic Sonic is your friend! More of a 3d speed section fan, modern Sonic is the guy you want! You'll have to play with both of them to complete the game but don't worry, you'll enjoy it.
The music consists mainly of older Sonic themes being remixed. For example, when you go through a stage you will hear two versions, a classic version and a modern version of the original stage theme. And they are absolutely a joy to listen to.
Other things also make a return or are brand new. There are mission gates which allows you to go through stages with an other goal than reach the finish, and there's a skill shop in which you can adjust Sonic's gameplay style to your own. Want more speed? Buy the blast off skill. Want more grip? The acceleration skill is something you want.
There are only two negative points that I have to mention with this game, which are the length and the story. The length of this game is only 4 hours long, not counting the missions and collecting red rings or achievements, so that's a bit of a let down. The story is pretty akward. There are barely any cutscenes, and making a story including time travel tends to fail easy if done wrong.
I would advice this game to any fan, wether old skool, modern lover or not a fan of Sonic overall.

I consider Jedi Outcast one of the best narrative Star Wars games ever. It's a simple and straightforward story, driven by the most classic of action hero motivations: revenge. It's a fine line to walk for our Jedi protagonist, Kyle Katarn. But he's no Luke Skywalker. From blasters, grenades, mines and more, no weapon goes left unused by Katarn in his quest for answers. And yes, that includes lightsabers.
In fact, the Jedi Knight series still possesses the best lightsaber combat to date. Every swing, every thrust has the potential to be deadly, whether it's your lightsaber or your enemy's. No florescent batons here: swings cut through enemies neatly and quickly, as they should. Enable the dismemberment option for increased pandemonium.
The greatest con might be the series' age. The visuals definitely diminished with time. But see if that still matters when the game hands you a lightsaber, a room full of Storm Troopers, and John William's score begins swelling.
Oh, and did I mention they got Billy Dee Williams back to voice Lando? Because they got Billy Dee back to voice Lando. Awesome.
