It’s been 20 years since Sonic rolled into the realm of games, and with him he’s brought us speed, clever level design and wonderfully imaginative set pieces. He has, however, also brought with him hideous 3d cameras, piles of buggy messes and a hedgehog who drives a jeep and carries a gun. Mixed legacy? You bet it is, and nowhere is the schizophrenic nature of the series better displayed than in the historically minded “Sonic Generations”. Is the blue blur back to his best, or is this simply another false start?
Sonic Generations begins optimistically, blasting through Green Hill Zone before being introduced to a charmingly “nod-nod wink-wink” opening cutscene that hints at a more light hearted Sonic adventure than other games have attempted. This reassuringly fun opening is cemented when, after finishing the first level with modern sonic, you think that you’re safe. Modern Sonic played fine, Classic Sonic was great, maybe we’re going to make the long haul here, maybe we can see the game through and not hit any major speed bumps. This goes on throughout the first third of the game, the level design is charming, the cutscenes are small and for the most part amusing, and the music is great. Then something happens, and a cold sweat sits in.
Challenges? There are challenges between the levels? The pulse quickens and blood drains from the face. Oh no. They surely didn’t mess this up, they were doing so well! Please don’t make me replay the same level to pad out gameplay please don’t... then the first genuine surprise happens. The challenges are not only really fun; they’re entirely different levels, for the most part! New power-ups are dished out in the form of Sonic’s friends and the level design shifts entirely. OK so these levels are much shorter, but they’re good, they’re fun, and best of all they take about 5 minutes at their most extravagant.
Then the first boss fight happens. It’s a mess; spotty controls, frustrating design and uninteresting music leads to the first true lull in the game. You can forgive it though, it isn’t too bad and it ended quickly once you figure out how to hurt the boss. But then you open up the Dreamcast era, and like Sonic does when he needs to go quicker, it goes downhill from there.
It’s incredible how Sonic Generations manages to pinpoint the exact moment Sonic jumped the shark but the history lesson is well taught. The level they chose from Sonic Adventure is a city level. The level they chose from Sonic Adventure 2 is a city level. The level they choose for Sonic 2006 is a city level. Suddenly it becomes very apparent that Sonic stopped existing in a sort of fantasy realm and started becoming an urbanite. All of the charm starts to drain, the level design gets, not exactly harder but more finicky, there’s more awkward jumps and bad precision platforming. Even worse are the glitches which suddenly pop up in Modern Sonic; blasting through walls, clipping on the edge of a platform and falling your death. Throw in more unexpected and unfair traps and it all gets a bit frustrating. Classic Sonic seems lost and bewildered in these later levels, outside his 3 games he has to wade through 6 modern titles and in almost every single one of them he is chased by something. I know Sonic being chased is a fun idea, but my god the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ must be magnetic or something.
This is Sonic Generations biggest problem, while it’s great to celebrate Sonic’s past, it’s his present that is the true villain of the piece. What’s baffling is how the designers missed a trick in doing as little of the bad Sonic games as possible. They chose to include Sonic Heroes and Sonic 2006, and both of the “new levels” for those games are horrible. Why on earth recognise these infamously bad titles when you could have had a proper Sonic 3 level (the one in the PC version is Sky Sanctuary, a fine level but from Sonic and Knuckles) and brought in Sonic CD for a real nostalgia trip. Instead we get a bad beach level and a third (third!) city level. A terrible decision was made in development, but it could have been worse, we at least didn’t get a Shadow the Hedgehog level.
Towards the end the game feels like it might be getting a little stale, so it stops. With only 9 levels, and only 2 Sonics to play them with, Sonic Generations is short, but rightly so. The challenges become a little more cumbersome and tricky towards the end, and the final bosses are a teeth gnashing nightmare, but they are at least beatable. With 90 challenges to play and time trial modes to master some players will get tons out of the end game, but most users will be satisfied to put down the game after the final foe is foiled. I certainly am, and it’s an amicable separation, for £20 I felt I got what I paid for, and the game seems to breathe a sigh of relief that I’m asking no more of it.
As Sonic games go, Generations is a fun tribute. It remixes its ancestry but adds little to the series other than a recognition of when to bow out. Classic Sonic was fun to see again, but I doubt he’ll be back and it’s perhaps better that way, he’s had his day and now it’s his older, more jaded self that has to prove his worth. Modern Sonic is not redeemed by this title, and the later levels remind you that he still has his fair share of issues. But maybe he can move on, maybe someday we’ll get that 9/10 Sonic game that blows us away. This, though, is not that game, but it seems it was never meant to be. Short, silly and satisfying, Sonic Generations is a snacky game, not an epic event, and it’s nice to see something that knows its limitations. No melodrama, no over the top score, a fun run through the past of one of gaming’s most contentious icons and then off home with a smile on your face. It’s a better tribute than it ought to be.

Fills the void Sega left in my heart when the broke Sonic's spine over their knee during that boardroom meeting.

Good roguelike game, with cheap price and good replayability.
However the game can become repetitive when you know all the mechanics ...
But the experience is recommended especially for the game ambiances.

Years later, I've had more fun with a $3($1 if it goes on sale!) game with its ~$6 expansion than some $30+ games I've owned.
Despite being a more traditional roguelike, OWH is a lot more accessible than ascii roguelikes. Featuring some simple but readable graphics, it's also not too difficult. With a lot of replayability through multiple endings, multiple difficulties, classes, and challenges, it's a simple game that'll provide a lot of hours of gameplay.
The art is a bit anime but it's pretty toned down. I don't think anybody will really strongly hate it.
For gameplay, it's a pretty well balanced game. Obviously as a roguelike theres a degree of inventory management and there aren't many instances where I felt like the game deprived me of a resource leading to me losing only because of RNG. All the classes are unique enough to give each a different playstyle, a pirate has different strategies than a swordmaster, a hero can take on enemies differently than a bard will.
There's also a surprisingly deeper story to the demon lord and the darkness, it really never is the highlight of the game over saving the world, but there are some more hidden endings.
I'd strongly recommend anybody who enjoys roguelikes or even wants to get started to try OWH. It provides a perfect mix of difficulty for people who want something to ease into playing roguelikes, and people who are masochistic enough to seriously enjoy the hardest difficulty. And with how low the price is, it's really not a tough choice to just pick it up.
The expansion OWH+ is also recommended as it effectively triples content through new npcs to meet, more endings, new items, rebalancing, a new postgame mechanic(Which is more just more QoL stuff), and improving QoL/UI.

This is an easy-to-learn roguelike based on the idea that the left edge of the screen is some sort of Darkness that is always creeping to the right.  You have to stay ahead of it by crossing a mostly randomized landscape -- you start in the grasslands, but can move on to places like deserts or volcanic regions, each with their own twist on exploring and fighting.
You have a limited number of turns until the Demon Lord comes after you, so while you're running away from the darkness you encounter tiny forts with treasure, enemies to fight, townspeople to talk to or trade with, etc.
The farther you get and better you do, the more you can pass on to your next playthrough, get permanent upgrades, or unlock new character classes.
One Way Heroics is tough but not absurdly punishing, and the limitation on where you can go (not too far up or down, but always being pressured to go right) helps keep you on track instead of wandering aimlessly.  I felt that this encouraged repeated playthroughs without being frustrating -- I usually got a decent sense of advancement/accomplishment from a session.
The standard price is, what, under $5?  I'd say it's worth that, but it's often a lot cheaper during sales (as I write this, it's $1.74, and I've seen it for under $1.00).  If the idea sounds at all decent, add it to your wishlist and grab it next time it's under a buck.  Or just grab it now.

One of the best games I have played in a while, certainly faithful to the Shadowrun spirit and a great start for those who don't know the universe.

It's hard to recommend this game if you're coming from the previous releases. These games have always been about the narrative but the pacing in Hong Kong is really off. Imagine if every text in the prior games were extended about three or four times in length, that is this game. Extended Edition indeed.

I loved Returns, and Dragonfall is amazing, and Hong Kong follows in a similar vein and this might be my favourite yet. They kept the permanent team of companions that you can get to know, including your character’s estranged brother which I thought was a great extra connection to rope you into the story surrounding the two of you from the start. The other members of the team, some of which you pick up on the way, are also interesting, and surprisingly engaging from a text based narrative.
You never really lament the lack of voice acting; the writing really does do the characters, story and the environment justice on its own, as long as you are comfortable reading as much as you have to. As per usual, I’m not a great fan of the hacking mechanic, but I’m notoriously bad as timing myself around three other moving things and not being seen. But that’s just my short comings and not a reflection of the game at all.
The artwork is gorgeous as always, and I’d love some of the street scenes on my wall at home. I’ve always loved Jon Everist’s music and Hong Kong’s soundtrack is no different, it’s beautiful and lends to the setting perfectly.  All in all, I can’t find fault with this game that isn’t my own personal preferences, and wouldn’t necessarily bother other players, depending on their own likes and dislikes.
If you haven’t played this, I strongly recommend you do. Whether you buy full price or wait for a sale is entirely up to you, but I don’t think you’d regret it either way to be quite honest.

Hello WoWS, tempted in by the loving care given to real historical ships I thought, hell, what's the harm in giving it a go.
100 hours later I'm addicted. The only game I've ever played where I choose full PvP every time. In over 300 battles so far I've yet to see anyone do anything other than take the game seriously and try to help their team, and the rants in the ingame chat are simply non-existent for the most part.
It's also anti-twitch, this is moves played out over minutes not seconds, and the joy of pulling it off, and the slow agony of getting it wrong and knowing you're doomed, all adds to a superb atmosphere.
A special mention too to the way the game opens up modes and sections as you progress through your first hours, never overwhelming, always exciting, and perfectly paced.
Also, loot crates done right imo. You can't buy them, it's not hard to earn at least one per day after 1-2 battles, and in 4 weeks I've had two super containers drop containing real world valuable items.
Finally, no pay to win. Yes, you can pay to advance quicker (premium increasing XP and Credits awarded) but all premium ships come with drawbacks to balance them out (just check the wiki for each). Nothing is a game winner by default, and yes a day one player can buy a high tier ship and jump into 'end game' battles but they won't have fun and they won't do it for long. The road to success, and the fun of the game, is learning to fight effectively through the tiers.
If you acknowledge the learning curve and take the time to learn how to play each class you're interested in at each level, there is a ridiculous amount to do here, with every battle unique, and a ton of campaigns and time limited events to focus on, what's not to love?

At one point I was into this game, edging on Tryhard. It was an amazing game. I put very much emphasis on
.
During the winter sale a year or two back I purchased this "unique" title, I was nervous and hoping for a new game I could play for hours on end without getting bored and this caught my eye.
Blade Symphony; or BS for its shorter possibly literal term, was the game that occupied much of my time.
As any gamer I was raring to go, but stopped as I played the Turtorial to grasp the basics. Only to be thoroughly confused at the poor quality of the walkthrough. Regardless I pushed on, ignoring the poor walkthrough eager to test my mettle against other players, which I did. Over and over I lost, and sometimes won by learning the ways of the game on the fly or browsing YouTube for the in-depth explanations of mechanics and gameplay that the game so thoroughly lacked. But I knew that I wouldn't win right off the bat, not without much,
practice and failure.
This game is not for the easily disuaded. For you will be deterred by the complexity of the game, and even the most smallest of mechanics will be difficult to grasp. Unless you persevere and learn by trial and error for sometimes the longest of times as I and other have. The learning curve is immense and only those who want to succeed, will.
Months had past, and I had become regular on BS. Frequently I would marvel at new ways to play, new tips and tricks that gave me that edge in a time of need. Or playing with new-made friends, enjoying the time spent together.
But this is a community that is rancid with poison and toxic behaviors. People acting like immature internet teenagers, threats, put-downs, and flatout hostility is a common thing. Browse the forums, look to the past as they do not, and learn from it, as they
do not.
So I left BS, only to return having heard that changes were made a few months after my departure. Only to see that the game I had enjoyed to an extent, was rendered virtually garbage in my eyes. Nothing had changed, things weren't better. The game wasn't balanced as it should, and it never was. Nor will it
be if appropriate steps are taken.
I cherish the time I spent there and I always will, but it is clouded by memories of frustration and forced ignorance towards sour behavior.
Overall Summary:
Gameplay - Fun at first, Interesting and unfinished, repetitive reletively soon and difficult as Hell if you aren't committed.
Community - Terrible. Aside from the few who aren't. You know who you are :)
Developers - Learning, as all should. But never act /  learn enough with / from the knowledge given.

The videos make the game look polished, finished, and requiring skill to play.  In reality, the game is nothing like that.  Yes, the graphics look good, but the rest of the game is pretty horrible.  They have you run through a tutorial on how the mechanics of the sword dueling goes.  They somewhat explain how the different styles work.  Then they throw you against AI to let you try them out.  Afterwards, you are left to go find a match and test your metal against other players.  Finding a match is a bear and because the matches support multiple contestants competing in a 1:1 battle, you usually find yourself sitting around spectating for a good portion.  Horrible matchmaking aside, that's not even the worst part.
The game mechanics you learn from the tutorial do not translate well against other human players.  Against AI who react and use dictated techniques the gameplay is fine.  But against users who can change styles, combo attacks, cancel actions, and can move anywhere of their own free will, it's VERY different.   Half the time you find yourself against people who are new (not their fault) and who rage over "cheap moves", which are really just the usage of the different "styles" to counter other styles (which is a game mechanic).  The other half are people who have realized that they can do things like cancel a combo at a certain time and instead choose a single move.  This means there's no consistency in the dueling.
The game sounds awesome in theory, but when they executed their ideas, they did so poorly and without proper testing (I assume, otherwise they released the game knowing of the issues and thought breaking the mechanics they set up was a good idea).  It's really not worth the money.  I picked the game up with a friend and even between the two of us, we had a hard time having fun with the game without mixing in other players.  The second you do, the game becomes even more miserable.

Remembering my early days playing Sonic 1, Sonic 2 and Sonic 3 & knuckles this game was SPOT ON with bringing back that nostalgic and great experience. Hell, this game even exceeds that level of quality (except for MAYBE sonic 2).
Soundtrack 8/10, The music just fits in so well with the flow of gameplay, it also fits the theme of the level perfectly!
Story 7/10, The story is decent but has plotholes that needs to be filled in, still interesting enough for me to keep my cutscene skipping habit away.
Graphics design 9/10, the placement of colors is a very fine work of art, and this game did a fine job of it, the detail in the animations (such as the animation for grabbing a ladder while moving horizontally) and the colorful artwork makes this game eye candy.
Gameplay 9.5/10 The different characters almost changes the way you play the game when you change characters, it gives the game lots of replayability. The boss battles require timing yet they are relativley fast placed and the graphics design really draws you into the game. The movement and combat abilities...just feel right and goes in synergy with the game's platform-ness, would be a perfect score if you could grab ledges though! Freedom Planet is a 2D action-platformer that borrows a lot from 16-bit SEGA, Treasure, and Capcom games, but manages to feel fresh and unique through clever design, a folded-in story experience, and obviously a lot of thought put into the game's excellent design.
Freedom Planet tells the story of a group of previously rogue animals, Sash Lilac and Carol Tea, who find themselves involved as one of the few with the knowledge that their home planet's being invaded by an alien overlord, Arktivus Brevon, and his army, who are after a stone of great power that rests on their planet, the Kingdom Stone. Getting involved with two other animals, Milla Basset and Torque, the four of them team-up to try and save the world.
The voice acting of the game takes a bit to get used to at first, but in the end the actors did good on delivering on their roles, and what I pretty much expected to be a pretty lackluster tale tacked onto the game actually provided characters I did end up caring about, developed through the course of the game, and even got pretty emotionally touching, dark, but with the right amount of humor thrown in to keep it entertaining. However, if you don't care at all about the story, when starting a game you can choose to play 'Classic Mode', which lets you play through all the stages with no story whatsoever.
Freedom Planet features three playable characters, Lilac, Carol, and Milla, all of who control and play completely differently. Lilac is the most straight-forward character, with a focus on speed and acrobatic ability. She can dash madly through stages and will be a favorite of those who have an inner speed demon. She does a variety of beat-em up style combos with slices and kicks for enemies, and uses a charge meter for a variety of her swirl and dash attacks. Carol is slower than Lilac by default, but when she collects gas from stages, she gets the ability to ride a motorbike, which she can use to do a number of spin attacks, wheelies, drive up walls, and a lot more. However, even when off her bike, she can be tactful, with a dagger with longer reach and damage than Lilac's attacks, a jump dash, wall jump, and can use certain devices in stages Lilac can't. Milla is the slowest of the crew, and needs to be played the most tactfully. She can't attack enemies directly easily, but is very good on the defense. She can fly using her ears, summon a green cube at any time which she can throw, use to collect and pick-up nearby objects like bombs, or generate a barrier shield with she can use to defend from attacks. And when she breaks her shield, it forms a laser that delivers high damage to enemies.
All three characters go through mostly the same stages, but there are a few stages that are exclusive to each character and some stages that two characters may visit while the other will go to their own unique stage. It's very interesting to see how all three tackle the same stages very differently, however.
Most may expect the game on first glance to be a Sonic-clone, the game started development as a Sonic the Hedgehog fan game and has been in development for about three years. However, while playing what I was most reminded of was games by Treasure, such as Gunstar Heroes. The Sonic influence is definitely there, but this game forms itself as a beast all its own through its own unique level design, bigger focus on combat and stage gimmicks, and constantly escalating gameplay.
The level design is absolutely ace and really impressed me. The stages are unique, fun, and challenging, while both building up difficulty slowly but surely while also introducing a number of new situations and mechanics. Most stages feature completely different enemies and stage gimmicks, but manage to really use them in ways you get familiar with them quickly and then go all-out, which feels natural and progressive despite each stage having a high number of unique gimmicks. You'll do everything from climbing from spike traps, riding disco-ball Ferris Wheels, avoiding drills and kicking them into walls to bypass them, jumping between missiles to get from airship to airship, swimming alongside and avoiding missiles from a submerged submarine, and a lot, lot more. Stages are usually actually fairly meaty, being of pretty decent length and with many multiple paths to take through almost all of them.
Several times through most stages you'll fight a number of bosses, usually 2-5 before the stage is up. And they deserve particular mention, as the boss fights are challenging, fun, creative, and feature both strategic yet satisfying encounters that come in a large variety. In a single early stage, you'll fight a golem made of blocks you've been pushing around, a skeletal chicken, a vehicle with a devastating iron claw, and a giant pray mantis with a T-Rex roar, and that again is only in a single level.
And this all goes to an extremely awesome and rocking soundtrack that delivers something like a mixture of a Treasure and SEGA soundtrack from the 90s. Each stage has two different songs for the two different halves, and there are a number of boss and cinematic songs through the course of it as well.
Honestly speaking, this is a very solid platformer. It has a good amount of optional content, from a training dojo stage in time attack to collectible trading cards you can find in stages and a variety of challenging achievements,  to replayability with the three very different characters with unique stages to each of them. It is a lot of fun to play from start to finish, and backs itself with some great style, design, and a pretty good story. The end of the game is actually pretty challenging, even on normal difficulty, and this game may feature in my opinion some of the best bosses to ever grace a platformer.
If you like platformers, and can get over the fact the game features anthropomorphic animals, this game is excellent in its own right. Its not merely a clone of anything, it's a solid indie release and maybe one of the best indie platformers to come out in some time. If you liked SEGA's and Treasures platforming games of the 90s, you need to try this game out.

I had never heard of this game until a friend recommended it to me. I have had lots of fun with the game so far, and I'm really loving what it has to offer. The sprite animations are really well done, and there are a lot of them, making the characters have far more personality than I expected.
I was expecting more of a Sonic clone based on how Lilac's levels appeared to play out during the video for this game, however; I got more than that. I feel the game combines elements of Sonic the Hedgehog and Rocket Knight, and while those comparisons are fair and easily made from a first impression, the longer the game goes on, you can see how the developers built off of those designs and were able to create their own unique personality with the game.
The voice acting itself is cheesy, and it may be hard for some to bear, but even this gives the game charm, and I can identify each character through their voices and traits. It is cheesy and over-the-top at times, but I've grown to love it. It's also nothing worse than you would encounter in any Sonic game.
Also, I want to make a nod towards the battle system. It's simple and fun, and it makes the boss battles in the game engaging and enjoyable. Some say the platforming is easy and the bosses are hard, and I just do not agree with this. The platforming isn't the hardest since you can fly through a level and not worry about falling to your death, but there are definitely some tricky parts in later stages. And bosses are mostly pattern memorizations. They do require timing and skill, but after taking the time to learn how their attacks play out, they are quite enjoyable to fight, and add even more to the game. I guess what I'm trying to say is that I don't see why boss fights being a challenge is a bad thing. Call me an old-timer or old-school gamer, but I like it when boss fights are a challenge, and they aren't just flashy set-pieces meant to be defeated in one life.
I will say, one boss in particular reminded me of a fight from the game Mischief Makers back on the N64, and that only makes me love this game even more.
Try out the demo if you're not sure. Look up some more reviews and videos on the game, but I am definitely not regretting my purchase.

Modern Sonic is broken by design and no game illustrates this better than Generations.
The game is structured between traditional 2D-ish Jump'n'Run levels and the 3D high speed chases introduced in Sonic Adventure (or even the Sonic 2 Bonus levels, if you're really nitpicky). The traditional levels are a blast to play. Ingenious level design, fair challenges and new ideas around every corner that mix gameplay up just enough to be interesting while preserving the core of the experience. It always "feels" like a Sonic game.
The "modern" stages, however, drown under the sheer amount of bells and whitles Sonic Team had to add to keep the levels from feeling too samey. Notable Exceptions are Rooftop Run and Green Hill Zone, which come the closest to being enjoyable on their own. Modern Sonic throws new mechanics at you every new Level to keep you interested, and it works for the most part. Compared to the 2D-Stages though (which remain mostly the same all the way though), it is a desaster.
The Main game is also a bit too short, with only 9*2 levels and a few Boss battles thrown in between (with the final boss being the most disappointing and frustrating battle in the entire game). It is a fun title. The big renaissance of Sonic Games, however, it is not.

I will give an honest review of the current state of the game from my point of view. Have been playing on and off since the day it launched in 2008.
FIRST OFF IF YOU ARE CONSIDERING THIS GAME FOR YOUR KID IT HAS HALF FRONTAL NUDITY (BREASTS). ITS MA RATED!
I play on Fury PvP under the name Laethiel I have made updates and changes to my old review, see below.
PVE side
You can level to 80 but along the way you will have a very hard time finding groups for any low level dungeons on the pvp server Fury, You will have better luck on the the crom pve server. Unles you play on EU prime time. They have a bit higher population on Crom. I had to power level my buddy to 80 on Fury due to all the missed content because of lack of groups. At end game (Level 80) you can do 6 man dungeons which aren't bad and are quite rewarding. and you will be able to do 24 man raids.. If you can find a raid.. on Fury PvP raids are rare or non existent , on crom they are somewhat more frequent since pve is all they do. They have since added a Raid finder which i hear mixed reviews about. Sign up and join a pub queue for raiding.
The 24 man raid. These generally consist of 4 groups of 6 combined to form a 24 man "raid". Most bosses are tank and spank time sinks with need/greed loot rolls that are open to all regardless of class. This leads to ninja looting on occasion. Most raids will be very controlling in dispersal of loot. There are on average 2-3 pieces of epic gear that drop per raid boss and raid instances can vary in how many bosses. from 1 to 8. Raids can take a few hours to complete so set aside some spare time on raid night, especially progression raids. expect alot of elitist attitude and assholism. and don't be surprised if you come away completely empty handed.. alot... I raided for 6 months once to get a piece of tier 2 gear. PvE Can be very Grindy.
The 6 man dungeon, There are many variations of these. from revamped low level dungeons called "unchained mode" to the khitai expansion pack dungeons. They are mostly quick and like i said very rewarding. I would recommend these starting out for quick epic gear. Problem is you have to be subscribed to play most content in the game so dont go in expecting a free ride, this game is hardly "free to play". You will find yourself having a difficult time getting to max level as a free to play member.
Free to play model: Improving slowly. you are limited to 10 gold currency,  You can do all pve and pvp content provided you own the content. Festival,minigames and world pvp. Baby steps
Global chat - A fun time if you have a thick skin.. Think barrens chat in WoW. This can be worse. But they do ban people for blatant non political correctness like using the N word or spewing homophobic slurs etc. I rather enjoy it. This alone kept me coming back for years.
The PvP side
The PvP Festival
The pvp festival, which pvp players enjoy more than our pve ?????tain counterparts, consists of daily pvp zones that switch around at approx. 8pm est every day to a new zone. In these zones all pvp is encouraged and guards will not intervene! this is great if you're like me, bad if you're not... plus you get pvp daily quests you can do to get pvp xp which is ok.
The monthly event.
This feature takes place on the 3rd week of every month starting on Tuesdays and lasting for 7 days. It takes place in one randomly picked zone (it cycles through 5 zones) and you and your friends must fight for objectives such as control domination, kill count, and the like. the rewards are pretty good. This event draws crowds of old and new players alike so get into a group/guild for it. They have group dm, solo dm, group domination. and chosen of ghullah in which you become an epic boss and try to score as many kills as you can before you die . They are at random locations in the zone and happen every 20 mins or so. There is no real notification system,youll just have to keep your eyes open.
As for the rest of PvP, You have open world pvp which comes with ganking (Fury) and all that fun and now mostly happens in the daily pvp zone due to there being no guards. You have minigames you can queue up for which consist of 3 x 6v6 ctf maps, 1 x 6v6 dm map where you can smash the enemy spawn and end the match quickly and 1 x 12v12 domination map which half your team goes afk most of the time because win or lose you still get a token which you need to buy pvp gear. But you get more if you win. Problem is there jut aren't enough people left playing to even get minigames or world pvp.
PvP Balance - It's like paper rock scissors.
The minigame queue which i will describe below is horrible. The "balance algorithm" they supposedly installed in 2010 or so cannot seem to balance teams. So you'll end up on a good team or a lousy team. One team will have all the high ranking pvp players and healers while your team will be all low ranking players and no heals, aka cattle. This is an ongoing problem. Deal with it. Update: Lately teams haven't been too bad.
Minigames - The thing is in age of conan you CAN'T join pvp minigames with a group or a friend/friends. Unless you are doing a full 6v6 tournament like a premade match and you have 2 full groups ready to go.. The public queue is completely random. You CANNOT decide who is on your team. This will induce episodes of rage. Granted there is a 50% chance you'll get your friend on your team.. They will never change this aspect. We have tried and failed to convince them for years that making it a random queue is a bad idea. They are afraid of premade stomping pugs which to be honest i would rather deal with.
PvP Gear dependance is fairly high in pvp but having high gear wont make you good. AAs (Alternate Advancement Feats - do your own research) also play a role. They have lowered the requirements to obtain pvp gear significantly so it's easier than ever to get in the game. By pvp 3-4 you are already a pvp contender and it took me and my buddy less than a week and a half of steady pvp.
Sieges (48v48)noone sieges. Forget about this aspect. If you try to siege a battlekeep youll have a carebear consortium allying to defend it from you. Not to mention it costs a fortune in game currency to launch an attack.
The expansion pack "Rise of the Godslayer" no longer requires a sub to use so this is good. You no longer need this to get access to the AA feats tree, also good.
Guilds -- It takes a long time to get off the ground and this game rewards large guilds not small ones. You can make a small guild but you'll never get anywhere without a guild city and those take time and or money and lots of manpower. To put it bluntly a guild consisting of say 200+ active unique members farming resource nodes daily would take 6 months to a year to build a guild city to full tier 3. . Some people sell these guild cities that are abandonded... I recommend buying one in this case. Again this game rewards zerg numbers. small guilds get crapped on usually. There is no alliance system and no faction system. You cannot kill guildies but you can kill anyone else.

This game is just too old without any love shown to it. For example, there is not a vertical sync option in the game, the UI does not scale to higher resolutions, and it continues to have a ton of junk loot with even a found boss mob alligator dropping just an item to be sold for a small amount of cash. It's an interesting historical look at MMOs though as some of the game mechanics show off what used to be acceptable. For example, the voice-acting takes place only in dialogue scenes instead of happening during the action to provide narration and context to the world, so instead of enhancing the experience, it interrupts it. Also, they've pulled back heavily on the gore that was the most fun thing about the game. I used to get ridiculous, sick kill effects, but the kills for my character were all boring and standard. Plus, it used to have the maiden you find in the tutorial be chained up with breasts exposed but now they've covered her up. This game's mature (and Conan appropriate) edge was what made it stand out. . .  I'm amazed they've lost the good bits and haven't seemed to have any engineers working on keeping the game engine fresh and viable. . .   but then this is a game that launched incomplete, so maybe their time has been focused on completing the game. . .  or maybe since it is 8 years old, they're just milking it with a few employees and keeping it open for fans. However, if you're returnign to see if it has improved, I'm afraid the opposite is true.

For a game that was born below the WoW shadow , where every other MMO wanted to clone the giant to get a piece of the cake, FC decided to make something diferent, oriented to the adult players, based on the world made by Robert E. Howard, with all the lore, and the feeling of the conan universe.
Yes, they made a terrible launch, but now, the game is different, after all this years, you can set all that hatred and disapointment away for a moment and give it another try. i can't asure you wont be disapointed, but i speak in my own experience, that since i played this game for the first time, couldn't see another MMO the same, and i've tried a lot of them.
what you can expect is:
-a unique combat system
-an adult oriented enviroment
-a different kind of fantasy
-boss mechanics that actually need coordination and comunication
-beautiful graphics, for a 8yo game
-amazing soundtrack, fitting to conan lore
-blood
-real character customization, no "meta" builds, that everyone uses leaving every other option unusefull for the end game
-Fun PvP, where skill is above gear
-a game that you can play with limited time and still get to participate in the endgame, but with a semi hard learning curve for each class
-a mature international playerbase, you wont find a lot of teenagers like other games around there.
yes the game has many flaws, but surely, it deserves a try.

Graphical Appearence[8/10]: It's nice, funky, new looking graphics with a lot of fun and color. The chararcters and costumes have a funny looking texture too. The landscapes are great. My favouite world was the 5th (BIT.TRIP)
Sounds/Music[9/10]: Scenario-fitting music and sounds. Sometimes really calm, sometimes really speedy. And the sounds are just great. Really good job.

Story[5/10]: I think the story could've been better. It was a little dull to me. I didnt really knew what was going on. Make the 3rd game's story better :).
Gameplay[6/10]: For my side, I've played with the keyboard, since I don't have a controller and oh man.... It was really bad. I've always mixed up the buttons(A,S,D,W,H,J,K) and it was not fun. I can only blame myself for it, I will buy a new controller. But in the end I've experienced the controls. I'd say though the moves were pretty nice, and it was a lot of fun playing it. The obstacles had a nice variety, too
Uniqueness[8/10]: I think you can't be indifferent with this game. You either love it, or you either hate it. And this virtue gives it a really nice feel.
Difficulty[2/10]: This is one of if not the hardest games I've ever played. I might be a n00b, but sometimes i had a really big struggle playing it on QUITE EASY gamemode. It isn't unfinishable though. I feel SMB is easier than this ;-;.
Characters[10/10]: Very nice variety of characters. I died at the costume called "F♥♥♥ing Turkey Suit". Has more than 20 costumes which you can choose from. Has 7 unique characters. It's really funny.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Pros:
+character and costume variety
+beautiful and funny landscapes and graphics
+lots of unique moves
+lots of unique obstacles
+collectable things
+funny gamemodes
Cons:
-hard bosses
-hard difficulty
-sometimes repeatable landscapes
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall[8/10]: I think you should try it out. It's great fun.

It's a great collection, and one that should be considered by Disney fans and Gamers alike. The collection itself gets about an 9/10. DuckTales - 10/10. The game is a classic. It controls perfectly, the levels are mostly well designed, and the soundtrack is godly. Plot isn't much.. even for a game on the NES. There's a few cheap moments (or expensive i guess), but with skill, they can be avoided. There's even a few secrets that i still haven't discovered probably. Like i said, it's a classic and is a must play
Chip and Dales Rescue Rangers - 10/10. While not as good as DuckTales, the game is still a classic. There's a lot more levels, but they can be short. There's a lot more Plot going around, although still not much. The real highlight of the game is the 2 Player Co-op. 1 player controls chip, 1 player controls dale. Enough said. The soundtrack is also something worth listening to, it's pretty great.
DuckTales 2 - 9/10. Small nitpick, but why couldn't this be on the Super Nintendo? I don't see why it was on the NES. oh well. The game is great, but doesn't surpass the first DuckTales. The game adds a little bit more plot, and fixes a lot of the bugs and glitches the first game had. You can just tap B while in air to perform the pogo cane move now instead of holding down and b, and you can get cane upgrades. The shop system is pretty neat, although some items are pricy, The music, while good, isn't great. The only songs i found pretty memorable was Glomgold's ship and Niagra Falls. Also, why do you lose all of your money when you die? Yeah, you can buy the safe item, but you have to buy it every time you beat a level. and why does Gyro call Scrooge "Uncle Scrooge?". Overall, the game is great, just not amazing
Darkwing Duck - 8.5/10 - Put it simple, It's a barebones Mega Man game. It plays VERY similar to Mega man 5. The plot is A LOT more detailed, great soundtrack, and most villians from the show are here. You don't take their powers though. DW has a gas gun, and he can have some nifty powerups for the gun, although he can only hold 1 at a time. you can also hang on platforms, which is a game changer and can be used for nice tricks. put it simple. It's Mega Man 5, add Disney Characters, Take away about 2 levels, make the levels less memorable, and add better music. That's basically Darkwing Duck on NES.
Chip and Dales Rescue Rangers 2 - 7/10. This game came out in 1994, a year after DuckTales 2 came out. Again, why was this on NES? anyways, The game isn't great.. it's just good. Think of it as, It's C&DRR 1, but less fair, an OK soundtrack, not so fun bosses, and too much plot. Put it simple, it's fun (especially 2 player), but i'd rather play RR 1
TaleSpin - 6/10. This game is either ya love it or ya hate it. and i don't think it's fun. The music is eh.. not memorable, but nice to listen while playing the game. The game doesn't play like a Run & Gun game or a Platformer, it plays like a shooter, which might seem a perfect idea for TaleSpin game. The outcome was just... off. The plane flip system can either make your day or kill you. 70% of the time, it killed me. Some of the levels don't cater to this gimmik. The bosses... OH THE BOSSES. They are just unfair. 90% of the time i felt like whenever i died, i felt like it was the game, not me. I'd Skip this one if you don't like shooters.

I often wonder if the reason I think I like a game is simple nostagia. So, I picked up this set of games from when I was younger to see if they held up. And...they are even
than I remember! Here's a quick run-through of them:
- This game is classic and is STILL so much fun to play. While the remake is out there (and is a great game in its own right), the orginal is still an amazing, fun and well-designed game.
- While the level design is not QUITE as good as the original, the addition of three upgrades makes up for it.
- This is another great game. While it seems a bit odd, the weapons you use are only what you can pick up and throw. Picking up and box and ducking lets you hide in the box, but enemies that are defeated by throwing a box at them will hit the box and still be defeated. It's funny at first, but it becomes a valuable attack very quickly.
- Same as DuckTales 2, really.  The level design is not quite as good as the first game, but it is more of the same, so still a great game.
- My favorite of the cartoons when I was a kid (and still a great show to go back and watch as an adult). This feels more like a MegaMan game than anything else and that is not a bad thing. This one is probably a little tougher than the others. You can pick up a different ammo for your gas gun but, like Castlevania, you can only hold one at a time.
- The weakest of the games, really. But still a pretty good one. This is more of a shoot-em-up and the controls are not quite as clean as the other games. However, it is still a good game.
All the games play almost identical to the orginal releases. While it's not quite 100%, it's close enough to let you play the games just like they were almost 30 years ago.
Chiptune beauty. It is incredible how good these songs sounded then and they still sound good today. Plus, you can play the music for each game from the menu.
This is a great collection of games. I got it on sale for $9 and it is easily worth that. Is it worth $20? For me, yes it probably would have been. But I rememebr playing most of these games as a kid and the nostalgia makes it well worth that cost. If you don't have a history with these games, maybe try to catch it on a sale.

Freedom Planet is a wonderful, charming, cute, epic, and endearing platformer that harkens back to Sega CD, Playstation 1, or early 90s PC platformers like Sonic CD. I didn't even know this game existed, let alone the amount of time it took for the developers to make this game! Now that I have my hands on this game, I can tell you that it might be one of the best 2D platformers of all time. Now, Shovel Knight deserves this honor as well, but it is nowhere near as fast paced as Freedom Planet! This game is an adrenaline rush of fun and excitement from start to finish!
With three differing playstyles from the three differing characters, you can play through this game in a myriad of ways. The levels are fairly large, and have multiple paths, allowing plenty of exploration. Secrets are everywhere, and there are tons of crystal shards to collect which are as addictive as coins or rings! You can also play other game modes, such as Time Attack or the "Target Minigame" included within that one.
I never found a dull moment during these adventures either, there was always something to smile about during the surprisingly epic storyline (such as this avian guard who always lets out a quack at the end of a scene). The characters, although they appear as cute as can be, are butt kickers in every sense of the word, and don't get me started on "Lord Brevon"! The voice acting is mixed, but I loved it, and it had a lot of heart very much like the characters themselves. It was a pure JOY following the epic journey of Lilac and her friends to stop an evil alien overlord! It truly was!
Freedom Planet's grand and varied adventure is a feast for the eyes or ears. The visuals remind me of a cross between a SNES game and a Sega Genesis game. The music is EXCELLENT! Absolutely memorable tunes are at every turn, with the "mid boss" and "major boss" tunes being some of my favorite tunes. With a soundtrack so incredible and fitting, you will be dancing in your seat as you play!
There really isn't much I can complain about, besides a few bugs. I am sure a few jerks are going to say this game is "way too girly" or "too cute". There also have been criticisms about this game being way too much like a Sonic game, but if anything it builds upon what made Sonic great AND more. You don't have to play Lilac if you think the game is too much like a Sonic game! If anything, the game feels like a loving homage to 90s gaming, with a story full of heart. It might be cheesy and corny, but it's full of heart.
Freedom Planet, in a nutshell, is a fantastic little indie gem. It has way more value than it seems, and is an adventure worth embarking on over and over again.

This remains to date the only game I have ever pre-ordered. I did that on the strength of the previous two outings, "Shadowrun Returns" (which, while it had its issues, I thank forever for introducing me to this preposterously perfect fictional universe) and "Dragonfall" (which included a tighter story and a home crew as well as the new setting of the Flux State of Berlin). But "Hong Kong" easily blows both out of the water in several respects in terms of the story.
First, you DON'T start the game as a shadowrunner. You fall into it while trying to make heads or tails of what your foster father was talking about in his last message to you. Before you get to that point, you're labeled a terrorist, on the run from the cops and have to rely on a notorious fixer to provide the backup you need to keep going. How your character reacts to that is up to you. Second, your character is much more plugged into the plot than in the previous two outings. Your character comes with an intimate backstory, regardless of what character you create at the start (though, again, how you react to your circumstances is up to you). From start to finish, you're intricately plugged into every aspect of the story in terms of relationships to your fellow characters, which you can expand upon with dialogue and the "loyalty" missions with your crew. Third, the shopkeepers are more than just handy places to get supplies you need. More than a few have some interesting backstories of their own you can pursue and possible get Karma from. Finally, you're up against one of the scariest things in the whole Shadowrun universe. I'll hold my piece on the nature of the threat. However, I would highly encourage you to go by the magic shop (even if your character doesn't use magic) for details on it through the gameplay.
The game mechanics are much the same as they were before (though I have to say that the character upgrade screen is the most refined of the three games in terms of breaking down what can be upgraded), including combat. You either love it or hate it at this point. Me, the turn-based combat brings up fond memories of the original Fallout games and Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magickal Obscura, so it's no problem for me. Besides, what other game can you have a drone with a working laser cannon, a classical fireball-slinging mage, a gun-toting hardcase and a summoned elemental spirit on the same battlefield?
It is a pity we won't be seeing another Shadowrun game from HBS for the foreseeable future. But what a high note to end this series on for the time being. Oh and anyone who doesn't want the fun to end should check out the Community Hub. There is a "Caper" that is worth your time.

This game was fun for its time, but it hasn't aged well. It's a game full of cliches that comes with having Czech developers write a New York (or Empire Bay) mafia story. For starters, the timelines for the war are very loopy. Vito goes to Sicily in 1943 and then they say "a few years later, I got shot." 1947 would have been after the war ended. They then backtrack on that and say he got shot "three years" after his drop in Sicily (1946, again after the war ended). Then it says 1945 when the story begins. They really can't keep to the story.
But it's really one cliche after another. All the mobsters are New York wise guys with trademark New York accents. The story is about Vito's rise in the Empire Bay mafia scene. You can travel around Empire Bay (pretty much 1940s NYC) in between missions and do some side quests, but the story is pretty linear and it forces  you to go in a singular direction. I played this on the XBox 360 a while ago and I forget if the story forces you to reset (lose all of your weapons/cars/etc.) twice, or if that was Godfather II: The Game. Either way, it just kind of slogs along.
It is kind of fun just cruising around in Empire Bay in old-time cars that handle like giant refrigerators and listening to old-timey music on the radio with period advertisments that say smoking is good for you. It's not worth full price, even if it is $20, so just wait for it to go on sale and if you've never played it before and like a decent mafia story to burn some time, give it a play.

Mafia II is simply amazing. The gameplay, the story, and the cutscenes. The game feels like a movie and should be played and reviewed like one. I have purchased this game during the 2015 summer sale and refunded it because I didn't like it, but I bought it again and my mind was changed. Mafia II is truely a work of art and it is a gem in the open-world genre.
!!!!SPOILERS!!!!
You play as Vito, a World War II veteran who comes back to see find out his dad borrowed $2,000 when he was overseas, and his father passed leaving the debt on his family. Now, $2,000 dollars doesn't seem like much, but it's 1945, which is about $25,000 today. So, to pay it back you link up with Joe Barbaro, your childhood friend with Mob connections. After doing a car jacking and getting $400 for the car, he sees the easy money from doing hits. His mother, still want's him to work at the docks like his dad, and when he does to the docks, hes met with slave labor. When he's about to leave, Steve, one of the mobsters, says "Had enough already?" where Vito replys "I'm not going to be like my father, I can make 10 times this in a day working with Joe Barbaro." Steve replys "No guy working for Joe should be moving crates for $10, come in" Vito then gets his second job, making $100 by collecting money from dock workers. After doing some illegal hits, he meets up with Harry Tommasino, who is part of the Clemente mob family.Vito steals Ration cards and sells them, only t be ratted out and having to serve 10 years in prison. In prison he meets Leo Galante. Leo, consigliere to the Vinci family, befriends Vito and gets him 4 years off his sentence, and gets Vito into the Falcone family. Joe and Vito kill Alberto Clemente, Don of the Clemente family, after feuding and the death of Joes friend, Marty. After Vito has a nice living, his house is torched by the Irish mafia and he loses everything. He then moves into Marty's old apartment, and Henry, Joe and Vito start buying dope from the chinese and selling it in the ghetto. Henry is killed by the Chinese because he was a government agent, and the Chinese blame the Italians for the "setup". Don Vinci then kidnaps Joe to find out what went down when they we're blamed, and Vito frees him. Soon, Leo offers Vito a chance at redemption. Kill his Don, Falcone. He does this with the help of Joe. The game ends with two cars, one with Vito and Leo, and the other has Joe. The one with Joe, is in front, and it makes an unexpected turn. Vito then shouts "Where are they taking him!" and Leo replys "Sorry Vito, but Joe wasn't part of the deal", Leaving the fate of the two characters unknown, but the Mafia II community believes Joe is killed. There is then a sweeping view of Empire Bay, and then fades to black.
I was in love with Mafia II, from the radios, the story and the art style. I felt a particular bond to Vito, which a lot of people could say because he was the main character, but I can truely relate, being an Italian immigrant. I can see what the attraction of the mob was, more power, more money, and protection. Since the Italians were a hated minority, which was protraited in the game by the excessive use of "Dago" and "Wop", it only makes sense that they would choose protection within one another, and thats shown throughout the game. The gameplay felt kind of bland in the combat, the game truely shined in its driving and cineamatic appeal.
+Story
+Cutscenes
+Driving
+Gameplay
+Graphics
+Variety in cars
-Ending
-Combat feels uninspiring and a copy of GTA.
Overall, I give this game a solid 8/10 for its cineamatic appeal, yet boring combat weighs it down.

I have not played with many Star Wars games throughout my "gamer career" but what I do remember is the fond memories I have attached to Jedi Outcast. I believe it is supposed to be a sequel to Jedi Knight 1 which is the sequel to Dark Forces 1... all FPS games and very old now and completely missed out by myself.
In any case, Outcast is a blend of FPS and TPS genres. Both perspectives are available throughout the game and they determine the weaponry used to dispose of your enemies. Obviously, weapons such as blasters are for the FPS perspective while wielding your lightsaber is the easiest from a third person perspective.
The game has an excellent story and some recognisable faces appear here and there (strictly following the storyline of the trilogy from the '70s / '80s). Music is, of course, the good-old John Williams-composed score and since they are really good why would we need anything else?
The only issue with the game is that I remember playing it in FPS mode, at first, but once I obtained the lightsaber I finished the rest in TPS mode. I mean, if having a lightsaber is de rigueur in a Star Wars game then why would you want to switch back to the general assortment of weapons? Also, your lightsaber coupled with the many jedi powers available is the best way to play such a game.
The game can be difficult at times but allowing you to follow both paths (i.e. Light and Dark sides) it deserves a second walkthrough. Outcast runs on the Quake 3 engine which, years ago, was quite beautiful but now is somewhat of an obsolete engine. In any case, this is an all-time classic and you are to purchase it especially if you played it already 10 years ago. Collecting classics is always a good pastime!

Jedi Outcast's strongest point is undoubtedly combat - a mix of classic FPS and great lightsaber/force system. Some powers/weapons are obviously better than the others but on Padawan difficulty level you can pretty much play around as you like. And play around you can! Force Pull stormtrooper's rifle from his hands and watch as he runs away in panic! Grab one enemy with Force Choke and shield yourself from his friends fire! Finally, I recommend playing with a certain cheat code activated - g_saberRealisticCombat 1 - It allows you to cut apart enemies a lot more than the base game (although it's a bit buggy and results in beheaded characters screaming and other weirdness. Nothing gamebreaking though). Word of warning - it makes the game both easier and harder since it makes some hit zones an instant kill (for both player and npcs). It causes shorter, more frantic duels with Dark Jedi and can end the final battle in seconds (which is hilarious when it happens). Overall I rate the game 8.5/10 (-1,5 for all the annoyances along the way). It's not a perfect game but still loads of fun and worth it's price.

Age of Conan.  I’m not entirely sure where to start with this review.  I started playing the game in October 2015, after a friend told me that it was their go-to MMO, so I thought I would try it out.  For the age of the game itself, the graphics are not too shabby at all, and would happily put a few more modern MMOs to shame.  The downside to this comes when it’s World Boss time, and there are spells being cast, and exotic damage graphics galore, which really leech memory and induces spectacular lag.
The play-style I found clunky at first, with the need to use key combos to make attacks work, but I got used to that.  Not being able to use a mount to get around the game until level 40 was a bug-bear, especially with the sheer amount of running around maps that’s required.  The map interface is pretty poor if you want to see where you are in relation to the rest of the world as there is no button that takes you directly back to viewing the area you’re in – you need to know the name of the area you’re in and select it from a drop-down list.  Local travel merchants in-game: location names not always accurate, so if you’re new and don’t know where you’re going, it can get expensive.
Like most other MMOs I’ve played, Age of Conan has an in-game “item store”, where you can buy un-lockable chests, better mounts, un-lockable areas, etc..  Funcom (which will further be referred to as
recently “re-vamped” this, in presumably and effort to make it more snazzy.  In my humble opinion, they failed miserably.  It is now open by default when you log-in to any toon, and it pops up at random intervals, usually when you’re in the middle of fighting something vaguely important.  The prices for the items within it also seemed to change – somewhat unsurprisingly they made everything more expensive, so you get less bang for your buck.
Another of their latest “re-vamps” to the game is a daily login “reward” system.  This entails having yet another pop-up window in your face when you log into your toon, but not just the first time you log in each day, it’s there every time regardless of whether you’ve claimed your daily “reward” or not.  The “rewards” themselves are okay.
On top of this, if you’re a subscriber you also have the loyalty reward system, which is claimable from the item store, once per toon, but require you to have been subbed for different amounts of days depending on the reward being offered.  These don’t change month-to-month, and are only claimable as long are you are a subscriber.
The latest update included a number things, one of the most notable being opening up pay-to-play/purchasable areas to free-to-play players who’ve already purchased the areas, but not raising the in-game currency cap for free-to-play players.
In terms of PvP, I have no experience of this in-game, and I'm not likely to venture into it either.
Offline levels have disappeared in the lastest update too.  These were one of the perks that subscirbers could enjoy, where every few days you gained a level token you could use on a toon to level it up.
While the game's fun to play overall, I won't recommend it.

Sonic Generations is a 2D/3D platformer hybrid. Developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega, it was released in 2011, celebrating Sonic's 20th Anniversary, for the Xbox 360, Playstation 3, 3DS, and PC. It was met with good reception and came after a long string of bad Sonic games. It doesn't feature a expansive plot or any of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that other Sonic games tried to do before it. Rather, it focuses on good level design and fun platforming, making a return to earlier Sonic titles.
Sonic's world is ripped apart by this scary clock-thing (The scientific term for it), and Sonic meets with his mute (Younger?) counterpart, along with a different Tails. Together they must fix everything that broke. By running really fast. (I wish it was that easy in the real world.) The plot is really just an excuse to remix old Sonic levels and string them together. Many of the levels take inspiration from older Sonic titles, like Green Hill Zone, or City Escape. Every level has an exclusively 2D stage, played with the chubby Sonic, and a 3D-that-usually-transitions-into-a-2D-level stage, played by the "enthusiastic" Sonic, both of which are well designed and play well. (The stages, I mean. Sonic is alright if you're into that kind of thing.) The 2D platforming feels good, and the 3D play is fluid. The levels are well made, offering multiple paths to follow, depending on your skill. Do well and it's a fast, fun level. Do poorly, and it's a slow, fun level. (But you wanna go fast, right? Thought you did.)
Having never played the older Sonic games, I really enjoyed this. The platforming is good, the levels are colorful and fun, and the 2D and 3D levels offer different styles of playing that no matter which you prefer, you will have fun.

The pack contains 6 games, Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers 1 & 2, DuckTales 1 & 2, Darkwing Duck and TaleSpin, and all 6 were originally released on the NES back in the 80's and early 90's. I beat two of these as a kid, Chip 'n Dale 1 and DuckTales 1, and have played TaleSpin in the past, but only briefly. So there might be a bit of nostalgia involved here, clouding my judgement.
I'll review these in release order (as that's the order they're listed in-game, and the order I played them):
The first, and probably most well known, of the games included in this collection, DuckTales made quite a splash on the NES. Much like in MegaMan you get to pick the order you want to play the levels in, but apart from two pickups that give a permanent health increase, there's no advantage in playing the levels in any particular order.
The levels are very varied, some offering more than one path, some being more maze-like and some having more involved secrets. It's all good, and the secrets are telegraphed enough as to not feel unfair, without being overly easy to find. The level design is mostly strong, and it's fun to explore the levels to see if there are any alternative paths. And for a game released in 1989, it looks and sounds surprisingly good.
Your main attack is to jump on enemies, but with a slight twist. You can use your cane as a pogo-stick, and landing on enemies with the cane out will usually kill, or at least harm them. The pogo controls can be a bit finicky though, and this is my only real gripe with this game. Sometimes it feels like the game ignores input when trying to pogo, but this is more down to wonky controls than the game actually doing that. This was an issue with the NES original as well.
Overall, this is a very nice game, although someone with a bit of platforming experience under their belt is likely to be able to beat it in under 1h from the first time they start it. It's easy.
This game was a graphical powerhouse when it was first released, and it's the earliest game I remember people buying because of its amazing graphics. The actual game though, it's not bad. Although why does Gadget look like a zombie? As Chip or Dale you need to stop the dastardly Fatcat, who's (as always) up to no good.
You've got an overworld map in this game, and you've got some say over which levels you'll play. The layout of this map is strange though, with one level being entirely optional, and one path being longer than the other. It would have made more sense if they had just made it a traditional linear game. It's good that the level design is overall very good, and the enemies fun and varied.
You can't attack enemies directly, instead you need to pick up crates, apples and other small objects to throw at enemies. It's a nice twist on the traditional formula, and combined with how agile the characters are, Chip 'n dale is a joy to play!
Out of the 6 games in the set, this is the easiest, and it was a game I remember blasting through in an evening as a kid. It's incredibly easy, so it would probably suit a newcommer to the genre quite well.
I've heard a lot of bad said about this game over the years... and having played through it properly, I don't get it. It's a pretty good entry-level shmup, with an interesting twist.
As Baloo, who for some reason flies in the world's smallest airplane, you need to navigate a bunch of different, and very varied levels. Actually, Baloo himself seem to be hit by a shrink ray, because he's tiny compared to most of the things in the environment. While the scale makes sense for some levels, the haunted house level is just odd.
The gimmick in this game is that you can turn around. On any horizontal scrolling sections (but not vertical scrolling ones)  also reverses the scrolling, which is important for getting through a lot of tight passages. You can't flip when moving up or down, which takes a bit of getting used to, but once you're familiar with it, it does work well.
This is a very easy game (are we seeing a trend yet?), and someone who's a bit familiar with the SHMUP genre, who can get used to flipping back & forth, should be able to get through this game without seeing the game over screen even once. Easy, but still fun.
Based on Disney's counterpart to Batman, Darkwing Duck is another platformer. This time you've got a weapon, and a cape that deflects bullets. Like with DuckTales you get to chose what order you want to play the levels, though this time you get them in sets of 3. Beat the first three, and you get 3 more, and once you beat them, it's time for the final boss.
The level design is once again strong, but a bit less varied than in previous games. All the levels play roughly the same, but the game is short enough that this does not become an issue. And much like in DuckTales, the order you play them in does not really matter, apart from the fact that you get to pick up sub-weapons, like in Castlevania (you can only hold one at a time), and having the right sub-weapon can make certain sections easier (hint: stick with the Arrow one, it allows you to reach some secrets).
This game is a mild step up in difficulty, and one of the bosses was actually not easy. It's still not a hard game though, and someone who's good at the genre can still probably beat this one without ever seeing a game over screen. It's still a good game though, even if it's not one of Capcom's best.
The often overlooked sequel of DuckTales, DuckTales 2 gives us more of the same... but slightly worse. You've got a few abilities that you unlock through the levels, so the order you play them in matters a bit more here, but you can still beat any level without the right powerup.
The main letdown here is the level design. It's a bit bland. The game never becomes bad, but there's not much energy to it, if that makes any sense. They're also structured more similarly to each other than they were in the first game, giving you less variety, and they're on top of that a bit less visually distinct, even if they do still have their own personalities.
This is the first disappointment out of the set. No, it's not a bad game, but having played it, I get why it's so often overlooked. It's just not a good as the first game. Still a very easy game though.
And finally, we have Chip 'n Dale 2. Much like DuckTales 2, this is basically more of the same, but worse. At least Gadget does not look like a zombie anymore.
Gone is the overworld map, instead you need to play the games in order. And that's not a bad thing. The main issue I have with Chip 'n Dale 2 is the level design, which much like in DuckTales 2 feels bland. At no point does it become terrible, but there's not a whole lot of imagination put into the way you navigate the levels. But at least they play with the idea that you're actually a very small creature in some levels (which makes a lot more sense than when Baloo was very small). The game does improve in one area though, and that's the bosses, which are more challenging and more fun than they were in the first game.
This game is a little bit harder than the first, but still a very easy game. But it's simply not all that good. If you've got the collection, then sure, do give it a try, but it's not worth buying for this game alone.
Despite finding two of the games to not be anything special, I do think that the Disney afternoon collection is quite a nice set of games. It's a great start for people who are new to platformers, or who are just a bit rusty, but for experienced platform players, you'll probably be able to beat this in about 5h. And the price point of 20€ might be a bit too high for that.So unless you feel like you have to play these games now, wait for a sale. It's well worth 10€, but not 20€.

After finally getting through the story (extra included), I felt I needed to write a review. Now I'm sorry if my opinions go against yours, as I will be comparing this game to the other two Shadowruns.
I heavily enjoyed this game, and that is mainly because of the characters and how they were presented, occasianly going against stereotypes for the videogame industry. More often than not video games will attempt to make every corporate worker as uninteresting as usual, and scientists perfectly fine - if not happy- with crushing baby seals with the baby seal's dead mom. In shadowruns case; corporate workers have little personality because of the fact that they work or die, and the few scientists showed fear, desire for redemption, not being totally evil, etc. All of the characters had little insights to their own lives (a cop liked painting when not on the job) that while not completely fleshing out the world, it added a little bit of muscle to the structure. Shadowrun also attempts, and in my eyes, succeeds with turning over stereotypes with the things that go bump in the night (play the game or look up spoilers to understand).
I do not feel like the party member's stories can be put simply alongside the majority of the other character's stories. There is arcs, and there is an overall lighthearted feel to the relationship among the party members (thanks Gobbet). You have your brother, a very angry person. You have a rat orc, a dwarf that has memory issues, a russian, and a very smelly japanese guy in the basement as your possible companions; and I enjoyed fighting alongside and for them. I enjoy their stories very much more than to dragonfall's, because I felt that dragonfall's party members were way to happy to comply with whatever you said, barely having their own opinions being shown (there may have been moments yes, including the one member that was seeming always against what you wanted), however I do not believe that the party members are better than that of shadowrun returns.
The atmosphere, being rather depressing, is in hong kong and revolves around a contained slum that I feel is trying a little too hard to be depressing. The hud area where you get your jobs I liked, with the vendors (the ones that I remembered to talk to) showing character in little ways, but not to sublty that I didn't notice. The story (as accustom to Harebrained Schemes' works) is very good and still felt your decision mattered.
Now I'm going to get to my problems with the game as I let Hong Kong pull back up its pants and I go get a bottle of mouthwash. It felt like there was either the option to be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or be a funny guy which even though I wanted to be the funny guy it didn't feel quite right with me. And the lighthearted tones set sometimes felt like it had bad timing and was forced sometimes. And since this game is text based mainly, one of the worst things you can do is have a typing error (I only noticed 2, one in regular game and one in bonus) which jarred me out of immersion for a second.
Overall I heavily enjoyed Shadowrun Hong Kong, thanks Harebrained Schemes for allowing me to actually like a videogame character compared to laughing as my shooter companion glitches into a wall.
TLDR: Magical Noodle Machine and cosmic horror oh my, how much did I love this game. Now hopefully I didn't have any cuts in my mouth as Hong Kong tends to have STDs

A Story About My Uncle is a game that gave me similar feelings I had playing Portal 2 for the first time.  It is an immersive first person experience with what I describe as grappling parkour with a brilliant story and wonderful narrator.  It is worth your time to play through this delightful adventure.

TLDR: The game is short with some replayability, but it's great. Performance is solid.
A Story About My Uncle is a platformer game that utilizes mechanics that include jumping, (both regular and suit-assisted jumping which consists of high jumping and jumps with a running start to reach further objectives), grappling, and rocket boosts. The main character narrates the story by telling the story to their daughter as a bed time story. The jist of the story being while trying to find your uncle, you stumble across a suit and by chance stand on a platform and are transported to another world where the game starts.
The game is pretty short. Some people have said they beat it in 2 hours. Personally it took me more like 4 and a half hours, since sometimes I misjudged a jump and lost my way which did slow things down.
Although the game is rather short, there is some replayability. In my first playthrough, I did not earn a single achievement, since the majority of them have you limit your grapple usage or play a level without falling. Those who are all about challenging achievements will be pleased with this game. Also, after beating the game for the first time, you unlock time trials, where you completely a level as fast as you can (also has some achievements). However, it’s completely personal, so you can’t compete with other players on achieving the fastest time for a level. Not that it really matters to me personally, but something to mention.
The Linux version took it’s time to be released, but it was worth the wait as they sure did polish it. I had no performance issues on the highest settings, and I don’t have the best hardware. So excellent job on that! Thank you for the Linux love!!
Overall, I had fun with this game and I defiantly recommend it!

This is getting too long, and i can't leave my games waiting for too long. So i'll jump to something i found average.

:
You'll either love it or hate it. But you'll have options either way, remember that.
There are three ways to save your adventure (which can turn out to be some pretty long and hardcore expeditions).
1. Find a save attendant.
A young elf will offer a save feature when you find her. I won't say much more, that's up to you. But you'll be able to find her pretty often.
2. Save stone.
A crystal used to save the game. Save attendants sell it, but you can find one in your adventures if you are lucky.
3. Goddess gift.
Once in a while, a goddess will offer a save option at the cost of 5 levels.
Did you see what's so different here?
All saving methods include finding something. This is not a game you can start and leave every 8 minutes. So no gaming at work i guess.
Personally, i love this feature. I like to have to save some money for save crystals and use them wisely. As i said, you'll either love or hate this.
