Первая часть Bit. Trip Runner, если вдуматься, является, по сути, обычным endless runner’ом, коих особенно много в последнее время развелось на Android и iOS. Но именно умение сделать из проходного проекта нечто большее и отличает по-настоящему талантливых разработчиков. Во второй части Gaijin Games не стали ничего менять, а попытались довести уже имеющуюся концепцию до совершенства.

Название сиквел получил довольно странное — Bit.Trip Presents Runner 2: Future Legend of Rhythm Alien. Главное изменение, которое замечаешь с первых секунд — игра перешла от Minecraft-образного кубического стиля к более привычному 3D со сглаженными углами. А вот бонусные уровни по-прежнему стилизованы под восьмибитную аркаду. Сложно сказать, пошла ли смена стилистики на пользу, но Runner 2 выглядит как минимум свежо. В главной роли снова симпатяга Commander Video, но теперь есть возможность поиграть и за несколько других персонажей, включая женскую ипостась Commander‘а.

Геймплей до смешного прост — персонаж бежит вперед, а все,что нужно делать игроку — это вовремя прыгать, делать подкаты да еще пару несложных действий. This game came as a surprise to me. I heard nothing of it prior to launch but I was interested right away. Freedom Planet is a throwback to the old school Sega Genesis days of mascots like Ristar and Sonic The Hedgehog and it pulls it off fantastically while still being able to stand on it's own. I can safely say this game is every bit as fun as the trailers made it seem (even more)! The levels are really diverse with different pathways, the physics are great, boss battles are creative and fun, the voice acting is really good and the sound track is top notch!
Besides the story, the game packs a Classic Mode that strips away all the cutscenes and plays all the levels in order, and a Time Trial mode. More features will be added and free so it won't get dull. It's a highly replayable game with huge levels and a lot of collectables. It also comes packed with achievements that let you look at the game a bit differently, for example there might be a different way of taking down a boss so experimenting and going through the levels more than once is highly recommended.
The controls can be configured to your liking so the button layout is never a chore to learn. The characters are easy and fun to control and it's a blast to play through each level. Everything pops out and is beautifully colorful, the sprites and character designs are amazing to look at, and every level still feels fresh after continuous playthroughs. I honestly can't think of anything wrong with this game, it's the perfect example of an Indie game done right! Do yourself a favor and buy this game! If you're an old school gamer you'll love it. It's highly inspired by the old genesis games but there's so much to love. It has a compelling and interesting story and it should not be missed!
I give it a 10/10!

There is good games, and then there is great games. Freedom Planet turns out to be latter, thanks to developers paying attention to details more than i remember seeing in quite time.
Story is not exactly Shakespeare, and amateur voice acting isn't best i have heard, but both turn out well and fine in the end. Atmosphere is still both exciting and charming, and characters are actually memorable. Visuals and art design are fantastic, despite i wouldn't call them as strong point of the game. Meanwhile soundtrack has well deserved it's place on my mp3 player, and sound effects are top notch as well.
Those less-meaningful things aside, most important thing here is gameplay, which is mix of various classics, without ever falling into most typical pitfalls of retro-style-indie-game cliches, and it works incredibly fine as long you adjust sensitivity settings to fit your taste. There is so far 3 characters, all with very unique gameplay styles, and all of them have worked outright fantastic, from what i can tell.
But what is game without it's meat? Level design here is surprisingly varied and detailed, with lot of interactivity put into worlds. Enemies and Bosses are the main challenge, though, but even on their worst they seem decent. Game even occasionally has some clever tricks and strategies to use against them.
However, the main problem of Freedom Planet is difficulty balancing issues, which are still around, even after some great patches. Levels themselves rarely get too hard, meanwhile bosses will beat you again and again. Hardest platforming parts also sometimes rely on some annoying contraptions. Only way to avoid the contrast between difficulty of levels and bosses, is to set difficulty on casual, which basically makes game ridiculously easy to play, and you won't really die at all. Even on harder difficulties, levels won't get much harder, meanwhile bosses are total killing machines.
Extra stuff includes collectible cards, Mahjong and Shang Mu academy, series of mini-challenges so fun that it must be illegal. And the best thing about this already content packed game is... there is still (as far as i know) more to come!

As with Shadowrun: Dragonfall, I have really mixed feelings about this game, and wish Steam had a 'maybe' or 'neutral' option for the recommendation. Unlike Dragonfall, however, in the absence of a neutral option I'm erring on the 'yes, I'd recommend it' side.
The Good
The combat is fun enough. Turn-based strategy with a number of decisions to make without being overwhelming (eg. which of two or three main 'attacks' to use; what order to use special skills in;  where to position yourself). Special skills are fairly limited, but with different character combinations, using different skills in different combinations is probably the most fun part.
The stories are still complex and multilayered, with great plots, and plenty of political and philosophical depth.
The decking/hacking/matrix aspect has improved in two ways, making it feel unique.  It's honestly minimal, but even a slight twist is a huge improvement over earlier versions.  It now feels like a mini-game, just like it always should have.
The Bad
The stories are still almost entirely told through walls of text - minimal cutscenes, no voice acting, minimal use of gameplay to tell the story. Even when the visuals do all the work necessary, there are still walls of text describing it like a novel;  and when NPCs have nothing meaningful to say, there's still a wall of text describing the manner in which they say nothing.
Luckily, this time, there is just a drop of animation and voice narration in the games few cut scenes.  It's not enough to make it a good game; and it's very cheaply done (basically a few drawings with zoom effects and narration to make it feel fuller than it is).  Just enough to create the 'I have to get back and finish that game' feeling that was missing in the earlier versions, but nowhere near enough to be a strength compared to other games.
Similarly, there is a little bit more storytelling through gameplay than previously.  Again, just enough to make it worthwhile and better than previous versions, but far from enough to make it a great game.
The cash and shop system is just as lame as before. You only purchase things for your main character, so the vast majority of shops and goods just get in the way.  All you really do is buy 3 or 4 upgrades for your main one or two weapons or your main three or four spells; and maybe spend a little on one-off items like medkits.  There aren't really any options with different effect types to add to strategic choices or variety; and you don't make enough cash to play around with options anyway.
Most of the time there is no point to exploring. There are a couple of scenarios in which you can find alternative routes or complete side-events that make the main part of the scenario easier to tackle.  But most scenarios are the same as with previous versions - exploring just means: waiting a minute for your character to run to where you want; clicking on a white magnifying glass to get some useless healing pack or a tiny bit of cash; waiting a minute to run back. You don't uncover interesting enemies, side plots, unique items, secret areas, mini-games, etc.
All in all, I enjoyed the game while I was playing it.  I more drive to hurry up and start again than I did with previous versions.  But I eventually gave up on reading the walls of text (click, click, click, hurry up and get to the point) or bothering with shops (four or five checks to see if a proper upgrade is available, otherwise ignore).

Absolutely a must for fans of the first Shadowrun(Deadman's Switch) or Dragonfall.
I think the most apparent change here is the models. Gone are the stumpy characters, everyone is slim-er(except trolls, they continue rightfully huge), which give the game a more sober vibe. You'll also find new augmentations: weapon mods such as arm claws, hidden whips, and shock hands. They answer to the Body attribute, so I suppose synergize well with fighter/melee characters (myself, I'm a sword fighter, did not go for offensive mods).
As for the single player story and gameplay: the writing here is absolutely incredible and to me is the one thing that stands out. I mean, every character is written from head to toe, these are characters that belong to this world, and most have stories as thick as your teammates. I can picture most of them going on runs with me! This is a breathing world, with locations, professions and events, and the writing works wonders on painting it for you. But... it's great because I cared to flesh the characters out by talking, AT LENGHT mind you, with them. If you're not looking for this, reading a lot essentially, then I suppose the game may be equal or inferior to Dragonfall, generally speaking. Here, you're not the team leader. There's someone pulling the shots, so you don't feel that big of driving force behind your team and your quest, as Dragonfall did. The runs surely are varied, and all the foreshadowing and climate of the story is nicely executed, but still.
Scenarios are beautifully layed down, and the Eastern feel is there. Soundtrack is great also in this regard.
Another accomplishment for the developers. Make you think what they would do with a triple A budget, a Deus Ex Human Revolution caliber... but then it would be another game entirely, right?

Short, objective version first, subjective ramblings below. Just to be safe, that last part will likely contain spoilers, possibly for all three Shadowrun games.
Pros:
-Great Story
-Tons of references to Shadowrun Returns and Dragonfall
-Great Soundtrack
-Very interesting and fun missions
-Interesting new Matrix
Medium:
-A bit much dialogue, though I didn't care unless I had to replay a section
-Hacking Mini-games, lot of people don't like them, I generally do, but they overdid the amount of them, especially at the end
Cons:
-Definitely not the best start for newcomers, go grab Returns first and then Dragonfall, Hong Kong last
-Noticeably less polished than its predecessors
-Played a male elf at first, stopped rather quickly because of his really stupid walking animation (saw similiarly stupid animations later on female Trolls)
With that outta the way, let's get to the more extensive part. First of all, I binge-played this game in two days, trying to complete as much content as possible. The story really gripped me, it was a lot more personal than in Returns or Dragonfall. As I mentioned above, I found quite a lot of cool references to the previous games all over Hong Kong, the most obvious and at the same time maybe the least obvious being Racter, your rigger teammate, is mentioned in a single line in Dragonfall in a dialogue with a character I actually missed the first time I played it. I'm talking of course about Lucky Strike, whom Racter mentions a few times now in Hong Kong. I've also found a few internet references, which mostly were hidden pretty well. Flying Spaghetti Monster, 'nuff said. The soundtrack was awesome, a lot better than before IMO, mich may also stem from the fact, that a few old tracks had been remixed and thus had both a cool new sound and evoked a nostalgic feeling. Might get repetitive though for some people. The missions were really cool and some of them could be solved with near to none bloodshed, which was a nice change from the usual bulletstorm you unleash in Returns or Dragonfall. The new Matrix was quite interesting, it felt a lot more...alive than before. In Returns or Dragonfall, the Matrix was all about running from one node to the next, blasting apart any IC you could see. Here in Hong Kong though, it was a lot more about thinking - though not necessarily. You could either think your way through the riddles the movement patterns of the IC posed or just go for the good ole run-and-blast, I didn't discover much of a penalty for the latter. Concerning the Mini-games, I liked them, they ware not hard, at least if you can remember a sequence of 4-8 numbers and then the look and position of a few symbols and compare them to the given solutions. To go a bit more into detail, you start with up to 7 rounds of Simon Says with increasing difficulty (at least measured in the number of digits, as I once had something along the lines of 666662, not that difficult) to gain more time for the second step, but you can stop after only two rounds which will only have four digits each. Once you've done that, you move to the second riddle, where you get a selection of around 10 symbol codes with 7 symbols, I think, not sure about the numbers here. Anyways, you are shown one of the smybols of the correct code every few seconds, sometimes faster, and subsequently have to find the right one. I usually got the solution in around ten seconds - while having time for about a minute. Like before though, there's always an alternative to these Mini-games, namely simply breaking the barrier, which will raise your alarm status a bit, or, in a few cases, a password. The dialogue was too much for some people, I didn't really care about the amount, unless I had to replay a mission, then it could be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ just like the Mini-games at the end, where you had to enter the matrix multiple times per mission with at least three Mini-games per visit. Moving on to the bad stuff. It's less polished than the other Shadowrun games in a few ways. First of all, there's this main menu glitch, were the buttons are halfway off-screen, though this fixes itself by hovering over where the buttons should be. Next up are quite a lot of typos and a few grammar errors in the dialogue. If I had to guess, there was too much dialogue for anybody willing to proof-read. Most of the time it was minor stuff, that didn't impede the reading process or change the meaning of the sentence, but a few times I had to re-read a line to understand what it's trying to tell me. Last but not least, the animations on a few chars. Admittedly, I've only played female humans or elves before, but I've seen enough of the other characters to know they had normal animations. Here...well....let's just say, the way a male elf or a female troll walk around doesn't exactly fit a Shadowrunner, at least not a more or less sane one. On that point however I want to mention that the both the animations and the new appearance of both male and female Orks were great.
Phew, what a wall of text. For anyone still reading this, congratulations for managing to bear with me and for officially reaching the end of this review.

I am a platform lover, and this game came very close to being a recommendation. It has a completely unique playstyle, some really interesting environments, and a story that remains just interesting enough to want to see it to the end.
The sense of momentum you get through several successful grapples feels really fluid, and this ability, combined with a pair of rocket boots that adds additional propulsion, lets you traverse vast environments quickly. The amount of safe platforms are few and far between, which means you will spend most of your time in freefall over bottomless chasms, trying to reach the next grapple point that seems just out of reach.
And that's when you hit your first major problem: you will always struggle to know exactly what is out of reach. The aiming point in the screen lights up when you can grapple, which does help a lot, but the proximity you have to be in order to reach these points is never clear, and oftentimes closer than you actually are. The game could have easily rectified this by having a scalable aiming point, that is to say one that would change shape, let's say a circle that gets smaller as you get closer to the object you're aiming for. This could have helped to player begin to more easily visualize safe distances to attempt. In reality, you launch yourself towards floating points hoping to grapple, and begin clicking furiously as you fall just short of it, hoping for a last-minute grapple success. The fact that this strategy occasionally works to save you is not a positive thing from a gameplay perspective.
And that awesome sense of momentum I'm talking about only works occasionally. An attached grapple will always bring you all the way into the anchor point until you slam against it, thereby killing all your momentum, which means that you have to let go at a safe distance to keep your momentum going away from that object and onto the next. The issue is that your momentum vector is constantly in flux and awkward to manage, and it's very easy to clip an object as you're passing it and fall. The opposite problem is letting go too early, which means you will not have enough speed built up to keep the sequence going. Furthermore, you actually have very little aerial control of your character, and although the intention is to make the grapple your singular tool for traversing the environment, it is much more cumbersome to use than your average platformer's jump techniques.
The rocket boots I mentioned could have helped alleviate this issue had they been designed differently. Any good platformer (one that feels nice and precise) gives the player a decent amount of mid-air control. You only get the boots towards the end of the game. Usually they're designed to traverse distances otherwise unreachable with your grapple, and you can only use them once per midair sequence. In other words, they are pretty useless in error correction, Having a pair of boots that could instantly change your direction and accelerate you into a different vector could have really helped in making this game feel more forgiving.
I am teetering on the edge of complaining about the game's difficulty, but it's ultimately fair once you get the hang of it. A speed run through the entire game will take you less than an hour, but new players can expect to spend 4 or 5, and most of that time is learning the grappling mechanics, the distances, the momentum, and everything else the game expects you to understand without really explaining it. This leads to lots of trial and error. This is typical for a platform game though, so it seems fair to demand it of its players. What I judge a platformer on is based on how fun that trial-and-error is, and honestly the fact that you can rarely build up a good sense of speed while learning the game makes the learning curve not too exciting to experience.
Fundamentally, the time it takes to understand the mechanics is time spent hitting your head on floating rocks, vectoring yourself in slightly wrong directions, and coming within two feet of your target and coming up short. A Story about My Uncle doesn't give the players enough tools to really feel in control. Had the story and graphics been a real selling point, I may have recommended it, but the voice acting is poor and the animation is very crude. With only 5 levels to play through and only occasional moments of fun, it doesn't have enough going for it to justify a purchase.
I will say this though: as a VR release, I would play it immediately.

Honestly It's not that good.  I have been playing civilization building games since the 90s, from HOMM, to TW, to EUIV, to space ones, etc.  I've seen it all, I've been there done that.
Though the Civ games stand as pretty decent in general, and this one as one of the best in the series (if not the best), after coming back to it these years later, I realize how crappy it actually is.
Once you get past the illusion of depth (EUIV has real depth, if that's what you're looking for), you realize there really isn't much going on here.  Nothing you can do to effect combat, very little diplomatic interaction with city states, limited diplomatic options with other civilizations, almost no military movement options (there is no patrol, skirmish/run, speedy advance at the cost of vulnerability, etc.)
The WORSE is the Barbarian system.  I recently started a new campaign on the fastest speed setting, and barbarians set to normal.  Despite wiping them off my entire continent repeatedly, they just automatically respawn bases endlessly all game on your borders.  Even in the 1700s you're being raided by garbage tier 10,000BC axemen, when your army is off across an ocean fighting a global war, all your developed lands are being pillaged and destroyed.  Which take TURNS to recover and repair from.  And you BETTER be sitting on gold to fast-produce a military unit to go deal with them, or you're screwed if you're going to wait the 5+ turns it takes to make one.
THEN the water, omg don't get me started on ocean travel.  You cannot stack units anywhere in the game, so the only way to protect vulnerable units is to layer other units in front of them and use terrain to your advantage.  BUT in the ocean, none of that counts for♥♥♥♥♥♥ and units don't just move a predictable 2 or 3 spaces.  A garbage barbarian boat from OUTSIDE your fog of war can come in, and snipe some tier 1700AD riflemen in an ocean vessel.  There is no transportation vessel, military vessels cannot transport troops, nor can they patrol or automatically engage boats that enter their vision.  You just get your valuable♥♥♥♥♥♥sniped by garbage barbarians.  Don't even bother playing a map with water.
Then the tech system is so resource dependant... If you don't spawn anywhere near Iron, you're pretty much screwed.  Late game, if you can't get access to Uranium, you will literally never get nukes.  Those are just a few examples.  Yeah, you can trade with them, with some AI, if you're on good terms, and they usually want to♥♥♥♥♥♥and take you for everything you're worth.
ANYWAY, long story short TL:DR, the TW games are MUCH better, just about as much campaign and diplomatic depth, and TREMENDOUSLY more military depth.  Especially the new warhammer series. I've only just installed it on steam, but I played since release back in I guess 2008ish, and levelled about a dozen characters up to level 80.
The game got harsh reviews on release due to lack of endgame content, which was something the game suffered from for about the first two years.  Fortunately, they've listened to the players and now there is a mass of content.  There's no level up grind because there are more than enough quests to see you through, you could start as one of the four races and follow a completely different quest line from levels 20-45ish.
Graphics are beautiful even after a bunch of years, and the combat system is good, balanced, and easy to get used to.  The f2p version lets you into a lot of the game, you can play it through without paying and still have more content than players had on the original release, but if you want to raid regularly you'll probably want to sub to the game.  I've also noticed that a lot of groups looking for players will insist on anyone joining be a subbed player with epic gear and a particular AA build (not the games fault, players can be jerks).  That coupled with the relatively low player population can make it a bit of a solo game once you get to 80 unless you're willing to put your hand in your pocket.  That said, you can solo most of the content.
The music in most areas of the game is great-the original game came with a soundtrack CD, even if you treat this as a single player game there's enough content to keep you happy for a lot more time than it'd take you to play through skyrim.  In todays world of dumbed-down games (particularly MMO's) AoC is a breath of fresh air that after some 7 years still has me coming back to it every now and then.

What a fantastic little gem! Having played the original, I can say that Runner2 is a huge improvement over an already excellent concept.
Running to the right has been done many times before... BUT the BIT.TRIP Runner series is great in that it is the love child of a side-scrolling platformer and a rhythm game (such as DDR, Beatmania, or dare I say Guitar Hero).
Adding the dance move to be done in between jumping, kicking, sliding, and blocking adds an element of danger to the game. You need to dance to get the highest score possible, but dancing makes it so much easier to miss things. I also like the addition of checkpoints. Some may think it's unfair to the original, but with the new additions of the sequel, I welcome a mid-level checkpoint with open arms. I am glad that the decision was to put only one checkpoint per level, it would be too easy with more.
And the graphics. The graphics! Everything is so nice and soft like the art jumped into a bathtub full of cotton swabs, except the stick part was taken off and it's just a bathtub ful of the cottony parts of the swabs. I guess that would be a bathtub full of cottonballs... Regardless, everything is very smooth, and for the lovers of the original, there are some retro levels thrown in as well. The good friends character pack DLC also has some impressive graphics and animations, but that's a different review.

Sonic Generations is a game that tries to please both fans of the classic Sonic, and fans of the modern Sonic. Each stage has two acts, one act for classic Sonic, and one for modern Sonic. After three stages, you have to complete 3 challenges that take place on those three stages you just finished. Each challenge you finish, unlocks a key. When you collect three keys, you go up to the boss door, and it becomes unlocked so you can fight it. In total, the game has nine stages, and four boss fights. The game's story can be completed in 5-6 hours, but I found myself going back to certain stages and replaying them, because I enjoyed them so much. The game's story isn't that great, but most Sonic games aren't known for their great story.
The gameplay is very well done and fun. You can purchase skills and customize your skill sets. The only issue I really had with the gameplay was forgetting that I didn't have a homing attack when I played as classic Sonic, though that is a personal problem. The game's music is fantastic. The graphics are also very well done and beautiful, for the most part. I had a couple of glitches happen during gameplay, but nothing major. The game runs pretty smoothly, but it had a couple little hiccups while playing (could just be my PC). The only thing about this game that I didn't really enjoy, was the last boss. It wasn't really difficult, just annoying. One of my favorite parts of the game, were the rival battles. There are only 3 in the game, but I really enjoyed them. In the end, I'd say this is one of the best modern Sonic games released to date. I give it an 8/10.
Unless your computer can handle it, this game would be a lot more fun to play (or even record gameplay) on an Xbox or PS3. Other than that, this game is flipping awesome!

YOU KNOW NOTHING! Play the demo, check the gameplay, read the reviews! This game is a Saturn-era platformer that NAILED IT. We are talking here about levels of quality used to describe games like: Shovel Knight, Megaman X4 or Sonic 3 & Knuckles. While game certainly is a nostalgia trip, it firmly stands on it's own in this day and age. Whole experience is delivered in awesome package with suprisingly varied gameplay mechanics, great level design, smooth controls, soft esthetic and top-level, adrenaline pumping boss encounters (better quality than all Sonic's bosses and on the level of the best from Megaman). On top of that, three distinctive characters to play means high replayability that easly justifies the initial price tag. Game may look like Sonic initially but in reality it plays like a improvement and modernization of Blue Blur's formula with many influences from other awesome platforming classics. It evolved from this ground-up and at the end Freedom Planet does it's own thing.
It looks well, sounds well (amazing soundtrack) and even the voice-acting, that is clearly more of indies level of quality, is most times solid. Not amazing mind you, but not bad either. Storyline is nothing super special, but characters are likeable enough to let some plot problems and incosistencies slide. Cutscenes can be really lenghty sometimes. I liked them, but those who highly prefer gameplay over story can disable them by choosing Classic Mode.
Some people also complained about difficulty curve. Bosses are in fact a bit challenging on Normal difficulty, but for me, fair checkpoint system and painless continues are more than enough to balance this out. If you are not reckless and do recognize some boss patterns, you should be fine. There are also plenty difficulty settings to choose from - you can pick Easy or Casual, if you want a sweat-less experiece.
This isn't a flawleess ride, but the overall quality of the game is unbelievably high for the first major project from this developer and only $25,000 gained from kickstarter. Again, check the demo. It gives a correct glimpse how the game really looks like and it should definietly tell you if you will enjoy the game. All in all, I highly recommend this game! It is much more than it looks at first glance!

Fun, fun game.
This is a party mix of some of the best elements of the 2d platformer model.
It's a action packed 2d platformer. That on the surface borrows a lot from Sonic & Knuckles. Which to be honest, if your going to clone a 2d Sonic game - that would be the one to choose. [Sonic CD taking second place, albeit not easily since it's really good.]
Freedom Planet does however, put it's own spin on things. Each character has their own unique moves. Lilac has a spin attack. Which can also be used to break special walls or even get a boost while in the air. Carol jumps up walls. Flurry kicks enemies. And has a motorcycle as a pickup that you can ride up walls. Best thing about Carol's motorcycle, is it doesn't feel like a cheap add on. You know, like in some other platformers. Where it's restricted to an area? None of that bs here. You can take that bike anywhere! So long as you have the skill to keep it intact. Milla can dig. And do creative things with her ability to shield. Of course, I'm only scratching the surface with this. I just want to give you an idea.
The story is surprisingly entertaining. The opening scene (before you press start), is a bit dark to my surprise. For a game in this genre. And I've played more then my fair share of platformers. Overall, the game's story seems to reveal an influence by anime. Which is still good in my books. The story won't win any awards in drama, but it may make you laugh. I like it.
There are numerous influences that can be seen in the game of the retro games of old too. From Megaman, to a whole range of Treasure developed games (Mischief Makers, Dynamite Headdy, Gunstar Heroes, etc). I feel it most with the bosses. Something about some of them remind me a great deal of the aforementioned Treasure games.
The bosses are just the right difficulty. Though it feels like there's a bit of a difficulty jump at some point. Or maybe it's just me. It's a hurdle that can be overcome with patience. And luckily, the checkpoints before a boss are forgiving.
There are two different modes. Story mode obviously, as well as classic mode which is story free. You also have access to a gallery. In which you collect various cards in each level. And there are a lot of these. There's 56 achievements you could work towards unlocking. Adding replayability to these levels on top of speed running if that's your thing. I know in shorter games, I like speed running. It can be a nice challenge once in a while.
I give this game a 4.5 out of 5. With some part of me having an inner debate on adding that .5 back on. But, that's where I'm at now. Fantastic game. This could be one of the best 2d platformers out there. In my opinion.
If your still on the fence about this, there's still a demo on the official site. I'll post the link below. For $15, it's pratically a steal. And as I see it, if you DON'T like having fun - then this game isn't for you. But if you do like fun, then get it!
As a side note, when I first tried the demo I got addicted. Seriously. Multiple speed runs with Carol on the first level in the demo alone. Then, wishing there was more game after. Making the wait for the full version that much more painful. Luckily, you won't have to wait if you decide to get the full version.

The platforming and combat are both very tight, thanks to excellent controls and the visuals are a retro treat.
The game is quite challenging on normal difficulty, however dropping the difficulty to easy makes it almost impossible to lose, even in the boss fights towards the end of the game. I haven't tried hard mode yet, but based on my experiences with normal, expect a considerable bump in the level of challenge. One thing I found very welcoming compared to a lot of platform games is the lack of cheap deaths. There are very few bottomless pits and the few instant death mechanics in the game are telegraphed well ahead of time with visual and audio cues, so they never feel unfair.
The audio needs a mention too, the music is fantastic throughout with a lot of subtle and not so subtle nods to old genesis classics. The voice acting is generally good, but can be inconsistent at times, more so in the earlier scenes in story mode. Some voiceovers are better than others, too, not only in terms of performance, but recording quality - unsurprising since the voicework was recorded on different hardware for different actors. But you have to remember this is about as indie as a game can get and the Troy Bakers and Tara Strongs of the world do not work for free. Fortunately for those who might be bothered by this, the game can be played in a "classic" mode, where all of the cutscenes between levels are skipped in favor of continuous action.
In terms of bugs, there is one very noticeable visual glitch with the airship not showing any thrust from its engines, but otherwise things behave as they should visually. Gameplay wise, I've had one major glitch so far where I phased through a solid ceiling when a block spawned on me - the block pushed me up through the ceiling. Oh and the unlockable Mahjong game's controls are very twitchy and prone to ignoring commands unless you turn control sensitivity right down.
Bottom line though, this is a fantastic piece of indie game development, especially given its humble origins. I'd fully recommend it to anyone with even a passing interest in retro platformers and doubly to anyone that enjoys speedrunning.

This game includes 6 classic Disney NES games; Ducktales 1 & 2, Chip and Dale Rescue Rangers 1 & 2, Darkwing Duck and Talespin.
It's a very nice nostalgia trip with new features. The new features include Time Attack and Boss Rush, you can also rewind in the game which I can only assume is for speedrun practice purposes.
However, there's a few negatives which really has nothing to do with the games themselves. I feel like there's way too few options in this game, where a lack of audio options is a very obvious fault. I don't know what it is with Capcom and not having sound options in their collection games (Mega Man Legacy Collection didn't have sound options either), but they need to step that up. It's tiresome to go into volume mixer to turn down the volume of the game.
Other than that, it runs nicely and the games are solid.

So far completed DuckTales, DuckTales 2, and Chip & Dale: Rescue Rangers, the three games I'm most familiar with in the pack.
This is a 1:1 re-release of the listed games. It's easy to tell that the game wrapper itself is a glorified emulator with a lot of bonus features, but what's important is that it's done well. The game has no apparent visual bugs and scales properly by resolution, has proper v-sync, etc. The games themselves are presented in a very nice "arcade" atmosphere with a game select that lets you instantly go into a Boss Rush or Time Attack mode if you wish, and even allows for a two-player local competitve mode on those challenges. A great setup if you want to challenge a friend.
Every game appears to be from the original ROMs for the US releases of each game. I can't tell any differences from previous playthroughs on the actual carts and I was able to complete each game smoothly enough. I'm no speed runner but I know these particular games quite well. One slight issue is what seem to be a very slight delay on control responsiveness which I think might have to do with the emulation, but I tend to feel that happening even on a Retron (which uses emulation software to run properly). You won't get the same exact experience as playing on an original NES cartridge, but you'll be so darn close only a speed runner or someone really sensitive to controllers will notice.
I've only tested this with a standard Windows controller (XBox / XBox One), but the controls are smooth besides the delay factor.
While the bonus features such as art galleries contain nothing special, it's a nice little bonus since the games themselves are a steal. $3.33 on average per game sure beats the average of $50 I paid between the original carts. (Talespin and DuckTales being around the $15 range while DuckTales 2 and Chip & Dale 2 being hundreds of dollars if you buy them straight up from collectors. I was fortunate to hunt down flea market copies.)
Overall, this is definately worth a buy if these games were special to you as a kid, or even if you just want to experience the original games for wha they are.

It's the six games listed in a slick collection. The majority of these are classics that still hold up extremely well today and are worth the asking price for the convenience.

It's six Capcom NES games based on licensed Disney properties from the 90's, and most of them are really quite amazing. You have one or two that aren't all time classics or anything, but overall the price of admission is well worth it. None of these games has been released outside of their original carts before, and you'd be hard-pressed to find one of them for $20 USD these days, let alone all six in one bundle. You have extra bonus stuff like a rewind feature to undo mistakes and whatnot, Time Attack and Boss Rush for those with a competitive side, and a bunch of neat art and music assets to take it. This is well worth the price for the quality and quantity of games you're getting and if you're at all nostalgic for these or generally down with 25 year-old video games then it's a must-get.

It does what you'd expect, it lets you play 6 classic Capcom Disney games on Steam. The presentation is good, the games run well, and there are bonus modes to try and Steam achievements to collect. There's also a gallery of artwork and all of the soundtracks from each game.
Whether or not it's worth $19.99 that's up to you. My personal reason for buying the collection is that I loved DuckTales 2 back in the day and wanted to play it again with the modes/achievements. I'd recommend waiting for a sale if you don't have any nostalgia for the games, but it is a well packaged collection.
PROS:

- Steam achievements and online  leaderboards
- Will scratch the nostalgia itch
CONS:

- The "retro" filters don't add much to the experience

I was really astonished by the sheer amount of quality this game delivers for the amount of money that I put down. It reminded me of the good old times, that I would reach out for a game in the heavily discounted bin and discover a gem. So what kind of game is Faster Than Light?
Faster than light is a management game set in space. The game starts you off with your own spaceship and crew. You will unlock more spaceships and layouts of those spaceships while completing challenges and winning the game. When you start the game you are immediately informed about your mission. You are part of the federation fleet and you have crucial information which needs to be delivered to the main fleet. The problem is, rebels are chasing you down to make sure you are not able to relay your crucial information to your fleet. Thus begins the challenge, you need to explore as much as you can without falling in the hands of the rebels. The places you can visit are marked on your map. Every point has lines attached to them which indicate where you can access that area from. It is very important that you strategically choose your destinations in order to explore as much as possible without falling in the hands of the rebels. Every time you travel, the rebels will come closer to you.
The amount of things that you can do and find in this game, is astonishing. While exploring you will encounter shops, people in need, enemies and other kinds of encounters. If you complete them, you can gain resources like: scrap metal, drone parts, fuel, crew members, missiles and sometimes even upgrades for your spaceship. These resources are vitally important because you are going to need them in order to defeat the final boss.
You will be managing your ship in a fight by: placing crew members in rooms that you want to see operated, dividing your energy over multiple spaceship systems and closing and opening doors. The rooms that are present in your spaceship are the: medical bay, shield generator, engine room, pilot room, camera’s, co2 room, weapons room and more. Some of these rooms need power where others do not. You can increase the effectiveness of these rooms by: upgrading the rooms with scrap metal, allocating more power to them and placing crew members in them.
Your crew members will gain experience by working in these rooms which will make the rooms more effective. For example an upgraded crew member in the weapons room will give you an increased reload speed. Each crew member has its own merits, for example humans will learn faster but some alien races will give power to a room or fight more effectively. You can find these alien crew members in shops or in encounters( some spaceships start with different alien races). Besides the rooms that you can upgrade, you can also invest in weapons, drones, systems and augmentations which will really help you out.
Weapons have different kinds of effects ranging from setting rooms on fire to temporarily disabling systems and of course dealing damage to the hull of the ship.  Most weapons will only deplete energy but some use missiles which you only have a limited amount of.  Drones will also deplete a resource named, drone parts. Drones come in different versions such as  defensive drones, attacking drones and hacking drones. In order to destroy your opponent you must deplete your enemies hull integrity to zero. In some instances you can avoid an fight by giving up resources or making a deal with the enemy. If you feel outgunned you can always warp away with your spaceship after a set time has expired.  Enemies can also try to warp away if they are damaged enough. you can however stop the warp by damaging systems that are needed for the warp.
Combat in this game is further enhanced by the addition of environmental effects. Some places you visit have ION fields or sun flares which will disable space ship systems or effect the maximum amount of energy you can use.
Systems  grant additional options  such as hacking, mind control and cloaking which makes this game more interesting and engaging. Passive boosts can also be found and are called augmentations.
The visuals suite the atmosphere of the game quite well.  What really stands out though is the amazing soundtrack! The music is extremely mesmerizing and really fits the theme of the game. I cannot stress you enough to at least check it out on Youtube or even better, buy it from steam.
If I have to discuss a negative aspect of the game, it would be the RNG. The game randomly generates enemies and random encounters which can screw you over big time. Some of these situations can be avoided however by knowing what the possible negative effects are of the responses you give. This does not change the fact however, that there are situations where it’s  better to start over instead of trying to reach the end.
In conclusion I really recommend checking this game out.

Well, I just beat this game, and I found it to be one of the worst experiences I've had as of late. And I really wanted to love this game, I really did: colorful, well-designed world, interesting characters, engaging plot and great soundwork. What completely ruined it for me, though, was the gameplay, it's been one frustration after another. There was no pleasure at all in traversing this beautiful world, and every time I found myself trying sections over and over just because jumps and grapples have to be stupidly precise. This gameplay reeks of when 3D platforming was in its infancy, when developers hadn't figured out how to do it well yet and didn't understand that having to make precise jumps in the third dimension needs to allow for much more leeway than in traditional platformers. In this case, the grapple points were often too tiny to be of use, not to mention that the actual controls are way too floaty; the right way to do this is to make sure that the controls are spot on, they're not working against you and the game helps the player in reaching the expected objectives. Maybe it's my fault for playing this with a controller, but some sections were downright impossible to pull off (I actually had to enable fly mode right at the very end, or else I would get an ulcer from this thing; not even kidding). What baffles me the most is that with 40-something testers nobody thought that some sections were too annoying to play, so maybe it really is my fault. I hated it wth all my guts, and I wanted to enjoy it so much.
Good game worth getting if you like this style of game.

I have been eyeing this game for a while and was fortunate to get it in a bundle.
If you like swordplay, dueling, and heavily-skill based gameplay, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are fantastic with very detailed models, skins, and weapons. There is strong mod support for user-based content, adding a large variety to the customization potential. The music is very good at keeping you engaged in the extremely intense combat.
Although you will be primarily using the mouse, the controls can be very tricky to master without lots of practice, and the learning curve is moderate to high - depending on whether you are used to aggressive, all-out-offense gameplay (you will find this game very difficult if that is your preferred playstyle). The tutorial is very helpful and critical to understanding the mechanics of the game - playing practice fights with the AI can help you get a grasp of how each character + weapon works. The combos are not complex since you are just moving and using the mouse, but things like timing, switching stances mid combo, parrying, and dodging are important to balance and master.
The feedback for where and how your sword will strike is provided by a faint aura showing the weapon path. Manipulate where you will strike by using the mouse and also by moving around. You can do air attacks by jumping first.
There are different types of weapons, like katanas, longswords, and scimitars. Each weapon has different characteristics - for example: the katana is a fairly advanced weapon, inflicting heavy damage during counterattacks, but weaker in overall regular attacks. The longsword is pretty balanced and has a good blocking move.
You have three different stances, fast, balanced, and heavy - you can switch at will by rolling the mouse wheel. Using these stances, there is a rock-paper-scissors element that becomes integral to survival in this game. When two swords hit at the same time, a parry happens; however, different stances will override the parry, inflicting damage and creating a window for counterattacking. You can switch stances in the middle of your combos, and this makes the game very intense when you are trying to strategize and outmaneuver your opponent.
You can also cancel attacks to feint, and the tutorial does a good job of teaching you how to do this.
In the beginning, when you are first learning to play, be prepared to die. A lot. If you play roguelike games or Demon/Dark Souls, you should be well accustomed to dying - it will be the same here. Even when you are defeating the AI consistently and with excessive ease, you will still die when you play online. Just remember, its all part of the learning process.
I noticed that the connection time can get pretty lengthy, so that is something to consider - there is also no average wait timer, so you can't know for sure how long it will take to find/enter a match. There is also a lot of complaints about the card drop rate - if this is something you care about, I have found this game to have the most ridiculous drop rates. I still have 3 drops left, and others have reported only 1 drop in 8 hours. This isn't too big of a deal if you intend to play this regularly, but definitely be aware.
This game definitely takes a significant amount of skill, and I advise you to stay away if you intend to play casually or do not like games that are too difficult. Otherwise, give it a try, and you may find the challenge to be to your taste.

A fast way to describe this game is like Jedi Academy meets Bushido Blade.
If that isn't enough then the best way I can describe playing this game is with a story of my first win in a Duel.
There are two kinds of servers you can play on, Free For All servers where you can practice and talk to other players or Dual servers where you go one on one in ranked matches.
Whilst you are cued to fight you watch however is currently playing. The game operates on a "Winner stays on" system so a good player can stay on for dozens of matches. That was what was happening this time I was playing. The player who was controlling the ring was using a rapier, a sword that can break through a players guard easily and get a lot of low damage hits in. He had completely wiped the floor with me the first time we fought and so I got to watch him fight three other players before I got another try.
I spent that time watching his tactics, the Rapier is great head on but does almost no damage if you try to swipe with it, so he was forcing the other player to come at him from the front. Either by throwing knives at them when they hung back or by diving in himself. In a sword clash or parry the Rapier will almost always come out on top so he was able to take people down with ease. Over the three fights I watch I figured out a strategy to take him down.
I was using the Tone Death, the first Longsword you get in the game which is good for wide sweeping attacks. When the match started we bowed and then I started to circle him, trying to get in a position where I could get around and past his guard. He didn't seem to be expecting it when I finally came at him and, instead of meeting him head on, rolled past his guard and brought my sword round in a wide horizontal swipe that took of a good sized chunk of his health.
The rest of the first round continued like that, with me chipping away at his health until he finally fell. The second round started differently, he came right in on the attack, striking at me and putting me on the backfoot. I rolled away as fast as I could to get away from his attack. I managed to land a few hits hear and there but he was hurting me more than I was hurting him. I was going to lose if that kept up
Charging up for a fast strike which would take of a huge chunk of my health if it landed, he came around for a final strike. You can shuffle back instead of rolling, it doesn't carry you as far but also doesn't leave you vulnerable to attack. So I started shuffling like a 50's singer and managed to dodge all three of his attacks along with the follow up. In the moment after his attack I brought my blade down it a heavy vertical strike and took of the rest of his health.
His body slumped to the floor and I sheathed my blade as I let out a breath I hadn't even known I was holding. I don't think I have ever felt happier at winning a game in my life.

While I do recommend AoC, I wouldn't suggest it for a long-time commitment.
A game launched ahead of its time (which is not a good thing because it kind of needed a better engine), with incredibly fun questing due to the background lore, unique combat mechanics combined with fun PvE and PvP battles and one of those games that were worth calling a potential "WoW killer" at the time. It had everything that somebody could ask for even now; beautiful graphics, graphical violence, detailed lore based on the Conan universe, fun combat, voice-freaking-acting and a lot of promise right off the start. That is untill you get to leave the tutorial area....
It's still a great amount of fun and worth throwing a little bit of money at it to get some extra areas and quests. But that's it really. The end-game is generic raids and that's about it. Some areas are locked to subscribers only, which are the end-end-game areas that you will have to go if you want to progress even further. Thankfully they improved their payment model, but it still is bad. There is some PvP to be had, but unless you are in the most populated server AND in one of the active and big guilds, you won't get much out of it.
It fell short due to it being rushed as all hell, which is painfully obvious. You get to be introduced to mechanics at the tutorial area that are NEVER used again in the game like a single-player mode for story quests and a nice hub city to link everything together. After that you are thrown ALL OVER the map in a fairly generic area system. No quests apart from a few that can be easilly counted with maybe just 1 hand and the story quests are voice-acted afterwards. You get to have to do group quests which requires pure luck of finding somebody at your level to do them with and due to you not having them done you will fall short later on (depending on your class, some are simply too OP on everything) and have to tediously go through annoyingly hard quests.
Also as I mentioned, some classes/builds are simply overpowered. Doing insane amounts of damage without long cooldown abilities and/or having too much survivability. It's one of the reasons that unless you are purely into the PvE part of the game and join a PvE server, you won't have too much fun unless you pick the objectively good builds.
In conclusion, it's still a great game due to the lore and the environments and Funcom 101 stuff that they have nailed in both their MMOs and I could even argue that you are missing out if you don't give at least the tutorial area a try. As a "Conan" game it also does what it does very well and you will love the world you are in. However, it has many issues including the payment model itself so playing to rush to the end-game is not adviseable.

As someone too young to have grown up with an NES, the phenomenon of River City Ransom passed me by. I'm not even sure how I came to hear about Underground- but I did develop a liking for beat-em-ups over the years, enjoying everything from the Ninja Warriors Again and Natsume's Power Rangers on the SNES, to the Scott Pilgrim game on XBox 360, to oddballs like Mutation Nation on Neo Geo. It's a genre that I've always found entertaining. But RCRU is more then just a beat-em-up. Like its predecessor, it is heavily dosed with RPG elements: a city to explore at will, shops, experience, upgradable stats and levels, a few sidequests, and a storyline delivered more eloquently then the average game in the genre, as well as a cast of playable characters more akin to a fighting game in sheer size.
Set 20 years after the events of the NES game, Underground stars a new generation of River City Highschool students, as well as an older, wiser Alex and Ryan, now co-owners of a local car repair business and still prone to dispensing well-deserved beatings. Local business mogul Merv's sweetheart has been kidnapped, and the blame has been pinned on your gang, "The Flock." A considerable bounty has been placed on your head and every two-bit punk in the city is out to collect. What's a highschooler to do? Why, bust heads from the school grounds to Ocean Heights and back until you get to the bottom of things, while enjoying a colorful and lively cityscape full of street fights and references to Back to the Future, Aliens, True Lies, Double Dragon, Sinistar, Akira, Newgrounds, Shovel Knight, Castle Crashers, Hyper Light Drifter, Hotline Miami, the greater Kunio-Kun franchise and more. If you've got a serious pair of rose-tinted sunglasses about the NES/SNES era, Underground will feel like coming home, in a way similar to but more accessible then Retro City Rampage.
RCRU's list of player characters is long indeed, though some must be unlocked, either by finding them in the school or simply by progressing in the story. Each has a different fightning style and varied attacks, combos, grapples and specials. You can switch characters at any time by visiting a hideout, which also function as save points, so feel free to try each one out until you find one that fits: my personal favorite was one of the starters, a breakdance-fighter named Provie, whose rapid movements, double-jumping and devastating specials made her ideal for me. Other options include luchador Bruno, boxer Paul, shotoclone Glen (complete with hurricane kick, shoryuken and hadouken), wrestling heel Mike, zangief-esque Rudy, and more.
Defeated enemies grant XP and cash, however, leveling up increases your stat caps, but not the stats themselves. To do so, you purchase food and items from shops. You won't know what item increases which stats without trying them out or consulting a guide, however there are extensive guides available here on Steam concerning this, as well as movelists and inputs for characters, where to buy new moves and how much they cost, where to find the secret move books and so on.
The game recommends you use a controller, but I honestly had more success using the keyboard. Try both if you're unsure which you prefer.
The game is divided broadly into three acts, and supports drop-in/out coop for up to four players. There's also an arena mode with an even larger playable roster, including various enemies, bosses and NPCs. It's great fun almost the whole way through, and even if it feels like the final boss phases are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and they kinda are, don't worry- the game saves after each phase, so just stick with it and you'll win much sooner then you think. RCRU delivers so much on sheer fun factor that the rest of the polish it has is almost superfluous. I highly recommend it.

Even then...
I *could* somewhat play this game, both on and offline, and get some enjoyment out of it, I could do some CRAZY combos, and kidnap people with Mike. Good enough fun to keep me coming back to RCR for a long time, truth be told.
A good example is this GIF. This is probably patch 12.
Cant do ANY of that anymore. They added pointless extended animations, which severely limit Mike's throw game. Its a utter♥♥♥♥♥♥move to literally remove what makes a character fun. Imagine if they removed Paul's Air-Combos, or nerfed Glen so he wasnt a OP, braindead, money stealing scumbag . You'd never hear the end of it, but nobody cares about Mike, so he will most likely remain like that. I had never played a River City Ransom title before, but just from what I had seen of the old games' footage, I knew it was up my alley. It seemed like the game was being made (and kickstarted) by a third party studio that was fans of the series so I was looking forward to playing it. Sure enough, I liked it. The game is relatively fun, but very rough around the edges, in an NES-game sort of way. I find that a lot of the design choices are questionable, and even though the developer's intent may have been to stay true to that NES feel mechanically, I believe there was room for some improvement to make the game more enjoyable.
THE BEST part of the game is its retro pixel asthetic with some gorgeous pixel animation. Could not get enough of it, and the quality of it alone is enough to justify buying the game. Despite some internal troubles at the studio, they ended up with a solid 8-bit soundtrack that accompanies the game very well.  The basic beat-em-up mechanics are great! But the more I played the game the more I began to experience design choices that made the game less of a fun romp, and more of a vague repetitive grinding land.
So here's a detailed breakdown of my gripes, from biggest to smallest:
- THE FEEL OF THE GAME IS WRONG. I purchased this game wanting to play something that felt either like a sequel or updated follow-up to the original River City Ransom title, both in gameplay and in setting. The feel of the game is certainly more North American rather than Japanese (understandable since the studio is Canadian), and that works in the favor of the developers: rather than try and emulate a culture they don't belong to, they doubled down on Western tropes for characters and school. It started out pretty all right. Unfortunately, the further I progressed with the game, the more it started going really off the rails story-wise. If you wanted a down-to-earth story about tough guy high-schoolers who fight other gangs, this is not it. It feels like the developers were trying to emulate the world of Scott Pilgrim, with fourth-wall breaking  dialogue at every turn. And while I don't mind an occasionaly self-aware wink at the player, this game seems to want to remind me constantly that I'm playing a video game, and to me that's doing a disservice to the world of RCR. I cannot express how much of a non-sensical mess the final act is.
- THE STAT PROGRESSION AND LEVELING may have been features present in the previous titles, but their implementation here just feels outdated and like an encumberance. Even though characters level up, their stats don't actually go up until you consume food (which is prohibitively expensive in the beginning of the game, when you need stats boost most). And when you do purchase food, there's no way for the player to know what stats will actually be increased until they consume it. They will then be greeted by an incredibly slow line-by-line message box that lists every single stat that was being affected by the food and whether it was maxed out or not. If you don't know which stats the food your are eating boosts, you may just end up eating food that tries to boost stats that are already capped for your level. And even then, the game doesn't explain what any of the stats even do. I resorted to using a guide for knowing what foods to eat, as this aspect of the game was just too opaque.
- So much vagueness: the game IS meant to be open world (to an extent), but objectives and information are communicated extremely poorly. Even though I would often go to the correct objective location, I often had to resort
to using a guide to figure out what else I needed to do to trigger the objective, mainly because little information is given to the player to tell them how to actually progress. This could also be an attempt to emulate old-school NES games, but this is taking some of the worse aspects of that era.
- AI is not particularly fun to fight after a certain point. I started to feel like the only viable strategy the AI uses is to have a second enemy flank me from behind to hit me. All the time. So much so that fights basically became me running to edge of the room or avoiding enemies until I made sure no one was behind me before I could safely attack. Even though the game offers a variety of environmental weapons, I found myself never using them since enemies seemed to easily knock them out of my hands whenever I used them, and would then proceed to pick them up and use them against me.
- The subway system (fast travel) was just confusing and unclear. It often involves you taking the same train multiple times, and each time you take the train you are stuck fighting a wave of enemies for 30 seconds and then waiting for the next train to arrive. Often, it was just faster to walk everywhere.
- The difficulty spikes in incredibly inconsistent ways. About 2/3 through the game I was basically plowing through everything (which didn't feel great) only to have new, much stronger enemy types thrown at me out of nowhere, in an incredibly long stage. In some cases these new enemies would appear in starting areas of the game, which made it impossible to grind or level up lower-level characters. Effectively, I had been playing the whole game with Glen, but it had become so excessively difficult to level up anyone else that I was just stuck using that same character the whole time. Strange design decisions.
Ultimately, I don't "not recommend" the game. I feel like it kept the most outdated aspects of the original title, while throwing away its charming setting. Not every story needs to be an epic. I enjoyed SR:Dragonfall despite its many flaws. It redeemed itself with its characters; they were all interesting, multi-faceted, and most importantly, they felt like
.
SR:Hong Kong had most of the same flaws, but the team was just awful in my opinion. I didn't like a single one of them. My first companion was so whiney and maudlin I brought him only on missions in which he was absolutely essential. None of them felt like my friends, ever. Maybe that's a more authentic Shadowrun experience in LARP, but it was disappointing here.
Hacking was tolerable in DF, but they really screwed the pooch in HK. I quickly got fed up with it and console-commanded my way through every hacking scenario thereafter.
There are some notable quality-of-life improvements, but mostly the gear and outfits are recycled. The scenery was good, but the character models were as terrible as ever. Portraits and other artwork were beautiful as always. Shadowrun-specific concepts like Rigger, Street Samurai, etc., are still very pale imitations of their LARP versions. Technology like Smart Links, rigger vehicles (non-existent) and drones, cyberware, etc. are all just flavor - everything has a homogenized, nerfy feel.
The writing is serviceable, but definitely not as good as the previous installment. By the end of this game I was rushing through just to tie it up and be done with it. I did feel compelled to finish it, so that's something.
I'd recommend the game, because it's well designed and there's nothing else making use of the IP at the moment. If you haven't played SR: Dragonfall, I'd suggest playing it first. It's a better game overall and will give you an idea of whether you'll enjoy this one.

The Ugly: In my experience the matchmaking has been sub-par-I have been in a couple close matches out of nearly 300 battles. New players can be placed with veterans-# of battles and your destruction ratio are NOT taken into account when "matchmaking". Also, losing 10 games in a row doesn't encourage one to continue to play. The game lags like a son of a gun whenever I mouse over, or click, anything on the port screen and in-game if I tap the "Esc" key by accident(I have v-sync disabled btw).
Overall I like the game well enough, but sometimes it is really frustrating and feels like it doesn't want me to play it. You can go from hero to zero overnight. If Steam had a 1-10 scale(like they should have done) I would rank WoWs as a 7/10. Ah hell, it's free-go ahead and try it!

Coming from somebody that played the original Bit.Trip, I can tell that this is quite an upgrade with a wealth of content when compared to the original. Check points, retro cartridges, keys, chests, alternate routes, and some clever methods of varying scores have been added to the Bit.Trip formula.
If you're one of those people that strives to be number 1 on the leaderboards, then the developers have kept you in mind. You can now press the right trigger to do a short dance to gain some extra points in between obstacles. Loops have also been added that have you use the left analog stick to follow commander video to rack up more points. Keys and chests are also point modifiers. AND you can jump over a checkpoint (one of the greatest new additions in my opinion) to get a huge point boost.
My one big issue with the game is that it seems pretty pretentious. For some reason, the developers got Charles Martinet (the voice of Mario) to be the narrator. At the risk of sounding unprofessional, the first thing I thought when I found out about this was "okay...?" Sure he's a great voice actor and all, but the real issue here is that the game doesn't need a narrarator at all. To the game's detriment, story elements are added at the start of the game and between levels. Sadly, I care as much about the story presented here as the Angry Birds story. Both the story and humor (if you can call it that) both fall flat here. The game would have been much better if it just stuck to its roots. Running and jumping.
Whether or not the game is worth $14.99 is highly debatable. I can say that I would never spend that much money on this game. However, I got it on sale for $1.19 during a Fall Steam sale. Needless to say, that was an excellent price for this game. If you can get it on sale for around $4.99, I'd say it's a must buy. I highly recommend this game.

THIS REVIEW IS OF MAFIA 2 AS WELL AS THE DLC CONTENT: JIMMY'S VENDETTA AND JOE'S ADVENTURES
Mafia 2 is in my opinion an absolute masterpiece. This game caught me COMPLETELY off guard when it came out. I was not expecting it to be as good as it was. You play as Vito Scaletta who joins the Mob life thanks to the help of his friend in a 1940s city. You will be shooting, driving fighting and even getting involved in a few sneaking sections to get through the game. What keeps the game going is the story which constantly gives you context to keep playing through the game, similar to what TV shows do to keep them addictive. The game's story is absolutely stellar and always gives you a good enough reason to keep playing. There is also a very good hint of realism which I loved and also helped keep the game fun and addicting to get through.
The game also gives you plenty of opportunities to explore and go to shops to purchase guns and clothing to make your character look badass. The shooting is also solid and the game feels like one giant interactive movie. And I absolutely love it. I cannot reccomend this game enough. I LOVE IT. I'm not going to spoil the game, just know that the story is amazing and the mechanics, while not the best in the world, do work and work well with the game and it's story.
Can the same be said about Jimmy's Vendetta though? Unfortunately, no. This DLC was boring. Very boring. It actually highlights how good the story is, but also highlights that the game's mechanics on their own are actually not that brilliant. All the missions involve going to the mission point (which can sometimes be on the other side of the map), going to point A, kill someone, steal something, blow something up and/or fight someone, drive to point B and do it all again, sometimes while trying to avoid the police. Every mission was like this and there is no story surrounding the missions so things get very dull very fast. Also you have a lot less health in this than you did in the base game, and since there is no checkpoint system, you end up having to replay missions all over again including the tedious driving which tells you off whenever you try to speed which can frustrate you alongside bore you. I only played about 20% of this DLC content before getting bored and frustrated and turning it off. DO NOT BUY THIS DLC, it is not worth it. Also, the ending mission is the same thing again and the ending itself is about 30 seconds long. Yeah, don't bother.
What about Joe's Adventure's? Well, if you are reading this now, I am still playing through this DLC pack, however this review will be updated once I have completed it.

A great value that gives you plenty of bang for your buck.
I don't normally play rogue-like games, but this one was a total blast that kept me coming back for more until I finally conquered it, and I still plan to go back and play it again. I also plan to check out more rogue-like games due to how much I enjoyed this one. The music is solid, the gameplay is an exciting challenge, and the pacing is excellent, with the incoming shrouding darkness that stalks you throughout your journey (or several) putting a great deal of pressure on you to keep moving forward, but still giving you plenty of time to explore to your heart's content, powering up your character to prepare for your epic battle with the demon lord, the game's big boss. And the game gives you many ways to do so.
You can go all around the map killing everything you see to level up as much as possible in the limited time you're given before the demon lord strikes. The second difficulty ensures that the demon lord can show up any time, which really amps up the intensity.
You can explore dungeons to loot rare items while taking out whatever lurks within.
You can stop at various buildings in the areas you visit to save your game, sell items, buy better items, and talk to NPC's.
And much more.
Depending on quality of your build, you will die often when you first start playing, especially if you aren't used to playing these types of games. However, you'll notice yourself becoming increasingly better every time, and when you finally accomplish that perfect run you've been planning after several failed attempts, it's extremely satisfying. And really, just experimenting with different builds is fun even when you die, because frustration is infrequent. You learn from each and every death and the game is rarely every cheap. You can see all of the enemies coming towards you at all times, giving you plenty of time to prepare your next move. Plus, with a reasonable agility level, avoiding enemies altogether is a relative breeze.
One of the best things about dying in One Way Heroics is that it doesn't feel like the end. There are brief descriptive endings for every death you experience, plus every time you die, you're given the option to read advice, transfer items to a new run if you want to start fresh, unlock new classes to play with, and plenty more. Exploration rewards you with more items, many of which you don't know the details of until after your run ends, whether by victory or death, but there's an item you can pick up that allows you to see all your inventory details on the spot, which really comes in handy.
Overall, One Way Heroics is one of those rare indie JRPG's where everything just clicks. It has very little in the way of flaws, it has tons of replay value, and there's almost always ways to freshen up your experience, with multiple updates and campaign variations keeping things interesting even after multiple hours of play. It's a great game with plenty to offer even to the most seasoned Japanese role playing game vets, and a shining example of indie development at its very best. Don't miss out on crafting your own incredible journey.

When I bought this game, I loved it. It was fun to play a fighting game that, unlike mortal kombat (in example), did not require me to learn 80 buttons to do 1 move. -Prior to certain updates some characters had extreme strenghts when people started complaining an update was made that bumped up every character... except Ryo  (downgraded since he was the most complained about)

Blade Symphony is a game with great potential and can be a fun game. Ranking system should be, perhaps, more complex as it is to plain to be accurate. The characters are lacking balance and makes the game more about picking a character for each fight as opposed to allowing the individual to progress with the character they like the most. fps issue and certain bugs must be dealt with. Overall broken combat system makes this game less and less realistic as a fighting game (in that I mean this game is currently all about jumping and running around) to include the aweful parrying system and poor tracer effects. Perhaps a game I would suggest to buy on sale as I do hope that the devs will fix these issues in which case I feel this game could be very good. But I would not purchase it at full price.
