Sonic Generations is a hidden "gem" among the other pretty terrible Sonic games out there. After beating the game I found it to be fun, but lackluster, nothing that stood out as a reason to recommend it; however, once I figured out that there was a huge modding community out there for the game my outlook on the game changed and I felt I had to mention it, if only briefly.
Team Sonic has been doing some bad and some good in their games. The epitome of this mindset has to be Sonic Unleashed - there's a really cool part of the game where you go flying around through well designed levels at breakneck speeds collecting coints and almost getting dizzy from the camera movement while you race against time to reach the finish line. Those levels were amazing and fun. Then there were the "God of War"-esque levels coupled on there as well, which were slow, boring, and, sadly, mandatory. I bought that game on PS3 and hated it - not so much because the Were-Sonic sections were terrible (which they were) but because of the lost potential the game had. Well, Sonic Generations takes it in the right direction, utilizing those same awesome level types where you fly around at lightspeed but instead of a Were-Sonic you are granted an Oldschool-Sonic for Type B levels. This would be fine if that Sonic didn't handle like a 12-Ton dump truck. The physics seemed to work fine but the stopping and starting of the character were just awful, and I found myself using my trademark "spin" while accidentally moving so I'd be going at about 2 miles/hour while the time keeps ticking away and I keep getting more aggravated. Those levels weren't nearly as much fun as the other levels, and normally I wouldn't recommend half a game, but Sonic Generations on PC is unique in that the modding community allows you to turn the game into what you want to play. Want more of the good levels? Download the Sonic Generations Unleashed Project. Want to change the physics up to more of a "classic" Sonic feel? Go ahead, there's a mod for that too. The ability to swap in and out parts of the game that you don't like or want to experience more of really turns Sonic Generations into a hidden gem that can provide hours of fun for any level of Sonic fan.
Pros:
Mods (see above)
Full Controller Support
Great Level Design (for the most part - Modern Sonic levels shine)
Good Music
Cons:
Handling/Controls (especially Classic Sonic)
Fixed Camera (makes some platforming awkward)
Unnecessary RPG-esque Upgrade System
Leaderboards are a fun idea, but it's rampant with cheaters - first hundred or so entries on all boards are 0 second runs
As I said, I wouldn't recommend the game without the modding community backing me up. That said, even if you're only going to play vanilla, the game isn't terrible, and the Modern Sonic sections shine and show the level design genius Team Sonic has. With mods Sonic Generations squaks by with a B+

The best Sonic game by far (my opinion), Sonic Generations has something for both kinds of Sonic fans: the classic platforming that put Sega on the map, and the high-speed action the series is now known for. The game is fairly short but has great replay value, most of the achievements are either story related or challenging enough to not be boring, and if you've played any Sonic game you will experience TONS of nostalgia when playing. Great game. Great franchise.
P.S. Rooftop Run Act 2 is my favorite level.

To me, the first Company of Heroes is one of the best strategy games made, and my favorite world war 2 game.
That being said lets take a look at its successor.
Company of Heroes 2 brings us to the Eastern Front with the Soviets and Germans. We also have the Ardense Assault DLC bringing us the Battle of The Bulge, The western Front armies DLC bringing us the US and Oberkomando West German faction. The British Faction DLC and numerous Theater of War DLC's as well. With all the DLC complete the game definitely brings some content to the table to keep any fan engaged for NUMEROUS hours and the amount of content is definitely great and helps justify any cost alone.
Now looking at the game as a whole.
Graphics:  The game looks great, sounds great, the explosions are awesome, the intense fire fights are a sight to behold, weather effects add that touch lacking in the previous one. All in all there is nothing lacking in this department.
Gameplay: The game is a mimic of the orignal game brigning us some tight nit squad focused combat where unit management takes precision and each battle and encounter feels personal. If you liked the original then you cannot complain here.
Campaign:
Tho the scenery of the campaign is great, I found the story to be a meh... You have the story told from the perspectice of a Russian soldier re counting the events from a humanitarian perspective. This kinda makes it awkward when you have a hard fought victory and instead of feeling epic you get this feeling of meh when the protagonist simply goes on about the Soviets and how they were cruel too. I think they were times when they could have brought forth the actions of the Soviets in the war and moments when they could let us have our epic moment of victory. On the plus side the missions are well made and is definitely worth playing thru for that alone. There is also a weather mechanic that makes the winter deadly and interesting and slows down the pace of the game.
DLC Campaign Ardense: Even tho this praticular campaign doesn't have a central plot and protagonist, it gives us a strategic campaign map where you pick and choose your stage of combat and have this tug of war with the germans playing as the Americans. It is good fun and is a concept they could expand upon further.
Theater of War: now this was a good addition, with scenarios and challenges, as well co-op mode. My only gripe is that all the theater of war DLC is focused on the Soviets and Germands, they could have added 1 from the US perspective and Brit perspective.
Multiplayer:
The game as of 2017 still holds a solid multiplayer base and games are not hard to get, with 5 factions to choose from there is some variety as to what you will see on the battlefield with each faction having a distinct play style.
The game supports from 1v1 to 4v4 games that can also be played against the AI solo or co-op if u got a buddy. There are tons of maps and community spotlight maps to add some serious variety and the inclusion of modding gives us an ever gorwing catalog of maps and scenarios.
The game has been contantly updated in its ever going quest to be balanced, and tho not every one is pleased with that, we know the devs are invested in the game in that regards.
Now my main gripe with this game is the amount of Micro Transactions in it. I generally have no problem with micro transactions as long as there is a good chance of you being able to obtain the items on your own. In this it does not seem so. After playing 40 hours I have not gotten anything but the ingame currency whch takes alot of to buy anything. It seems the devs defintiely wanted you to spend extra cash to get the commanders and abilities you want and that I am NOT cool with.
All in all, this is a GREAT game and I would have given it a NEIN (pun) out of ten if it was not for the micro transactions.
The game gets a solid 8 / 10 , it is no doubt a must have for any strategy game fan and even more so for the WW2 fan. With hours of content, numerous unlocks and an amazing display of warfare this game is definitely awesome and cannot be recommended enough.

This game made me feel more than any AAA-produced title ever could. The story can switch from side-busting laughter to gut-wrenching depression in a single scene. While potentially jarring, it never feels out of place, as the world shown here is hilariously bleak and fully realized. This might be one of the darkest games I've played, but oddly enough, it is one of the funniest as well.
As far as RPGmaker games go, this one is simply the best. It was made with plenty of custom scripts, so it's not obvious as to the software used. Aside from that, the soundtrack is *incredible! Appropriate as well as satisfying, particularly the tracks used during fights and important story events. Austin Jorgenson has definitely created a masterpiece here, in more ways than one.
This is a story-driven game, make no mistake. There is a lot of re-playability though, especially since the game features something like 30 potential party members for you to recruit (these vary in difficulty, from dialogue, fetch quests, minigames, fights, etc). Lots of easter eggs and hidden material to flesh out the world nicely, as well as one of the strongest main storylines I've ever seen in a game, especially an Indie.
Speaking of which, I can safely say this is the best Indie game I have ever played. The gameplay is different yet satisfying enough to rank up there with the great RPGs of the past, but the story is in a league of its own.
TL;DR: Highly recommended for everyone, except if you are sensitive to dark humour or *very* dark themes.
P.S. LISA: The Joyful isn't as satisfying as the main game, but if you have an interest in the story, I recommend it highly. The gameplay is also altered *just* enough to make it feel like a whole new game.

TL; DR
Pros-

Cons-
-Poor mission design
-Extremely difficult/ punishing (Cops will come after you constantly and attack you)
-Annoying gameplay choices (Innocent people will get in your way, you and your team mate will constantly be knocking each other down even if friendly fire is off, objective isn't always clear, and enemies will swarm you.
- VERY UNBALANCED (My special move did less damage than a single punch.)
Let me preface this by saying that I wanted this game to be fun, and that I did enjoy it at some parts, but the majority of my play time was spent annoyed, frustrated, angry, and disappointed. The game started out really fun, with a few hiccups here and then. Then the first chase mission happend. Then the second. Then the third. All of the chase missions were frustrating and extremely unenjoyable. You have to run after an enemy and hit them, while avoiding being hit by other enemies, and not running into a wall/ obstacle. Then after that, the milk delivery mission. You have to bring a glass of milk to a npc on the complete other side of the world and if you get hit while holding the milk, you'll break the glass and have to start over. But, I thought that I could over look the poor mission design, and enjoy the game play. But even that was challenging because enemies just swarm you and overwhelm you to the point of frustration. You will be fighting one enemy, and while your attack frames are active, a random enemy will come up from behind you and hit you. You could try to block, but blocking only works against attacks coming from in front of you. You could also try to turn and block, but that still leaves you open to the OTHER enemy behind you. Another poor gameplay design comes from the police. They look for any excuse to come after you. If you accidentally run into a parking meter, it will count as vandalism and they come after you. If you accidentally hit an innocent civilian, who blend in with the enemies and run at you because they want to make an insurance claim, the cops will come after you. They will also throw teargas at you that can literally stun lock you FOREVER. It's not an exaggeration. The time it takes for you to recover from teargas is plenty of enough time for them to throw another one at you. Then there's the friendly fire. I play this game with my brother and it's super irritating when you constantly knock your team mate on their butt. Sure you can turn friendly fire off, but you can't turn off knock down on your team mate. No matter what you do, if you hit an enemy into the air and they collide with an ally, your team mate will also fall to the ground. The biggest issue with this game imo is how unbalanced it is. I was playing Bruno and I thought that he was the worst character in the game, but it turns out he's actually decent. He's just bad compared to Glen, who my brother was playing. My "special" move essentially required me to do a four button input for a move that did as much damage as a single punch, whereas Glen's special move did four times as much damage as his punch. Most of the moves that you learn are TERRIBLE. They have long start up times, horrendous recovery times, and small hit boxes. Examples of these moves are Bruno's Poof Kick, and Glen's Dark Rainbow. Just look them up, they're actually more useless than their normals. You would think that moves that cost energy to use, require you to be a certain level to use, and require you to buy in order to unlock them, would be better than a normal punch or kick, but no. Using punches and kicks are generally more viable than trying to land a move with a miniscule hitbox. What really sets me off about the balancing is that throwing enemies won't deal damage to them. Not even the initial enemy that you throw takes any damage. There's a certain character, Mike, who relies on grapples (his fighting style is listed as Grappler). His special grab deals 0 damage. It actually is a useless move. You can increase Mike's throw stat all you want but it won't turn that 0 into a 1. I don't so much mind how grindy the game is. As long as a game is fun and addicting, then grinding becomes enjoyable. But this game is more irritating and frustrating than anything which is a massive shame because it looks great. I really hope that the devs take a look at the balancing of the game and change damage values to more reasonable numbers, because I love old school beat em ups like Final Fight.

Negative sides? Like every game of this kind, sooner or later it becomes boring. Not so much "endgame content" in it. Grinding for the next ship in the next released tech tree is not the thing worth the time spent. But in this game there is, basically, nothing else to do, but to grind :(
Situation improves, though. Clan battles are now available, some fun events (like Halloween)  do happen from time to time. This helps to keep me playing.

Returning back to the franchise with Shadowrun: Hong Kong feels very familiar yet fresh thanks mainly to its own Asian flavor we didn't really get to see in previous two entries. As befitting my take on these other games, this one is also not a singular experience and is most definitely worth talking about.
If you're not familiar with my previous Shadowrun reviews I'll give you a quick summary: it's a cyberpunk future meets fantasy; meaning you have your cybernetic orc-augmented street samurai running around with their group of freelancers-for-hire aka shadowrunners, but the twist this time around is we've going to Hong Kong. Specifically, second incarnation of the Kowloon Walled City mostly. I believe this game's big draw lies in exploring the Chinese part of Shadowrun setting where myths and legends are more real then anywhere else and vicious mega corporations aren't as massively influential as much as they ARE the government.
Not everything is perfect, of course. With such a great setting in-hand and for the most part likable and varied characters, I'll get back to that in a second, you might be thinking it's an amazing game story-wise. Sadly that was not the impression Hong Kong left on me. Not in a sense it's a bad game or even badly written as much as the fact it comes off as disjointed with main story missions just kinda connecting without any real investment. That of course depends on how much you care about a particular character in your party and his connection to the main character as well as overall story motivation for good three quarters or so of its run time. If you're not emotionally invested in what you're being told instead of shown, and you spread out with side missions, this story will not do much for you until it escalates later on following some pretty decent foreshadowing. One thing that took me by surprise, but was something I enjoyed because it played into my tendency to explore and talk to everyone, was that some resolutions and options only become available to you after following up on unrelated and completely optional side activities or dialog. This even affects the very last decision you get to make in the main game, which might irk someone used to games clearly presenting your options.
As far as gameplay and mechanics overall go it's your familiar Shadowrun package – that of tactical turn-based RPG, although they did commit to some tweak. Primarily in the Matrix in a sense that now you can move around in real-time until you engage in combat. I'm heavily split on guard programs running their patrols and having you avoid them, but I did enjoy the new pattern matching hacking mini-game. I assume this feeling is not unanimously shared by everyone. It is worth noting that unlike the previous two games Hong Kong seems to have either pushed the Unity engine to some limit or memory leaks lead to game running choppily after couple of hours of continuous play. Bad experience also came from scripts not playing properly couple of times and game hanging up during some engagements, but that's nothing worth really dismissing it over.
In closing I'd like to mention the bonus campaign Extended Edition introduced by saying it certainly had some meat on its ones and ran for at least good four or so hours. I do wish it gelled better with the main campaign or continued it in some more meaningful way as opposed to having you chase an antagonist you may or may not even remember at the end. Good point is that it does offer you a pretty big decision at the end, even if the entire campaign comes of as weak compared to what you did earlier.
Time for me to say I do recommend this game wholeheartedly although your mileage will vary depending on how much you end up caring about the emotional angle. See you around, chummers.

Shadowrun Hong Kong is a third and last installment in Shadowrun returns series. And I am happy to say that in my mind it is almost as good as Dragonfall.
HK feels a bit weaker in story department, compared to Dragonfall - combining cyberpunk and fantasy cliches, it still however menages to deliver a well crafted and thoughtful story, with a diverse cast of interesting characters. It provides rich roleplaying options as well- both on mechanical and social levels of interaction with the game world.
Mechanically SR: HK shows a lot of improvement, in comparison to earlier games- while the combat is still slow and boring, most missions are designed in a way that allows you to minimize playtime spent fighting, if not outright skip most of the fights.
First hour or so feels a bit off-putting, with slow and downright boring exposition, but after that the story picks up and the fun begins.
So, to summarize :
Good story
Amazing characters
Nice writing
Boring fights
Slow first hour
The bonus campaign consists of 4 missions and holds up to the original game (if just barely), by providing a definitive ending to the story.
So, if you re into CRPGs, then do yourself a favor and play both SR: HK and Dragonfall- they are worth it. (Mostly, by being 1 of the best RPGs in recent years).

This game is simply amazing. The fighting styles, the techniques, the way in which it's not just continuing clicking on the same damn button as if it was Mortal Kombat or any fighting game that requires amazing combos to beat a person yet they use the same button. ANYWAYS, this game let's you have the fun of kicking someones butt. Despite how many times you're going to lose at the beginning, you'll begin to understand that this game is not easy at it seems to be.
Set aside from this, Blade Symphony is a third-person 3D swordfighting indie game which focuses primarly on multiplayer. It takes you to the basics of how swordsmen actually battle. Every attack has an opening so timing in this game is efficent or else you'll lose badly. You choose how you want to attack the person and which every attack, there's a different set of styles depending on the character you chose to play as. Advanced play has been primarily used by players who are masters in this game while the newcomers only know basic mechanics and so on. While the masters use all their flawless techniques, the newcomers would only not know how to time their attacks but also use basic fighting styles with little less combos that create openings for the masters. Many newcomers will not want to learn how to play the game therefore leading them to not only not knowing how to play it but losing in an instant to the masters or other players who had been learning this game for quite a while.
Other than that, this game like I said before, I love it. It's awesome. The community in this game is not so mean but at the same, not so friendly. So you could say it's in the middle. I see no reason to get bored of this game when it's gamemode is primarily on multiplayer with Steam Workshop items you could download from. Learning how to play something will increase your benefit of actually having a chance to win at a battle rather just going on full force with one blow.Well, have a nice time in this game and wish you the best of luck!

Flanking manoevers, blitzkrieg tactics, and strategic artillery strikes. Company of Heroes 2 has all of the action from the original entry and packs it all into the eastern front of the European conflict. If you haven't already played Company of Heroes 2 be warned, it is an extremely precise and highly addictive strategy experience-- catharsis aside it has its balancing issues, some of the units seem incredibly powerful while others seem to collapse the moment you stop micro-managing them. Rest assured though, anyone looking for an in-depth World War 2 strategy game need look no further.
Scorched Earth
Coh 2 offers, among other improvements, the ability to play as the Russian army. Unit types for the Soviet allies are varied and true to their historical counterparts; conscripts are cheap and plentiful, T-34s are lethal and only available late game, while units like Partisans add varied tactics that rely on neighbouring countries support in the war effort. I played most exclusively online and have found that most players prefer to play as the Wehrmacht and Germans.... though I have found that *certain* enemy types seem extremely effective, coupled with regular server lag and hacking issues, this can extremely hinder the player's experience and make a well-plotted strategy come undone with the drop of the server.
Fight on the Beaches, never surrender
Since it's release, there are a number of expansions available for the game. I played as the British Forces and found that their role and abilities from the original COH have been somehwhat diluted. Gone is the ability to move your base (this ability has been restricted to the Axis) and other changes (C.O.'s are gone) have made playing as Great Britain feel less distinctive than in their previous appearance. Still, the units' dialogue and the addition of new units like the 50 Cal. Sniper, and armoured cars make playing as the empire an enjoyable experience. Though, if you have the base game, you might save yourself the $15 for the expansion.
Lend Lease
The addition of the real money marketplace has, unfortunately, made this game less enjoyable than it could have been. Additions like commanders, special abilities, and (less importantly) unit skins are a compromising addition to a game that has the potential to be so effectively competitive. Depending on who you talk to the ability to pay for better armies is a good and bad thing, but in either arguement it affects the game by preventing the player from settling into a dynamic real-time strategy, and instead (like many pay to wins) shifts the focus on to the better units.
Closing Days of the War
If you liked the first company of heroes, and are looking for a deep war-strategy experience, then by all means buy this game. But do yourself a favour, wait for a sale and pick it up cheap.

--What Runner2  does well:
Runner 2 is an engaging and challenging rhythm game game/quirky platformer. It plays a lot like Guitar Hero, except instead of colored buttons you are responding to puzzle/platformer enemies and jumping puzzles. This makes it feel much more like a true Game than most rhythmers, since there is a much more diverse set of "commands" and input possibilitiesi. For that, it's a lot of fun.
--What it does poorly:
The 2.5d really interfered with the experience for me. There are a lot of depth of field issues which will have you jumping over pieces of the background or running into things in the foreground. Also, the 3-d hitboxes are all slightly off. This, combined with slightly-too-loose controls, means a lot of "aggggghhhh I swear I hit that button," controller-throwing moments.
The death sequence is way too long, making those moments of frustration even worse.
Also, the difficulty scaling could stand to be retuned. On the "normal" setting, I usually could perfect a level on the first run. On the "hard" setting it would often take 20+ runs to get right. There's got to be a happy median in there.
--What I liked
Runner 2 sucked me in and made time sometimes disappear, which is the highest praise for a rhythm game. When I was on a roll, I didn't want to stop playing, since the system of pass/perfect was tuned just right for my perfectionist gamer streak. Unfortunately, the issues above would often break that spell and I would alt-f4 in frustration.
The building climax of the music feels awesome when you beat a level, but can be disorienting when you have to restart mid-song.
Also I like that the game has 'rhythm' in the title since the Steam interface doesn't have spellcheck.
What I didn't like:
The art direction could have been a little more diverse. Going through on hard, aiming for perfects, the art assets and music got extremely repetitive, which can be hell in a game like this.
I didn't really like the musical themes for three of the five worlds.
--Finally, the "bonus game" at the end of each level seems pretty pointless. There is little emotional payoff for "winning" it, and it is infuriating to lose. Definitely a bit of filler that should have been trimmed.
--Conclusion:
A very fun game that is exactly what you would expect. Just watch a LetsPlay of it on Youtube. If it looks like your speed, you'll probably like it. If not, you won't.

Pros:
- Good plot/writing (including most side quests)
- Characters that you get curious about, even those not on your team (I frequently checked in with the Club 88 among other places)
- Hacking is implemented in a way that makes being a decker interesting for the long run (hacking in itself is akin to combat)
- Lots of combat styles to pick between (Want to be a hacker with a flair for magic? Sure! Want to be an♥♥♥♥♥kicking monk with cybernetics? Go ahead! Be creative, have fun)
- Not all situations have to end with blood splattered on the wall, often you can use other methods to solve problems
- Some characters from previous games show up
- Free DLC
- Good Workshop community - they make good stories / changes to the game worth checking out
Cons:
- AI can be questionable at times (instead of attacking, they'll move back & forth)
- Re-loading takes WAY too long, between loading times I'm reading several paragraphs of a novel, news story etc)
- Bugs which won't be fixed (Conjecture on my part, but seeing as they still haven't fixed bugs that was reported almost a year ago...); see next point
- Choices can sometimes carry over to older saves (Example: I killed someone for blabbing, wanted to try a new approach but after loading my older save, the person was already dead and replaced)
- Talking to people can be a clumsy process if you need to do it repeatedly
- Memory leaks (Longer you run game, slower it gets - the more saves the slower it loads them)
- At least one puzzle is nigh-impossible to solve without googling despite the hint(s)
Not really cons but:
- Being unable to use hacking skills to disrupt enemies with cybernetic augmentations, smartlinked weapons etc
- Sometimes the RNG is ridiculous, missing twice in a row with 91% chance of hit? Yeaaahhhh....
A rough gem that could do with some more polishing, worth checking out - especially when the game is on sale.

Game type -- Shadowrun's unusual setting (cyberpunk mixed with fantasy elements; entirely possible for a cybernetically augmented pistolero to be magically hasted by a shaman while dealing with hostile abominations from the astral plane) set in Hong Kong rather than Seattle.   Stats-based RPG, heavy emphasis on small-squad tactical combat, fixed-perspective isometric view, mostly-linear campaigns w/ a small number of non-random side missions available.  If you've played either previous Shadowrun Returns game, this will be pretty familiar territory for the most part.  Strictly single-player.
Played through main and bonus campaign w/ an elf pistol-specialist street samurai with a fair side investment in charisma; typically had a rifle samurai, a decker, and a shaman in the party.  Don't expect to build a character who's good at everything and wielding the best of everything as resources can be fairly tight and this isn't a game with repeatable quests to farm (in the included campaigns, anyway; UGC can be as generous as the author feels like).
Positives incl. -- true to setting (for a CRPG, anyway; can't really replicate a human GM's ability to incorporate and handle all the wacky ideas a player might have, so your options will always be limited), combines some tongue-in-cheek humor with a cast of suitably shady characters, revamped Matrix system (but can rely on a particular NPC decker if you don't build your player character as one) favoring stealth and timing, often multiple approaches to getting to the next stage.   Charisma isn't a complete dump stat, and knowledge of the right etiquettes can give you opportunities.  Still, do not expect to be able to avoid all bloodshed by any means; you will need to kill, and frequently.
Mixed -- There's Workshop support, but there seems to have been less modding done for it (notably few story UGC) than for Dragonfall or first SR iteration.  Combat mechanics are improved over original SR/Dragonfall with cover and positioning matter more, but it's still fairly light -- if you want a game where you can shoot an enemy on the floor above you through the ceilng or collapse a staircase with explosives, this isn't it.  You won't have to spend twenty minutes per turn meticulously planning, however, as if it's some hardcore complex military simulation with a gazillion things that you *could* do where many of 'em will eventually doom you from wasting too much time or too many resources or getting too many limbs removed from IEDs you didn't spot.   Complexity is a matter of taste.
Negatives -- pretty short game (main and extended don't take all THAT long to play through once), story isn't anything to write home about over the long run.   One can also argue that it's not terribly innovative over Dragonfall, aside from the revamped Matrix sections.  There's also one bit of cyberware that's fairly sketchy, because once it shows up (and it shows up pretty frequently in the bonus campaign) grenades are drastically less useful, and that removes options from the board.

This is a very solid, fun, game that has some flaws that bog down the experience a bit. However, I still reccomend it for beat'em up fans, as this is one of the best additions to the genre this side of BOR in a long time.
PROS:
- Combat is excellent (for the most part). Smacking things feel good. Combos are easy to execute and very free form allowing for a lot of creativity. Granted that you spend money wisely, you'll learn moves at a fairly steady pace throughout the game.
- Plenty of characters to choose from, and you'll unlock more as you progress through the story. Each one has their own fighting style, and play differently. Unfortunately, you're better off not switching characters throughout the story (see below)
- About 8-10 hr long story mode, depending on how much grinding you do. I feel like this a good length for a budget title. There are $60 triple A games that offer much less in this department.
- Fantastic art design and pixel art. Sprites feel both nostalgic and modern. Colors pop and are vibrant, and go well with the overall humerous and cartoony tone of the game.
- Enemies feel unique. The different gangs you'll go up against all have their own quirks about the way they fight. Whether its Nerds throwing beakers from afar, Luchas dropping kicking their way in, or Rich Kids double teaming you into oblivion, when you fight groups of these enemies together, you're forced to change your tactics up, which helps the beat'em up combat (which is notorious for becoming repetitive) stay relatively fresh throughout the game.
- Humor abounds. This game is funny. The things characters say are hillarious, the plot is totally cheesey and self aware, and there are louds of references and satires of pop culture.
- River City feels alive. This is perhaps the first Beat'em Up I've played set in a city where the city feels like people live there. On most screens there are NPCs going throughout their daily business. You'll see people walking dogs, riding bikes, taking subways, driving cars, ect. If you assault civilians or commit crimes, cops might come after you, forcing you to hide and lay low.
CONS:
- AI can be tedious. As you progress through the game, enemy AI will become more dangerous, but this mostly includes almost like a game of keep away. AI will maintain just enough space between you and them for none of your moves to close this distance effectively, while they rely on charging attacks (most are very fast and hard to react to, but not all) that close the distance, hit for a large amount of damage, and the AI will usually use this attack when your back is turned. By end game, nearly every battle plays out this way, and it does begin to feel monotomous.
- Grinding Heavy. In order to upgrade your stats, buy new moves, and heal, you need money, which enemies drop. However it isn't until mid game where enemies start dropping what feels like a fair amount of money. For much of the early game, enemies drop only a few cents. While it does add up, be prepared to do a lot of screen clearing to afford a burger.
- Switching characters is not advised. Your XP does not carry over between them, nor does your money. Past a point, all of the starting characters (assuming you've put no time into them) are incapable of lasting even one screen. You have two options really: stay with the same character you've been using, or grind and work on all of them, switching characters regularly. For a game with such a colorful cast, seeing most of them become non-viable after a certain point is a touch dissapointing.
- Boss are bland. I found most bosses to be too easy. The last few end game bosses are a good challenge, but many of the early game bosses are so easy to overpower and get on the ropes real quick. They never really get the chance to show off their cool traits.
- There are way too many start-up and recovery frames on a lot of moves and animations. Whiff a grab at your own mercy. The reason this becomes an issue is because it gets to the point where enemies are able to avoid your moves with ease, and in many cases punish your specials with their own because their's seem to start up faster than yours. This is very prevelant in the later game. Also getting up after being knocked down seems to take forever, even with maxed out stats. I'm not saying I should be able to get up instantly, but there's definitely a few frames that could be shaved off here and there to make the combat tighter, faster, and less tedious at times.
- Weapons feel useless. One of the best parts about Beat'em ups is the weapons you'll find on the streets to smack people around. River City Ransom Underground has plenty of weapons, but mostly all feel relatively the same. While weapons do more damage, I found that weapons are not that effective because they are slow, and after about two hits, enemies will close the distance and damage you, knocking your weapon away before you can swing again. You will do more damage with normal attack strings in a much faster time.
- When you die, you lose half of your money. This wouldn't be a problem if there was some way to store money away in one of your hideouts or something, but you can't. Instead, you are better off spending cash as soon as your earn it.
- Other flaws include platforming that is difficult to line up correctly, a few chase sequences in the early game, and an infuriating fetch quest involving a bottle of milk. These however, are minor, and once you pass them, they do not come up again.
Coop in this game is fun, and eleviates some of the combat problems single player has (i.e. keep away enemies, being blindsided...) but you and your friends need to be in it for the longhaul. This is not a game where a friend can just drop in. They need to join you from the begining, work on their character alongside yours and grind just as much as you. Be prepared to add a few hours onto the play time for a coop playthrough.

This is just....Saints Row! Like it should be.
If you've never played any Saints Row game, I really suggest you at least play Saints Row: The Third before you go at this game, simply to close up on a bit of story and the characters.
Saints Row basically is a parody of some other games and movies, taking the really good parts of them and putting them into a big playground. The game plays like any typical GTA game, including the open-world and most typical GTA features, but extends that with:
- Weird, crazy, funny weapons (e.g. MERICA, a flame-launcher/rocket-launcher/minigun/grenade-launcher combined)
- Complete character creation similar to GTA Online, but with a lot more configurable details
- An enormous amount of character customization options and unlockables
- Awesome and funny vehicles including space-ships, multiple kinds of tanks and other WMDs
- A story that reminds of Matrix. I mean really, it's basically Matrix. But with Saints Row flavor. It's funny, good enough to keep you interested and doesn't force you through the game.
- Superpowers similar to InFamous/Prototype. Fast running, high jumps, walking up walls, fire-blasts, telekinesis, you get it. And yes, it controls really well.
- An extensive set of attributes and bonuses you can get by unlocking them for money or finishing side-quests for them
- Explosions, everywhere. If you love big massacres in GTA, this one will satisfy you for sure
- A whole lot of different missions, meaning you won't be just killing people and destroying stuff all the time. Many mini-games, bonuses and stuff to collect etc.
- The 18+ requirement has a good reason
- -> Coop <-
and much more...
You know how serious Rockstar is in GTA, this takes it to a next level. Prepare to get run over by d*ildo-cleaving aliens while shooting back with black-hole launchers, jumping 100m into the air and throwing fire-blasts wearing nothing but sneakers.
Some ideas for improvement (For, maybe, Saints Row V? :)):
- The vehicle handling is quite not as good as GTAs. Especially the tank controls shouldn't follow where you look at, but where your vehicle is pointing at and any turns feel really different compared to a lot of other games, the vehicles are turning quite slow. You don't need a lot of vehicles in _this_ specific Saints Row, though.
- I did have one or two crashes at some point. Nothing is perfect.
- I miss a real whilte color and many colors look shabby on some clothes
I can really recommend this game for anyone that loves some relaxed and fun third-person shooter action with a lot of laughs and good jokes. People that liked GTA really should give this game a shot.

I loved playing LISA - it's an oldschool RPG with an "earthboundish" style and approach, but overall much darker. LISA felt to me like playing an absurd and depressing trip through a doomed world, full of threats, mysteries and morbid humor, yet it managed to be one of the best games I've ever played!
In LISA you're forced to make very hard decision and - as many reviews say - even if you try to play righterous and make everything right things still wont turn out the way you intended them to do.
The setting is placed in a somehow post-apocalyptic, run down world, full of perverts mutants and bandits.
You'll be playing Brad, an aged man whos trying to survive in the apocalyptic wasteland of "Olathe". One of the most remarkable things is the whole setting itself - The apocalypse was caused by the disapperance of all female humans, leaving the world behind in a chaotic and slowly dying state. I will not write any further about the story but I can tell you; It's pretty damn good, and it'll probably wreck your feelings!
The gameplay consists mostly of walking, picking up items, recruiting new and unique party members - by finding them or completing their quests - and batteling in a typical JRPG battle system. Due to the amount of recruitables and different endings the game offers plenty replayability!
The atmosphere of LISA can reach from claustrophobic and disturbing to open and sort of "light hearted" and the music as well as the "earthboundish" style will help you to immerse into LISAs story.
In short: It's an extremly depressing but even more fun and cynical (J)RPG to play and I would recommend it to anyone how likes dark humor, post apocalyptic settings and RPGs.

Lisa is a good game. A good game where everyone is bad, including you. The twisted, charming world of Olathe, a post-apocalyptic wasteland scattered with men, is filled with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, addicts and rapists. It's a tough place, but the game has ways of smoothing things out with its own brand of humor.
I don't have much to say beyond that in terms of coherent thought, because I'm fairly poor at doing that. So, I'm just going to organise thought into pros, cons, you get the gist.
- Battle system keeps things rather fresh for a turn-based RPG with combo systems and a variety of character specific skills.
- Charm, it has a lot of charm. When people can do whatever they want, it opens up a lot of opportunity for "absurdist" humor.
- If you like anything about the Mother/Earthbound series, go get em'. The charm and aesthetic bring that to mind.
- Great OST. The music is unconventional, but are memorable nonetheless.
- Good pacing.
- A lot of replayability. The endings, outcomes and achievements keep things fresh.
- It does a good job at having a "show, don't tell" policy where you have to infer plot points through the details hidden through out the game.
- Choices are a big part of the game. Most of the time, the ultimatums provided have a way of having long term effects, but at times, the choices you make can fall flat. These few aren't superficial choices per se, but they don't have too much of an impact in the end.
- The themes are really heavy and I wouldn't want to recommend this to anyone who's particularly sensitive to certain subjects. Just a heads up.
- It's still a turn-based RPG, so the fights can drag at times. The game's pacing does its best to combat this, but the process of "your turn, your turn, then your turn" can draw things out with an enemy with 20,000 HP.
- Visually, the pixel art is not bad by any means, but it's the resolution that may keep you too a small windowed screen.
- It's made on RPG Maker, so there're issues present with the environmental pieces shaking as you walk. It can be hard to notice, but it's there at times.
- Some back tracking is present. Evens out as the game progresses.

He takes some drugs called JOY that cause one to forget their troubles and release happiness in their body. This resultes in one becoming a JOY-Monster that appears to attack harshly only when someone agitates it, with a smile still slashed acrossed their face.
Another 10 years later, Brad adopts a lost baby naming her Buddy, who is the only woman in the world. Months and a few years pass by, Brad arrives to his home to dscover that Buddy is gone and his friends brutally murdered.. Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast is a game in the series of Dark Forces and Jedi Knight. In my opinion it is the best game in the whole series (some may disagree) because it contains a very nice single player and and very good (and well balanced) multiplayer.
Singeplayer: The SP is set after the collapse of the empire. The ex-Jedi Knight Kyle Katarn is working as a mercenary for the new formed republic, trying to find outposts of the Remnant troops of the empire, who still work against the republic. In the process of the singleplayer Katarn regains his jedi power and discovers the real aims of the imperial troops. The story telling is very well embeded in the normal game flow, which is a good mix of action (fighting with weapons, lightsabers, force) and thinking (solving puzzles, finding ways). There is an option to set the level of difficulty, so the game is demanding, no matter how good or bad you are.
Multiplayer: After the SP (which is quite long), you may want to play MP. The general MP is very similiar to other Quake3-Games: You have Gametypes like Deathmatch, TD, CTF etc. But there are also some special gamemodes like JediMaster (one player is the jedimaster with every force power, the rest just owns weapons and has to kill him), CTY (like CTF but the flag-stealer isnt allowed to use force), Holocron (the force powers are spreaded at the maps in little boxes which you can pick up).  After you joined a MP server you'll have to set your name, your skin and your force powers, where you can choose either the dark or light side and disturb force points in the different powers (like lightning, absorbation, healing, jump, speed). Note that there servers which disable weapons or forces, leaving you with nothing more than your saber ;)
The MP experience itself is unique - you can have normal deathmatches there, but also nice chats or exciting light saber duels; the lightsaber fight is the best I have ever seen in a Star Wars game: you can choose your style (fast, medium, slow means: less, normal, many damage per hit) and the saber reacts to every mouseclick you do, so with a bit of training you can do really nice combos. Also, back then, the modding community was quite active, giving you access to dozens of very good maps, tools and server mods.
Sooo all in all - buy the game, you'll not regret it :D

I'm no expert on roguelikes. But this game at base price costs about as much as a cup of coffee from a mid-market coffee chain. I've played it for twenty hours, and it still feels like I'm scratching the surface; after each run, I feel like I learned something about how the game works, about what it wants from me and how to succeed. It's a good feeling. The game is fair but challenging, and for those of us for whom that isn't enough, offers a highly modular difficulty system (base difficulty plus class plus perks, all of different usefulness) to challenge yourself with. There's incremental progress and upgrades to unlock if you'd rather have a barometer of progress other than your own growing skill at the game, which is difficult to quantify, but grinding for these things isn't really an issue -- classes and perks are pretty cheap, at least for the useful ones, and everything else is bonus stuff.
If you buy the expansion, you're basically getting a game that has double or triple the content of the base game, and also includes a whole bunch of quality of life UI upgrades and balance changes. A lot of the things added are very simple and unobtrusive but satisfying -- things like turning to face the enemies automatically, a little screen to track all of the things you've achieved as each class, more dimensions to facilitate the psuedo-multiplayer. Other additions are bigger -- new classes, new allies, new npcs, new bosses and objectives and missions. While the price of the dlc is triple that of the base game, it's absolutely worth it -- even more so if you can get it on sale. The hours of gameplay/$ ratio is excellent.
It's also in the class of games that are easy to play while doing something else, like holding a skype conversation or queuing for a match in some other game. It takes very little processor power, deals with tab switching quite agreeably, and time stops while you aren't moving.
All in all, I think it's a great way to spend an hour or two between doing other things, and ends up being quite moreish once you've wrapped your head around the basic steps to survival. Then, it's all about the rng and your own wits. Recommended.

One Way Heroics is a tile-based, rouge-like, J-RPG. There is a constant threat, the darkness, consuming the world. There's only... a 'few' ways to resolve and save what is left of this world.
One Way Heroics has a constant threat; the swallowing darkness from the west, and thus one can travel only eastwards or risk being consumed themselves. There will be many opportunity costs because of this. One can only explore only so much north-side and south-side in such a time-frame that you may miss a dungeon, or a town, or even rare holy loot; or unfortunately encounter a powerful foe that will devour your lifepoints in a single blow. Unable to fully loot everything because of a weight limit, you will have to take a limited amount of supplies and equipment and give up what is necessary for survival or end up blowing your own self up because someone lit up explosives in your inventory.
It comes along with many classes starting with the sharp Swordsmaster and agile Hunter, to the charming Bard and sexy Hero... to a traveling Tourist
? Each a journey without rest and different abilities for each class.
In terms of difficulty, you choose the difficulty before you start your adventure; from
and
, to a
. As time goes on and as the darkness consumes more of the world; foes will be buffed and be stronger in level. It can be tough understanding every little mechanic there is, but after a few Walk in The Parks, you'll get a solid grasp on what and what not to do.
In terms of the game-play time, you can probably expect each normal journey to take thirty minutes to an hour (or an unfortunate eight minutes if you get caught off-guard), depending on how much you're willing to balance exploring and fighting. There are save points for each journey if you're slightly lucky to encounter them in towns, so don't worry if you end up having to sleep for yourself in the real world. Don't worry, that darkness won't eat you.
The DLC (OWH+) is not strictly necessary, but it does change and add more content to the game as it should. Get it if you enjoy the base game for how it is, and you'll definitely enjoy what the DLC will deliver (classes, choices, and stories!).
There are many win and lose conditions, multitudes of endings, and things to learn about the origins and the characters you meet along the way; certainly a lot to adventure and explore outside from the adventure itself.

Played 100's of hours before steam release. Below is review (as short as possible) on the features of the game, including the ships, captain, maps, currencies, game interface, gameplay itself, a take on the game being called pay2win, and community/esports stuff.
Ships - Mostly from WW2, a few exceptions included. Ships are quite customizable in various ways, both cosmetic & performance wise. 4 classes of ships that all have their pros and cons in the grand scale of the battle. There's various countries, and overall the amount of ships in the game may seem excessive at first.
Captain - Only relevant thing about captain is the captain's skills. You customize these to suit your playstyle (usually there's a cookiecutter way of doing things, though).
Maps - Several exist, more are on the way. Main change in maps is their objectives and the locations of islands and ship spawns. Islands offer great utility and can be used for sneak attacks, defensive gameplay, shooting at someone without being detected, and turtleing with torpedos. Objectives are pretty straightforward, mostly capture a wide circle to gain points (points are also gained by sinking enemy ships, and lost if you lose your own).
Currencies - Doubloons is the 'Pay2win' currency (more on that below). You can buy it with real money, and ocassionaly you get it by playing, doing missions for example.  Credits is the currency for most stuff. It's what you earn in battles, spend on ships, their post-battle repairs, their upgrades & such.
Game interface, menu, etc - Pretty clunky, though goes to decent amount of detail on options. Main menu is sometimes laggy. In battle it's alright.
Gameplay - Lots of depth, high level of gameplay requires extensive knowledge on ships & their weak/strong features, highly predictive aim especially when fighting from long distance, and most importantly nerves. In pvp, just like in any other game, you don't have much control over the actions of your foes or allies. You will ocassionally ram into an ally and do damage, get torpedod by your careless teammate, and a few other things. Gameplay is sometimes a bit slow, but not to the point where you'd fall asleep. Queue times are around 1 minute, sometimes a bit longer depending on the time of the day & tier you're playing (there's certainly a lack of carrier players). Oh, and there's lootboxes that you get through playing. And missions. Gameplay is either normal pvp battle, players vs bots battle, or ranked pvp battle. Ranked pvp rewards are a bit underwhelming as of now, but it's an alternative to normal pvp battles. There's some events every now and then that spice up the game a bit and bring new ships, colors, and game modes.
Pay to win, Y/N? - Short answer: no. Long answer: a bit. Features you can buy is essentially levelling through ships faster, or just buying premium ships. Premium ships are sometimes better than their corresponding nation's ship of same tier that's not a premium ship. This isn't that common though, and the highest tier doesn't have premium ships. There's also a few upgrades that are quite minor, that can be purchased with doubloons. Overall though, you won't have to spend a dime on the game, and you can be just as competitive as anyone else.
Community, esports, etc - There's a rather big community around WW2 ships (thanks to few animes and this game), and there's threads and small forums on large websites that are ran by the community, aswell as the game's official forums which are semi-active. There's roughly around 25k~ players online on average throughout the day. There's also several sites that track your progress & statistics, where you can compare yourself to others and see how well you're doing. As for esports... well, it exists, there's clans that play competitive and so on. It's very small though, and not active in terms of tournaments. Definitely not a main attraction to the game.

This whole series is near the top of my list for any game I've played. Absolutely fantastic, and I hope they keep making more.
PROS:
- This is the best-written CRPG series I've ever played. Tons of interesting characters, and it seems like they put a lot of thought into their motivations and backstories. And little pieces of lore like the BBS and the nobodies you run into on the street are a nice touch.
- Pacing keeps it interesting. Not too long, not too short. Never feels like a grind, and each mission has its own "flavor."
- Combat is fun, characters play uniquely. Not so much combat that you get sick of it, or that it feels like you're playing an MMO.
CONS:
- Sort of easy. Most of the way through on Hard difficulty, and I've only had to revive one teammate. Some climactic battles end up pretty disappointing. And I'm not playing a power-build character. Then again, maybe I should nerf myself and not abuse Is0bel's grenade launcher so much :D
- For an immersive RPG, character customization is pretty bare-bones.
- Weapon and armor choices are still pretty linear, but they've put in some unique items this time. Still needs a bit more variety IMO.

I loved Dragonfall. Really, really loved it. And you can pretty much say that I agree 90% with most of the positive reviews of this game. However, I'm not finishing this game for a big reason.
The whole
issue. In Dragonfall, the game occasionally buckled under the strain of the designers' wishes. Too many enemies and the occasional complicated environment led to long loading times, awkward enemy behavior, and the enemies taking very long turns "thinking". This game takes the same engine and goes crazy-go-nuts. Two or three times as many enemies, large maps, vendors on combat maps, complicated mechanics, and teams of helpful NPCs make the game go really weird.
I've had the game repeatedly take a long time "thinking" about turns for enemies I had not aggroed, so the long turns just resulted in them taking no action. I've had friendly NPCs block exit doors and I had to trick them into fighting enemies so I could get past them. I've had both enemies and friendly NPCs take weird turns where they just kind of wander around the map. It seems like whenever enemies summon a spirit, it inevitably starts wrecking them and they don't fight back against it (yay!). I've had really weird item management when vendors are present on combat/mission maps.
Overall, it's like someone decided to take their stock Toyota Camry to the race track; the game just doesn't do what the designers wished it would. The weird stuff makes a game that
isn't as good as the last game really lose whatever luster it still had.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong (Extended Edition) is a disappointment.  I would only recommend this game for the serious fans who care more about the story than the gameplay.
The addition of stylized "cut-scenes" with voice acting, and the visual overhaul of the matrix are welcome improvements.  However, there are far more glitches in the actual gameplay than in the previous games.  The UI and movement are cumbersome at the best of times; reloading a quicksave is sometimes necessary during normal gameplay becuase of glitches.  The most common glitches I encountered were being unable to click on objects in the environment (such as terminals) and the game freezing during combat.  "Misclicking" is still a big problem during combat when multiple actors are close together.
The redeeming quality of this game is the story, which is quite good and keeps me playing long after I would have otherwise quit in frustration.  The numerous choices in dialogues adds to immersion, as do the many choices and their consequences.  Unfortunately, one of the glitches in this game involve dialogue scripts breaking, which requires reverting to an older save.
Also, the matrix overhaul is terribly implemented.  The decking sequences are tedious and full of glitches.  The "real-time" movement in the matrix exacerbates the flaws/glitches in the "real-time" movement system.  The matrix is practically unplayable even after all of the patches they've released.  These glitchy "real-time" sequences don't belong in a turn-based tactical game.
I do not recommend buying Shadowrun: Hong Kong unless you are a fan of the series and you don't mind the major gameplay flaws.

Magic, cyberware, dwarves, dragons, elves and corps who want you dead. Harebrained Schemes has put out a truly amazing title in Shadwrun Hong Kong, their third Shadowrun title on Steam.
If you're not familiar with the Sixth World, the year is 2056 and magic has made it's return to the world. Along with it, elves dwarves and even dragons have returned. Shadowrun Hong Kong takes you to the seedy underbelly of its namesake, within spitting distance of Kowloon City. The streets are filled with gunrunners and organ leggers, and you're a shadowrunner trying to make it.
The game itself is indepth, with multiple classes to tweak as you please and a deep story waiting for you.

Back in the day I was a big fan of the Abe games so when Munch came out (and I didn't have a p̶l̶a̶y̶s̶t̶a̶t̶i̶o̶n̶Xbox) I was quite disappointed.
The good: the puzzles were generally all pretty clear. I very rarely got to a point and had no idea what to do next. Decent enough story and execution thereof.
The bad:
- Limited level designs, like maybe 2 major types of area are used in nearly all the levels,
- The group that ported it to the PC clearly did the least amount of work possible. Want to quicksave? You have to go to the menu every time.
- The controls! Space is both jump and interact, order to work and attack are on the same button, etc. I can get why you need to do that for a p̶l̶a̶y̶s̶t̶a̶t̶i̶o̶n̶Xbox release but it just makes the game super frustrating when you're playing on a PC.
- The camera! Oh god. :( It will swing around based on the room layout and where you are, but because the movement is relative to the camera you'll be running, the camera swings, and bam. Dead. A significant amount of time I had trouble with puzzles not because I didn't know what I needed to do, but because the interface got in the way and made it difficult.
So yeah, unfortunately I can't recommend it.

I've been an Oddworld fan since childhood, and started Munch's Oddysee with enthusiasm, only to be disappointed on the first moments. This is not just a bad Oddworld game, it is a bad game in itself, for any kind of player.
There were the usual intro cinematics, for the title screen and for the game itself, as good as always, with that familiar feel and style. The creepy design of the creatures, the dark mood of the plot, the toilet humor, everything was fine. Then, inside that cave where we start playing and learn the commands, I press the jump button and Abe springs cartoonishly on the air in an instant making a muffled "boing" sound. This is the condensation of the main flaw of this game, it is too goofy for what it tries to do, with almost no sense of menace.
When I played Abe's Exoddus, I loved its unique style, gameplay and personality. I was scared by its mood, challenged by the threats, amazed by the crafstmanship of the design, animations and backgrounds. The humor balanced well the overall tone of the early Oddworld games, and I assume every fan will agree that these traits were their main qualities and the soul of the franchise. Munch's Oddysee took the challenge of taking it to the new generation, but did not make it successfully.
It's understandable how the early formula would not translate to 3D, but what formula does this game adopts then? A generic platformer not unlike many others from the Nintendo 64 era, with bland gameplay and with every of the characteristic Oddworld traits either absent or toned down. For example, in the early games, it was amazing how the characters moved in a very organic, realistic way. Abe jumped a small height upstraight, runned smoothly, and climbed ledges with effort. In Munch's Oddysee, he moves like a bad version of Mario or Megaman, severely breaking the gritty feel we all love so much.
The level design was very rich and pleasant, with that Ridley Scot Alien vibe on some environments, and a fantasy native vibe on others. Here, the backgrounds are very basic and unpolished. The first level, for example, wich is a set of woods, fades into a fog at a short distance. None of that huge constructions, ruins and statues on the background are to be found. None of those rich details like the coccons with skeletons on the walls of Necrum, or the structures os Monsaic Lines also. The industrial levels are as generic as they can be.
The gameplay is, probably, the worst part, because it really strays off the spirit this game tries to convey.
First, now everything you do depends on these bright green balls you collect on your path, from the possession powers to opening doors. Yes, bright collectible itens inside an Oddworld game. It's a really clunky way to limit your possession powers and it just does not fit well on this fictional universe. Instead of sneaking your way to sabotage some machine or find some lever or control pad, you walk through an obvious trail of globs and chant to a door when you have gathered enough.
Second, the enemies. In the early games, you were almost completely helpless for 99% of the time, and almost everything could kill you instantly, because there was no lifebar. Guards, wildlife, machines, everything was either a monster or a murderer, and you were just this malnourished running slave with near zero fighting capabilities. Then, the emphasis was on stealth, puzzle solving and occasional ofense when the circumstamces allowed. In this game, there is a lifebar, wich means many of those old enemies are now much less of a threat. The sligs, slogs and scrabs don't scare anymore. You end up runnig past many of them just because you don't have the patience to deal with them, not because it's your only option.
There is also a combat system. You still interact with characters like in the old games, but instead of them being more helpless than you, needing nothing but rescue, now they can fight for you, weather you play as Abe or Munch, and is really disappointing to see an unarmed slig being slapped to death by a mob of wisecrack mudokons. The vikker interns being eaten by fuzzles are just a little better. In the end, it is just too silly and you don't feel any menace or urgency, which means that killing the enemies is not very satisfying, so the combat gets repetitive and boring.
Storytelling was always simple in Odworld, but the franchise tries to create this epic universe, which Munch's Oddysee tries to expand, and such would require more thought through. The plot then just throw events out of nowhere, leaves many things unexplained, and doesn't really know how to pull off its ambitions.
Certain franchises just do not make good transitions to newer game designs, but on top of that Munch's Oddysee makes many bad decisions that undermine all the key features of its legacy, specially the dark, menacing setting. This leaves the humor unbalanced and the overall mood uncharacteristic of the franchise's style. But, as a standalone game, this is also a poor effort, with not many good points to make it a fun game.

Who would have thought that after 25+ years of spin-offs, sequels, and remakes that barely saw any exposure outside Japan, we'd ever get a successor to River City Ransom like this. It's about damn time.
Though the game does pay due respects to the original source material, the "Kunio-Kun" series, this is far more a sequel specific to the westernized version of "Downtown Nekketsu Monogatari," known throughout the USA and Canada as "River City Ransom."
The gameplay is surprisingly faithful to the source material, something I'd probably describe as "enjoyably frustrating." Enemies have numerous bad and annoying habits, including but not limited to pacing outside your reach, hitting once and running away, and attacks that knock down from a distance. All of this just makes me ravenous for♥♥♥♥♥kickings, which is practically immersion for a game mostly centered around punching out a stream of interchangable dunces between boss fights. Getting in synch with the enemy AI and figuring out how to punish their odd habits is part of learning to play. Character building returns as a big feature of gameplay, as well, increasing parameters and learning new abilities from stores strewn across the game world. While infrequent, the game does demand trail-and-error puzzle platforming during a few segments (including three chase sequences and one fetch mission). While most of these felt needlessly difficult on the first few attempts, they became considerably easier after I had completed them once.
If there's any parts of the game that gets a "needs improvement, see me after class," it's the character balance. There are 10 available characters for story mode, each with some diverse gimmicks and a suite of unique attacks. However, at least half of the characters have some flawed attacks that fail to hit correctly, combinations wherein a strike knocks enemies out of reach of the following move, or have a warmup animation that is too long to legitimately hit anything with (the AI is programmed to walk outside of range). Most of these, however, seem accidental and are likely to be fixed via the game's frequent updates.
This is still an extremely fun game with a banging soundtrack that's even better with some friends. Old timer or newcomer, you owe it to yourself to give this a try.

One Way Heroics is a tile-based, rouge-like, J-RPG. There is a constant threat, the darkness, consuming the world. There's only... a 'few' ways to resolve and save what is left of this world.
One Way Heroics has a constant threat; the swallowing darkness from the west, and thus one can travel only eastwards or risk being consumed themselves. There will be many opportunity costs because of this. One can only explore only so much north-side and south-side in such a time-frame that you may miss a dungeon, or a town, or even rare holy loot; or unfortunately encounter a powerful foe that will devour your lifepoints in a single blow. Unable to fully loot everything because of a weight limit, you will have to take a limited amount of supplies and equipment and give up what is necessary for survival or end up blowing your own self up because someone lit up explosives in your inventory.
It comes along with many classes starting with the sharp Swordsmaster and agile Hunter, to the charming Bard and sexy Hero... to a traveling Tourist
? Each a journey without rest and different abilities for each class.
In terms of difficulty, you choose the difficulty before you start your adventure; from
and
, to a
. As time goes on and as the darkness consumes more of the world; foes will be buffed and be stronger in level. It can be tough understanding every little mechanic there is, but after a few Walk in The Parks, you'll get a solid grasp on what and what not to do.
In terms of the game-play time, you can probably expect each normal journey to take thirty minutes to an hour (or an unfortunate eight minutes if you get caught off-guard), depending on how much you're willing to balance exploring and fighting. There are save points for each journey if you're slightly lucky to encounter them in towns, so don't worry if you end up having to sleep for yourself in the real world. Don't worry, that darkness won't eat you.
The DLC (OWH+) is not strictly necessary, but it does change and add more content to the game as it should. Get it if you enjoy the base game for how it is, and you'll definitely enjoy what the DLC will deliver (classes, choices, and stories!).
There are many win and lose conditions, multitudes of endings, and things to learn about the origins and the characters you meet along the way; certainly a lot to adventure and explore outside from the adventure itself.

Sonic Generations is a double-shot throwback to the classic Sonic that we knew in the cheap day-cares that attempted to make kids want to stay there, to the light-speed Dreamcast Sonic whose coolness shamed the ice caps. It's been ten years since I've played a Sonic game worth playing, and the 3DS version alone was good enough, but Sonic Generations for the PC (or a console, if you still think they're the pinnacle of gaming) gives hope that the blue blur can still be as great as his glory days.
The game has stages from the classics and the times when I cried at how Sonic just wasn't the same, but all of them are fun, and you definitely have a little bit of an edge if you've played a stage on an original game that may be featured in this. On that note, the G.U.N. truck was a bit nasty back in SA2. Here, it's VICIOUS!
There's a shortage of downloadable content, so far being only Casino Nights pinball, but the shortage of content is by no means a bore. Casino Nights pinball has some fun slot action from StH2 (Genesis), classic pinball feel of Sonic Spinball (Game Gear), and the... how to say... refined appeal of Casinopolis' pinball stages from Sonic Adventure (Dreamcast).
Knowing what I know now of the game, I would've paid $30 to $35 for this (I'd pay more if we were given Mushroom Hill on the PC and consoles), and I'm most certainly proud to have snagged it on a $7.50 deal!

Bit.Trip Runner 2 is the sequel to the original Bit.Trip Runner game, with lots of changes to bring another fantastic game. Since this game is a directly numbered sequel, there are some similarities between the two games. One thing to note is the series's trademark pixelized art style is changed to a more stylized and cartoony look. Overall, the worlds are less brightly colored and flashy but still are trippy or weird in nature. The music is also not chiptune in nature, but still has the style of Bit.Trip to it. Some songs wil be familiar to those who played prior games like Runner, and the music is still electronica based. Most fans of the original Bit.Trip games might bemoan these changes, but they actually are a refreshing change and still carry the same kind of charm and style that makes this a Bit.Trip game. The story continues from the ending of Runner, with all of Commander Video's friends and Mingrawn Timbletot being in the cutscenes. However, Commander Video is sent into an alternate dimension and chases after Mingrawn Timbletot in this more cartoony dimension.
The gameplay naturally takes after Bit.Trip Runner. Players keep running and must dodge obstacles using several abilities. Runner 2 adds new objects in the levels to mix things up, such as a loop the loop, speed boosts, and rails. Additionally, the player has a few more abilities to use to navigate new obstacles. Included in every level are checkpoints that players will restart at if they hit an obstacle after that checkpoint. The checkpoint may be skipped to earn bonus points, but at the expense of starting from the beginning of the level if they mess up. Alternate paths are showcased more in the game, and even have signs showing which paths are easier or harder. The harder paths tend to give more points, but may also have a treasure chest to unlock costumes or even unlock a new level with an alternate exit. Some levels also have keys which must be activated first from a Key Vault level. The levels with keys then are to be replayed to unlock a padlock and get another treasure chest. The difficulty tends to be easier than Runner on the Just Right difficulty thanks to the checkpoints making levels more bearable and the difficulty curve not being too extreme like in the first game. Runner 2's Hard mode should give a challenging set of levels with a difficulty not unlike the previous Runner game. There are more levels overall in Runner 2, which should make this game longer than the 5 hours of gameplay expected in the first Runner game.
Bit.Trip Runner 2 might look a bit different in style to other Bit.Trip games, but this game is just as fun as the first Runner game. Runner 2 boasts more features in the gameplay and is a longer experience while having the signature Bit.Trip style to the game. With a fun cartoony style and a variety of levels with good music, different level designs, and more fair difficulty, Runner 2 is sure to be a great experience that gives challenges and different things to be expecting.

LISA is emotionally forgiving as a nuclear bomb.
Its lewd. Its raw. Its about pain ,family ,drugs and all combinations of those three. and how that amalgamation of pain gains a hideous life of its own as a contagious parasite.
The creator is a pretty cool guy too. I cant sing enough praise for it.

To me, the comparisons to Mother seem to ring true because it's a story-type game rather than a strategy/skill game. Lisa seems to employ a different kind of storytelling mode, however; one that is much more adult and perhaps deliberately more slow-paced (and at times, repetitive) to really let the point sink in.
Pay attention to the characters, names and their motivations, as a lot of them will appear again throughout the story. There is also a lot of imagery used, so take your time to appreciate the plotline instead of trying to rush to the end.
I would recommend it because it is pretty impressive for a game to be able to explore such deep themes. Almost like watching a (really long) movie. It was a bit too slow for me at some points and I came close to abandoning it a couple of times.
TLDR; Good storyline but can be a bit slow-paced. Not much strategy/skill required so can get repetitive and boring.
