Though I never grew up playing the River City Ransom games, it had a reputation of being a fantastic beat-'em-up for NES, and its reputation carried over into other games that I did play and enjoy, not the least of which being the Scott Pilgrim vs. The World game on the 360/PS3. I only ended up playing the original RCR after playing Underground, and I will agree that both games are quite different, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, though it may upset some players.
I'd say if you're looking for a classic RCR game, look elsewhere, such as River City Tokyo Rumble for 3DS. If you're looking for a solid arcade beat-'em-up that throws references to other media in left and right, and that anyone can play without knowing much about the genre or about River City Ransom, this is a good choice. As a comparison: Underground plays more like the Scott Pilgrim game than like a River City game, which is slightly ironic considering the inspiration behind the SP game.
I'll get the bad things out of the way first.
-Unclear objectives. Even though you're given hints by NPCs as to where you need to go to progress the story, some objectives aren't that easy to find on intuition alone, so if you're attempting to survive a horde of enemies while plot is happening around you, you'll be lost quite easily. Don't be afraid to look up a walkthrough. Move lists also suffer from this; a handful of characters' moves are executed only during a combo, but the combo string is never specified, and you have to use trial and error to figure out what move went where.
-Bugs. There are a few annoying glitches to be found, though nothing too gamebreaking. The worst I've come across has been getting stunlocked by tear gas that a single police officer would continually throw, with no easy way to escape. There's also the annoying habit of running into invisible walls on screen transitions, though that can be avoided by jumping into said transitions.
-Lack of solid plot. The original RCR had a simple plot, but the idea of being a street thug beating up on all rival gangs in the city was solid enough to keep its successors going. Underground flip-flops between a revenge story, a rescue mission, a sci-fi, a different sci-fi, and gang war, which is a bit bothersome to keep up with at times.
-Tedium. A lot of the time, you can find yourself doing one thing over and over for one reason or another. Grinding for level-ups, grinding for money, moving from point A to point B then back to point A because of story, punching the same dude who's already dead despite being able to be air-juggled, and so on.
-The milk quest.
Now for the good things.
-Varied characters and moves. The amount of dedication put into giving all 10 playable story characters their own unique movesets that benefit their fighter type is astounding to me. References to other media aside, the characters all feel great to play as in their own way, and none of them feel the same as anyone else. They are also all animated brilliantly.
-References. Pretty much anything that was popular in gamer and geek culture at any point (mostly during the 80s) has probably been mentioned ingame somehow. Phrases are not exempt from this.
-Upgrades. Characters all can level up to Level 40, and upon a level-up, their stat parameters' maximum value increases, and the maximum is different depending on the type of character you're using. Stats can be increased by purchasing food, books, music, etc., and moves can be bought at three different dojos in the city. Unfortunately, there's no way of knowing what items or moves do what until you buy them, which is a bit of a deterrent for some, but there are guides out there to let you know what's what. There are also hidden moves for every character that are fun to use, but ultimately pointless for a handful of characters.
-The fighting system. Unlike the original RCR and its successors, Underground seems to have more of a focus on pulling off combos and air juggles. Rather than buying moves to have varied ways of doing extra damage, you would buy moves in Underground to further stylize what you normally do to inflict damage. In other words, Underground is flashier with how you attack enemies, which, to the right audience, is a lot of fun.
-4-player multiplayer. The game allows for up to four people to play online, locally, or over LAN, and this is true for both story mode and Arena mode, the latter of which is PvP. There are quirks programmed into the game to account for more players, such as increased amounts of enemies, additional text at plot points to give a sense of group togetherness, and group saunas. As fun as the game is solo, playing it with others is another level of fun.
A lot of love went into the creation of this game, which is clear to see. Despite the flaws it has, I still have a ton of fun with this game and its quirks. It's not for everyone, admittedly, but I hope I touched on the topics that are of the biggest concerns to people.

Easily the best Sonic game since the Genesis titles. It's not perfect, but for the first time in a while the developer seems to really get what makes Sonic fun. Running fast and moderate platforming. And not anything else.
No playing as Sonic's slow moving friends, no fishing, no lengthy treasure hunting for emeralds, no werehogs, or any of the other experimental gameplay that diverged from what makes the series memorable. Just running fast and platforming.
The gimmick is having a mix of oldschool 2D and modern 3D Sonic levels. Thankfully both are a blast and capture the best parts of their respective styles. While the game stumbles due to some frustrating optional levels that guest star Sonic's friends, overall the gameplay is well paced and pushes the strengths of the series.
Plus it features both Vector the Crocodile and Blaze the Cat! Vector because his 90's cool attitude can't be held down. And Blaze because the game had room for one cat character and she is clearly superior to Big the Cat in every way. At least as far as anthropomorphic cats go.
Highly recommended to Sonic fans who may have abandoned the franchise sometime after it went 3D.

As fun as many of the super powers are and as wacky as some of the weapons are I think I liked SR3 slightly better. The story is decent but late game SR4 even makes fun of itself on stretching out the story, with events from SR1, 2, and 3 occuring in missions. I've played through it several times trying different combinations (Unlocking everything, only using base powers, not doing any side missions, etc.) and I've found that no matter the difficulty you need the experience and money from side missions (which are all activities) to upgrade yourself and weapons whereas the powers make certain areas easier except that there are a lot of ways the missions will temporary take away your powers. There are no decisions to make in SR4 that really encourage replayability like there were in SR3 and even with not having done coop on either game I've played SR4 about 50 hours less than SR3.
There is more activity variety in SR4 but many of them offer only 3 (sometimes 6) instances and it can be easy to gold level them on the first try once you know what you're doing so it doesn't take long to go through the fun activities. The garage is mostly useless due to the running and flying abilities with those times when you want a vehicle it's easiest to just steal one. Rampages aren't as fun, except in missions/activities, and once you reach level 3 threat there is pretty much no way to get rid of the threat besides starting a mission/activity, portaling out, or fighting until it maxes and sends out a Warden.
All in all it's a fun game with some of the missions being some of the best in the series while others are tedious. The DLC offers a decent return so it's worth it to pick up the GOTC version. 1. Definitely an improvement from BIT. TRIP Runner 1 with simply having checkpoints.
2. Really beautiful graphics and music.
3. Mechanics are fun and difficulty isn't because of something cheap/cheating -- rather just a matter of timing (very doable)
4. Easy controls for the controller.
Cons:
1. I needed a controller to really progress through the game. I believe it is also HIGHLY recommended to have a controller for this game.
2. The last world/part of the game gets rather difficult to distinguish between the level course, your character and the background. The complimentary colors and theme is waaaay too much.

The *BEST* Shadowrun game to date! Finally, just about everything I wanted Dragonfall and Returns to be: Hong Kong is. Dragonfall was a vast improvement over Returns: much better storyline - characters you can actually converse with - the ability to level-up your squad as you see fit. Hong Kong keeps those improvements, and then even more.
+ Longer, more fleshed out storyline. Far more conversation options and a squad to actually care about (Gobbet <3). Feels like a vastly more immersive experience! Finally feels like there are some actual decisions to make in conversations with your squad, on missions, and even the shopkeepers around Hoei.
+ Updated UI and the ability to not just send every pickup to stash: can finally swap items around and send them to a squadmate if you're inventory is full. Very helpful feature that's finally been added. Also, you can now enter combat mode before (some) fights break out, allowing you to properly position your squad instead of finding yourself clumped up for grenades/mage AOE before a fight even starts.
+ Armor no longer gives stats (aside from armor rating) = You can buy anything to customize your looks rather than being locked into one particular armor set based on your class. Very cool! Can be a shaman and look like a decker if you really want. Personally, I just go with the ninja outfits from Shen... but that's just me.
+ Classes finally feel more balanced. My main gripe of previous Shadowrun games was how much better any gunslinger felt over any other class. But more cyberware (!!!) and cyberweapons = Melee classes feel far more competent in Hong Kong than they ever have. And Mages finally get a VERY useful spell: Chain Lightning! IMO, just what mages needed to really feel powerful. A cheap (AP-wise), multi-target spell that deals good damage and AP damage, and isn't limited by a 2x2 square AOE.
-/+ Updated Decking system: Still not sure about this. In some ways I enjoy it: it's different. But it's a little hampered by being a bit unresponsive and awkward at times. But at least it's no longer awkward battles in the matrix with Blitz..
- Still some bugs present. Nothing game breaking, but some minor lingering issues that can be a bit bothersome. Sometimes can't interact with NPCs/items until I spam ALT. Once got stuck in a conversation with Duncan while simultaneously picking up an item during a mission and had to restart because I couldn't get out of it. Matrix sometimes feels unresponsive and awkward. But all-in-all: minor and doesn't affect my experience too much.
** On the whole, absolutely love this game! It's been really fun playing all the Shadowrun games and seeing the progression. Returns was short, with a simplistic storyline and no real squad to care about. Dragonfall improved quite a bit on all fronts, and now Hong Kong improves on everything Dragonfall did over Returns: making for a much more fulfilling experience into the Shadowrun universe.
Would highly recommend Shadowrun: Hong Kong - 9.5/10 game for sure! And an absolute must play if you're super into the Shadowrun series and have played the previous games.

Ah, Shadowrun.  The IP that just never really quite gets the attention it deserves.  Originally based on a tabletop RPG game that lovingly mashed together cyberpunk literary classics such as Neuromancer with the traditionally high-fantasy festooned world of elves, orks, and dragons.  If you don't remember Neuromancer, just picture the baby of Lord of the Rings and The Matrix and you'll do fine.
Since it's tabletop days, it has had a few different incarnations as a video game, to very mixed quality and success.  Hong Kong is the 3rd in a line of well-received CRPGs that have all been enthusiastically supported by Shadowrun fans through Kickstarter.  A success story for both fans and developers, and it shows how much of a cult following the IP has maintained over the years.
It is also this cult following, however, that has given something of a critical pass to this series.  Remove the Shadowrun license and you'd be left with an RPG that does
things with text and...  Well, just competent things with everything else.
Don't get me wrong.  It's fun to play and the gameplay isn't
. it just doesn't stand out.  Also, for every step forward Hong Kong has taken from it's predecessors, it seems to have also taken one back.
Combat is turn-based and
tactical.  Meaning you want to take advantage of cover and positioning and prioritize your targets carefully.   I only say
because most fights for me tended to degenerate into stun-lock and DPS rinse/repeat cycles.  Use Action Point-damaging abilities to stunlock enemies that aren't immune to it, then have your close range DPS monsters tear apart everything else.  Also, RNG is as strong of a mechanic in battles as your tactics are going to be.
Cybernetics have gotten a bit of a rework, with a new ability-tree to that effect.  While being able to get perks for a cyber-focused build is neat, the ability tree itself is a bit of a head-scratcher.  All but ONE of the cyber-weapons are melee and use Strength and the Close Combat skill.  One weapon, however, the mono-filament whip, is a ranged weapon and uses Quickness and Ranged Combat instead.  The problem here is that you will start with the claws if you invest points into the Cyber Affinity tree, a weapon relying on strength.  If your intention is to use the whip, then you are basically either wasting points in Strength to use the claws until the whip becomes available, or you are left with a weapon you won't use taking up essence until you can get the whip.
The decking component of Hong Kong has been fleshed out and is no longer
a stripped-down version of the normal combat.  You must make your way past patrolling "Tracer IC" and getting into any combat will increase your System Trace.  If that hits maximum, then the system goes into alert mode, spawning a deathsquad of attacker IC at your location.  Also, hacking into data nodes now includes a mini-game that is a simple pattern memorization, and reminds me of the "Help Me Rhonda" bit from Short Circuit (what a terrible, terrible movie).  However, despite these additions, Hare Brained has also taken a step back here.  I found Matrix runs to be sometimes very tedious.  The added stealth mechanics of avoiding Tracer IC isn't particularly enjoyable when you have to have to clumsily float through them, making the passive "Boost" program that increases your float-speed basically a slot-eater on all of your decks.  Direct IC combat has not become any more enjoyable for the changes either.  Instead of finding a good position, it's often much better to just use the accuracy buff "Sniffer" program and then use all of your AP into dealing damage.  Often cover is impossible to get to anyway as the Tracer IC will be sweeping through it.  Altogether, the decking scenarios themselves just weren't as well done as the regular combat scenarios, which already left some to be desired.
Thankfully, the story-telling is still top notch.  There is no voiced content still, and it's
text heavy, to the point that you'll be forgiven if you think that you're actually playing a visual novel instead of a CRPG.  On the whole, I did enjoy the story quite a bit.  I liked that there is a lot more moral ambiguity in Heoi, a setting where even the "good guys" are still bad guys, over the relentless idealism of Berlin and the Flux State.  Your Johnson isn't a well-meaning teddy bear, but a
ruthless ganger kingpin.  You rub elbows with thugs, not hippies.  That said, I still ended up loving the story and characters of Dragonfall over those in Hong Kong.  They all somehow managed to grow on me.  It's not that the characters in Hong Kong didn't - I loved Gobbet, Rachter, and Gaichu.  However, Duncan and Is0bel were entirely disinteresting to me.  That could be just my tastes, but they both seemed to be lacking depth.  Duncan's only character progression is basically in direct relation to you (something that ends up not even mattering at the end depending on which ending you get), and Is0bel's problem is similar.  I get that she doesn't know how to interact with people well, neither did Eiger, but she has very little to add outside of her character flaws.
I also enjoyed the setting of the Walled City, with the host of lore and superstition surrounding that den of squalor.  However, being familiar with the actual Kowloon Walled City, I don't think the terrifying scale and density of that place was very well-depicted unfortunately.
If my review sounds overly-critical of a game that I'm actually up-thumbing, it is only because I feel that a good series, while being just that, good, is stagnant.  Given the great stories, it has been relatively easy to overlook the dated visuals, the just-okay gameplay, bugs and sometimes wonky AI, and very static NPCs and environments.  With Hare Brained now having several other pans on the burner (other games in development) I am thinking that maybe we are at the end of the run here, chummers.
I truly do love what Hare Brained has done with the Shadowrun IP - they've basically taken the Doc Wagon to it and saved it from death quite honestly - but if they want to continue to lead the way for Shadowrun CRPGs, they are going to need to take some great strides forward.
The developers should look toward some of the great creativity that modders have come up with to create much more appealing environments and mechanics.  I'd love to see worlds that really pop and come to life rather than feel like a low-poly character dropped into a static painting.  Open up the tactical possibilities of combat and make me rely on the environment more, make weapons more interesting, and choosing combat abilities less straight-forward.  Make the Matrix like a 2nd world.
Until then, I'll be in the shadows, lah...

The gameplay showed some expected flaws, such as Sonic spindashing or boosting in the wrong danged direction because he takes too long to turn around and his direction can't be changed during these actions. Sometimes the camera will bug out, and sometimes you might fall through terrain. Enemies can be a big pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ All that said? The modern levels are great to play through, being able to literally blast through stages and enemies while still being able to explore the levels as you desire. The classic levels feature many classic enemies and gimmicks, but with so many new stages, it all feels very fresh, even when Sega took on old stages. Every single act I've played through so far has had a myriad of alternative paths, and it quickly becomes very evident that they put a lot of love and care into designing each and every one.

Once you actually start to go for achievements or the time trials, the flaws of this game are heavily highlighted and actually start to become unbearable, which is an experience that I would not recommend.
That being said, this game is incredibly short. I played through this game very leisurely my first time through and really took the time to soak in the environments and explore areas that I thought were interesting, and it was only about two hours. Those two hours were fairly captivating, although I honestly don't know if the asking price is equal to the amount of enjoyment derived from playing. I would highly suggest buying this game on sale, since I think that otherwise, there are just better alternatives to A Story About My Uncle.

I'm gonna go ahead and just quickly address all the mentions (for good or for ill intentions) of Undertale here with an "Honestly? Stop that". Comparing the two games unfair to either, as both have their own unique identity. We get it, you really hate or really love Undertale. Now shut your facehole and let people enjoy other things without dragging your stink into it. Goddamn.
Anyway...
This game does a LOT of things right, which makes it one of my absolute favorites. In terms of gameplay it manages to stick things as familiar as turn-based combat and moral choice system while still managing to keep things fresh. Things like the combo system for characters like the protagonist and a few recruitable party members, along with the chance of an enemy having an ability to permanently kill any of aforementioned crew, keep your attention without the "spam the A button to make everyone attack until thing dies" that many RPGs today suffer from. It's simple, but it's also unique.
And on the topic of the moral choice system, can I just point out that anybody writing a post-apocalyptic setting should take some notes from this game's writing? Because LISA does a damn good job of blurring the lines of morality, as a world where everything has gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥and everyone's just doing what they can to survive should. Personalities will warp, chances for even a fleeting moment of relief or happiness will be taken, but there still can be even the smallest speck of good in there.
Where LISA really shines through though are it's story and characters. The mood is portrayed really well with a wondeful mix of soundtrack, storytelling, and visuals. Little bits where the game doesn't take itself too seriously are sprinkled about the story, but it's still able to remind you just how bleak the situation is. It's also one of the few games where you don't HAVE to play the prequel, LISA: The First, to enjoy the story. But at the same time doing so will explain a lot of things about the trilogy's namesake character.
Speaking of the prequel, another thing I really adore is how this series touches on sensetive subjects without using them just for shock value. It also doesn't portray said abuse victims as beautifully broken people who can do no wrong because of what they've endured. You can sympathize with the trilogy's three protagonists, yes, but their actions in one game or across many will still make you question the kind of person they really are. As a survivor of abuse myself, the personalities of Brad, Lisa, and Buddy all speak out to me very much. And speaking of people...
The party members and the NPCs! How could I write a review for this game without mentioning these colorful ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s? I've only seen a handful of games that offer a variety of recruitable folks to join you that still make them all unique! The game manages to not draw out their time to the point where some would nitpick about it, but still manage to give them some pretty powerful personalities! The NPCs, albeit important to the story or not, are also solid proof about what I said about blurring the lines of morality. Across the trilogy, reoccuring characters aren't written off as inherently good or evil, but as burdened by their various pasts and coping with it in different ways. A character you could hate in one game could redeem themselves in the next, or a character you loved in one game could do something unforgivable in another.
I've heard a few complaints about the world of Olathe, in that it's very linear. And honestly, I'd have to agree. But at the same time it's vast enough for you to discover all sorts of hidden secrets or just fun easter eggs. Linear doesn't necessarily equate to bad, but the variety always helps.
Another I've heard is the ever popular "it's too hard!". To which I have to respond: Dude, it's known by its fans as "LISA: The Painful RPG" and even has a harder difficulty called Pain Mode. If you walked into this game not expecting it to try and kick your♥♥♥♥♥ Then I'll probably assume you're also one of those people who expected Dark Souls to not be hard and not really know what to say to you.
All in all: this game is a masterpiece and well worth the 15 dollars for both the game itself and it's sequel-DLC, LISA: The Joyful. And on top of that? LISA: The First is entirely free. I would definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a good story with some challenging gameplay!

Now, I'm a simple man to please and I don't have much to complain about, except the lack of graphical options. Though it may not be necessary to tweak this game as much as modern, more demanding games, it would still have been nice to at least be able to choose resolution because though the games looks and play really well, some people might want the original resolution since the cinematics have been stretched and they look pixellated. I would've liked having an option to have original resolution cutscenes and higher resolution gameplay. This game has a really slow start but it's worth the wait. Some of the best 3rd person lightsaber combat in any Star Wars game, with characters, locations and a soundtrack directly from the films. Jedi ownage at its finest.
Full video review:

(EDIT: I was under the apparently mistaken impression that Jedi Academy came first. That was a mistake on my part when I made a comparison at one point.)
(EDIT 2: I have posted a video at the bottom that very briefly demonstrates the shifting position of the crosshair.)
It's time to face an uncomfortable truth: no game is perfect. I tried as hard as I could to enjoy Jedi Outcast, and I tried more than once. It's unfortunate, but if you are curious about what problems this game might have, you are about to find them all listed in one place.
One of my first irritations was trying to aim. Your reticle does not stay in the center of the screen: it shifts between the center and the lower right corner depending on the distance of your target. This greatly complicates aiming. Many enemies move around wildly, and your weapons have very slow moving projectiles that usually don't do much damage unless you can get one of those exceptionally tricky headshots. Both you and your target will be moving, so when you combine that with the shifting reticle and slow projectiles, hitting anything at all is an extreme challenge. I have often missed targets at nearly point blank range because the reticle was never where I expected it to be. Bear in mind that you will be shooting for the first large chunk of the game.
One of the most appealling aspects of the game is lightsaber combat. And I found that to be little more fun than shooting. The very first level after you get your lightsaber pits you against snipers -which can't be blocked with your lightsaber- and grenadiers -which your lightsaber not only doesn't protect you against, but I remember it actually detonating the grenades. Timing your swings is tricky, so you might take a shot before you actually kill your target.
And then there is lightsaber vs lightsaber combat. And I was never able to figure that out. (This coming from a lover of Dark Messiah of Might and Magic and Severence: Blade of Darkness.) The Jedi Outcast tries to replicate the look of (highly correographed) lightsaber combat in the movies, and what we get is hard to read. What I would end up doing was trying to always keep the enemy in front of me and keep using force heal. By the way, do you remember those attacks your lightsaber won't protect you from? Like explosives and sniper shots? Enemies with lightsabers are immune to such attacks from you.
Force powers try to spice combat up. But gone are force choke, force drain, and other useful abilities from Jedi Acadamy. (Not to mention the ability to immediately level up your force heal and skip the very worst levels.) In fact, you get less combos in general than you did in Jedi Academy.
Jedi Outcast features the most monumentally confusing level design I have ever seen. It is clear that none of the levels were designed to be like a place that would have had an actual function for actual people before your character shows up. Rather, levels tend to be slightly abstract. One problem is that there are often several similar rooms copied and pasted together, making environments more confusing and repetitive. Jedi Outcast delights in making it unclear what you have to do to progress through the game. I would literally get stuck for 30 minutes and then achieve progress only by shooting a random thing out of my frustration or boredom. There were usually no visual cues at all that I was supposed to shoot said thing, and these incidents happened many times. I have said before that if Valve designed these levels, there would be honorable suicides taking place.
And now for the most frustrating mechanic by far in the game, the mandatory stealth section. If one enemy sees you and presses an alarm, you immediately get a cutscene of Mr. Katarn getting executed. There was literally no reason that I couldn't have sliced out everyone's nipples except the game wanting to pis me off. This section contains the type of hyperlinear gameplay executing the player for not guessing what specific thing they had to do to avoid execution that frustrates me in modern military shooter campaigns. The elephant in this particular room is that stealth mechanics don't really exist in Jedi Outcast. As Kyle announced the beggining of the mandatory stealth section, my already high frustration immediately spiked yet higher. At my first feel of this section, I immediately decided that the game had tested my patience in too many other ways, so I cheated past that part in the hope that the game would begin to get fun after that.
It never did. I reached a point where I fought three lightsaber wielding enemies simultaneously, and I gave up. I'm pretty sure the game was not going to get better after that point, and even if it did it would be far too late for that.
Shooting is broken, lightsaber combat is broken, and level design is broken. What is left? Storyline? First off, the enjoyability of a game's story is always going to be bottlenecked by the quality of the gameplay because you must play the game to progress through the story. Ignoring that, what is the story? That joke of a leftover empire does things, and we contrive a way to have an army of red lightsaber wielders. Just like in Jedi Academy. And this constantly contriving armies of red lightsaber wielders in Star Wars games rings a bit as B.S.
Every time I try to play it again, I always rediscover frustrations that I hadn't quite commited to memory; there are too many for me to remember all of them. I literally consider Jedi Outcast to be the worst first person shooter I have ever played. (Haven't played Revelations 2012, Rogue Warrior, or Garry's Incident mind you.)
Now, the vast majority of players say this game is awesome, and it has nearly a top tier metacritc score. For those reasons, I can't guarantee that you will hate this game like I do. But if you do pick up Jedi Outcast and find it to be one of your most frustrating experiences in gaming, I just want you to know that I called it.

There may be stages to how one approaches this game.  I'd never played the original River City Ransom, and I'm sorry I missed that one.  But I was always a huge fan of the old school beat em' ups like Double Dragon, Renegade, Bad Dudes, and the like.  So, upon seeing the trailers, I was jaw-to-the-floor-in-a-puddle-of-drool with desire to play this thing.
When I got the game, and played my first round of the retro scenes, I was reminded quickly of how difficult these older games can be.  But once I got out of the flashback, into picking fighters and trying out their different styles, eventually beating up Abobo in the principles office and fighting off  riot police while trying to escape the high school when the plot thickened, I was struck by how much you can get out of a simple premise with some clever hidden paths.
Now this game is hard at first, really hard!  It will test your reflexes, and have you micro managing every quarter you pick up from the floor after a hard won fight or a loose parking meter.  And there are lots of things to find in this game, fences to climb, and a city map that has very little to do with the actual lay out of the game (it's more metaphorical, pay attention to it's inconsistancies, and you might figure it out).
But after dying so many times, reincarnating back at your hide out and figuring out how to dodge the cops, you start to get honed on the depth of control of the fights, even with the most basic of moves, on how to stay alive, manage your cash to get the next fight move at the dojo, or a burger just to stay alive, and you do that enough times and something awakens in you that you haven't felt since, well, back when...
This is what classic gaming is all about.  And that's why River City Ransom: Underground is pure awesome in sack of kick♥♥♥♥♥  Now go buy this game, and get ready for some retro knuckle busting thumb thumping!

I love RCR on the NES. It's still one of my favorites. But this game wasn't what I was expecting. The map system is awkward, the game is LOADED with stuff I want to skip, terrible dialog, long drawn out conversations and a lack of understanding where to go next. After the first section is done, you warp ahead in time and pick a character and you fight for 40 minutes before you can get any upgrades or new moves.
The enemies run away a lot, forcing you to keep chasing them, when you need to kill them all to exit a level this gets amazingly frustrating. I have no idea where you can save, it's always grayed out for me. You have to read a lot and follow the dumb plot to know what to do and where to go. I just wanted to make people barf and collect coins, but they added a bunch of stuff that really ruined what I liked about the original. It's tedious and bloated, enemies are sponges and the most annoying parts are left in, like running into slightly off pixel items causes you to take damage, fall down and take a few seconds to get up. This happened in the original, but the added depth just makes it even more annoying.

If you want a trip down memory lane, it's worth the buy.  If you never played the first game on the NES, it's probably skippable.  After finishing, the NES game left me more satisfied.
Without spoilers...this game just gets weird near the end.  Even near the start, you don't fight bosses...you CHASE them.  It's not fun.
I'd wait for a sale on this one, though I spent a lot of time with it.  Cheers!

HBS is back with another gem of a Shadowrun game. Keeping to the pattern that  made Shadowrun Returns and Shadowrun: Dragonfall fun, as well as keeping to the source material, SR:HK is a fun step back into the world of magic and cybernetics.
As far as lore and story goes, the devs have hit every nail on the head (aside from a couple of small editing errors in the text). You get fun, interesting characters, dialog that keeps you both hanging on the story line and laughing with the poetry on the Shadowlands BBS.
Technically the game is much better than predecessors, with the ONE downfall I can find. In SR:DF Director's Cut you got the ability to manage your team's karma spending, able to develop them as you chose. HBS turned to the "dumbed down" format this game, allowing you the ability to pick one of two ability modifiers every few levels, a la XCom. It takes away some of the fun, but still allows you to do some customization of the team based on your main runner.
Graphics are good, control is still solid, aside from the new real time Matrix movement. It's added, I'm sure, to add tense, interesting Matrix interaction, but the ability to move your character quickly around real-time IC is...irritating to say the least. At least the hacking minigames are fun for me.
in all, a 10/10 for me and any Shadowrunner out there craving good story over run-and-gun-non-stop.

Picked this game up on a whim. Dived straight in. Ignored the tutorials. Built a fleet of 23 Colony Ships thinking I could storm the solar systems and pick up the production from the awesome gas giants that orbited the sun.
Then I discovered that you could only colonise Rocky planets to start with.
And so having grasped the basics of the controls and UI, I'm starting again. "properly" this time. If anyone wants a preview, I'll be streaming the game for maybe an hour or two at the weekends (GMT) so check in to the channel's discord for the times.
So far in this game's favour
+ Nice art style
+ Consistency
+ Plenty to check out and uncover if you don't do the tutorials *cough*
+ Recognisable influence from games like Civ
+ Not too many nags, handholding
+ Tutorials included for those that want them (and you should want them!)
+ Quick to load, small download
+ Very responsive developer, helping with my noob questions and taking feedback for the next version
+ easy and quick to pick up and put down. I don't always have hours to spend at a time, so this fills the void
+ Having come from just playing Homeworld: Desert of Karak, I really like the freedom to go anywhere.
+ Game starts off very chilled
+ I've not uncovered any game breaking bugs
On the negative side
- UI has some less-than intuitive elements
- Research tree seems to be a little too understated, there's a lot going on, but I don't feel like I'm progressing through it with any meaningful choices at the moment, it's just set-and-forget.
- You have to do the tutorials
- It's not  up there with Civ or Stardock's Sins (but then why should/would I expect that?)
Conclusion
So it's an early release game. If you like early release games, being part of the development of the game, and having a responsible ,responsive Dev to chat to about what you're experiencing, then great. If you like indi games rather than AAA titles in the same genre, then there is a lot to commend this title.

This is kind of a mix between MOO and Stellairs. On one end, you have Masters of Orion, the game that made 4X games a genre back in the mid-90s. The other end you have Stellairs, which was just released a year ago, but in my opinion it added features and changed how the whole 4X genre is handled.  Children of the Galaxy is a weird mix of simple and complex that blends well together. It does some things not seen before, like moving galaxies, which has it planets obit around there sun. When you target a planet if it takes more than one turn to get to, you must target its next movement location. It’s displayed on the map, so It’s not a complete guessing game. Another cool thing is warp magnets, you build these in a system and they make ships warping land around them. It’s a resource hog but who doesn’t want to know exactly where the enemy fleets will drop in at? Little things like this give it an identity that stands out from all the other 4X’s.

Let me start by saying that i have high hopes for this title, but find their "6 months" (6+ minimum) in early access to be ambitious to a impossible degree. Currently, what is in the game works - but calling it fleshed out is a massive stretch. Also taking the currently missing features along with that - there is years of work here to rival other titles in the genre.
Lets break it down:
Exploration mostly boils down to "let it auto explore" with little to no influence you want to expand to doing - you just create a bunch of scouts and send them into the void on their own. Anomalies, unique finds, planetary exploration, systems and galaxies are mostly flat and have no depth in terms of unique elements in them.
Expansion is also... flat. Outside of a few research points that provide passive buffs here and there, most of your expansion is spamming all possible buildings on a new planet and building a ton of stuff floating in space to mine and defend it. There is no customization and depth in terms of expanding your planets, borders and supply-lines, adaption to different planet biomes or even differences in resources available outside of the hard number. Basically again - planets are fire and forget.
And these two already illustrates the issues with the game.
The building works, the expansion works, the exploration works, the production empire expansion works. There are no game breaking parts to the game in any of these. But they are so very limited in gameplay interaction. Most of the early to mid-game consists out of queuing a bunch of things and pressing "next turn" 20 times.
And while the research systems has hints of greatness in the way you can assign a % to a type of research to focus on - the nature of needing those pieces of tech to get anything done means that multiple search items at once doesn't benefit you until the very late game stages.
I've not touched on diplomacy much, nor on combat and the fact is that these are... non existent in my eyes. Diplomacy they've said is still in development, so that aside - the combat is a rock-paper-scissors affair that mostly requires "lots of rocks" and little else, with balance being messy and combat interaction having little to no weight.
Again, the core idea is great and the "in world" combat that allows for smart movement and usage of the environment as needed is great - but its so damn shallow.
So with enough time in the oven - this could be great, and with the level of quality they have on display it is clear the developers care immensely about this product - but it's not there by a long shot, even on systems they are already advertising as implemented, that are missing anything but the barest of bones.
For now i'd be hesitant to jump in with the current lack of content, but the game shows promise to keep iterating on good ideas down the line.

Lisa is a hidden gem if I ever saw one. When reading the description I was convinced the game would just be wacky, weird, and a little odd. Instead the game was all those things, and then some.

The story itself is much darker than what you might originally think, dealing with hard choices like sacrificing part of yourself in order to save another team member, or choosing him to die just to keep yourself out of harm's way.
A thing to be noted is that the game can be quite challenging at times. More often than not there are limited resources in areas, so you cannot grind your characters up, and as such funds to buy items are in scarce supply.
The game is charming, dark, and humurous, and definitely makes you think about the choices you make.

I bought this game during the summer sale, since a reviewer had described it as "Undertale, but for adults." While the two games have some major key differences, the choices you make during your journey do affect your game and yourself as a person. Will you be selfish and risk the life of your party member in roulette just to earn magazines (the game's currency)? Will you sacrifice your party member's life in order to keep your own arm? Will you give in to the drug called Joy, which makes you feel absolutely nothing? Just how far will you go save the life of someone you consider your daughter? The choice is yours.
LISA has many unique characters, some of which you will hate (and in the end perhaps love) and some of which you will love right from the start. While the game does not go too in-depth with backstory, some of the flashbacks throughout your journey give you enough information to piece mostly everything together. And holy hell, is it depressing. There's a lot that I can't say since I don't want to ruin the story, but let me just say this game is an emotional train wreck. It makes you laugh, makes you angry, and it makes you cry.
Every aspect of LISA is what makes it such an amazing game. The crude humor, the complex characters, the soundtrack, the storyline - it's all amazing. LISA is definitely one of the best games I've ever played.

One Way Heroics is a Roguelike adventure game that takes place in a fantasy world that is being consumed by darkness. Our brave hero must quickly travel ---> and defeat the Demon Lord in order to stop the darkness from consuming the entire world!  The constant pressure of the dark wall of doom closing in behind you forces you to plan ahead and takes a bit of getting used to. Labyrinthine dungeons are there for the plundering, but if you spend too much time looting you may find yourself without an escape route!
Don't let the word "roguelike" scare you off! The game has a save system, so if you really want to continue your adventure after getting eaten by that dragon, you can restart from the last time you saved. Keep an eye out for villages to save at! Also, there is an "emergency save" feature that allows you to save anywhere provided it has been at least 5 (in-game) days since your last save. Of course, you get a higher end-game score if you clear the game without dying, and with minimal saving.
In the beginning, you can choose between two classes, and more can be unlocked as you earn hero points (awarded at the end of each run). Each class has a trait unique to them that offers its own style, from the straightforward Swordmaster: master of slashy stuff, to the Force User: a squishy mage-type character.
Without spoiling anything, the game has a surprising amount of depth to it. I'm still discovering new stuff and I have been playing for quite a while already. There is a dark brotherhood, NPCs to befriend, an adorable fairy guide, witty dialogue, and some interesting sidequests you can find. The DLC is well-worth the cost, almost doubling the amount of content in the game.
Give this game a go, at a price like this you'd be hard pressed to find a better value.

Locations

Puzzles

Story

Value

This review assumes you played Puzzle Agent 1, and contains spoilers for the ending of it.
Puzzle agent 2 picks up right where Puzzle Agent 1 left off. Personally, I adored Puzzle agent 1's "Unsatisfying" ending, where you are unable to solve the real mystery because you achieved what your job actually was, I thought it was a perfect way to maintain the mystique of what was going on, and end on a good joke. So of course this game picking up where it left off, entirely undermines that ending.
I would have preferred a new story entirely for agent tethers. That said, while it undermines the joke of the first games ending, it doesnt do so poorly, it doesnt feel shoehorned in to start answering questions that should remain unanswered, really you could have put the two games together and released it all as one game, and nobody would have bat an eye. The story retains all the charm and humor of the first.
The puzzles themselves are, roughly on-par with the original, though with the addition of sliding block puzzles that both controlled poorly and hurt my brain, those were the first puzzles I every had to look up outside guides for. And mathamatical puzzles that I just couldnt get without using all 3 hints immediately. But none of them were outright unfair, they just werent something I personally was any good at.
The games length is also on-par with the original game, pretty much everything is just as good as the original, so its really up to you, if you liked the first game so much, you would have been willing to pay double the price for it, then Puzzle Agent 2 is worth it.

Hong Kong is the latest iteration of the Shadowrun series, and it really doesn't deviate much from it's popular predecessors.
The new stuff worth mentioning:
- A more complex Matrix, with stealth elements, and a little memory mini-game to hack.
- You can now enter turn-based mode as soon as you see the enemy, giving you the opportunity to attack before they do.
- New Cyberware skill-tree and new Cyberweapons, weapons, spells, and enemy types.
- Improved item handling. You can now use medkits on anybody on the team when not in combat, and item pickups can now go to teammates instead of stash if your character doesn't have room for it.
Nothing groundbreaking for sure, but it makes for an altogether more refined experience, and a thoroughly enjoyable Turnbased RPG with a strong story. I must confess that it exceeded my thresold for how much I can endure reading, even though the writing is very good. I would've paid 50% more for a version with voice acting.
The AI can still be considered stupid, odd or buggy at times:
- I've cornered a foe, who decides to use his "strip armor" spell on my rigger who's by far the furthest away avoiding combat.
- The enemy tries several times to toss a grenade at Duncan even though he has the ability to toss it back (every time).
- A foe will make a move towards my team, but then instead of attacking, he moves back into cover, clearly wasting action points, as the direct route to that cover was shorter.
And in the just plain silly category, I discovered that my summoned Rat Devil spirit could operate a computer during combat. Judging by it's avatar it really shouldn't have a clue what its doing :)
The extended version I bought at 50% off has a quite lengthy, high quality bonus campaign included, bringing my total playtime to 20 hours.
Unlike Dragonfall DC, I found Hong Kong to be very easy on normal difficulty, and I was only challenged in the end fight in the bonus campaign, until I realized I was missing an item that gives you control of a powerful spider tank.
Bottom line - if you just cannot get enough of Shadowrun, or you're a fan of the genre, but haven't tried the previous Shadowrun games, then this is a recommended purchase even at full price - especially if you don't mind reading A LOT. If you've recently played a Shadowrun game and felt it was a okay/good experience, there's no reason to throw money at Hong Kong - it's fundamentally more of the same.

I found the game to be incredibly fun, the art design is lovely and the writing of the main campaign and a mini-campaign follow-up to it is solid and interesting. The same can be said about the characters, I pretty much fell in love with one of them.
The best of Harebrained Schemes' Shadowrun games so far, Hong Kong offers improved combat, cyberware, matrix systems. I hated playing the Mage in the previous games, had tons of fun doing so in this game, particularly to improved ley lines which clearly make a difference this time. Matrix is more stealth-focused, requires the decker to avoid detection from constantly patrolling cameras and has them perform a hacking mini-game based on remembering numbers / symbols. Though if one dislikes it, they could just run through the cameras and force their way through, which will cause hostile ICs to arrive.
The game's main disadvantage would be the amount of bugs in the game, like items not doing what they advertise (specifically adding stats). Fortunately, until it is fully & officially fixed, there's a Workshop patch to help.

This is is the pinnacle of Harebrained Schemes' take on Shadowrun, building on the shaky-but-promising foundations of Shadowrun Returns and the excellent follow-up, Dragonfall. Like its predecessors, SR: Hong Kong is a narrative-based tactical RPG born out of the pen-and-paper Shadowrun setting. The Hong Kong location gives things a different flavour, sufficiently differentiating it from the other two games, but what really sets it apart is the extra attention paid to the NPC runner crew. Shadowrun Returns had only a couple of returning characters, while Dragonfall introduced a true party of the kind you'd expect to find in most computer RPGs. Hong Kong takes that and runs with it, and I think a large part of what you get out of the game will depend on how attached you become to the characters. For me, Hong Kong is easily my favourite of the three games, though I still need to go back and play the Director's Cut of Dragonfall.
Gameplay-wise, things are mostly similar to the other Shadowrun games, but the interface is further refined, while cyberware and Matrix hacking have seen a lot of attention. The Matrix work in particular makes playing a decker a lot more interesting, and the hacking minigame for cracking blocker IC is pretty neat. It's a lengthy story, too, especially with the Shadows of Hong Kong mini-campaign added with the Extended Edition. At time of writing, that epilogue campaign seems a little rough around the edges, but is a welcome follow-up with a couple of interesting runs.

River City Ransom: Underground is NOT the type of sequel that gives you more of the source material - this is evident within the first five minutes of gameplay (barring the humorous throwback tutorial). Conatus Creative has made the combat of River City Ransom far more robust and complicated than the original - in the beginning, you will feel as though you are fighting nearly impossible odds, but once you spend some time with the variety of combat options given to you, you will find how to best handle the problems thrown your way.
Visually, the game has been crafted with love and care - every background is incredibly detailed and every character oozes personality (with the exception of the generic "Thug" gang, but that's probably the joke in the first place). The only complaint I have regarding visuals is that it sometimes gets a little challenging to keep track of your character if you are playing local multiplayer, but the chaos and fun more than make up for it.
Speaking of multiplayer - the game has both couch and online play. I haven't run into any issues when playing with friends; the game felt practically seamless and lagless for me and the others.
The sound design is stellar as well. Disasterpeace put together a solid arrangment of music, considering it appears that Conatus was not able to get permissions to re-use any old music from the original River City Ransom. That said, Disasterpeace's songs will grow on you over time to the point where they'll get stuck in an endless loop in your mind.
As I briefly mentioned before, the mechanical side of the game. RCR:U's heart and soul is the brawling and street fighting; your enemies are smart and aggressive, you WILL need to learn how each opposing gang member fights and how to best make your openings. Generally speaking, rushing up to your opponent is the worst approach, as they'll perform a quick backstep and counterattack, or they'll slowly adapt and block your combos if you continue to re-use the same combo chain. Unfortunately, while weapons exist, they often are not as useful as you might like. Enemies tend to ignore the weapons so long as you don't touch them, but in the case that you do, their behavior then becomes unpredictable and far more dangerous.
As far as plot and pacing go, this is where my only real complaint crops up. RCR:U generally does a good job of informing the player of their next goal... up until Act III of the game. Acts I and II flow really well and feel just about right, but Act III just kind of feels sparse and confusing. It's the only point in the game where I had to look up forum questions and such, as it turns out I had been entirely misinterpreting what the game was
to demonstrate to me... but it really just wasn't obvious.
While the game does suffer a little bit toward the end, I cannot hold the entire game at fault for that. This is a game that's worth playing - the people making it put their heart and souls into this and you can see it when you look for it. They have been very quick to respond to bug reports and other problems that happened after launch, so I cannot recommend this game enough if you're up for a challenge and a good old street fight.
Despite some flaws that other people have brought up, this game is still immensely fun to play.

I commend Oddworld for having the guts and the will to revist a port of one of their old games, and it just so happens to be the one I've actually played in the past. Sure, there might be better game they've made, but dammit, this is the one I've actually had memories playing.
The past horror stories about the then-current PC port made me hesitant to get this version of the game, but the updated port beta was interesting enough - and I'd say it's won me over even in its rough state. Actual game is pretty much a typical 3d collectathon platformer, which would feel instantly familiar to anyone who played Crash Bandicoot, Spyro, Super Mario 64, or (in my case) Rareware's 3d platformers. However, as should be familiar to players of past Oddworld games, this game heavily relies on puzzles from the two playable characters, both of whom play differently and offer their own host of challenges.
So far I've only played enough to get my bearings, but this new port is really well done. On my 2k monitor and GTX 970, it runs like a dream, without many visual flaws for something that's originally from 2003. I would probably add post-processing sharpening and shaders, but the visuals could keep me playing. This game also controls well on a 360 gamepad, though I had to turn down the walk speed on one of the characters, who felt a little slippery to control in my opinion. Camera controls well, though I had to remove the inverted X axis for it to feel natural. Options are a little lackluster right now, hoping that resolution and quality options can be added in the future, and that the X360 controller controls could be more clearly indicated than using "Button 10" and such.
I have a few issues with this while I've been playing. For one thing, the tutorials in Abe's section - can that shaman tutorial guy shut up and not halt me in my tracks with obvious crap when I'm trying to enjoy myself? I've also found it fiddly to grab Mudokons in order to toss them, feels like that could use a more generous collision box. Also, in order to active an environmental trigger, I found that you can't be right next to it, contrary to my own instincts. Finally, when multiple Mudokons chant, the audio of them becomes obnoxiously loud. I'm hoping that these issues could be addressed or tweaked in future beta releases.
For $5, this would be a purchase that's well worth your time. Just remember to use the beta version of this game for now.

Even though i've always taken a liking to platformers, i was never much of a sonic fan like so many are. Untill this game came along, and now i finally 'get it'.
Clearing a level isn't that hard, but to master a level takes time and practice. Sonic rewards you for it like no other platformer, with so many routes to take, so much speed to build up while creating a flow that just hits every right note.
In order to keep you fresh and excited in this process, it offers you an enormous amount of challenges. The stages never feel repetitive, and the surroundings are gorgeous. On PC only it runs on 60fps, and it shows.
All the content is doubled by giving you an option to play the game in 2D or 3D at the start of each level/challenge. Both operate on a high level. The soundtrack is great and in tune with SEGA's great work in the past.
The only downside are some of the boss-stages, where you feel like you're on rails for a large part. But they are just a small piece of the content, so hardly something to bother yourself too much about.
Highly recommended!

I usually just♥♥♥♥♥♥out dumb reviews about games, but here goes nothing:
LISA is a side-scroller RPG, nothing too super duper cool. It DOES give the game a better look as Austin could make the characters much bigger and stand out much more with this setup.
The game's story is as follows (SPOILERS):
An event characters refeer to as "The Flash" occurs, causing every woman in the world to vanish. You live in this world as Brad Armstrong, a man who is addicted to a drug named "Joy" which makes you feel nothing. Years after the apocalypse, our good old addict Brad hears a cry... A baby's cry. Of course, he goes to the source of the noise to see if it is truly a baby.
After playing with the baby for a while (and accidentaly dropping the baby to the floor) he goes to his home to show his friends his new finding. As soon as his three friends see the baby (Rick, Sticky and Cheeks) they ask him to check what gender it is.
As it turns out, this baby is a female. Brad's friends suggest that they should give the baby to Rando so they can live a good life and esentially save the world. Brad refuses however, as he thinks this bay is his "second chance". The game explains why he says this in a really good way, you need to see it for yourself.
His friends agree to keep the baby, and they name her "Buddy". After a while, Buddy gets kidnapped, Brad's friends die and Brad goes out to Olathe to save his little adopted daughter from addicts, monsters (again, check that for yourself) and perverts all of which have a desire for SKIN.
The rest is up to you.
The game is one of the only RPGs to give you more than 4 party members and actually make your choices matter. Unlike the classic "Do you want to watch THIS guy die or do you want to watch THIS girl die?" choice, the choices you make bites you in the♥♥♥♥♥through the whole game. I do not mean like, people remind you of it and call you a "monster" or something among those lines. No no, your choices heavily effect gameplay. There's one choice that's a weirdly obvious choice and won't even effect the gameplay if you choose one of the options, but other than that they are awesome.
The designs given to all the characters greatly favor them by causing them to perfectly stand out. I am guaranteeing you that you won't be able to find  a party member that even resembles another character in look/personality/move set, let alone being the same.
LISA is also a painful (haha funi), emotional roller-coaster. It tries it's best to kick you in the balls and spit at your face and it does the job perfectly. Unlike Undertale, it does not push you to feel only good or only bad for a specific character. In LISA, it will give you many reasons to HATE and LOVE the characters. For example (SPOILERS); Brad tries to protect Buddy from a sea of perverts, but kills many others in the process. It is fine, though. Cause Buddy is the only woman alive and she should not be used as a sex toy, right? Well, it's up to you.
The battles are fair and fun to go through as well, I am %100 positive I've never gotten♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at an enemy because of how "unfair" their attacks were. Yeah, getting stunned is♥♥♥♥♥♥but at least not all of their attacks do that to you. Even if they heavily rely on stunning you, they are given a lower chance of doing those attacks with the stun de-buff. You won't get "stun then rapidly hit with deadly attacks" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t from this game, I am guaranteeing it. There are insta-kills that permanently (I do mean this) kill a party member, but they are often set to low frequency. Meaning that you won't have a hard boss insta-killing your party members one by one.
Do not even get me started on how good the music is, I would say it's the best soundtrack I've ever heard. Yeah, every boss and random battle is not given a specific theme BUT Austin used the pitch setting in RPG Maker to make each boss fight music feel different. You can hear, say, Summer Love 20 times through your run but you won't get tired of it due to how he changes the pitch each time to make it feel and sound different. One time it's a relaxing song, then another time it sounds like a song you would hear while hanging out with your lover on the beach.
Overall, I would say this game gets a A+ for execution. Go pick it up or beg your friends to buy it for you, or how the ♥♥♥♥ you guys get your video games these days...

After playing more than 500 hours of this game. I'm finally writing my total review.
For those who dosn't want to read a wall of text here is a short summery:
This is a Pro-Nazi game in disguise. So unless you love being dominating overpowered axis power, or have hard BDSM fetish for playing Allies. You will quickly learn the dev's hugely favor the Axis forces.
No back to the review:
This game graphics is pretty good and detailed, with terrain shaping as the battle goes with craters, wrecks, ruins and so forth after heavy bombing/artillery etc.
The tactical gameplay is nice, your units arent you dumb single tab target unit that does x damage per shot at all times. or as pure rock paper scizzors as your classical rts games are.
Here combat feels more real, your infantry takes cover, jumps into nearest crater, wall or bush, to give itself advantage over the enemie. Recon, and knowing your effective range is the key of this game. Flanking and so forth.
There is alot of tought and details into the strategy with units having abilties and each faction being unique and interesting to play.
However, for each and every update that comes, the German forces are turned stronger and stronger while allied forces are getting weaker and weaker. (well especially if you look on US forces)
If you dont believe me. take a look on this site:
There you will have overall win to loss ratio statistic over the faction. You will see that OKW and Wermacht (German forces) have far stronger win ratio than the allied forces.
In all aspects. 1v1 to 4v4.
This further proves that the devs are quite pro nazi but in a subtle way.
Then you take a look into the game units.
The allies have quite few doctrines and unit diversity (except soviet)
Alot of the allied unique units have to come through special doctrine. Wich severly limits your play style during a battle.
While the German Forces are pretty good all rounders.
They get good mobile artillery, solid heavy tanks and solid infantry. And can quickly adapt and change play style after need. Any good German player would know how to prone and poke the allies to figure out what doctrines they went and then just adjust to a hard counter towards that and win.

So my conclution of the game:
It is a great RTS, however it severly lacks in the balance department.

Children of the Galaxy has the smooth shine of modern polish, but sadly lacks the depth to engage in many ways.
Video:
Text:
Let me start by saying that i have high hopes for this title, but find their "6 months" (6+ minimum) in early access to be ambitious to a impossible degree. Currently, what is in the game works - but calling it fleshed out is a massive stretch. Also taking the currently missing features along with that - there is years of work here to rival other titles in the genre.
Lets break it down:
Exploration mostly boils down to "let it auto explore" with little to no influence you want to expand to doing - you just create a bunch of scouts and send them into the void on their own. Anomalies, unique finds, planetary exploration, systems and galaxies are mostly flat and have no depth in terms of unique elements in them.
Expansion is also... flat. Outside of a few research points that provide passive buffs here and there, most of your expansion is spamming all possible buildings on a new planet and building a ton of stuff floating in space to mine and defend it. There is no customization and depth in terms of expanding your planets, borders and supply-lines, adaption to different planet biomes or even differences in resources available outside of the hard number. Basically again - planets are fire and forget.
And these two already illustrates the issues with the game.
The building works, the expansion works, the exploration works, the production empire expansion works. There are no game breaking parts to the game in any of these. But they are so very limited in gameplay interaction. Most of the early to mid-game consists out of queuing a bunch of things and pressing "next turn" 20 times.
And while the research systems has hints of greatness in the way you can assign a % to a type of research to focus on - the nature of needing those pieces of tech to get anything done means that multiple search items at once doesn't benefit you until the very late game stages.
I've not touched on diplomacy much, nor on combat and the fact is that these are... non existent in my eyes. Diplomacy they've said is still in development, so that aside - the combat is a rock-paper-scissors affair that mostly requires "lots of rocks" and little else, with balance being messy and combat interaction having little to no weight.
Again, the core idea is great and the "in world" combat that allows for smart movement and usage of the environment as needed is great - but its so damn shallow.
So with enough time in the oven - this could be great, and with the level of quality they have on display it is clear the developers care immensely about this product - but it's not there by a long shot, even on systems they are already advertising as implemented, that are missing anything but the barest of bones.
For now i'd be hesitant to jump in with the current lack of content, but the game shows promise to keep iterating on good ideas down the line.

Pros: A fun and somewhat-realistic sword fighting game, from what I can tell. I don't really know much about swordplay but the sword arts seem pretty realistic. Nice workshop support. Regional servers to choose from, frequent events, VAC secured.
Cons: Not a very good fighting game. Predictable opponents are still very difficult to defeat despite a built in rock-paper-scissors counter system. Many attacks have a deceptively small range while others have an equally deceptive and explosive range. Attacks seem to sometimes go straight through your opponent. Hit and block stun are well off at times, leaving you vulnerable when you hit your opponent and unable to counter when you block. All of this makes for a highly frustrating experience.
There's also a very limited number of fighters to choose from, as well as weapon types. They're not very well balanced either making for some false choices on the customize/character select screen.

And that's probably all people need. But there's absolutely no single player experience at all and the last time I played, lag was somewhat of an issue still. I also didn't notice too much different between the current version and the version I played when it was still in early development other than the AI opponents were added (and I'm assuming that a lot of glitches were fixed, but tell me what else I’m missing). The AI opponents are laughable since they won't really help you get better being that you can beat them by doing the noob strategy I mentioned earlier.
Overall, if all you want is a competitive online multiplayer game then you should be fine. But if you wanted something more than this isn’t for you.

Puzzle Agent 2 is a point & click puzzle game that continues the story of the mysteries introduced in the first game.  There are some minor improvements to the gameplay (more interactive puzzles means I didn't need paper and pencil this time), however the story and flow didn't feel as cohesive or intriguing.  For example, certain scenes would just end and you'd suddenly be in a different location.  The puzzles are mostly the same, but I still had a good time solving them and finishing the storyline.  Recommended only if you play Puzzle Agent 1 first.
PROS
+ Fun revisiting Scoggins, MN and seeing same charming characters
+ Most puzzles are fun and challenging
+ Same great art style, music, and voice acting
+ Achievements
CONS
- Storytelling feels rushed and wasn't as interesting as PA1
- Many puzzle types recycled from PA1
- Some puzzles are confusing or poorly explained
- I experienced more bugs/crashes than in previous game

delivers everything fans of the original were looking for – more puzzles, more Scoggins strangeness, and some proper answers to a mystery that was only half solved in the first game. If you’ve already played and enjoyed Puzzle Agent, this one is an easy buy. If you haven’t… well, Puzzle Agent is pure gold for fans of quirky stories and head-scratching logic puzzles, so pick up the original first, and then dive into Puzzle Agent 2 the moment that game ends.

A great sequel with very interesting and thrilling follow-up story. Puzzles are brain teasers. If you enjoyed Puzzle Agent 1 then do play this game because it has more puzzles and you need the story to finish up.

Good:
-Still pretty good story
-Nice art style (this is subjective but I like it)
-Well written dialogue with good voice acting
Bad:
-Puzzles are similar (and some more boring) to Puzzle Agent 1. I started getting bored of the puzzles in this game.
-The story gets very strange in this game and will take some unexpected turns. Some will view it as a plus but in my opinion the craziness at the end of the game didn't make for a very satisfying ending.
-If you want to get all of the achievements in the game, you must complete every puzzle on 100% on the first try, in one playthrough (since I have already failed one puzzle once, which was a misclick, I would have to replay the whole game to get the last 2 achievements). This is very frustrating if you are a completionist (I would very much like to get the last 2 achievements, but I have no intention of replaying the whole game to do this).
-Pretty short like Puzzle Agent 1
Conclusion:
-The verdict is that if you liked Puzzle Agent 1, and want to find out what will happen in the story, then you should probably buy this game (So I am recommending it as part of the series). However, I would say the game is considerabely worse than Puzzle Agent 1 and the creators should really have invented some new, more interesting puzzles to keep the game fresh.

Puzzle Agent 2 tries to be twice as fun as Puzzle Agent, while making the "puzzle" part worse (ambiguous rules, culture-specific puzzles, assumptions about the player's factual knowledge, etc.). I'd recommend playing the game only if you've played the previous part, and are looking for closure. If you're looking to play the game solely for its puzzles, you will probably be sorely disappointed.
That, of course, is my opinion.

Before i start i have to mention this game's story is the biggest reason you will enjoy this game, meaning if you did not play the first puzzle agent you will have absolutely no idea what is going on. Gotta love episodic games.
If you played the first puzzle agent game, you're definately going to want to play the second but bewarned that some corners were cut in the second half of the game.
The story is still by far the strongest part of the game, but even it be less engaging towards the end and the bits that were bad in the first game are still bad. Remember how in the first game it felt slightly off that the FBI were grading you for every little puzzle you did? Not to spoil the story but it feels even weirder, though i do like the idea of grading our performance on the puzzles themselves since if we weren't they would feel a bit too easy. Remember how the first game had all this suspense and mystery that kept you attached to the story? The second part feels like it's trying to keep building tension, but it never really amounts to anything important as far as the story is concered. I can imagine the devs talking as i play the game like "Hey here's a spicy love interest, you should talk with her. Whoops she's actually completely irrelevant to the story nevermind tee-hee." The puzzles are even jankier than last time and the last 30 minutes or so of the game is a bit of a mess in terms of presentation. Feels like they had a good idea for how to end the series, but didn't give themselves enough time to actually make the end so you get all these jump cuts and plot holes that don't really make sense.
That said for the most part the story gets tied up and the mystery of the town gets explained in a relatively interesting way. It's still got a lovely world full of mystery to unravel, and if you played the first game you are already super invested in the ending and will probably be ok with the little stuff. Despite it's flaws, puzzle agent two is still a perfectly good ending to the puzzle agent series.
Now get rid of this episodic nonsence and just make one solid consistant game please.
