Nearly 30 years after it's initial release River City Ransom for the Nintendo Entertainment system gets an official North American sequel. Kick, Punch, Jump and BARF your way through city streets and rescue River City from the clutches of Slick... again.
So this game's been in development for nearly 4 years and there are still numerous problems that need to be worked on and fixed. The development team was small, so to the mass majority of people think it's a resonable excuse as to why a 2D pixel art game took so long... To me, it just sounds like inexperience and incompetence. As someone who heard about this game before it's kickstarter inception, I have to say I'm incredibly disappointed with the final product, the wait wasn't worth it in the slightest.
The game itself feels unfinished, from terrible and clunky U.I., lack of description in menus and by the middle portion of the 2nd act you'll get a feeling of a complete lack of vision on the writers part. The first few hours of the game feels like River City Ransom but it slowly starts to deteriorate and it starts to feel less and less like a proper RCR sequel and more like a parody game and it's just completely whack.
I tried to give this game some credit and the benefit of the doubt but after having completed it within the first few days of release I couldn't bring myself to ever return to it due to save files being corrupted because of bad programming and how generic the game just feels.
Here's a quick rundown of issues that haven't been fixed and / or issues that still plague the game.
There's more, like bugs, glitches, save files being erased randomly, New Game+ not working as intended and the abysmal PVP mode but I could write a book about it so I'll just leave those issues as footnotes.
I want people to enjoy this game (including myself), I want to recommend it to you and tell you it's the greatest thing that ever happened to River City Ransom, but it's not. Instead it's a mediocre and tripe entry to an otherwise legendary franchise that will never receive the justice it deserves.
If you find this on sale for 10 dollars, maybe give it a go but don't expect to start netplaying with 3 other friends and have a jolly good time. I myself never tried the online portion but I've only heard bad things about it. Even the local co-op play has it's issues as I've tried that with my brother and we laughed the entire way through just because of how terrible the camera rubberbanding was.
RCRU is a one shot deal unfortunately. Where the original RCR had tons of replay value just due to how short and simple it was, RCRU requires way too much investment all while overlooking game breaking bugs / glitches while playing... it's just unpolished and it shows. Boasting a character roster of 10 playable characters each with their own unique and diverse skill set, it takes days to master their combos and that's only after you've leveled them up completely and maxed all their stats and bought all of their abilities... which also takes days of grinding.
Once you beat the game once, you'll never want to go back as it's just more of the same. I held off for 3 months on this review trying to give them a chance but considering there hasn't been a significant update for this game in over 3 weeks, I've given up trying to bite my tongue on the issue. These guys need to be exploited for this trainwreck they've delievered upon us. It pains me to say this but I wish a team of more competent people developed this project.
It's a 6 / 10 at best... It's passable, it's playable, but you won't want to come back to River City after you're done.

I was concerned over some negative reviews, but this game is genuinely everything I wanted from a sequel to RCR.
If you've played the original back on the NES (you may enjoy giving it another play through before playing this, as it's amazing how much care was taken to both adhere to and improve on the original formula), then you know what to expect here, only with more characters, better graphics, more locations, and beautiful sprite animation. Note that you don't have instant access to the full roster, not all characters are unlocked in the same way, and each has their own skills, levels, and money independant of the others. This means you can swap if  you want to start fresh, or try a different play style, or even possibly if you're frustrated and want to bring in your best guy to win a tough fight.
Some carry overs from the first game you should know to expect:
-There are multiple gangs. Each feels unique in this one rather than pallete swaps with different stats. You'll need to learn how to deal with each, and might want to pay attention to how much money each tends to drop.
-The AI can be tough! RCR is not a beat em up where you can just wade into groups of near-mindless enemies. Groups will often sit to the side and send one foe at a time at you, and if you ignore this and try to take them all on, you better not have a lot to lose...
BTW- the system where dying cuts your cash in half is back as well!
-There are a LOT of things to spend your money on, and you will find out what things do as you progress. I don't personally consider this a negative. The majority of the purchases I've made so far have been very very easy to save up for, so buying a random food item and finding that it boostes a stat I'm not concerned about is never a big deal. Also there are far more abilities to purchase in this game compared to the original RCR!
-The game is an open city which you can freely explore, though in this outing you have a map you can check, so it's much less trouble to figure out where to go when they tell you to find so-and-so at "The bridge" or "The abandoned factory"
All that said, I'm having a blast. If you and your buddies have fast and stable internet, you should have no trouble teaming up online as well! I've had ZERO issues playing online with friends so far. No noticeable latency issues or disconnects! And unlike the first RCR, this one allows for FOUR players! You can also host or join public games, though I'm not particularly interested in playing with randos, so I have no experience with that.

I actually do recommend this game despite everything I am going to say, but things need to be said and everyone - especially those responsible - needs to read this review. RCRU is a cheap cash-in on nostalgia. The game looks and plays great, but after replaying the original NES title I realised there are some outright inexcusable setbacks in this modern sequel. The addition of a grapple is great at first, but the punishment for failure quickly gets old as enemies get faster and there is no way to perform the grabs more quickly unless you are certain characters in certain situations. The police in this game make the police in GTAV seem tame; Once you hit the open world you must follow two NPCs and survive brawling alongside them until you've completed your objective. If at any point you hit an annoying civilian then a wave of cops come after you, fighting them makes them call for backup, and the only way to lose them is to reach a hideout or hide in a dumpster, and the only way to do either of these things is clearing every screen of both mooks AND cops until the open world is finally free. And the worst part? The cops grant no money or EXP for defeating them. I'm not entirely sure what the point of EXP has in this game. Instead of a typical growth rewarded in most RPGs, RCRU increases your potential maximum stats with no growth at all and occasionally allows a new move to be bought at dojos. I assume this was to stop players from farming up cash to buy the most expensive specials at the start of the game, but more powerful moves require more Special to use anyway. I can't say I've ever seen techniques handled this poorly in any other game. Speaking of farming, you sure do spend way too much time doing it. Enemies are all over the place, you can mug civilians, and you can even vandalize some objects to knock change out of them, but the yields are just pitiful for the first half of the story, once again putting the whole level-limited moves from dojos into question as grinding has become more of a chore than ever. And the absolute worst part about this game is the items. A freaking tutorial message reads "Buying and using items is an essential part of this game" and that's about as much honor as the devs give to the classic. I played this game with some friends on release, hyping up how great it was to beat people up for lunch money and grow stronger by eating sushi and burgers. The first mall in the NES title offered a café with cheap health items, a bakery with single point stat boosts for under $1, and a sushi bar with FOURTEEN different items of different effects ranging from $2~$29. Meanwhile in RCRU the first mall has ONE shop, selling expensive and useless cats. You can't access the selling point of this eat-em up until after defeating the first two bosses. And when you finally access the shops you slowly begin to realise that the items just suck. The best stamina item in the whole game costs as much as a Special move and only heals you for 60 - which isn't much to a character with ~600. The single item in the whole game I can recommend anyone buying is Dry Beef Stick as it is affordable and provides the only two stats that matter. The stats in the classic weren't perfect, but I could at least say "buy X if you want stronger kicks and buy Y if you want better maneuverability." You can't define your playstyle with stats, then there is an illusion that the characters set playstyles through their different max stats. The truth is your playstyle is dictated by each character's special moves. It doesn't matter if one character has a higher THR than the rest because just throwing enemies doesn't damage them, you need to use a Special move, which is powered by the character's ATK. Seeing this game boil its legacy down to a single concept is worse than disappointing, it's betrayal. To summarize, I can only truly recommend this game to anyone interested in watching 8bit sprites do flashy special moves after hours of tedium, and to look elsewhere for the RPG/Beat-em up that RCRU claims it's being.

LISA is a game about hurt. You play as Brad, a middle-aged nobody residing in the wastes of a ruined world. Brad lives with his lifelong friends in the middle of nowhere. Olathe, the name given to Brad's homeland before everything was destroyed, is sparse with human life, rife with monsters, and is entirely devoid of women. All except for Buddy.
"Where are we right now?"
LISA is a game about hurt. People will hurt Brad. People will hurt each other. Brad will hurt people. Brad will hurt. It's not uncommon to hurt, especially when it's the end of the world. Although, even in the end of the world people don't like to hurt. Maybe you'll take Joy and forget about all the pain and hurt, because Joy helps you forget - at least temporarily. Plus, when you can forget about everything that makes you so pathetic, then you can truly become strong. Besides, you're not the only one using Joy, and Joy has virtually no side effects - save for withdrawal.
"Why are we having this conversation?"
LISA is a game about hurt. The game begs the question of whether or not a few strong men can save the world from a sea of dip♥♥♥♥♥. Are you a strong man? Will you do the right thing?

The partial controller support isnt much better because by "partial" it means not only do you still have to navigate menus with the keyboard, but that only the cardinal directions register as inputs on the analog stick. If you press it to the diagonals it doesnt pick up at all. Furthermore the camera controls are on the D-pad rather then the right stick, so you have to use the same thumb to point the camera where you want to go before pressing forward on the stick to actually move. This renders any precision movement impossible rending some parts of the game nearly unplayable.
In conclusion, if you want this game, go find a console version of it instead.

And long, and rambling.
I've had this game sitting in my Library for a few months now and after trying to get back into it after the release (free release, mind you) of the bonus campaign; I've finally hit my limit of general disgust. And I haven't even gotten to the bonus content. I likely never will.
The bugs I encounted when I first started playing are still resident and still potentially crippling if not monitored. I'll hash some of those out in a moment. This is my major hang up: As a turn based strategy game, even a game that has a "Rewind" feature; mistakes in skill planning are game breaking. The first instance of this rears it's ugly head in the first real mission "The Walled City". The player character, the NPC Duncan and one other NPC selected from two possibilities are required to run an errand in a Chinese slum. No biggy. However, your choice of that third NPC can have an impact on the Karma (Player Character build points) that you earn durring the mission. One example of this (hacking a computer terminal) requires a piece of equipement that the PC doesn't even have access to that early in the game and bringing the optional NPC that can Hack it means missing another optional objective and reward because you can't bring the other Character. I can earn 2 Karma for muggung a mugger and returning stolen property, but only if Strength AND Unarmed Combat are at certain levels; but if I have those, I won't have either the Magical skills to earn Karma for aiding a Spirit, or the social skills to not completely screw up an encounter with a guard. Great, can I have Duncan beat someone up since I have to drag him along anyway and clobbering people is his specialty? No. Again, my build points are based on characters and situations outside of my control, and that causes a nickle and dime cascade effect that will make the game even more unsalvageable later. The cause of this error is the very "team" mechanic that the game is trying to enforce. The Player Character can't do it all, but the NPC can do considerably less.
Now take this into account: This is a Turn Based Strategy game. There s a lot of real world time that goes in to just a few moments of game time. Even with the rewind option, it just too much of a time sump to run into a brick wall and have to start even one mission over again. Too bad a complete re-build and replay from start is usually the only real option.
Bugs:
For no reason that I've noticed, when Characters are moving across the map durring fights, they stop animating and instead, the Sprites just slide around. This only seems to occur when the Sprites are moving from or to tiles that make up paved streets, but it happens randomly and to random characters. Not a serious issue as this is a TBS, but it does show that after all the updates and exxtra content, a core mechanical issue has been completely ignored by the Devs. Character pathing should alway be considered important. If the pathing is glitched, will line if fire, transition points and area events also fail?
NPC Movement: The NPC Gobbet (a team mate) lags far behind whenever the team moves across region maps. Sometimes, she wont even start moving until the rest of the crew has reached the point they were directed to. Since the game uses Icon transition points on the map, to prevent crashing (it happened to me twice, so far), I have to sit there and wait until the Character finally shows up before having the team move into a new map. Not a game breaker for the patient, but for anyone who doen't notice the discrepency, it could foul up an autosave and thus royally screw over a gamer. Unlikely, but possible.
There are many other bugs as well. Some involving sound and music files, some involving inventory. These are all well documented in the Community pages here on Steam. Please, check those out before even considering this game.
Biggest Bug: The Karma (character Upgrade) Menu. When I click on the in game menu to spend the points I have managed to farm, the Karma submenu takes so damn long to open, that if I don't jiggle the mouse every once in a while, my comp will go into Hibernate. That's bad. And yes, I know that I can change the Hibernate fuctionality on my end, but that isn't the point. The bugs I've listed have been evident since I first DL'd this game last summer and after all this time and all this content, are still here. And though they may seem minor, they all point to some very serious "lurking issues" in the engine that I for one, have no idea how to resolve.
TL;DR
This is not a multiplayer game, so why am I being penalized for the inability/availabilty of teammate's skill when I don't have a say in the skillsets of teammates? Why is the ONLY actual character in the game denied advancement because Teammates can't perform thier roles as written? This is a game breaker and it's the failure that has finally warned me off of Harebrained Schemes.

The sequel / spinoff to Bit.Trip Runner. If you played the first game, you know what the deal is. Control a new 3-D CommanderVideo through the stage and dodge everything in his way. They added a few new tricks to Commanders courses that makes the gameplay a little different from the first game like jump-sliding, and rail grinding. The visual style has shifted dramatically from the pixel and 3-D blocks to this wild cartoony style, and I know it's not everyones cup of tea, but it does make the stages a lot more interesting looking and it's nice seeing all the little quirks and fun things in the backgrounds of stages, even if it leads to a deserved bonk and reset. In terms of difficulty, it's slightly easier on the mind now that they've added checkpoints to stages so that if you hit something, you don't reset all the way back to the beginning, and they made a difficulty setting that actually works if you find the game too hard or too easy.
For completionists, this game is both harder, and easier than the first one... Easier in that you the retro stages are easier to get to as their hidden portals in the level instead of a reward for finding all the gold. Easier in that collecting all the gold is an easier rhythm to get into, though I can see how it might not be for some players, maybe it was for me because I played the first game? Anyway, it's also harder in that to get 100% on a level, you have to beat it, with all the gold, on each difficulty. So you'd have to play a minimum of three times per level if you get it all the first try. For achievement hunters, there's even an achievement for hitting the bulls-eye at the end of each stage for bonus points on each difficulty for every stage, which would definitely increase the amount of times you'll need to replay a level for 100%.
I'd recommend, it's fun, has fantastic visuals, the music feels like a step-up, and I believe it succeeds as a good sequel to the first Runner.
Also, who couldn't love Charles Martinet as the narrator?

In the tradition of its predecessor, Dark Forces 2, Jedi Outcast succeeds in making you want to stab out your eye sockets and replace them with voltage beans. What's a voltage bean? Why don't you ask Kyle Katarn?
Or...Dasani? Am I spelling that right?

The adventures of everyone’s favorite Kyle Katarn continue in another thrilling Jedi Knight game.  And who doesn’t love Kyle anyways?  He’s often been referred to as the Chuck Norris of Star Wars.  And to people that care about Chuck Norris that probably means something.  For me personally, Kyle as seen in these games is more annoying that the Kyle you read about in many of the books.
But I’m not reviewing the latest Fate of the Jedi book, is that series still popular?  I’m way behind on my Star Wars novels unfortunately.  We’re here to talk about the next in the Jedi Knight series, Star Wars Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast.  This time Kyle is back, and what starts with a blue milk run quickly becomes a quest fueled by anger and revenge.
As the Wikipedia blurb said, assuming anybody actually reads those, Jedi Outcast uses the Quake III: Team Area engine.  This means we are guaranteed to have a pretty good looking game, ID Tech III was first seen in Quake III Arena back in 1999.  It was a beautiful game then, and personally is still a beautiful game.  While there will always be things that could be picked at about the engine, and all the games that run on it, it will remain in my book as one of the best looking engines out there.
Jedi Outcast starts off kinda slow, but does pick up its pace once you get your hands on your lightsaber.  Which for me took about 4 hours.  I’m not going to lie, I had a really tough time with this game for some reason.  I’ve played it through in the past, but long enough ago that everything was still new to me.  In fact it wasn’t until I got the lightsaber that I realized that I had in fact play Jedi Outcast.
Something about the combat mechanics didn’t agree with me, and while there were some valid complaints.  Things like the Imperial Officers take more damage than the Stormtroopers.  Stormtroopers that are wearing armor while the Officers simply have their dress uniforms.  It would appear that a cotton polyester blend can withstand blaster fire better than the standard issue plastoid armor.  Someone should tell Requisitions about this, could save the Empire billions of credits.
You know that line from A New Hope?  Where Ben Kenobi says that a lightsaber isn’t as clumsy or random as a blaster.  Thereby implying that blasters are both clumsy and random.  Well it seems like the developers took that line from the movie and placed it at the core of their combat mechanics.  You could fire a blaster six times without moving the mouse and you’ll hit at six different locations.  The blasters have a fan effect, one that is made worse if you use the rapid-fire.
While the previous games had a similar fanning of the blaster bolts, they also had an auto-aim that counter balanced it.  You didn’t have to be a perfect shot, the blaster would make up for what you lacked in skill.  Here they’ve done away with the auto-aim, but left the fanning.  Personally, I don’t think Ben was being very literal when he made that statement.  Not to the extent that this game makes it seem.
The story I’d call above average, but still falls to some standard video game issues.  As with many games there are aspects or parts of the story that feel like they are only there for something to do.  Otherwise, were it simply a written story, the segment would have been left out.  But I’d can’t blame a game for these moments, as all games tend to have them.  The developers want to keep the action up, or to showcase a specific feature or ability in the game, and write a level into the story just for that purpose.  Its a common trait, and one that we games have gotten used to.  And the better writers and developers can do this, and blend it into the story so well that we tend to not even notice it on the first pass.
Jedi Outcast has the expected character cameos of Luke Skywalker, Mon Mothma, Jan Ors, and Lando Calrissian.  And best of all is that Billy Dee Williams actually voiced Lando, giving the character a little more love than the others.  Although it was a pretty big coincidence that Kyle should happen to be stranded in the same place where Lando is locked up.
But convenient coincidences aside, the story holds it own with the average of today.  As well as the bulk of the gameplay, controls, and puzzles have all aged well.  The blasters could use a little work, and perhaps a texture update and you have something that beats a lot of today’s releases.  In fact this would be a great game to get a HD remake.  And there are probably a couple of other things that I just can’t think of right now, but I guess they’re not that important.

So I went through the effort of downloading and launching this game for 5 minutes just to write this review. So if you are new to the game and genuinely wanting an honest opinion on it, please read my words carefully.
I've been playing this game for a little over a year now on Wargaming's client.
I have over 2000 battles and 4 tier 10 ships grinded out as well. And am well on my way to more.
Alright I'll get down to what everyone seems to be clamoring about and try to give an overview on it from the perspective of someone familiar with the system.
Free to Play.
All the skill needed in the game comes from a willingness to learn and the time invested in improving your skill.
There are players I know personally who are quite good if not better than average without spending a dime.
Most of the money that gets whaled on the game is spent by naval enthusiasts who just want to collect another historical ship.
So how does this ingame F2p economy work?
Game progression works where each ingame nation has several tech tree lines to progress through in various classes of ships. Each line is divided into 10 tiers which determine the matchmaking the ship gets as well as it's overall power relative to other ships.
Each battle you play you will earn credits and exp. The amounts are infulenced by things such as winning or losing. Surviving a battle. As well as individual performance.
If you do nothing you will earn nothing.
In terms of exp grinding you are about halfway to a tier 10 ship in amount of exp grinded once you own a fully upgraded tier 8 ship.
What can you do with real money?
Well the obvious and most dramatic thing you can do is buy a premium ship. This is something I do not reccommend a new player do for many reasons.
YOU ARE NOT GOOD ENOUGH. Im serious. No new player posesses the skill necessary to pull their weight in a high tier premium ship. You may get away with it with the gimmicky tier 3 and 4 premiums but this is not worth it, since the main perks of premium ships is increased credit and exp income, which at low tiers is moot as you make profit easily.
PLEASE do not buy any premium ships of a tier you have never played before.
You not only will be disappointed at your results and regret your purchase, but you can and will throw a game if you are high enough tier and do not pull your weight.
The next thing you can buy is doubloons. This premium currency allows you to do multiple things. First it lets you convert exp earned on ships you have grinded past and allows this exp to be spend on other tech trees. Note: you still need to have played the game and have a substantial amount of exp saved in these ships. YOU CANNOT GENERATE EXP OUT OF THIN AIR WITH JUST CASH. Doubloons can also be directly converted into credits. But remember credits are useless without earning exp. Finally doubloons can be used to respec skill points put into your ship's commander, demount a placed upgrade for use in another ship without spending credits and to retrain your commander instantly when placed on a new ship.
None of these actions are impossible for a ftp player it just takes time or costs an amout of credits. For example if you have a maxed out commander. You can use the excess exp as if it was already converted by doubloons.
RNG elements.

Dispersion as your shells leave the barrel is determined by an RNG mechanic. This mechanic is listed in port and the lower the number, the better. The number is basically saying that at your maximum range shells fired have a chance to land anywhere in an oval shaped area with a length of that many meters.
This really isn't that big of a deal at all, unless you are playing low tiered battleships that have♥♥♥♥♥dispersion by design.
Real life balistics on this scale of artillery were not laser accurate. They could put a shell where they wanted, mind you, but by no means were they as accurate as tanks or sniper rifles. Simply put, If you know how to aim and are skilled in leading and prediction, you can and will have a few shells hit your target per long range salvo. Medium to ideal engagement ranges, you will see most of your shells hitting. Which is pretty realistic if you ask me.
As for armor and damage, That system is less realistic, but it is more consistent.
Shells will do the same things under the same circumstances depending on where they hit the ship.
If armor is too thick and and/or the shell isn't large enough, It will shatter and deal no damage.
If the shell impacts a certain thickness of armor at an angle, and the shell isn't past a certain size, it will bounce and deal no damage.
If a shell is too large and the armor of a ship is too thin, the shell will over penetrate and not have a chance to detonate it's warhead inside the target for it's regular amount of damage.
Note: The above only applies fully to AP shells, HE shells have their own mechanics, but are even more consistent.
The chance for an HE shell to set fire is also a random % chance as well. But most ships that need to set fires have incredible rates of fire and large shell volume so this isn't too terrible.
Knowing your targets and how your shells interact with them is key to dealing damage. Otherwise you are wasting ordinance on something that isn't effective.
MOBA Elements.
This game is a MOBA through and through.
You are on teams, Placed in an enclosed map with key areas that you need to take.
There is a 2 point capture the flag mode,
a 3 or 4 point domination mode,
and "epicenter" where you have a large set of cap zones inside one another. Where the deepist zone is worth the most points.
Because it is a MOBA, it is not a sailing simulator. You can and will encounter players at every tier that are playing to win and maintain their stats. Just like any online game, expect some toxic ingame chats if people have slighted each other. It can largely be ignored.
I must stress PLEASE do not go into battle and ruin another players experience by not contributing, refusing teamwork, Teamkilling/damage etc.
Conclusion
From my experience this game is not near as ruined by being f2p as other games.
Trust me I've played a few of those.
Where literally every ingame action has a purchase option.
Where if your pockets are deep enough, all content is available to you instantly.
Where power creep runs rampant every month with new mechanics and items.
After having dealt with the worst of the worst of f2p games, this game is absolutely nothing to worry about.
Yes things will take some extra time and effort than if you invest money in the game, but paying players and free players all have to still grind a significant amount. And no amount of premium ships or economic grinding bonuses will make someone a skilled player.
I reccommend this game if you want/interested in
-Naval history and ships.
-A competitive online MOBA played at a slower pace than most.
-A free to play system that isn't pay to win.
-An absolutley massive learning curve.
-Are a fan of naval anime such as Kancolle, Arpeggio, or Haifuri. As there have been collabs in the past and some interesting weeb skins and mods available.
Great game, but pay to win...
I would say that this game should be at the top, along with Dota 2 and TF2, one of the most epic free games on steam!

I Highly… highly recommend this game. This is one of the most Fun and addictive games I have played in a long while. It’s not often a game comes along that makes you feel good and excited to play it when you get home. This is one of those labor of love games.  Before I get started I do recommend using a gamepad. Trust me it’s worth it.
The game is not just an homage to the original but adds a new layer of depth a detail to the original without fixing what isn’t broke as so many sequels do. The Gameplay, Graphic style and original characters are all kept intact for the sake of the story as well.  The Tutorial is even a playthrough of the last stage of the original game setting up the events of this game for those who weren’t born in the 80’s. The heroes, villains and gameplay is all explained seamlessly all while punching your way to the top like a badass in less than 10 minutes of the game. Genius.
The Gameplay is insanely satisfying.  Nothing feels so gratifying as playing Paul the Boxer, setting up an epic string of right hooks, jabs and Overhand rights then slamming your opponent’s crashing into 5 other guys like he just got hit by Vegeta.  Rudy in my opinion is this games Magilkarp who later turns into a Roid-Raging Gyarados (Pokemon fans know what I’m talking about) with his earthshaking attacks. And if sports aren’t your thing you can just go Glen take on the entire city Ryu-style.  Provie is my personal favorite cause who doesn’t think Capoeira is cool in any media. Each character has a style and martial art all their own just like Overwatch but without Bastion (thank god) that only gets better the more skills you learn.
The Graphics are perfect just as they are.  The decision to keep this game in “8bit/Old school” style graphics and not turn it into some cheap 3D remake was just as brilliant a decision to keep Frank Miller’s Sin City in black and white.  The animations each character in the world has its own personality.  The renditions of the city itself are amazing and the open world aspect allows you to explore areas that have nothing to do with plot just for fun and easter-egg hunt.
The city itself is filled with an entire cast of NPC citizens that you probably pass by everyday in real life like dog walkers, joggers, business men/women and even people driving to work. They are part of the game too. There are music stores, subways, suburbs and slums all adding to the feel of being in a real breathing city.  Attacking them or destroying their property summons the police just like in Grand Theft Auto. So, it doesn’t pay to be the bully.  At least it should make you aware after a while of your surroundings especially if you are outnumbered and low on health. Even still after summoning my 3rd wave of cops to try to stop my rampage at level 40 I always like to imagine Gary Oldman’s character from the professional screaming “….EVERYONE!!” in the distance.
I can’t guarantee everyone will know who Abobo, Mr. Kim or Billy and Jimmy Lee are but that therein is the beauty of this game. I will say I really wish we got to see even more of Ether, Calvin, and Prison Slick. The characters were so cool to fight it makes you want to see them again if a sequel is hopefully made.  Even the yearbook in the title screen just makes you remember that all these guys are not completely faceless mobs and are just students at your school. Some have turf like the Jock over the Football field or the Rich Kids in the Suburbs; some are spread everywhere like the muggers ambush masters of the city.
What is a sadly undersold feature of this game is that every enemy boss or minion in this game is 100% playable in PvP or Arena. Each comes with a complete book of unique to each character. Extremely cool.  You can play with friends or fellow RCRU players if you ever want a player 2, 3 or 4 anytime you want with a WLAN or Steam connection.
To sum up, if you ever wanted to feel like you can take on the whole city and win here’s your chance. I haven’t said anything about the plot because honestly everything outside of the original RCR plot is too funny to spoil or reveal so I encourage you to play that on your own and only use the guides if you get lost or need advice knowing how to level your character. There are surprises, 4th wall breaks and pop culture references galore so be prepared for a great story with a great cast of memorable characters you will want to see again.
If you haven’t already buy this game and get a copy for your friend. Ignore the trolls who try bash this game as this game is un-friggin-believably fun.

Before I say anything about the story, I’m going to point out that, since this game series is based on a book series, I realize I can’t exclusively blame the game for my problems with the story. They’re just working with what they have. However, I haven't read the books, so I don't know how accurate the game is or isn't, and a lot of this game is about the story more than the puzzles, so I think these are still pretty valid criticisms. Disclaimer over.
The first Puzzle Agent game was
. It was exciting, mysterious, challenging, a little spooky, (okay it was a lot spooky, but I might just be a big baby), and it had me on the edge of my seat the whole time. You uncover the mystery of Scoggins bit by bit and everything gradually starts to piece together leading up to the big event at the end. But, of course, it ends on quite a bit of a cliffhanger. The factory foreman is still missing and you still don’t really know why the Hidden People are there or what they want. So, obviously, you would expect Puzzle Agent 2 to address these issues. To find the factory foreman, to solve the mystery of the Hidden People. And it does. Unfortunately.
Here’s where my problem lies. I can’t figure out a way to express my disappointment without spoiling practically the entire thing, so I guess all I will say outside of a spoiler box is that Puzzle Agent 2 feels like it undoes what Puzzle Agent did so well. There’s not much tension. There is a mystery to solve, of course, but it’s all very linear and honestly a little boring. Somebody gives you a clue, so you go investigate it, that leads you somewhere else, you go investigate that… so on and so forth. And what is there is just… unsatisfying. It all seems like a bunch of plot twists that aren’t really necessary instead of using what they had already set up. So many details are added in this process that, even though the original story is technically wrapped up, there are so many more loose ends that you’re left way more confused than you could have ever been before. Again, I don't know how much of this is the game and how much is the book, but it’s still quite disappointing and I honestly feel like I probably would have been more satisfied leaving myself at the cliffhanger than I am now after knowing what actually happened.
In a few more spoiler-y details:
The puzzles in this game are a pretty good balance of difficulty, though there's admittedly not a lot of variety. I can only think of 4 types of puzzles right now, which is not exactly great for a game with the word 'puzzle' in the title. With that in mind, the variance in difficulty might have just been which types of puzzles I was better at/worse at. I’m not exactly bad at puzzles but I’m not great at them either, so I played this along with somebody who I consider to be much better at puzzles than me. A few were quick and easy solutions, a few were easy to figure out but took a while to finagle correctly, a few were challenging but definitely possible, and a small few were so frustrating that we had to look up a guide in order to solve them. There are plenty of in-game hints that I imagine are plenty helpful, but if you use them, be prepared to have to do a second playthrough of the game if you want all of the achievements.
I know it seems a bit odd to have a section about the controls in a review of a PUZZLE game, but I mostly just wanted to rant about the sliding puzzles for a hot moment. It should be easy to move a sliding block around a tiled area, right? But hoooooo boy. I was clicking and dragging with all of my heart and those pieces just would not move more than one square per click. It was extremely frustrating, to say the least. There might have been literal screaming at one point.
I do genuinely have another reason for this controls section, though, and that is that it’s VERY easy to accidentally click on things you don’t mean to click on. It seems like you're supposed to click and hold the mouse button to see what’s in the room, then wait for the symbols to disappear before you let go of the button and continue on. But if you ease up on the button even a little bit, it will just start clicking on things. Also, even if the symbols have disappeared, you can end up clicking on things when you release the button if your cursor is anywhere near where one of the symbols is. I will admit that I played the first game on the PlayStation, not Steam, so I might just not be used to it, but I find it a bit finicky.
The bugs I experienced during Puzzle Agent 2 were small and forgivable, but present nonetheless.
Toward the beginning of the game, there’s a puzzle where you have to split numbers to make new totals all adding together to make 50. It wasn’t too hard, but it took a lot of guess and check, so we decided to quit the game and figure it out while we ate some lunch. When we came back, the totals at the bottom were still there adding to the actual totals we should have been getting no matter how many times we reset the puzzle. We eventually gave up and started over in a new save slot, which was annoying, but the puzzle was pretty early in the game so it wasn’t a huge deal.
There was also a cutscene near the end of the game where the sprite of Nelson turned into a black square right before the game crashed. It was pretty hilariously timed,
and it might have had more to do with Steam than the game itself, but it did make us do the puzzle right before over again. Again, not a big deal.
I realize this review focused way more on the negative than the positive, but I really did enjoy Puzzle Agent 2. Regardless of how you feel about the story when all is said and done, if you enjoyed the first Puzzle Agent at all, you should at least give Puzzle Agent 2 a try. It’s just the right amount of challenging, considering the focus should be on the story, and it’s nice to revisit good ol’ Scoggins, Minnesota and all of the strange people who live there. And if, afterward, you’re as disappointed with the story as I am, you could always read the books.

I really wanted to like this game. I played the original extenisively and considered it one of the best games on the NES. This game however, has some really broken gameplay. Early on it's fine, but as you progress in the story, the enemy AI becomes unbearable. Swarms of enemies will surround you on all sides, they will attack you simultaneously from every possible direction, making it impossible to block. They will constantly use special attacks which knock you down, and there is no way to quickly get up, you just have to lay there for several seconds while the enemies perform ground attacks on you. Many enemies will walk backwards away from you so that you cannot attack them. The enemies also have an almost psychic level of knowing exactly what to do, moving away the instant you press the grab button, and then hitting you with a special that knocks you down. There is a reason most beat-em-ups over the years have limited the number of enemies or at least made some of them hang back and wait to attack you one or two at a time. Not in this game. The AI is cheap and dirty and ultimately super-annoying. Two other major flaws are the random NPC's who will walk into the middle of a brawl and seemingly get hit on purpose which immediately causes tons of cops to show up and start attacking you, not the thugs, just you, only you, only ever you. There are ways to lose your wanted level but it's annoying and ridiculous that the NPC's have no self-preservation instincts. The other big flaw, was also a flaw in the original, and that is the way boss fights, that are necessary to progress the story, are often very hard to locate. Sometimes they only appear at a certain time of day, sometimes it's unclear where they will be located, based on the one or two lines of dialogue you get, to give you a clue how to find them. If I wasn't constantly referring to a walkthrough, I would still be stuck looking for the boss under the bridge, because I never realized you could climb the fence to get to a new screen, which only is possible in this one location. Dumb, unintuitive game design decisions like this, make the game frustrating.
There are plenty of good things about this game, but the bad outweighs the good, more and more, the further you get in the story. I hope the devs make some changes to fix these problems, but if they don't, then this game should be avoided like the plague. I assume they won't.

I love the original NES River City Ransom. Rented it tons as a kid (not sure why I never owned it) and emulated and beat the classic as an adult. Having played with friends and alone, it carries a lot of nostalgia. I absolutely love the idea, art style, and fighting gameplay of its successor -- and indeed I backed it on Kickstarter -- but I just can't get into this game as a whole. I played on "Normal" difficulty. This review comes after playing it enough to get "Nintendo thumb", but admittedly I have not put a lot of time into the reincarnation. Frankly I'm not enjoying myself, and I don't have time for games I don't enjoy anymore.
While the enemies are fun to fight with various characters, the fact that they mirror your every move instantaneously and come in a never-ending deluge make trawling through screen after screen tedious at best, and a battle of attrition that you *will* lose at worst. That combined with the fact that hideouts are difficult to find (particularly with the confusing low-fidelity world map that really didn't help me locate them, even when they were displayed on it). In the early game (which is as far as I bothered to slog) I didn't come across shops to buy healing, and dying took me back to a boxing ring, where I'd visited to purchase moves, over and over, from whence I'd have to grind my way back to my search for anything interesting and novel (which I wasn't able to find before I gave up).
I found two other things about the enemies annoying:
1) The uninspired AI, and other than their special movies and cool art style, there wasn't much distinction between the gangs/cliques. The primitive AI is also easy to exploit if you get a height advantage -- they come at you generally only one at a time. This is actually a blessing in disguise given the game's level of difficulty. And yes, I am saying this despite my opinion that fighting *is* fun overall.
Another time, I got the negative attention of the riot police, and one repeatedly threw teargas at me, which stunned me. It drained my health only very slowly, but I could never become unstunned as the cop seemed to be in an infinite loop of throwing teargas. So I died despite starting with a decent amount of health. Another time in a gym I got caught in a loop where I couldn't control my character and kept taking incidental damage/stun until I died. This seems to occur when there's a heavier prop that can be used as a weapon around, as it will probably be knocked around in the mêlée and hit you (e.g., big yoga ball, trash can, tire, etc.). Pure frustration!
2) After defeating a foe, the coins they drop as loot bounce randomly in two dimensions and are are often difficult to pick up in the middle of a fight with multiple opponents. It's a small thing, but given that they also disappear after a short delay, combined with frequent deaths that halve your held money, accumulating cash becomes quite a vicious cycle of futile grinding that gets you nowhere. Difficult to locate hideouts of course exacerbate the problem, as you will have to fight back from wherever you last chanced upon one.
So while generally I feel that just a few gameplay tweaks hobble it from reaching the heights of its classic ancestor, it's with great regret that I cannot recommend this game. I will undoubtedly give it another shot in a few weeks or months with the hope that I can break past the wall preventing me from enjoying it. If I can, and garner any sharable insight into how to improve enjoyment of the game, I will update this review.

To begin with, I bought and started playing Blade Symphony because of the multiple 'Recommended' reviews given to the game. I honestly have to say that so far it is money worth spent.
The game has incredible, deep combat mechanics which allow you to attack your opponent basically however you want. Graphics are futuristic and top-notch with all of the flashy effects one would expect from current gaming titles, still not requiring that much from your rig. The additions you can buy with in-game currency are purely cosmetic and define your look and style more than combat prowess.
In all honesty I hope this title will get the acclaim and popularity it deserves and will become an e-sport in the future. It trully touched the honorable swordsman in me :).

Where to start with this game? I guess the most important thing to say is that I haven't put 40 hours into it in the last few days for nothing, the game is good, addictive (I wanted to keep following each quest line) and lots of fun and I do recommend it.
That said there are both good and bad things as with any game, and it has taken quite a while to get over what I perceive as negatives, and that has included playing almost all the Shadowrun predecesors in order to do so.
First, and the thing that still bugs me is that - and this is a problem with the Shadowrun universe not the game - once you complete what is essentially an epic quest nothing happens and nobody cares. All that effort and then you get told that the world would have been exactly the same even if you never bothered, the people you 'save' still live in misery, the bad guys get away with it, and life moves on. The whole ethos of the Shadowrun universe is pretty much that no matter what you do you make no real impact, but it sucks in a game.
Now I have got that off my chest I will move on with the review proper.
Good:
Gameplay - An evolution from the previous games, moveing your team into cover, flanking people, setting up defensive positions or going on the attack never really god boring. And this is despite that every fight really is very similar but it always manages to feel different which is good.
Story - I found myself staying up late because I didn't want to go to bed half-way through a quest for example. The 'twist' is visible a mile away and sadly there is no emotional investment so makes almost no difference to the game, but the actual story itself is nice. If you don't know much about Shadowrun then it can be very unexpected.
NPC's - There is a limited selection to pick from but each fills a specific role so you always have a veried party and I actually liked all their personalities. I found myself a little sad that sometimes I had to leave a favourite behind to bring someone more suited to a particular mission.
Choice - Each mission has multiple ways of completion, you can fight, talk, sneak, hack, use drones in vents to get where people can't go etc. Each quest often gives you instructions on how you need to complete it (IE: The client wants no deaths) but you don't have to follow the instructions.
Environment - Different areas feel different, what you do is more or less the same, but they manage to keep it from getting old.
Bad:
Character creation - Far from the only game with this issue, and not something that bothers everyone, but you pick a portrait, and then try and make your avatar match. Sound simple but why do they include portraits that have no matching avatar?! They also took away the portrait I used in all the other Shadowrun games!
Skill choice - This is intentional because they want to stay in tune with the Shadowrun universe, but you can only really be good at one thing and they don't want you getting too powerful. The problem with that is you miss out on a lot, and I know the only way to not miss out is to play a character that I won't enjoy, there isn't enough flexibility. Specifically all the talking skill checks are done against Charisma, but that stat only benefits one class and is a 100% waste for other classes. There are skill checks against the other skills, but they are few and far between. To stack things even more in favour of Charisma is the 'etiquette' choice, essentially the ability to pretend you know how certain peopel act (Such as a gang member, or a socialite) as they are unlocked through points in Charisma only.
Weapon varity - Shotgun, pistol, SMG, rifle but no real difference between the weapons you get in each category, and no real benefit to not using a rifle which is good from point blank to sniper range.
Replayability - Because the character development means only one enjoyable looking path I have no reason to play it again. I would love to, but that, combined with a fairly linear story just stops me.

Shadowrun Hong Kong is the latest (and, hopefully, not last) entry in the Harebrained Schemes' TRPG franchise. It features a familiar "fish out of water" scenario, a cast of colorful characters and a long-awaited setting - the mysterious, energetic city of Hong Kong.
If you've ever come across this series before, then you know how
the slums, sterile office spaces and warehouses can get. Hong Kong lets you visit the more pleasant locales too - restaurants, pirate ships, underwater laboratories, and that's not everything this game has to offer. Sadly, what you get to see has little to do with the actual city, but it does grow on you faster than, say, the gray and brown streets of the Flux State.
If it is optional content you're looking for, then you're in for a ride... or should I say "in for a
"? There is a lot of extra dialogue trees that you don't really
to delve into, but if you do, you get to immerse yourself in one of the more lore-rich universes. As usual, if you bond with certain characters, you get several side missions. Yet again, they don't offer much in terms of stpry consequences, aside from some more dialogue stuff and a few stat gains here and there.
In terms of player freedom, Hong Kong is on par with Dragonfall. You have a clear goal and a final showdown to look up to, but it's up to you how far in the world of crime you'll go to get there. Quite often the player is presented with more choices than the standard "cause trouble" and "talk your way out of trouble", however morally gray they may be. You get to choose the order in which to do the runs (and which runs not to do at all, if they don't sit right with you). This prevents the difficulty from spiking, but doesn't offer much challenge in return. Only two routes have managed to cause me anal pains, both of them in the bonus campaign.

it's 👌👌👌 top-shelf stuff. Hong Kong is grittier than Returns, leave your
and
at the door. Since it's the first PC-only installment, the game feels much more lively and content-rich than it's predecessors. However, despite being consistently good, themes from the OST don't manage to stand out, unlike, say, Dragonfall's end-boss theme and No Overkill.
In conclusion, I'd like to say that I definitely recommend the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game for you. It was worth every ruble I paid for it, and possibly more. It is more of an RPG than most of modern titles are, in fact, it is one of the better games I've played in my life.

This game has many things going for it other than just an open world city to fool around in. It has upgrades, fleshed out character creation, and hundreds of secrets, collectibles, and activities to complete. I've played this game on both current-gen and next-gen consoles, and the game still feels fresh to play now. Sure, the city is more or less a copy of Steelport from Saints Row 3, but there's enough original content to overlook that. However, this game reeks similarity to a bad PC port of a popular game, like we've seen many times before. If you want to look at the positives of this game, I suggest reading one of the positive reviews, but I will only be covering the negatives so that you as the consumer can judge whether or not you want to buy the game still.
I've had several problems with the menus, where options aren't highlighted when I mouse over them, making it confusing to navigate. It doesn't help that the game seems to read my left and right analog stick inputs on my controller in reverse, while it works just fine in other games.
While some glitches are intentional effects to remind you that your character is in a simulation, others are very, very real. Missions not being counted as completed, character trampling over each others' lines, and
One of the main reasons I got this game on PC was to play Co-Op with my friend, because Co-Op campaigns are far superior to small boring minigames that are an excuse to add a "Co-Op" tag to the game. The problem was that the Co-Op feels like a fanmade mod for a game that wasn't designed with Co-Op in mind.
The way cutscenes work are somewhat inconsistent. Sometimes the cutscene show your character while your partner sees his/her character. Other times the cutscenes show whichever character reached the cutscene trigger first to both players, which can result in a glitchy camera transition for one of the players. Sometimes the QTE icons are only shown to the player who reached the trigger first, in which case only the player who can see the QTEs has to do the actions. Other times each player has their own replica of the QTEs that they control for their own character. There's never a cutscene that is altered in a way that incorporates both characters into the cutscenes without being
Co-Op doesn't feel like you're meant to play through the entire campaign with a buddy. Side missions are sometimes only completed for one player, leading to one player having a weapon that the other doesn't. Power upgrades and regular upgrades aren't shared, making it hard for us to stay at the same skill level. When entering or leaving the simulation, it doesn't drag your friend along with you. Spawning into the game can sometimes spawn each player thousands of meters apart. Glitches are also a major issue. Problems such as your co-op partner frozen in an "on the floor" position, a vehicle that appears in a different place for each player and then teleporting, and laggy player models that make the character look as if he/she is gracefully floating away, which also makes PVP minigames difficult.
If you have enough money and you have the right console, I'd recommend you spend a little bit extra to get this game on another platform. If you're dying to play with amazing graphics and mods, then you might want to get the PC version, although it'll have many issues. It's a fun game, but the PC version is lazily done, and the Co-Op intergration is subpar.

So, I'm gonna start off with why I wouldn't recommend this game, and then get to why this averages out to a thumbs-up, mkay?
Fact is, it's just... bland. And I'm not sure if that's better than it being actually bad, because at least when a game is bad, or even mediocre, there's something to point at and say: "Hey, you know that dumb design decision? Yeah, that's the straw that breaks the camel's back." This game doesn't have that.
It's cute. It's got a wonderfully Star Trek aesthetic to it, the interface makes me warm and fuzzy inside, and the away missions are a nice game element that is rare if nonexistent in similar games. There's resource management, building elements, and honestly a really pleasing art style.
But that's the problem, too. Once you've seen all that perty stuff you start to notice how small the game really is. The question I find myself asking is why I'd want to play it, without really being able to come up with any reasons not to.
Sure, I can build a trading port thingy to get more of the stuff my spatials want because reasons, but if they don't get them... oh well? And if they do... oh well? That's the main sticking point of this game, for me at least. It's not that this game lacks anything similar games have, it's just that it fails to give any of that meaning.
That being said, this game has a lot of cool elements (reminiscent of a casual game mindset) that other more popular games in the same vein could learn from, and for how long I played it I actually found it to be quite fun. Sure, that fun tapered away into an existential feeling of "Sure thing, but *why*?" but it was still there.
So, given the price point, I figure it's worth a spin. Maybe I just haven't played it enough to find paydirt.

Quickly reached the point where I had no reason to do anything. Normally in a game like this it takes 15+ hours to reach the idle point, where a base or city or whatever is self-sufficient and can exist forever without player input. I hit that point in The Spatials after 3.
Nothing costs credits to maintain, not the infinite sources of resources, nor anything on the station, nor your Spatials themselves. All of these are one-time costs, and then cost nothing for the rest of the game. Spatial needs are unlocked at levels, so the entire base can be crewed by level 1 Spatials and they'll be free labor. Spatials stationed in embassies are free as well. Spatials can't die on missions either, so the away team will be the ones to have any upkeep at all. But that upkeep only comes in the form of consumed resources, resources you're already creating for your visitors.
I built up a base to 2 star ports, with enough amenities to keep my visitors and away team, and that's end of the game. There's no impetus to expand beyond that. I was making consistent money. Everyone's needs were met. I had no grand goal to achieve. The missions aren't interesting enough to engage in for their own sake. There's no increasing flow of mouths to feed and heads to shelter, there's no increasing demand for resources, no long term goal to dump resources into achieving. There's a long tech tree to go through, but no reason to down it. There's nothing.
It's a game that's interesting for a short while, but peters out very quickly.

Billed as "The Painful RPG", it goes out of its way to make the journey of Brad a miserable one even if it's loaded with bizarre, wacky Earthbound-style humour along the way. Themes are dark, mature and extremely cynical to the point of making me a little apathetic by the end, but more than the narrative there are loads of punches to the gut in a gameplay sense along the road to infuriate anyone who goes in blind.
I feel the overall experience can be summed up by listening to the soundtrack. Filled with odd samples, heavy bass, and swerving in unpredictable ways, sometimes not really matching up what's on the screen, it's sometimes catchy, always unpredictable, and occasionally jarring. Sometimes it's just annoying seemingly for the sake of being annoying. Still, it hooked me for the desire to see not only what happens next in the game, but to hear what strange music accompanies the next weird event.
Reasons You Should Try It:
+Carries on that same Earthbound style of humour, but even more insane. Individual jokes are hit or miss, but overall it made me laugh out loud several times.
+A whole bunch of party members to recruit scattered around the world, which reminds me pleasantly of Suikoden. You can explore, experiment, and eventually settle on a party to call your own out of the weird cast you find.
+Aside from a few small areas that have random encounters, most battles are hand-placed and unique.
+It veers into incredibly mature and dark territory and gets downright brutal at times.
Reasons It Should Go ♥♥♥♥ Itself:
-Pits of death are everywhere in the world, resulting in an instant game over if you walk off a cliff.
-Samey backgrounds can get confusing and difficult to navigate, especially given progression is pretty open-ended. One slip and you're in one of the instant death pits mentioned above.
-Some enemies randomly use instant-death attacks that kill your party members for good, forcing you to either reload or replace them. The only way to avoid them is to stunlock the enemy.
-Camping can randomly result in major or minor inconveniences whenever you need to rest. Generally not anything too bad, but it can lead to backtracking and tedium.
-If you're like me and hate the idea of wasting experience points on characters you don't plan to use, this game will drive you insane. There's eventually an area to quickly grind up your party if the people you want to use have fallen behind, but it comes fairly late in the game.
Many of the user-unfriendly design choices can be chalked up to its subtitle, as it's fully intended to simulate a painful journey. I'm not sure if I'm entirely sold on this excuse, but they do all fit thematically. Choices you're forced to make along the way can be a punch in the gut, and there are little tricks and traps and general trolling scattered around the world that seem placed specifically to extend a middle finger to the player. Though while the game is more than happy to screw you over, it's never actually too overly difficult, and even if you've been screwed and weakened in all number of ways, it's built so you can still get to the end regardless of your choices along the way.
Though the game♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off plenty of times, especially early on, once I started to really get a sense of what it was all about, and got on its wavelength, I really did start enjoying it. I couldn't wait to see what was around the next corner because I really had no idea. The mood jolts suddenly from horrifying to wacky to depressing without a moment's warning, and every door could be holding something you didn't see coming. It took me a while to turn around on it, but once it got its miserable hooks in me, I was very pleased.
So if you're a fan of old-school RPGs and/or games that are as weird as they are dark, this has my recommendation. It's the very definition of not for everyone, so I wouldn't blame you if you hated it. It kind of hates you too.

Finally, a Fallout-esque concept done right.
In a world where women have disappeared, a baby girl suddenly appears and shatters the manly harmony. Can
disillusioned drug addict Brad do what is right to save humanity from extinction, or will he bring doom and destruction to the world? Or maybe both?
Lisa is a post-apocalyptic RPG that can be dark at times (particularly towards the end), but is mostly weird and funny. It's often compared to Undertale, but apart from the obvious Earthbound inspiration and great soundtrack, they don't really have much in common.
+ Eccentric and overly "manly" setting, with many fun characters and situations
+ Lots trippy / unsettling scenes and monsters
+ An actually balanced implementation of RPG Maker's default battle system, for once
+ Somewhat open exploration and hidden secrets
+ Choice and consequences, multiple endings
+ Hard mode with limited save points, asking you to plan ahead
+ Amazing soundtrack (which also has some narrative aspects)
- Falling from cliffs, seriously they're as deadly as in Dark Souls
- Somewhat limited consequences of choices outside of gameplay repercussions
- Dark / Gay-ish humour that might not be for everyone (though I find it hilarious)
8/10 Get this if you want a strange humour-centric RPG. Get the DLC as well, since it expands on the ending.

LISA is a laidback and very plot-based RPG. You play as Brad, a man who was abused by his father and blames himself for the suicide of his younger sister. Not to mention that Brad is addicted to joy, a very addictive drug that will cause you problems in your journey through the game (Withdrawal). But anyways, the game fast forwards to Brad as a young adult who then finds a baby (Buddy) who ends up to be a girl. If you don't know, LISA is in a post-apocalyptic state and there are only men left in society so this means that Buddy is the only women left in existence. Instead of revealing Buddy to Rando and his army, Brad decides to hide her along with his three childhood friends Rick, Cheeks, and Sticky. The years past by and Buddy is now a older child but not yet a teenager, but then Brad fast forwards to him being drunk and high in the middle of nowhere. It then transitions to Brad helping out your first recruitable character, Terry Hintz, Terry is a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ character until the ends and he achieves a high level so i recommend keeping him around. But anyways, Terry Hintz joins your party and you proceed back home to discover Cheeks outside gushing with blood and he tells you that Buddy was taken and she is gone. You then can walk inside and pick up a weapon and then you can go outside and proceed to left to climb down a rope to start the story. You then come across many enemies and three crossroads, and the whole journey is based off your decision-making and how you take the fights to your enemies. There are many recruitable characters to accquire across your journey, i prefer to have Terry, RT, and Olan but those are just my personal preferances. But anyways your entire journey is to find Buddy and i suggest you prepare for your final fight against Rando, he is the boss of the Rando Army and is your final boss of the game. I suggest you wear him down to when his mask breaks because the mask reduces fire damage, because of this I recommend you use to Charging Headbutt to stun Rando and then when his mask breaks you should use the Diesel Firebombs. Once you have defeated Rando the game is practically over, you just have a scene when Brad talks to Buddy and you can pick your ending. Anyways, you will not be dissappointed after purchasing this game, i suggest you buy the bundle with LISA: The Joyful and The Original Soundtrack & Artwork. I haven't gotten the two DLCs but I am looking to accquire them soon and I'm sure LISA: The Joyful will be just as good as LISA. I hope you have as great of an experience with this game as I have, have fun and good luck!

On the whole this game is okay, but initial impressions, I nearly chose to uninstalled. I dunno if it's just that I sucked in the beginning or if you're NOT SUPPOSED to win cos I've had it for a while now and I have just had my first victory online. And that's real frustrating cos without wins you can't upgrade your character.
The combat moves look pretty cool and slick and there's definitely some skills to be proud of, but only if the moves are actually done correctly to the nanosecond. If not, you can expect to die pretty quickly in the duals (in training or online).
First impressions on the online game lobby were that it was just a mess of numbers and titles. Took me ages to work it all out, so I would not call it new-user friendly.
Until a couple of my friends joined, I was losing dual after dual which was a real downer cos I felt terrible.
In the training, I can't find a dificulty setting. For some people, this might mean a choice of either: hard, hard or impossible which doesn't really help, unless you got friends who are kind enough to 'train' you in a private dual online.
Customization options are pretty decent, leveling up with currency to 'buy' new gear seems fair in most games like this. But if you're like me and suck at the beginning you gonna need a LOT of patience.
Tutorials can be a bit misleading; yes, they do teach you how to swing a sword but there's more that had to be learnt outside of the tutorials if you want to stand a chance online. AKA learning the hard way.
Suggestion for Improvement:
What would make this game a touch more attractive is if at the end of dual, the game played a badass slow-mo of the killing strike, like they do in Skyrim or LOTR: War in the North.
Another would be just liven up the online lobby a little bit, when you first enter, it can be like looking at a psuedo-code programming. Black and white, parenthesis and anacronyms everywhere. Just jargon that had to be researched to make sense of.
Bottom line: for the adept rpg "swordsy" gamer, this game would be awesome. But if you're like me and a newby, patience is key. And if you don't have that, don't waste your shinies on this game cos there are way better ones out there.

I went into this one assuming TellTale had learned from their missteps on the first Puzzle Agent, namely its lack of puzzle variety or challenge. I even hoped there would be a little more to do, maybe some side paths or dialogues to explore. I don't know why I thought this, other than my brain is chemically imbalanced towards unwarranted optimism. Instead of improving on these points, Puzzle Agent 2 looks to the elements that worked so well in the first and throws them clean out the window, opting for a game that is less challenging, more confusing, and all-around dumber than what came before.
The case at the eraser factory is closed, but with too many lingering questions for Agent Tethers' liking. He returns to Scoggins, MN on his own to delve into the mystery of what REALLY happened there, and soon finds matters reaching far further than he ever dreamed. There are some kooky new characters to help him on his way, as well as plenty of familiar faces who generally aren't that happy to see him. And there are puzzles, of course.
The story is important here, but not as important as the puzzles. My big problem with the first Puzzle Agent was the lack of variety and challenge to the puzzles, almost to the point of dragging down the entire game. Inexplicably, Puzzle Agent 2 scores worse in every way with its puzzles. There are even FEWER kinds of brain-teasers this time, with the vast majority of them just retooled versions of puzzles from the first. I guarantee you're going to be sick to death of making paths and adding numbers by the end of this one, and the only new kind I can recall were reprehensible sliding block affairs.
And they're not even harder! There were a few puzzles in the first game that gave me pause or required a few attempts, but I solved every single one of Puzzle Agent 2's puzzles on the first try! Including the three "secret" puzzles at the end! They may mostly be copies of previous puzzles but they're even easier than before, with many being obvious the moment you lay eyes on them. Instead of taxing your brain they beg for loose brain change and then scurry off into the shadows no matter what you toss them.
Building on the bizarre and creepy story of PA1 could maybe be enough to save PA2, but it faceplants on this hurdle as well. The highlights of the first game were the unexpected moments of terror and the sinister mystery hiding in the corners of sleepy Scoggins. PA2 drags all that out into the light, dissolving the horror with ridiculous explanations and over-complications. The story pulls in all different directions with new characters that end up being irrelevant and revelations in entirely new genres. I don't know what you're imagining the ultimate secret of the Puzzle Agent saga is, but I guarantee that (a) you're wrong and (b) the truth is way dumber than what you came up with.
The only way I can imagine Puzzle Agent 2 coming into existence is that TellTale diligently compiled a list of all well-reasoned criticisms of PA1, and then did the exact opposite of what they indicated. Everything that was bad in the first is worse in the second, and everything that was good is somehow twisted around to be bad. I implore you, if you took a chance on Puzzle Agent 1 and enjoyed what you experienced, stop there. Proceed no further, for this is easily the worst thing that could have happened to this series.
