The story takes place years after Agent Nelson Tethers solved the biggest case of his career. He heard that one person related to his solved case has gone missing but that's not all, a whispering madness is still creeping from mind to mind, and a troubling recurrence of... creatures... is lurking into the town. And on top of everything, the FBI's Department of Puzzle Research has marked the case closed.
There is only one thing that can do Agent Tethers, he must go rogue and venture back to the eerie town of Scoggins, Minnesota to solve the mystery of "the Hidden People" once and for all.
- I made the mistake to play the sequel instead of playing the first game, but it won't spoil the first game at all so you can play them in ny order you want. -
As a point and click, you can move freely. With your truthworthy scooter you can fast travel to any locations you've heard from many town folks. You'll need to inspect and solve puzzles in order to uncover the truth of what is happenning to this town. You'll also be able to talk with the town folks to help you in your investigations as you can't do it on your own even if you know almost everything about this town excepting the current events. You'll uncover that something bigger is related to these events : something creepier and very dangerous.
Since the town did a "gum censure" you can't buy gums which are very precious to you to help you to concentrate on the case and on the puzzles. Hopefully our man still like to chew old gums found here and there, under a table... And maybe on the floor. Anyway, these gums help you to get hints for any puzzle you want.
You can stop and resume a puzzle at any moment. (You still need to get back to where you found it) Each puzzle works the same : you have a guideline and sometimes you have rules if there are. After that you can try to solve it or use hints to help you. When you submit it to the Puzzle departement you'll get a rating : a gum bonus if you don't use any hint, a tax bonus if you've made no wrong answers and a 10-star rating as an overall rating.
As said the difficulty ranges from Casual to Puzzle Gamer, many puzzles are easy but some need more time to solve. There are some harder puzzles like the Monosaki Puzzles, Logical suits and a few puzzles. Monosaki one require you to think out of the box in term of mathematics.
The game also have a small mini-game at the nearly end, to beat, different from the other puzzles. This one is the only one which ask you to think and act fast but you can always retry it until you get it right.
Finaly only 2 achievements can be missed. The one that requires to get 25 gums in Minesotta, even it's hard to miss. And the one that ask you to get the "Puzzle Agent" rank : mostly perfect all the puzzles including the 2 bonus one but not the tough one.
You can backtrack everything even if you hit the point of no return. You can try any missed or shelved puzzles including the ones in space and the mini-game.
I can only recommend this game and maybe the whole sequel. It's different than a Professor Layton puzzle game but still very good.

Picks up where the first one left off, straight back in to find out what is going on.
Puzzle Agent 2 is a lot like it’s predecessor in all ways but very few. The main difference being that the sequel has achievements I guess, which I’ll go through later.
The story unfolds in this one and despite me being a little lost along the way it came together in the end. It’s definitely unique and a little weird but that’s what kept it interesting enough to continue. I imagine it isn’t easy to keep a game about an FBI agent who solves puzzles for a living intriguing.  The game seemed to have some kind of Nordic or Scandinavian influence to the story and it’s characters which I found quite interesting. I’m not very well educated on those things so that might even be wrong, but nonetheless the involvement of folk law was interesting.
As I said in my previous review, I can imagine these game being quite good as something to play with kids. I don’t know about other people but I find that puzzle games are especially fun when you have someone else to bounce ideas off of. It’s light-hearted and I think this is something you could get a kid to engage with.
The puzzles themselves are a high variety of good puzzles. I’m not sure whether it was because the first game got me used to the kind of puzzles in the game or not but this one felt easier somehow. I felt like I did a lot better in this one, right up until I realised I’d have to play the entire game again to 100% it.
Which brings me back to the achievements. I got quite lucky with this one as throughout these games I did a lot of scribbling on pen and paper to help solve some of the puzzles that were a little harder to visualise. If you want to 100% this game you need to manage a playthrough without using any hints or getting any wrong answers.
For that I highly suggest you just do a super quick playthrough after you finish the game while it’s still quite fresh in your mind. It’s also worth noting, if you are a pleb like me and manage to get an answer wrong right near the end of your 100% playthrough, if you don’t really feel like doing the entire thing again, tabbing out or opening the task manager and straight up closing the game worked for me to be able to re-boot up the game just before I fudged up.
It’s a tad tedious to 100% but it’s definitely doable and not too hard. My playtime counts for a full playthrough of which I took my time, and a whizzed through playthrough skipping all text and just doing the puzzles as fast as possible.
All in all these games were quite enjoyable. They aren’t the best or the most exciting but I found them to be quite charming. If you are a fan of Tell-tale, puzzle games and/or point and click adventure games then I think you will enjoy these.
TL;DR : Decent enough story if you own both games, seems like something that would be good to play with kids and high variety of good puzzles. It’s a little tedious to 100% but definitely doable.

Warning: Spoiler Alert...
I've never had so many mixed feelings about the implementation of a game as I have this one...
The game is obviously a sequel to the original 'Puzzle Agent' and literally carries on where that one left off. Certain events were left unanswered in the original, such as what did the 'Hidden People' want with Ed Davis? And where is he now? Though the Scoggins eraser factory has reopened and Agent Tethers has been taken off the case officially, his curiosity of wanting those questions answered gets the better of him and takes it upon himself to take some vacation time and return to Scoggins to do some personal investigation.
Like before once he arrives in Scoggins he gets treated to some creepy cold hostility being constantly reminded that his presence in town is not very welcomed. This makes Agent Tethers conclude that there may even be a bigger darker secret the town is holding onto other than the fact that there is a religious brotherhood who believe in the 'Hidden People', but what could that be?
He soon discovers that he may even have a secret padre in town as a note is pushed under his hotel door informing him that 'Ed Davis does not exist'. This is strange as Agent Tethers saw Ed Davis with his own eyes and that the whole town practically testified to knowing Ed who was married to Gloria the one who runs the town diner. So with all that in mind what could the note be implying? The further he pushes on in his investigation the more he begins to realise that there is a whole string of missing people from Scoggins and that Ed was neither the first nor the last to mysteriously disappear. What do these thing have in common with the hidden people? The brotherhood?
Three things make the pursuit of truth difficult for Agent Tethers, 1) many people are being deceitful to him. 2) His own bureau have arrived in Scoggins with an army of MIB and are preventing further investigation and 3) Agent Tethers begins to question his own sanity as he not only begins to see Hidden People in the forest, but now discovers wandering astronauts too. All these baffling and quirky elements sets up the scene for a Pulitzer which Dean Koontz and Stanley Kubrick would stand up and applause, but unfortunately it is here where someone throws a sleeper over the tracks and the story train starts to derail leaving nothing more than a jumbled mess.
The game is from Tell Tale (
) who often deliver strong punchy and meaningful cartoon games on the other hand the animation is delivered from an Oregon Cartoonist known as Graham Annabel who produces the 'Grickle' series (
) who seems very haphazard in his cartoon telling’s, but has laid himself various iconic themes that constantly perpetrate in many of his cartoons such as people who result to their primal state and bellow out monkey screams.
As noted in my previous review on Puzzle Agent the story is loosely based on a real folklore about the hudufolk people in Iceland which people even today still believe in and have gone to some extraordinary methods to convince others either through trickery and deceit. Why? For one thing some people need to believe, secondly a small town and individuals simply prosper in money ways from the publicity. Examples of this flourish in all corners of the globe from Lochness, Bigfoot, Alien Sightings and more bizarrely here forest gnomes. Some passionate believers have performed even illegal activity in the interests of the hidden people and often blamed the sabotaging and vandalism on this folklore as proof. Others have experimented in drug and meditational related exercises in order to make contact with these hudufolk often forming small social groups/fan clubs. You would probably agree with me that some important and interesting statements could be made about this controversial matter. Here we have none. Zip. Which leaves me with nothing more than the question what is the point of this comic series? What statement is Graham trying to make? Is this series simply for entertainment purposes? What target audience is he trying to reach here and what is his overall message?
The target audience is a serious question mark, because while for the majority of the game the story has teetered in the morbid and foreboding ‘twin peak’ slightly adult medium. Here it now finishes with the kindergarten concept that the garden gnomes are from the moon and were stranded here on earth from a space ship hoping to return. Seriously? That was the best you could come up with for a cartoon saturated with adult concepts?
I honestly felt more and more disappointed with the ending as it veered off its structured roadway and ploughed into absurdity. The story telling seemed more and more structured to support the already known animation style of Graham Annabel and his ability. It seemed like the animation was the one that was calling all the shots rather than the story telling calling all the shots, and the animation was there to enhance its nitid telling’s.
I guess in the end Tell Tale has seen that this story harbouring no meaning, making no statement and swaying constantly between adult espionage and childish finger painting has a limited market value and that their valued expertise is best marketed on other profound statement and products.

** Decent Game, BUT IT IS NOT River City Ransom and is Basically a Beta **
**DO NOT BUY if you want ACTUAL River City Ransom **
River City Ransom: Underground can best be described as a River City Ransom Like or Lite as opposed to an actual River City Ransom game.  That doesn't mean it's bad, but I do need to stress that anyone who wants a new version of River City Ransom to play on their PC will be disappointed.  There are elements of the original that the devs either didn't understand or willfully ignored for their own vision, and while it doesn't necessarily make the end result bad it might upset fans of the original.
I've edited this review after putitng more hours in.  After discovering some baffling bugs, I have to say this game is basically a BETA posing as a finished product.  It's fun, but damn I don't know what they were thinking sometimes.
Thus for this review I need to break it down into The Good, The Bad, The Ugly and The Different -- the Ugly being ideas that in themselves aren't bad but implemented poorly and the final category showing the differences between a classic RCR and RCRU.
For those finding this review too long to read:  It's a good game, it's similar to RCR, but it's not an RCR game.
*** The GOOD ***
Graphics:  It really does look like a RCR game, it looks like a first rate NES game.  There's a lot of really nice touches hidden throughout as well.
The Sound:  While its soundtrack isn't my cup of tea it really does have the NES sound down as well so if that's what you're into, you'll be happy.
Combat:  Every character plays very differently and for the most part the flow of combat works pretty well.
Comically Eating Everything:  It was funny in RCR, it's funny now.
Shout-Outs:  Lots!  Big props to the original password screen at the start.
Characters:  Each play very differently; there's surely someone for everyone!
*** THE BAD ***
Controls:  Way to finicky for a beat-em up.  Combinations (UP+S) that would come out on any other game result in the wrong move in this one.  Some moves are glitchy or only pop out in very situational times.
Movesets:  Many moves are far too situational to be worth the cost to buy or are excessively taxing to use compared to the results.  Some moves like Bruno's Elbow Drop are perfectly balanced while others (especially the desparation moves) don't do nearly enough damage.  Combined with the finicky controls and you're far better off just using bread-and-butter combos.  Some moves do no damage due to devs clearly not thinking before making changes.
Progression:  Characters have moves that they can buy before they can purchase the prior requirement moves.  Others might only have one functioning attack button while running until they buy their other running attack which isn't different enough to warrant not having it from the start.  Story progression isn't obvious and sometimes can feel buggy and the game play isn't deep enough to have trying to figure out where to go next to be fun.
Tutorial Screen:   There needs to be an option to disable it for people who've played before.
Balance:  The balance is "Did you test this at all?" level of bad.  Some moves are tricky or situational with poor payoff, while other characters have "INSTANT MURDER BEATDOWN" with the push of a button.  Many moves not worth using.
Lack of Testing:  There are a lot of really obvious things that should have never made it into the live version of the game that did, such as characters with broken move sets or move sets that get broken later due to some not-at-all thought out changes.  This appears to be the team's first game but some of these things one would think would be pretty basic.
Enemy AI:  Bosses are stupid, mobs are cowardly and get more defensive as the game goes on. Considering you grind on the mobs for cash (as bosses award cash once only) it makes taking down mobs a chore and taking down bosses a breeze, making for some really backwards design.
Chase sequences.  They have no place in an RCR game; either make it a fight or don't include it at all.
*** THE UGLY ***
Day/Night Cycle:  Neat idea, but there needs to be a way to quickly shift between day and night other than waiting it out.  This could easily be solved by making the beds OBVIOUSLY usable to advance time.
Civilians:  Neat idea to make them attackable, dumb idea to have them wandering around in a gang brawl.  Either have them all clear out immediately, turn them into combatants (ALA one of the Kunio Kun games on SNES), or restrict them to shopping centers, or allow them protection via Friendly Fire OFF.  This isn't the kind of game to have to worry about idiots wandering into your attack combos, which leads us to....
Cops:  Neat idea, terrible implementation.  Cop weapons should be usable, and they should be worth XP/cash.  This is supposed to be RCR, not Grand Theft Auto.  If you want to make them a penalty, then cops should only protect safe zones (of which there are none).
No Safe Zones:  RCR had them for a reason, they give the player a breather.  A lot of the troubles with the cops and civilians could be cleaned up in one go by restricting them to safe zones like the traditional shopping centers.  Then it would feel more like a punishment for behaving badly.  Especially key for New Game+ when things are supposed to be "Back to normal".
Weapons:  RCR and RCR EX both had variable-range weapons, but in this game while weapons are really klunky and have poor hit detection.  Weapons that should have range don't, and what should be light bulky weapons like trash cans are super-slow while the old body-weapon element of RCR is the same as it always has been.
Hit Protection:  Probably the most baffling element in the game.  It's not implemented universally between players & enemies (which is something RCR and RCR Ex does) but the worst part is it applying to normal mobs.  The player has to beat down a mess of these enemies, why would you give them a 'cheese hit' (3rd from weapons, applies to certain air combos) protection?  It's never appeared in any RCR game proper and it's annoying when you just want to beat down some mobs.  It's hardly game-breaking and easy to circumvent, but it shouldn't be in at all.
Tutorial Pop-Up:  GO AWAY.  If you're so concerned with players "missing" tutorial pop-ups just have it be an option on the pause menu.
Cash:  Bosses no longer drop money on repeated fights.  It's in the other RCR's for a reason; bosses aren't really quick to farm unless you're very strong.
NO GENERIC DUDES.  How can you call it "Rivery City" WITHOUT the GENERIC DUDES?!!!!
*** THE DIFFERENT ***
- No "safe zone" shopping centers
- Set Combo system as opposed to classic RCR "free flow" (RCR had a fun, chaotic system that really did treat players and enemies equally)
- Special Moves much more situational and meant to be used into the designed combo system as opposed to simple (RCR) or on-command (RCR EX).  Very few straight-forward, "open" use specials.  This will be most noticeable for RCR vets because it really does change game play entirely; instead of the move being open to use whenever and letting the combo opportunties occur based on stat/situation variables, the devs had a very narrow idea of how a move could be used.
- Character-restricted move sets; part of RCR has been that special moves could be used universally.
- Bosses no longer drop money on repeated fights, cash grinding on mobs only.
- Level-Up system.  Levelling up restores all your health but without levels your ability to increase your attributes is capped.
- Lore.  It doesn't follow Kunio-Kun, although there's a few shout-outs here and there.

FTL is probably the best rogue-like game for short or medium length play sessions. It certainly has the best replayability  and ability to surprise the player. The RNG is there, still the game feels fair. You can fail due to some unlucky chain of events and then you can suddenly realize that there actually were the things you could've done better and there was the way to save the situation.
You can chose the difficulty and ship at start to customise the experience, to adapt it to what you have in mind for the run. You can make it crazy hard and unforgiving or a breeze, or all the things in between. Also the playstyles may vary greatly, you can be effective in many mutualy exclusive ways. By breeze I mean for experiencied FTL pilots. Before you learn the basics by trial and error method the game will punish you repeatedly and destroy your ship with every new unexpected threat.
Every run is a story on its own. It can be the epic tale of struggling and prevailing. The things could happen according to the plan or every jump will surprise you and force you to adapt and improvise. You may calculate your every move with great caution or rush just blindly. You may win and lose hundreds of times and still learn something new, find new tactics and new uses for the things you thought you know everything about.
In short: this game is a timeless classic of the genre.

When you boot up this game, it immediately charms you with a clever little "brought to you by" screen that changes sponsors each time you play, and wonderful narration by Charles Martinet. Wonderful narration that quickly becomes a jumble of important-sounding terms in what I guess is supposed to be humorous, but which sadly sums up the experience itself: a jumble.
People praise the art style. Personally, I find it really, really creepy. I found myself avoiding checkpoints lest I get the image of the living, seemingly-drunk pickle man standing there burned into my brain, and then it turns out jumping over checkpoints makes him angry and he chases after you, so that doesn't help. Outside of the game and on the menus, though, the game is a treat for the eyes. Or it would be, if it didn't stop for a plain black loading screen upon every single button press.
Where it actually matters, though, is the gameplay, and that's why I'm giving this a thumbs down, not any of the petty stuff above. First, it seems simple. Run, jump. It's classic. Then they add sliding. Okay, this works. Then they add kicking, and springing, and spinning, and bouncing, and dancing, and it all becomes a confusing, frustrating mess as you try to amble your way through even the first world without being bombarded with eighty new button presses to memorize. Any time you hit an obstacle, you are forced to watch the game drag your character back to the start/checkpoint, a simple addition that feels like a cruel, merciless taunt after a while, as if to say "now you have to do all this again because you missed this stair!"
Simple stairs remain insanely difficult even before the game piles on this stuff. It's already hard. It just feels brutal in a way that isn't fun. One twist I very much like is being able to get a much higher score by taking a risk and actually dodging the checkpoint. This is rather creative, and puts some high stakes on the affair really quickly. However, if you do manage to get every gold piece and red plus throughout the level for a perfect score, then wait, no, you don't have a perfect score yet! Time for a cannonball minigame! And if you don't hit the bullseye, it doesn't count and you have to do the whole level again to try again!
It tries, it really does. But it feels quite often like this game doesn't want you to have fun. Just when it hits a good stride, it finds a way to undo it. The rhythm aspect doesn't even fit, as the music sort of plays out of time with the actual level and regardless of what you're doing. So this is a game, yes, but I have no idea who it's for.

If you're looking for a one-line recommendation for Runner2, then here you go...
"If you've ever had a group of friends over, and wished you had a modern game that let you pass the controller around the room like you used to back in the old days, then don't even stop to think about it...just buy Runner2, right now.  In fact, go ahead and save yourself a few bucks by picking up BIT.TRIP Complete because you're going to want the other games eventually anyhow."
BIT.TRIP Presents Runner2: Future Legend of Rhythm Alien is a fantastically fun, beautifully constructed, musically catchy, and perfectly balanced challenge for gamers of all shapes/sizes/skill levels.  In my opinion, there were only a few ways that Gaijin Games could've improved on the formula that made the original BIT.TRIP.RUNNER such a massively fun and soul-crushingly addictive experience.  A) Add an optional mid-level checkpoint for those of us who have a rage-quit tendency, B) polish the graphics and improve the contrast between character/obstacles/background, and C) create a more stand-alone story and game experience by improving the corrolation between the worlds/levels, making their visual appeal and location-specific music stand out from each of the others, and spread these ideas throughout the game menus/maps/etc.
All of these ideas and so much more were applied to Runner2, and I can't recommend it enough.  This game has provided hours upon hours of laughter and massive fun for me and the rest of my family/friends.  Given the price point that it's at even when it's NOT on sale, I'd say it's an absolute no-brainer.  Thank you, Gajin Games!!!

LISA got me all sorts of stressed though...
LISA: The painful RPG is a western take on the established formula of the traditional turn/party based JRPG.
LISA is about a man named Brad. Unlucky in life, in more ways than one; He finds himself in a world devoid of women, a true “Children of Men” situation. However he happens upon a young child whom he adopts as his own. As if you'd never guess, she is kidnapped and our adventure begins.
Retro styled, two dimensional worldscape with different plains to explore. 4 person party, extra people to choose from for almost any play style. Some characters use SP while other use TP. SP must be recharged though resting or use of items. TP is charged through doing basic attacks or getting hit. Additionally there are characters, including Brad himself,  that use a combo system to enter in special attacks. Of course, they can also be selected from a skills list should you desire that method. If you've ever played the game “Legend of Legaia” it's a very similar system.
The Perma-Death is real, at least for your party members. Many events in the story cause the death of party members; There are even some enemies that can insta-kill. There is definitely some RNG at play and “save scumming” is definitely a viable strategy for these sections and to be fair this aspect is going to push a lot of people away. However, these areas are not that egregious and the story itself far outweighs those frustrations. Another thing that is relatively unforgiving is that fact you very easily can fall off of cliffs and get a game over. Well.. I hoped you saved recently.
Each character has a relatively unique aspect such as Jack and Birdie, two of my favorites. Jack, a magician still learning the trade has skills related to failed magic tricks which often grant random status effects. And Birdie, a posthumous drunk who gains stat buffs relating to drinking alcohol and has attacks regarding stumbling around as well as buying drinks for everyone for health regen as a support character.
There is also a mechanic that is rather story driven with Brad being addicted to a drug called “Joy” which I'll leave for you to discover.
The story is very dark but remains humorous. So long as you think committing a copious amount of murder to save someone has a certain unique irony to it. The story telling is VERY good. It's extremely effective. There is a sequence of events roughly half way through that made me feel very icky. To the point where I almost (quite literally) stood aghast at the scene before me. The ending is also quite something to behold. The journey there is nothing short of dramatic.
The soundtrack is also rather dashing if I do say so myself. Ironic when it needs to be and adventurous when you need a push. It reminded me of something that sort of gave the vibe of “Pulp Fiction” set it a “Mad Max” setting.

This time you not only play as our old friend Abe, but also the new and polite Munch! You play as the two and together you have to save Munch's species, the Gabbits. As Abe is now a free mudokon, you get to roam the villages and wilderness of his native land. As Munch, you get to slowly make your way through the industrial environment of the Vykkers, until the two finally meet and you now have to control two characters. This works very good and opens up for alot of new puzzles and ways to approach the game.
The game is executed very well and with a controller, the controls and gameplay works really good. The levels is a mix of puzzles and action, as you always have to figure out some puzzle, while taking care of enemies and saving your friends. With two characters you also get two different sets of playstyles. Abe who can move fast and agile, will posses and do most of the physical work. Munch, who is native to water, moves slowly on land, but often have to move around sneaky and open up the paths for Abe, while fighting alongside his new friends: the Fuzzles. Munch even has a newly attached neural implant, that can shoot electric shocks if boosted enough! This makes him able to take control over mechanical structures and weaponry, for an explosive exit.
The graphics are nice (compared to the time) and the cutscenes are just awesome. Sometimes the puzzles can get a little tedious, but that stops as you progress further into the game. While playing you are constantly entertained by funny minor things such as jokes, posters or items found around the world, that has that special oddworld-humor about them. I had a lots of laugh as I played while listening to Abe and Munch debate, or reading the newspaper, that shows after each level. Some items are just so lame, that you have to laugh, like the Vykker's invention; The Buttflo! <- Yeah for a hard stomach I guess. The story is very good and deep, which leaves you really cheering for Munch's cause.
We are introduced to new things and species, such as the Vykker. If you paid attention in Exoddus, then you'll have noticed a blocked doorway to their lab. We even get to see more of how the lives and such are inside the industrial world of Glukkons and Sligs, which is really interesting and fun. Yet we still get to see familiar things such as Mudokons, Slogs and our dear friends, the Paramites and Scrabs.
One sad thing is that 2 achievements does not work, and some a bugged. This is really sad. Another problem is that you can't change the axises for the camera in settings, which is annoying. After you get used to that, it won't really affect your gameplay, but can be tricky at times. I also read that alot of people have had problems and crashes. Some were never even able to launch the game. I must say though, that I had zero problem and the only crash I had was when I Alt-Tab'ed alot in a short period of time, so that is most likely my own fault.
I will suggest that you take notice and think of how well you PC has been doing previously, when handling games that could be a bit tricky and fragile. If you have had alot of crashes and such in previous games and don't really have the info to fix it yourself, I suggest you may not buy this game yet. If your PC usually play edgy games or ports good and you rarely have had crashes, then just buy the game.

I feel really split here.
Early on, River City Ransom: Underground hit a lot of my classic brawler nostalgia buttons. Unlocking new moves and discovering new enemies was fun, but as the game went on, cracks started to show. By the time I finished the game, beating the final bad was a chore to get over with rather than feeling like an accomplishment.
Compared to the original, RCR:U is a big improvement. There are a lot of characters and moves to unlock, and the enemies have more varied arsenals as well. The animation is expressive and sharp, and the enemies are now unique with movesets of their own. Exploring shops and finding what you need to level up is still charming if shallow.
Unfortunately, the game is obtuse. What you need to do to progress is often unclear, and though they seem to be trying to emulate old-school games in this regard, it's not fun. As with the original RCR, there's no guide to what stats food will improve, even after purchasing it. At the very least, being able to see what an item does after you purchase it would add a lot to the game's quality of life. Early "bosses" often consist of races where you need to catch a bad guy, which mainly consists of double-tapping and holding a direction and just knowing the obstacles to avoid. It's also not fun. Many bosses, though colorful and creative, are vulnerable to what I've always called "edging" - using the up and down directions to close in safely into close quarters, hitting them once or twice with a weapon, and retreating and repeating. Most are utterly helpless against this, having little or no vertical space to their attacks. Grinding is necessary to an extent, but towards the late game most enemies don't even award money, making it harder to level up when you need it most. Some characters are locked away in locations you have no particular reason to visit, which might have worked if the game actually rewarded or encouraged exploration, but as it is, players might miss them until they glance at a guide.
It's frustrating because a lot of the game is creative and clever but doesn't quite make use of it. There's beautiful animation and pixel art all over the place, but most of it doesn't matter too much. Even when it does, like the tunnel full of a line of animated cars that can knock people over, there's not much reason to interact with them. There's a mini-golf course just screaming to at least have golf clubs scattered around. And so on.
There were a lot of complaints about the AI difficulty, but those have been addressed for the most part and the maddening backstepping enemies of the original release have been fixed. Overall, this is a lot better than it was at release - but core issues remain. This is, at heart, very much a sequel to RCR in both good and bad ways. I like a lot of what I see here and hope it might get cleaned up in a followup here. The writing is clever enough but is largely tucked away in the bottom of the screen where it's easy to miss. I have mixed opinions generally, but when it comes to recommendations, I just think back to how I feel after finishing it and the last miserable slogs that were the concluding areas, and that feeling is uuuuugh.

It brings the best of the beat em ups and the absolute worst of the NES into one title.
I so badly wanted to recommend this game. It has so much potential and great ideas. I love brawling in the streets. I love how different gangs have different turfs. I love the goofy sauna animations and the dragon dojo. I love the GTA wanted system they added that makes no sense in when it's triggered. (You're in a town and enemies attack you, when you fight back if you even slightly touch property or an NPC you are flagged for wanted)
Sadly, all the great parts of this game are buried under the most obtuse systems. Even worse, the "questing" in this game to complete side missions and main missions are absolutely atrocious. The direction you're given is so vague (just like the NES era) and the world map is so unhelpful that it makes you not want to play. Let me set up exactly how my first real mission went down.
You are told to head to the River City Bridge to find someone connected to the villain. Fair enough, I check the World Map and it gives me two objective markers. I assume the two indicate that I have to search between those two spots. I fight my way across the bridge andddd.. nothing. Nothing happens. I clear the bridge of enemies, nothing happens. I walk through the town past the bridge trying to find a loop around beneath the bridge. Nothing happens. I go back to the other side of the bridge and clear it, trying to jump over things to find the path and NOTHING HAPPENS. I finally have to lookup a walkthrough (which at the time of writing this there are none in text), I find a YouTube video of someone literally doing exactly what I did. For 30 minutes they walked around aimlessly until by luck they jumped near a TINY FENCE at the end of the bridge and their character started to climb it. At no point is it ever indicated that you can do this. There is no previous mission where you have to climb a fence and you learn that you can do that. There is no indicator that it's anything more than a background prop. You are set up to fail and waste your time. Exactly what they used to do for NES games for you to call the tip hotline or to buy the strategy guide.
Also, no items, shops, or upgrades have any descriptions so you are buying blindly every single time. You just bought a cat? Good luck figuring out what that does! It's unnecessarily complicated for no reason. We moved past these systems.

A Story About My Uncle is a first person adventure platformer by Gone North Games, the same developers behind Goat Simulator. You must jump, grapple, and rocket boot your way through amazing locations in order to find your Uncle Fred.
A Story About My Uncle (which I will now on abbreviate to ASAMU) is an extraordinarily beautiful game for a US $12.99 indie title. The worlds/levels you must traverse are outstanding. From dark icy caves to floating islands, the art department at Gone North Games have my complete respect for the way they were able to construct such a beautiful world. The only complaint I have regarding visuals would be the humanoid creatures you encounter (the Villagers and the Strays). Although they don't look too good, they aren't a major part of the game and you can avoid them for the most part if you'd like.
The soundtrack for ASAMU is for the most part really well done. I quite enjoy the Main Theme of ASAMU as it really sets the tone for the game; an adventure game with a deep sentimental backstory. Most of the music in the ASAMU soundtrack is extremely adventurous enhances the adventure atmosphere of the game. I don't really like the music in the Caves (the first few levels of the game) but the music only improves more and more after you emerge from the dark caves. Overall the music is really well done.
The voice acting, however, is in my opinion poorly done. The voice acting for the main character and his daughter were pretty well done and I quite enjoyed listening to their voices. The voices of  pretty ever other character in the game were godawful. I couldn't stand their voices, and I often wished that they would get to the point.
Oh my, what do I even say about the gameplay. What I can say from the getgo, however, is that the gameplay of ASAMU had me HOOKED! I absolutely love the feeling of intense freedom and adventure when you grapple and fly through the air across mystical islands and caves. I really enjoy the artificial feeling of zipping through the skies and finding your way across the expansive worlds. ASAMU is a platformer game unlike no other platformer. You have the power of magical crystals at your disposal, allowing you to jump great heights, grapple, and rocket boot your way towards your long-lost uncle. After beating ASAMU, I found myself constantly craving another game to quall my lust for more adventure.
My only complaint with the gameplay aspect of the game is that I often get lost in the huge levels. There aren't any markers that point you to where you are supposed to go, so you can find yourself at the start of the level by accident like I did many times.
A Story About My Uncle isn't really a story about the protaganists uncle. It is however, a story about your adventure finding your uncle, an adventurer who found his way into a new world (which is all I'm going to explain without spoiling the story). ASAMU is a rather short game. I managed to beat the game in 2-3 hours with the rest of my time either idling or replaying levels that I really enjoyed. I feel like the story was really hindered by the poor voice acting but the exposition delivered by the main character and his daughter are sufficient in getting the point of the story across. You play as a father retelling the story of him travelling to another world to save his uncle who had been missing for quite some time. Along the way you meet many different people and traverse incredible areas. ASAMU is truly a story to experience if you can get past the voice acting.
Overall I really enjoyed ASAMU. If you enjoy First Person Platformers or Platformers in general, I think you'd have a blast in ASAMU. The game is rather short and pretty easy to beat, so if you don't have too much time to play then I suggest you try out ASAMU. Although there is no sequel or prequel to ASAMU, you can replay levels to reaquaint yourself with jumping through the skies.

Let me start by saying that this feels like a very refreshing throwback to flash games, the kind I used to play in school, with just enough gore so that it would have been blocked in my school. I like games that I can pick up and put down in a moment's notice, so this suits my needs wonderfully.
The controls are elegant and simple. The rules are easy to remember: you are a pig ninja, wolves are jerks, kill wolves. It is simple enough so that you can immediately start having fun with it, while leaving room for style and improvement. I can see youtube gamers showing off their ridiculous high-scores for this game in the near future.
That being said, there is a reason this game is free-to-play. The whole game has two settings: normal and 1-hp. If you're not a psychotic perfectionist or from Korea, you will probably check out 1-hp setting, play it a few times, then go back to the normal setting forever.
Still, I can see this game eventually becoming something I would pay actual money for and I really hope the game makers will continue to update.
Sidenote: the enemies sound too much like animals. I know, that sounds obvious, but I don't like the idea of beating up animals. It's a small niggle, but I feel making the characters sound like people would make the gameplay more satisfying
Update: I bought this game back when I had no money. Now that I can actually afford to buy games, I'm still coming back to this game for a quick round and to see if there's been a significant update. That being said, I really like the new content that's been patched in. The City level is not only an aestetic change, but also provides just enough change in the gameplay to make you switch up your old play pattern. Every enemy is decked out in fancy attire or pop culture references, which can be thrown back into their dumb hipster faces. I love the developer's commitment to this project, which is even more admirable considering the game is available for free.
I think I can safely say that, at this point in Iron Snout's development, I would pay at least a dollar for it. Other developers have charged more for less gameplay and I would be willing to throw a buck or two at SnoutUp if they were to shoot me a link *wink* *wink*.

Probably one of the most balanced and well put-together strategy games I've played. Its graphics are pretty nice and I really enjoy the diversity of the different Civs you can play as and their different personalities.
The economy system is very balanced, such as how much gold you make per turn compared to units and buildings and such, and this makes it to where you kind of have to choose wisely about what building to produce in one of your cities. Even the system for production is great because you can choose to not produce a building until later when you have more production per turn in your city to finish it in just a few turns.
Speaking of turns, I adore the different modes put into the game, by modes I mean quick, standard, epic (I believe?), and marathon. Each mode affects how long a single game takes and marathon is definitely harder because you have to be able to plan ahead to be able to take care of things as easy as quick.
This is just one setting in the game setup that is very, very customizable. You can choose your map (i.e. pangea, present-Earth, just continents, archipleago, and the list goes on), temperature (I believe this decides whether you get a lot of tundra or desert, or the in-betweens), age, and more.
Social policies and culture is another factor in this masterpiece of a game because social policies can boost empire growth, militaristic capabilities, gold, production, happiness, and just a bunch of other misc things.
As I'm mentioning culture I may as well mention how you can achieve five different victories, so there are multiple ways to approach the start of your game. They are a culture victory (finishing 5 social policy trees and building the Utopia project), diplomatic victory (essentially getting every civilization to vote for you as world leader), time victory (having the highest score-affected by so many factors in your empire, but it essentially means whoever is the strongest all-things-considered-by a certain turn), domination victory, or a science victory. If you have a lot of jungle tiles around your cities for instance, a science victory (finishing the tech tree before anyone else and pretty much going to space) would be a good victory to attempt. If you have a lot of militaristic power, land, and gold, a domination victory (taking over every civ, personally my favorite, it's the most exciting for me and in my opinion requires the most strategy to prepare for.) would be possible. If you want the game to last a while you can even disable particular victory types so you can enjoy a thriving empire and whatnot to achieve, for instance, a domination victory, I do this a lot.
I could go on and on about all the different kinds of things in this game, but if you're reading this review, if you're not inerested I don't see why you should read on, however if you are interested, I don't really need to say anymore do I? Buy the damn game!

Aside from "Sonic Rush" on the DS a while back, it is a common opinion that the last  decent Sonic game was "Sonic Adventure 2" and its port to the GCN. "Sonic Heroes" signaled the descent of the series into games including the "Werehog" Sonic and whatever made the black hole that is my memory of Sonic in 2006.
However, "Sonic Generations" is both a love letter to the series and an apology to the fans. One level from each major Sonic game since the first "Sonic the Hedgehog" is taken to compose the series of levels in this game. Except, in a lovely twist, each one has a 2D and 3D version. One for original, Genesis style Sonic and one for modern Sonic, who plays like he did in "Sonic Colors."
It works wonderfully. This game rekindled my childlike love for game. Aside from two mediocre levels (Crisis City and the one from "Sonic Colors"), both parts of every level work wonderfully. That's right. 2D City Escape is just as good as a 3D Green Hill Zone.
Combined with collectible artwork, homage boss battles, a plethora of challenges, and remixed music for every level, the game will last you for a while and is generally just fun. For the first time in a while, Sonic is fun.
Please play this game, even if it's only to let Sega know that these are the types of Sonic games we want.
It's a really great game especially with big picture mode. I highly recomend this to sonic fans who havent played this game already and to people who like action/adventure stratagy games.

Braindead speed at its finest, not to say it doesn't have its redeeming factors, such as in City Escape, where it fits... somewhat. Where I really started to cringe was when I hit the end of the game - nine levels (split into two acts, one for each Sonic) and only FOUR BOSSES. Sonic ONE had more content than this. Sonic Team tries to mask up the lack of substance with their missions in between every boss fight - you need to beat six out of 25 rehashed missions of each level to continue the game. After you beat missions, you get an unlockable item, and sometimes a powerup which you can buy at the shop. Anyway -  art. Yes, really. You get over one hundred unlockables of art. Really. The best part of the unlockables is the feature to be able to replace the normal BGM of a level with unlocked music (or in my case, Live and Learn or Open Your Heart)
The plot-line is some♥♥♥♥♥♥on time-travel, most of it is pieced together before the final boss fight, it is also extremely predictable after the first boss fight victory cutscene - if you have half a brain, the game's essentially over for you after the first three levels.

While I like the idea, and do belive this game does a good job at execution, I strongly hope the developers are working on the competitive aspect of this game. When you play games like this, you want to become skilled, you want a stats that show you how well you are doing compared to others. While this game does offer that, it offers it in a very lackluster way. To a new player it is very hard to know what server is ranked and what isn't, causing most people to have a bad w/l ratio from the begining. Past that you can ONLY get elo from people in your divison, which is ridiculos. You can lose to someone 3 divions below you, or in return beat someone 3 divions above you and get nothing. Second off your rank is based on your world chart rank. Diamond is the top 2-10%, and master is the top 1%. This means that the longer the ladder is up, the harder it is to get division promotions, what sound like a good thing is acctualy a very horrible thing, as the game does something very stupid to help new players get diamond/master.
When you win/lose a game, you gain/lose mmr bassed on your "expected" performence against that player. Lots of variables are used, their w/l, your w/l, their elo, your elo, and worse of all... time. If you play ranked constantly you will start gaining little to no elo, making it impossible to rank up.
The ranked system is complete trash, you can go from oak-iron-diamond-master-oak all in one day, and it fels extremly unrewarding. It needs a massive improvment, along with a better matchmaking system. Overall its a solid game, but the ranked system is in DIRE need of work.

I normally don't write reviews, but this game really caught me of guard and it's even hard to compare it to anything I have played so far.
Lisa follows the path of a broken man named Brad Armstrong, who lives in a post apocalyptic world where all women have vanquished. He finds the last female baby and decides to hide her away from the world because he knows what the outside world would do to her. One day she gets kidnapped and Brad has to set foot on a self destructive journey to find his daughter.
The humor is so refreshingly dark and silly, but then at the same time the main story just slaps you in the face and it's like BAM feels! I keep seeing people comparing it to Undertale, which is a good game on it's own, but it's generic animu ending stuff compared to what Lisa has in store. In a way it is an Undertale for adults without the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fanbase.
The gameplay sorta feels like the classic Earthbound styled games, which is alright for an RPG maker game. Lisa also comes with a permadeath function, sacrifice options and a Hardmode setting. At parts it can be frustratingly hard, but overall it is a really good game, with lots of places to explore and characters to recruit and play as, which all come with unique movesets and little stories.
Overall I can totally recommend this game if you are in for a challenging RPG and lots of emotional pain.

Munch's Oddysee is a mediocre game. Let's just say it's not one of the better transitions of a series from 2D to 3D. It just doesn't hold a candle to the first two games and even Stranger's Wrath.
IMO it feels rushed and not very well thought out, the game is supposedly mostly about Munch, however I found myself playing as Abe about 80% of the time. Surprisingly, there isn't too much story around either, although all of the present cutscenes are expectional. There are fundamental issues with the game's tone and nature of the gameplay though. It is one thing to give Abe a life bar and a completely different thing to see him slap a Slig to death. Arming fellow Mudokons and sending them to battle is kind of hilarious at first, but gets old quickly and doesn't fit in at all with already established concepts. Lastly, the game's just too repetitive, most of the levels see you doing the same thing and it just gets uninteresting and old real fast. It's not a bad game, but it certainly isn't a good one.
The PC port is pretty bad as well. The original 2010 release was full of bugs and crashed literally every 2 minutes. They've got rid of most of it, but it is still pretty bare bones. Controller support is rather bad, the analog control on my XBOX One controller was insanely off, the game crashes on modern hardware when trying to use Anti-Aliasing (thank god for Super Sampling), in-game options are incredibly lacking (Sound Effects & Music have 3 states, Mute - Soft - Loud, good job lads...). And yet it still crashes from time to time, so I'd recommend you quicksave often.
Overall, I'd pass this one. If you played the first two games and want to see how the story unfolds, just watch the cutscenes on YouTube and move on to Stranger's Wrath which is a masterpiece.

The game itself suffers from horrendous balance issues and blatant pay-to-win problems. The developers have consistently been deceiving, insulting, and even threatening the playerbase.
The game is player-vs-player focused. It features ships from various points in time. There is a progression system for advancing up tiers in a tech-tree. There are numerous different tech trees for different nations. You earn credits and XP from battles - winning, killing ships, dealing damage, capturing objectives, and spotting enemies all award you varying amounts of credits and XP.
In a battle, you can have ships of various nations and various types distributed amongst 2 teams. Furthermore, you can have ships of varying tiers. Up to tier 4, you will always either be in a highest tier ship or only ships one tier above yours in the battle. Starting at Tier 5, ships can be up to 2 tiers higher than yours.
The higher tier the ships, the more powerful they are. So the game is inherently designed around you wanting to get to higher tier ships, so you can more easily beat your opponents.
If you are in a Tier 10 cruiser facing off against a Tier 8 cruiser, you will probably win - same if you are in a Tier 10 Destroyer, Battleship, or Aircraft Carrier.
You can either try to make the most of your ship and let yourself be pummled over and over again by higher tier ships (with the occasional game where you are the one beating the lower-tier enemies), or you can pay money to skip past lower tier ships rather quickly and directly upgrade to higher tier ships.
The higher your tier ship, the better the odds of you being in a top-tier match.
However, ship progression is far from the only progression present in the game. In fact, it's probably one of the least important progression systems present in the game.
What probably amounts to the most important progression system is the captain system.
On any ship, you can slot a captain. This captain gains XP along with your ship - and once you accrue enough XP, you unllock a skill point for him to spend.
These captain skills are incredibly powerful - making your ship that has a seasoned veteran just straight up better than the equal tiered opponents you face that do not have a captain of their own to match yours.
If you wish to advance to a ship and take your captain along, your captain suffers what is called "retraining". During this time, you need to play with the captain on your ship to grind out XP to "familiarize" him with the new ship. The problem? The more you invested into your captain before, the longer retraining takes on a new ship. Except you can spend money to by-pass this problem entirely.
Keep in mind that these captain skills are not trivial. There are entire ship classes (like destroyers or light cruisers) for whom these captain skills are essential to deal damage and survive. Without the correct captain skills, they are simply anemic XP and credit Pinatas for the enemy team.
Additionally, Wargaming (the developer/publisher) has  the habit of continously powercreeping content with new ships released. That means that unless you invest an unfeasible amount of time into this game or fork over vast quantities of money, the line you are grinding will easily be obsolete in a few months, displaced by something that is just straight up better.
They will milk the paying players for money and let them have overpowered ships for a few months. They eventually nerf these ships once the people who are likely to spend money to get them have done so, and then announce a new line a month or two later that will repeat the cycle.
Additionally, this game features premium consumables and premium ships.
Premium consumables are buy-for-each-battle items, that are direct upgraded versions over regular consumables. You can either pay exorbitant, non-sustainable amounts of in-game credits for, or you can pay real money for premium account time, premium camoflagues, buy in-game currency, or premium currency, all of which enable you to continously use these consumables.
Premium ships are ships that you can only attain by paying money for them. They are virtually never changed from their initial state. They are typically released along with new ship lines. This means that while newly released regular ships are just as good as the premium counterparts, the premium ships will remain overpowered, while the regular ships are subject to balance changes.
Just think about that; if you pay real money for a ship, it will never be nerfed. In a PvP game.
When players point out the disparity between regular ships and premium ships, the developers will do any combination of the following things:

None of this even addresses the combat in this game, which is absolutely attrocious.
All guns you shoot in this game have dispersion. Absolutely staggering amounts of dispersion. We are talking "divine intervention" levels of dispersion here.

You can be randomly one-shot from a single shell striking your ship.
Fires and flooding (damage over time effects) are based off of chance.
And you can pay real money to skew the chances in your favor.
"Oh boy, will the salvo I just fired instantly obliterate that ship over there?"
The sound effects in the game itself mirror those you might hear on slot machines. Big explosions, sounds effects, and all.
This game is fundamentally manipulative, deceiving, and exists to give a power fantasty to those willing to pony up the cash. I would go so far as to label it and its makers as evil. Please, do not play this.

I've been playing this game extremely casually for the past years, that means a few hours a day to once every 2-3 months.
I have to say this is the best naval battles game out there by far, if there even is a competitor. If you are drawn to it by KantaiCollection like me, you will marginally be disappointed but nevertheless still impressed by it, and hey the mods can fix your addiction, even through the mods are of extremely poor quality, the limitations placed on them are a factor i presume, for me slapping kancolle(and other) art on ship skins is indeed poor quality.
While all is good and the game is satisfying to play, WarGaming themselves are taking it in the wrong direction since the beginning and that shows, part of it has to do with insane 40 to 60 euro prices for ONE premium ship, the only vanilla skin in the game so far is the Bismark skin which you cant get anymore, and camouflages which are a consumable that pretty much ruin the look of ships to me. They have done a good job with the Halloween event ship skins for one mission available during halloween, but that is it. Personally i feel like ships skins and maybe even voice packs(preferably in cooperation with kantai collection team) would be the right direction instead of ultra expensive ships.
Okay aside from that, you got premium account benefits which frankly are equivalent to nothing. Let me put it like this, the major problem you will inevitably face is buying a new ship which requires EXP obtained only and only by the previous ship in a line of tiers to unlock the next tier, and game currency to buy the next ship. The EXP itself is a massive grind you have to go through at high tiers, especially for casual players ( i play for 2 and now close to 3 years casually and i still only just got to tier 9 out of 10, getting to 10 is much harder due to: read on), and CREDITS(game currency) the game offers you a insane ammount at the start to buy your ships, this will take you to atleast tier 7 maybe as you get some from grind too. Now heres how it works, you get credits, like exp, from participating in battles(grinding) roughly around 50k to 100k on a good game, and lets be real you wont be as good as youtubers of this game and be the carry to get a more than that, the problem again rises when you reach tiers 8,9,10 where the cost(yes there is a credits cost) to enter a battle with X ship is pretty much higher than the credits reward for winning/losing the battle, this becomes extremely obvious with tier 9 ships where even if you win, if you plaid poorly you are still in the negative... so... the tiers at which the game is most fun, the developers pretty much said no to that.
Now what im getting at is premium account time MARGINALLY fixes this, you get more EXP per battle so theres less grind, and more money and lower deployment cost(participating in game) this basically makes it like this, people say its efficient for non premiums to farm with tier 5-6 for money to buy and play tier 9-10 ships, and this is an insane grind ( i forgot to mention credit costs to buy ships go from 5 million at lower tiers to over 10 million credits for tier 9 or 10 )  so instead, with premium account time, you can farm money with tier 6-7 without losing money if you dont win the game.
Theres EXP conversion cost which means you convert EXP accumulated with a ship ( the one you grind with duh ) to something called Free EXP that can instead be used to unlock ( and then buy if you got the credits ) any ship, this costs real money currency and the same system is in place for commanders and resetting commander skills (im not going to get into this) both of which have a decent cost, but the cost being decent is a direct result of how insane the grind has to be in the first place, which is not a good thing. On top of which you dont outright buy Free exp, commander EXP.. etc, you first grind it and pay to convert it to, hopefully, be used on buying t9 and 10 only.
All in all a very great core game with rotten wargaming elements, i do recommend it because its extremely satisfying to play, the explosion sounds which they keep improving, that time you get citadel hits(massive dmg) all is very fun to play and everyone should give it a try.

Noting on some key-point elements of the game:
- You have a vast free roam map of several districts, each district with it's own theme, military, industrial, domestic etc. It's a trully sandbox experience.
- You get the feeling that you have so many things to do, follow up on the main quests, catch up on some side quests, try out your newly aquired weapon or skill, roaming free around the city delivering mayhem on the streets, killing countless of innocent pedestrials just because...you can. It's up to you.
- The controls are pretty straight forward and simple, but actually effective, with the exception of driving the motorcycle and flying the aircraft.
- At the start of the game, and later on in specific stores, you are given the opportunity to customize your avatar in ways I never thought I would see in a game. That is all I am going to say:)
- The variety of weapons and powers it's impressive, plus everything is upgradable. There's a bit something for every taste and style. Also, there is a number of challenges that, when completed, provide you with very usefull upgrades.
- The story is interesting, with twists and developments. I was tempted to take on the next main quest, just to see what would happen.
- Despite it's light and humorous atmosphere, if you dont take your enemies seriously, there are times that you might actually die, I find this a good thing, otherwise it would had been a bit boring.
Overall it's a pretty fun and exciting game, full with content that will keep you occupied for over 100 hours, at the momment of writing this I'm at about 60% of completion.

I've spent quite a bit of time on this game (since day 1) and while I initially thought it wasn't that good, I just could not get my hands off this game as it is so addictive.
So let me start off by saying that this game has bugs. Some that are just too obvious like: some combos not working correctly, last boss glitch, and multiplayer saves (as of 3/20/17). While this got frustrating at times, it is nice to know that the devs are working on them and from day one until now, I am getting a much better experience and game.
Positives:
+ Graphics: Love the sprites and they are animated beautifully, especially when you do combos. It's like retro art in motion.
+ Characters: The diversity in characters will have you playing this game for hours, as each character is different and fun to master. I wanted to main one character, but after 40 some hours, I ended up mastering all of them. This is what really sucked me into the game, as I love diversity in characters and moves.
+ Sound: I love the music in this game and is reminescent of the 8-bit era of gaming with a more modern twist.
+ Control: These controls are super tight and precise. Gotta give it to the devs for making a game that controls really well and is satisfying when you perform a combo. Highly recommend you use a xbox controller for this.
+ Local Multiplayer: works like it should an dI love playing this game with my wife and friends.
Negatives
- Bugs: A handful and they are obvious at times. Just know that they are working on them and each update the game gets even better.

- Difficulty: for those who have never played the original, this game is a major shock to them as it can be very difficult. I am a glutton for pain and therefore I have a tendency to level up a character to the max. If you put time into a character the game gets easier. If you don't it can be frustrating for newcomers.
Neutral:
~ The dreaded milk mission. This mission can be very difficult and frustrating for many. Once you get past it though, all the other missions are fun.
There is definitely more positives than negatives with this game, and I highly recommend it for those who miss old-school fighting games like double dragon and the original river city ransom.

=================Original Review===============
Pains me to say this, but no I don't recommend this game
Yes, I bought it. Yes, I've played it a bunch. Yes, I'll continue playing it. No, I don't recommend you buying it until several issues are ironed out.
1) Network issues. The multiplayer/co-op are prone to lag causing odd interactions like characters warping. It's neither consistent, nor terribly overbearing, but it is an issue.
2) Network issues again. Good luck playing this game with multiple people behind the same router. The devs were nice enough to enable a command line argument to help this issue. It's a workaround that works for two players on the same network. Good luck with players three and four.
3) Shop issues. As you play the game, you will acquire character levels and money. You can take said money and visit various shops and dojos to buy items and new moves. What's that item you want to buy actually do? No idea sir/ma'am. You'll have to buy it and use it first to find out, then make a (mental)note of it. You want to buy this move from the dojo. You have enough money but the game says you're not a high enough level to buy it. What level do you need to be to buy it? No idea. You'll just have to come back each time you level up and hope you can buy it then. By the way, the move you saw listed when you were a level 1? It's available at level 20. Hope you enjoyed the repeated trips back to find that out. Oh, side note. Yes you bought the move, but it requires a certain amount of special attack energy to use. No, the game doesn't tell you how much or even tell you that any special energy was needed for that move. Just keep eating items that increase max special energy (after you've figured out which items do this) until you can actually activate the move. You'll be able to use it eventually.
4) Stat and combo issue. The Strength stat increases your damage. Awesome. It also increases your knockback for each hit. Sooooo, as you level you'll increase your STR through items which will result in your combo strings having more knockback. Sounds good? Here's the problem. This game's combo system requires that the previous hit land or the next hit won't activate at all. So when your STR increases to a certain point (varies per character, but all of them suffer this) your hits will start to knock enemies back far enough that the next hit can't land. Yes, improving your stats breaks your ability to do your own combos.
5) AI issues. The enemy AI is terrible. It's not overly difficult at all, it's simply cheap to the point of annoyance. This is a beat 'em which usually means enemies will be more than happy to engage you. Not in this game. Enemies will routinely back away from you and mirror your footsteps pixel-for-pixel as you advance and retreat. What results isn't a difficult fight, it's a dull one where you spend more time chasing enemies than fighting. It gets tedious quickly and boring. The other problem is that the game very
clearly reads your controls. Say you're throwing a jab when the enemy is in range. The AI has the ability to backpedal
just out of range of your jab, then walk back into range and hit you before you can recover. I repeat, this sort of thing happens with your fastest combo starters and it happens more and more as you progress through the game. As opposed to other classic beat 'em ups where the challenge lies in beating crowds of enemies without being overwhelmed by numbers, this game has you quite literally chasing crowds of enemies that are all too tentative to engage beyond running in to land a poke before retreating again.
6) Character balance issues. The various characters you get to play vary wildly in viability. Some characters like Ryan, Paul, Provie, and Glen are solid as soon as you pick them up. Others like Bruno, Mike, and Rudy are borderline terrible until you've purchased several moves. This might put some people off as some characters are an absolute chore to play until around level 15 when they finally get some usable and fun moves added.
7) Move list issues. The movelist is flat out wrong a LOT of the time. I don't know how this happens frankly, but you'll buy a move in this game then check the movelist to see how it's done only for the movelist to have the wrong controls listed. Heaven forbid the move you just bought is part of combo. The movelist will simply say "punch" for example where as the move you just bought can only be activated after a kick-punch-kick string has been landed.
Some of these issues where present in the original River City Ransom from 1989. Here's the thing, they were problems then too; so hanging on to them for charm or nostalgia doesn't fly. YMMV, but I haven't found it particularly interesting seeing the same problems that I saw when I played the original game almost 30 years ago as a child.
Nostalgia keeps me playing this game. If it didn't have the Kunio artstyle and I didn't have such fond memories of the original I would have put this game down permanently. There's a
game hiding in here, it's just buried under a mountain of mechanical, enemy AI, and UI issues.

Besides being a unique procedurally-generated RPG with an appealing soundtrack, this game has another worthwhile distinction that isn't frequently mentioned in positive reviews: One Way Heroics is conducive to playing in short bursts, or for hours at a time. On a low difficulty, you can clear the game in half an hour, provided you have some idea of what you're doing. One Way Heroics (OWH), is a Quick paced Rogue-like RPG made from the RPG maker Series. Sounds simple, and is easily hidden amongst the other "Maker Games" on Steam. But this is one RPG that you should not miss. It's Challenging, Fast-Paced, and Addicting. As the name implies you will be going one way with your "heroics" as you battle the Darkness that is plaguing the world you inhabit (as the different world are classified as alternate dimensions in-game)
Pros
- A Decent array of Classes, 2 to begin 8 overall (3 more if you get the expansion).
- No two world are the same allowing for a new exciting experience each time, and if you liked a world you played before you have access to that in your logs.
- Simple yet thrilling combat: with the unique "one way" mechanic, the combat does not allow you to dawdle and grind. You will have to defeat enemies Quickly.
Con (As the only one i can really think of as of writing this review)
- Slow Start: the Game is tough, While it's nice that the first two classes you start with are easy to play, the Classes you unlock will take a bit of practice to get used to making it a tad difficult to unlock early achievements.
Otherwise One Way Heroics is a fast paced RPG that looks generic but should Not be Overlooekd just becasue of that. IF you like Simple yet thrilling RPGs then One Way Heroics is a Game for you!

This is, without a doubt,  a great little game. It's got a lovely premise and theme, and the gameplay mix between game modes (strategy and tactics) is very well balanced.
I can't recommend it, though. Its tutorial and help system is not nearly sufficient for the gameplay present. You kind of get thrown into a game and given a few tips, and you're left to figure out stuff on your own. In these days of quest markers and other player-catering behaviour, this 90's throwback to how you treat your player - an obsessive mathematics-inclined nerd - is not how to make games anymore. Don't buy it unless you're willing to put some time into learning what it's all about.
That said, I eagerly look forward to Weird and Wry's next title, and I hope they either figure out the magic of approaching players and UI design, or hire a designer to guide their methods. The Spatials has touches of genius within it, and at the same time, a voice that suggests neither brother was willing to take the spotlight and argue for the audience's experience or take responsibility for the title.

The controls are tight, and combines the best of both the old school 2D Sonic games with the Next Gen 3D Sonic games. Theres a wonderful little story that ties it up, and the best part for many will be the fact that Sonic's friends take a backseat completely and only serve as a motivation for Sonic to run at the speed of sound.
I do not like Platformers. So take what I say with a grain of salt, but I really enjoyed Sonic Generations, mainly because of all the wonderful BGMs (City Escape and Rooftop Run). Sonic Generations hosts a collection of the best momments in the Sonic franchise sprinkled with alittle bit of Next Gen quality with old school care. No matter if your a fan, a hater, or someone who could careless about Sonic, you'll find enjoyment in this game.

Blade Symphony promises a fun deep sword combat game, and instead delivers:
- An extremely poor tutorial that tosses you into a bunch of situations without fully explaining them or your controls, giving incomplete instructions, and humiliating you with "simple" stuff that is too hard to do.
- Terrible, illogical naming and documentation. Why does "block" not block on half the swords, and which swords do what? What in the name of all that is good is a "string" and why do I care?
- Poor, laggy control scheme. Expected better out of a game where timing is everything.
- Bad clipboxes
- Bad event detection (parry happening well after one player finished swinging, swings going through one another)
It feels like an extremely gimmicky game to be played only by its devs, or the few people determined enough to find out all the quirks making gameplay difficult. For the rest of us, it's an experiment in futile button mashing hoping you get the ever so elusive "timing" right. Count this sword hobbyist and gamer disappointed in this utter waste of money (even at its sale price)

First and foremost, the game is awesome.  The game dynamics work a lot like they did with the previous Shadowrun games but the experience I feel is more evenly weighed.  The only real complaint I have is how the racial bonuses are handled.  In the original table top version of Shadowrun, a player figured their stats and then added the racial bonus.  That means that if you start with a 5 in charisma as an elf, you should only have to spend 4 karma to get it.  And at each subsequent level your karma expense should be 1 less than the actual final result (i.e. raising from 6 to  7 in charisma should only cost you 6 karma due to your racial bonus).  As it is, you get the bonus at character generation and then it disappears.  Without that contingency, the other races really seem worthless despite their overall caps.  I really hope this is given some attention in what I hope are future installments of this series.
That being said, the game is good.  The story starts off a little slow without anything to really pull you into it.  However, as you play it, the story starts drawing you in.  The side missions and quests begin to mean something as an overall plot starts to take hold.  More is happening behind the scenes than just what your character is doing.
I've not completed the game yet.  I will say I predict that in the end, the story has one basic ending, as most do, that will happen regardless of character choices or actions inbetween.  That is the nature of these kind of games.  It is a story that unfolds and the final chapter is more or less the same.  In most cases.  However, I liked the first in this series and this is definately an upgrade from Dragonfall (a great story in its own account).  I think the developers, overall, have recaptured the atmosphere and feel of the original table top in the way it was originally written and intended to be played.
Overall, I love it.  4 out of 5 stars (check the racial bonus tiffe).
