The best part about this game is how it cleverly combines several different genres. You build a base for your crew, but also for aliens that come to visit you. Then you have to meet the needs of both your crew and the aliens. They crave all kinds if different products you have to craft from resources you gather. Finally there is the action part; take your crew on away-missions to distant planets where you'll find plenty of pirates, robots and aliens to blow up!
The caveat of course is that because the game combines so many different elements it doesn't excell in any of them. Nor does it bring any revolutionary new gameplay. But is that really necessary? All the elements in the game work, and more importantly they work well together.
My only real critisicm of this game is that I found it to be rather easy to beat.
Still, for the price I can only recommend this game. I've had many hours of fun with it. If it ever goes on sale, this is a total no-brainer; buy it!

This is a really fun space colony game where you explore other planets on little quests, exploring that planet and gathering resources strewn about the map and killing various enemies and receiving a reward for doing it.  Completing the mission lets you harvest resources periodically from that planet.
Meanwhile, you can also send your officers on quests of their own that take time (5m for example) to complete - higher level officers are required to be ambassadors to the galaxies so you have a lowered time on harvesting resources you've unlocked.  The base is built SLOWLY.  It will be a while before you can allow visitors in my experience, because you have to meet their needs.  My first base I built a bunch of stuff and everyone got ticked because I didn't have the stuff they wanted, especially food.
Concentrate on getting resources and officers in the beginning before building a lot of amenities, or even unlocking them in the tech tree.  Some products you need resources for you won't get until you're in the 15th galaxy area, and likely beyond but I've just made it that far, so unlocking extras in the tech tree aren't very beneficial for a while.
Its a very in depth, yet light weight game it never feels like you're grinding.  There's a lot to do, spread out between different tasks and all giving a relaxing feeling.  A lot of upgrades in weapons and abilities for your officers, special decorations and such to find on planets.  The cool part about the planets and missions is they all look different.  There's a lot of graphic content and neat environments to explore.
Absolutely recommend buying this game.

I am a big fan of the Shadowrun universe and Asiatic settings, so this game was a no brainer for me (pledged on KS). I am happy to tell you that this game is all I wanted it to be: great story, great npcs and great design, in a very fascinating setting like Hong Kong. The game looks even better than Dragonfall and maps are bigger; the matrix has become more dynamic and cyberweapons were added to the mix.
It definitely doesn't revolutionize shadowrun games made by HBS, but it improves most of the aspects of Dragonfall. I say most because this game does have some minor flaws, notably:
1) Maps are most of the times bigger, but that increased space is not filled with characters, secrets and so on
2) Your companions are great, particularly Gaichu, but overall they do not reach the level of greatness of Dragonfall ones
3) The game is too easy even at hard difficulty
4) Dialogues are great, but sometimes they drag on for no reason, making the read somewhat boring.
Despite these flaws, I vividly enjoyed the game and I still play it from time to time: ABSOLUTELY RECOMMENDED.

Thankfully, some stuff on the workshop fixes most of this, so remember to install that before starting your first playthrough.
As for the positives: I really enjoyed this game. The music and sound effects are as usual.
The plot is rich and very interesting, full of scary Chinese monsters and corporate backstabs, as you would expect after playing the previous iterations. Dragonfall seemed longer to me, but from a quality angle the writing remains very good. I wish more games were like Shadowrun, when it comes to telling a story.
Seems like every new installment brings in some improvement. This time cyberware and skill tree get expanded, making the customization of the PC more interesting. Only thing that might put off old fans of the series is the new matrix. I liked some of the changes (the fact that it's not all turn based) and hated some others (damn sentries), but I'm not here to judge.
If you never played a Shadowrun game, I'd suggest you start with Shadowrun Returns, because it's great, and costs less (a good thing since you may end up not liking it), while if you played and liked one of the previous games jump on SHK right away. You won't regret it.

I never understood why it seems so hard to make a decent cyberpunk(ish) game. Shadowrun Returns is on the right track, definitively.
As a longtime player of the P&P-RPG Shadowrun, I thoroughly enjoyed this latest installment. Of course it has its problems, but on the whole I can recommend it to anyone not too hooked up on graphics or other shinies. This game further improves on the original Shadowrun Returns and its first official successor Dragonfall.
As with Dragonfall in regards to vanilla Shadowrun Returns, Hong Kong makes further small improvements on the gameplay and mechanics that I personally welcomed as good additions (for example having a Mass Effect 3 like skilltree for your team to give them certain powers as they progress in level).
PROs:
- Story is very good. In fact I'd say it is the best so far.
- Very well written dialogue with interesting special options if you developed the right skills, providing a satisfying RPG experience
- Atmosphere is very immersive, the texts (yes reading! see below under CONs) are painting a pretty good picture of the Awakened Hong Kong in all its corrupt glory and misery
- Quite a few points in the storyline where you have to make decisions influencing your later game in small ways.
- Interesting characters as fellow runners with good backstories and their own missions. I never used hired help.
CONS:
- A LOT of reading involved (didn't mind that myself, but it is not for everybody). Nothing (exept pro- and epilouge) is voiced over
- Limited possibility to equip your fellow runners. They mostly have their own weapons and equipment and don't need stuff you might want to give them. That is on one hand fine, as you won't earn enough money to equip everybody with the best stuff anyway but it takes away some of the fun (for me at least).
- Occasionally ATROCIOUS AI in regards to neutral NPCs in combat (had a physical adept - supposedly helping me - run circles for the whole fight while his mates and my team died)
- Same for the odd enemy AI (not to spoil anything but the final boss hardly even attacked my team during the whole fight).
- The hacking minigames during matrix runs are an interesting feature but it gets old very quick.
- the odd bug (had bought equipment like spells disappear between runs occasionally)
While on first glance the number of cons does seem to outweigh the number of pros a little, this is mitigated by the fact that the cons are - to me - minor annoyances as I play primarily for the story experience not the gaming challenge.
If you played and liked Shadowrun Returns and Shadowrun Returns Dragonfall, Hong Kong is a must have in my opinion. If you didn't, you might want to check them out first, as Hong Kong features improvements over them that you will probably miss when going back and the lack of which might lessen your enjoyment of the earlier installments (especially of the original).

Which is good because that's a type of game you're meant to finish many times to get the many different endings and face the many different daily challenges.
The graphics and soundtrack are also good in a 8-bit kind of way, but the real draw is really the gameplay.
It's a very solid recommendation for anyone who likes roguelikes and don't mind jRPGs. If you're a fan of jRPGs and can stomach roguelike mechanics, you should also definitely give it a try, it's an experience you have to make. Easily one of my favorite games.

Easily one of the best roguelikes out there. I'd put it at number 2 in my book.
The companions are terrific; each have their own stories and quests. I don't think I've ever seen a roguelike with a story that was actually compelling.
The spell casting is phenomenal, something I could never enjoy in Nethack, Slash'em, and other turnbased roguelikes.
Terrific soundtracks, another thing that many roguelikes lack. I'd say on-par, maybe better, than FTL soundtracks.
IMO, this game has an excellent balance of luck vs tactical sense (Its not a total crapshoot but there is enough randomness to make repeat playthroughs rewarding and fun.
Incredible sense of adventure as you flee the oncoming doom from the west; different biomes offer unique challenges and enemies.
Most people don't realize there are actually THREE ways to win. If you think you da man just because you stomped the demon lord, think again. You ain't done yet, lil ♥♥♥♥♥.
And... its 87 cents during sales. You could buy a soda... or you could save half that money and buy a game with at least 20 hours of content. What a time to be alive.

Simply put: I didn't find this game fun.
The gameplay mechanics are interesting and I especially like the idea of character progression through new characters, but the content is just... lacking. Going through the game and advancing my character gave me no sense of accomplishment or progression. Nothing immersed me in the world or made me care about the Demon Lord. The interface was frustrating and took away most of the enjoyment I could get out of the rougelike aspect of it. Oh, and the lack of language support in the game itself is frustrating--I decided I wanted to play through in English this time instead of Japanese and changing it via Steam (the only way) wiped all of my data. There's no real excuse to not have proper language support these days... except that I'm pretty sure this game was made with RPG Maker, which has absolutely no localization support.
Anyway, despite the low price I'd recommend giving this game a pass.

Do not be fooled by the cheap price, this game is worth way more than what it's up for. At first i thought it was going to be another cheesy sidescroller game, and boy was I wrong. This game is absolutely fantastic, a real gem, and I'm suprised it's not exploding. The game is fun. Anyways, enough ranting about how fun it is, here's my pros and cons.
PROS: Massive replay value. There is a lot of hidden content, and a lot more to the game than what you see on your first clear.
Multiple classes for your own style of adventuring. While this may not seem huge, the differences in classes are a lot more diverse than what you think. Join up with a party of a few people, or go completely ham solo with a knight. Choice is yours

Difficulty. This game can throw some suprising difficulty at the most unexpected places. I've died at some very unexpected places. There is a lot of strategy into this game. Very good for those who enjoy a challenge.
CONS: Well, I haven't run into anything that would deter me or anyone i know away from the game yet, but I'll update this if I do.

A distinctly (but not stereotypically) Japanese take on the (real) roguelike. Kill things. Collect utility items. Find good gear, hopefully. Carefully contemplate your options as a cabal of imps breathe down your neck. Probably get killed, or more likely kill yourself in a nearsighted blunder. Every once in a blue moon, reach the the Big Bad only to lose your head to a casually-flung fireball. Every once in a hundred blue moons or so, actually kill the guy. It's simpler than, say, Nethack, but bears more depth than grandaddy Rogue.
In true roguelike spirit, there is a leveling system, but progression is heavily biased towards gear, and by extension very random.
The advancing wall of doom is a unique spin on the roguelike formula, forcing you to budget your actual turns. Can you make it back to the entrance of the dungeon? You can easily kill the enemy harassing you, but do you have time? It creates a real sense of urgency without imposing actual time limits. You have plenty of time to think... about the 8 turns you have remaining before the darkness consumes you.
Another unique mechanic is the final boss periodically shows up and harasses you before running away. It's a double-edged sword; this gives you an opportunity to slay him early, if you got lucky enough or twinked over powerful items from your vault. At the same time, you have to know not just when, but HOW to run. The game does warn you when he'll be showing up soon, so you always get a chance to put your pants back on.
And unlike your average roguelike, it's controller-friendly, being largely driven by graphical menus as opposed to keystroke commands.
If you like very unusual games, buy it. If you enjoy a proper roguelike, buy it. Hell, it's dirt cheap even without a sale. And quite good.
Starts off slow when you first play, but that's when it starts to get exciting.

Worst game I've ever played. This is the first time I've ever been insulted by a game's existence. This game takes ideas from all over the place, with level designs similar to Antichamber, No Man's Sky, Dr. Langeskov, The Tiger, and The Terribly Cursed Emerald, and The Beginner's Guide. However, the game takes most of its inspiration from The Beginner's Guide, as it's practically a copy. While retaining its own story, it is so clearly trying to be the same game The Beginner's Guide was, even though this kid could never understand what made that game so special. Davey Wreden had a hit, a real hit, with the Stanely Parable, so it makes sense to see him go down a rough road of depression. That game, The Beginner's Guide, is one of my favorite games of all time. Its message is that people often look too deep into meanings for everything. People get obsessed with work, they distort it unitl it's not even real, all because they want to feel like it's speaking to them, when usually it isn't. This game throws that all out the window and gets all the wrong messages from The Beginner's Guide. This kid has the standard teen struggles, yet he thinks he's special, or at least story worthy. Nothing in this game is interesting. This kid's problems are as simple as, "I want love," or, "I want to be confident," and it's just not anything interesting to see.
Basically, this game is trying to be something that it's not. This kid obviously loved The Beginner's Guide and wanted to make a game just like that. He wanted his story to be known, for his insecurities to be known. But The Beginner's Guide had subtlety. This game is more like a toy box that spilled open, releasing everything in a messy, unorganized way. Point is, The Beginner's Guide was made for people just like this kid, and obviously that went right over his head.

Game: Puzzle Agent 2
Developer and publisher:
Released: 30 June, 2011
Genre: Point-and-Click Mystery with Comedy
Setting: Winter, 2010, Scoggins, Minnesota, U.S.A., Earth
Spoiler-free plot summary: About a month after the events of the first Puzzle Agent, Agent Nelson Tethers is still obsessed with the mystery behind the Hidden People of Scoggins. During his vacation, he travels back to Scoggins and attempts to solve the mysteries haunting his mind.
Full review: Not much to say here really. Puzzle Agent 2 is set in the exact same location and has the exact same mechanics as the first Puzzle Agent. All that's really new here are harder puzzles, remixes of puzzles seen in the first Puzzle Agent, and the answers to the unsolved mysteries of the first Puzzle Agent.
Again, I can't talk about the plot of Puzzle Agent 2 without spoiling anything as everything kicks off right from the getgo. What I will say, however, is that all of the mystery and eeriness is completely thrown out the window as the plot, even though it starts out strong, ends very weakly.
Do I recommend buying Puzzle Agent 2? Yes, but only if you're really desperate for answers that weren't given at the end of the first Puzzle Agent. You're really not missing out on much, and it would have been best if the mysteries in the first Puzzle Agent were left unsolved and open-ended. For NZD$11.99, I'd wait for a sale for when this game is $2 - $3 before buying it.

Gameplay wise this one feels like it really is designed to be played with a controller, using a keyboard and mouse is better for aiming but having too many controls signed to same key will be annoying. The combat is alright, but it's clunky enough, it's clear they probably should have gone with a new engine to do all the superhero tricks they wanted for the simulation to work effectively.

Some things that the BIT.TRIP games have always done well are pacing and rhythm. With this installment, not only do these tropes continue, but with flair that the series has never attempted. This is the same old rhythm platformer you know, with more personality and accessibility; a refreshing step from the classic, and in my eyes, a damn good sequel. The new art style is a particularly welcome feature in my book. The visuals are very slick and aberrantly fitting. The music is encapturing, as one may expect from a BIT.TRIP game. The controls are responsive. Everything seems to mesh together well into a melting pot of skill, reflex, and sometimes, luck. This time around, the gameplay is expanded to make the experience more accessible. Hardcore rhythm challenge-seekers (or challenge-seekers in general) shouldn't worry; the difficulty is just as punishing as one would assume, it can simply be toned down. Casual players also are welcomed due to this, and that is why I would recommend the game to players of all types. It's for everyone.

Whether you have or haven't played the original BIT.TRIP RUNNER, this game is far superior.
Putting aside the gorgeous graphics (which mean nothing if the game isn't fun), this game is just far more forgiving than the original RUNNER. The reason for this is because of the checkpoints in the stages, the levels can be difficult without making you want to tear your hair out when you get hit near the end, and if you don't like that kind of thing, you can just jump over them.
And being a rhythm game, the music is critical, and this game delivers. The songs that play are really upbeat and get you in the mood to play. It's not easy to describe the music, and I wouldn't say it'll get stuck in your head (though the world 3 theme did), and the controls are dead on.
There's also a bunch of unlockable outfits and game cartriges in certain levels, the outfits are completely cosmetic (but look nice), and the cartriges take you to 8-bit style bonus levels, I don't know what happens when you beat them all, but I'm assuming it's how you unlock retro Commander Video.
Overall, a great buy, definitely worth the money.

The music and art style are great, and I've been craving base building games, but I just don't find The Spatials fun.
The only difficulty in this game is figuring out the rules for how to optimize base building and combat. The rules aren't complicated, they're just not explained well through the tutorial or interface. Once you've got them figured out, the rest of the game is just grinding.
The grinding is really obvious too - enemies are just "Pirate (lvl 10)", weapons are "Phaser (lvl 10)", the buildings & activities have different names, but it's obvious that each level is just an improved version of the previous level. There's no complex supply chain, nor any high level unlockables that make the game interesting again.
Optimizing your base feels more like a chore than anything - if you try to make neat, isolated rooms, you're wasting 50% of your space and you won't make much profit. You're better off smushing everything together, and filling all the gaps with statues of a bald guy, because decor helps, but it doesn't matter which decor you use.

The Spatials is yet another game that came out of nowhere for me and what a nice surprise it is. I’m fairly big fan of the city-building sim genre (except for The Sims for reasons I won’t go into now) and Weird and Wry decided to put the genre in space. (It may have been done before, but this is a first for myself.) With a bit of a nostalgic Star Trek look and a bit more complication in the genre than I’ve played, The Spatials has taken a lot of my time lately and I’ll gladly give it more.
So you start with just an air-lock and you build out from there. You can build a lot of different facilities that one would expect like sleeping and storage areas, but once you get a little further in you can build bars with dance floors (which the humans aren’t too fond of weirdly enough) and sell fancy drinks. I had to do a lot of extra work to get the ingredients to be able to make the drinks, but what are you going to do. I also haven’t got to build a Duty Free shop, but I’m on my way. With as many airports as I’ve been in during my life… I kind of need one in my space port or it just won’t feel finished. *Insert end-game goal here!*
*EDIT* In the middle of writing this I realized that I have actually built the Duty Free shop so the new goal is the build the second version of it and a freaking Holoarea because it’s a Holode… Holoarea and that’s awesome!
That does bring up a few things that weren’t the clearest in the tutorial. Granted, some of the issues I had could have been solved by… you know… reading, but that’s neither here nor there. Sometimes you’ll do a tutorial and just assume that you can handle the rest of it. Well it turns out, I’m not capable of handling The Spatials without reading the in-game notes (go figure). It is good to know ahead of time, for those of you who haven’t picked it up, that you can build facilities that create items that use materials you can’t get for a while. It is easy enough to unlock more solar systems, but the difficulty goes up as well.
Moving on from there you build the places where food and/or goods get created and then you also have to create a place for your people and the visitors to your space station to purchase or consume the goods. That means if you make a kitchen to make a pizza, you’ll also need a cafeteria where you can sit down and enjoy it (or procure it and enjoy it in this instance). It makes sense, but it’s a nice and small touch that adds a little complexity. I really enjoyed figuring it out and the process of making the space station work efficiently. To really get it, you’ll want to have a little bit of everything crafted just in case someone comes in and is craving pizza or yogurt or a cold one for those who like their drinks shaken, but not stirred (if you’re over 21 of course). You’ve got to be prepared.
If you want to be completely prepared you’ll have to work for it. While you can expand and conquer more planets, that won’t really help you get enough supplies to be able to create everything fast enough to be able to keep all of your people and visitors clean and satisfied. After beating a mission on a planet, you should go back and beat the harder difficulty setting to double-up on the supplies you get from the planet. (The “WTF” difficulty in later levels are not very nice at all.) Also, remember to hire more people so you can have people to staff the so that you can get your supplies faster as well. It’s a delicate balance between hiring too many, making the right products and having just enough for everyone. The nice part is that it’s not really frustrating to do this, it’s actually quite fun. I’m not completely sure how Weird & Wry managed this, but they did a great job.
Last thing, because I see people complaining about this, there is a little complexity to this game. Not a lot. It’s not overly difficult if you’ve got the capacities to read and remember things. While you may be maintaining your space station and making everyone happy by supplying the proper goods DON’T FORGOT YOUR AWAY TEAM! People complaining about how “you can’t raise their happiness levels back up in time to keep them from leaving” aren’t being very observant. When you’re out on missions you get hungry running around blasting fools and picking things up. Not to mention how dirty you must get. You need to give your people time to get cleaned up or yeh, they will leave. Wouldn’t you? All work and no soap or food make these Spatials look for another port were their fun-meter can be filled properly. (You know… like my station when the bar will actually serves drinks…)
Score: Tasty!

i had really hoped to love this game, but came away pretty disappointed.
i love "base" layout and planning games like this (evil genius dungeon keeper) but found that there wasn't much to this game.
my main problem with the game is there is no real incentive to progress your station, or your resources.  everything you "unlock" is basically the same exact thing as the thing you just had, so the base gameplay you will experience pretty much in full at the first solar system.
away missions are a neat mechanic in idea, but are ultimately really boring and tedious.  they are procedurally generated form a seemingly tiny pool of options... most every single mission is "kill all the things"  which gets really really boring quick as combat is basically hold down L mouse button and hit hotkeys for bland abilities periodically.
in the end i played this game for a couple days, progressed about half way into the galaxies, and just got bored and didn't want to come back.  i didn't really want to expand my base, explore the system, or complete the tech tree... which is saying a lot coming form someone who LOVES this "base building" type game.  i rate evil genius as my favorite alltime game if that says anything, and this game just left so many empty feelings inside me...
i don't know, the game should be ALL about the base, and it should make or break you and your team... and there just isn't anything like that here... bases are just money-generating and officer pleasing zones... i found myself not really "planning" layouts or logistics for rooms... after a while i just was plopping♥♥♥♥♥♥around just to have it... and that's not a good thing for a base building game.
however i really hope the developers get something out of this game, cuz the genre is my favorite and would love to see more games come out for it.
TLDR:  disappointing, boring and tedious base builder that disappoints the hardest of hardcore base building genre fans.

TL;DR I love the management, simulation, RPG, RTS style of this game.
This is the game that I thought Spacebase DF-9 was going to be. It's way more in depth and almost has the Dwarf Fortress feel I've been looking for. I played 6 hours on the first night I got it, so that says a lot. There's a bit of a learning curve and it has these different modes that the game forces you to play: base-building, RTS, RPG, and management. To advance building your base, you need to venture out into space in search of other planets to get the resources you need. You can then assign three officers per solar system to produce resouces at those solar systems quicker so that you don't need to constantly keep going out to space. Eventually you will have to level up your officers to get the next level of resouces to fulfill the needs of higher level officers (it's all relative). The item level also isn't dependent on the level of each officer, which is good, but you have to have officers at a high enough level to get them in the first place.
Honestly, this game has a lot of depth, and tafter 6 hours of playing I still feel like I'm only 1/4 of the way to end game (maybe?) and I there's a lot of replayability, unless you don't like the grind and repetiveness. The replayability comes from the randomly generated solar systems, resources and base-building. It's sort of a mix between Starbound, Rim World, Prison Architect, Spacebase, and Prison Architect.

Firstly Id like to say that Im a huge River City Ransom fan all the way back to Nintendo. This game has good qualities. The art is nice and the animation is wonderful. There are nods to the original formula here but not in an intrusive way to where you wont "get it" if youre not a fan. There are some nifty surprises in here as well. Cool little easter egg art and places to see pretty backgrounds. The developers are working, at this time, on fixing the games problem areas. It is a fun game. Id come back once the issues are fixed. Dont get me wrong. The game was fun for a time and when it works its wonderful, unfortunately what youll also find is a semi broken and unfinished mess. Drink in that pretty art!
I guess Ill begin with the meat and potatoes of the game. Its really the main relevance since everything else is negligible to some degree. When you start a toon youre missing moves. Theyve attempted to correct this and in doing so seem to have removed throw damage...good luck, grappler types. So here is how the game works in a nutshell. You hit people in the face and they turn into spare change. However you have to buy moves, basic moves sometimes, to get to do better combos. There are guides for moves that are seemingly broken and requirements for each move you get. Sometimes you buy a move and try, try, try, to get it to work, unknown to you that its the end part of a 3 hit combo and you cant do it until you have the 2nd hit in the combo. The in game guide is worthless as sometimes it displays the wrong command prompt and most times just will not work due to you not understanding the use and timing.
Enemy A.I. is frustrating to the point of being easier to ACTUALLY go out and fight a gang of people. Ever played Double Dragon 3 the Rosetta Stone? Well welcome back friend. The computer will seemingly input read your controller commands and the longer you play, the farther you get will do so to greater and greater accuracy until youre trying in vain just to get a hit off on any of the some 5-10 baddies on the screen. Seriously. I wasnt kidding when saying that video up there is mostly false advertisement at this point, with what Ive witnessed. You eventually get to a point where you pick up weapons and hurl them at a baddie just to see a group...no Im not even kidding a bit, a whole group, jump, in unison, over the object or attack youve just thrown. Use a special and they will go from blocking to just literally stepping just inside or outside of yer hit box and you miss, however they connect a hit every time. There are charge times to most moves that are interrupted by the overly fast and completely accurate computer players. Their moves, by comparison, are almost instantaneous and will almost always hit with almost no discernable warning.  The special moves you do just dont hit. Most of the time during the later chapters of the game its just you, swinging on like 5 people, all of which are blocking, and dodging everything you dish out. The only way to really fight is to kind of trick the A.I. by walking around and hitting them as they approach yer hit area or jump onto a trashcan and attack as they jump. The A.I. will do its best to gang up on you and just hit you in the back as much as possible.
So you basically....no, literally end up standing on a dumpster next to a spa in a part of town, and kick dudes that jump up to fight you. Most of my game experience has been standing on that damned dumpster and just kicking people. Wanna use a grappler character? There is another issue. Grabbing. You attempt a grab and mostly the computer just walks away, at full speed, backwards as you run to grab them. Grab and miss, there is a 2-3 second penalty where you just stand there looking like an idiot and the computer? You guessed it, pops you in the face...a lot. Actually grab someone? Sweet....do you have a move for that? If not you cant do anything with the enemy grabbed and you stand there while....a computer baddie hits you in the face, breaks up the grab and reinforces the knowledge that youve wasted yer money.
You can check the forums about the frustrating fighting for even more details. Ive been flat out told by a dev, who I wont name, because I dont like to call people out publicly unless your name is Dean Hall, Ive been straight told that enemy A.I. is not working as intended. Will they fix it? Who knows. Will it matter? Doubt it at this point. There are other problems which need to be discussed. Lets move onto them. Boss fights. There are almost none. In fact there are a few that are "good" if you let the boss actually atack you. There are chase missions where you should have boss fights. Ill get to that crate of bull$#1t in a minute. The bosses are weaksauce. Some are interesting in animation and do some cool things but theyre incredibly easy.
Some of the cooler boss fight set-ups are in fact chase sequences..........holy....crap. Theyre terribly thought out, buggy, and just stupid. Theyre either slap happy easy or frustrating to the point of breaking a toaster near you, from rage inducing randomness. For instance the character Tex. He runs  through a sewer area and sometimes he jumps to his death. Has nothing to do with you its just...well.....stupid programming. Then there are chases that bug out and dialouge on screen after a chase or a boss fight thats interrupted by people beating the crap out of you while youre trying to read the text as its spoken.
Lets move on to the characters. I loved Rudy. I play usually as the bigger, slower, guys because theyre fun to me. By about 2/3 of the way through the game you will no longer be able to physically touch the overly perfect ninja computer players unless you use some real trickery. Look at that video of Rudy, just tearing through like 4 dudes at a time! Yeah. No. In the actual game its a lot more like "RUDY! WHAT THE HELL ARE YOU DOING!? Grab that guy GRAB HIM!!! FOR THE LOVE OF PETE JUST LET ME HIT SOMETHING!!!!" but that doesnt happen. In most cases youll just swing, get blocked, get hit in a counter, attempt to grab, miss, and be hit again, then rage and spam yer special, the computer will walk backwards, youll miss and be hit after.....rinse and repeat. Mention this on the forums and be met with the resounding cry of "Git gud noob" or "Uze FAzter Chakter! Herdee herp a derp" Basically.....there are people that will literally come in here to my review and tell me Im no good because I think frustration is not fun and I dont like the A.I. being overly defensive to the point that you almost rage quit after fighting a wave of dudes that just beat you half to death.
Lets move on. My fingers are starting to hurt. Platforming. What the hell is jumping on platforms, overly small and sensitive platforms sometimes, doing in a beat-em-up? Its confounding frustrating trying to jump on the logs in one part its frustratingto fall in a river when you get too close by accident. Moving on. Jumping in this game sucks.
Missions are not explained well. You go to the mission giver and the explanation of what to do are vague at best. "Go here and good luck!" Then you go to a place and its like a mystery of what the heck to do. Hell, the first time you see Tex you think yer in for a fight but in fact thats the first running mission you have. Getting him to appear? You beat the baddies in that area....how do you know to do that? You dont. Frustration prompted me to just beat the crap out of the gang members in the area where hes supposed to be at.
Lets finish this journey. Put the nail in the coffin, so to speak. The achievements are borked. A lot of achievements just do not work. Theyre vague and buggy.

On the surface, it's a prettier RCR, but once you unlock everything you can create characters with custom looks and customized movesets that add so much replayability.  If you haven't played that game, dooo it!
Anyway, on to RCR:U, as I said, I came into this hyped and ready to punch things.  But my enthusiasm was quickly bled dry.  Having multiple characters to choose from is great but they all feel crippled out of the gate.  All of them need to be upgraded multiple times at the dojo and it's not cheap.  And that's on top of the money you'll need to spend improve your stats and heal.  But it's worse because now you have to grind with half your move set locked, meaning you can't fight effectively, meaning more frustration and more time grinding.  Now, add in the pedestrians who blindly walk right into your attacks while you're getting mobbed by the AI, which brings out the cops, which means you have to run and hide, further extending the amount of time you're doing non-fun things instead of making progress.
The original was grindy but it was basically a beat-em-up RPG and grinding was just what you did in JRPGs at the time, we accepted it as a small side-effect of creating a breakthrough genre-bending game.  But today almost every game genre encorporates RPG elements, that's no longer an acceptable reason for grindy gameplay.  The other thing is, what made RCR tolerable was that the base game play was enjoyable.  But here the grinding is boring and frustrating.  The AI is obnoxious, they're fast, they swarm you, and they constantly hit you with cheap shots.  You're hamstringed by incomplete move sets, idiotic pedestrians, and psychotic cops.  You never get a second's respite, even in town / malls, the enemies are still there, they're constantly buzzing around you like angry bees.  It feels like you're constantly being pestered, it's annoying.
Anyway, save your money.  If you're looking to relive a retro beat-em-up experience in a brand new way, go get Mother Russia Bleeds, a game that is the spiritual successor to Streets of Rage in every way possible.  You could almost call it Streets of Rage "4" on drugs.  :)

Honestly, this is one of those games that you want to be good, but it's actually pretty bad and broken.  I keep seeing people talk about how this game is a tribute to the old RCR game and to "old school difficulty".  This game isn't really much of a RCR/Kunio game, and that NES style difficulty? It's not tough, it's just straight up broken.
Who wants to play a game where the enemies become psychic blocking machines halfway through? Who wants to chase a boss down instead of fight them? Who wants to play a Kunio game where the only way to progress is to became a frame counting combo master when what we really want to do is chuck garbage cans at dudes heads and rip around town WITHOUT HAVING TO HOLD DOWN THE D-PAD!
I think the devs started with a good idea, they just got too ambitious, added way too much extra junk, and lost sight of what makes a goofy beat em up game fun.

Long story short, the devs got an official license from Arc Systems (that's actually super risky and rare btw) to make their own RCR game which is called River City Ransom Ungerground. Game got kickstarted, developed and released on Steam! Everyone was hyped for it including myself. So how good is this game to the RCR series? Let's find out.
Now this is coming from a player who has experience and played 3 RCR games. I first played a Japanese version of it on the Gameboy (where Kunio/Alex went to Japan), River City Ransom EX on Gameboy Advance and a spin-off, River City Super Sports All-Stars. My experience and opinion may be different from yours which I respect. I may be a fan of the game but I still will give criticisms because that's what fans do. Also, there might be minor spoilers so be aware. Anyway, let's start.
River City Ransom Underground is a beat em up game with some RPG elements that pays homage to the old NES game, River City Ransom. The first game was an amazing hidden gem during it's time and still is today. RCRU is the sequel to the game that took place couple of years after the first game where the two main characters, Alex/Kunio and Ryan/Riki join up with a brand new variety of characters to beat up bad guys and explore the story. You will unlock new characters to play in Story mode and a whole lot more for Arena mode. (I do hope we can play all of them in Story mode, probably in future patching). This game also has online and offline co-op and competitive. Let's go section by section shall we?
From first impressions to now, I love how amazing the pixel/sprite work is done here like it feels like a big upgrade or leap while keeping the RCR style consistent. Animations are smooth and satisfying to look at as well as how colourful the backgrounds and levels are. It's basically nostalgia done right and improved in this section. I don't have anything to criticize here since this is one of the game's biggest strength. Though, I guess some people might find the style weird for those that never seen a RCR game before. Still, whoever did these, you have my kudos and props man.
If you love the old school 8-bit/16-bit/32-bit SFXs and music then you'll find RCRU's one to be pleasant and nice to hear. Since I grew up with Gameboy games and all, it felt nostalgic and cool for me. The OST/music is fine and fitting too. Not really memorable but it fits well and earns a pass. HOWEVER, I was disappointed there was no remix or even any iconic music from the old RCR game like the Boss Fight and the Downtown theme. Those are like the most memorable themes of the game and it kinda saddens me. I do hope they add a mod/feature where we can add our own custom musics or they add their own version into it if they can. Probably due to licensing but still, it's a nostalgia miss.
Oh boy here comes the main part on why people love/hate this game and I can see why from both sides. Before I go any further, let me remind you that this game has grinding like it's prequel. You're gonna need time and patience for a game like this though thankfully community guides make it easier for you by miles. Let's start with the positives.
+ Lots of playable characters to play and unlock, each with their own unique movesets, theme/fashion and styles. Though you can only play 10 in Story Mode while the rest like playable grunts and bosses are in Arena Mode, they are still fun to mess around with. Hope the devs allow us to play them in Story Mode+ or so.
+ Smart enemy AI. I'm pretty surprised how smart the enemies are since they can easily dodge my attacks be it melee or projectile. They are smart enough to jump, block, counter-attack so you can't just go gung ho unless you have the right moment which is always rewarding when you finish them off with a stacking combo. Players criticized that they are too hard to beat but that's how beat em ups are in general. There are some bosses that gave me trouble but once you understand their moves and your situation, you can easily make a comeback and succeed in the end. (
) I do wish there could have been an 'Easy' mode for newcomers or casual players. Other than that, they're cool to fight with.
+ Lots of combos. styles and moves. Always satisfying to grind for them and use them. Heck, some of them are actually references to other games (Glen is freaking Ryu from Street Fighter, Provie has badass break dancing and Ryan can go MUDADADADADA) though the devs should fix a few issues with the button inputs/instructions on a few moves.
+ Variety of shops and places. There's plentiful of them which I bet are some of the backers from Kickstarters. There's even characters from other games or so like Shovel Knight & Newgrounds making cameo appearances and so. Also, you can buy cats.
+/= Civilians made the game feel more lively for me since the first one had barely anyone in it. Personally I actually like it myself. You can also hurt them to get some extra cash but that leads to one of it's downsides: the cops. Players complained that they only serve to hinder the enjoyment because accidentally hitting them just makes it harder and I do agree since I have a few experience myself. Luckily the devs nerfed it to make it easier but that's still the downside part.
Lukewarm/neutral + negative parts:
= Police/cop system. Think of GTA's cop system. Honestly I kinda like beating up cops since it provides enemy variety and a challenge (they got electric tasers and a SWAT shield and fight with bare hands. I love it) but the problem is to some players, it's more annoying than rewarding. Yes you can have bragging rights and personally I don't want them to remove the cops but they should at least drop like big money should you beat them. If you're seeing this devs, make the cops more rewarding to beat up and make them less likely to 'get attracted' from the accidental stufs players do like vandalism or such. I'm fine with it but others may not.
= Bugs. This is from day 1 to now. On the first day, there were bugs on multiplayer, story, moves, etc which was one reason I had to stop after 4 hours. But after patching, balancing and fixing, I was able to enjoy the game again and in the end, I forgive the devs for being passionate in polishing and listening to community feedback. I would have turned this review to a negative had it not been for the patches.
= 2 or 3 missions involving chasing + that freaking milk mission. Good news is that the devs made it a lot easier this time but it was frustrating to do the latter one. Reason I find the chasing missions not the best is because
.

I praise them for caring for the game because we rarely get a RCR game nowadays and these guys are also huge fans of RCR with the creator of Double Dragons helping them in a way. So what's my verdict?
8/10 after patching, lower like 7 or 6 if it wasn't patched. I highly recommend it for RCR fans and anyone interested. If you are not sure, wait for sale. Thank you for reading this.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong has a good story but the whole thing felt a little long; kinda like when you notice you are checking the time watching a movie kinda long.  Returns was great if short. Dragonfall was great; building on what Returns started by adding missions for the squad and cleaning up game mechanics and UI.  After playing it, I would buy it on sale or not.

As a fan of the old SNES Shadowrun, I happily bought all of these 3 new Shadowrun cRPGs.
All of them good, some with more problems than others.
Shadowrun Returns was quite easy and too straightforward; it didnt feel much of a RPG. The base system was solid though, and it captures the lore of Shadowrun very well, so even with limited playability it was a solid game.
Dragonfall mastered the problems of the first game and made it a truly great game. Great story, characters, more challenge. The way it is constructed reminds me a lot of Mass Effect 2-3 games though, heh. Suppose it is because you get to choose which mission to do next, and between the mission you go to your base and talk to your crew, which will make you know about them better and build up your relations. And get their character missions etc.
So the latest/last part to the new Shadowrun games, Hong Kong. After the great Dragonfall, they had to try hard to surpass themselves. In fact, the biggest problem of this game is, that they probably tried too hard. Way too hard in some aspects.
The progression and spacing of the game is just completely broken, compared to most RPG games. You will do a fun but short mission in 20-40 mins, after which you will go to your base city and talk with your crew and other NPCs to learn about their past and opinions... for hours. After every single mission.  They have given a detailed backstory to every NPC in the game, and they sure didnt cut anything out of it, but it all is told to you in very bloaten, repetitive and overly detailed way. The ammount of past stories the characters have is just too much. Its hard to get focus on what part of those backstories they blabber about are meaningful, so at some point you will stop caring at all. But since talking to your crew is also a way to unlock their quests, and sometimes actually interesting as well, you still have to force yourself to read through the thousands of lines of their past history with their past friends. Its shame they didnt just edit the text more and focus on writing what is important instead of just writing every single thing they can come up with, as the characters themselves are super interesting. The Russian rigger is one of the most interesting characters I`ve ever seen in RPGs.
Even though I dont mind some reading, I still see games more of an visual media like films are. When you have a story you want to tell; show it, dont tell it. If Hong Kong was a movie, it would be a 5 hours long movie where characters talk about their past yet you are never shown it but just the faces of the characters talking. If the game actually took you to their past and let you play through them, well that would have been incredible. Obviously it wouldnt have been possible to their budget and time, since the game would need 10x more locations in it then...
Another problem is, that while the missions are super fun and varied in settings, combat wise the game is way too easy even on Hard. Most of the missions only have 1-2, or even 0 combat situations in them. I think I only had to use 1 medkit in the whole game. In later stages where you get 3 AP instead of beginning 2, your team will be next to invincible and its rare that you get hit even once if you utilize tactics even a bit. The game just lacks balls to throw enough strong opponents at you, it just throws the handfull of 3-5 all from 1 direction, which are then easily taken care of, even if you gimp your main character with poor choices. Only hard parts are in the computer world of Matrix, which are hair-pullingly irritating when you dont play as a decker yourself but need to use the NPC decker. Had to do some annoying save&load in some of those. They are not fun either, as controlling 1 character in simple turn-based tactical combat really doesnt give you many tactical possibilities.
Because of how easy the battles are, you really are not encouraged to play the game again with different classes, even though in theory you could play the game in 20+ very different type of characters. The ammount of dialogue between the missions furthermore gimps your interest in giving it a second playthrough. Which is shame. The game has excellent world, full of interesting people, nice grapchis and sound and atmosphere. With edited dialogue and harder combat, this could be a worthy successor to Dragonfall and a cRPG which I could recommend to everyone, but now with the problems I only recommend it to the fans of Dragonfall who dont mind reading a loooot.
For the ones who have not played any of the these Shadowruns yet, I recommend getting Dragonfall first.

Finished it some time ago. Overall the game was fun, although far worse than amazing Dragonfall.
-Racter and Gaichu are great. Those two are among the most well written and interesting companions in the genre in recent memory. Both are quite morally ambiguous, shady and somehow maniacal. Talking with them is fun as well as reading their barks during missions.
-Goblet was alright. HBS tried with her dialogues to mirror a way players were taught by Dak'kon in P:T and it was successful enough to be entertaining. I don't care about Duncan and I think Is0bel was bad. She might have been a good character but HBS went for too much drama in her lines and she became tiresome.
-Many of new portraits are amazing, they are the best of all kickstarter cRPGs. They can even compete and win with Baldurs Gate 1 portraits.
-Writing was pretty good. Kindly Cheng scenes often felt quite menacing. Sometimes the writing feels it was suffering from graphomania, and the game is badly paced.
-Story starts really strong, even better than Dragonfall. And then it stops. Game forgets PC is hunted by the police and let him go to the parties and do his businesses. Until endgame the story is nearly completely abandoned. There are less endings than in Dragonfall and there is a lack of wonder if choices made were correct.
-The lack of the Lodge and Schsssomething miniquests makes runs far worse. Loved that those quest were often in conflict with each other and made runs far more varied and richer in C&C.
-New augmentations system was fun. The choices are now quite big, we have new slots and I liked weapons like a whip of being overpowered.
-Dragonfall had a really good encounter design. APEX mission was it highlight. Hong Kong only good encounters are the ambush in the first mission, the boss fight and a battle in the tomb raiding mission. From which only the last 2 are not questionable.
-Runs were often very good conceptually but weakly designed. Great example of that was Feng Shui run where the player is tasked with sabotaging the company Feng Shui flow. It's done by clicking on things...
-Combat difficulty was lowered. Very High setting was cut from the game.
-Most encounters are skipable. Sounds great? Never have I thought it is possible to use this feature to make the game worse. Actually I think it is the first time ever something like this has happened in the cRPG genre. How it failed? It is because skipping combat is easy, does not require much player input. It actually felt I was naturally drifting towards peaceful resolutions which takes fun out of outsmarting foes. I honestly and non cynically think HBS has added something to the pool of knowledge of cRPGs design by this mistake.
-Music was ok, but not as great as Dragonfall. Visuals were an improvement from previous installments.
-New matrix was a total letdown. Instead of improving it, HBS made it worse. Was actually cursing when playing it, cannot imagine how somebody thought the design was good and was not slapped for it by his colleagues. Gone are the simultaneous meatspace/matrix battles, instead we have minigames.

A clear effort can be seen in this game by its developer. The game is inspired a lot by the Beginner's Guide. The player can even hear, at one point in the game the song "Va" from the Beginner's Guide. Anyways, what this game tries to convey feels, in a way, overly "edgy", or even pretentious at some points.
For what I expected to be a walking simulator, the environments lacked detail. Some places were too dark, some way too bright. I found myself turning off the lights on some scenes only to navigate the level. The player's movements are not responsive at all and unreliable, especially during the levels requiring some sort of platforming. The cursor's movements have also been smoothed a lot. Personally, this choice affected my experience when exploring the levels.
As far as music goes, much of it feels a bit abstract and just plain strange. There is a piece or two that enhances the atmosphere and sounds nice. However, most of the soundtrack is not listenable. Sometimes the music's volume increases to the point where the player cannot hear the dev speaking.
The gameplay feels unoriginal. A scene in particular concerning a small room is heavily inspired from the Beginner's Guide. Some levels are excruciating to complete as well. The highway scene, for example, jolts the player back every couple of seconds and becomes very jarring over time. There is nothing that the player can do in that level. Another example is the ladder level, or even the level where the player has to hold his breath. Once the left mouse button is let go and pressed again, the audio is started from the beginning.
The Beginner's Guide does similar things, but things in that game transitioned smoothly. Levels were entertaining, and environments were more compact. The player knew where to go and the dev talked along the way.
Overall, this game feels pretty amateurey. Everything was serviceable, if not painful. Although it can be unfair to compare, the Beginner's Guide is a far superior game, but not only that, it is wholly original. This game tries to mimic the Guide with little success. The overall message is not thought provoking and does not leave an impression on the player. It did make an hour go by though, albeit a bit painfully.

Here are a few items of interest within
:
Gameplay - Aside from other roguelikes, this title’s complexity is derived from its tactical display rather than gameplay, as
utilizes a turn-based approach to combat and item usage. Each in-game action made by the hero utilizes said turns, which advances the daunting foe. The term ‘turn-based strategy’ does not entirely cover this game’s spectrum, however, as
action, whether it be equipping a new weapon or item, or consuming a potion to gain back energy, summons evil one turn closer to the player’s character. Adding to the ominous theme, the darkness swallows the lands you have passed through, and the notification of non-player character deaths can be heard as they disappear into mist. Controls are rather simple on both keyboard and controller, but can be adjusted in the case that they feel awkward. Equipment can be modified within the menus to alter the method of play by adding boons to weapons and armor, but, as stated, this increases danger; these items are gained either as loot from defeated enemies or may be distributed throughout the map. With a high enough Charisma score, the player may also gain discounts from various shops and recruit non-player individuals to the party that will assist in combatting foes and leveling up.
Character Creation & Upgrades - Characters comprise of several customizable components, such as name, class, avatar, and perk and statistical preferences chosen by the player; perks may also grant players companions or other game modifications such as quicker swimming or improved unarmed damage. These adjustments allow the player to modify how they would like to play according to the class. Additional equipment may alter damage totals to enemies or reduce them toward the player’s character. Levelling up in
operates in a similar way to other titles, as it improves the character’s base statistics depending on which class was chosen.
Unlockables - Depending on how far the player’s character progresses in the campaign, a number of Hero Points are rewarded to the player to purchase game augments. These modifications increase the amount of content usable by the player, such as said hero classes, perks-with selections for both combat and other skills-, and expanding what’s known as the Dimensional Vault: an item-storage system in which adventurers may donate a number of items from preceding generations to the next living hero. This expands play so that the entire game is not just an uphill battle with no reward when so close to the resolve, but rather contains encouragement toward progression.
TL:DR -
is a fun, simple, and rewarding title with incentive to advance toward the Demon Lord time and time again. There is a great amount of challenge involved in this title, but does not evoke frustration due to its Hero Point system. Though the accolade of defeating the ultimate evil may not be reached every time, the journey is a fantastic ride filled with choice, vicious battle, and sacrifice. I highly recommend this title to anyone who enjoys roguelikes and simple roleplaying mechanics. This game has a great deal of replayability, and I hope you enjoy upon purchase. Thanks for reading.

Even though I really love Abe's Oddysee and Exoddus, Munch's Oddysee is still a worthy successor considering the 3D approach. Besides the somewhat awkward controls, which are generally easy to get into, the story is what makes the game incredibly strong, which shouldn't surprise you. Every level and piece of detail that's presented still makes you feel you're wondering the native and industrial grounds of Oddworld. While saving Mudokons and Fuzzles, you'll be going head to head with more innovative enemies that attack in various styles, forcing you to adapt and strategize depending on the current situation. The game also has a status record called Quarma, which moves positively or negatively depending on your actions. In order to obtain good Quarma, you have to save Mudokon Scrubs, Fuzzles and egg crates. However if you kill the Mudokons and neglect the Fuzzles, you'll receive bad Quarma. So overall, the game ending will depend on the score of your Quarma.
So if you're an Oddworld fan or have just started out playing these games, definitely check this one out after playing the first two.

World of Warships has come to steam! Ignore the reviewers angry about not being able to link their existing account - it won't impact you as a new player. The short playtime is deceptive - I've played a little over 10,000 battles over the course of the past two years. As a veteran player, I would recommend this game, but not without a few provisos.
Overall, it's a fun game. One of the better naval battle games out there, at least on the arcade end of the arcade-sim axis. Driving around feels pretty good - the time it takes to maneuver has a feeling of inertia without being actually as slow as it takes enormous warships to turn or accelerate. Each ship has its own handling characteristics, from nimble destroyers to slow battleships.
The advancement system works pretty well - ships are fitted into a tier, 1 through 10. By playing games in a ship, you earn experience on that ship that goes towards unlocking the next tier of its nation and class. You also earn credits, used to purchase upgrades and boats. At lower tiers, advancement is very fast; you can reach a tier 5 boat in a couple evenings. Higher up, it slows down so unlocking a new ship is a real achievement.
Playing a battle earns silver, but it also costs some - a pittance at low tiers, but repair costs scale up. The flat repair cost for tier 9 and 10 games is enough to leave you in the red unless your performance based earnings are very high. One of the primary forms of monetization is a premium account - a monthly subscription that increases your experience & gross credit earnings per game by 50%. This makes playing at higher tier possible without grinding out games on cheaper servicing mid-tier boats. Premium account will let you advance to new ships faster, but won't give you any advantage in battle. A "pay to grind less" model that's generally pretty fair. The premium account is also shared with Wargaming's other "World of" titles, where it works the same way.
The other form of monetization is selling 'Premium' ships. These ships aren't available through play, only by breaking out your wallet, but for the most part they're not pay to win. Most premium ships provide a unique experience or gimmick that makes them situationally strong, but have other drawbacks that keep them at about the same level as the free techtree ships at the same tier. A few are a little on the overpowered side, as the developer avoids nerfing premium ships to avoid backlash, but it stays out of pay to win territory for the most part. All premium ships also earn extra credits, a way in which they add to the 'pay to skip grind' model.
The main game mode is 'Random Battles,' 12v12 PvP games including ships of three tiers - 8 through 10, for example, or 5 through 7. Unlike World of Tanks, bottom tier ships can contribute. While the top tier ships certainly have advantages in range and firepower, lower tier ships can still win confrontations. Battles have a 20 minute time limit; at high tier where the meta is fairly passive they often take close to that long. Lower tier battles are much faster. You can join random battles with up to 2 teammates in a 'division' to play together with friends. Larger groups are disallowed, as they'd unbalance matches. Other battle modes include both individual and 7 player team competitive modes, Co-op battles that mirror random battles with one side composed of only AI, and special co-op scenarios that provide interesting challenges for a group of up to 7.
Balance passes are about what you'd expect in such a game. The developer is active in trying to fix issues, but not perfect at it by any means. There's a bit of an issue with power creep - due to their refusal to nerf premiums, ones that were mistakenly too strong can only be balanced by strengthening the other ships at tier. New lines have their own gimmicks, which often end up making the older ships weaker in general.
Aircraft carrier balance in particular is a mess. Wargaming promised a complete overhaul this year, but it's november already and there's no sign of one - though there is a balance pass in the works to (hopefully) improve the USN carrier line that's been underpowered for a very long time. Unfortunately some of the recent changes have been very much for the worse - like armour-piercing bombs which can delete ships with little to no counterplay. Meanwhile, the interface can still be quite unresponsive, and carrier battles can be very frustrating.
Another problem is that the game doesn't have the best new player experience - a real failing in a free to play title. While it's easy and fun to tool about in low tier co-op battles, there is very little in the way of tutorial materials, and jumping into random battles can be intimidating. Find a friend who already plays to show you the ropes, or ask questions at the very active subreddit at /r/worldofwarships.
Still, I'd recommend World of Warships overall. It's a fun game to play with friends or on your own, and it's devoured more of my time than I'd like to admit, and it's totally playable without paying a cent.

Before I start the review, I'd like to clarify that I do NOT have 12+ hours of active playtime in the game, I spent around 9 hours inactive and at the time of writing this review, I apparently do have 12.4 hours on record according to Steam.
Anyway, let's get into it:
A Story About My Uncle is a game about a father telling a bedtime story to his daughter, the story is about the father's youth when he set off to a different world to find his uncle that's been gone for a while. I don't want to get into the story in too many details in order to avoid spoiling any experience  for you, whom are reading the review and considering buying the game. I just want to say, the story is not any extra rich and there's not too much of storytelling in general, but I still found it sufficent.
Gameplay:
So you're a nephew that took their uncle's adventure suit and teleported in a different world. There, you are stuck in an environment highly above the ground, having to jump over flying parts of land (call if flying islands if you want) in order to progress. At start, you only have a little gear, but later on the arcade around jumping over the flying platforms gets more and more fun. All features you get throughout the game are:
Ability to jump really high (1 use)
Ability to jump into long distance (1 use)
Grapple into a place you're aiming at (up to 3 uses)
Rocket boots boosting you into any direction you look into (1 use)
>The uses of abilities reset everytime you stand on the ground
And all you have to do is pretty much not to fall down into the abyss (there are a lot of checkpoints though so don't worry too much).
While that may sound simple, I actually found it really fun. Overall I don't find the game any challenging, it's easy for the most parts. If you want a challenge, go for the Steam achievements this game has, that may actually make it harder. Also I'm sure this is a great game for speedrunners, the game is not too long even for someone clumsy at such games as me as it took me around 2.5-3 hours of actual time to get through the game.
Design:
I found the graphics pretty, it's just one of those games that shine in their visuals. The environment later in the game looked beautiful, no cons graphics wise except for the fact a lot of the textures were inaccurately placed, as i sometimes happened to clip through them. Mostly because I got into places I wasn't intended to be in, which I'll talk about later on in the review.
First half of the game felt a little sinister to be fair, the sound effects and some of the environment (note there was a monster in one part which I found totally unfitting to the game), nothing too bad, but if you're weak to creepier atmospheres, this may probably be one of the very few reasons why not to buy the game, although I think that could be fixed with just turning your sounds off. In the second half of the game, I didn't find anything that would really feel creepy, I found the atmosphere much more relaxing.
Sound effects were in their place, although as I said, there was a bunch of eerie sound effects in the first half of the game.
Bugs/glitches:
I'll just summarize them here really quick.
-Sometimes, you can find a place you are not intended to stand on, this could make your gameplay severely easier either because of being able to recharge your abilities or clipping through the map and skipping large part
-Some stones or places were literally just textures, meaning that when you though you could land on an offside part of the game and be safe, you actually fell down and respawned back on the checkpoint
-Sometimes a little weird interaction with the characters in the game
-Not being able to grapple something you should clearly be able to grapple on can ruin your mood easily in this game
Performance/controls:
-You have a lot of graphics settings, you can really set the game to ultra low or ultra high settings.
-I cannot say it'd really be optimized, I played the game on a low-tier laptop and had to set my settings to as low as 640x400 in order to run the game on decent framerate, I can run games like Overwatch or GTA V on the same graphics but far smoother.
-Controls were fine, I have nothing to complain about
Personal opinion on the game:
If you like games of this genre, I'd say it's worth it, maybe not really for its full price but it's discounted quite often I believe (I grabbed the game on 80% discount). I did like the graphics and enjoyed the playthrough most of the time, only felt a little annoyed by the bugs/glitches in this game. I found the story ok, not anything that would grab you into the game and want you to keep playing but it did go just fine.
Summarized pros/cons:
Pros:
- Fun gameplay
- Good looking textures even for low settings
- A decent story
- Often highly discounted game on Steam store
- Easy game pretty much for anyone
- Good for speedrunning
- Challenging-to-get achievements
- Easy, good controls
Cons:
- Glitches/bugs, nothing too critical but still could ruin a run for you here and there
- Around 2-3 hours of gameplay if you're not playing for the achievements
- Quite bad performance
- High base price on Steam store, for the game length
- A little horror-ish environment for the first half of the game, didn't find that fitting the gameplay at all.
If you're seeing this game on discount and you like the game based off how it looks, then go for it, if you read my review you can probably get an idea of what you can expect in the game.
Thanks for reading the review. Have a great day.

Because all you will be doing is driving from your house to your friends house, you and your friend will go do the mission, you then have to drive your friend back to his house, and then you drive back to your place. A good Sim-Tycoon type game with some unique mechanics, unfortunately the additions are a mixed bag.
The spatials puts you in charge of developing a new human space station to expand and explore the neighboring systems. To do this, you need to put together a team to send on away missions to local planets; Success allows you to buy access to local resources, unlock tech, and progress to new systems. There's nothing wrong with the game, it just feels like most of the game mechanics are just slightly off. They either don't quite go far enough, or seem to be more complicated then necessary.
An example of this is the resource collection. Once you complete an away mission you can buy resource nodes on that planet, which deliver raw crafting mats to the station for you to use. The system is complicated by the fact that you need to devote officers to the system in order to speed up harvesting, and that you can repeat a planet at harder difficulties to get more resources. While playing I never felt that this added anything to the game, it just prolonged the grind required to get some resource chains up and running.
Another example is the crafting system. You put down rooms and stations for your officers to create new consumables for your visitors to buy. You need to queue up the number of each item you want to create at the crafting section, but volumes fluctuate so rapidly it's rarely useful to set anything but 'build infinite' at each station. It feels like they were setting up a system that allowed you to 'keep x items in inventory', but it was never finished or too complicated to work properly. As a result you either need to over recruit to keep all crafting going or micromanage, which is almost impossible because the station operates while on away missions.
There may be systems in place that handle my grievances but the tutorials are terrible. They're not much more then a text overlay and they only cover the most basic systems in the game. You will have to figure a lot out for yourself.
If you're willing to put up with some rough sections, the Spatials is a pretty decent game. The mechanics are solid, and there's enough progression to keep you going for quite awhile. I recommend it, just have an idea what you're getting into before buying.

Really fun and relaxing to play. Despite the cutesy graphics, there are a lot of systems to sink your teeth into. Explore planets with a little expedition crew and try to upgrade your colony at the same time. Fun stuff!

The Spatials is an unusual game. imagine a mix between Theme Hospital and Cannon Fodder and you are halfway there. Fun to play but could do with a little more variety. There is also some inbalance in the economy but overall a game worth checking out.

The first playthrough is very entertaining and will glue you to the screen if you like this sort of game. Both aspects of the game (building and questing) are entertaining and well thought out. Though the missions are really just five guys running after your cursor and shooting things, they still managed to make it not boring somehow. Every character has a role and if someone gets killed your entire team will feel crippled and be much less effective for the rest of the mission.
Everything seems reasonably complete which is a lot more than you can say about a bunch of other indie titles, and the dev page still has a list of interesting features they want to add. The game has stellar ambiance. Some of the best music and ambiant track I came across. I sometimes found myself just staring at the screen, watching the little guys run around my station and listening to the sounds of space.
After a while the game becomes a bit too easy as you secure enough of the basic raw materials and are making profits like crazy. The main hurdle I think isn't really the profit, but making the visitors leave satisfied with your station. As I was playing through I was constantly looking at the happiness meters for the different species trying to figure out what to build where to make this or that alien more satisfied with my services. Really the only problem is that the shooting part gets way too difficult after a while where even your most experienced crew can berely kill the level bosses, often just by running away and sniping, whereas the management gets too easy as profits keep mounting up. I don't know if the devs are planning rebalancing, but I think the later stages of the game could use some.
All in all this is a very nice addition to your librarly if you are into management with a twist.

I'd like to set the record straight. If you're looking for Dwarf Fortress IN SPAAAACE, this is not it. I've heard a common complaint is that there's really no threat in this game. Indeed, your biggest threat is officers threatening to quit if you don't fulfill their needs. Other than that, no one tries to invade your station, and, really, even off-station combat is fairly inconsequential even if the whole squad is wiped out.
What this is is more akin to Sim Theme Park. Your goal isn't survival. It's the year 5781, survival is easy. Your goal is to build a thriving, booming business based on attracting visitors and tourists and selling them stuff. The challenge is in making your little corner of space as massive, flashy, and successful as it can be, instead of a rinky-dink little asteroid focused on efficiency.
It is a fun game, and mostly well-done, barring some poor sound design and strange interface graphical choices, but you have to go in with the right expectations. Go into this expecting danger and tense thrills and you'll be disappointed. Expect a game about effectively making a cruise ship based off an asteroid, and you're in the right place!
