Pros: What I did enjoy were the deep dialog trees that you have to take the time to read and figure out how to lead the conversation. To get all of the special endings, the game really does expect you to take your time and talk to pretty much everyone in Heoi between runs. Remember to sleep!
Cons: I'm not in love with the real-time stealth mechanics in The Matrix. I was initially opposed to the hacking minigame, but once you understand it, it works pretty well.
Bugs: I did encounter several bugs (more annoying than game-killing) involving disappearing items and some choices on complicated missions. Hopefully they will take the time to work these out.

This is one of the best renditions of the shadowrun universe to date. It also continues in the top down gameplay style of the other 2 previous games, but does not have a continuous story, although some honorable mentions of reoccuring characters or subplots is necessary. Algernon, for example, can be found in this game.

This is the third of the Shadowrun games I've played so far - and the one I've most enjoyed. The music is creative I found. I liked the ambience. The notes and themes were definetly different than the others. You get to see some specific cultural themes from this one, which really brings out the setting of the game. All in all - it seems to bring itself more into its own as a setting.  While Dragonfall and Returns were nice, you had to really know more about the social structures of the area to discern that you were in two different countries. You're a merc. You do stuff. You get money. You beat the bad guys. Corps are out to get you. Copy Pasta with some nice differences. In Hong Kong, the area is different. The background, the character images available,  the dialogue options and buildings reflect the setting, even some of the Matrix reflects their change in location. Spirits too are caught up in this - and reflect the area; which I thought was a particularly nice touch.
The cyberware system is a bit more friendly. You can finally go whole hog and upgrade your character to be Robocop. The bonus mechanics of basically purchasing more essence with exp is an option. This means that even mages/shamans/adepts with the inclination to do so, can get themselves some of the tuneups without feeling the pinch. In practice, I had an Elf Shaman who had  Kevlar Bone Lacing and Dermal Plating - with the final costs bringing my essence back down to 6. But that being said, I lost some of the versatility I could've otherwise used (like having access to mage spells instead of just shaman spells). Still - a nice customized choice. There are cyberware weapons - which any fan of the dice game can tell you there are a lot of those in the books. Its really nice to see them displayed. You get access to things like throwing grenades back (imagine that in Dragonfall), using powerful stun weapons, built in swords, and even a whip (which works for ranged characters - giving them a reason to go into it).
The NPC's are... very well fleshed out. Every so often you find the 'I'm a jerk because I'm a jerk' stereotype in a game. Some use it more often than not. This game however, is a bit more lenient on the action. Characters have reasons for their motivations. They have backstories and drives. Some dialogue options will recurr in future follow ups - and if you paid attention to the wording, you can change how events go. As with text based games - and a lot of RPG's, it can be a trial to wade through all the dialogue. Not gonna lie, I fast clicked some of these options when my interest was gone. Your character - in a lot of such situations - can also be fatigued by the conversation; and be rude, trying to end and get out of the talk as fast as possible.
Combat is a bit nicer. Weapons still carry over the same as they did before. Your NPC companions have their own unique tasks that make you weigh whether or not you want them in the party based on what you were going up against. Some characters can outright knock out some enemies, while others make excellent tanks. Certain wombo combos are possible - fencing an enemy in with a barrier, then throwing an acid fog or a land mine at their feet; setting up the combat in your favor. You no longer have to necessarily rely on 'I need to hit'. Could just be 'you have to be in this general area'. Spells get ... amazingly modified by ley lines now. Where as before it was like 'this could be cool' - sometimes it more along the lines of "... I really do not want to step on this". A single spell meant to hit an enemy suddenly bounces three times, hitting your party member in the process! That being said, it brings a nice mechanic to the casting system.  The only gripe is that I had gotten used to having a medic on the team in Dragonfall; so always make sure you have multiple of the Doc Wagon kits!
Since the last one I played before this was Dragonfall, I will use that by comparison. In Dragonfall, you had a set goal. You could see completion.  You had to manage your finances and/or your missions to be able to get what you needed. In Hong Kong, you can conceivably finish the main storyline with some of your runs holding out. There are quite a few.  The cash flow isn't as strong though - so if you plan on playing Street Samurai, be judicial. If you're thorough, you should be able to raise enough funds to accomplish most of your dreams. By contrast - on my second playthrough, I had so much left over I bought every flashbang I could carry and loaded up on meds and chems for the final mission - with about 2k in the bank.
And finally... the Matrix. I've seen some people complaining about the Matrix use in this game. I actually enjoyed it quite a bit. It was... more true to the setting in my mind. True it became a pain relying on NPC's kits to solve the issue, but hey - if you wanted your approach, you could play a decker! That being said, their are some memorization puzzles along with matching, stealth involved, and management of resources. Going into the Matrix becomes getting more nuyen, more gear, more consumables, and - more plot objectives. If the stealth is a problem, the option of going loud - like it was in most of Dragonfall, is always there. If you are unable to complete enough tasks or handle enough situations against the grain, you will go into the familiar Matrix Combat. So - its  a choice there.
----
TLDR:
Cons: Lots of talk. Can have problems with cash if you're not careful. Can miss important clues if not careful, which are not always logged in your mission journal.  Matrix mechanics can be challenging. Gear no longer gives stats (something to be aware of).
Pros: Fresh setting. Revamped cyberware mechanics. Renewed magic system. Can go through almost every mission with like three fights if careful (not counting matrix engagements).
Would buy again. Would gift to a friend.

Well, a lot has definitely been said about this game. Having played all SRs, I'd like to add a few brief words about it... It's a good game if you're a fan of the series, but this is really a buggy affair, no way around this. Expect a lot of replaying, specially the last few missions, so SAVE often because you will do some backtracking.
The interface is glitchy and buggy, animations are stuttery and click capture laughable at best, here a better job could've definitely been done.
OTOH, the game looks gorgeously hand drawn throughout, and it's still Shadowrun as far as creating a new build and playing through its countless missions.
I did enjoy the fact that the game has become longer, so there's a lot of time for fighting and developing your character throughout, as well as enjoying the process of learning how to fit in the team and make the best out of every possible roster member you decide to bring along. The strategic aspects of the game are impeccable as always and just a blast.
Lastly, the matrix engine was "ok-ish" for the first play-through, but just taxing and not fun second time around. I guess I won't be doing any more experimenting on this one because I don't want to have to go through all the hacking sections, they've become long and boring fillers between otherwise good missions.
SR:DF blows this one out of the water, so if you haven't played that one, do yourself a favor and go for it. If you have and crave a bit of SR fun, go for this one knowing that there still are too many bugs all over this one, but that the storyline and strategic bits are great.
So, recommended with a pinch of salt...
Played the previous Shadowruns, this one tops them.  Love the gameplay and story.

I would only recommend this game if...
- You are a die-hard fan of the SRR series
- You can put up with game-breaking bugs
- You like playing any class except a decker
While I have played the previous two installations and enjoyed them, somewhat, this one struck a few nerves.  There are bugs that will require reloading of save games (make multiple save games, by the way) and cause outright frustration.  Plus, the story seemed lackluster in comparison to the previous iteration.
First off, the reloading bugs.  There are 2 that come to mind immediately.  In the beginning when you have to talk to your new contact, make sure you go to your shelter afterwards.  Do not save and quit, even though it is about 4 hours in and you need a break.  Doing so will cause the shelter to be inaccessible and the new contact to not do anything.  Thus, you will have to reload.  If you are like me, and only made one save, then prepare to play those 4 hours again.  The second majorly annoying bug is towards the end of the campaign.  Gather the four items before interfacing with the computer.  If you interface with the computer first, you'll have to reload and start the battle over again.  Also, even if you do this correctly, there is still a chance it will bug out and you'll have to reload.
The second deal-breaker is that the enemy AI has not improved since the last iteration.  If the main character is in LoS, they will gang up and kill it.  If the main character dies, then it is game over.  Sure, if you like playing the tough type (street samurai / something beefy), you will be fine.  I like playing a decker and was looking forward to the improvements to decking in this version.  However, since AI will hunt out the PC and deckers are not known for their ability to take a beating, it was pretty frustrating to try.
Not really a dealbreaker, but worth a mention is that there are no graphical or combat improvements since the last iteration.  Character development is minimal.  There are very few skills which makes combat pretty repetitive.  After a few chapters, I found the 3 teammates that were most useful and never changed them around.  There was no need to.

I loved this game. They managed to give me a chance to make choices about my character's personality and backstory by way of the dialogue options. And it was made meaningful later.
The upgraded Matrix experience pleased me.

Excellent isometric CRPG reminiscient of classics like Fallout 1/2 or Arcanum. A worthy successor to the previous Shadowrun game, Dragonfall, and superior to it in many respects. Varied engrossing/fun missions, very engaging companions, lots of shooting and throwing fireballs. And yet one can still skip most of the combat by being talky.
The world is actually very bleak, despite elves and wizards and all that. Many situations are rather morally grey and there are no real happy endings. Yes, I have enjoyed it greatly.

If you are a fan of the original NES game you are going to love this. RCRU takes the original formula and improves upon every aspect. This is a really fun beat em up, that is a blast multi-player. It still retains the feel of the original but adds combo moves, multiple characters to choose from, up to 4 players multiplayer, and way much more to explore. This game is a grind, and waves of enemies don't seem to give you a chance to rest (except for in your hideout/shops) so expect to die a lot. Your characters will level, and you can buy/eat food to increase your base stats, so you are at least on a forward momentum. You buy your moves in Dojos this time around, some of which are gated by character level, and add a lot more variety to how the differnet characters play.
Writing this review as of patch 5 release. Yeah there are still some bugs and areas for improvement, but nothing that detracts from the player experience at this time IMHO (thank the gods multi-player saves are now working), and the developer roll outs have been addressing the main sticking points so far, so I feel pretty confident all the little gripes will be handled.

This game would be fun if they didn't bog it down with the police and chase 'systems'.
The former would be fine if the pedestrian AI wasn't so stupid -- but that's something you eventually get used to.
The latter is a steaming pile of cow dung that is very close to making me quit playing.  RCR's engine wasn't made for chase scenes, so a facismile of it certainly isn't either.
Other than that, the game is a nice facismile of the original.  The only flaw outside of the above mentioned issues is how poorly the game teaches you moves.  They really should have taken a page out of the GBA remake of RCR (or even the slightly inferior Tokyo Rumble on 3DS) no guess work there.

Pretty solid game all around. It's clear that much more effort went into this remake than their half-hearted Double Dragon 4. Interesting old school graphics. A very large variety of characters and moves, which keeps things fresh. Lots of content included and the save system is nice. Dying sets you back some time, but you maintain most of your progress. Funny easter egg inclusions of other indie game characters.
The game is rather grindy at times, however, and much like DD4, can be annoying when it decides that it wants to be a platformer. It definitely does not control well enough to be a good platformer. Also as in their DD4 attempt, they didn't bother to program in controller support, which is disappointing. Keyboard controls work fine, but I wanted to play two player locally and couldn't really do that without the controller.
On the whole, it's an inventive game with a unique blend of styles. Worth checking out.

It's a lot of good, clean fun that takes the old RCR and makes it better... not much else to say as far as that goes. River City Ransom Underground
With the Online Multiplayer bug seemingly Fixed, I can finally recommend this game.
This game retains much of the charm of the original, with adorable sprite-based chibi characters pummeling each other over lunch money, and then using that money to buy hotdogs, comic books, and cats to help raise your stats.
Where in the original, each character could learn every move, and you 'defined' your character by choosing a name and which moves to get for them, now there is a roster of selectable characters each with different moves, a la Street Fighter.
Each Playable character outside of the 3 selectable at the start of the game can be found somewhere in the world. After finding them, recruiting them can be as simple as defeating them in a fight, clearing all te enemies in the area, or helping them defeat the enemies harrassing them. After that, they will head back to your base of operations and become selectable as a character the next time you go to a Safe House to save your game.
The character variety is nice, with at least one character to represent each of the games numerous different gangs fighting style. This adds much more gameplay time, as each player has a whole stable of characters to switch between and learn moves for.
But there are still a few things that have not managed to be as good as they were on NES, somehow;
- Double-Tap Over to run should not require you to hold Over to continue to run.
- Players in Multiplayer will get stuck Zoning on and off the screen, either by running or being hit.
- Timing on Jump Attacking and Jump Airtime both seem abrupt either Press Windowns that are too shot.
- The Camera Stutter in Couch Co-Op is extremely jarring, almost unplayable with 3 or more players.
These are all almost certianly nitpicks by a super-fan of the franchise, however, and shouldnt stop anyone from spending the amazingly low price of this great game to get a look at the amazing gameplay and world that was River City Ransom.

SEGA promised the fans and they delivered. Classic sonic is back wearing the correct shade of blue jumping from platform to platform in his whole new 2D world, of course with Modern Sonic tagging along with his 'Sonic Unleashed' style stages.
Sonic Generations alternates between the two Sonics as they try and subdue the villain 'cleverly' named the 'Time Eater'. There are 3 eras in the game with 3 stages within each, 2 decades of 'Sonicness' for both Classic fans and Modern fans to enjoy.
As you progress through the not so great story, you will play through 1 Classic stage, 1 Dreamcast stage and 1 Modern stage all of which have 2 levels for both Modern and Classic sonic.
Watching Classic Sonic 'run' not 'blast' through each stage is wonderful and fills the air around you with sweet nostalgia and success. Not to forget Modern Sonic with his finally mastered 'Unleashed' controls, playing as Modern Sonic is just as enjoyable as it was in Colours and Unleashed but this time with an extra "uummph".
I must say SEGA have finally captured the essence of our beloved Hedgehog and have made an excellent game which makes you forget about the many mistakes they have made in the past (Sonic 06). Overall Sonic Generations is an excellent game and a 'must have', even though the game has a fairly bland and predictable plot, and not to forget that Modern Sonic is still... Well... Modern Sonic, but even with all the Complaints from other fans it seems like a meaningless excuse to just hate on our once beloved Sonic.
Sonic is finally getting his s*** together not to forget that this is an improvement from his last 2 games or 3. In 1 vs. 1 or 2 vs. 2 multiplayer battles the game runs alright, could be better, but still alright with around 40 fps (see system specs below) but when playing anything above that (3 vs. 3 or 4 vs.  4) the game tanks frame rate to about 4-12fps after about 20 minutes. I generally play with 2-4 friends vs. the AI and we all start to get these problems eventually. When playing alone this can happen too, although uncommon.
The game also suffers from an unbearable syncing issue. The frame rate drop is still playable even at 4-12fps but shortly thereafter players will start noticing input lag (Move soldier here > wait 10 seconds to 10 minutes, we timed it > solder moves) and the game clock on each client will no longer display the same time, 10 minute difference in an hour game)
All in all if the game ever gets some attention from Relic except to add more DLC then I can recommend it but otherwise I advise spending your money elsewhere.

An excellent sequel. It takes what was wrong with the first game and revamps it to make it more enjoyable.
Gameplay is simple to get a hold of, and the difficulty curve rises at a good rate. The three difficulty settings allow you to tailor your experience to how much of a challenge you're after, and the "Just Right" difficulty provided enough of a challenge for me to enjoy the game from start to finish. There is a good amount of incentive to replaying levels with unlockable characters and costumes as well as collecting Retro cartridges.
The biggest difference from the first game to this one is the addition of Checkpoints - and the best part about these is that they are optional. For someone like me, who grew rapidly frustrated with the first game, the addition of Checkpoints is a welcome change. For those who enjoy the challenge, you can simply jump over them for extra points rather than using them.
Another change is the implementation of multiple pathways, which is a neat idea but I always went for the "dangerous" route regardless - and I did not feel the need to go back and do another path unless there was an alternate exit or a hidden treasure. Both pathways lead to the end and have the same amount of gold, so unless there's a treasure there's not much point to making the choice other than, again, deciding how much of a challenge you want.
Visuals are very aesthetically pleasing and the design for the menus, cutscenes, and world map are nice and consistent. Some of the character designs were a little -too- weird for my taste but for the most part they are fun and interesting. Sound is great; Charles Martinet does some great voiceover work and the music - as to be expected - is well-suited to the gameplay and easy on the ears.
I highly recommend this game. It's a fun platformer with a neat twist that will easily fill some spare time.

Imagine if DF-9 and Cosmonautica had a baby and it was tutored by Dwarf Fortress.
You build a base for two groups:  Tourists who will visit your base and give you credits in exchange for goods and services; and officers who build the base, staff it to produce those goods and services, and go on away missions to unlock more planets/systems to get more resources to unlock more goods and services to make more tourists and officers happy.
As officers complete missions they level up and their needs change.  At first they just need to have a place to sleep, then eat, then drink, then hygiene etc.  Higher level officers give better bonuses but are harder to keep happy.  Unhappy officers leave.
Combat is very casual.  Death is not an issue.  Failing is not an issue.  This game does not appear to have a fail condition.  And I almost did not recommend because of that.
But it is fun.
I enjoy the sounds of laser fire as I smash yet another pirate raid.  The visuals are pleasant to look at.  It is rewarding to watch your officers grow as you groom them for their future jobs, be it leading the away team, governing a solar system, or forcing poor Jerry to be a fry cook for the rest of his life.  The choice is yours.

Hong Kong...The place where dreams come from!
Ok, not dreams. More like nightmares. And demons...
●▬▬▬▬ஜ۩۞۩ஜ▬▬▬▬●

Overall Rating: ★★★☆☆ [3/5]
Story: ★★★☆☆
Gameplay: ★★★☆☆

●▬▬▬▬ஜ۩۞۩ஜ▬▬▬▬●
★OVERALL★
Reminiscent of expansion packs in the 1990's, Hong Kong is a standalone story staying true to the already established world within the previously released Shadowrun Returns. Once again, just like with the release of Dragonfall, Harebrained Schemes has given us an entirely new game. There have been some much needed improvements to the combat system, a rebuilt UI, new cyber-skills, and the addition of illustrated cinematic transitions for the storyline; however, they made some changes to the Matrix and Decking that you may or may not like. It's not easy to follow up such an epic story with great characters as was in Dragonfall. And if you played it prior to Hong Kong, you may be left feeling a bit wanting by the end. Much like a warm-up band playing after the main concert. You might feel the urge to leave the show early...
★STORY★
This time, you *don't* start out as a shadowrunner. Long estranged from the man who raised you, you've lived a comfy life in Seattle and have all but forgotten your childhood. Until, without warning, your father sends you a trid requesting you meet him in Hong Kong immediately, but gives you no explanations as to why. So, out of guilt or a sense of loyalty, you drop everything and hop on the next flight to China. But he's not there to greet you when you arrive. Instead, the boy you grew up with, Duncan Wu, now a member of the Seattle police force called 'Lone Star,' is there on the docks. Surprised to see each other, you discover that neither of you know what's going on and quickly things take a turn for the worse. Suddenly, you're forced into the underground and to survive you must become a shadowrunner in one of the most dangerous, and profitable places in the Sixth World- The Hong Kong Free Enterprise Zone.
Unfortunately, SR:HK falls short of the glory that was Dragonfall. Which is disappointing given the interesting and rich setting of Hong Kong, especially since they had a pretty clean slate to work with as Shadowrun lore doesn't touch on much of the Asian side of the world. It has some of the most annoying characters I've ever seen in a video game, the worst of which are Duncan Wu and Is0bel. Their dialog sounds like emo teenagers and I just want to slap them. Hard. With a bullet to the face. And if it were me, I'd outright resent having my father drag my♥♥♥♥♥all the way to China to fix *his* problems! It's no wonder your character left him to begin with. In spite of all this, it might be forgivable if the plot wasn't so predictable. After 25 hours into the story, the only reason I continued was out of a compulsion to complete the damn thing so I could shelve it and never return.
★GAMEPLAY★
I've come to think of the Shadowrun Returns series more as an interactive virtual novel with tactical and roleplaying elements. Because the true lure of this game is not the gameplay, but the story. I'm not saying that it's bad, it's just not what makes the game entertaining. While you're able to change some elements of the story to your own unique perspective, the main storyline arc remains similar. And customizing your character has little impact on how the story develops, instead offering a different perspective on the same events.
However, there have been some improvements to the combat system. Now the floating combat text includes events such as "Dodged," instead of only telling you if you hit or missed. Also, your percent chance to hit seems much more accurate than in previous games. I don't know if a layer of RNG was removed or just tweaked but combat is much more enjoyable than it was in SR:R and SR:DF. Sadly, it seems this improvement has come at the cost of a weak story.
★SOUND & MUSIC★
Jon Everist has composed the music for both Dragonfall and Hong Kong, and he was one of three composers that created the original soundtrack to Shadowrun Returns. As usual, his talent is one of the shining highlights of this series. He successfully mixed traditional asian instruments with modern techno music to create a unique sound that feels appropriate for the futuristic setting of neo-China. I recommend buying the deluxe edition for the added bonus of the game soundtrack. It’s a welcome addition to anyone’s music collection.
★BUGS & BOTHERS★
Unfortunately, there exists a bug that can be very game breaking. Sometimes, items left on your characters will disappear after the mission is completed. Items like weapons, medkits, and spells. It's extremely frustrating to say the least… There’s no workaround that I know of and there’s no sign of a fix in sight.
Now let's talk about the overhauled Matrix. While the look of the Matrix is much improved from the previous Shadowrun games, the mechanics are completely different and not for the better, in my opinion.
Deckers can now “eject” from the Matrix at anytime, but doing so severely hurts your Decker’s HP. Making it an unacceptable risk during combat and basically unnecessary out of combat. Never once did I use the eject ability during my playthrough. It’s a good idea, but the cost is too high.
Once again Deckers get the shaft. While combat in meatspace has been much improved, combat in the Matrix has become more difficult. In previous games, it wasn’t hard to raise your programs skill high enough to reach a 99% hit chance. In Hong Kong, however, that’s only possible at max skill. And the further you are from your target, the more severe the penalty to your hit chance. It’s almost like they swapped combat systems between meatspace and the Matrix. And since you can’t level up your companion’s abilities, Is0bel, your resident Decker, remains a mediocre choice when trying to hack your way through a security system.
While in the Matrix, you must dodge watcher programs that follow a specific path and if they spot you, it will raise the alarm level by +20 each turn for every watcher that has spotted you. And they're absolutely everywhere. Some areas of the Matrix are literally crawling with watcher programs to the point of madness. On top of that, you must bypass Blockers using their new Hacking system. Blockers are basically giant virtual walls that stand between you and your objective. You must hack, enter a password, or override it at the cost of +50 to your alarm level. This wouldn't be so bad if the Hacking system wasn't an annoying mixture of "Simon Says" and "Guess Who?" using pseudo-geometric shapes that don't make any sense combined with yet another level of RNG. It's not that hacking is difficult, once you understand what you're supposed to do, but it's just so damned *annoying* since you encounter the blasted things multiple times on *every* mission!

Ok, honesty time. I will not play this game on Steam. I already have an account outside of Steam with plenty of hours invested since the game came out originally.
Now, there are many many issues with WoWS. Here are just a few of them...
-Balance - There's a distinct feeling of inability to compete after a certain point. T5 is ok, IF it faces it's own tier or below. Anything else makes you essentially obsolete and means you can do nothing against your opponents.
-Progression - Rewards mean basically nothing. Getting through Tiers 1-4 are fairly easy. T5 is a mediocre grind, and anything else is near impossible. You earn what is pretty much nothing from "an ok match".
-F2P model - Now, this is a thing with a lot of different games, but WG takes it to a whole new level. Between premium ships ("Special" ships that are just normal ships you can get for free with a skin, a few minoor model changes, and a large pricetag), buying premium account (gives you a bonus to match rewards), and buying various other consumables or premium currency WG is simply milking the community for money.
-Game Mechanics - Lots of issues here. Spotting consists of a set limit, meaning if a ship is just barely outside of that limit, it's completely invisible. THis means you can sit just outside an enemies view range and just shower them with shells, while they can't shoot back becuase you're invisible. Another mechanic issue is the fire damage. Fire is basically the "Be all, end all" for damage. It kills EVERYTHING. Full health battleship? Burned to death. Carrier? Burned. Cruisers? Burned. This needs fixed, has been requested for fixing by the community, and WG has done nothing.
-Accuracy for damages - Another massive issue. Damage and how it is caused is fairly spotty. Sometimes you can go out and just wreck every enemy you see, and then the next match, you do nothing at all. Lots of this seems to be related to how WG did their damage/physics calculations for shells. However, this isn't the only WG game that has this issue, so it might just be how they do things.
Yet, not everything about World of Warships is bad.
-Great models - The ships are extremely well modelled. Overall, they are completely correct and minus a few ahistorical things created for mechanical balance (Bismarck being able to equip/launch floatplane Me-109 fighters...) everything is correct.
-Beautiful maps - The maps you fight on are beautiful. They have great water modelling, great designing of islands and land (except for what appear to be some extra small buildings...)
-Decent community  - You can and will find friends in this game. Among all the mean people who will berate you ingame for apparent poor gameplay, there are great people who will help you.
So yeah... If you love WG stuff, sure, get this game. If you want something balanced, avoid it like the plauge. If you want to have an enjoyable time shooting digital ships, leave this game alone.
Overall, DO NOT INSTALL THIS GAME.

River City Ransom Underground is exactly the RCR/Kunio-kun game that it should've been. It takes the formula of the original and dials everything up to 11, without changing the dynamic of what made the original game a classic. It's silly and self-aware as most modern sequels to classic franchises are, but doesn't devolve into complete lunacy like Double Dragon Neon did. It looks and feels like RCR, and fans of the original won't be disappointed.
The addition of new characters, each with unique playstyles makes it both interesting and fresh when experimenting. Some characters feel much better than others, but the team at Conatus are actively supporting and rebalancing, so the game can only improve from here.
The online multiplayer was completely painless, and now that the progress saving "bug" has been fixed, the game's value has jumped immensely.
The game's unfortunately had a rough year due to a disgruntled contractor hitting it with bogus copyright claims, forcing them to pull their soundtrack and recommission a new one, but now that the new soundtrack is implemented, it's safe to play (and show on YouTube) once again.

Conatus Creative bought the licensing from Arc Systems for this game as part of a poorly managed Kickstarter campaign.  So if you've played other games in the franchise like the 3DS River City Tokyo Rumble and are expecting that same degree of polish, then you're going to be sorely disappointed.
The game is really glitchy.  There was no beta testing, but even if there were the final release of this game is far worse than any game I've seen starting beta.  They're really struggling to patch the errors in post, but like the rest of the game its sloppy.  They patched the dreaded "milk run" quest after enough players complained, but even after another patch the final boss is still just garbage.
The game has some great ideas, perfect for selling you on Kickstarter, but the execution is very poor.  Each of the characters have custom skills, but nothing carries over.  So leveling each character is like starting over from scratch making an already grindey game just excessive.
As soon as you beat Merv the game goes into an "endgame mode" that's pretty tiresome combined with a glitchy final boss.  All subway transportation is closed and all of the enemies are replaced with grey clone versions of themselves that are a bit tougher, rarely drop money, and often follow you into shops.  Earning money in this mode is much slower and leveling another character from scratch is nearly impossible.  The combination of starting this "endgame mode" so early and unexpected with its many drawbacks and a final boss that's glitched is a really poor design decision.  Furthermore, you don't get to go back directly to the glitched boss so expect a 15-20 minute reset every time it glitches you into an infitine stun loop.
I really want to like this game, I bought a gift copy for a friend right away, and I have high hopes that their continued post-production patches will stop some of the bleeding, but in the end this game has a lot of fundemental problems that cripple it from reaching the heights this project promised.  There have been a lot of success stories of independent studios this year, but sadly this isn't going to be one of them.

The original River City Ransom is one of my favourite NES games ever and also one of my favourite brawlers. Conatus Creative had a lot to live up to. River City Ransom Underground is indeed a worthy sequel but some of the old-school design choices it sticks to might be off-putting to some people. It's also not the most polished release, despite a lengthy beta for Kickstarter backers.
The original RCR was a very early version of what became the open-world genre. Your goal was simply to rescue your kidnapped girlfriend but you could approach this quest in any number of ways, either hanging back to farm currency and items to level up or just pushing right through the story if you were good enough. You can do the same in RCRU, though you're going to have to be exceptionally skilled to do it.
You choose between one of a number of different characters, each of which have their own talents and moves. You can swap between them at hideouts you find (which is also where you save) but each of them levels up independently. You gain levels by taking out enemies but this only raises your maximum possible stats, which can affect your health and special moves. You increase the stats by spending money that you pick up from downed foes at various shops on food and other items. You can learn additional moves from these shops. Much like a Dark Souls game, you're not told what effects different items will have before you buy them. You can look this up if you want but the idea is to encourage discovery and experimentation.
The new River City is much bigger than the old one and you'll go to a number of different areas (some of which have not so obvious entrances) as you brawl your way through a number of different quests to further the intentionally ridiculous story. Unfortunately, a lot of these quests involve frustrating chases or escort missions that require you to go several screens back at least to retry and the outcome of which is often dependent on RNG. These tend to get pretty old pretty fast, as can some of the cheaper boss fights. They also added in cops, which spawn infinitely when you accidentally do things like punch a civilian or a parking meter, are very hard to take out, give no reward, only attack you and will keep coming until you find a hideout. For better or worse though, this is a retro design mentality and this game isn't being pitched as anything else.
There's 4 player co-op available, either local or online, though it's not really worth it if you don't play with friends. The online lobby system doesn't tell you anything about the point in the story a host is at so you're usually just dropping into some random midpoint of their game, which can have a lot of spoilers and also be far too high level for you. There's also zero in-game communication and players all have to be on the same screen so co-ordination with randoms is a nightmare.
The art and music of RCRU are absolutely top notch. Pixel art is often overused in indie games these days but the hand drawn art and animations are some of the best around here, as is the original chiptune score by Disasterpiece. Unfortunately, for a PC exclusive game in development for this long, it's buggy and has some notable omissions. Only Xbox One and Xbox 360 controllers are supported and rumble doesn't work. The combo screen doesn't show actual controller buttons, making learning new combos difficult. Playing online doesn't save any character progress unless you're the host. I also had several instances where certain events didn't trigger to progress the story unless I exited the game and reloaded. They are planning to fix all this but again, this game was in beta for a long time, these shouldn't have been there at all.
RCRU isn't for everyone. It's for people who want a challenge, want to figure their way through the story without handholding or direction and who enjoy the design methods that made retro games tough. If you're someone who grew up with the original though, this scratches that nostalgia itch, while also adding in a lot of modern amenities. It's definitely best played in multiplayer with friends. Just maybe wait till they get the progression fixed.

There are 2 types of rogue like games. The first type you actually progress your character accross playthroughs (Dead Rising, Rogue Legacy) where you get your sense of accomplishment despite not beating the game.
The other type consists of losing literally everything stat and possession and see if you roll the dice better this time around. Thats much harder to remain satisfying since from a stat angle you can't tell who has 80 hours of play time and who has 5 hours. So why invest the additional 75 hours?
This game is the latter, sure certain games can pull it off like Faster then Light because you unlock ways that alter the game in a dramatic way that getting those unlocks feels worth it even if you lose. This game has a few different classes but they control and play almost identically and their bonuses would only be noticed if this game was in the former catagory. It wouldn't be hard either, you remove weapon degredation (since you can save items between playthroughs) and allow perminent base stat increases using the levels you gain in playthrough as currency. Make this playthrough harder so that future ones will be easier sort of deal, they already have something like that but it only applies to the current playthrough
TL:DR this game is very much worth if you're buying it for literal cents on the dollar. It goes on sale frequently

By far the best of the 3D Sonic games (no offense to any of the other ones). The level design, the gameplay mechanics (and how well they flow), the nostalgia (even if a few of the levels are tributes to very recent games)... Everything about this game is beautiful. The two different kinds of gameplay (the old-school 2.5D platforming Classic levels, and the 2.5D/3D platforming Modern levels) keep the gameplay fresh and exciting, and the different missions in the game add a bit of flavor to the whole game (even if some of them are a bit tedious). But it's fun nonetheless, and it's one of those games that makes for good speed runs and self-improvement. Overall, it's an excellent game, it's great for both life-long veterans (such as myself) and newcomers, and I can't think of a reason NOT to play it.
Mind you, the final fight IS a bit disappointing...
And the momentum-based physics of the old Sonic games aren't present in the Classic stages...
But hey! No such thing as a perfect game. :3

There are two philosophies in making Roguelikes: The classic Roguelikes like NetHack had dungeons that weren't terribly long with permadeath, but were excessively lethal because the point was that you,
were the one "leveling up" by learning new techniques for beating the game that you never thought about before you had YASD or hit the oracle; The other usually eschews permadeath to have a more classic RPG sense of character progression through nigh-infinite procedural dungeons.
One Way Heroics goes the ultra-short game route with none of the character progression, but it also manages to be so rules-light that it fails to really give the player any sense that they learned anything.  I "beat" the game on my second try, and it just said, "Yay, now try again!"... WHY? What goal do I have in playing through a 10-minute game I've already beaten to get more loot I don't need to beat it again?
It just feels like it gutted the biggest reason I enjoy RPGs - the sense of customization and development of your characters - in favor of nameless forgettable nobodies, and there's nothing in the game that replaces that or gives me any sense of reason why I'd want to play any more than that 10 minutes it takes to see the whole story play out once.

An extremely fun little game, a light kit-bash of mutliple gernes. Full of goofyness, jokes and sci-fi puns (Star Trek, Star Wars, Space Oddysey, etc.), it is a welcome break from all the tripple A games we got showered over the past 6 months. I love games that do not take themselves seriously. I love games that just let you fool around with them till you feel like it, and then just save and quit, without the feel of being bound to them and forget your real life till you finish it a few times over.
As usual in my guides, let's take a look at the good and the bad.
The GOOD:
1. Pleasant, isometric 3D graphics - very nice and colorful, with plenty of goofy looking guys and animals.
2. Kit-bash of genres - I can list base-building, resource management, exploration, RPG, and I am sure you will find plenty more in this game.
3. Relaxing gameplay - while you can still lose, you can still enjoy every aspect of the game to its fullest without biting your nails like it is an Ironman Impossible XCOM run. This is a game that allows you to lay back and relax in your chair and click your way to victory.
4. Great replayability - all the systems in the game are randomly generated, making you adapt to the start that you are given.
5. A plethora of varying maps - exploration missions take place on a huge variety of pretty maps with varying flora, fauna, climate and enemies.
6. Very decent tech tree for a game of this calibre - unlocking new technologies allows you to build more rooms and further expand your starbase.
7. Progress in every aspect of the game - whether it's gear or base expansion, you always feel like adding more stuff to the pot, learning more about the game and seeing more prettier things show up.
8. Pew-pew-pew lasers - come on, who doesn't like shooting lasers?
9. Your starbase never gets attacked - you can sit and relax and play for fun. Like fun FUN. Not the "I beat the game, whew" fun.
10. Multicolored Spatials - strategists, scientists, engies, diplomats and doctors all have a different color. Cute - and a small Star Trek throwback.
11. Character progression - whether you send your guys on away missions or on tasks (AI controlled missions with % chance of success), they always progress and you won't have anyone lagging behind.
12. Progression is meaningful - leveling your guys actually matters. You need leveled guys as ambassadors on conquered systems. No more slave labor!
13. You dont lose Spatials - when they get knocked out, they go in stasis and can reappear after a while or through a skill, allowing you to relax and play.
14. Wonderful music to fit the whole Sci-fi theme.
The BAD:
1. Exploration missions are a pure rinse and repeat - go kill this guy, go kill another guy, then some more guys, maybe a facility or something inbetween. While there is some variation in the system unlock missions, everything else is painfully average.
2. Your space base never gets attacked - it could be a turn off for some players, even if I find it a good thing to promote casual gameplay.
3. You don't lose characters - if a character goes down to 0 health, it immediately goes in stasis, and then reappears on the battlefield after some time, or through a skill. While it promotes casual gameplay, there is no tension and worry about losing someone like it exists in games of the sort of XCOM and This War of Mine.
4. The huge amount of point and click could be a turn off for some gamers. You can literally do everything with the left and right mouse buttons. Even only the left one.
The CONCLUSION:
If you want a casual game that doesn't take itself seriously, with goofy stuff, pretty graphics, lots of great gameplay and very decent replayability, this game is for you.

This game has some major flaws, but it delivers on everything it promises.  Building the station is fun, combat is fun.  Managing resources is fun.  I basically didn't stop playing this from the day I started.  However the game needs some serious rebalencing:
It encourages you to walk away from your computer, leaving the game running to pay for all the things you need since there is no reprecussions for not managing your station other than you don't develop as fast.
Combat has the right idea but movement is clunky at times and near the end the only stratagy to fight hard monsters on WTF mode is to kite them like a hunter in WoW.  For 5 mins at a time.  Not hard to do, but boring.
Getting ambassadors later on is tedious and expensive.  The system that levels your non-main party is expenive and slow and relies on taking advantage of leaving the game running for many hours at a time as it doesn't appear to be possible to make money fast enough to keep up with your advancement.
Some special powers are not ever useful.  As kiting is the only method of beating higher ranked bosses, close range weapons just don't do anything.  Scientist only should ever use one ability.  Diplomats can only use two abilities without being gimped.
That sounds like a lot of complaints (And I have more) but despite all that the game is super addicting and well worth the cost.

Combat takes place on away missions where you are in direct control of your crew.
The graphics are nice and friendly and the game runs well even on my older and outdated laptop. I turned off the music because I wanted to play my own, but for the short amount of time I had it on it was enjoyable.
I got this game at a discount, but even at full price it is still very much worth it. Not too stressful. Not too boring. Just right.

A lot of the reviews for this game are negative, and it disgusts me about why  they dislike the game. The game is a look into the creator's life, his ups and downs and the struggles of the real word. Rejection, self criticism, depression. The game's not made for you, it's a passion project. That being said, I enjoyed it. Each level of the game is a seperate memory or dream. A memory of a beach in Berwick, a memory of being rejected by the one he loved, a memory of his childhood friend who got him into game development. There are a few levels that struck a chord with me, spoiler alerts I suppose. You're in a room with a 2 minute timer on the wall, "Countdown to self destruction." On the ceiling tiles, depressing thoughts. As reflected on in the developer commentary, most players would never see the outside of this room. The timer would run out, and out of frustration, skip the level. Look around a bit, and a note will tell you to pay just the littlest bit of attention to the painting in the room. Doing so unlocks a door to an infinite ladder, climbing it starts a video of the creator performing theater. As you climb, you watch the video of  the creator destorying his art and his self portrait he wanted you to admire not long ago. Turning around however shows screenshots of Gamejolt games, all with harsh self criticism on them. This level was a look into the mental state he was in, and the pressure he put on himself to do well.
In the end, I enjoyed it. It made me feel plenty of emotions, and for the price of absolutely nothing but a little of my time, I would put it in my list of favourite games.

I've played both previous Shadowrun games by Harebrained Schemes, and in my opinion they keep getting better. Hong Kong is far from perfect though. If you're not familiar with the setting, the game is a lore heavy CRPG set in a cyberpunk/fantasy universe. Robots and elves. Expect a lot of neon.
The Good
+ Strong writing and dialogue. Characters have a lot of depth, and the plot is intriguing.
+ Fun and distinct class builds. Word of warning though, don't spread yourself too thin.
+ Multiple ways to approach combat, puzzles, and scenarios (cover mechanics, brute force, skill checks, charisma, chilling out with spirits, etc.)
+ Great art style.
The Not-So Good
- A little too much text. This is subjective, and I personally like all the reading, but there is a ton of it and you may not be into that. It does affect the pacing. Luckily, most of it is optional.
- Spelling errors. I've noticed more in Hong Kong than the previous games.
- The new Matrix. In the previous games, the Matrix was basically standard combat with even more neon painted on it. It was boring. This time around, Harebrained Schemes added a stealth mechanic you can use, and a hacking mechanic that has you memorizing patterns of numbers. I really like the hacking part, because is feels more immersive for that kind of character. I've heard others complain that they don't want something that requires actual skill instead of your character's skill, which is a legit criticism. I will say this though- the stealth option kinda sucks. It requires precise clicking and timing to avoid cones of sight, and the game just isn't built for that. It's not responive enough. The changes in the Matrix are optional though, you can still just kill everything if you prefer,
-I've heard reports of bugs. Haven't encountered anything major myself, but everyone's experience will differ.
Summary- Punch people with a robot arm, read a short story, memorize a few numbers, then upgrade your robot arm.

Alright, I had to rewrite my review on Lisa, as I've finally figured out what makes this game absolutely perfect.
It appeals to both old school and new game designs.
When you talk to most Old School video game fans, they'll usually claim "that games were just better back then." While some can't narrow it down as to why or just tell you "because," most tend to lean towards the systemic game design of these old games. That sort of seamless transition from an area to the next without being scripted by story, but by the emergence and progression of game mechanics as the game went on. You didn't have your hand held throughout the story, and while there were usually set levels or dungeons you had to clear, you weren't told which one you had to go to. These games, of course, lacked an intricate, well written story that many of today's single player games thrive on. These games are masterfully written, with story arcs and plots that put many novels published today to shame. With me being the former and my girlfriend more the latter, we couldn't figure out why we both absolutely loved this game despite us having such different tastes. Lisa did it
right.
This game in no way holds your hand. Challenging mechanics and a surprisingly well crafted overworld that has plenty to explore. While the central area hubs got confusing at times, they led to countless areas to explore with new characters to run in to, many of which were not required to progress in the story whatsoever. While these areas were eventually driven into a bottle neck in order to progress story wise, you didn't have to rush to the bottle neck, leaving you to figure out what to do on your own through game mechanics. But it's not like you wouldn't mind getting right back to the story either, though. I mean this game did it perfectly. The  world building was done so subtly yet beautifully, with the backstory of the world and our main character given as the game progresses, rather than being laid out in a scripted one-scene cut scene. And done so indirectly as well, with many of these important aspects being implied rather than told, you're left to interpretation on so much of the game that it's refreshing and intriguing. Not to mention the overall tone of the game, being such an incredibly dark story offset by its lightening dark humor. The humor isn't in poor taste, if anything it only accentuates the most crucial story elements of the game. It acknowledges everything the player has gone through, with nothing put in on accident. Subtle story hints and characters are reintroduced so seamlessly it's hard to catch them at times. The emotionally driven story paired with the challenging yet organic game mechanics pull literally everything together for something of all cliques to enjoy.
Damn near all of my problems with this game were technical. Shortcuts like using shift to hop off of your bike could not be used to hop
to your bike as well. The cruel (yet probably intentionally) punishing overworld which allows a player to straight up die because they mis-stepped. What kind of inventory system what that even? Mostly just things along those lines, which, coming from games developing along the lines of Lisa, is a common yet acceptable trait.
If you can get past that, which you should, literally everything else about this game is beautiful.
Challenging combat system, incredible story, and addicting as hell.

Even though this game isn't in early access mode anymore, I'm pretty sure it isn't 100% finished yet. At least, I hope so. If you're really, really into sword fighting games, you might like this game, otherwise I wouldn't recommend it. So far, this game kept getting slower and slower. For example, you used to be able to jump high into the air and, even though it wasn't very polished yet, it did have a lot of potential. But now they made it so that you're barely able to jump over a curb anymore.
Okay, I get that that's just one of my preferences and there are probably some people who actually prefer jumping to be almost completely removed, except for triggering Air attacks, but there's a better reason for not playing this game: It has NO singleplayer mode (nor multiplayer PvE of any kind), which means that it's exclusively PvP. The problem is that there's just barely anybody to actually play against. You can literally run this game, check the server list, and see a maximum of about 11 people playing. On the same server. Which might be an American server too. Which isn't a very good thing if you're in Europe yourself. This game just doesn't get advertised, enough. It sometimes does have a small amount of people playing it, like right after the game goes on sale, but eventually people keep leaving and leaving until it's just the same handful of people who still play it consistently.
My conclusion:
If you're really into a game that exclusively offers you PvP sword fighting (with a little bit of dress up) and you don't care about any additional content, you might enjoy playing it for a while.
If you're just "curious" or think it "might be interesting" to you, I wouldn't recommend it, even if it's solely because of the almost non-existent player base.
(On a side note: I don't hate the developers of this game. I don't know that much about them, but they appear to be friendly people who really do care about their small playerbase, and even host small, official tournaments every now and then, with a unique item reward. I just don't think every update has been for the best.)

I wish I could say I enjoyed this game, but that would be a lie.  I'm a fencer in real-life, so that coupled with the screenshots and trailer led me to have some high expectations for Blade Symphony.  The premise is strong, but it's executed very poorly, surprisingly.
The servers are usually unpopulated, and lag is persistent.  Yes, I've tried all the usual tricks to negate as much lag time as possible.  It did not change the result.  What follows is spotty hit detection and unexpected deaths.
The combat isn't simply hack'n'slash; it's more profund than that.  However, I learned the best path to vicotry involved that line of strategy....
The game is also very unforgiving to beginners.  I understand I'm a noob, but after ~100 duels, I can count on one hand how many of them I've won. I "am" going to blame the lag here, because I "know" I'm not THAT bad.  The customization doesn't come to the rescue because you have to win to attain a decent amount of points to unlock anything of value.  In my four hours of recorded playtime, I unlocked only one thing with my accumulation of the game's currency.
Overall, this adds up to playing the same people, getting your tail handed to you repeatedly, usually in a very inexplicable manner, and rarely changing your outfit to fit your playstyle.  It looks and sounds pretty, but that's not enough to have me recommend Blade Symphony to you.  And that hurts more than the unfair defeats. :-(

I know not why I left it so long to review this game again (I wrote a review years ago but it was, looking back, terrible). Mafia II is still, even by today's standards, a very well-made game, and one that I must immediately recommend to all who may consider making the purchase.
Admittedly, the hype of this game is significantly less than that of its yesteryears, not helped at all by the recent release of Mafia 3. I have not played Mafia 3, but having seen some of its content I can say with some confidence that you would in fact be better spending money on this one.
Mafia II is, as far as story is concerned, is almost a perfect game. Without spoiling it, you are dropped into a world as a mislead young man named Vito Scaletta - an Italian. The development of this character alone made this game immensely enjoyable to play, as one bad deed leads to another, and eventually his life is consumed by them as he keeps making bad decisions time and time again. In a sense, the player can't help but feel sorry for Vito, and empathise, as no matter how wrong the things are that he does, we grow to love him - not hate him, for we never really feel that he is a malicious person. The game essentially takes you through this phase of his life, and the progress that he makes within. Mafia II's story is both gripping and exciting, and I thoroughly enjoyed playing it through. It stirred emotions and piqued interest at every corner, making a very memorable experience for all who play it.
I cannot, admittedly, praise the playstyle of the game quite so highly as the story though. While not in any way bad, the combat in the game does become extremely repetitive, and at times feels like a bit of an obstacle - something you must get past that is preventing you from progressing with the story. Combat in this game uses a very simple basis of softly punching someone or doing it really hard, allowing for stuns, within which the player has a chance to finish the opponent. Shooting is very much a case of hiding out of the line of fire and picking the enemies off. I did play the game on 'easy' first time round as I was new to gaming in general back then, and I never felt like combat presented any challenges where any skills were really needed. It was always a case of taking out wave after wave of enemy, and that lost the fun factor after a while.
Driving was another thing that did get tedious occasionally. While not entirely unpleasant, there is much of it as the story forces you to do your fair share of driving across the game world time and time again. I found the driving took some getting used to as the steering and general feel was not like that of any games I've ever played. Cars feel heavy and lack massively in agility, which helps them feel authentic, but it does, as I said, take some getting used to, especially when you are used to driving feeling like it does in games like Grand Theft Auto - a game to which Mafia II is very similar in a lot of ways.
Otherwise, as far as sounds/music and graphics go, there is nothing to fault the game for. Authentic music makes the game feel immersive in all areas. The voice acting was, to my memory, flawless, and considering the age of the game, the graphics both in the game itself and in the cutscenes were stunning, even by today's standards. I found the game gave me many of hours of play time that I really enjoyed. I must say though that despite the extra content it adds, the DLC is, in my humble opinion, overpriced. It amounts to more than the game which is not great in my books. It should also be said that when you finish the story, the world lacks anything to do. I felt the same about GTA 5 but at least that offered heists or races. Mafia II does not. The shops are useable, as is your garage and vehicles, but just about all you can do is drive around aimlessly. This is something I found most detrimental to the quality of the game. It may as well have just ended there and not given you the chance to enjoy an empty open world. Overall, I would give this game a proud 8/10. The developers did a really good job with this title.

I think some of the people went into this game without reading the description. It states that in includes "a teenager coming to terms with life and growing up." So, obviously this isn't jsut supposed to be an ordinary walking sim. It even states that the game has "less traditional interaction". I think if people read the "About This Game" before playing, they might not be so disappointed.
As for me, I thoroughly enjoyed the game. The themes really got to me. The music was amazingly well done. I can see where the creator is trying to go with the old-school sounding monologues, like a distressed teen from the 90s making audio journals. I really don't think anyone can say that audio then was as good as it is now (heck, it's even better than 5 years ago).
I also noticed, these levels aren't random. They go in chronological order, starting from when the narrator was a kid. This is obvious when you climb up a certain something in the first level, and compare it to images shown in later levels.
The levels were pretty fun, some of them a bit tricky to figure out at first. The last level was probably the hardest for me. Most of them give you a lot of space to roam around and find some little hidden easter eggs. And they definitely are unique. I wonder what inspired them? The puzzles that I encountered were fairly enjoyable, my favorite probably being the art one, just because of the creativity.
There were really only a few things about this game that nagged me. First, the controls. They were a little wonky, I felt that movements were too quick and exaggerated. Jumping that high was a bit unrealistic. The second thing that nagged me was pacing. Sometimes, you'd have as much time as you'd like to look around, see all the details that were put into a level. Other levels seemed like they had a time limit, so you couldn't really see anything. Though, a few of those are SUPPOSED to be that way, and it would ruin the level otherwise. Models probably could have used a little more work too, though it all still looked pretty nice.
Overall, I think this is a good game. Looking for a generic walking simulator? This isn't for you. If you're looking for something out of the ordinary though, that will mess with your feels with colorful, crazy settings lots of interactivity, and a deep dive into a hormonally struggling and totally relatable teenager's thoughts, this would be a good game to try.

I backed on KS, I never played the original game, and I've only played single player. I was intially really excited about the game before release. On Day 1, I felt a bit disappointed because I think I was expecting more of an action-adventure game. Once I realized that it's really an ARPG, it started to be fun again. Also, you really have to start unlocking character moves before the fights become fun. Now on to the bullet points:
+ The brawling is just generally awesome. Probably even better in multiplayer, which the game seems designed around.
+ The art and animations are great. Character movements look and feel very fluid, and a lot of detail has gone into flushing out River City.
+ Great soundtrack.
- Some really annoying mission design, often at odds with the things that make the game fun. Chase missions are boring to repeat, the infamous milk run is a pain, etc.
- I've only played as Glen and Paul, but it seems a lot of other characters are much more difficult to play as. Especially ones that rely on holds and specials, as basic combos have much higher DPS, and are much, much easier to execute. Which is a shame, because it makes more interesting strategies less useful.
- Late game enemies have very obnoxious and predictable AI. They will always block and move out of the way. This really limits which moves are useful against them, which in turn makes the combat less interesting. It also makes slower characters very difficult to play with.
- The entire final act feels like a mess. The story is random and under-developed, and there don't seem to be enough new art assets to really sell the changes that take place.
- At least in single player, fighting through the city gets very samey, as there isn't much variation in the encounters. Roughly the same number of enemies appear on each screen, all enemies always attack you and never other enemies, etc. This really limits the variety of interactions you'll see in the game. Would be less of an issue in co-op, as fights are probably much more complex when you add more players to your side.
= Overall, if you want a brawler, this one is awesome. It has some issues, but some of those are being addressed by the developer. Still a lot of fun in spite of the problems I have with it.

As it currently stands, the game is not worth purchasing... which is too bad since the core combat is not bad and sucessfully adds to the original game formula while adding some modern enhancements.  Unfortunately everything else wrapped around it feels like a system trying to directly pull you away from the core combat.  To list a few things:
There is a lack of move information so you do not know what you are purchasing for your characters and how the moves work without going through trial and error.
There is a large number of chase sequences in place of boss fights.
There is a milk run section that can be lost due to RNG based on screen loads (ie you load a new section and immediately get hit based on enemy placement).
The final boss has a very boring attack pattern that requires you to be perfect or you will be infinitely juggled.  And when I say infinite, I mean you can literally be juggled infinitely until you force quit the game because can get into a juggle state where you cannot die, but cannot do anything.
All of the above not only detracts from the game's enjoyment.  I get the sense the developers were trying to add extra components to give the game some variety, but they did so at the cost of making the game far worse overall.
Hopefully they will be able to resolve some of this in a future patch, but for now I would not recommend purchasing this.  In fact, this is in many ways worse than a straight up bad game, because in a straight up bad game you can usually figure out that it is bad pretty quick and then stop playing.  For this game, it has a lot of promise so you end up playing for a bit only to realize there are terrible walls (ie milk run, final boss, etc.) awaiting you which turns the whole thing into a large waste of time.

This is the best game I've bought this year.
I purchased it on an impulse buy and I'm glad I did. I would pay a lot more for this game, had I known it was going to be this much fun.
At first glance, it's a simple game. Once takes a group of Officers on an Away-Team mission, conquers a planet by completing a quest, then gets the resources of that planet to use in building their base, crafting goods and services for visiting humans and aliens to purchase and use, working their way up a Tech tree to get access to even more goods and services.
But, it's not really just that simple. One has to acquire the gear for their Officers, level up their Officers, hire more Officers to work shifts and to take on missions while other Officers rest and have a little bit of R&R, satisfying their own needs for food, drink, fun and a bit of rest.
The decisions ones makes, not only during the mission, but when giving weapons and augments to Officers or choosing the properly outfitted Officers for the mission are critical to their success. Combat isn't just point-and-click, but many times I've found myself having to kite angry robot bosses around a map or manuever my team into a good position to get the drop on a bunch of pirates.
Since I bought the game, I've been playing non-stop, for the most part, only pausing long enough to grab some sleep. And, that's not something I normally do with any game, even the great ones. This game is "special." It's got that "certain something" that demands that I keep coming back to it. Whether it's the constant incentive to journey to the next system or the allure of dropped loot and leveling Officers, or even building the next expansion for the space-station and watching the money roll in as aliens plink away at pinball machines or have a go on the dance floor... Whatever it is, this game has "it." It's fun, it's addicting, it's a great game that doesn't take itself too seriously, but still manages to provide a great experience.
If you like tactical-rpg, building, crafting, Startopia meets Space Cplony meets Action RPG games, you'll want to buy this game, right now...
I'd buy it again.

My first impression of this game after 4 hours of play is pretty good. In spite of the kiddy graphics there's a surprising amount of depth to this game. Each game is randomly generated giving you a different experience each time. I haven't played too far into the game yet so I don't know how it develops later on, but I'm certainly enjoying the early game.
The Spatials is basically split into two parts: first you have a base-building tycoon style game, second you have a real time RPG game where characters go on missions, level up and so on.
Base building is the core of the game, your goal is to build a large space station that will attract many visitors from different alien races, supply them with their needs and of course, make money out of them. To do this you'll not only need to build the station, but supply it with resources, and there are many different resources to be found on the hundred or so planets out there.
Research is necessary to unlock new room and equipment types and there's a tech tree that you progress through, making your station more advanced over time. To unlock new techs you need to gain research points by going on missions. This is also how you discover and acquire the resources you need.
Your station requires staff. There are five different types of characters, obviously modelled on Star Trek - the diplomat, the science officer, the doctor, the strategist and the engineer, each with colour coded uniforms making it easy to tell them apart. Not only do they work in the station but more importantly, they go on missions to various planets. This is where the real time RPG part of the game comes in.
Each character possesses different skills and items. Going on missions gains them experience which causes them to level up and further develop their skills. They also develop increasingly sophisticated needs that must be fulfilled, like certain foods for example. Oddly, their only need at the beginning of the game is sleep, apparently they don't even need to eat at the start, which is just as well, because you don't have any food or the means to cook it.
Missions consist of choosing five characters, landing on a planet and performing certain tasks, like destroying enemy bases and so on. The combat is pretty simple once you get the hang of it, with each character having a certain special skill that can be activated with a keypress (1-5). It's very important to keep pressing the 4 button to keep healing your characters. They can't actually die in combat, but if their health is reduced to zero they are put "in stasis", so they can no longer take part in the mission. If this happens to all your characters then you've failed the mission. You can easily try it again later though, perhaps with different characters and equipment.
Once you've won a mission you get certain rewards, such as resources and items, as well as experience and research points. You also have access to the planet's resources, which you can start harvesting, to add to your station inventory. You can upgrade your characters with new skills and new weapons to make them stronger in future missions.
You can also accept contracts which are like missions, but you don't actually play the mission, you just send up to three officers on the mission, pay a fee and get a result a few minutes later.
New staff members can be recruited at embassies, and every system has one career mission which unlocks a new star system. Over time, enemies grow stronger and your characters level up, making them stronger. All the while you have to keep growing your base and providing more and more services for the visiting aliens.
While the graphical style is a retro isometric view, it's detailed and colourful and serves its purpose. It won't win any prizes but that's not what the game is about. The gameplay is straightforward, easy to learn and enjoyable. It may become quite challenging to satisfy all of your visitor's needs once the station grows large enough, but I haven't got that far in the game yet.
My first impression though, is very good. It's a fun game, an interesting challenge, and very relaxing to play. I recommend it.

Good things first: The game looks great and the soundtrack is amazing. It has a really polished UI. At the beginning the game seems interesting and even though the tutorials don't teach you everything but leave a bit to discover (like removing items when your inventory gets full) it's quite easy to get.
Unfortunately that simplicity also is the root of the problem with the game. It's just too simple. There's no much strategy involved - you just need to build everything your visitors require. The game doesn't allow you to do much planning or optimization. Soon you also start to run out of resources, which can be helped with the away team and "diplomacy". Unfortunately there are also some weird requirements for materials you just don't have or will have in long time (like fibers). The campaign starts to feel one long linear path you're unlocking.
Speaking of the away teams and exploration mode. It's interesting, challening and funny at first, but becomes mundane quite soon. All the missions are basically variations of three architypes: find items, kill pirates, destroy buildings. After dozen of levels, you feel you've seen it all.
The difficulty levels in exploration is quite uneven. At first the missions are extremely easy (12 first planets or so), but the you hit a huge wall where completing a level becomes a true (much needed) challenge . Unfortunately the game still repeats the same pattern, and with no chance of strategy throw in, it becomes boring. The difficulty comes from the fact that enemies have more health and they do more damage. They always behave the same: go to the attack range and attack. No specific AI or anything.
