Alright, I had to rewrite my review on Lisa, as I've finally figured out what makes this game absolutely perfect.
It appeals to both old school and new game designs.
When you talk to most Old School video game fans, they'll usually claim "that games were just better back then." While some can't narrow it down as to why or just tell you "because," most tend to lean towards the systemic game design of these old games. That sort of seamless transition from an area to the next without being scripted by story, but by the emergence and progression of game mechanics as the game went on. You didn't have your hand held throughout the story, and while there were usually set levels or dungeons you had to clear, you weren't told which one you had to go to. These games, of course, lacked an intricate, well written story that many of today's single player games thrive on. These games are masterfully written, with story arcs and plots that put many novels published today to shame. With me being the former and my girlfriend more the latter, we couldn't figure out why we both absolutely loved this game despite us having such different tastes. Lisa did it
right.
This game in no way holds your hand. Challenging mechanics and a surprisingly well crafted overworld that has plenty to explore. While the central area hubs got confusing at times, they led to countless areas to explore with new characters to run in to, many of which were not required to progress in the story whatsoever. While these areas were eventually driven into a bottle neck in order to progress story wise, you didn't have to rush to the bottle neck, leaving you to figure out what to do on your own through game mechanics. But it's not like you wouldn't mind getting right back to the story either, though. I mean this game did it perfectly. The  world building was done so subtly yet beautifully, with the backstory of the world and our main character given as the game progresses, rather than being laid out in a scripted one-scene cut scene. And done so indirectly as well, with many of these important aspects being implied rather than told, you're left to interpretation on so much of the game that it's refreshing and intriguing. Not to mention the overall tone of the game, being such an incredibly dark story offset by its lightening dark humor. The humor isn't in poor taste, if anything it only accentuates the most crucial story elements of the game. It acknowledges everything the player has gone through, with nothing put in on accident. Subtle story hints and characters are reintroduced so seamlessly it's hard to catch them at times. The emotionally driven story paired with the challenging yet organic game mechanics pull literally everything together for something of all cliques to enjoy.
Damn near all of my problems with this game were technical. Shortcuts like using shift to hop off of your bike could not be used to hop
to your bike as well. The cruel (yet probably intentionally) punishing overworld which allows a player to straight up die because they mis-stepped. What kind of inventory system what that even? Mostly just things along those lines, which, coming from games developing along the lines of Lisa, is a common yet acceptable trait.
If you can get past that, which you should, literally everything else about this game is beautiful.
Challenging combat system, incredible story, and addicting as hell.

It's quite hard to start this review without saying something overwhelmingly positive about this game. Sonic Generations is one of my all time favourite video games, with a good reason. It's hard to find any better 3D platformers in Steam, at least at time when I'm writing this review.
Sonic Generations is a fast paced platformer with highly colorful worlds and enjoyable mechanics. There's two different play styles: first, there's "Classic Sonic" that plays just like in the 90's. What I really like in these 2D sections is the fact that it's not TOO much focused on just speed alone. In recent 2D Sonic games, there's usually all kinds of boost mechanics that gives you maximum speed from anywhere, but there's nothing like that in here. You basically only have all the moves that the original Sonic 2 had in 1992, and nothing else. There's no boost, no homing attack, no grinding. It is meant to be nostalgic, and it really works. Levels are built around these mechanics, and should make you feel like home if you've ever played any of the classic Sonic games. Yes, there's even some real platforming sections where you have to stop and jump carefully! In my opinion, this is the best 2D Sonic action we've got after the first Sonic Advance game in 2001.
The other play style is the "Modern Sonic", the 3D sections. Gameplay is straight from the Sonic Unleashed or the Sonic Colors. This play style is much more focused on the speed than platforming. Some could even say that the modern sections are more like a driving game rather than a platformer, and I can't blame them. Basically in these sections you go really fast and try to react in different obstacles that comes in your way. There's some really cool stuff that happens in the levels, and you can even find some alternatives routes if you're good enough. In contrast to the more slow 2D sections, these fast pacing 3D action stages create a good variety so one game style never gets too repeative.
Sonic Generations has nine worlds and each one of them has its own classic and modern sections. Every main Sonic game until the Sonic Colours has been represented with one level that was chosen with fan polls earlier in the game's development. There's some ups and downs with this decision. At least we got what everyone loves, but there's a little bit too much focusing in city levels. Like I said, there's nine worlds, but three of them are city levels. Well, some could say four. I would have wanted to see more variety, for example a ice or a desert stage.
Still, every level IS the fan favourite of the original game, so there's absolutely no bad levels in this game at all. Stages are quite short, and should take you less than few minutes to clear. If you just want to clear this game once, it won't take you very long, I'd say about 5-6 hours. But you won't also find the most fun from this game in that way either. Since the levels in Sonic games are built in a way where you can find alternatives routes, this game gets better as you do. When you find some new shortcuts, try to make past enemies asap, and finally get good, it just feels amazing. When everything is going smoothly, you can feel at that moment why people still loves these games. If you want more slow paced platforming and hate the idea of speedrunning, I wouldn't recommend this game too much for you. Still, there's very small amount of trial & error in this game, so even the first time should be enjoyable.
In top of entertaining gameplay, there's also some really good visuals and the soundtrack is awesome. In 1080p/60fps, this game is one of the most beautiful games ever released. I love the art style, everything looks crisp and detailed, and scenery is just breathtakingly gorgeous, especially in modern sections. Soundtrack is a collection from all of the earlier games, and most of the pieces are remixed versions of the original songs, so it does not feel cheap. You can use default music and feel awesome, but the game makes you to choose background music in stages, so I recommend trying all of the songs.
In Sonic's history, there has been some great games, and then there's been some really bad games. This one is still one of the best ones, and should rise the series' reputation. At least it was my favourite game of the year, back in the day, and I already 100 % it two times. This game just does not get old.

One Way Heroics is adorable, but it's not super deep.
There's enough customization to keep you absorbed for a while. Once you've unlocked all the classes, defeated the demon lord, seen the end of the world, fought the darkness, and seen a few endings... It's not as interesting. The gameplay gets a little repetative, especially considering that an unlucky run might run 5-20 minutes. There's a surprising amount of hidden story in here, but I'm not sure if I'm patient enough to see it all.
But it's so cheap. So cheap. I got it for less than a dollar. For that amount, it's worth it. I've gotten about 8 hours of fun out of it so far, and that's *definitely* worth a buck.
The DLC is... meh. It makes the game harder. In the original game, a "friendly settlement" will usually include a save girl and someone selling food. In the DLC, it might be a merchant, a trainer, a mercenary, or lots of other things that won't feed you. Also, your food rots and raw meat poisons you. All this  means that running out of food is a *way* bigger issue in the DLC than in the original.
The DLC's okay--you get some classes, more achievements, and probably more plot--but I don't find it as enjoyable as the original game.

I seriously enjoy this game. One of my favorite aspects of a randomly generated world is the fact that you're not going to see everything the first play through... Or the second play through... Or even the twenty-second! I still have not figured out how to recruit other party members during the journey, but I'm fine with that because I've been so preoccupied with discovering all the other things you can do with different classes.
Speaking of classes, I normally hate class systems in an RPG. When you have to devote to one for the entire game and you're not even sure if it's your favorite because you haven't got to try the others yet. But in One Way Heroics, many runs are fairly short, so you can try every class that you like. Get a feel for all of them. Then play the one you feel like playing based on your mood. It's kind of like a fighter game in that aspect; you pick a character based on the kind of match you expect to have.
Another great thing about the classes in One Way Heroics is the fact that they all have something unique and interesting to bring to the table. Each has a special skills, and each has regular skills that they perform better or with a bonus. It's balanced pretty well and it makes picking a favorite for your style of play easy.
The variety of items is the last good point I'd like to touch on. One thing I almost always start out with is increased inventory ability, because I love picking up as many items as I can and using them effectively. One Way Heroics exhibits great balance between character stats and the necessity for equipment. You can make your character strong, sure, but if you don't find a rare and powerful weapon or some really good armor, you're going to be running from the demon lord many times before you can hope to fight him.
The one down side to this game I'll mention is the character design. The artwork is a little sloppy looking, though charming in it's own way, and the character dialog, while funny at first, is a little lacking in terms of variety. Well. during gameplay anyway--Dialog is actually pretty good during cut scenes, as I am hit with something new almost every new game and end game. Finally characters feel a little flat. Even though the after story of you and the fairy continuing your journey after the world is saved is rather touching, it feels awkward because I don't really feel connected to the characters. They're too generic, but then, maybe that was intended.
All in all, great game. 9/10

Hard to recommend the game, but still do:
Amazing concept, awful execution.
The joy of the game is the feeling you get running/jumping/swinging through mid-air in death defying stunts and grabbing hold of a bit of floating rock just in time! However, the level design is glitchy and you can’t tell which bits of floating rock are in range or not. So, that amazing experience is mired by a frustrating fall to your doom again and again and again. It’s hard to keep the momentum going and spoils the experience. Level design typically has one path for the player to take, despite seeming open for problem solving. Forcing that one in-game path only exacerbates the frustration from falling just short of where your creativity wants to take you.
It’s one of the few games where I actively ran past optional in game collectible so get to the end.
But that actual ending though, straight shot to the heartstrings. Voice acting is wooden, sure, but not without its charm.
It’s only a 5-hour game, tops. Buy it if it’s on sale for no more than $3-$4. Great potential if the developers wanted to use this concept in a cleaner style.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong, the third installement in the Shadowrun reboot.
The game is based (just like previous installments) around a protagonist whom gets his/her bum marked as a shadowrunner after bad happenings.  Along the way, the player meets new NPCs, gets info around the current predicament and trots around the hub to talk with people or buy items.
The game's heavy on dialogue, choices and repercussions, just like in the previous installments.
If you're a fan of Shadowrun, then this is quite an easy pickup. If not, I'd highly suggest to start with Shadowrun Returns and Dragonfall.
What I liked about the game is that it's story rich, much like the previous games. The atmosphere is great, the hub area is rather nice to explore. The NPCs are alright, the alternative storylines are alright... And that's sadly it.
There are several NPCs to choose from and have dialogue with. Sadly, aside from 2, they all fall under the 'meh, seen this character before' category. Aside from those 2, I personally didn't care much about their predicament.
Sure, some of it was like: Woah, what's going on... But it fell so flat on its♥♥♥♥♥♥ because it later got the 'we've done it, yay' treatment.
The missions that the player can pick up are, for the most part, well done. Some turn into a complete nightmare, but unlike the previous installments, it's not as well worked out this time around.
It feels more 'safe' compared to the previous installments. There's only 2 missions where I was generally taken by how things turned out (only to be classified as 'yay, we done did it' in the end) which is a huge letdown.
The focus was probably more on the combat and hacking. The combat is amazing, hands down. It's fluid in nearly every way eventhough it feels a little easy.
The hacking is a lot faster and it feels more down to earth. Yet... Did we really need to get a memory game and then a sequence of markings?
The ending is lackluster. I saw it coming a mile away. Not because this is another installment of Shadowrun, but because the game didn't even try to mask it. I do like that there are several different options, but the general showdown felt weak.
The pacing of this game has to be the most horrible thing I've experienced in the last 2 years though.
I felt myself becoming really bored after playing it for a while. You go on a mission which doesn't take 15 minutes, then hang around the hub area for an hour, reading arbitrary dialogues.
Then there's the 'role playing' aspect. I'll compare this to Fallout New Vegas and Fallout 4, because this game does the exact same thing. Aside from some decisive factors, 80% of what you say/respond, doesn't even matter.
The big choices issue has even broken the game in 1 level, where you can't proceed if you didn't spend the right karma points.
Another reason I couldn't play the game in long runs, is, because it's a dialogue heavy game... With LOADS of typos in it. It doesn't just come down to a letter wrong here and there... There are whole sentences that aren't proper English. There are commas missing, misspelled words littering every conversation, as well as plain lazy writing.
As a big fan of Dragonfall, this is a major disapointment. I found myself not caring for some of the dialogue anymore, even when it sort of started to become interesting... (And then it usually dried out right after in most cases).
All in all, even if the review seems mostly negative, because this installment's a huge step down from the previous ones, this is still a pretty enjoyable game. The combat feels good and responsive, the atmosphere is great and it feels like a Shadowrun game. It just lacks what made the previous installments a great game.
I'll not play it again for a while, unless, perhaps, the pacing gets improved and the numerous typos get fixed.
I don't mind a typo here and there, but like I said, the game is riddled with it.
On that note though, the sound and music effects in the game are well done. Some even improved from the previous versions I might add. But I still wonder why my heavy pistol sounds like a dart gun...

When I backed Harebrained Schemes' Shadowrun Returns Kickstarter campaign in April 2012, I had no idea that Jordan Weisman's young studio would eventually become one of my favourite RPG developers. While I was actually disappointed in Shadowrun Returns, Dragonfall more than made up for it and I still believe that it is one of the best recent CRPGs. With that in mind, I had high expectations of Shadowrun: Hong Kong yet Harebrained Schemes did not disappoint. The Hong Kong campaign offered everything I liked about Dragonfall but on a bigger scale. It is hard to discuss the story without spoiling the experience and as satisfying as the main campaign is, it's the side-missions that I enjoyed the most. Here the improvements over Dragonfall are the most apparent as there is very little repetition. Each mission is memorable in its own right, whether you're intentionally disrupting the flow of Qi in a corporate office or kidnapping a from a gaudy seafood restaurant. There are always multiple approaches to take, shortcuts to find and relevant party dialogues to experience. Speaking of party members, the shadowrunners of Hong Kong are just as interesting as those of Berlin and you can spend hours arguing and discussing transhumanism or poetry with your party members. Overall, Shadowrun: Hong Kong is an excellent game. If you like traditional isometric CPRGs like Fallout 2 or Planescape: Torment, if you enjoy turn-based combat and if you have the patience to exhaust every dialogue choice for every NPC, you will enjoy this game.

A somewhat dissapointing game after Dragonfall.
Overall: not recommended, some game changes that have not been made good enough for release, a poorly integrated and not especially interesting story, some small improvements over past games but not enough of them
The new hacking system is an easy, uninteresting puzzle game that doesn't seem to scale with difficulty (easy even on Hard mode). So it just becomes an annoying delay.
The use of realtime stealth mechanics in the hacking system is a bad choice, the game engine is not suited to realtime mechanics and is also quite jarring to include when everything else dangerous is turn-based.
The inability to use programs outside of combat is also annoying, as that is exactly the time you most want to use repair programs or security supression programs and it doesn't make any sense for it to be barred out of combat.
The game still has the problems of the past games of being quite slow-paced, with lots of tedious running back and forth between vendors and quest givers without anything interesting on the journey.
The dialogue is also quite restrictive and doesn't often reveal interesting information. The options are all very heavily "toned", kind of telling you who your character is a bit too much, not leaving you much freedom to play a character.
The good points are pretty limited:
* some interesting new cyberware ideas (though the magnet arm is a laughable concept, it's at least an interesting and useful option to have)
* they fixed the problem with the enemy always shooting first while your guys are standing dumbly in the open (since you were in dialogue mode not tactical mode at the start of combat), they normally either move into cover on their first go or you get to go first, which is a welcome change
* you can initiate combat without going through dialogue! a much-needed addition!
* you can trade items between party members
(spoilers)
The story is not well integrated and thought out. For example when you utterly wreck the mission with the whampoan council by killing the council, you barely get a slap on the wrist from the *ruthless triad boss* employing you. I at least expected to have to convince her not to exact punishment (like by explaining that the ghoul is a good asset + the council are unreliable liars so better that they be replaced). In addition the actual investigation into the whampoan council is somewhat dissapointing in the "investigation" side of it. There is no real puzzle or deduction to the game and I find I can just keep clicking through without thought.
edit:
I have now attempted playing the extended edition campaign. I say "attempted" because I couldn't bear to finish.
Within minutes I was finding sloppy proofing errors in the dialogue, extra words in the middle of sentences, dialogue that makes no sense. The player is forced into a mission and given no option of resistance or any good reason why they should do it (not everyone is evil enough to hurt people just for revenge). It railroads the character.
This could be tolerated if the gameplay is good, but it isn't. I didn't play very long but I soon found fights had no clear indication of what the parameters of the fight are so you're left guessing blindly and only find out what you missed when you fail to do the thing you didn't know you needed to do...
Overall. The expansion seems like a sloppy, half-hearted attempt at meeting their KS obligations. I am increasingly disappointed by HBS.

First off let me say... Amazing!!! A huge thank you to the developers and backers of this title, what a stupendous job!
I was a huge fan of the original River City Ransom, and, like many others, always hoped a sequel would be released. Almost 3 decades later we finally have that sequel, and it was worth the wait.
Right from the introduction, it truly feels like you are back in River City. The characters are well done, with great new fighting styles. The levels are beautiful and really help to draw you in.The story was well done in my opinion, keeping in mind what the original story was, and flowing right into this one. I enjoyed the new challenges added, they gave the series a new level of difficulty in all the right ways. I also enjoyed the boss fights, they were challenging on the first playthrough, but really fun, and I really liked their moves. Plenty of classic River City fun, with a healthy mix of new, yet somehow familiar material, that holds true to the original style in every way. Solo, Co-Op, Arena... yea it's all here. There are a few bugs, but these can easily be fixed in updates and should not deter you. One bothersome thing was the in-game move lists for all the story characters were either lacking explanation, or just wrong. I have posted a guide on how to correctly do the moves, I hope it helps to take away the only frustrating aspect of the game, although I suppose these could also be updated. The story does get dry towards the end. The main villain is just thrown in, with no back story or legitimate connections. The boss fight is fun and challenging however, and i thoroughly enjoyed the ending. Nice nod to Contra 3, don't think I didn't notice.
In conclusion, I highly recommend this game. Whether you are a fan of the original or a newcomer to the series, if you feel like kicking some serious butt and having a blast doing it, this is the game for you.
Side Note: If anyone knows where to get an extra Nes cartridge copy of this game, please let me know. I didn't hear about this being in the works until it was to late to help on the kickstart, so I missed out on a copy.
By the way Rollingwood Station and Merville Station have there names switched. Still throws me off...

I've gotten to level 12 planets and all of the away missions are these pedantic kill squad missions. You have a diplomat, science officer, and engineer on your away team, but your ONLY MISSION IS KILLSQUADS. Just lemme take all Marines, that's all we do. Honestly i did not expect that much - i was just looking for a small sim, not too expensive.
But i was really surprised by this game. First of all you get 4 games in one.
Simulation - Manage and build your base, train your crew and make your visitors happy.
Strategy - Decide which missions to do to get the different resources of the different planets.
Tactical realtime combat - You play with your 5 man landing crew on the planets to solve mission, fight bosses.
RPG - Decide how to develop your crew, equip them with stuff you find or get in missions. Control what they should do, and what not.
All these for parts of the game are more or less lite versions of each genre.
The simulation part makes fun, but it is not so hard - crew members can leave if they are unhappy, but in my game they did not yet. You gain money permanently, but you decide what to spend it on and when - so you should never reach 0. But still their is enough micromanagment possible to make your base work better and better.
They strategy part is nice to have, but easy to handle. If you level your crew up to fast, they demand goods you can only produce with later ressources. So you have to ensure to get this resources quick before your crewmembers leave. You have to decide, if you want to spend money on gather resource or put personal on the systems embassady, to maximize the output of the system.
The tactial realtime combat part makes a lot of fun, i easy at the start but get very difficult later. Each planet can be played in 3 levels, normal, hard and wtf. And if one crew member "dies", he just goes to stasis and can join you later after the mission - so its not so frustating, as you dont lose long trained crew members.
The RPG Part seems to be not so important, but later in the game the importance grows. You have 5 different types of crewclasses and each member has its own "carreer" to get better. Addionally each class hat 6 equipmentslots for equipment of a specific type. The carreer attributes can buff your abilites to work on the station or buff equipmentslots to get additional stats for the missions on the planet. This does not matter at the start. But in my game for example, i recognized with level 22 crew, that my doctor is always close to dying and has a lot less life then all the other crewmembers, even with the best equipment. When i checked his carreer i saw that this guy has 0 % bonus on life, where the other members had 50-90%. But therefor he was a perfect worker, so threw him out of the landing crew and picked up another doctor who was level 20, but had already 65% bonus life.
And in this more then 25 gaming hours i did not find a single bug.... this is really impressive. Ok the pathfinding is not perfect and the crew does not always the most clever thing, but everything work. And each option they a thought of while playing, is already there - but sometimes not easy to find (Sort crew by class would be nice - Ahhh, there is the button on the bottom of the list / Some statistic would be nice - Ahh, below the notifications there statistics to show me almost everything).
I bought this game just for some our between other really good games.... now i have more than 25 gaming hours in less then a week and dont play anything else. So i suggest to buy this game. For me it is PERFECT!
Update 6.4.2015: Played 50 hours now and finished the campaign at normal difficulty. On the 2nd run i will make a lot different - so here some hints:
- Visitors and crew always want to fulfill their highest demand. This means if food is on 40 and sleep on 39, they will run and get sleep, even if they are in the bistro and would be more clever to eat first. After sleeping the will run back to bistro, but wasted much time.
- Each person has different demand and craves. Later it makes sense to reduce rooms which fulfill demand on lower levels. Nevertheless you still need all of them, because some persons want special stuff from low level rooms. Example: Later i build about 10 suites all around the base and deleted my 3 baracks, but kept one. So i force the people to use the better beds to gain more sleep at a time. But some still need the low level soap, so i kept one barrack, without beds, but 2 showers.
- You can build large rooms (you really have enough space), but it makes no sense. You need to build more than one room of the same type at different locations, so people dont waste time to run around your whole base to fulfill 2 or more demands. So i built many small rooms of the same time everywhere.
- Use corridors and security gates. With this you can ensure that vistors and worker dont get into the same areas. This way you can optimize the paths between the rooms for both of them. If you ways go through rooms, this get more difficult and you need to change gate settings many times to build.
- Free your landing crew from production so they gain happiness faster, cause they fulfill demands faster and you can do mission after mission - but let them still be builder for rooms and so on. If they got stuck behind some security gates in the visitors area, they will be free after doing the next mission.
- Free the workers from building, so they dont run long ways between building and production.
- If you feel unpowered, use lemurian sniper rifle and rockets to kite your enemies - it take some time but you will be able too finish each fight successfully.

LISA: The Painful is quite frankly one of the most fun yet devestating rpg maker games I've ever had the JOY of playing. However I honestly believe LISA is a game better played with no plot context, so for that reason I'll leave the plot element at "This plot has legit made me laugh, cry, and feel just uncomfortable enough to say it was disturbing but never to a point where I wanted to quit playing." All of this and enough ambiguity to leave some things up to the player themselves and I'm always down for games that let you come up with your own interpretations of certain elements.
Don't get me wrong, this game would no question go on my personal top 10 list of rpgs (or dare I say any games in general) but the experience is what I would call an aquired taste and it really isn't the type of game I'd reccomend to everyone. But if you've been on the edge of wanting this, think it's your kind of game, I'd say it's worth every damn penny.
Reasons you might really like LISA:
-The story is one of the best I've seen in recent years
-The game in general take inspiration from Earthbound and actually pulls it off really effectively
-Terry Hintz
-Decisions in a game that actually drastically effect gameplay as opposed to feeling weightless to the overall experience
-A fish lawyer on legs
-The difficulty never goes into the "Impossible" territory, It's always pretty much in the "hard but fair" range.
-30+ Party members for a lot of combination potential
Reasons you might NOT like LISA:
-The game works off a high amount of dark humor, which works well for the setting but isnt really everyone's cup of tea
-Laaaaaarge amounts of gore/body horror, again, not everyone's jam
-Family abuse is a really heavy and prominant theme of the game
-Mandatory Russian Roulette (with permadeath)
-The ability to savescum might make some of the game's choices a little less impactful, but that's more of a personal play preference thing.
-You'll cry
-A lot
-No I'm serious you're gonna cry I promise.

In Early Access: Incredibly underpolished game.

Are they based on opinion? Yes, what review isn't. Freedom of speech is a thing, guys. The internet would be rather boring if you were only permitted to post positive outlooks.
Graphics:
Graphics in this game, are decent, with polished textures. However, the animations can be a little underdevelopped, such as running, but what do you expect from an Early Access game? I'm sure they'll tweak it once the game's fully prepared. However, in terms of graphics in general? Mechanics/Game Play
This game has a very innovative, good, and interesting concept, and it is definitely a reason for it being so popular. A game which is entirely about duelling with swords, combining styles and stances to create your own personal sword fighting technique, and testing it out against other players' own fighting styles. The concept was a sell to me, and after watching the preview on the store page? I had to give it a shot.
But it is really painful, to see that the execution of the concept, is sorely lacking ;~;
I hope, yet again, that I can just slap the 'EARLY ACCESS!' sticker on it, and expect it to get refined in the future. Don't get me wrong. I 'want' it to get refined. I 'like' this style of game, truly, why else would I have it!? But right now, the mechanics are bulky at best, and require some intensely impressive keyboard sorcery to manage the wrist breaking controls effectively.
Stances are options to increase the level of customization you can do with your technique, enabling you to pick and choose what attacks work for you, and which don't. Something I personally have trouble with, is the way you change stances. Considering how they expect you to change stances 4-7 times depending on the level of difficulty you're trying to master, and that you either change stances by the 1,2,3 buttons, or scrolling your mouse wheel? When you have to move around to keep yourself out of your opponents reach, it can become difficult to both manage WASD as well as 1 2 3.
They have also added some eye-candy features to the combat styles which, I think, are honestly not neccesary, such as flashy dance-type animations that makes it take longer to actually strike. The female character in the game, appears to be dancing more than fighting, and it quickly gets frustrating when your 'to the point' opponent strikes 5 times where you strike 3 times.
The choice of swords you can use here is actually pretty awesome. No 2 swords are identical, and to add some extra customization options to your style, you have around 4-5 different types of sword to choose from, such as standard medieval long swords, to japanese katanas, to central european rapiers, and more. I actually like this idea, but what I don't understand, is how they've decided to base the general 'combat style' (how your character moves) on what character you choose, not what weapon.
For example: I like the look of the female character, but I don't really like the way she fights, her spinning and jumping etc. It blocks the view, and makes it less enjoyable, and harder, for me personally. I much prefer the combat style of one of the male characters, who does dashes, and super quick forward attacks. I wish the attack patterns were based on the sword type you use (Slashing for Katanas, thrusting for rapiers, and a jack of all trades for the longsword). I personally think that'd make the game more fair, and add another element of customization.
Instead, you're forced to choose your physical appearance based on the character's fighting style. I don't like this too much.
Lore/Storyline
Far as I know? There is none. I havn't seen any evidence yet of a storyline to explain the appearance of the characters, why they're fighting, or what the ultimate goal is, nor what their pasts are. I may be wrong, and simply missed it(I plan to give this game some more time to redeem itself to me), but black on white, I can't find it. As an RPG/Lore fan, I like when my game has an answer to the worlds simplest question, the first question a child asks after grasping the basics of speech: Why? A game that cannot answer this question, or won't answer it, cause it considers it redundant, or pointless to the bigger picture, is not a game I'm very interested in. A game where you're given an armor, a sword, a place, and an opponent, and expected to simply raise your sword and strike them down, because that's just the goal of the game? I apologise, but to me, that's just shallow, as I like to know 'why' I'm raising my sword to strike them down, before I actually do it.
Overall?
I won't recommend this game, RIGHT NOW! Since it's in early access, changes are bound to happen, and just like with Warframe, the much desired melee combat rework was done in combat 2.0 recently, which made the game far more desirable, and true to its nature. This game? In my opinion it needs alot of work, both in balance, concept reconsideration, and immersion. As it is now, the game is trying to do too many things, much too quick, and it makes the game appear as if trying to be made of gold, when it's honestly just a really fancy brass.
As is, I can't claim it to be worth it's pricetag. Perhaps if it was free? I'd say its worth a shot. But if you want a game with fun combat, and customization oppertunities? I'd rather recommend Warframe for you. Somewhat the same concept...Samurai in full body armors that're customizable, who can pick and choose weapons. Except Warframe is primarily Co-op player(s) vs. AI, whilst this is kind of like Warframe's PvP brother, Player vs. Player, little to no A.I.
Hopefully, I can make this a thumbs up in the near future. \o

Blade Symphony
Everyone loves swords. There is just something appealing about being a master swordsman able to slice through enemies like paper. It might just be my fascination with weaponry; it might be that I'm currently watching a lot of sword related TV; it might just be that swords are universally appealing. Whatever the reason, I have desired a way to legally satisfy my urges. The practical output of this is that I will buy almost any game which features a sword as a weapon. In some cases this leads to me purchasing the mediocre/dregs of gaming (Shadow Warrior), but sometimes I end up with a game in which I truly feel like the mighty warrior I am (Mount & Blade). Thankfully, Blade Symphony falls into the second category.
At its heart, Blade Symphony is a fully 3D sword fighting game. Its low-key release hides a game which has a startlingly deep combat system. The beauty of the game is in how many options are available to you, and finding your own particular style within that. While the game only offers 5 sword styles and 4 characters, each offers a unique playing style and combination. The longsword for instance is a heavy hitting blade, with strong but fairly predictable attacks. When combined with the character Phalanx, it makes for a long range, but slow jab. Combine it with Pure however and it becomes a whirlwind of attacks, but with less power and versatility. Finding your own style of play really is the crux of this game.
The combat will feel familiar to anyone whose played games like Jedi Academy, Mount and Blade etc. Attacks are controlled by movement of your character as well as the style or stance you are in. Light attacks are fast and easy to chain, with heavy attacks taking a long time to wind up, but capable of taking enemies down in seconds. While this may seem simple, stances can be changed mid combo, leading to attacks of varying speed. Thankfully, button mashing is heavily punished, and instead timing and bluffing is the order of the day. Characters warily circle each other before hitting out with a few choice attacks, before backing off and reassessing the situation. This makes fights tense and efficient; with neither player wanting to risk an attack which may leave them open.
I say player in this context because currently there is no single player option for the game. Aside from a brief 20 minute training mission, which covers the basic controls and not a lot more, the entirety of the game is online only. There are a number of game modes ranging from the traditional 1v1 duel to my personal favourite the free for all. In this mode, up to 12 players can all enter one arena and battle it out. While this does sometimes happen, what usually occurs is that players group off and challenge each other to 1 on 1 duels while others watch. The beauty of this is it enables you to watch and learn from other players and also use the excellent arenas to form impromptu viewing galleries.
The game does have some glitches, mostly with some slight lag and dodgy wall running. While not game breakers they do detract from the overall polish of the product. The wall running in particular seems to have no real use other than being able to climb around some of the maps, but they don't really seem geared to making use of this in any way. It mostly seems to be in place to add a cool parkour edge to the game, but this falls flat on its face. Every time I attempted it in a fight, my opponent would deliver a swift counter and id be dead before I hit the ground. Two of the fighting styles also seem slightly redundant; relying on one set of spins and flips which just gets endlessly repeated. This tends to take the skill out of the game slightly, and is the one area where button mashing can take a slight foothold.
As a budget game, Blade Symphony offers a surprisingly robust experience with the potential to become a cult classic. The community are great ambassadors for the game, and show respect to new players, with very little bad mouthing or aggressive posturing. For someone looking to sate their need for swordplay, or someone who has grown tired of the usual COD shooters, it represents a worthy alternative.

Agent Tethers is back on the case! Despite having reopened the eraser factory in Scoggins back in Puzzle Agent 1, Tethers is still unconvinced that all is solved in the town. He returns to finally put the case to rest and end the mystery of the little town in the middle of nowhere.
Puzzle Agent 2 plays exactly like it's predecessor, with you playing as Agent Tethers and traveling all over Scoggins to interrogate townsfolk and solve various puzzles you'll come across. The puzzles are again quite varied and will give you a decent challenge, however some are more out there than others. There was one puzzle where I had no choice but to consult Google due to how much mathematical knowledge the games assumes you'll have playing (you'll know it when you see it.) There are also plenty of puzzles that are trickier than in the original so with the exception of those few really obtuse ones, you'll feel a bit more challenged than before.
Without spoiling it, the plot is rather weak... several of the familiar townsfolk do make returns, but they aren't quite as utilized as well as before. They're all pretty much moved aside from the plot come the second half, which is a real shame considering how lovable and off the wall they were in the first game. Also, a lot of the ambiguity in the previous game is stripped away in this game, which may not be such a good thing, in my opinion. Part of what made the original so great for me was the abrupt ending, and the resolution in this game leaves much to be desired.
They recycle a lot of the music in the original, but do manage to add some other tunes, which sadly didn't really stick to me as well the previous game. The animation is still Grickle, which is just as slow and choppy as before, but if you enjoyed the style before, you'll be getting a lot more of it. The voice acting is still top notch.
All in all, this game feels like an expansion to the first one and should really be bundled with the first one when you buy it. I'd wait for a steam sale or humble bundle, but if you have a fix for puzzles that the first one didn't leave completely satisfied, then this game is a must buy.

I played this game with a friend in coop, and when the game wants to run smoothly without issues, it's fantastic. While the story was lacking, the references and comedy were all on point and the game was action packed. I can't wholeheartedly recommend a game where the devs refuse (or straight up ignore) to fix problems that have been causing coop players to crash since the game's release.
One of my minor complaints though is that it feels as if the map was recycled from Saints Row 3, with a few extra features/buildings, although this wasn't that bad to be honest, just wish that there was a lot more on offer. My main issue with the game however, was the constant disconnections and lag spikes that my friend and I experienced, which really took from the enjoyment and overall experience of the game. We found ourselves regularly disconnecting from each other's lobby multiple times, and upon doing some research on the topic, many others have too (especially during Fraud, the final mission, and some others), and apparently this has been a ongoing problem since the game's release. Once you or your partner disconnects from the lobby you're forced to restart the mission from scratch, and during longer missions this becomes 100x more annoying. The first DLC was hilarious, and as for the second, well the constant disconnections made the second one completely unplayable.
The game itself is fun, the powers are amazing and unique, the guns are great, but these problems made the playthrough take 2x as long as it should have, and doing the exact same thing over and over again hoping you don't disconnect is annoying af.
If you plan on playing this with a friend, you should be wary of these issues as they can become really frustrating at times (keep in mind that this doesn't happen to everyone, but has happened to a lot of people), otherwise the game is great, and is also a great solo experience!

Ah the world of organised crime. So fascinating. I'd honestly like to experience the mafia life, you know all the parts that don't involve killing, because I'm a pacifist hippie. But I'm not Italian, or American. So the next best way to experience it -behind The Sopranos and The Godfather trilogy- is Mafia II.
You play as Vito, a typical Italian-American bloke coming home from fighting in ze old country in World War II. You meet up with your best mate Joe, who manages to secure a deal for you so you don't have to fight again. And so you live your life in post-WWII New York City. You do some missions to get a bit of cash, and of course you end up working for the Mafia, and then finally becoming a made man; and official member of the Mafia.
The game is divided into chapters. The first few are set in the Winter of 1945. But then you get into trouble and go to jail for six years. And then the majority of the game is spent during 1951. This is pretty much a Grand Theft Auto-lite game. You can roam around a supposed Manhattan, Empire State and all, but it's absolutely tiny compared to the real thing. However it's a fair size for a video game I suppose.
You do typical mafia work, stealing cars, selling them, whacking guys and whatnot. Each chapter usually begins and ends with you in bed. You wake up, drive somewhere, kill some guys, go back to bed. There is a lot of driving from A to B. But the cars are really nice and classy. I mean, I don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about cars, but these are swankay. They are stiff to handle and weak as♥♥♥♥♥♥ easy to crash and conk out. But I guess that's just part of the realism.
With an excellent era comes an excellent soundtrack. Those developer blokes have secured some top 40's-50's artists. Chuck Berry, Bing Crosby, Buddy Holly, Little Richard, Dean Martin, and many more. Yeah that's right, I know that stuff. Video games taught us, granddad. Most of the game takes place in '51, however most of the songs are from the late 50's, even a couple from the 60's. I guess the guys were trying to make the music aspect a general 50's experience as opposed to a restricted one before rock n' roll started.
The same thing goes for the Playboy magazines. Yes. Spread all over the map are Playboy magazines you can collect. They each contain centrefolds of sexy nude 50's chicks. Makes you think, many of these women must be grandmothers now. Everyone who plays this game is going around collecting and possibly JERKING OFF TO SOMEONE'S NAKED GRANDMA. Anyway, Playboy didn't actually exist until 1953. But I am certainly not gonna complain...
However I must address the flaws. There is bugger-all else to do other than story missions and collecting mags. No assassinations on the side or races (classic hot rods do feature in one mission though). The story is great, however the ending I felt was kinda wanky. I think they were going for an ending akin to The Godfather, where the ending is not apparent, and the cycle of mafia life just goes round and whatnot, I dunno, hard to explain. But it just came across as flat.
Overall a solid game. The post WII America was done really well. I look forward to the next one.

Being a long time RCR fan I was more than excited to see a development team bring us this amazing sequel. This is exactly why the Indie market is so great. I've put over 40 hours into this one and honestly, knowing what I know about what it takes to design a game like this one while staying true to the original; I think they did a terrific job. The fact that they are patching updates as frequently as they are says a lot. The truth of the matter is that a lot of the complaints I'm reading are coming from people who have never even considered the back-end side of development on all the games they normally enjoy. This takes a great amount of team-work and most certainly demands a large amount of time. One thing to remember is that this was not a major development team so expectations of the "fix this now!" is rather ridiculous. All in all (at least from the story perspective) this is a true sequel and a lot of fun to play. The multiplayer problems will certainly be fixed in time but we'll have to be patient.

Some thoughts after doing a playthrough:
Overall I enjoyed the game a lot even though it has some flaws. It did a great job of capturing the feel of the original while improving on it. It was fun, had a good sense of humor, tons of old school references peppered throughout the game and a good selection of fighters with different styles to choose from.
For anyone having some issues with the difficulty, it's best to think of the game just as much of an old school rpg as a brawler. You start out weak without any special moves. Invest a little time in building up your stats and moveset and your character becomes much more effective.
The greatest flaw of the game however, (and a common, valid complaint) is that once you reach a certain stage of the game, the enemies become hyper reactive to all of your attempted moves and movements so the third act becomes this annoying and frustrating dance between you and the npc enemies as you each jockey for position. You rush an emeny, they rush backwards (at great speed). You rush back, they rush forward. You throw a projectile, they jump over it. They will spend more time trying to flank and get behind you than time trying to fight you. A large portion of your moveset effectively becomes useless because you will hardly ever be able to land them which completely defeats the point of saving up for them in the first place.
I suggest getting the game while on sale.

Well, that was painful.
I expected this game to be some walking sim where I could chill out in weird places. At first, it was exactly that, and even though there was some non-walking gameplay somewhat tacked on, I was willing to forgive it since the environments were nice.
Then roughly halfway through it, it became something else.
The dev started to talk. That's understandable. I'm used to semi-autobiographical games about the devs' childhood, their families, their aspirations, their dead parrots, etc. I usually like those games. They're more or less windows opened into another person's world.
Except this time, the window opened into an extremely loquacious teenager's world. I don't think I've witnessed as much angst in all my high school years combined, and I was the kind that wrote bad poetry during math class. I listened politely at first. Then, after I realized the dev's monologue was still going on after like 10 minutes (during which my disembodied character slowly crawled up a ladder while a video was playing in the background), I started to feel annoyed. Later, in another map, when the monologue turned into some cacophonic counterpoint, I wanted to throw bricks at my screen to make it stop. Thankfully, I don't keep a supply of bricks around. I seriously considered turning the sound off though, which is a shame since the game's music is actually good.
I don't know why I bothered to finish the game (maybe something to do with masochism), but I was glad when it was over. Towards the end, I spent more time staring blankly at the screen for the dev to finish his speech than exploring the maps. In a walking sim, that's pretty sad.
+ The environments are interesting. Apparently the assets are all custom-made, which is quite a feat.
+ The music is fitting.
- Very annoying monologues. Their poor audio quality doesn't help either.
- Repeat the previous point five times.
3/10 I don't really like writing negative reviews, but this time I was extremely irritated. Dear dev, if you're reading this review: you're obviously good at expressing yourself through videogame environments, so you don't have to talk our head off while we explore them.

Like many cross-genre games, this one suffers from not deciding which genre to focus on. The squad-based real-time combat portion feels like the controls are incomplete (where's the option to "fight things you run into while moving"?). This suggests that the station construction and management should be the main focus, producing bonuses for the squad to make up for the reduced controls. However, the only bonus that can be gotten from the station is xp, and only at early levels (according to the help screens). This in turn makes the station management seem nearly pointless, in addition to the lack of achievements for doing well at it, as the main goal of managing the station becomes simply supplying all the needs of your away team so that they don't quit on you or go into combat with penalties. The tourists are self-balancing: the only penalty, at least so far, for not satisfying all of their desires is that they arrive more slowly. Station constructions are limited by the away team's adventures, both by the need for tech points (gained from exploration, not building/research) and by the need for resources. So both the combat portion and the building portion are crippled: the former by poor controls; the latter by lack of incentive and challenge.
This is a nice casual game. Has some of the mechanics in old-school city/complex builders; some of the stuff you find in phone games nowadays; and a nice homage to Star Trek adventures.

I'm addicted to The Spatials. This game has elements of some of my favorite classic sim and rpg games. Visually it reminds me of Roller Coaster Tycoon 2, but in space and theres no rides. Start off colonizing an asteroid, and build a station to sustain your crew. Explore nearby planets to obtain resources and credits. After completing the planets mission, use credits to unlock the planets resource nodes to import goods to your station after a time period. Hire new crew members and employ them at the solar system's embassy to reduce the time period it takes to extract resources from the planets in the system. Once you get supplies rolling in start building for guests to visit the station and spend credits, and expand accordingly. Explore the galaxy and unlock alien races to visit your space station, play through missions and discover your enemy. Visitors will be satisfied if they can fulfill their cravings before leaving the station.
It can be very easy to get ahead of yourself in this game, and if you're not careful you can unlock the expansion nodes too early before you have set up incoming resources and will constantly trying to keep products in stock and guests satisfied. I advise new players to unlock the research nodes as your crew members or visitors need them. You can unlock the next level by beating the first planet in the solar system, but skipping planets will limit your production. Also planets have difficulty levels, and clearing a higher difficulty will increase the resources a planet produces per period, so there is replayability even after completing the first levels.
There are two ways to level your crew in the game, by defeating enemies on planets with your away team, or sending crew members out on contracts for experience, resources or items. The contract system is great for hiring new crew and levelling them up to be ambassadors for a solar system's embassy. A strategy I recommend to start is hiring low level crew members as workers, and choose specific ones to level with contracts. As a crew member's level raises, so does their cravings and needs, which take away from production time and takes longer to get in a good mood. Higher level crew members will consume more advanced products which could be sold to guests instead, but also have production bonuses so you will have to balance your worker's levels with your available resources. Also item drops will increase your away crew's power, so equipping higher level items makes a lower level away team stronger.
9/10 I recommend this game to anyone who loves theme park style games and space exploration rpgs. It has a fun and colorful art style. There is room for it to grow, so far I don't think the camera angle can be rotated to see the station from different directons but otherwise its a great start from new devs, thanks guys! I'm hooked.

Lisa: The Painful is an entertaining journey through a post-apocalyptic land called Olathe, where all females have disappeared from the face of the earth.
The story centers on Brad, a middle aged man out to rescue the last female.... his surrogate daughter.
Equal parts humour and drama, the plot can entice you into becoming emotionally invested in Brad and the many quirky and entertaining characters he comes across (which a good twenty or so who can be recruited into helping Brad).
The turn based combat, the soundtrack, the humour, the story and the choices, YOU, the player have to make.
It all comes together to create this wonderful game which can absorb you into this world.
The game covers some pretty mature topics that will test your morals and Brad's, he may be a mostly stoic and driven man, but you will piece together more about him as you go along. You will have an effect to some extent on who Brad is, based on your choices.... but some things are just set in stone.
Addiction, isolation, depression, sadism, murder,♥♥♥♥♥♥ Lisa: The Painful covers all this and more and yet keeps the game balanced in between light and heavy with it's plentiful bouts of jokes and japes throughout.
Combat is kept interesting with plenty of various and sometimes hilarious combat styles that are used by the cast.
The cast, who, apart from Brad, can die in combat and other scenarios. None of them are out of Death's reach.
Soundtrack is quirky and fun, complimenting the game style and scenarios perfectly along with some of the more somber tracks, which help emphasise the emotional moments so well.
While humour can be very subjective, I challenge you to get through this game without laughing or cracking a smile.
There's a little bit of something for everyone in this department.
The game has decent replayability with multiple "bonus endings" should certain conditions be met, forcing at least two playthroughs to see it all and potentially three playthroughs to get all achievements, if you are a perfectionist.

The biggest change Hong Kong makes is to the Matrix system, the virtual world that deckers, Shadowrun’s version of hackers, inhabit whenever they “jack in.” Decking is a common occurrence in these games to collect important data and shut off electronic dangers like turrets and cameras, but it’s no longer just a different coating of paint on the combat system. A stealth system has now been implemented with the player having the ability to avoid detection from patrolling defense programs. Accessing nodes containing information now requires the decker to participate in a mini-game of sorts that involves playing a game of “simon says” with the number pad, and matching an encrypted password that is easier to find depending on how well the decker performed in the previous mini-game. Failure in either the sneaking or the mini-game results in the decker being easier to track in the system, filling up the system trace meter. Getting discovered by a patrol forces you to fight it, and there are still defense programs in certain parts of the Matrix that will automatically attack you when entering an area. While the movement controls aren’t particularly adequate to perform these stealth sections, it is still more than doable. Personally, I’m glad that the Matrix finally feels like its own component and not a re-hash of what’s already in the game. The additional hacking mini-games provide a much welcome change of pace, and at any rate, not going for stealth in the Matrix is still viable albeit more difficult. As it should be.
Aside from the Matrix redesign, not much has changed from Dragonfall, but that’s in no way a bad thing. Hong Kong provides a new campaign, a new setting, a new tileset for those interested in building their own campaigns with the built-in editor, and many incremental improvements to an already good game. Get it if you like Shadowrun, get it if you liked either of the last two games, get it if you like strategy or tactical rpgs.

For some reason, even though I liked Shadowrun Returns and ADORED Dragonfall, Hong Kong felt extremely repetitive and tired, like a copy of something better that I had enjoyed previously. After 15 hours I simply had no motivation to go on. It played like a sweet pulp novel but there was not enough "X Factor" in it to keep me interested or going. Maybe I'm getting old, but reading through page after page of screen text for something that ultimately interests me little, is not my idea of fun anymore.
That being said, the story missions are spot on and "true" Shadowrun. Now if only all that needless merchant NPC exposition and endless companion monologues were somehow more appropriately integrated into the actual flow of those missions, it'd be a most agreeable ride. As it stands, it's good, but comes with heavy reading caveats.

Another great Shadowrun adventure.
Having polished the engine and mechanics with Dragonfall Director's Cut, developers focused on world building and the story. The game is at its most beautiful, music is great, combat is crisp, missions diverse and interesting. Atmosphere sucks you in and you really feel the tension building up to something as the game progresses. The best part? I wasn't disappointed with the conclusion at all. Personally, I find the characters somewhat more alive and peculiar than Dragonfall ones. The game is also more liberal with karma points than Dragonfall so I don't feel as forced into metagaming and can actually allow myself sculpting a roleplayed person and still be an effective runner.
That being said, there's also one major downside that hurts replayability. Harebrained really went overboard with text and exposition to the point where it feels as if you're spending more time reading than doing actual runs. Even if you click through most conversations it still takes a lot of time to visit everyone between missions. This makes Dragonfall feel much more focused and intense. (In particular I feel the whole Ka Fai family business could've and should've been cut. Maybe Spider Shen too.)
One more minor gripe of mine is that the engine isn't particularly well suited for the new stealth mechanics in the matrix and one of the missions. It's bearable at best, but some of the more tricky and complex sections had me savescumming in frustration at how my character was moving. Although overall I like the new matrix minigame. It certainly makes me feel more engaged.
These two issues are why I wouldn't rate the game at 10 (for the record, I named Dragonfall Director's Cut my game of the year for 2014). But then again, despite these the game is certainly worth at least one playthrough for the story and definitely more if you're into Shadowrun and/or turn based combat by Harebrained. Can't wait for the promised mini-expansion.

I backed this game, and definitely enjoy it, but it isn't the crown jewel of this series by any means.
Hong Kong tries to take all of the things that were good about Dragonfall and adds more of it.  This is nice, because you have more game, but in some ways, it really kills the balance, especially in the writing. There's no arguing the writing is great -- I think it's what made Dragonfall, and the quaility remains. However, in Dragonfall, the mission and dialogue balance was very nice. It really felt like it would shift to one game element, just as you would start to fill up on another. This is a rare and beautiful thing. Some of the new additions to the matrix also seem a little bit too involved for what it should be. Having to play Simon to hack through nodes sort of pulls you out of the experience I feel.
Hong Kong is very 'clicky'. Just finish a mission. Great. TIme for clicky. Clicky through the fixer's dialogue: clicky through the musings of every party NPC, (you don't want to miss anything right?) clicky through the people at the nightclub, clicky through the dudes playing games on the dock, clicky through the computer and BBS to get your money, etc. On first play, this is probably fine, but on subsequent plays it gets old. It's sort of annoying, because the new additions to character customization are very cool, and you'll probably want to replay with a new build.
I only gripe on it because its legacy is so good though... As a package, Hong Kong does a good job of keeping the classic-style CRPG game alive, and is a great entry in the Shadowrun universe and cyberpunk for those interested in either. Though, ultimately, It's shadowed by the greatness of its older brother.

So after playing this game for a good little bit, I have found that this game could easily be one of those games that you could play to kill time, ALOT of time.
One of my friends sent me the game and expansion as a gift through Steam, and I tell you what, It's quite an amazing game especially for use old heads that like our RPGs and video games in general with a more retro feel to them. The graphics, by today's standards, aren't the super realistic HD sculptures that a lot of people have come to expect from video games. Instead, the graphics are more of a 16-bit sprites with beautiful choices of color palettes throughout the game. It is very easy to tell when you traverse through different environments, desolate deserts, cold artic tundra, lush beautiful forests and plains. The guards, townsfolk, and inhabitants of the world are just as carefully designed and all look unique.
Probably one of the biggest things that makes this game so great is the gameplay. Imagine a Japanese Style Action RPG with a lot of Rogue like aspects that do nothing, but add to replay value of the game. Everything can be randomized, and like most Rogue Likes perma death is a real thing. About the only thing that you can save, aside from the game, is your character's inventory, or rather a select few items to continue playing with. You get a super awesome sword that when roots your enemies and burns them to death, and you don't really want to let it go? Well there's something called a deminisonal vault that you can use to keep that sword through multiple playthroughs.
Speaking of that deminisonal vault, the way you get it, and use it is through things called Hero Points. You acquire Hero Points by either completing a full run of the game, or dying. If you die, by some random Dragon Knight in a structure you were checking for loot, drowning in water, or trying to climb to the point of exhaustion and just collapsing. There's also one other very unique way of dying. In this game, you visit a town and you can't revist it, you can't go back the way you came at all. This is because the Dark Lord (boss of the game) is spreading darkness throughout the realm, you touch the darkness and you die. Well the screen scrolls to the right, just like an old school platformer, but instead of being able to go back you can't because of the darkness, if you try, you die. This adds for a significant amount of challenge, you can easily get stuck in areas of the game because of mountains, walls, or whatever other obstacle that impedes your travel, and the darkness catches up and you die. Actually, every action you take, wether it's attacking an enemy, moving, using an item, casting a spell, or whatever moves the darkness closer towards you.
The Plot is a throw a way plot you are X hero out to slay the Dark Lord and stop the spread of the darkness throughout the world. There's other campaigns that you can do that are fixed maps that have their own story as well, but it follows the same formula.
Probably one of the coolest things about the game is Character Creation. At the beginning of the game you start with two classes, a Swordmaster Class and a Knight Class. You can chose what your sprite looks like, and also give your character perks to help with his stats, or whatever skills you have for the class. You start with three perk slots, but as you play you can unlock up to five perks. Puzzle Agent 2 is a game marred by plot inconsistencies and an unsatisfying story. While the characters and atmosphere pull the player in, the gameplay and story problems are overwhelming.
After competing Puzzle Agent 1, I was excited to play the sequel. Unfortunately, this game doesn't hold up. The story has suffered, as the overloaded plot crashes and burns in a chaotic confusion, leaving plothole debris everywhere. A list of which includes:
The list goes on. This is totally unacceptable and unprofessional story-writing. You can beat the game in under 2 hours (I've played the game a couple times to get all the achievements) and the number of plot-holes is unbelieveable. Why else would a game so short have a plot explanation on Wikipedia that's as long as a PhD dissertation?
I've heard great things about Telltale's more recent work, but there's still no excuse because Puzzle Agent 1 was satisfying as far as story goes. Yes, there were loose ends and mysteries at the conclusion, but the main goals were achieved and the mysteries were largely related to things out of Tether's control the whole time: He couldn't understand this odd little town, and he never would. It was over his head, and he caught a glimpse of something greater than he could ever imagine. The player is left intrigued. In Puzzle Agent 2, parts of the mystery are revealed and simply make no sense, leaving the player very frustrated.
The biggest problem with the first game were that the puzzles were inconsistent in difficulty and clarity. Here, it seems the difficulty has been smoothed out a bit, but they have lost variety and at times still have difficult to interpret rules. The biggest problem I had was that the puzzles had little to do with the story and actually broke the pace.
Not to say I disliked everything. Sheriff Bahg was my favorite antagonist from the first game, and his condescending skepticism of the meek FBI man Tethers is always so well-played. The voice acting for Bahg is excellent. The atmosphere in the game also retains it's X-files allure, and Tethers searching for clues is still exciting. Korka was an interesting new character, and she gave the story some funny payoff and comedy relief. I always liked Tethers as a character; he's an excellent straightman in a world full of insane people. He also always has this idiotic confused look on his face that's actually pretty endearing.
ACHIEVEMENTS: Since this is a point-and-click adventure game, this is pretty hard to screw up, but Telltale pulled it off. One achievement requires a perfect run of all puzzles in the game. Even if you beat the game with one failed attempt at one puzzle and go back to that puzzle after the conclusion of the story, it doesn't matter. You have to open a new file and play the entire game over and do everything perfectly. Kind of a waste of time.
Overall, the game is atmospheric, exciting and well-acted, but the gameplay and story problems are too great for these high points to overcome. Not recommended unless heavily discounted, you have played the prequel, and are looking for achievements.

I played this game with a friend in coop, and when the game wants to run smoothly without issues, it's fantastic. While the story was lacking, the references and comedy were all on point and the game was action packed. I can't wholeheartedly recommend a game where the devs refuse (or straight up ignore) to fix problems that have been causing coop players to crash since the game's release.
One of my minor complaints though is that it feels as if the map was recycled from Saints Row 3, with a few extra features/buildings, although this wasn't that bad to be honest, just wish that there was a lot more on offer. My main issue with the game however, was the constant disconnections and lag spikes that my friend and I experienced, which really took from the enjoyment and overall experience of the game. We found ourselves regularly disconnecting from each other's lobby multiple times, and upon doing some research on the topic, many others have too (especially during Fraud, the final mission, and some others), and apparently this has been a ongoing problem since the game's release. Once you or your partner disconnects from the lobby you're forced to restart the mission from scratch, and during longer missions this becomes 100x more annoying. The first DLC was hilarious, and as for the second, well the constant disconnections made the second one completely unplayable.
The game itself is fun, the powers are amazing and unique, the guns are great, but these problems made the playthrough take 2x as long as it should have, and doing the exact same thing over and over again hoping you don't disconnect is annoying af.
If you plan on playing this with a friend, you should be wary of these issues as they can become really frustrating at times (keep in mind that this doesn't happen to everyone, but has happened to a lot of people), otherwise the game is great, and is also a great solo experience!

Ah the world of organised crime. So fascinating. I'd honestly like to experience the mafia life, you know all the parts that don't involve killing, because I'm a pacifist hippie. But I'm not Italian, or American. So the next best way to experience it -behind The Sopranos and The Godfather trilogy- is Mafia II.
You play as Vito, a typical Italian-American bloke coming home from fighting in ze old country in World War II. You meet up with your best mate Joe, who manages to secure a deal for you so you don't have to fight again. And so you live your life in post-WWII New York City. You do some missions to get a bit of cash, and of course you end up working for the Mafia, and then finally becoming a made man; and official member of the Mafia.
The game is divided into chapters. The first few are set in the Winter of 1945. But then you get into trouble and go to jail for six years. And then the majority of the game is spent during 1951. This is pretty much a Grand Theft Auto-lite game. You can roam around a supposed Manhattan, Empire State and all, but it's absolutely tiny compared to the real thing. However it's a fair size for a video game I suppose.
You do typical mafia work, stealing cars, selling them, whacking guys and whatnot. Each chapter usually begins and ends with you in bed. You wake up, drive somewhere, kill some guys, go back to bed. There is a lot of driving from A to B. But the cars are really nice and classy. I mean, I don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about cars, but these are swankay. They are stiff to handle and weak as♥♥♥♥♥♥ easy to crash and conk out. But I guess that's just part of the realism.
With an excellent era comes an excellent soundtrack. Those developer blokes have secured some top 40's-50's artists. Chuck Berry, Bing Crosby, Buddy Holly, Little Richard, Dean Martin, and many more. Yeah that's right, I know that stuff. Video games taught us, granddad. Most of the game takes place in '51, however most of the songs are from the late 50's, even a couple from the 60's. I guess the guys were trying to make the music aspect a general 50's experience as opposed to a restricted one before rock n' roll started.
The same thing goes for the Playboy magazines. Yes. Spread all over the map are Playboy magazines you can collect. They each contain centrefolds of sexy nude 50's chicks. Makes you think, many of these women must be grandmothers now. Everyone who plays this game is going around collecting and possibly JERKING OFF TO SOMEONE'S NAKED GRANDMA. Anyway, Playboy didn't actually exist until 1953. But I am certainly not gonna complain...
However I must address the flaws. There is bugger-all else to do other than story missions and collecting mags. No assassinations on the side or races (classic hot rods do feature in one mission though). The story is great, however the ending I felt was kinda wanky. I think they were going for an ending akin to The Godfather, where the ending is not apparent, and the cycle of mafia life just goes round and whatnot, I dunno, hard to explain. But it just came across as flat.
Overall a solid game. The post WII America was done really well. I look forward to the next one.
