There's always been a huge audience for anything related to the Mafia, but with an increasing number of people looking out for such things, we've seen more than a few unneeded spin-offs to what an Italian Mafia story was meant to be; luckily Mafia II returns to the roots of that concept, just like the game before it, concentrating once again on making a name for yourself in a corrupt world. The takes place in the fictional city of Empire Bay, inspired by the look of major U.S cities like New York and Chicago during the 50's, including some of the major landmarks from the real world and combining them with a unique map design that makes Empire Bay feel like a real place in space and time. The map here is enormous and with that comes the main problem while you're out exploring it as it feels empty for most parts, and to be honest during the story there are lots of well-made locations that you'll probably never visit unless you're just into exploring without actually doing missions or challenges. The lack of side missions or challenges is clearly felt in this one, and that has nothing to do with the story being organized in chapters whatsoever, but it feels disappointing that even after you're done with the amazing story there is nothing else to keep you roaming on the streets of Empire Bay. On the brighter side, this is probably one of the best stories you've seen in years, and 2K does a great job introducing you into the world controlled by the Mafia in the late 40's all up to the 50's. Everything about the atmosphere of that time period seems right and this is one of those stories that will probably remain in your mind for a very long time. You play as Vito Scaletta, a veteran finding himself back into Empire Bay after suffering an injury during the war and being sent back home for a while, time which extends permanently once he gets in touch with some old friends. The menus are easy to browse and the loading screens will get by you pretty fast; in addition to that you can view all your collectibles in the game from the main menu. The characters are well-made and have personality in every single aspect, although having the ability to change certain decisions would've been nice, adding to the replay value, but the story is awesome enough to be worth your time as it is.
There's not a lot of diversity in gameplay here as you'll probably spend most of your time in cover, trying to aim a headshot towards an enemy who is also hiding in cover or getting him while he's advancing for another place of cover. There is nothing wrong with that as the game is fun to play and the controls work well in that environment, but don't expect to rush into a group of enemies without strategy and succeed, because it probably won't happen. There are a few moments in the story where the basic cover shoot-out will be replaced by activities like lockpicking cars, throwing molotovs and so on, but those are few and easy to forget. On the bright side, the range of weapons that you have at your disposal and new ones that will constantly keep showing up as you advance the story forward will keep making things more interesting, starting from basic things like pistols and later moving on to epic mafia weaponry such as the Tommy Gun. Even with the shooting mechanic as basic as it is, the environment in which it takes place changes the strategy every time, as lesser cover spots will require you to stay longer in one place and snipe out everyone in your range, while plenty of cover will give you the opportunity to move more freely and surprise your enemies from behind. Driving around the town is fun and there are plenty of cars to try out and upgrade to make your collection bigger, but unfortunately those services are only meant to provide a few minutes of extra fun after you've completed the main story as you'll probably ignore those features at all the first time you play through the campaign since you will be too preoccupied following the story, and since there are no additional missions apart from those following the main plot, there is little reason to take a break from the story. The thing that will keep you going in this game is the motivation to see how the story unfolds, and even if there's nothing much else to do after completing the story, robbing stores, evading cops and challenging achievements will keep you going for a while.
The landscape of Empire Bay looks amazing, leaving you drooling over the beautifully detailed buildings and admiring just how authentic everything looks, despite areas being so empty due to the lack of side missions or challenges. There is detail to everything you'll find in the city: the cars look as they did in the 50's, the city features old landmarks like The Brooklyn Bridge or The Empire State Building combined with other digitally created locations that make the city feel alive. The main characters certainly look like they're out of the 50's and the one thing this games does best is to keep you attached to them. Throughout your playthrough you'll encounter lots of different characters from different families in the Mafia, each one being unique and keeping you interested in their personal stories as well as their own part in the main story that the game wants to tell. Unfortunately this realism of characters will often be interrupted by bad facial animations and even worse lip syncing.
The voice acting is well done, having Italian accents specific to the time period and the birthplace of the characters, and combined with the amazing dialogue and the lines that never get old, including Mafia classics, the experience doesn't get any better than this. The soundtrack is amazing including hit tracks from the 50's divided into 3 radio stations that you can change whenever you want while in the car. The use of certain tracks during mission makes the sadness of someone getting shot feel authentic and make you experience what being a gangster really felt like. With very few exceptions, the sound effects are a blast for the ear and a pleasure to hear over and over again, especially those classic Tommy Gun shots that you're already familiar with from Mafia movies.
There are lots of collectibles in the game, some which you'll have to find across the city and others awarded for completing a mission on a certain difficulty level. If you're hunting for achievements or simply want to see all the playboys, this will keep you occupied for a while, however the lack of multiplayer or leaderboards for missions is felt, and after collecting everything it will take you a while to jump into the story all over again. The difficulty levels on the other side are well done and it's a good addition if you want to replay the story on a higher difficulty level.
This is an amazing experience if you like killing people and Mafia related stuff; too bad the game does suffer from the lack of extra content to keep you engaged into the game even after completing the story. If you are looking for a brilliant story this is a must buy no doubt, and with the price being lowered since its release it's probably worth your bucks.

The ability to reaccomplish missions and the contract system makes it fairly easy to level a new crew up in your current ones get disgruntled enough to leave.
Not for someone looking for a fast paced game.

***This review was written using a key provided by the Developer for review purposes***
The Spatials is a space station building sim crossed with an isometric ARPG meets Tycoon game which recently released on Steam. In The Spatials not only do you build a space station on an asteroid to satisfy guests and earn their hard earned cash you also take a crew of brave men and women on hundreds of missions across an expansive randomly generated galaxy. Completing missions earns you valuable resources and money which can be used back at your space station or, in the case of money, can be invested into planets where you have completed missions in order to regularly receive supplies.
+Simple and colourful graphics which suit the game well and look nice
+Easy to follow tutorials which are very helpful in teaching you the basics of the game
+Great UI which is very easy to navigate
+Building is very easy thanks to the grid that appears when building and it's also very easy to correct mistakes if you accidentally build something in the wrong place
+A reasonably sized Tech tree with a good variety of things to unlock over the course of your game
+The galaxy is randomly generated each time you start a new game and contains over 100 planets with increasingly challenging away missions
+Missions on planets have you go around completing objectives such as killing enemy pirates or destroying guard towers
+When on missions I found the combat to be fun though it seems not everyone would agree with me on that
+A good number of different room types and objects for your space station
+You're provided with a simple breakdown of what your staff as well as visitors want while they are at your space station
+After completing missions you are able to spend your money unlocking resource slots which then provide you with whatever resources that planet has every few minutes
+A large number of weapons and upgrades to be found on missions for your crew to use making them stronger
+Simple controls when on away missions
-It's very hard to earn money early on and I often found myself just sitting idle while I waited for more money to be spent in my space station so I could buy something
-It's not in the slightest bit challenging. Firstly, your crew can never die on an away mission, if they run out of HP they simple get beamed back to the ship and then they're perfectly fine for the next mission. Secondly, there's no environmental dangers or any enemies where your space station is nothing to slow your progress or make it harder like there are in similar games. Finally, even if your visitors are unhappy they still spend money while visiting your space station so it's impossible to ever run out of money
Verdict:
8
A great building/ARPG/Tycoon game with nice, colourful graphics and a wide variety of things to do while playing that's easy to get in to for new players.

I bought this game for $9.70, and like someone already said, it is well worth this price.
This casual space-exploration game blends time-management with simple mouse-clicking combat. You started out with one room on an empty asteroid surface with a few employees. The goal is to explore neighboring planets and galaxies to exploit more resources to build up your home base.
The control interface is easy to learn, although I wish there would be more guidance on manufacturings. However, after a few trial and errors, you can definitively get a handle on those things.
The main thing here to progress through the game is to send your employees to explore other planets and gain expereince, resources and money. There are a lot of planets, so you wouldn't worry about play time; if you do though, you can always revisit those planets to get bonuses. So far I feel this game follows a linear progression, that is explore-upgrade-explore, interspersed with quirky story lines here and there. But I have yet to explore the majority of the galaxies out there, I will update my review once I finish it.
tl;dr
Pro: Rich content and long gameplay
Con: Simple, somewhat linear, progression

Premium ships are ships that can only be acquired (relistically) in 2 ways

A Story About My Uncle (ASAMU from now on) is a rather unusual platformer which attempts a new take at the genre.
Literally, the game requires you to jump or "fly" while grappling with a sort of energy-based hooks onto various objects, mainly small rocks and platforms.
The game starts with a short introduction about your uncle, in his house, where you start to travel to a fantasy world, looking for him and Maddie. The plot isn't really very elaborate, although there are a few moments where you'll find yourself touched by the relation between your uncle and the world inhabitants.
Overall, there are 5 levels plus the introduction and the ending - the game won't last long, probably around 4 to 5 hours, maybe more if you can feel compelled to go for the time challenges (imho not that worthy).
The matter worth mentioning is that at least 20% of that time will be wasted in trial & error, because all the game controls rely upon are your mouse buttons and the spacebar, WASD obviously required for moving on the ground, BUT while you fly in the air you can only adjust your direction with a mix of inertia and the height + the spot you choose to grapple to. This does not only mean that the controls are sometimes very imprecise, but that is hard to repeat a step in the same exact way several times (which you will have to, because of trial & error). You will need to be quick and creative in the way you choose your path.
Visually, lucky enough, the game will help you out with a few hints, and everything is nicely layed out so that you can have a look around, and despite the difficulty, get an idea of how to get to the next platform. Particularly, ASAMU is well thought in a way that lets you enjoy every single flight across, with some puzzles working around revolving/rotating objects. It really "feels" like flying, maybe even more so that the experience from Bioshock Infinite (where you'd simply grapple your hook physically to a rail).
All of the levels make use of a good colour palette, and feel consistent with each other.
The one point where ASAMU might have failed is the character rendition: they simply look awful, there is such a strong difference in rendition between them and the landscape that you cannot simply ignore it. Lucky enough, they're voiced quite well, which makes them alive in some manner (the playing character rendition is the best one, a warm and smooth voice).
Sound wise, i wouldn't have minded a few more bits of soundtrack and especially sound hints and sound bonuses you could trigger once reaching a platform. There's some sort of "sound notice", but it's short and simply serves you to notice you reached a checkpoint.

I must preface this review with the following statement:  I love this game.  Not only does it capture the feeling of the original River City Ransom, it improves on it in many ways, from expanding the very narrow plot to having more intrigue, adding a greater variety of characters to choose from, and varied environments that change a bit based  on time of day AND story progression.
That said, this game has some serious problems.  First of all, the characters.
The only character I can honestly ENJOY playing as right now is Paul.  Why?  Because he's BALANCED.  He has a good set of moves that allow for juggles, crowd control, and dealing with downed enemies.  Let's take Rudy as a contrast.  He's a wrestler that doesn't even start with wrestling moves, he's ponderously slow to the point of being interrupted on moves,  and his specials rely on almost pinpoint precision to hit targets -- though that's not limited only to Rudy.
Why is Bruno a Luchador?  He doesn't even fight like a wrestler!
Most of the playable characters seem to suffer from flash vs. substance, where their special moves, WHEN THEY WORK, tend to have such a narrow margin you find yourself in turns frustrated and exhilarated when they fail repeatedly only to land a hit once.  A great example of this is Paul's Dash punch, where it has such a narrow chance of hitting an enemy that 40%  of the time you pass THROUGH them (harmlessly), and the other 30% you fall short  of  hitting them.
This problem is pervasive with many of the specials, and believe me, I've tried most of the characters at this point, from Bruno to Mike to Glen to Alex and Ryan, their specials (when they trigger at all) often have really, REALLY  bad collision radii.  Add to that the preternatural ability of the enemies to detect when you're going to do one and you end up relying on basic punches, kicks, and counters A LOT.  Which is unfortunate as the specials can be cool.
I really wanted to play as Rudy and Alex from the trailers, and sadly they fall well short of balanced characters, often getting their asses handed to them on the high difficulties, which is all I'll play at since I get the most value when there's a real challenge.  With that in mind, the main new characters (Provie, Glen, Paul and Bruno) have clearly had the lion's share of focus by the developers.  They are more balanced, more varied, and more survivable than the backup characters and it shows, unless you want to count Wes who is more of a cheat code than a character :).
The other major issue I have with the game as it stands are the platforming elements that want to borrow from sidescrollers but with PIXEL PRECISION.  The log jumping is atrocious because of the per-pixel vertical motion, when what they SHOULD have done was make the logs snap points you jump between.
Another little problem is transitioning between rooms.  I believe you should have to hold down a button to avoid accidentally  moving off-screen or being punched off-screen, because while it's funny to punch enemies out of the area, it's not funny at all to clear most of the enemies and then stumble out of the screen or get thrown and have to go back.
Aside from that, I find it a highly accessible and largely victorious sendoff to the original.  If they would take some time to digest some of the criticism leveled at the playable characters and IMPROVE the balance of the rest of the characters rather than GIMP the few that ARE balanced, I think this game would be a blast to build up all the characters in.
As it stands, I just play as Paul  and spin punch the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of enemies because it's fun, feels good, and the challenge is there without me feeling like half the moves are useless or broken.
As far as the multiplayer, my friends and I haven't had any issues so I can't say much about it.
I  recommend this game, but I do hope the devs take another look at Rudy, Mike, Alex and Ryan as well as address the precision issues with the specials and skills that don't actually trigger at all.
If you are a fan of the original definitely pick this up.

One week and 30 hours played through the entire storyline, I feel like I can now fairly review this game.
River City Ransom: Underground is the highly anticipated sequel to my favorite NES game of all time. Ever since discovering its Kickstarter campaign I have been waiting for this game's release. So is it up to the hype? Will RCR fans like it? Let's take a look.
Even though it is a PC game, free from the 8-bit limitations of the NES, RCRU still keeps the retro feel of the original game, with some extra flashy things not possible on the original console, such as full-screen animated cutscenes in that quirky Technos art style. There are so many homages to RCR and other Technos games like Double Dragon and Super Dodge Ball that experienced gamers like me will appreciate the nostalgia hits that RCRU provides. Lots of locations in RCRU re-create similar landmark areas in RCR, with a bit of modernization and artistic liberty in re-rendering those scenes, so they are familiar, yet fresh. The character animations feel very fluid.
Alex and Ryan are all grown up, and even though they can still fight, they are spiritually passing the torch to the new generation of high schoolers. With 10 playable characters, there is a lot of variety in move sets, and many of the characters have received praise from the players in choosing them as their mains.
Without giving away too much, the closing portions of Acts 2 and 3 will blow your mind.
Let's face it, playing a beat-em-up like this with your friends is the best way to play.
RCR had its quirks that RCRU faithfully reproduces, but they really should have had a modern redesign.
-Willpower is automatically understood by RCR fans but new players won't easily grasp its purpose. No up-front explanation of what any of the stats do, you just have to figure them all out.
-There is a plethora of shops selling oodles of items, with no explanation of what they do until you consume them. Some items are purely cosmetic, and again, you have no way of knowing. The first thing RCRU players did upon release was assemble guides for this.
-You gain absolutely nothing on level up, and only gain stats from eating things. This is even worse than RCR because the level system imposes an artifical cap that you have to grind XP to raise, but Stamina/Energy/Special don't even display the upper cap for your level, you just have to keep on eating stuff until it says you're maxed out.
-Bottomless pits, everywhere!
Most shops are only open in the daytime. No way to control it other than waiting. Some quest elements depend on day or night too. This isn't explicitly mentioned. You just have to "know."
A completely unnecessary game element. Do a bad thing and get swarmed by cops. And it's quite easy to accidentally do a bad thing. They give no XP or money, and are just there to be a nuisance until you go out of your way to get rid of them.
New characters are weak and don't have much more than a punch, a kick, and an aerial attack. Starting out, this is OK because it reinforces the RPG aspect and the enemies are very weak. However as you progress, the enemies get stronger and smarter, and if you feel like switching characters, then you will have a hard time leveling up because there is no way to scale down the enemy difficulty. You only lose half your cash from dying, but not even being able to kill a single enemy makes it impossible to progress. You pretty much have to resort to cheese tactics to win fights. Once you can gain some levels and quick cash and turn that cash into STR, then the momentum begins to swing in your favor.
There are level caps for learning new moves, but the dojos won't reveal what they are. Then once you've gotten your new moves, it's nearly impossible to tell how to use them. Some moves are simply marked P and K when they are actually steps in a longer combo, but the move list doesn't explain this. The devs have promised to patch this.
Many quest steps have vague or even no explanations. And then there is the content of certain quests. Chasing the Zombies. Delivering Milk. These are the story elements people gripe about the most. If you those mess up, you have to start over, and it is VERY easy to mess up.
This is the mood killer. Broken stuff that should have been caught and fixed before release.
XP not saving in multiplayer games. Broken Achievements. Broken Vending Machines. UI errors. Quest glitches. Two subway stations have their names transposed. Again, these things can be patched, but the multiplayer bug is the biggest deal breaker right now, and the devs' highest priority.
So, the big question, is it worth it? In my opinion, yes, it is. RCRU delivers a lot of fun, humor, nostalgia, and new gameplay to an old NES classic. RCR fans will love it the most, but retro beat-em-up enthusiasts will also find enjoyment. Playing it with friends (or even strangers) makes it even more hilarious. Yes, it has flaws, but it also has a passionate development team working to correct them. Give it a little time for the issues to be fixed, but definitely give it a try.

There's a lot about The Spatials to like, and a lot that falls flat. The away team leveling process is pretty cool and works reasonably well as a game mechanic. The base building and visitor attraction mechanic is a cool concept, though the economics of it are extremely simplistic and not really that interesting. There's also a big mismatch between when nodes in the research tree unlock and when the corresponding resources required to use the stuff you've researched unlocks. You end up with a substantial amount of time where you can't use anything you've researched. Worse, later on, once you hit level 13 or 14 officers, their vital needs get complex enough that if you happen to fail a mission and they become unhappy, you can't raise their happiness levels back up in time to keep them from leaving, even if they started at near-full before the mission began. And because you lose all their items when they leave, it's hard to replace people.
Essentially, there are major game balance issues right now that keep the game from reaching its full potential. But the game is also a diamond in the rough. Fixing the game balance issues really shouldn't really be that hard. A few of the planets around level 6 or 7 should get a couple of the more advanced resources sprinkled in to tide you over until level 10 or so when the advanced resources really start becoming available in bulk. The AI for officers should be smarter about fulfilling their vital needs and cravings more quickly so that they don't time out when unhappy through no fault of the player. It's certainly possible right now to get totally screwed by suboptimal base design, but you don't know the base design is suboptimal until you're frantically trying to make someone happy again with a timer ticking on you. And the game needs a lot more variety in the missions, particularly in terms of different types of enemies. Every mission is the same couple enemies with very little variety. After the 10000th pirate you kill, it gets a little monotonous.
If the game is on sale for < $5, or if they fix these issues, it's worth your time, otherwise, probably not.

This game is almost perfect. It is one of those rare gems that you can run for hours and hours only to realize the sun has come up and you may need to sleep at school/work before putting in another night with this game.
It is also available for Linux (currently as a beta), which is a big plus.
Do I recommend this game? Yes.
There are, however, some issues that may affect gameplay:
1. While the soundtrack does a good job of being ambient enough to not be an immediate bother, it starts to get grating when you're playing it for several hours at a time. Grating as in there's this one track that sounds as if it's glitching and it gets annoying fast.
2. There is no way for tall objects (Like the spaceport) to become transparant while moused over or when using the wall-removal button, making it fairly difficult to see what may be built directly behind them.
3. Apparently you can't put corridors side-by-side, yet there's no obvious other room that could be used to make corridors which are two or more squares wide. Yet, when exploring planets somehow someway the people building there CAN add corridors side-by-side, making for some interesting doorway and hallway combinations.
4. You can't (de-)construct the initial teleport room, mostly because it's the only place where your officers spawn. But you can't build anything in there, not even ornaments, making it a fairly useless 3x3 square block. (5x5 if you consider you can't put rooms up against other rooms.) It's also the only place which has walls with big giant windows which I'm sure my visitors would enjoy seeing on the outer edges of my spaceport. From a glance at the research tree, there's also no way to unlock being able to (de-)construct this particular room type. I would welcome the opportunity to expand upon it and use it as a 3x3 hallway with ornaments, but alas.
5. Emptying your inventory during a crisis gives you 1C for stacks of 0~1999 units, 2C for stacks of 2000~2999 units, and so on. It's pretty much useless even while you'd imagine there's a bit more compensation for the hard work your officers put into making end-products as opposed to raw materials. This is not taken into account at all and all stacks are treated equally in this.
6. When sorting officers, the three category buttons do not have their expected behaviour. When all are turned off, one should see the entire list, which happens fine. But when sorting on only diplomats, one still sees the entire list. When sorting on only exploration crew, one still sees the entire list. It is confusing. A similar sorting option is lacking at the Diplomat screen, where I often have to scroll past my exploration team and already assigned diplomats before getting to the candidates I can actually put in the vacant slot I am trying to fill. This could use some optimization.
7.a. Officers will walk away from big building projects after they have only put down one piece of floor or an object instead of being automatically assigned the next build order since they are the closest worker to it. Especially in big projects this may lead to officers from the farthest reaches of your station to come wandering over, slowing down the build project immensely.
b. In a similar manner; officers will randomly decide to hop from one factory module to another without clear indication of what is behind their decision to do so. They would make one dessert only to hop over to the machine next to it and make another dessert at it, only to then walk over to another factory room and start making spare parts. And this is with enough officers in the station to occupy all of the factory objects simultaneously.
So yes, the game runs stable (Tested on Windows 7 & Debian 8). It's playable. It's enjoyable. It could use some optimization, but there has never been a perfect game.
So, If you're happy enough dealing with the issues I listed in this review, by all means buy the game. It /is/ enjoyable to play and a decided timesink.
For all intents and purposes, this is what Double Fine's Spacebase DF-9 could have been. And it made me think of games like MuckyFoot's Startopia in terms of station-building, a real-time version of MicroProse's UFO/X-Com series in terms of planet-exploration/combat, and even Sierra's Alien Legacy which had attempted to combine the two elements before.

Mafia 2 is an open world third person shooter that follows the life of Vito Scaletta, a Sicilian immigrant who soon finds himself falling into the criminal underworld with his best friend Joe. All of the characters are beautifully crafted, not only in development and personality, but in graphics as well. Empire Bay looks amazing, and it really embodies the spirit of all of the gangster films that you know and love. However, once you have finished playing the game, you're left in a bit of a rut. There is no free-roam mode, so you'll have to replay one of the missions to do that. I can understand why they did that, the game takes a massive twist at the end that would really screw up the world of Empire Bay as Vito sees it, but I still feel like it would have really turned this into an alternative to GTA. My other issue is that there is not much that you can do in the city that doesn't assist the plot. You can't go into buildings or bars until they come up in the story, or sometimes not at all. Driving is fun, however hard it may be, but you will grow to love it with all of the vehicles available and customizations that you can make. The story is one of the best currently on steam, with imaginative missions, great characters, and compelling twists and turns that will make it a ride to remember. Mafia 2 will take about fifteen hours to complete if you stop and smell the roses.
Conclusion:
One of the best looking games out there, terrific plot, but don't go in expecting a GTA4 that works on PC. Also, amazing soundtrack made up of jazz and rock. If you want a fun time, and want to get eaten up into a great plot, then I guarantee that this will become dear to your heart.

Found this game in a stored library and thought, hey, why not give it a try. Just finished it on hard difficulty and here's my oppinion on this game:
Atmosphere, music, animation, voice acting all good quality. I mean, ye, some bad synchronization at some points, but nothing that inhibits the game flow.
The gunplay itself is simple... yet fitting for the game. The mostly destructible environment really gives the game a great feeling. Because what's better then a barfight (with pieces!) which leaves the bar in ruins?
The story itself is fairly long, reasonable and interesting enough to keep you playing, albeit I did miss the luxury of being able to make choices. Because at some points I was literally facepalming and saying 'WHY WOULD YOU DO THAT VITO?!'.
Now, what are the downsides? For once, the game consists of 70% driving around. The car physics are reasonable, albeit the other drivers are less so (I can't count the number of people I shot for wrecking my tuned high-expensive car by suddenly pulling over just half a meter in front of me). As well, if you don't like driving/travelling for a minute in between each mission location, this game will bore you QUICKLY.
As well, I had a few moments where I was fairly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at the game's checkpoint system. Usually they're fine, but on the on or other mission they clearly forgot to place some. Example: Track a guy 3 minutes through the city in cars. Absurdly easy. See him enter a factory and sneak in through a disposal pipe. you cant even die here, because it's just a 2minute-scriptey walking scene. After that? Stealth episode, if you're seen you lose. Guess what happens when you lose? Back to last checkpoint. BEFORE THE CAR CHASE.
On the same note, the hard difficulty is... let's call it lazy design. The enemies aren't smarter, they just hit harder. To the degree where some enemies can INSTANTLY kill you. Which would be a fine difficulty mechanic, if it's the kind of 'takes skill to avoid' kind of thing. But sadly, it's RNG-based. You see that tommy gun spraying across you from the entire room? 9/10 reload it wont hit you, 1/10 it's a headshot and you die instantly, back to last checkpoint. Walk through a door and the game scriptspawns an enemy around the doorcorner? Instant death, back to last checkpoint.
Combine this with 30 enemies in between check points (at later missions), and you get a lot of restarts, praying that the enemies miss during those 0.5 seconds you need to pop out of cover to actuall kill one of them.
In my eyes, this is arbitrary difficulty and lazy design.
Anyways, in the end this is a solid game, albeit any longer and it would have turned repetitive. And the game design has it's flaws.

I was consistently impressed with the writing and design of this game. Many RPGs profess to let you build your character and play the way you want, but Shadowrun Hong Kong delivers in ways that other games do not. There are a variety of intriguing character options from spirit-summoning street shaman to hacker drone commander to cyborg warrior. In terms of character personality and history, the story lets you flesh out your character's backstory through dialogue in surprising ways. Most importantly, you can play through virtually any mission without violence if you select the correct dialogue options and your character is skilled and charismatic enough. This is a role-playing game in the purest sense,
There's more than one way to skin a cat in Shadowrun Hong Kong, and I found myself reloading misions to try them all. Particular standouts for me are the mission where you solve a murder mystery in one of Hong Kong's tech district and the mission which requires you to infiltrate a party hosted by TV serial producer who has a mysterious new girlfriend.
Most of the characters you recruit are fairly intriguing; true to the genre they have dark secrets in their past that come back to haunt them in one way or another. Conversations with your teammates are alternately thought-provoking and comedic, depending on who you talk to. The game is incredibly text-heavy, if you do not enjoy reading or dislike Hamnett-esque noir prose, this is not a game for you.
I was also impressed by the game's respectful use of Chinese culture. The game draws heavily on Hong Kong action film stereotypes and settings, but the writing suggests a familiarity and depth of research beyond a few viewings of Hard Boiled and Infernal Affairs.

Coming off the back of running the Berlin shadows, I'll admit: Hong Kong is something special.
I'll say one thing about the campaign; It is solid, a lot of questionable things happen no matter how you play.  In essence, the tale captures the spirit of the setting well, especially the arbitrary way society has devolved in dystopian but throughly human ways.  Spoiler alert.
Now that we have that fluff out of the way, I'm going to point out that mistakes are even more a recipe for disaster than usual.  Your first run of the game will be full of failed checks, out of reach items/cyberware, etc.  The game requires a lot of frugality and planning if you want to make the most of your experience.  A single missing karma point can really mess up your day, so be prepared.
And yes - the dreaded easy misclick of doom still exists.  Fear it chummers.
Also a word of warning to vets of the other modern Shadowrun games; don't expect the matrix to be a cakewalk.  It is simple; but it requires a lot of patience - something the new hacking system barely allows.
I believe that covers it with as few spoilers as possible.  I wouldn't call this perfect; but it is a step in the right direction.  Would prefer the loadscreen to go by faster, though.  Worth the price of admission, nicely done Harebrained Studios.

While I have played and finished all three Shadowrun games in this vein, I feel that they play similarly enough that a single review can basically cover the other two games (Stories aside. More on that in opinions.)
So this review will focus on SR: Hong Kong specifically. Additionally, while I enjoy the Shadowrun setting I am by no means knowledgeable regarding deep setting details or lore. It's got dwarves, so that's good enough for me.
This Shadowrun by far as the more interesting story compared to the previous installments. Your character is the adopted street urchin of a elderly businessman who pleads for your help to resolve some sort of conflict in Hong Kong. Your character is forced some personal background, but you get to customize it partly as the game progresses. Eventually, you end up as a Shadowrunner (illegal mercenary.)
What follows is contract work to kill/steal/kidnap various targets while you try to figure out what happened with your foster father. Also all of Hong Kong's government wants you dead. That's a thing too.
Given how new this installment is, along with its tools to create content, I can't give a yay or nay on the potential of such stuff. Only time will tell what kind of quality stuff the community produces!
It's a simple game, with an interesting story that I enjoyed. Cover based, turn-based RPG combat that allows you freedom to make your character how you like. The core NPC team all have good stories, and their character's were enjoyable to me. Hong Kong's story was the most fulfilling out of the three Shadowruns, to me personally, and the ending was satisfying.
Got $20 and want a single player RPG in cyber-punk future? I'd pick this one out of the three.

I suspect I'm about halfway through, and I have nothing but great things to say about this game. I've never played a Shadowrun game before, but this has me hooked.
The visuals are not fancy, but they are extraordinarily well-crafted. They create a sense of place with economy, and likely allow the game to be played on a wider variety of hardware. They also allow enough ambiguity that one of the finest pieces of the game - the text - is emphasized all the more. Characters subtler actions are conveyed through the dialogue text boxes, and it actually makes the scene more visible and compelling in the mind's eye than if avatars approximated those actions.
Speaking of text, the writing is utterly superb. The player feels as though he or she has simply stepped into something like "Blade Runner," as a noir tale is laid out with plenty of options for customizing response. The player effectively builds the character, not only through choosing from an extensive skill tree, but also through responding to dialogue. I am not sure what impact it has on the story, per se, but the characters are so well-drawn that the player wants to respond in a way that enhances their interactions.
Finally, perhaps most important, is the gameplay. There are two modes, so to speak. 80% of the time, the player is free to roam about with his or her companion characters following. In this mode, one can interact with the environment or other characters by clicking on them. The remaining 20% of the time is spent in action sequences, which play out in a turn-based fashion reminiscent of the recent XCOM: Enemy Unknown. Customization is so extensive, though, that each of your characters will bring unique abilities to the fight, which can be accessed along a panel at the bottom of the screen. Each action sequence felt strategic without feeling like it was overwhelming. Difficulty is just right - perhaps a bit harder than many modern RPGs but a bit easier than XCOM or similar tactical strategy games.
The TL:DR version of my summary: buy this game. If you like cyberpunk, if you like strategic combat, or if you just like a well-written noir tale, you will enjoy yourself.

For a game that regularly goes on sale for less than a dollar, it's absolutely amazing, the dlc for the game, while making the game harder, adds so much convenience to the interface. Now for the breakdown
Music
The music is never really downbeat, though there are times when it's calmed down.
It tends to pick up to a rousing adventure theme when combat really begins to happen
The music in towns is really calming, to the point that I've just sat in towns listening to the music playing
I tend to reccomend listening to the music of any game prior to purchase though, and there's an awesome playlist on youtube containing all of the music from the game.
Interface
The interface in the base game is kind of unintuitive, with the keys being used as follows: R T W A S D Ctrl Shift
There might have been more, but either never needed them, or they just didn't come up.
The intro menu here is really simple, but the opportunity to rerun a map you like just because you remember its seed is awesome, but there's not much that's all that interesting in the intro menu.
The in-game menus are interesting, but I do have just one issue in that you can "use" a bomb, by which I mean it will just explode on you. I don't know why this is an option but I accidently use the bomb instead of throwing it more often than I'd like to admit. But beyond the occasional issue with that, the menus are easy to understand, just getting into it the first time is a bit interesting.
The interface in the expansion is much more compact with the numbers on the keyboard being used for quick acess inventory slots. The rest of the keys are: Z X C V Shift Ctrl W A S D or the arrows
The expansion makes the menus even easier to use, as well as picking up dropped items.
Gameplay
It's a Turn based roguelike with the opportunity to overcome every map that I've come across, though it may take several attempts to do so.
The combat is really intuitive, where the combination of shift and direction makes aiming easy, and there's only one attack button, which allows you to really take advantage of the turn-based global interaction.
It is possible to get all pooped on by the spawning of the enemies, or even by travelling to the wrong bit of the map and getting stuck behind a wall of mountains, but so far, I've had only a couple of instances where this happened.
My complaints here are really just twofold, with the first one being the bomb issue. There's a number of games I lost because of that, but it's my fault. The other is how slow the game can be on the longer runs, but the expansion allows the speeding up of movement so I no longer have this issue.
Story
Nope. not telling you. If you want to find out, do so yourself.
It is a compelling story found out through gameplay if done correctly though.
Really, as a quick sum up of all that: the game is really well put together and the expansion just tightens some controls and adds to the game as a whole. I spent $7 on this and as you can see I've put in 40-ish hours into it. I love it, and it's something that, if you like the gameplay, you'll love the game. If you don't like the aesthetics and or the gameplay, you won't really feel bad about it because you've probably spent more money on worse games.
Enjoy! I did.

One week and 30 hours played through the entire storyline, I feel like I can now fairly review this game.
River City Ransom: Underground is the highly anticipated sequel to my favorite NES game of all time. Ever since discovering its Kickstarter campaign I have been waiting for this game's release. So is it up to the hype? Will RCR fans like it? Let's take a look.
Even though it is a PC game, free from the 8-bit limitations of the NES, RCRU still keeps the retro feel of the original game, with some extra flashy things not possible on the original console, such as full-screen animated cutscenes in that quirky Technos art style. There are so many homages to RCR and other Technos games like Double Dragon and Super Dodge Ball that experienced gamers like me will appreciate the nostalgia hits that RCRU provides. Lots of locations in RCRU re-create similar landmark areas in RCR, with a bit of modernization and artistic liberty in re-rendering those scenes, so they are familiar, yet fresh. The character animations feel very fluid.
Alex and Ryan are all grown up, and even though they can still fight, they are spiritually passing the torch to the new generation of high schoolers. With 10 playable characters, there is a lot of variety in move sets, and many of the characters have received praise from the players in choosing them as their mains.
Without giving away too much, the closing portions of Acts 2 and 3 will blow your mind.
Let's face it, playing a beat-em-up like this with your friends is the best way to play.
RCR had its quirks that RCRU faithfully reproduces, but they really should have had a modern redesign.
-Willpower is automatically understood by RCR fans but new players won't easily grasp its purpose. No up-front explanation of what any of the stats do, you just have to figure them all out.
-There is a plethora of shops selling oodles of items, with no explanation of what they do until you consume them. Some items are purely cosmetic, and again, you have no way of knowing. The first thing RCRU players did upon release was assemble guides for this.
-You gain absolutely nothing on level up, and only gain stats from eating things. This is even worse than RCR because the level system imposes an artifical cap that you have to grind XP to raise, but Stamina/Energy/Special don't even display the upper cap for your level, you just have to keep on eating stuff until it says you're maxed out.
-Bottomless pits, everywhere!
Most shops are only open in the daytime. No way to control it other than waiting. Some quest elements depend on day or night too. This isn't explicitly mentioned. You just have to "know."
A completely unnecessary game element. Do a bad thing and get swarmed by cops. And it's quite easy to accidentally do a bad thing. They give no XP or money, and are just there to be a nuisance until you go out of your way to get rid of them.
New characters are weak and don't have much more than a punch, a kick, and an aerial attack. Starting out, this is OK because it reinforces the RPG aspect and the enemies are very weak. However as you progress, the enemies get stronger and smarter, and if you feel like switching characters, then you will have a hard time leveling up because there is no way to scale down the enemy difficulty. You only lose half your cash from dying, but not even being able to kill a single enemy makes it impossible to progress. You pretty much have to resort to cheese tactics to win fights. Once you can gain some levels and quick cash and turn that cash into STR, then the momentum begins to swing in your favor.
There are level caps for learning new moves, but the dojos won't reveal what they are. Then once you've gotten your new moves, it's nearly impossible to tell how to use them. Some moves are simply marked P and K when they are actually steps in a longer combo, but the move list doesn't explain this. The devs have promised to patch this.
Many quest steps have vague or even no explanations. And then there is the content of certain quests. Chasing the Zombies. Delivering Milk. These are the story elements people gripe about the most. If you those mess up, you have to start over, and it is VERY easy to mess up.
This is the mood killer. Broken stuff that should have been caught and fixed before release.
XP not saving in multiplayer games. Broken Achievements. Broken Vending Machines. UI errors. Quest glitches. Two subway stations have their names transposed. Again, these things can be patched, but the multiplayer bug is the biggest deal breaker right now, and the devs' highest priority.
So, the big question, is it worth it? In my opinion, yes, it is. RCRU delivers a lot of fun, humor, nostalgia, and new gameplay to an old NES classic. RCR fans will love it the most, but retro beat-em-up enthusiasts will also find enjoyment. Playing it with friends (or even strangers) makes it even more hilarious. Yes, it has flaws, but it also has a passionate development team working to correct them. Give it a little time for the issues to be fixed, but definitely give it a try.

This game is like the first dark souls game. Satisfying combat and enemies to fight. With a large open world and secrets tucked away here and there. But it also suffers from lack of modern game design mechanics which can make the experience frustrating to certain player demographics. But I have a feeling that this game was purposely designed to lack modern game design choices. I was born in 1990. That’s when the original came out. And with the games ultimate feel and game mechanics, I think I can safely speculate that this is how games felt like at my birth. It is a true throwback game with prettier 16 bit art and a lot of extra content chucked in for good measure.
Funny thing is that the combat missions are fair and fun. However, your most challenging obstacles will be non-combat missions. Chasseing bad guys down and fetch quest, along with trying to find the mission starting point or objective will leave many players frustrated. Best to play the game with someone who has already beaten it or just look for a walkthrough when/if you get lost. In addition, be prepared for some grinding if you want to toughen your fighters up. I recommend to stick with 1-2 characters during a play through. Mine were Paul & Mike.
Ultimately I am proud to put this game in my top 10 retro games list. The game is humorous, pretty and full of satisfying combat. Despite the frustrating points, I feel more then capable to dive right back in to the game and kick its butt. It's not made for everyone. But I sure love it. I give this game an 8/10.

I've never played the original River City Ransom, but I later became a fan of brawlers. I loved Dungeon Fighter: Online and I certainly like this, too!
The game can be difficult, but don't let that dissuade you. That said, the game has it's problems,  like the move system.
To obtain new moves for your characters you have to visit dojos around town and purchase the new moves with cash you "found" after "helping" your fellow "citizens" (aka you beat up lots of mooks for their lunch money. Particularly the nerds. They don't carry more cash, they just deserve it).
The dojos don't explain to you what the moves do beforehand, or what level you need to be at to obtain them (they'll just say you're not high enough yet). And some dojos will sell you moves you can't use yet because it requires you to have another move from ANOTHER dojo.
And then when you have the moves some of them are not properly explained at all in your own moves page! And some don't even give an explanation.
A lot of the moves you buy are actually extensions for your combos. By mashing Punch and Kick quickly in a specific order you can perform special combos for reliable and unavoidable damage. You may start out with your longest combo only being P-K-P, for instance, but when you buy X move you can suddenly tack on another P at the end of that for a 4-hitter ending in a punch that sends the enemy flying! So even if you bought a combo extender you can't use yet, it's not a total loss.
Other than that, the game has other issues, such as incompatibility with non-X-input controllers, so sometimes your inputs get janked up. And Multiplayer is basically in a beta phase right now, with it's own host of issues (but still worth playing just to beat up mooks with your friends!).
Some advice I have for anyone who wants to play this game and have fun.
1. Guard. The game becomes so much harder when you forget you can defend yourself. Defend yourself.
2. If the police show up, rush to your nearest hideout. This will make them leave you alone (until your next crime).
3. The police only show up IF A CIVILIAN REPORTS YOU. So as long as you avoid punching civilians and performing illegal activities while civilians are still around, the police won't even notice.
4. No, beating up aggro mooks doesn't count as a crime. Just make sure civilians don't get hurt in the crossfire.
5. Don't ever deny Paul his daps. Paul is just the sweetest guy and why would you make him so sad you MONSTER.

I suspect I'm about halfway through, and I have nothing but great things to say about this game. I've never played a Shadowrun game before, but this has me hooked.
The visuals are not fancy, but they are extraordinarily well-crafted. They create a sense of place with economy, and likely allow the game to be played on a wider variety of hardware. They also allow enough ambiguity that one of the finest pieces of the game - the text - is emphasized all the more. Characters subtler actions are conveyed through the dialogue text boxes, and it actually makes the scene more visible and compelling in the mind's eye than if avatars approximated those actions.
Speaking of text, the writing is utterly superb. The player feels as though he or she has simply stepped into something like "Blade Runner," as a noir tale is laid out with plenty of options for customizing response. The player effectively builds the character, not only through choosing from an extensive skill tree, but also through responding to dialogue. I am not sure what impact it has on the story, per se, but the characters are so well-drawn that the player wants to respond in a way that enhances their interactions.
Finally, perhaps most important, is the gameplay. There are two modes, so to speak. 80% of the time, the player is free to roam about with his or her companion characters following. In this mode, one can interact with the environment or other characters by clicking on them. The remaining 20% of the time is spent in action sequences, which play out in a turn-based fashion reminiscent of the recent XCOM: Enemy Unknown. Customization is so extensive, though, that each of your characters will bring unique abilities to the fight, which can be accessed along a panel at the bottom of the screen. Each action sequence felt strategic without feeling like it was overwhelming. Difficulty is just right - perhaps a bit harder than many modern RPGs but a bit easier than XCOM or similar tactical strategy games.
The TL:DR version of my summary: buy this game. If you like cyberpunk, if you like strategic combat, or if you just like a well-written noir tale, you will enjoy yourself.

This game is FANTASTIC. I love HBS and I want to support them in any future games. I want more Shadowrun, I want the new Battletech, I want them to be super succcessful so they keep giving me ALL of it. That's how much I love this game.
This review will sound a lot like my Shadowrun:Dragonfall review (in fact I copy/pasted some of it because it's true here, too). The writing is top-notch, I *love* the story, I love the art and atmosphere, I love the universe. The gameplay reminds me of the isometric games of old. The turnbased combat feels solid and has *just* enough tactical weight to feel fun. The characters are amazing and feel like real people. It feels like a real, interesting world. It's like reading a fantastic book.
Once again the decisions feel weighty and meaningful. Even though yes, this is basically a linear set of encounters it doesn't feel that way. It feels like a real world in which I am making real decisions. If you allow it you can really get sucked into the experience.
Additionally, I really love that they are weaving a story across all of their games and that they all intertwine. Yes, they are all in Shadowrun and so you expect part of that but it's really, really cool to hear references to stuff that you did in Berlin (i.e. Dragonfall). Stuff like that makes it feel like hey, this is a real place with real people!
I'll say what I said for Dragonfall: f you like RPGs, if you like cyberpunk, if you like turnbased combat, if you like *amazing* writing, if you like cool 2D art, then you owe it to yourself to pick this up.
This and Shadowrun:Dragonfall are two of the best RPGs I've played in the last 5 years.
Additionally, I'll say again that HBS really supports their games after release. Bugfixes and updates are guaranteed and I also know about an additional mini-campaign that they are doing because their Kickstarter reached a certain goal. You can tell that they really love doing this and it's not solely about money. It feels great to back such a company.
UPDATE 2/13/2016: The bonus campaign is out and it's MEATY. I think I'm maybe 5 hours into it and I don't see the end in sight yet. It's more great content in an already great game. HBS is the kind of developer we should all support.

Still, enjoyed the heck out of it, missions are varied enough and problems can be usually be addressed in several violent and non-violent ways, the writing is top notch. Recommended.

Hi folks! Been playing The Spatials for many months prior to the Steam launch (stoked that my save games transferred seamlessly).
As a DF9 refugee I have to say I'm loving The Spatials. It's not the same game DF9 was trying to be so don't think it's an exact replica. Main differences being the art style, you cannot explore directly outside your base (but you can perform away missions on planet) and most of all this game is actually complete!
The Spatials has more depth than you might initially think from a cursory glance. It's never a hard game but there is a bit of thinking and a bit of managment required. Mostly when it comes to leveling up your crew members so they can a.) fight tougher enemies in the away missions and b.) man the higher level embassies to speed up your resource production.
Equiping your mission team with a suprisingly large number of different abilities and special weapons is a fun and interesting dimension. I'm still finding new abilities (or new levels of power) that I didn't realise existed. Abilities are picked up as semi-random drops from completing missions.
Initially you may think money is your big hurdle but once you get a good tourist trade running (with the requisite food, drinks, merchanidise, beds and showers production lines running) money will not be an issue. Leveling your crew and opening up the tech tree will be.
Yes there is a (somewhat linear) tech tree which will gradually open up new rooms and items to start new production lines.
Have to also mention the two man team at Weird & Wry. Carlos is amazingly responsive to queries and feedback on the official Spatials forums and I couldn't fault the open communication, frank feedback and friendly rapport he has built with the community there. A note that The Spatials is released as a complete game and not Early Access. As such there is no feature roadmap to build out that I'm aware of. I don't mind, as the game is pretty darn good right now.
As I mentioned I've been playing for several months now (since Dec 2014) and haven't become bored (although some of the away missions do tend to repeat with increased difficulty). So for less money down than that other space base building, management game, The Spatials has more depth, missions, simple combat, a tech tree, deep chracter skills and abilities, a story line and fantastic devs.
Highly recommend for the price.

-day and night cycle, only exist to inconvience you, forcing you to wait for boss to spawn or for shop to open, it changes nothing else in the game.

A very fun and very reasonably priced little game. I think that there are a fair few “Spacebase Refugees” that have come to look at The Spatials. This is a completed game, although the devs seem to have ideas for improvement in the future. Speaking of the devs, Carlos is very good about responding to questions and concerns and generally communicating with the community.
The Spatials is a weird mix of activities, including base building, “dungeon” exploration, looting, production lines, economy simulation, and character simulation (meeting their needs/keeping them happy). Despite all of these different things sounding too disparate, the game does come together into a cohesive whole which is fun and different. I would say that there is room in the future to strengthen each segment of the game and expand upon them, but right now this is a completed game which (as all games should) stands to be improved upon.
The humour is delightful and it’s great to have a game where you don’t feel too much pressure (yet if you want to challenge yourself with low level characters on a high level planet you can!).
All in all, considering that I've played 30 hours of this game already, and I'm likely to play another 30 of it and get all the achievements now that it's on Steam - I'd say that it's a good game, a fun game, and a great buy. If this is your sort of thing, it will entertain
for ages too!
Most of your gameplay does consist of away missions, exploring the planet and defeating all the enemies. This gets a little monotonous after a while. There could be a tad more variety in the fauna, flora, and layout of planets as well as in the mission objectives.
Back at the asteroid though, you build up your base by choosing what to build and where to build it, albeit you probably want to eventually build at least one of everything. The idea is you need different sorts of rooms to provide goods to visitors (to earn money) and to your officers (to keep them happy). This includes things like sleep, hygiene, food variety, intellectual stimulation, and entertainment.
One fun feature of the game that is right up my alley is the inclusion of collectables. You have a garden and a museum room which allow you to show off your collectables, and you find the collectables whilst exploring planets. (Tip: they are generally found somewhere around the centre of a planet so that you don’t have to search every square inch of every planet).
I find mostly use the mouse, and it would be a little tricky to not use the mouse. On away missions there are hotkeys for using each character’s special ability.
There isn’t a story per se, however I’ve only got about halfway through the galaxy. There are hints at a storyline as you do major missions to unlock the next solar system, however this isn’t a story-driven sort of game.
Nothing amazing, nothing bad. The music is quite fun, although some tracks get on my personal nerves due to some repetitive high pitch noises. Meanwhile the phaser fire during fights can get quite monotonous. However this is a case of not being able to think of much to say about the sound, I just didn’t find it particularly remarkable.
I really enjoy the artwork in this game. It’s got a clear style and it sticks with it. The interesting thing is how the art style supports the game’s attitude of being a little bit of a star trek farce - it doesn’t take itself too seriously and doesn’t want the player to take it too seriously either.
I’ve had a lot of fun with the randomized portraits and my imagination to find characters that look vaguely like other characters. So far I’ve found a Locutus, Jean Luc Picard, Beverly Crusher, Geordi LaForge, Miles O’brien, The Doctor, Tom Paris, Katherine Janeway, Kes, Julian Bashir, B’elanna Torres, Wesley Crusher, and Lando Cairissian. I’ve also found a TARDIS collectable, which totally made my day.

What do you want out of video games?
Your answer is going to decide whether or not I'd reccomend it to you. Because it is a very unique game that excels as an piece of interactive art but struggles as an actual game. Maybe that last part is kind of the point.
This is more of an interactive performance art. There's a mix of music, typed text, voice over, and live action films. It is an emotional look at the life of an individual and excels at it. I could understand the developer and was able to empathise and connect with a real stranger at a level I haven't experienced in a game. He puts himself out there, warts and all, in this game. The landsacpes that you'll exlore are his feelings and memories portrayed through dream levels.
And here we get to the negative, the mechanics. The controls are fine, but platforming could become a chore. The jumping was airy and the distnace felt like it changed level to level, and I often had to experiment. It was easy to know where to go, but with levels that have multiple rooms that trigger different events it was hard to know what order the developer wanted me to go. Some instruction were a unclear on what button to push. But you figure this all out eventually. Honestly, it just plays into the dream thing, so while frustrating, I didn't let it get in the way of enjoyment.
Ultimately, it experiental mentality lifts this game beyond its mechanical limitations to be an intimate piece of art.
One technical thing: I was running this on a low-end laptop, so I don't know if other people will have this problem, but when I got to the level exit it took a few seconds to load the next level, making me think I did something wrong or entered the wrong way.

I was gonna give this a proper review, but honestly, I feel like it just needs nitpicking rather than a full overview.
In short - It's easily as good as SR: Returns, but it falls short of Dragonfall.
Dragonfall took everything that was wrong with Returns, and just bumped it up. All +1 and everything.
Hong Kong manages to do that as well, redefined some of your character choices - Armor now just gives armor, no more stat buffs, so it's down now to your cyberware to see enchanced stats which I like more. Stops making you more powerful than what you are. Adept got scaled to par as well, the mixing of Qi spells was pretty cool I thought, and there is a large selection of weapons available, which ultimately might lead to arbitrary choices but, it's still cool nonetheless.
The story, while fine,
Though they went all out with the additional storylines - Everyone you talk to on the side has pages and pages of text... Though, sometimes, too much to make your head spin.
The Matrix got a complete revamp and damn, was it worth it. Jacking in never felt so good. Combat is still roughly the same but the espionage part of it is what makes it tick now.
The soundtrack in Dragonfall was awesome, and while Hong Kong's is good, it doesn't evoke any feelings you'd come to expect from running shadows. You need some heavy beats when you're out there in cyberland and whatnot, but HK just gives you more.. "Mellow" asian sounding tunes, more atmospheric vibes. If you take a listen to
As a plus though, the combat music in the game is dynamic. As more bullets fly and more bodies fall, the songs'll get more intense. But it's still too hush hush to really care.
And, was it just me, or
tl;dr It's a fine game, not my personal favorite out of the current three - It has the most refined structure of them, but it just feels lacking in other departments.
If you had to buy just one, well, it'd be this or Dragonfall, but in the end, it's your call.

If you are looking for a heavy story driven RPG, then this is it.  There is a *lot* of reading within conversations if you want to go that route.  The reason I love the Shadowrun games is that in between combat and missions, the player can have deep side-story conversations with NPCs.  These stories don't always matter in the grand scheme, but they are an example of immersion at its best.  Shadowrun games tend to be like comic books.  There is a lot of text, you get an image in front of you, but your imagination is what takes it to the next level based on what you are reading.
If the side-stories and world mythos wasn't built up as well as it is, the game would be "ok".  The grahpics aren't anything spectacular, but they do the job.  The battle mechanics are pretty simple to understand but don't bring anything new to the table outside of the updated network "decking" which is much better than previous versions.  The soundtrack is also pretty good.  There are still some UI quirks here and there, but nothing major at all.
Again, the thing that makes Shadowrun: Hong Kong amazing is simply the story and the world it lives in.  The devs spend a lot of time writing quality back/side stories, which would be interesting in a book of short stories.  If you don't spend time reading through the conversations and each character's story (even simple vendors have stories), then you are doing yourself a big disservice. Since the world is so vivid and original, there is plenty to expand upon for future releases.
A definite buy for any real RPG lover.

Lately I've been pretty bored with video games. Couldn't finish most of them after I started. Thought I was just burnt out, too old for games. Turns out I was just playing mediocre games. Shadowrun Hong Kong gave me the joy of playing video games back. The anxious feeling to know what happens next, to explore the world, the curiosity about characters and their past. It's all there. I highly recommend this game to every RPG fan out there.

Let me start this review by saying that I really want to give this game a thumbs up, because I loved Shadowrun: Dragonfall so much. However, Hong Kong does not deliver and we need to be honest about it. I am not sure what changed in the development of this game, but the final result feels rushed and unfinished.
The first alarm kicked off as soon as I began reading the text. Namely, right from the start I began noticing errors, missing words and letters, to the point that it seems like nobody bothered to run this through a simple "Word" spell checker. Now, you might be thinking that this is nothing more than nitpicking, but the dialogues in general are horribly written. Most characters in the game seem to talk for no other reason than to make the game feel longer and they bring nothing of value to the table. This comes from a person who loves to read and I am a huge fan of games that do not shy away from text, but the problem with Hong Kong is that the text is just boring and bland. If the quality of the text was on the level of Planescape Torment or even Shadowrun: Dragonfall, I would love this game - but unfortunately it is not!
I mean, when the local blacksmith greets me with 3 pages of text describing how he is sharpening a sword and where he learned the craft, the game is just wasting my time. I have not learned anything of value about that blacksmith, I have not learned anything about his character, I have not received a quest, I have not learned anything about the setting or the story, I have not received a piece of valuable information... it was all just a big waste of my time. And this wouldn't be such a problem if it wasn't a regular occurence for almost every character in the game. After playing Hong Kong for 15 hours, you notice that 70% of the game is just reading these hollow meaningless walls of text.
It almost feels like there was more content planned, but that the devs ran out of development time. Makes me really sad, because I actually loved the general direction of the story. Hopefully they are planning to release a Director's Cut which will iron out all the bugs, flesh out the characters and rewrite the dialogues so that they actually lead to something. You can't have bad writing if writing is the crux of your game.

I had a hard time deciding whether to recommend this game or not. I started it straight after Puzzle Agent 1, so it almost felt like playing just one game that I generally enjoyed. And with that in mind, I can recommend Puzzle Agent 2
in pair with its prequel.
The story starts soon after the events in PA1 with you (Nelson Tethers) going back to Scoggins in order to find out what happened to the mysterious Isaac Davner (who went missing in the previous game). You soon end up with a lot more missing persons than you'd expected and your investigations take you to new characters that seem important, but provide little relevant to the case information. The otherwise straightforward mystery soon evolves into a mess of weirdness in which you start doubting the sanity of everyone, including the protagonist. And even though the case was closed for real this time, I was left a bit unsatisfied at the end and felt like some important questions were left unanswered. Storywise, PA1 was better, but I'm still happy that PA2 didn't end with a major cliffhanger.
The puzzles in PA2 don't really shine, but I can't say too many bad things about them either. Some felt way too easy and I was staring at them, wondering if I did something wrong. The vague descriptions of others made it almost impossible to solve them without using hints or googling the answers. Overall, I'm satisfied with the puzzle experience, but it could've been better...
I really like that PA2 has achievements, but if you're after all of them, you'll either have to be really careful with getting a perfect score on all puzzles on the first try, or use a walkthrough and spoil the experience, or be prepared to replay the whole game. It's a bit of a bummer that there aren't any checkpoints that could be used for replaying only parts of the story. Sadly, there is such mechanic for only one event near the end of the game (you can replay a short action part that grants the Nelson's Run achievement).
In conclusion, PA2 has the advantage of finishing the story, started in PA1, and answering most of the questions that were left hanging in the first game. The story is still interesting, but at some point it splits in several directions and becomes a bit hard to follow, causing even more "how"s and "why"s that don't receive an answer in the end. The puzzles are similar to those in PA1 and the presence of achievements is a nice addition. Again, I don't think I'd like it as a standalone game, so my recommendation is to buy it with PA1 and play them as one game.

___________________________________________
At first glance, One Way Heroics looks like it was made on RPGMaker. It wasn't. Its a completely custom engine, from someone in Japan.
And, boy is it unique. Seriously. Yes, its an RPG. Yes, it is done in 16 bit style. But that is about the only thing that makes it anything like the RPGs back then.
The description on the store page really doesn't do it justice. It explains the base game. But it doesn't explain how incredibly addicting it is to go just "one more run".
See, there's a bunch of dimensions - and they are slowly being swallowed up by the darkness. Meaning you can't go left for too long, as the darkness slowly advances from left to right across the screen every step you take. You are slightly faster than it, though.
The game is turn based, so like Rogue, everything only moves when you do. Its like Rogue too, in that all you have to do is hit the attack key near an enemy  You are trying to defeat the Demon Lord who's causing the darkness, but its going to be quite a few playthroughs even on the easiest mode to beat him for the first time.
You will die. A lot. No biggie though as it has permanent unlockables. A "vault" which you can upgrade to store items in. Perks to make your char stronger. And you can either choose to adventure in a completely randomly generated realm, or you can choose one of the "online" realms, 1 of which is random, and the others of which have "specials" (a certain character is there, darkness, better items, more XP etc). The online realms change every 24 hours. There isnt multiplayer as such, however in the online realms, theres a constant scroll of a pic and brief info about each other person playing. You can also set 1 of about 20 "online messages". One of the nicest features of online is you can also encounter the "ghost" of another player in your game at the spot where they died. They help you by giving you an item they were carrying and some of their XP.
Theres also 5 game modes, eacxh slightly harder than the last, but with better items and more story.
Oh did I mention that? Theres a story too. Each companion which you can find (and theres quite a few) has a story associated with them you can learn by talking to them. Oh, and both enemies and companions can have "prefixes". Some make them stronger, both enemies and companions. Some change dialogue with companions. (Really, EVERYONE needs to see Naughty Queen Frieda)...
The base game is I think around $4. Its totally worth it. There's also DLC, which is totally worth it as well, if you like the base game. It adds even more awesomeness.

TLDR
This game is worth playing if you're tired of bad storytelling in video games and want something eccentric and unique unto itself.
It's hard to write about the game without spoiling some of it, but I won't name critical points. It's a RPG with a 4 slot party system, EXP, levels, and mixing and matching party members as you discover them throughout an apocalyptic world populated entirely by men and all that entails.
It's a very *human* world, twisted through a bizarre tone that expresses itself through experimental and sometimes grossly unnerving music, the art, and the mechanics especially.
Great care's taken in making every single party member have their own theme and flavor. Even mechanics tied to resting in the wilderness speak to the game's theme of pain and hostility. To say this game is quirky and bizarre is an understatement though. I felt a constant sense of tension and unease as I played, but I think that was largely the point.
Plenty of humor kept it from beating me over the head with constant reminders that the world's screwed, and my main character's drug addiction getting in the way and tempting me to feed his demons. There is a drug called Joy that gives party members, and your permanent player-character, massive bonuses and chases off the heavily penalizing withdrawal status effects.
I'd highly recommend this game to anybody who loves quirky humor and darker, adult themes. It truly was a horror, and there are very few heroics to speak of except for the silly boys that made up their own rules in a traumatized wasteland that's both horrific and playful.
It's our Earth alright?
I could go over every little detail on why this game is more human than the trite Good vs Evil nonsense that typically plays out in other stories, but the sweaty wonderland is best experienced with an open mind.
