Mafia II is an action-adventure video game developed by 2K Czech and published by 2K Games. It was released on 23 August 2010 for the PlayStation 3, Xbox 360 and Microsoft Windows;[1][2] a Mac OS X port was released by Feral Interactive in December 2011.[3] The game is the direct sequel to 2002's Mafia: The City of Lost Heaven.[4] Set within the fictional Empire Bay (based on New York City, Chicago, Los Angeles, Boston and Detroit), the story follows a gangster and his efforts to climb through the ranks of the Mafia crime families.
The game is played from a third-person perspective and its world is navigated on-foot or by vehicle. Players control Vito Scaletta, a war veteran who becomes caught up with the Mafia when trying to pay back his father's debts. The player character's criminal activities may incite a response from law enforcement agencies, measured by a "wanted" system that governs the aggression of their response. Development began in 2003, soon after the release of Mafia: The City of Lost Heaven. At release, Mafia II received generally positive reviews from critics, with praise particularly directed at the story.

Mafia 2 is a great game.
It has good replayability and a huge, vibrant open world setting.
New York is very well rendered and has beautiful details and features.
All of the vehicles in the game drive really well, they feel weighty in the corners, but not so much as to make cornering a chore.
The game has some really nice little details in it, including things like hotdog stands, unique and personalisable number plates on EVERY vehicle in the whole game!!!
The car tuning is fantastic and means that you can really put your own stamp on your favourite cars.
I recommend downloading the 'free ride' mod, because it gives the game even more replayability and makes it more relaxing to play.
Overall, this is a fantastic game. I highly recommend it and the 'free ride' mod makes it even better!

SR:HK delivered everything I have come to expect from Harebrained Studios's Shadowrun offerings: great writing, complex characters, innovative quests, and solid gameplay.
On top of that, they managed to exceed my already-high expectations in two areas:
I spent about 30 hours playing the main campaign as well as most of the optional side content.
I played through SR:HK on Ubuntu 15.04 and 15.10, no issues encountered.
Additionally, I played the last ⅓ or so on a big screen using a Steam controller - the "High Resolution Display" option in the game settings made this a flawless experience.
Conclusion: if you like RPGs, if you like great story, if you like the idea of a neon-filled future where it never stops raining - play Shadowrun: Hong Kong

I'm not sure why this is rated as "very positive." Many of us are very supportive of Harebrained Schemes efforts, especially after the terrific "Shadowrun: Dragonfall." Unfortunately, most of the positive votes are unrealistic assessments of a very mediocre, tedious, and uninspired game. There are many reasons Shadowrun: Hong Kong is a failure of an RPG, many of them preventable by the developers.
First, the re-work of the Matrix is difficult to comprehend. How did this get past Quality Control? Where were the people inside the company who had the common sense to say "HEY, GUYS, THIS IS REALLY TERRIBLE!" The Matrix is a total, absolute, utter failure of both concept and game testing. It is thoroughly tedious, unenjoyable, and stupid. I rarely use the word "stupid" because it's vague unless you mean something is the result of incompetence. The Matrix in SR:HK is stupid. You are essentially playing a game of Pac-Man, in real time, where ICs play the role of the ghosts. If your tracing gets to high, well, you know what happens in Dragonfall, right? At any rate, they followed up this absolute disaster of a design with a game of Simon (you know, the extremely lame memory game?) to resolve the security around data nodes. Pac-Man and Simon. That was the idea behind the Matrix in SR:HK. A truly disgraceful product.
Second, the BUGS. What the hell happened here? You need to keep a large amount of saves because the possibility of saves failing to re-load during certain missions is quite high. During the museum heist, Rooster kidnapping, and Sinking Ship missions my save files would cease to re-load after a certain point in the mission. I would have to go back to the start of the level, or at least the last functioning save, and get through the whole mission without saving. The Sinking Ship deserves a trophy of its own for not working. If you look at game reviews right after release, you'll notice that the mission would get stuck for all sorts of reasons. Well, it still happens. Once you go down to the lower levels, two things will happen: one, the game will bug out and your character will stop responding to your cursor clicks, and you can't even scroll the screen. Second, the couple that leads you to the lower levels will 1) get stuck walking back and forth during the event, or 2) accidentally set off the event WHILE YOU'RE IN ANOTHER ROOM LOCKED BEHIND THEM. In both scenarios, the game cannot progress. On top of that, every rat encounter has the possibility of the rats getting stuck just like the couple.
Another bug I experienced was loaning a special pistol encountered during a mission to one of my team members. The weapon simply disappeared forever after the mission. Annoying to game breaking stuff abounds.
Last, the overall story writing is flimsy compared to Dragonfall. Hong Kong is full of cliches, predictable plot twists, unintendedly funny characters, and seemingly meaningless conversations.
There's a lot of potential in SR:HK if it gets a major reworking like Dragonfall did, although Dragonfall was already a great game when it received the star treatment. As it stands, I have to rate Hong Kong as the worst of the series by a longshot. The Matrix alone is a barrier to ever replaying the game, as no one in their right mind would want to replay Pac-Man and Simon that takes 3-5 minutes per re-load, depending on the mission.
Gotta say, usually love the stuff this developer puts out. SR:HK is a major disappointment, I don't recommend anyone spending money on this train wreck.

Shadowrun: Hong Kong is another very fine entry in the Shadowrun Returns games.  Apparently created under the school of thought of “If it’s not broke, don’t fix it,” Hong Kong doesn’t change much of the basic gameplay from the previous Shadowrun entry, Dragonfall.  It’s still a fun and accessible tactical rpg.  And in another similarity with Dragonfall, the story and characters in Hong Kong are top notch and really get the Shadowrun setting right.  Developer Harebrained Schemes really seem to know Shadowrun and I am darn happy to see them do justice to a fantastic property.
In short, if you’ve played a previous Shadowrun Returns games, then Hong Kong is more of a good thing.  If you’re interested in trying your hand at running the shadows, then buckle up chummer: this is a great place to get started.

As of Nov. 28 2015, there are still some gamebreaking bugs. There's a lot to love in the game, but the bugs I ran into detracted significantly from the experience.
Mission: Whistleblower
At the end of the mission, you may end up fighting two factions. If you move away from them so that they fight each other, the game can get stuck on "Enemy Turn". Left it there for half an hour before giving up and restarting.
Also, transition between realtime and combat mode has a bizarre wait time on it. After engaging combat mode, guards continue to walk for 10+ seconds, even pausing and resuming their walk, and can "ambush" you while you helplessly wait for combat mode to engage.
Mission: Uninvited Guests
At the end of the mission, there is a door to the escape vehicle. You can break this door directly by having a character "work on it" for a few rounds. Alternatively, there's a jack-in point around the side, which has some additional paydata. But, if you (1) break the door directly, then (2) jack in to grab the paydata, then (3) your decker gets wiped out in the matrix, you don't just get a stunned decker. No, it says "You failed to open the door, mission failed." And you are forced to restart.

Similarly with the indoor areas, mines, vending machines, walkways and ladders are placed with little consideration for either making sense in the setting or being interesting to play. On top of that, animations are rough and the sound effects grating. If there was any music I don’t remember it. Everything is ugly and un-designed. It’s almost like a freeware game, or a student game.

The Spatials is part tycoon game, part action game. The basic gameplay is that you build a space base to attract visitors, but to keep them happy you need to set up a production chain of food and items.
And in order to get resources for this, you need to send your crew out on missions.
The space building part functions much like any tycoon game: you lay out rooms and corridors, optimally in such a manner that nobody has to travel too far for it. You can also use decorative items to make the base prettier.
The missions are point and click: you get an objective such as  "track the items" or "kill the pirates", and you click your crew through the world. You can kill enemies (and innocents) by clicking on them or by using your crew members' skills.
After you cleared a planet you will have earned some resources, and you can now also set it to automatically deliver resources to your base on each turn.
Back at the base you will be able to unlock more room types, increasing the types of things you can build, increasing the number of resources you need... you get the drill.
The game has a cute visual style and Star Trek-like music. It is quite easy to get into, but at the same time remains challenging and fun as you try out new base layouts and new missions.

This game is an outstanding Indie gem.  It is deep, well balanced, well thought out, and runs very smooth.  It also included a help screen and a tutorial assistant that can be closed until needed at any time.  You will likely need to use the help resources a few times however as this game is very deep and complex.  The brilliance comes with th games simplicity however.  While it offers a lot to do, it never feels overwhelming and everything makes sense.
You start off with 5 random people as your crew in a tiny little room on some distant asteroid far, far away.  Every crew member has a name and a purpose and starts off at level 1.  At this early level their only needs to keep them happy and working for you is a place to sleep.  Easy enough, just use your starting 10,000 credits to have them build on add on room and toss in some beds.  They don't require micro-management and work without having to babysit them at all, which I love.
So now you got them a little space station started.  Next room to build is a warehouse, get another warehouse room added on and toss in some storage vaults and a recycling machine to help keep your inventory clean and uncluttered.
Perfect.  Now what?
Well, start exploring the vastness of this procedurally generated galaxy that is your game.  Start by looking in your own system and clicking on other plants or asteroids to conquer.  Conquer them by completing the missions given to you on said planet, usually killing mobs or boss mobs.  Once you conquer the planet, you now have access that worlds rescources.  Now use your points you've obtained conquering planets to research no technology on new stuff to make for your base.  Add on more rooms and more cool stuff.
Pretty soon, you'll be ready to host aliens from other universes to come and stay at your base, and by supplying them with food, drink and items that want to buy, you'll make them happy and start acquiring money.
Rinse and repeat, as you start conquering and exploring planets further and further out, as the difficulty increases, and as your base grows in insane sizes.
It's a brilliant game that seems to offer a bewildering level of depth, explortation, and balance.  But most importantly it is just plan FUN to play.
There isn't many Indie games that launch with the level of heart, soul, and quality that this little game contains in abundance.
This game is easily worth double it's asking price in my opinion because it is loaded with so much to do, so much to research, and so much to build.  At its current price tag, this is a no brainer for any fan of simulation or RPG fans.  Go click "Buy" and you'll thank me later.
My Early Rating...  88% out of 100.  A great bang for your dollar!!

Note: This Review/First Impressions was done with a key obtained from the developer. The majority of playtime (6-8 hours) was done via the key obtained via the Humble bundle, but an additional key was released for Steam.
A mashup of Roller Coaster Tycoon, Star Trek, and some parts action RPG. It's not a game for people who need high energy and high actions, but more so for people who like micromanagement, with creating your perfect space station and the perfect crew who specialize in certain areas.
+:
Lots of Management options, in and out of missions.
Lots of building options, with different items and materials.
Crew management and upgrades adds a sense of improvement and experience that you don't see in a lot of simualtion games of this type.
Lots of variety all over the place.
Good bang for buck in terms of content.
Slow, methodical gameplay for those who like control.
-:
Action RPG portions can get boring, not enough variety in missions.
Lack of controls on away missions could be better.
UI elements could be added to provide better information to the end user.

It was hard to understand how the game worked at first, but after a little bit I figured it out. It's a simple game with an interesting concept. You can only move in one direction, hence the title. If you are caught on the far left side of the screen, you can die. So you always have to move forward. Each move causes the screen to move, so the more time you waste in one position, the less time you have to escape the left side of the screen. It sounds weird but you'll understand when you get into the game. Now, the game is simple, you buy equipment, level up, and defeat enemies. It's pretty difficult to fight the first boss at first, but at least you can transfer items from your first playthrough to the next one, making it easier. You can also receruit party members if your charisma is high enough. Just like in Magicite, another permanent death game, the point is to play multiple times to increase your stats and chances of survival. You'll get more bonuses to your character and it'll be easier to move on. The game is great when it's on sale! I think I got it for less than a dollar.

Didn't like it. While it does feature proper randomization and varied starting options, I can't say I find it an enjoyable roguelike.
First of all, interface is bad, no mouse support, and various dialogues during each run start / end repeat every time without ability to skip them. Also, it was obviously designed for Japanese language, the information is crammed in too tightly, and those dialogues I mentioned are like something out of a jRPG/visual novel but, you know, this is a roguelike with many retries necesseary to achieve something, so you'll see those pop up every now and then, forcing you to rapidly skim trough same lines every time!
Next, it's... I can't really say it has that much tactical depth. I mean, there are special abilities which are not very convinient to use due to interface, some of them cost stats, some can be used just few times, but due to the price you pay to use them they are only handy in extreme situations. Same with items, they run out of durability and break, so you have to spare better ones, but even then there's no depth beyond "know when it's right time to use this".
Also, can't say I enjoyed either visuals or audio. Guess I'm just not weaboo enough to enjoy Japanese style. Although if you are into this sort of thing, you should probably enjoy it.
Finally while it has some nice simple ideas, the balance is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥ Like charisma is near-useless except for getting extremely rare companions, meanwhile other stats are essential for survival. While unfairness is a common thing in random roguelikes, having one of the essential stats useless outside of daily events and extremely rare occurences is just plain wrong.

Mafia II is an action-adventure video game developed by 2K Czech and published by 2K Games. It was released on 23 August 2010 for the PlayStation 3, Xbox 360 and Microsoft Windows;[1][2] a Mac OS X port was released by Feral Interactive in December 2011.[3] The game is the direct sequel to 2002's Mafia: The City of Lost Heaven.[4] Set within the fictional Empire Bay (based on New York City, Chicago, Los Angeles, Boston and Detroit), the story follows a gangster and his efforts to climb through the ranks of the Mafia crime families.
The game is played from a third-person perspective and its world is navigated on-foot or by vehicle. Players control Vito Scaletta, a war veteran who becomes caught up with the Mafia when trying to pay back his father's debts. The player character's criminal activities may incite a response from law enforcement agencies, measured by a "wanted" system that governs the aggression of their response. Development began in 2003, soon after the release of Mafia: The City of Lost Heaven. At release, Mafia II received generally positive reviews from critics, with praise particularly directed at the story.

Mafia 2 is a great game.
It has good replayability and a huge, vibrant open world setting.
New York is very well rendered and has beautiful details and features.
All of the vehicles in the game drive really well, they feel weighty in the corners, but not so much as to make cornering a chore.
The game has some really nice little details in it, including things like hotdog stands, unique and personalisable number plates on EVERY vehicle in the whole game!!!
The car tuning is fantastic and means that you can really put your own stamp on your favourite cars.
I recommend downloading the 'free ride' mod, because it gives the game even more replayability and makes it more relaxing to play.
Overall, this is a fantastic game. I highly recommend it and the 'free ride' mod makes it even better!

I haven't finished it yet, and will update when I do. But for now, I enjoy it. It's a very simple platformer, with jumps and a grappling hook. It looks decent and the controls are good. There's a definite sense of wonder as you roam around the world, and it feels genuinely good to fling yourself around the levels.
I will say, however, that despite the beautiful scenery, the game does feel rather empty. There's not a lot to do. I would have appreciated more puzzles other than "How do I get from A to B?", or perhaps stuff to collect. There are a few inspired set piece moments, but they're few and far between.
Some of the jumps are very unforgiving as well, mostly due to not being able to see what you can latch on due to distance. There's also sometimes not a clear path forward.
I could also nitpick the voice-acting. While the actors themselves are pleasant and well-cast, they have trouble delivering the lines. They're clearly reading verbatim from a piece of paper, and will sometimes hesitate, pause, and almost stammer, especially the main character. It's hard to believe a voice director would let that slide without another take.
Still, while that sounds like a lot of negatives, I still am enjoying my time with the game. Pick it up when it's on sale like I did; it's worth your time.

This is the story of a Hunter who threw away his puny bow and picked up a super-manly Sharp Holy Axe Elizabeth+6. Because this item was guaranteed to deal critical damage when it hit the target, this Hunter managed to kill every enemy that came his way in one hit. Even golems and polar bears. As a result his level grew very rapidly. Soon he had a level above 30, even, and enough Strength to where he could carry several battleaxes and greatswords with ease. But it all went to his head. For his head, much like every other part of his body except for his massive beefcake arms, was puny and weak. So it was, when he got cocky and decided to break into the hold of the Dark Brotherhood (not THAT Dark Brotherhood), that he soon realized he could only kill one of them, before all the other members inside would shank him from all sides and kill him instantly. And so they did.
That is the story of my... I wanna say my twelfth time playing through the game. I lost count, honestly. This game is wicked addictive. It's a really good buy if you're into rogue-likes and your computer is getting on in years or is otherwise not that strong. This section is dedicated to a much more in depth review and an added personal note.
Your either here because the game isn't worth the 15 minutes of your time to download or you've already played it, never the less here we go.
This game is not an ordinary "walking sim" as you may have been able to tell. This is not some hack game like Gone Home or Dear Esther either, this is a genuine expirience that's worth your time and gives somthing in return for playing. The non spoiler plot summery is this game is about the human mind and how it subconsciously interprets the life and struggle of a teenager juggling life on top of chasing his big dreams. The game is a roller coaster through confusion, fear, mischief, homesickness, danger, dred, gain, love, loss, frustration, anxiety, and a ♥♥♥♥ton of other emotions.
A bit of backstory to the creation of this gameis that this game is, obviously, a dream journal the creator would fill after waking up. This game would be created around the subconcious sights so that himself and others could experience them all with as much lucidity as possible. The rest need not be explained here as there is in fact developer commentary in the game.
On a more personal note, this game hits all kinds of home with me.
Wanting to have everything you want with the lack of difficulty that should come with it is by far the stupidest endevor iv'e ever participated in. It is certainly not the same level as Harmon's journey was here but every emotion this game had to offer was felt by me in the last three years and i get everything in its entirety. I waded through school, loved, lost, and drempt as big as they come but in the end it seemed to all fall through the cracks and i could only get SOME of what i wanted. When the game shoved these concepts back in my face i never cried harder, especially at "Get Over Her". It's quite possible that i've mega misinterpreted things but this is what the game says to me in its language.
But this game is not about me and i certainly will not pretend that it is.
This game was an experience that i vow to never forget. It will stay downloaded as a reminder of what you can do with a great idea and some talent. It's the least i can do aside from donating cash i don't have.
Still a well deserved 10 of 10

I was able to pick up Shadowrun: Hong Kong on sale at right around 13$, so lets keep that in mind whenever I discuss the worth of the game.  For everyone hoping this was another Shadowrun: Dragonfall, well, it's not - but that's okay, because it's still a strong entry into the franchise.
There is nothing bad about SH:Hong Kong, the only complaints, are those of omissions when compared to it's predecessor.  You won't find multiple sources such as the Lodge lobby for your paydata - that's all going straight to Shadowland BBS.  Not every crew member has their own optional story quest either.  Unfortunately, you can't help a killer AI inhabit a dragon, but I guess you can't really catch lightning in a bottle twice there, now can you?  I wouldn't call the game shallow, because everyone introduced is afforded a good amount of creativity to their personal story.  It's just not to the same extent that we saw in Dragonfall.
Still, the setting is intriguing, the characters are engaging, combat is fluid, and the overall eerie tone of the games voice resonates well.  Just saying teeth isn't scary - but the authorial description of 'too many teeth' and building slums, gnarling innward to consume you is... or it's at least unsettling.

I have really enjoyed the experience in Shadowrun HK. The design of the game, the music, and the NPCs really made for an immersive Cyberpunk experience. As a tabletop player, it was great to see such a great adaptation of this masterpiece that is Shadowrun.
The characters running with you are pretty deep, they all have their own story and you can choose to help them get some closure with it... or not. Up to you.
You can rush through the game, all gun blazing, with minimum interactions and go to the end, or you can stop and talk to everyone around, learn more about the world, the characters, the power in place.
It is pretty open and the choice is yours.
Be aware that the story is text heavy. I personally loved it but it might put some people off. I believe it is the only to have such a complexe game, and I think it is great.

off the bat i already enjoy the setting of Hong Kong a tad bit more then Dragonfall, it is a much more gritty atmosphere and the characters look more polished, everything seems to be more polished in general compared to the previous title and the ambiant noices of a futuristic hong kong are really good. the initial plot is also more to my personal tastes and is pretty cool, i really hope that it keeps up this plot line and i hope the next shadowrun has even more ui and combat improvements

SR:HK continues to improve upon the already successful formula of the previous iterations.  It's a solid followup to Dragonfall, with improved level design and a generally more dynamic and diverse gameplay experience.  I'd suggest that this one is more fun after playing through Dragonfall, but if you have played that one then this is a reliable, solid sequel.
Tips: 1) the new Matrix system is great, but definitely study the instructions before doing it for real. It's not completely intuitive and becomes much more fun once you understand it.
2) Experienced Dragonfall players will have a bit of an easy time with the final levels.  Recommend turning the difficulty up to “Hard” from about NPC level 4 to get the most out of the final levels.

Living up to my expectations for the third entry to the Shadowrun series, SRHK is an awesome RPG with a decent story and immersive gameplay.
Pro's:
+ Awesome theme and setting, and has captured Hong Kong really well.
+ Great characters and backstories present to other team members are fun to explore.
+ Great story.
+ Variety of missions is good and keeps gameplay fresh, with no drudgery missions.
+ Huge amount of class combo's and paystyles make for some good repayability.
Con's:
- Not as much character customization as the previous games.
- Some may not like the skills system not present in the other 2 games.
- Interface is a little bit janky, but have seen worse.

This review refers to the Linux version of SRHG... Let me start by saying it's a nice game with a good storyline, as was the original SRR...
The problem however comes from it being so buggy. On the linux version you can't even quit the game from the menu, clicking exit does nothing - you have to switch to a virtual console and manually kill the process. HBS have known about this bug since 2013 (it's in the original SRR game too) and done absolutely nothing to fix it (one of many bugs). There are multiple typos and issues with the storyline text (e.g. 'farther' being used instead of 'further').
I therefore cannot recommend this game in such a bad state for Linux, it might be fine for other platforms, but these issues should not be in all the games in this series for over 2 years.

A very fluid first person platformer.
This game uses a grappling hook as its main mechanic to allow you to move though an amazingly designed world. The further the game goes on the more tools it gives you to let you move through the levels faster and more fluidly. Nailing the level using the fastest possible route, sometimes multiple are available, feels amazingly good.
The graphics are to this day good enough, the shader quality is decent and the game has a lot of fancy effect which conceals the sometimes a little dated models and textures. The one thing that does look noticeably bad are the characters. Their anatomy looks very unnatural which in some cases can be excused by the game's "cartoon" look but most of the time just looks "off".
The environments though, that is where the game really shines. The art team really outdid themself here. The atmosphere of there areas are amazing. In combination with the music you can really immerse yourself into the world as you soar through the sky. A++ here.
The story is what I would describe as "cute". It is told using a narrator who tells a story to his daughter about, you guessed it, his uncle. The story does the job of making you want to keep going to find out what is going on very decently but it really is nothing special. The story really helps make the world come to life though, even if it is not really that special.
The game is not that long though, it took me 3 hour to beat, and does not really have any replay value. It is not really expensive either though and goes on ludicrous discount every now and then.
In the end I really enjoyed my time with this game and am still looking for news about some kind of DLC or sequel every now and then.

Let's get the important things out of the way right here at the start:
Is One Way Heroics a good game? Yes.
Is it fun? Yes.
Should you buy it? Yes, especially when on sale.
Is the OWH+ DLC worth it? Yes, every steam penny you spend on it.
Now for the unnecessarily long analysis portion:
One Way Heroics is a Roguelike with large amounts of Turn-Based RPG elements. Your character grows stronger as they defeat enemies, you can equip a variety of different weapons, there are multiple character classes, and there are even quests in the game which require recruiting certain characters or speaking with a specific person (OWH+ has quests to unlock extra character classes and a quest to return a little girl to her father).
Some other mechanics the game runs on include:
- Everything moves on a grid
- You have a stamina bar that allows you to climb mountains, swim in water, and use special attacks
- You also have an energy meter which is refilled by eating food, it also provides energy for force attacks
- Every recruitable character has affinity that goes up as you travel with them or do specific things on the way such as eat a specific kind of food or kill enemies
- The recruitable characters can also be levelled up
- Weapons can be given extra attributes via scrolls or other such objects
- Most items have weight (arrows and gemstones don't) and if you exceed the weight limit, you can't move
- You can unlock various perks that help you along the way
- You can find goddess statues throughout the world which give you special boosts for the cost of levels
- The Awakening ability, which allows you to take five consecutive actions without anything else moving
- The Dimensional Vault which lets you store items from a run and take them out again for a different run
- Your weapons and armor will break after a certain number of hits, given or recieved
Mechanics specific to OWH+
- Food can go bad as time goes on
- You level up upon reaching a new area
- You can add extra parts to the starting castle with Dimensional Gold Coins you find in each run, you can also place special NPCs in these extra parts
- Extra perks that make the game harder but greatly improve your rank and score
- Tons of extra items that aren't in the regular version
The biggest and most important game mechanic however, is the darkness. The darkness is always on the left side of the screen, and if you get swallowed by it, you die. Every time you do something, be it moving, attacking, equipping an item, or even talking to someone, the darkness moves forward. This means that ever action has to count, and you have to really think of possible risk vs. reward of doing specific things. Because if you go into a dungeon and can't get back out in time, you will be consumed and that'll be it. You can use the Awakening ability to get away, but it only has five uses per run, and the world goes on for a long way (10,000 km if I recall correctly).
Overall, a really good experience, and one I highly recommend.

Star Wars: Battlefront II (2005) is a serious contender for, "Quintessential Star Wars Game".
Beyond the surface, yes. Most factions play largely the same with the exception of different special units to set them apart. But in 2005, four factions and two dozen maps was quite the accomplishment, especially if you ported over the first game's absolutely stellar maps. The wonders of using the same engine twice..!
The Campaign, while it tramples then-EU-now-legends lore by placing the 501st Legion at Mygeeto, Utapau, and Felucia, is a remarkable look at the life of a Clone from the beginning of the war to the penultimate Battle of Hoth. A story spanning two decades as told by a veteran Clone Trooper voiced by Temuera Morrison, whos vocal performance is absolutely 10/5 in the delivery of a story told by a now old man.
Gameplay wise, Battlefront II was revolutionary. Alongside two eras, they introduced a fully realized naval battle system that allowed you to dogfight between the vessels, taking out priority bombers you could also fly to attack their capital ships, and if you were an early bird looking to strike hard and fast, you could stage a boarding operation to destroy the enemy vessel from the inside-out. This particular aspect of the game garnered much attention, and was seen as a proper escalation from the previous title. A future prospective title would promise seamless ground-to-orbit flight with all the same objectives, but of course, some things were simply too good to be true and were never fully realized.
I have very little experience with the online component, as I lived in a very remote area as the game made its debut. I would only be able to truly get into the online gaming movement in 2009. But I have heard excellent things.
The extremely rudimentary, but smooth-running engine has been an excellent playground for modders for years. BFX being one of the best out there, adding lore friendly vessels, conflicts, units and more.
But this is a game that doesn't need mods, that doesn't need DLC, that doesn't need introduction.
Battlefront II stands on its own two feet twelve years later, offering more than most contemporary titles of today- and such was true even then, at the peak of the AAA industry's offerings of good, solid games that asked for nothing extra, lest they had downloadable content to offer for then-non-standardized prices.
Star Wars: Battlefront II remains one of the greatest Star Wars titles ever made, offering endless action and variety to the player. I only became bored of it after easily, two to three hundred hours of gameplay. Maybe more. We didn't really keep track of those things in 2005. Just whether or not the game was fun and good.
And Battlefront II will for another ten years, score one after the other for The Republic.

This isn´t the newest of games. But even in 2014 when it was released, it wasn´t on the brink of tecnology. This said, QVADRIGA offers a lot of fun, for some time at least. It took me about 20 hours to play it through the Campaign on normal difficulty and static turns and there would now be the chance to play it through again with a harder difficulty and the so called "dynamic" gameplay mode. This makes the game a bit faster paced as it doesn´t pause anymore after each turn. Instead you have a counter which gives you some seconds time to plan your next move while the game is going on.
QVADRIGA is a fun game IF you are ready to read through some Tutorial TEXTS to tell you about the principle game funcitons. It has a very functional graphical style - so I guess the budget for this game was quite limited. Even though, the developper(s?) managed to get quite some renown for their little game. This because it combines a very unused topic (Chariot Races) with turnbased strategy and racing. This is indeed a nice combination and therefore as I said before, really fun to play. I even play it with my 6 years old girl and she starts to get the hang of it - even though she´s still a bit afraid of what might happen to her rider or the horses if she pushes them too hard and they fall of the chariot or get hurt. So - another cool aspect: It´s a game (if properly explained by the parent) that can even be played by a 6 years old.
I wold love to see a sequel to this game. But for me to  buy it there would have to bee some improvements on specific points I´d like to mention here:
- there is no kind of multiplayer function. Even though this game would be perfectly working as a splitscreen or LAN or even internetleague kind of game. This would be so awesome and could give the game so much more LONGTERM MOTIVATION. It would be awesome to have online playerranking lists, tournaments and so on... there is so much to be done here.
- once you complete the campaign (careful spoiler!).............................................................. there is only a simple screen telling you about the points you did, the percentages you finished 1st, 2nd, and so on, and a small "Congratulations, you won...blablabla" text. Once you leave the screen your hardfought campaign is over, you cannot continue with your team and there is no kind of medal - or something where you could see what you achieved before... it´s like you just recently installed a fresh game. Very disappointing actually.
- the graphics. Well of course, it´s a low budget and low personel production - i perfectly understand. And also the main game and concept work perfectly fine. But then again, the navigation screens, the team management screens, the skills of your horses, chariots and so on...omg, there is so much to be done here in terms of easier understanding and better displaying. And there are so many good examples for that kind of stuff out there, so all the menus and stuff really isn´t the developpers strongpoint. His strongpoint clearly lies within the core game - and as I said many times before - that is very cool :-)
- Introduction into the game. After a first start and trying to read through the about 20 pages of text the game offers as a "how the game works" tutorial- i quit the game quite fast again. Since I really didn´t have the time nor the motivation to read through all this until i actually get into the game. Luckily I gave the game another try on another day, and just tried the "learning by doing" thing, failing many times in my first races until I actually got the hang of it. So this was quite cool. But as I know, there are MANY gamers out there who would not have given the game another try after trying to read through all those pages of "how the game works" thing - and it´s a big shame because a lot of people are missing out on a really cool game here I am sure. Instead of all those pages...why not make a proper Tutorial video explaining all these things on the fly? Or make an introducion right into the game coreplay, explaining the different things in the very action of it and get the people right into the game itself. Would be much better I am sure.
- Steam achievements: There is not a single achievement to be get in this game. Not that I am actually an achievement hunter or something - but I am sure there is A LOT of people who would like this for a game like QVADRIGA. And QVADRIGA would offer soooooo many chances to get a cool achievement like for example:
- won a race even though the chariot chrashed
- win three races in a row
- completed the normal campaign
- got crushed under the wheels of another chariot (but survived)
- became the most famous rider of a region
- became the most famous rider of the world
and so on... there are litterally thousand of possible cool achievements you can imagine for this game.
Things I loved:
- the different events which differ depending on how well you fare and how well you are known.
- the core game itself
There is so much to write about the game and it has a MANY MANY cool things in it I wouldn´t change- like the teammangagement, the different chariots, riders and horses, the different arenas, the worldmap concept and stuff... but the things I miss most is the Multiplayer functionality. This would be a MUST for a Sequel to this cool neat game.
Congrats to the developer. I hope there will be more of this to come. Maybe next time with a bit of a bigger budget to include multiplayer and better playability/motivation.

So actually, now that the game has been patched and it's multiplayer isn't a complete mess, it can finally be an enjoyable experience worth playing. Took em long enough! It wasn't the PC side-scrolling beat-em-up I really wanted but it was still a fun experience that while is a good time, still has glaring issues. I found a lot of the gimmicky missions in the game to be aggrevating and not remotely fun. Unlike games like Scott Pilgrim you're not told what stats an item increases which is polarizing given how expensive everything is. It's also never implied how moves worked due to how poorly listed the move list is, and it's not easy to understand how to perform combos with moves you've wasted your life savings on. Bosses are a complete joke but controlling crowd of baddies is a superbly huge pain, especially since your character gets easily tossed around by everything. That's a staple in a lot of these beat-em-ups but the animation for getting knocked down and coming back up is super jank.
Actually, a lot of the animations in the game are just plain jank. They don't feel really smooth and give this very bad old Mortal Kombat vibe, given that there's a superb lack of frames in msot attacks. Kind of disappointing since the pixel art is really good. The game's artstyle and levels certainly pop with a lot of style, but when you see it all moves, there really could be more to be desired. It takes inspiration from the inspirations of River City Ransom like Scott Pilgrim and the newer JP River City games, but it chose to retain the stiff animation of the originals rather then trying to go for a more goodfeel kind of experience that I don't even have to play to notice in Scott Pilgrim.
also the music (composed by Disasterpiece of Hyper Light Drifter fame) is
. Like it actually is so repetitive it kinda hurts my ears and I choose to default to just better music from my iTunes list (like the hyper light drifter soundtrack).
I feel like i'm nitpicking but besides all of that, it's exactly what it is on the description. A fun beat-em-up with online (that finally works) multiplayer, a lot of replayability with tons of characters, moves, and such to go through. It still is a solid single player experience over a multiplayer one but if you're looking for a 4-player beat-em-up that's new and fresh, you've got it!

So, I *really* want to post a good review for this game. Unfortunately, I really can't.
To start with the good- the game's graphics and sound are extremely well done (assuming you like the retro NES deisgn at least), and the combat is genuinely fun to play.
So, why am I leaving a negative review? Short version is I honestly feel the developers are being dishonest with their customers. RCR:U is being sold as a finished game, and it is absolutely not. This is clearly an Early Access beta passing itself off as a finsihed product. There are *massive* issues with baffling design decisions, game mechanics that aren't explained well, or sometimes at all, and one of the most absurdly unintuitive  user interfaces I have ever seen.
There are non-hostile NPCs on many of the game screens, and hitting them summons literally endless swarms of riot police to kick the tar out of you. Unfortunately, there's no explanation of this, the NPCs you're punished for hitting aren't really visually distinct from the ones you *are* supposed to hit, the game screen is usually a confused mess of 12 people punching each other, and the non-hostile AI is stupid enough to wander into the middle of a fistfight. Once you inevatably accidentally summon the horde of riot police, your only way to get rid of them is to return to one of your safehouses (again, this is learned by trial and error, since the game never explains any of this), and restart your progress to... well, wherever you're trying to go, since the game never really bothers to explain what you're supposed to be doing, or why, and the map is utterly useless since it doesn't actually display where you're supposed to go (there's an icon in the legend for your next destination, but it never actually appeared on the map while I was playing).
In short, this is a game with immense potential to be an awesome sequel to RCR if the developers actually finish it, but as it stands today (March 5 2017), don't buy this game, as they're selling an incomplete product and claiming they're selling a finished game.

Although Shadowrun: Hong Kong was initially conceived of as a stand-alone game, it still builds upon the design of Shadowrun: Dragonfall.  Most praise and criticism in
of that game applies to this game as well.  This review will primarily focus on the changes.
First, the positive aspects of the design…
This is perhaps the most non-linear game in the series.  At any given point there are usually 3 or more missions you can choose from.
I particularly enjoyed Ractor's and Gaichu's backstories.
Gaichu's stance mechanic is great!  It's a pity a similar system wasn't used to make all melee more tactical.
The new cyberware is really nice, and now has sane essence costs, so you can actually make use of it!
A few new spells have been added.  However, the spell list is bloated with ‘moar harder’ versions of spells, when statistics should have been used for that, making it appear as though there is more variety than there really is.
You can now click the holster button to ambush enemies.  Ambush isn't just for enemies any more!
Now for the negative aspects…
As with Shadowrun: Dragonfall, the player may be waylaid mid to late game by having chosen to build a main character with a redundant class.  If you don't want to be redundant in this game, you need to play a mage.
Now armor only differs in its protection rating and aesthetics.  In previous games they also affected other statistics, requiring you to make trade-offs.
All companions have most of their slots locked, so you can customize your team far less than in previous games.
Completing a mission feels unrewarding due to being paid so little it feels like an insult.  Most of the time the payout is less than half of a
!
The music is not as good as in the previous games.  It's not
, it's just so ambient you are unlikely to notice or remember it.
The walking sound effect seems to have been changed to someone stomping as hard as they can, as if they're trying to get caught, and you only ever hear one set of footsteps, even when your whole party is moving.
Now for the big one; the matrix changes.  We've been asking for a matrix that felt more unique; different from meatspace.  Apparently we need to learn to word our wishes more carefully…
Remember that awful real-time stealth segment in Shadowrun: Dragonfall's Bloodlines quest that almost everyone complained about?  Apparently Hairbrained Schemes decided they could improve their game by making all matrix levels work like that, and requiring you to use the matrix on almost every mission.  Oh, and there's another meatspace mission (Whistleblower) like that in this game, in case you couldn't get enough.  But it's okay, because we gave them proper vision cones this time!  That might make it too easy though, so lets fill each screen with about 10 enemies, all frantically patrolling in tight circles, and hide most of it behind walls and fog of war so you can't anticipate the movement.
They also decided to add timed puzzles (in the same sense that the 100-yard dash is a puzzle) to barriers and nodes in the matrix.
If they wanted to involve stealth in a turn-based game, and improve the matrix, they should have looked to
and the 3rd edition Shadowrun tabletop role-playing game rules for ideas.
Hairbrained Schemes,
revert these matrix changes in your next game.

Having been a long-term fan of Shadowrun and a fan of the other Harebrained Schemes Shadowrun games, I was a Kickstarter backer for Shadowrun: Hong Kong (SR:HK), and I don't regret it at all.
The campaign is enjoyable and consistent with the Shadowrun world. I never played a PnP game of Shadowrun set in Asia, but the setting seems to me to be well thought out and realised, and a valuable part of the franchise.
Technological changes since the previous game (Dragonfall) include a few graphic-novel style cutscenes, a revamped user interface, improvements to combat, and significant changes to the matrix.
The NPC characters that make up the crew are very well realised and I grew attached to them throughout the game, moreso than in Dragonfall.
The writing was, unfortunately, a little disappointing. The setting and story were great and I liked the style and flow, but there were enough errors in grammar and spelling to make me cringe each time I encountered one, and they seemed to get worse as I progressed. Perhaps a little of the 'bagel money' could have been used to hire a contract proof reader? ;-)
I've completed the campaign once, taking a good 45 hours or so on it, and missed out on only one side mission goal. I think I have a little over half of the achievements. There's definitely good value for money here, as with the other Shadowrun games!
Overall, if you haven't played any of the Shadowrun games, I'd recommend picking up either Shadowrun Returns or Dragonfall next time they're on sale, and trying one of those first. If you like them, then by all means pick up SR:HK, as you'll no doubt enjoy it as well. It is a great game.

So of the three Shadowrun games made by Harebrained, this one falls firmly in second place.  It would have rivaled or perhaps even surpassed the already impressive, nearly-flawless Dragonfall with the improvements on decking, the expanded NPC list, and the equally intriguing plotline.  However, several bugs cause problems and knock this game backwards.  Most bugs are just amusing - I managed to open the menu on a neutral character's turn, only to see their character profile.  They were named "I am a Troll Ha ha ha" or something along those lines.  It was great.  But other bugs really disrupt gameplay.  They're rare, but common enough to be a problem.
That said, the game is a lot of fun.  Harebrained took everything people loved from the earlier games and added more of it, while redoing some things that were less appealing.  All the changes were intelligent and well thought out.  The improved items, the improved skill tree, the improved decking, alongside a plot that's just as good as Dragonfall, makes this another RPG gem.  And we need more cyberpunk RPGs.  For the money you won't find much better than this.
The decking upgrade is worth special mention.  Decking before was... kinda lame.  You popped in, killed any IC you found in a shootout minigame, and carried on.  They have now turned it into a stealth minigame, with alert levels, locked doors (blocker IC, whatever, shut up) and, if you're caught, a shootout.  It's much more involved and much more fun.
Absolute recommend

Munch's Oddysee was one of the few games I owned for the original XBOX, and to this day is one of the best games I've ever played. It's funny, dramatic, and has a long compelling story mixed with addictive action puzzles. It was one of the XBOX's best sellers for a reason.

Munch's Oddysee is the first in the Oddworld series to make the jump to 3D and is the unfortunate victim of a somewhat muddled development cycle. It was originally a PS2 game which was hastily ported over to the first Xbox when Microsoft realized they needed more exclusives. Due to the combination of those two things the game neither looks as good or plays as well as it should, but despite its flaws I found it to be an enjoyable experience in the end. If you're a fan of the series and can put up with some general jank it's definitely worth playing through.

I've wasted 37 hours on this game (as of the moment when I made this review- I guarantee you that number is going to skyrocket over time), and I have not regretted a single moment of it. I have no regrets about every second I spent, desperately drowning the determined German advance with tides of equally determined conscripts as I buy precious time for my T34/76's to make it to the frontlines to crush that StuG pounding that machine gun nest suppressing that sniper attempting to kill that squad of engineers as they repair the machine gun nest, while a trio of Panzers attempt to smash through the right side offensive spearheaded by a trio of American Shermans with two British Crocodile heavy tanks, and a M10 Tank Destroyer right behind them with German 8-cm mortars falling about the armor engagement as infantry fight and die all around them in the muddy trenches of Hill 331.
Yeah, it gets pretty hectic.
This game also has workshop support, meaning you have mods. And thank the God-Emperor for those, as the most enjoyment I've gotten from this game comes from two mods- the More Units mod, and the Resources for Players mod. Both of these have added more playtime on this game dramatically for me, and I've spent too many weekends in a single game for an hour or more, deploying intricate defensive networks and minefields in order to destroy any possible hope the four expert AIs have of dislodging my 500 population cap tank force inching bit by bit up their territory as I build up dozens of mortar positions on my side of the map with barrage units, to crush their pitiful 'armies'.
Oh. And OKW and British can be ridiculously powerful when played right. OKW has some of the most powerful heavy tanks in the game alongside Russia and Wehrmacht, while British use some extremely 'interesting' units.
The base game comes with only two factions, the German Wehrmacht and the Russian Red Army. Both are just as powerful as the DLC factions, as all factions have their strengths and weaknesses. Wehrmacht generally follow a early to mid-game infantry offensive with a gradual inclusion of armor, while the Soviets turn out hordes of expendable infantry in a grind to get to it's formidable armor forces like the daunting KV2.
OKW uses powerful but expensive forces overall, and it's early-game infantry and vehicles are devastating against other armies. Late game, it struggles until it reaches it's most powerful heavy tanks which can turn the tide of battle. More then just the units though, OKW relies heavily on how you play it, as many of it's units are highly situational, such as the thermal searchlight halftrack which can reveal enemies hidden in the fog of war, which is best used on the offensive with fast moving armor units.
British play somewhat differently from their COH1 version, but many principles are still the same. They have access to the Sherman Firefly which is essentially a Medium tank, given the firepower of a tank destroyer. Pretty neat eh? It also has access to some of the more decent Allied heavy tanks, in comparison to the Russians and Americans. They also use some really powerful defensive positions like the BOFORS gun, which can rip and tear through infantry and light vehicles alike.
Finally, there's America. The US army plays a somewhat intermediate game style, and depending on your doctrine, it can cater to several different playstyles, ranging from an airdrop heavy playstyle that can shred an unprepared opponent, to a slow and methodical armored push backed by artillery support. None of it's units are particularly spectacular, but that's because of the fact that the US Army has some of the best unit verastality currently available. Late game pushes with the US generally follow a mixed force doctrine, especially if you play a certain doctrine which allows vehicles and infantry nearby each other to coordinate fire, and to move faster.
I personally play OKW and British the most, due to their heavy tanks and bombardment options. There's just something that is so satisfying about dropping a Stuka Fuß bombardment square on the enemy defenses followed by a Schwerer Gewher artillery strike, as a King Tiger and two Jagdtigers smash their way through the enemy as Panzer IVs blaze through the devastated cityscape behind them, leaving nothing but ash and rubble.
That or sending a spearhead column of Crocodile tanks as they illuminate their way through thick undergrowth with spurting jets of flame as airburst artillery shells smash through the treeline, vaporizing infantry and light armor alike with HE shells smashing apart what few armor units there are with devastating accuracy.
All in all, 9/10. I would recommend this game to anyone, especially if it's on sale.

So, after finally clearing the game and seeing 95% of what it has to offer, I figured I could give my two cents to people considering wether to buy this game.
Simple version? Buy it. Longer version:
Plot
The setting itself is quite simple. You are the hero, saving the world from darkness that's devouring everything. And to do that you have to kill Demon Lord, who's somewhere over there ------>
That's basically it, but there is so much more, if you care to search for it. Game is filled with alternative endings, hidden classes, party members... Well, you get the point. It actually makes me really sad that only 4,6% of players have invested time to complete the game in some other way, than beating the Demon Lord, as they are missing out on great plot, that's just hidden within seemingly generic RPG storyline.
Gameplay
As you embark to find the Demon Lord somewhere over that ------> way in randomly generated world, the said darkness is chasing you, destroying villages, killing the monsters and, most important of all, keeping you from stopping.  On your way you'll encounter multitude of different terrain types, villages, dungeons, enemies, merchants, friends, (friendly) ghosts of other players and so on. The further you go, the harder game becomes.
Combat is very much in retro RPG style. You act ---> your party members act ----> enemies act. Extra agility can get you (or enemies) multiple moves in a row. There are status ailments, buffs, critical hits and plenty other things involved as well.
Difficulty
The game lets you pick the difficulty setting from Walk in a park, Afternoon Stroll, Grueling Campaign or Inhumane odysseu, but even the Walk in a park isn't exactly a cakewalk for newcomer, while Inhumane Odysseu often catches even experienced players by surprise. You also choose your class, perks, and wether you'd like to start with some items from your previous misadventures, so game lets you have very much control over the level of difficulty.
Overall
I enjoyed this game immensely. When i got it for around 0,60€, I felt like I was robbing the developer, because this game is a rare gem that has great potential. So I was just happy to pay the 5-ish € for the new DLC, as I felt I had finally paid him back.
The game is addictive (albeit a bit repetitive), and easily triggers the "ONE MORE RUN" -feeling, that made me waste many evenings while trying to overcome hardest ordeals the game had to throw at me.

Very fun indie rogue-lite JRPG. I think it's one of the more overlooked games on Steam which is a shame because it really is good, especially for its price. Basically the game is about you playing the role of the hero, and you have to venture through the land to kill the Demon Lord. You pick your name, class, perks, and start your adventure in a castle full of helpful knights that can give you advice, and also a fairy partner that you bring with you on your adventure to give you advice throughout the game. It won't be easy due to all the wild animals, bandits, monsters, and even the environments, and it's all randomly generated to boot. To top it all off, you absolutely cannot let the black darkness on the left of the screen reach you. Throughout the game the darkness will slowly creep up to you and try to engulf you. Although you move much faster than the darkness itself, doing things like moving through mountains and water, or exploring towns and dungeons for too long will eventually cause the darkness to reach you. The game has a lot of tactics involved as in you have to try and make the most out of the various dungeons you come across, or else you will either get almost nothing out of them or end up dying due to the darkness. Time doesn't move when you're standing still doing nothing, so you can plan out everything. You also have to be very wary of the enemies the game throws at you. If you're not careful and don't take control of the battle, you'll end up finding yourself in a lot of trouble as they are quite strong. Look for various Weapons and Armors you can find because they will most likely be upgrades to your starting equipment. Eventually at 400km the Demon Lord will confront you for a final battle, he has barriers and a lot of HP. Throw everything you can at him, and eventually reinforcements will come to help you. Once you defeat him, you will see the credits, and beat the game...well sort of. See after the end of every run, whether it be due to death or completion, the game will score you on how well you did and you will receive Hero Points. You can use these Hero Points to expand your dimensional vault (A vault where you can store your treasures to use in other runs), unlock new perks and classes etc. This gives the game a ton of replay value as you have to complete the game multiple times to unlock everything. There are some problems I do have with the game, unfortunately. For starters it's quite clunky where you have to manually aim your attacks at enemies and you have to look in the menu to select an ability/item, and your movement speed is quite slow. Fortunately I hear the Plus version which I haven't played yet fixes all of those issues and and adds more content as well. I give the game an 8/10.

I do recommend this game for it's retro charm, not for it's actual gameplay. If you never thought about buying this, you'll be very fine without owning the game :)  Short sum-up at the end, please refer to that to decide if this is a game for you at all.
The game is a really nice trading game - buy cheap, travel, sell expensive. Alternative money income is picking up the scattered boxes and selling it's contents (Value scales with time) or doing bounty hunter missions.
The trading itself is pretty simple, easy to get into, easy to organize and I have to be honest, fun. Reminded me of the old isometric Spells of Gold, where your income source was trading, and you expanded your trade (and your character skills) from the money. Here we have the growing trading parts, but sadly it lacks other progression. Buy more inventory space, then just haggle with the goods ; sidequests are either get X amounts of Y items, or kill someone - which is a bounty mission again.
The bounty missions sadly always start with just a pistol (regardless of your money) and take place on ~5 different map. It's charmingly broken in it's early 2000's ways, like a badly done Quake III ripoff. Aiming is bad, AI is horrible, there are pistol-SMG-assault rifle-shotgun weapons but you literally need nothing but the rifle. The map has respawning armor and healing items, and I think the enemies can pick them up, but they won't really go for it - so you can just stand on the armor, get max, go and shoot some enemies then go back and wait to heal/rearmor to max. Like I said, charmingly broken system, but works. And if you're shameless enough to abuse it, it's even easy.
The best thing in the game in my opinion were the sidequests, and *some* characters. There's no story of yours, but you can help a robot uprising to make them free, find a wizard (!), save Lieutenant Dan, a french robot cause reasons, Terminator references and have some pretty sly 4th wall breakings. These were pretty well done, and weirdly enough feels the most homogenous, good quality content of the game.
So to sum it up: Nice trading system in my opinion. Retro-ish, broken, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and abusable but kind of stylish FPS missions, good references (and like 15-20 character alltogether, somewhat ridiculous how many modells are re-re-reused)...  But it oozes the 2000's FPS game's cheeziness and I really liked it for it (Somewhat like Chrome) . If you never played those games in that era, the game will likely be just trash for you, don't get baited by it's usual 0.5$ price.

I literally have to rewrite this entire review, so I may sum up things more quickly than I should.  Sorry?
LISA: a 9 hour game (DLC included) for a net of $15 (DLC Included).  I've clocked 30 hours, and it could quite possibly be my favorite game of all time.  Here's why.
~Music
LISA's tracks are all unique in one way or another, and really help set the mood of a particular area of the game.  They take on a very quirky vibe that you'd be hard pressed to find in any other environment.  A few examples would be "I am Satan" and "All Hail the Fishmen".
~Comedy
LISA is, first and foremost, a depressing game.  The Add On/DLC LISA: the Joyful has very little comedy within it and is overall a very depressing game.  The first game, however, is absolutely LOADED with dark comedy.  From people being used as furniture, and the "Supreme lord of suprise" kicking you in the nuts, to a troupe of Power Rangers, and a WWE ring, the game can put a smile on your face with ease.
~Depressing S#!t
Opposite the Comedic side of LISA is what is possibly the most depressing and tear-jerking game to date.  I can reveal very little of these without spoiling the game itself, so you're just gonna have to take my word for it.
~Characters
Oh my holy mother of god, the characters.  The characters in LISA are its major strong-point.  There are 30 recruitable party members, all with distinct personalities, backstories, and all extremely unique.  From a Fish-Lawyer, to a serial killer wearing a goose mask, to Terry Hintz, there'a SO much this game has to offer in terms of character.  It's not just confined to your party members, no.  Every SINGLE person in the game has some story to tell, from a man with a cabinet on his back, to your old high school bully, every NPC you can talk to has something to say.  Even past THAT, almost every ENEMY in the game has a unique name and personality, with only around 4-5 places for random encounters in their purest form.
~Gameplay
LISA is an RPGMaker game, so the Combat is, obviously enough, Turn-Based.  But even in spite of that, LISA keeps it fresh with timed button presses and combo attacks.  Each character (Yes, more about the characters) has a moveset specific to their character.  Harvey's legal documents, Queen Rogers extortion, and, of course, Terry's Hottest Dance all add something to the character in one way or another.  You learn about the same amount from the way your character fights, and their dialouge.
~Graphics
RPGMaker also confines this game to some rather low-res sprites, but all you really have to do is look at the above pictures to get a glimpse of what it's like.  Everything about the graphics fits, all the sprites are well made, and the game's atmosphere is heavily carried by it's art.
~Who wouldn't want to play this game?
If you don't care at all for story in a game, this one's not for you.
If you can't stand Turn-Based combat even a little bit, than this one's not for you.
If neither of these apply to you, stop reading and play the game already!
Well, if you're here, and one of those two things do apply to you, here are some suggestions:
If you don't care for story:  Try Heroes of Pen & Paper, Santuary RPG, or any number of action RPGs.
If you hate Turn-Based gameplay:  Try Undertale, Thomas was Alone, or the Fallout series.

Look, I knew what I was getting in to. This game promises awkward dimensions to explore, and that's generally what it offers at the start. The places are kind of sloppy but they're still interesting enough to wander through. But about a third of the way through the game, it becomes a playable montage of the developers venting about his life and his experience making games. And I'm OK with that, genuine emotion comes from firsthand experience. I liked the developer expressing the struggle of creating games that are judged by people, what I disliked was that this game was boring and irritating to play. Many of the levels I just skipped when I couldn't tell how to proceed and assumed it wouldn't be rewarding to find out, which is the last thing any game should make a player feel like.
There are a few creative levels, like the floating blocks that loop if you fall off, the art gallery and the bedroom within the empty expanse, but some are just tedious. Yeah, I can forgive the rewinding city level for being interesting, making a point through gameplay and not overstaying its welcome. But then you have the escape room level, which ends with you slowly and painfully clambering up a ladder while viewing a series of negative reviews of previous games and a long, tedious video of the developer theatrically trying to deal with the complaints.
I don't mind being emotionally lured into art by what it means to the creator, but when you blot out half the screen with pictures of yourself and your friends it isn't enough to redeem lousy gameplay.
There's one level at the end which is literally a flat world featuring several fake Steam reviews, positive and negative, for the game. The last one brings up the reoccurring line that stuck with me from the game: "Just dream, because it's easier than living". If there's one thing I want to say it's that the developer has some nice ideas and should continue trying to make his dreams a reality, even if he gets negative feedback for what he creates.

Yeah... I wasn't a huge fan of the first, and this is worse in every way.
A list of downgrades:
1. Plot goes from passable and intriguing in the first game to a haphazard string of non-sequiturs in this game and still leaves a lot of loose threads, despite supposedly finishing the storyline.
2. About half the puzzles are a rehash of puzzles from the first game, which were already a bit repetitive to begin with, and a lot of the new puzzles are really easy. The developers discovered slider puzzles so those are all over the place. I guess, the instructions feel overall a bit better here though.
3. Shorter length. Only 34 total puzzles here and there's a few puzzle-gauntlet strings with little plot so the end result is a shorter runtime overall, despite this game costing double the previous.
4. Nothing's been upgraded aesthetically, the game's full of reused assets and the interface is completely identical.
5. Characters act inconsistent here for no apparent reason. The sheriff and Korka most notably.
Basically, take the first game, strip away any charm, rush out a sequel, and you get... this. Not like it's a horrible game but, noooo way is it worth its asking price.
Oh yeah and good job making players replay the entire game if they screw up a single puzzle on the first try if you want to unlock the last puzzle, that's -always- appreciated... e.e

Everything I wrote about the first "Puzzle Agent" game on Steam pretty much can be repeated here: It is a good, short adventure game that focusses more on solving puzzles (some easy, some pretty tricky) than on challenging adventure game moves, provided with sketchy but still very cool and funny visuals by Graham Annable, a great atmospheric soundtrack and a bunch of likeable (and some new) characters.
A new addition compared to the first game are Steam achievements, yeay! But no cards to collect ;(
That's the good stuff and if you liked the first game already, you definitely should play the sequel if you haven't started yet.
And I recommend to play the first game first since "Puzzle Agent 2" continues the open end-story (in the worst case you might just get confused by the plot).
Speaking of plot: Unfortunately I have one or two issues with it.
Without spoiling it I can tell that the story doesn't seem to be clear in the end. When I finished the game (thus the whole story) I just wondered about details that seemed to be forgotten halfway through and thus some questions remained unanswered. What a pity since the actual crime story is quite funny and crazy.
And the puzzles? Yes, some are very easy and some need real hard thinking and cleverness to be solved. And then there are one or two you might just look up on the guides or do trial or error (to me math idiot, that was a mathmatical puzzle). But at least you can't complain that the puzzles all were boring and crazy-easy. And it's a good mix.
So if you love to relax to a short, funny crime adventure based on puzzle solving, grab some chewing gums and try this! But as I mentioned, finish the first game first.
While you're playing, I'm hoping for Puzzle Agent 3.

Puzzles rely more on thinking 'outside the box' than on solving with information given. An early example is a number sequence puzzle that provides the numbers 11, 12, 1, and 2, and challenges the player to work out the next number. Multiple potential patterns present themselves, but none of them are relevant; the game intends for the player to guess that they must be talking about clocks, and assume that the 12-1 portion of the sequence is a reset of the pattern, none of which is information that can be presented or discovered ingame in any way. Thus, like many of the game's puzzles, it's impossible to appropriately solve without using the built-in help system or by simply guessing.
Another good example is the coinbox puzzle, which attempts to utilize binary, but does so incorrectly. That puzzle is literally not possible to solve properly because its understanding of binary is incorrect, or perhaps the solution was coded wrong. The 'correct' answer is a mirrored version of what the actual binary values should read, though there's no indication that the answer is mirrored, leaving the player to guess and check. Either way, it's another ready example of puzzles that are ill-planned and expect the player to guess or to have outside help.
This might be the right puzzle game for people who like to be stuck only to learn that the solution was hidden in information they never had access to. Probably great fun for people who like riddles that can't be solved with the data provided. Not a good one for puzzle solvers who expect cleverly presented clues and solid logic, none of that will be found here.
